articles.title: Rehabilitation and the post-intensive care syndrome across the recovery continuum: a narrative review.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Improved survival from critical illness has produced a growing population of intensive care unit (ICU) survivors with new or worsened physical, cognitive, and mental-health impairment, defined as post-intensive care syndrome (PICS), and frequent distress among families/caregivers (PICS-family, PICS-F). This narrative review synthesises the evidence in adults treated in high-resource settings. METHODS: Rather than a formal guideline process, we used a structured descriptive approach: for each recommendation, we identified the predominant study design, assessed the consistency of findings, summarised uncertainties, and assigned an evidence-strength label (high, moderate, low, or insufficient). RESULTS: We summarise the definition of PICS and its overlap with related constructs (post-sepsis morbidity, chronic critical illness, post-COVID conditions, and frailty); the mechanisms linking acute injury to persistent disability, including skeletal-muscle pathobiology, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial and neuroendocrine dysfunction, and epigenetic change; and the instruments assessing the three PICS core domains (recommending a two-step assessment approach), as well as quality of life, across the care continuum. We describe preventive and rehabilitative interventions from the ICU (e.g., the ABCDEF bundle that includes light/no sedation, delirium prevention, early mobilisation and family participation) through the ward to the post-hospital phase, the heterogeneous organisation of post-ICU recovery services, PICS-F, the educational and cultural change needed, and the health-system and policy context. PICS-F affects 20-60% of relatives; nurse-led family interventions seem promising. CONCLUSION: The evidence base remains limited and heterogeneous, preventing firm recommendations. Research priorities include harmonised outcome measurement, phenotyping of recovery trajectories, the optimal dose and timing of rehabilitation, and rigorous comparison of follow-up models.

articles.title: Ventilator-associated pneumonia after traumatic brain injury: a timing-sensitive ecological framework of neuroimmune-pulmonary vulnerability.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is frequent after traumatic brain injury (TBI), but its biological meaning and outcome impact remain incompletely defined. Traditional models emphasise mechanical ventilation, aspiration, colonisation, endotracheal tube biofilm, and hospital pathogens. These mechanisms remain essential, but they do not fully explain the early clustering, heterogeneous susceptibility, changing bacteriology, and variable mortality effect observed after TBI. MAIN TEXT: Severe brain injury creates an early vulnerable host state through impaired consciousness and airway protection, neuroimmune dysregulation, autonomic and endocrine activation, altered pulmonary immune surveillance, and, in many patients, extracranial trauma, shock, transfusion, or thoracic injury. These processes interact with ventilation, antibiotic pressure, and rapid respiratory microbiome disruption. Early VAP may reflect abrupt loss of control after injury and intubation, whereas late VAP may reflect persistent or secondary failure driven by biofilm maturation, antibiotic selection, multidrug-resistant pathogens, and intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired immune dysfunction. Clinically, VAP consistently prolongs ventilation, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and resource use, while its independent effect on mortality is phenotype- and context-dependent. CONCLUSIONS: This model proposes a timing-sensitive ecological framework in which established mechanisms may converge early and with particular clinical intensity after severe TBI, creating a vulnerable host-microbe state that may lower the threshold for clinically apparent infection. Future studies should distinguish isolated TBI from polytrauma, compare TBI with other acute brain injuries and non-neurological ventilated populations, and incorporate dynamic immune, microbial, and trajectory-based outcomes. HIGHLIGHTS: VAP after TBI should be viewed as a timing-sensitive interaction between ventilator exposure and early host vulnerability, not as a distinct disease entity or as a pneumonia pathway unique to traumatic brain injury. The TBI-focused contribution lies in the early convergence of otherwise non-unique mechanisms: impaired airway control, aspiration risk, neuroimmune-endocrine activation, treatment exposure, dysbiosis, and extracranial injury burden, rather than in any single TBI-specific mechanism. Isolated TBI and TBI with polytrauma are biologically different phenotypes and should be separated in future studies. Early and late VAP may represent different phases of loss of pulmonary host-microbe containment; this distinction is probabilistic rather than TBI-specific in itself and requires validation in TBI-stratified cohorts. Mortality remains clinically relevant but context-dependent; VAP more consistently modifies recovery trajectory, ventilator dependence, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and possibly neurological recovery.

articles.title: Inflammatory phenotypes in severe pneumonia: clinical evidence to mouse models for precision therapeutics.
articles.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
articles.abstract: RATIONALE: Hyperinflammatory and hypoinflammatory phenotypes previously identified in sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome may enable precision therapies, but their clinical relevance and translational modeling in severe pneumonia remain incompletely characterized. OBJECTIVES: To examine biomarker-defined hyperinflammatory and hypoinflammatory phenotypes in critically ill patients with pneumonia (pulmonary sepsis), test whether the biomarkers that define these phenotypes identify subgroups and outcomes in a mouse model of bacterial pneumonia, and determine whether the mouse phenotypes respond differently to therapeutic interventions. METHODS: We performed latent class analysis (LCA) in a cohort of 548 ICU patients with pulmonary sepsis to identify inflammatory phenotypes and test the association of these phenotypes with clinical outcomes using validated classifier models. We developed a mouse model of pneumococcal pneumonia that recapitulated key aspects of these phenotypes and tested responses to dexamethasone and IL-6 receptor blockade. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Two phenotypes were identified in patients with pulmonary sepsis: a hyperinflammatory phenotype with more lung injury and increased mortality, and a hypoinflammatory phenotype with more favorable outcomes. Despite uniform pathogen exposure and baseline conditions, LCA identified 2 phenotypes in the mice with divergent trajectories (lung injury and mortality). Therapeutic benefit from anti-inflammatory interventions was observed exclusively in the more inflamed mice. CONCLUSIONS: By integrating clinical data from human studies and experimental findings in a clinically relevant mouse model, this study provides a translational framework for developing phenotype-targeted therapies for critical illness, with the goal of improving patient outcomes.

articles.title: Establishing curriculum priorities for intensive care recovery education: an international Delphi study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To effectively support recovery, intensive care unit (ICU) clinicians require training to identify patients at risk of post-intensive care syndrome and implement interventions during and after ICU admission. This study aimed to identify and prioritise curriculum topics for educating interprofessional ICU clinicians on evidence-based ICU recovery care across the continuum of critical illness. METHODS: A two-round e-Delphi study followed by a structured consensus meeting endorsed by the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) was conducted. A steering committee generated an initial list of curriculum topics. In round 1, participants rated topic importance (9-point Likert scale) and suggested additional topics. In round 2, they rated newly identified topics and ranked priorities. Topics reaching consensus (≥70% rating as critical [7-9]; ≤15% rating as not important [1-3]) were discussed during the final consensus meeting. RESULTS: Participants' mean age was 43.5 (±10.5) years and they were predominantly female (n = 90, 66.7%). Priority topics included early mobilisation during ICU admission, post-intensive care syndrome, delirium prevention and management, implementation of the ABCDEF bundle, and cognitive support and rehabilitation. The final set of learning modules for a future curriculum was established. CONCLUSION: Priority topics and learning modules for an expert-developed curriculum framework for ICU recovery were established with interprofessional ICU clinicians through a structured international consensus process with moderate levels of participant retention between the two Delphi rounds and full consensus agreement among experts. This framework may support in delivering recovery-focused care across the continuum of critical illness.

articles.title: Comprehensive Driving Assessment to Enable Driving Resumption in Adults Recovering From Critical Illness: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Primary objective: To determine the driving ability of adult ICU survivors 2 months after hospital discharge. Secondary objectives: Evaluate driving resumption at 3, 6, and 12 months; factors associated with driving resumption; and acceptability of a comprehensive driving assessment. DESIGN: Observational cohort study. SETTING: Certified driving assessment center in the United Kingdom. PATIENTS: Adult ICU survivors who received mechanical ventilation (minimum 72 hr) and/or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. INTERVENTIONS: A Driver Vehicle Licensing Agency-approved, driving ability assessment comprising physical and cognitive evaluation, and practical driving skills using a driving simulator, private track in-car assessment, and on-road in-car assessment. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We recruited 40 participants (median age, 53 yr [interquartile range (IQR), 46-64 yr]; 13 [32%] female) from six hospitals. Of these, 33 completed the driving assessment at a median of 12.5 weeks following hospital discharge. Twenty-six participants (79%) were assessed as capable of driving a standard vehicle; however, only 15 (45%) had resumed driving. Seven participants (7/33, 21%) were deemed unable to drive a standard vehicle due to either physical ( n = 4/7, 57%), psychological ( n = 2/7, 29%), or cognitive impairment ( n = 1/7, 14%). Driving resumption following adaptations, retraining, or refresher lessons occurred in four participants ( n = 4/7, 57%) in the 12-month study period. Self-reported driving resumption at 3, 6, and 12 months was observed in 21 (62%), 28 (82%), and 30 (91%) participants, respectively. Time to driving resumption ranged from 7 to 274 days following hospital discharge. Median (IQR) driving confidence (10-point Likert scale) increased from 7 (5-8) pre-assessment to 9 (7-10) post assessment ( p < 0.05). Driving assessment acceptability was rated very good or excellent by 32 participants (97%). CONCLUSIONS: Using a comprehensive driving assessment 3 months following hospital discharge, approximately three quarters of this cohort were deemed able to drive a standard vehicle, yet less than half had resumed driving. Of those with a driving-related impairment, most could resume driving following intervention.

articles.title: Association of ICU Room Characteristics With Mortality and Length of Stay.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: In addition to medical considerations, economic factors are increasingly influencing hospital planning. While guidelines suggest ICU room design and layout likely affect outcomes, data supporting current recommendations are scarce. The aim of this study was to investigate the association of shared rooms vs. single rooms, high vs. low visibility, and distances of nurses' and doctors' charting areas to patients' rooms with mortality and length of stay in a large, mixed-discipline cohort. DESIGN: Retrospective observational cohort study. SETTING: Four ICUs at the University Medical Center Mannheim, Germany. PATIENTS: Critically ill adults with ICU admission between January 2019 and May 2022 for at least 24 hours. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Associations of the index variables with in-hospital mortality and ICU length of stay were assessed by multivariate regression, adjusting for biological sex, Simplified Acute Physiology Score II, need for vasopressors, need for ventilation, and medical vs. surgical admission. Five thousand two hundred ninety-three patient stays with a mortality rate of 18% and a mean length of stay of 6.3 ± 9.2 days in survivors were eligible for this analysis. In the overall cohort, none of the index variables showed associations with mortality. Patients admitted to single rooms showed a mean length of stay increase by 0.81 days (95% CI, 0.04-1.57 d; p = 0.039) compared with shared rooms with up to three beds. CONCLUSIONS: In this mixed cohort of medical and surgical ICUs, neither single rooms compared with shared rooms, high-visibility rooms compared with low-visibility rooms, nor distances to nurses' or doctors' charting areas were associated with mortality. The observed increase in length of stay associated with single room admission highlights the need to balance privacy and infection control benefits with potential implications for ICU capacity and operational efficiency.

articles.title: Sodium bicarbonate therapy for metabolic acidosis in critically ill patients: a Bayesian systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the effects of sodium bicarbonate therapy on mortality and renal outcomes in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis. METHODS: We performed a systematic review and Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intravenous sodium bicarbonate with placebo or usual care in adult intensive care unit patients with metabolic acidosis. MEDLINE, Embase and CENTRAL were searched from inception to December 2025, with an updated search on 2 April 2026. The primary outcome was short-term all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included renal replacement therapy (RRT) initiation, 90-day mortality, RRT-free days, vasopressor-free days, intensive care unit and hospital length of stay and adverse events. RESULTS: Four RCTs including 1544 patients were analysed. Sodium bicarbonate did not show a clear short-term mortality benefit (RR 0.94, 95% CrI 0.73-1.22), with a posterior probability of benefit of 72.1%. For RRT initiation, sodium bicarbonate was associated with a lower risk (RR 0.74, 95% CrI 0.59-0.98), with a posterior probability of benefit of 97.2%. Effects on other outcomes were small or imprecise, and no consistent safety signal was identified. CONCLUSION: Current randomised evidence does not demonstrate a clear survival benefit from sodium bicarbonate therapy in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis, but suggests a high probability of reducing RRT initiation. Further trials should define the patients most likely to benefit. PROSPERO registration: CRD420251246519.

articles.title: Impact of antibiotic prophylaxis on the occurrence of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia in trauma patients (antiVAP): a propensity score-weighted, retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Short-course antibiotic prophylaxis has been associated with a reduced risk of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) in selected populations, particularly patients with acute brain injury. However, its role in severely injured trauma patients remains controversial. METHODS: This multicentre, retrospective cohort study, conducted in 15 French trauma centres, included severely injured adults who required mechanical ventilation initiated within 24 h of admission and continued for at least 48 h. Propensity score-based analyses assessed the association between early antibiotic prophylaxis (initiated within the first 24 h of management and continued for up to 72 h) and patient outcomes. The primary outcome was early-onset VAP; secondary outcomes included late-onset VAP, extrapulmonary infections, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU and hospital length of stay, and 30-day mortality. RESULTS: A total of 1,321 trauma patients were included. Antibiotic prophylaxis was administered to 746 patients (56%), with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid used in more than 90% of cases. Early-onset VAP occurred in 240 of 746 patients (32%) who received antibiotic prophylaxis and in 195 of 575 (34%) who did not. After inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with early-onset VAP (weighted odds ratio [wOR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.66-1.22; p = 0.48). A cause-specific Cox model accounting for the competing risk of death before day 7 yielded similar results (cause-specific hazard ratio [csHR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.71-1.07; p = 0.19). Antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with improve of secondary outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis in severely injured trauma patients was not associated with a reduced risk of early-onset VAP. CLINICALTRIALS: Gov ID NCT07059039 - Registration date: July, 10th 2025.

articles.title: Chlorhexidine within a standardized oral-care bundle for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia: a pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover trial in six medical intensive care units.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chlorhexidine (CHX) has been a long-standing component of oral-care bundles for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), but recent evidence has questioned its benefit in non-cardiac-surgery ICU. We evaluated whether adding 0.12% CHX to standardized oral-care bundle provides incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU. METHODS: We conducted a prospective, pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover (AB/BA) trial in six adult medical ICUs of a single tertiary-care academic hospital in Bhubaneswar, India. ICUs were randomized as three ICUs of two Period of 9 months with the multicomponent oral-care bundle without chlorhexidine and three with the same bundle plus 0.12% chlorhexidine with a 1-month wash-in and re-training interval. Consecutive adults ventilated for ≥ 48 h were included. The primary outcome was VAP incidence density (Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (CPIS) > 6) as per 1,000 ventilator-days. Secondary outcomes were 28-day all-cause mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, 28- day ventilator-free days, Beck Oral Assessment Scale (BOAS) and Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) scores. The primary model was a population-averaged Poisson generalized estimating equation (GEE) and adjustment for treatment, period, sequence, age, sex, APACHE II, and SOFA. RESULTS: A total of 1,035 patients (637 No CHX, 398 CHX) accrued 10,024 ventilator-days (5,918 vs. 4,106). Groups were well balanced at baseline (mean age ≈ 55 years; APACHE II ≈ 19.6; SOFA ≈ 13.4). VAP occurred in 100/5,918 ventilator-days (16.9 per 1,000) vs. 77/4,106 (18.8 per 1,000) (No CHX vs. CHX). The adjusted Poisson incidence rate ratio was 1.08 (95% CI 0.84-1.38; p = 0.56). 28-day mortality was 28.7% vs. 26.4% (no CHX vs. CHX) (adjusted OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.65-1.15; p = 0.33). ICU length of stay was longer in the CHX arm (adjusted mean difference + 0.89 days, 95% CI + 0.19 to + 1.58; p = 0.013). BOAS and CPOT scores did not differ. CONCLUSIONS: In this trial, adding 0.12% chlorhexidine to a standardized oral-care bundle did not reduce VAP incidence density or 28-day mortality and was associated with a modest increase in ICU length of stay. Routine CHX use provided no clear incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU population. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical Trials Regisrty- India (CTRI) identifier [CTRI/2024/02/062201], registered [01 February 2024].

articles.title: Impact of acute kidney injury in different ECMO modalities: a multicenter retrospective study on risk factors and mortality.
articles.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and serious complication in critically ill patients receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), significantly affecting mortality and long-term renal function. However, risk factors and clinical course of AKI across different ECMO modalities remain poorly understood. Herein, our study identified independent risk factors for AKI in ECMO patients and evaluated the effect of AKI severity on 30-day mortality. This multicenter retrospective cohort study enrolled patients from three ECMO centers (September 2019-June 2024). AKI was defined and staged according to KDIGO serum creatinine criteria within 7 days after ECMO initiation. Multivariate stepwise logistic regression identified predictors of moderate-to-severe AKI (stages 2-3). Cox proportional-hazards models assessed the association between AKI stage and 30-day mortality. Among 210 patients, 110 (52.4%) developed AKI stages 2-3 within 7 days. Serial monitoring showed a progressive increase in stage 2, while stage 3 plateaued. Moderate-to-severe AKI was independently associated with 30-day mortality. In the overall cohort, VA-ECMO modality and norepinephrine use were independent risk factors for AKI stages 2-3, while high fibrinogen (FIB) level and a history of cardiovascular disease (CVD) were protective. In the VV-ECMO subgroup, elevated lactate, bicarbonate, FIB, procalcitonin, and blood urea nitrogen levels, along with decreased total bilirubin and white blood cell counts were significantly associated with increased moderate-to-severe AKI risk. Herein, our study indicated that severe AKI independently predicts 30-day mortality in ECMO patients. VA-ECMO modality and NE use increase moderate-to-severe AKI risk, while high FIB level and CVD provide protection.

articles.title: ICU-acquired acute kidney injury in critically ill adults: a retrospective cohort study of risk factors and KDIGO stage dynamics in a Brazilian ICU.
articles.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent complication in critically ill patients, and early recognition of risk factors may support preventive care. We conducted a retrospective cohort study in a single-center Brazilian ICU from 2015 to 2022 to identify factors associated with ICU-acquired AKI and to describe KDIGO trajectories. Adults with ICU stay ≥48 hours were included; patients with chronic kidney disease, AKI on admission, or no serum creatinine measurement were excluded. Analyses included a multivariable Fine-Gray model with ICU death as a competing event, a Bayesian network for conditional dependencies, and descriptive KDIGO dynamics. Among 2935 patients, 794 (27.1%) developed AKI. The final model retained age (sHR 1.05 per 10 years; 95%CI 1.01-1.10), chronic liver disease (1.95; 95%CI 1.11-3.43), immunosuppression (1.93; 95%CI 1.29-2.87), hypertension (1.26; 95%CI 1.06-1.50), underweight BMI (1.33; 95%CI 1.05-1.69), mechanical ventilation on admission (1.50; 95%CI 1.19-1.90), admission arterial lactate (1.06 per 1 mmol/L; 95%CI 1.03-1.10), and leukocyte count (1.02 per 10,000 cells/µL; 95%CI 1.00-1.03). Among AKI cases, the proportion classified as KDIGO stage 3 increased after day 7, largely driven by renal replacement therapy among patients remaining in the ICU. These findings highlight that early admission markers of vulnerability and illness severity are associated with ICU-acquired AKI and support early risk recognition and kidney-protective care in the ICU course.
articles.ai_summary: Researchers studied 2935 critically ill adults in a Brazilian ICU to identify risk factors for acute kidney injury (AKI). They found that several factors, including age, chronic liver disease, and high lactate levels, were associated with AKI. The proportion of AKI cases classified as KDIGO stage 3 increased after day 7.
articles.ai_significance: These findings highlight the importance of early recognition of risk factors for AKI in critically ill patients, supporting the implementation of kidney-protective care strategies in the ICU.

articles.title: Clinical practice guideline for renal replacement therapy in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury (2026 edition).
authors: Guideline working group of Chinese Society of Critical Care
articles.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and severe complication in critically ill patients, associated with high morbidity and mortality. Renal replacement therapy (RRT) is a vital life-support modality for critically ill patients with AKI. However, there remains a lack of unified clinical standards for core issues including the timing of RRT initiation, treatment modality, anticoagulation strategy, and weaning from RRT. In response, the Chinese Society of Critical Care Medicine organized a multidisciplinary expert panel to develop the "Clinical practice guideline for RRT in critically ill patients with AKI (2026 edition)" in accordance with the GRADE approach for grading evidence quality. This guideline was developed through systematic literature retrieval, meta-analysis, and evidence-based medical evidence synthesis, followed by multiple rounds of manuscript review and revision via online and offline meetings of the working group, and final approval by the Standing Committee of the Society. A total of 34 recommendations were finalized, covering key clinical topics including timing of RRT initiation, establishment and maintenance of vascular access, selection of treatment modalities, application of specialized membrane filters, anticoagulation regimens, replacement fluid formulations, prescribed treatment dose, and RRT weaning strategies. This guideline aims to provide scientific, standardized, and clinically actionable guidance for critical care practitioners in China, promoting standardized RRT management in adult critically ill patients with AKI.

articles.title: Guidelines for the prevention and treatment of stress ulcers in critically ill patients (2026).
authors: Guideline Working Group of the Chinese Society of Critical Care Medicine
articles.abstract: Stress ulcers is a common complication in critically ill patients, associated with increased mortality risk and prolonged intensive care unit stay. In recent years, several large-scale clinical studies on risk factors, prevention, and treatment of stress ulcers have provided new evidence for guideline development. Moreover, the lack of standardized protocols for the prevention and treatment of stress ulcers in clinical practice underscores the urgent need for authoritative guidelines to address inconsistent in management strategies. Accordingly, the Chinese Society of Critical Care Medicine established a multidisciplinary expert panel to develop the "Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Stress Ulcers in Critically Ill Patients(2026)". Following the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology, the guideline formulation process involved proposing clinical questions, literature retrieval and screening, meta-analysis and evidence synthesis, initial formation of recommendation items, panel reviews, three rounds of remote meetings, four rounds of face-to-face meetings, manuscript revisions, and final approval by the Standing Committee of the Society. The guidelines were finalized in the form of 23 evidence-based recommendations. These guidelines cover key aspects of stress ulcer management, including risk factors, prevention, treatment, and adverse effects of acid-suppressive drugs. The aim is to provide evidence-based guidance for healthcare professionals and promote standardized clinical management of stress ulcers in adults.

articles.title: Empiric Antifungal Therapy in Critically Ill Patients Undergoing Surgery for Severe Intra-Abdominal Infection: a Large Retrospective Single-Center Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intra-abdominal candidiasis is frequent in critically ill surgical patients and is associated with high mortality. Whether empiric antifungal therapy improves outcomes after surgery for intra-abdominal infection (IAI) in critically ill patients remains uncertain. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective single-center data warehouse-based cohort study of 1,061 adults admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) after surgery for IAI between 2018 and 2024. Patients who received systemic antifungal therapy within 24 hours after surgery were compared with those who did not. The primary endpoint was 30-day all-cause mortality. Secondary endpoints were day-5 renal dysfunction, assessed by the renal SOFA component and the creatinine-based KDIGO stage, and the need for surgical reintervention. Adjusted analyses used propensity-score overlap weighting. Prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses used a Peritonitis Score ≥3, the identification of at least one organism in peritoneal samples, and a yeast-positive peritoneal sample. RESULTS: Empiric antifungal therapy was initiated in 46.0% of patients. Peritoneal sampling was available in 957 patients (90.2%); 21.4% had no organism identified and 25.2% had a yeast-positive sample. In adjusted analyses, empiric therapy was not associated with reduced 30-day mortality (OR 1.53, 95% CI 0.83-2.78), lower day-5 renal SOFA score, lower KDIGO stage, or fewer reinterventions. Findings were consistent in patients with Peritonitis Score ≥3, with at least one identified organism, and with a yeast-positive sample. ICU and hospital stays were longer in treated patients after weighting. CONCLUSIONS: Empiric antifungal therapy initiated within 24 hours after surgery for severe IAI was not associated with improved short-term outcomes. TRIAL REGISTRATION: NA.

articles.title: From predictive signal to deployable value: EHR measurement-process features in ICU AKI prediction.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Electronic health record (EHR)-based clinical prediction systems increasingly use features that reflect how care is delivered and recorded. We evaluated whether creatinine measurement-process features add incremental, operational, and transportable value for dynamic ICU acute kidney injury (AKI) prediction beyond clinical creatinine trajectories. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cross-database study using MIMIC-IV for development and temporal testing and eICU-CRD for external validation. Repeated 6-hour landmarks began 24 hours after ICU admission. Predictors were derived from the preceding 24 hours, and the outcome was observed creatinine-defined KDIGO stage 2-3 AKI during the subsequent 24 hours. Clinical creatinine trajectory features were separated from measurement-process features, including count, recency, spacing, density, gaps, and calendar timing. Logistic regression models compared clinical-only, clinical-plus-process, and process-only feature sets. MIMIC-trained preprocessing and coefficients were frozen for eICU validation. The primary metric was patient-equal-weighted Brier score; secondary analyses assessed discrimination, calibration, fixed-burden alerts, redundancy, hospital heterogeneity, and model-class sensitivity. RESULTS: MIMIC-IV included 4571 ICU stays and 41,600 prediction windows; the eICU dynamic validation subset included 23,058 stays and 206,532 windows. Process-only AUROC was 0.560 in MIMIC-IV and 0.681 in eICU, indicating site-dependent marginal signal. Adding process features changed patient-weighted Brier score by + 0.00010 in MIMIC-IV and -0.000136 in eICU. At a fixed 5% alert burden, detection gains were modest. Process features explained 0.16% of residual Brier-loss variance, and conditional permutation changed AUROC by 0.0018. CONCLUSION: Creatinine measurement-process features captured workflow-related signals but added limited deployable value once clinical creatinine trajectories were represented. EHR process-derived features should be evaluated for incremental performance, calibration, alert burden, redundancy, and transportability before implementation.

articles.title: Distinct associations of age, frailty, and comorbidity with AKI occurrence, mortality, and kidney function recovery in older ICU patients: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is common in critically ill older adults, but the associations of chronological age and baseline vulnerability to kidney outcomes remain uncertain. We examined associations of age, frailty, and comorbidity with AKI occurrence, in-hospital mortality, and kidney function recovery. This retrospective cohort included adults aged ≥60 years admitted to six intensive care units at a Brazilian university hospital from 2023 to 2025. AKI followed KDIGO creatinine criteria; frailty was measured by the modified frailty index (MFI) and comorbidity by the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI). Modified Poisson (AKI occurrence), time-dependent Cox (mortality), and Fine-Gray (kidney function recovery, with death as a competing event) models were used. Among 2387 patients, illness severity and chronic kidney disease prevalence increased with age. AKI developed in 1396 patients (58.5%), rising from 56.2% (60-69 years) to 63.3% (≥80 years); age, MFI (adjusted risk ratio 1.030 per point), and CCI (1.028 per point) were each associated with AKI occurrence. AKI (hazard ratio 3.135, 95% CI 2.585-3.801) and age (1.039 per year) were associated with in-hospital death, whereas MFI and CCI were not after adjustment for acute illness. Of 927 survivors with AKI, 50.2% recovered by discharge. Age was not independently associated with recovery, whereas greater MFI and CCI were associated with lower recovery. Age, frailty, and comorbidity captured distinct dimensions of risk: AKI and age were associated with in-hospital mortality, whereas baseline vulnerability, more than age, was associated with kidney function recovery, supporting frailty and comorbidity assessment in ICU risk stratification.

articles.title: Transportable early renal recovery phenotypes and 30-day major adverse kidney events after sepsis-associated acute kidney injury: A MIMIC-IV discovery and eICU-CRD external-validation cohort study.
articles.abstract: Early renal recovery after sepsis-associated acute kidney injury is heterogeneous. We aimed to derive clinically interpretable early recovery phenotypes, assess their transportability through fixed-centroid external assignment, and examine associations with 30-day major adverse kidney events (MAKE30). This retrospective discovery and external-validation cohort study used Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV and eICU-CRD. Eligible patients were adults with a first intensive care unit stay and Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes -compatible acute kidney injury within 7 days of sepsis onset. K-means clustering integrated five renal, fluid, and hemodynamic domains across twelve 6-hour intervals after acute kidney injury onset. Stability was assessed by repeated 80% patient subsampling. eICU CRD patients were assigned to fixed MIMIC-derived centroids without reclustering. Modified Poisson models estimated adjusted risk ratios (RRs). Of 9725 Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV patients with known MAKE30 status, 2529 (26.0%) experienced MAKE30. Four phenotypes were identified in 7965 patients: low-burden rapid-recovery, preserved-diuresis intermediate-risk, oliguric kidney-failure, and shock-vasopressor. The four-cluster solution had a median adjusted Rand index of 0.939 (empirical 2.5th-97.5th percentiles, 0.892-0.990). Relative to the low-burden phenotype, adjusted MAKE30 RRs were 1.74 (95% confidence interval , 1.58-1.90), 3.80 (3.47-4.16), and 3.68 (3.34-4.06). In eICU-CRD, 4708 of 8771 patients (53.7%) could be assigned; corresponding RRs were 2.82 (2.45-3.23), 4.78 (4.00-5.72), and 4.99 (4.32-5.76). Unassigned patients had higher MAKE30 rates than assigned patients (41.1% vs 25.2%). MAKE30 associations persisted in landmark and distance-restricted analyses. Early renal recovery trajectories identified four reproducible clinical phenotypes associated with MAKE30. Fixed-centroid assignment reproduced the direction of these associations in eICU-CRD patients with sufficient trajectory data. Selective assignment and the observational design limit generalizability and preclude conclusions about phenotype-guided treatment.

articles.title: Structured Patient and Family-Centered Rounding in the ICU is Associated With Increased Family Confidence in Staff Compassion and Perceived Quality of Information Shared.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Determine whether inviting families to participate in structured, multidisciplinary rounding in the ICU can lead to improved quality of information shared and greater overall confidence in the care delivered to patients. DESIGN: Pre- and postimplementation observational study based on surveys provided by the Society of Critical Care Medicine-Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute initiative. SETTING: Academic teaching hospital with 21 medical (closed unit) and 25 surgical (open unit) ICU beds. SUBJECTS: Family members and care providers of critically ill adults of 18 years and older. INTERVENTIONS: Families and clinicians were surveyed before and after implementation of a quality initiative to promote greater patient and family-centeredness in daily ICU rounds, using a structured and scripted rounding template. Additional information was gathered regarding provider attitudes toward the incorporation of families in rounds. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: In pre-and postintervention periods, 36 and 28 families were surveyed in the MICU, and 44 and 42 families were surveyed in the SICU, respectively. In pre-and postintervention periods, respectively, 53 and 48 clinicians were surveyed in the MICU, and 46 and 28 clinicians were surveyed in the SICU. Clinician perceptions improved favorably in the MICU, with statistically significant improvements falling under the category of family welcoming, presence, and participation in decision-making; less so in the SICU. Family perceptions improved in almost all parameters in the MICU, with statistical significance achieved in perceived interest in patient needs, control of agitation and pain, and consistency and honesty of information shared. Similar patterns were observed in the SICU but did not reach statistical significance. CONCLUSIONS: Structured, multi-disciplinary rounding with regular inclusion of family members and bedside nurses was associated with significantly greater family confidence in the quality and honesty of information shared, and an increase in perceived compassion in the care provided by ICU staff. Clinician perceptions regarding family inclusion on rounds were generally positive.

articles.title: Association of medication burden and potential drug-drug interactions with acute kidney injury among critically ill patients receiving anticancer therapy at a tertiary care centre.
articles.journal: Journal of oncology pharmacy practice : official publication of the International Society of Oncology Pharmacy Practitioners
articles.abstract: BackgroundCritically ill patients with cancer are exposed to many drugs, including anticancer agents, antimicrobials and supportive medications, which increases the risk of nephrotoxicity and potential drug-drug interactions (pDDIs). The contribution of medication burden and pDDIs to acute kidney injury (AKI) in this population is not well characterised.ObjectiveTo assess the association of medication burden and pDDIs with AKI among critically ill patients receiving anticancer therapy.MethodsThis retrospective observational study was conducted in the intensive care units (ICUs) of a tertiary care centre from August 2025 to September 2026. Adults with malignancy who received anticancer therapy within 30 days before or during ICU stay were included. AKI was defined and staged by KDIGO criteria. Medication burden (total drugs and nephrotoxic drugs) and pDDIs (screened using a standard interaction database) were recorded. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of AKI.ResultsOf 210 patients, 86 (41.0%) developed AKI. Patients with AKI had a higher median number of drugs (11 vs 8, p < 0.001) and pDDIs (6 vs 3, p < 0.001). Independent predictors of AKI were ≥10 distinct drugs (aOR 2.62; 95% CI 1.32-5.18), at least one nephrotoxicity-related pDDI (aOR 2.87; 95% CI 1.43-5.76), APACHE II score (aOR 1.09 per point), pre-existing CKD, sepsis, and cisplatin exposure. In-hospital mortality was higher with AKI (39.5% vs 21.8%, p = 0.007).ConclusionHigh medication burden and nephrotoxicity-related pDDIs were independently associated with AKI in critically ill cancer patients. Routine pharmacist-led medication review and renal-focused interaction screening may help reduce preventable kidney injury.

articles.title: Association Between Succinylated Gelatin Exposure and Acute Kidney Injury in Critically Ill Trauma Patients: A Retrospective Five-Year Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Early fluid resuscitation is a cornerstone of trauma care, but the relationship between resuscitation strategies and acute kidney injury (AKI) remains insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to evaluate whether administration of 4% succinylated gelatin is associated with the development of AKI in critically ill trauma patients during the first seven days of intensive care unit (ICU) treatment. Methods: We conducted an observational retrospective single-center cohort study including 215 adult trauma patients admitted to the ICU at a tertiary care center between 2015 and 2020. Gelatin exposure, kidney function, and clinical outcomes were assessed from the pre-ICU phase through the first ICU week. The primary outcome was the development of AKI, at stage ≥ 2 of the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) staging. We used mixed-effects models, competing-risk analyses, correlation analyses and exploratory unsupervised clustering to explore associations between gelatin use and renal outcomes. Results: AKI occurred in 17% of patients and was associated with older age, higher Simplified Acute Physiology Score 3 (SAPS3), pre-existing comorbidities, and early signs of hemodynamic and metabolic compromise. Gelatin doses of ≥10 mL/kg/day were not associated with a consistent rise in serum creatinine or progression of AKI over time. Multivariable regression models revealed no independent association between gelatin and worsening AKI. Instead, KDIGO stage worsening was primarily associated with AKI present at ICU admission and with crystalloid volume. Clustering analysis identified a high-risk phenotype with increased gelatin exposure, but this cluster also showed pronounced shock and inflammation, suggesting confounding by indication. In a competing-risk analysis, gelatin was not associated with new-onset AKI, whereas higher gelatin doses were associated with a lower rate of ICU discharge. Conclusions: In this retrospective cohort of critically ill trauma patients, succinylated gelatin administration showed no statistically significant association with KDIGO-defined AKI progression across unadjusted and adjusted models. Gelatin doses of ≥10 mL/kg/day were more frequently administered in patients with greater hemodynamic instability, suggesting that gelatin use primarily reflected underlying illness severity rather than acting as a direct nephrotoxic agent. These findings provide no evidence of an independent nephrotoxic effect of gelatin when used as part of balanced trauma resuscitation strategies.

articles.title: Intensivists' Perspectives and Practices on Palliative Care in the ICU: A Nationwide Survey in Korea.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: While many countries have made progress in integrating palliative care into intensive care units (ICUs), implementation remains highly context-dependent. In Korea, palliative care integration within ICUs remains limited, and intensivists' perspectives on its role and applicability have not been well studied. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide, cross-sectional online survey of certified intensivists and fellows registered with the Korean Society of Critical Care Medicine between April and May 2024. The questionnaire explored knowledge and confidence in palliative care, current ICU practices, referral patterns, perceived barriers, and preferred strategies for integration. RESULTS: A total of 241 intensivists responded (response rate, 23.9%). Most agreed that palliative care should be incorporated into ICU care (97.1%) and were willing to make referrals (98.3%). Advance care planning, symptom management, and family decision-making were the most expected domains of support. However, fewer reported involvement in psychological support, end-of-life care, or bereavement services. Referral practices were more frequent in institutions with palliative care teams, while lack of resources, unsupportive institutional culture, and unclear processes were commonly cited barriers. Clinical guidelines, professional education, and reimbursement reform were identified as priority strategies for integration. CONCLUSION: Korean intensivists widely recognize the need for palliative care in the ICU but apply it within a limited scope. To strengthen integration, consensus on definitions, clear referral criteria, and supportive institutional and policy frameworks are required.

articles.title: [Correlation between acute kidney injury diagnosed by serum creatinine and urine output criteria and short-term prognosis in critically ill patients following non-cardiac surgery].
articles.journal: Beijing da xue xue bao. Yi xue ban = Journal of Peking University. Health sciences
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To analyze the correlation between acute kidney injury (AKI) diagnosed by elevated serum creatinine (Scr) versus only meeting the urine output (UO) reduction criteria and short-term adverse outcomes in critically ill patients following non-cardiac surgery, and to evaluate the association between even mild elevations in Scr and clinical outcomes furthermore. METHODS: This study was a secondary analysis of data from a prospective cohort study. A total of 1020 non-cardiac surgery adults admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) of Peking University First Hospital from May 20, 2019 to March 7, 2022 were included. According to Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guideline, AKI patients were classified into two groups: the AKI-Scr group (those meeting the Scr elevation criteria) and the AKI-UO group (those fulfilling only the UO reduction criteria). The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality in patients with AKI, and the secondary outcomes were major renal adverse events, post-operative renal replacement therapy (RRT), postoperative complications, postoperative mechanical ventilation time, ICU stay, postoperative hospital stay, total hospital stay, and total medical costs. Multivariate Logistic regression analysis was used to identify risk factors of hospitalized death in critically ill patients with AKI following non-cardiac surgery. RESULTS: A total of 1020 non-cardiac surgical patients admitted to the ICU were enrolled, among whom 429 were diagnosed with AKI. There were 91 cases in the AKI-Scr group and 338 cases in the AKI-UO group. The primary study endpoint: no statistically significant difference in in-hospital mortality was observed between the AKI-Scr and AKI-UO groups (5.5% vs. 2.1%, P>0.05). The secondary study endpoints: compared with the AKI-UO group, the patients in the AKI-Scr group had a higher incidence of major renal adverse events (9.8% vs. 4.4%), postoperative RRT (4.4% vs. 0.3%) and postoperative complications (50.5% vs. 24.0%, all P < 0.05), a significantly longer duration of postoperative mechanical ventilation (12.0 d vs. 7.5 d), ICU stay (2 d vs. 1 d), postoperative hospital stay (14 d vs. 9 d) and total hospital stay (21 d vs.17 d, all P < 0.05), and a significantly higher total medical expenditure (112000 yuan vs. 89000 yuan, P<0.001). Multivariate Logistic regression analysis showed that postoperative RRT (OR=33.164, 95%CI: 1.305-842.794, P=0.034) and sepsis during hospitalization (OR=23.096, 95%CI: 4.242-125.175, P < 0.001) were independent risk factors for hospitalized death in the critically ill patients with postoperative AKI. Compared with the ΔScr≤24% patients (Scr increased by less than 24% from baseline within 7 d), even in the patients with only a minor elevation in Scr (ΔScr increase of 25%-49% from baseline but < 26.5μmol/L), the incidence of postoperative complications was significantly higher (48.6% vs. 19.2%, P < 0.001), along with prolonged ICU stay [1(1, 3) d vs. 1(1, 2) d], postoperative hospital stay (13 d vs. 9 d), and total hospital stay (23 d vs. 16 d, all P < 0.05). Compared with the non-AKI group, the incidence of in-hospital mortality (2.1% vs. 0.3%, P < 0.05) and postoperative complications (24.0% vs. 18.3%, P < 0.05) was higher in the AKI-UO group, and the ICU stay [1(1, 3) d vs. 1(1, 2) d, P < 0.001] was longer. CONCLUSION: In critically ill patients with AKI following non-cardiac surgery, the short-term prognosis of patients with AKI whose diagnosis was mainly based on increased Scr was worse than patients who only met the diagnostic criteria of oliguria. Even a mild elevation in serum creatinine was associated with adverse patient outcomes.

articles.title: Association of Oliguria With Acute Kidney Injury, Chronic Kidney Disease, and Mortality: Determining the Optimal Threshold in Critically Ill Patients.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Oliguria is a key prognostic indicator of acute kidney injury (AKI), yet the consensus definition (< 0.5 mL/kg/hr) is increasingly questioned. We aimed to determine thresholds of lowest mean diuresis (LMD) associated with AKI, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and mortality. DESIGN: Retrospective observational study. SETTING: Uppsala University Hospital ICU, Sweden. PATIENTS: A total of 4999 adults (≥ 18 yr) without preexisting CKD admitted to the ICU between 2017 and 2024. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: LMD was calculated over 3, 6, 12, and 24 hours (LMD3h-LMD24h). Generalized additive models were used, adjusting for Simplified Acute Physiology Score 3 estimated mortality ratio and gender. Outcomes were AKI within 7 days of LMD (Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes creatinine criteria), incident CKD after ICU discharge, and 90-day mortality. All LMD time frames were significantly associated with AKI, CKD, and death (p < 0.0001). Thresholds for AKI were 0.43, 0.41, 0.42, and 0.53 mL/kg/hr; for CKD, 0.21, 0.21, 0.31, and 0.43 mL/kg/hr; and for mortality 0.16, 0.18, 0.24, and 0.39 across LMD3h-LMD24h. CONCLUSIONS: The risk of mortality or persistent kidney injury, reflected by incident CKD, increases at a lower urine output threshold than the current AKI definition. These findings support the idea of filtration deficit, urine output, and tissue injury as different dimensions of AKI and should influence future AKI definitions.

articles.title: Glucose control and clinical outcomes in surgical patients: A narrative review.
articles.journal: Nutrition in clinical practice : official publication of the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition
articles.abstract: Perioperative hyperglycemia occurs in up to 40% of noncardiac and 80% of cardiac surgery patients, frequently independent of a diabetes diagnosis; it is driven by the neuroendocrine stress response, inflammatory cytokine release, and postoperative insulin resistance. Elevated glucose promotes protein glycosylation, which impairs wound healing and immune function, and it has been consistently associated with surgical site infection, anastomotic leak, prolonged length of stay, and increased mortality across surgical subspecialties. This narrative review examines biochemical aspects of glycogen metabolism and stress-induced insulin resistance, synthesizes evidence linking hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) thresholds to surgical outcomes, and summarizes contemporary guidelines from the American Diabetes Association, Endocrine Society, European Society of Cardiology, Society of Critical Care Medicine, and Surviving Sepsis Campaign. Current consensus favors moderate, protocolized glucose targets (generally 100-180 mg/dL) while avoiding iatrogenic hypoglycemia. Preoperative optimization toward an HbA1c near 7%, judicious carbohydrate loading, and avoidance of glycemic extremes offer meaningful, modifiable strategies to improve outcomes in surgical and critically ill surgical patients.

articles.title: Acute kidney injury at a tertiary nephrology referral center: predictors of renal recovery and in-hospital mortality.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a global health problem associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Despite advances in prevention and management, in-hospital mortality remains high, particularly among critically ill patients. OBJECTIVES: To determine incidence, risk factors of AKI among patients admitted to Mansoura Nephrology and Dialysis Unit (MNDU), a tertiary nephrology referral center in Dakahlia governorate, Egypt, over one year, and to identify predictors of renal recovery at discharge and in-hospital mortality. METHODS: This prospective observational study was conducted from June 2022 to May 2023 and included adult patients admitted with various kidney disorders. Patients were classified into AKI and non-AKI groups according to KDIGO 2012 criteria. Clinical, laboratory, and outcome data were analyzed, and multivariable regression analyses were used to identify independent predictors of in-hospital mortality and renal recovery after AKI. RESULTS: A total of 839 patients were enrolled, including 330 (39.3%) with AKI and 509 (60.7%) without AKI. The most common pathophysiological causes of AKI were pre-renal (54.2%) followed by intrinsic renal (38.5%) one. In-hospital mortality was significantly higher in AKI than non-AKI group (17.3% vs. 3.8%), with septic shock being the leading cause of death (84.2%). Among patients with AKI, 45.2% achieved complete renal recovery, 21.8% had partial recovery, and 33.0% had no recovery at discharge. On multivariable logistic regression analyses, KDIGO Stage 3 AKI (adjusted OR 0.277, P = 0.046), kidney replacement therapy (adjusted OR 0.409, P = 0.004), and requirement of vasopressor therapy (adjusted OR 0.041, P < 0.001) were independently associated with lower odds of renal recovery, whereas necessity of vasopressor therapy emerged as the only independent predictor of in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR 420.511, 95% CI 97.451-1814.543; P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: AKI was common among hospitalized patients and was associated with substantially increased in-hospital mortality. Vasopressor requirement was the strongest independent predictor of mortality, emphasizing the prognostic impact of hemodynamic instability and critical illness severity. Severe AKI (KDIGO Stage 3), kidney replacement therapy, and vasopressor necessity were independently associated with reduced renal recovery at discharge. These readily available clinical indicators may support early risk stratification and guide closer monitoring of high-risk patients.

articles.title: Estimation of Soluble Urokinase-type Plasminogen Activator Receptor in Septic Acute Kidney Injury Patients: A Prospective Observational Study from a Tertiary Care Center.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Septic-acute kidney injury (SAKI) is one of the most common and most serious complications in critically ill patients, and conventional markers such as serum creatinine and urine output remain late and imperfect indicators of renal injury. Soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (suPAR) has emerged as a biomarker of immune activation and systemic inflammation and may have diagnostic and prognostic relevance in septic AKI. METHODS: In this prospective observational study, 113 adults with sepsis, were enrolled over 1 year. A total 77 patients had S-AKI and 36 had sepsis without AKI. suPAR was measured by ELISA at admission, 24 h, and 48 h. AKI was classified according to Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. Group comparisons, correlation analyses, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis were performed. RESULTS: Admission suPAR was significantly higher in S-AKI than in septic non-AKI controls (29.0 [19.0-92.0] vs. 9.0 [6.0-16.0] ng/mL; P < 0.001). suPAR increased stepwise across KDIGO stages: 20.5 ng/mL in stage 1, 33.0 ng/mL in stage2, and 46.0 ng/mL in stage 3 (P < 0.001). Admission suPAR was higher in patients with partial renal recovery than in those with complete recovery at discharge [46.0 (23.0-88.0) vs. 19.5 (15.0-41.2) ng/mL; P = 0.005]. ROC analysis showed excellent diagnostic performance for S-AKI with an AUC of 0.906 (95% CI 0.84-0.96); the optimal cutoff was 16.0 ng/mL, with 77.9% sensitivity and 86.1% specificity. CONCLUSION: suPAR was significantly elevated in septic AKI, increased with increasing AKI severity, and predicted incomplete renal recovery. suPAR to be a promising diagnostic and prognostic biomarker in septic AKI.

articles.title: A Comprehensive Review of the Underlying Mechanisms of Resistance and Therapeutic Options for DTR-PA in Bloodstream Infection and Pneumonia: A Clinical Vignette-Based Approach.
articles.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a ubiquitous opportunistic pathogen and a leading cause of severe healthcare-associated infections, particularly ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) and bloodstream infections (BSIs) in critically ill patients. Its remarkable capacity for both intrinsic and acquired resistance leads to complex phenotypic profiles, culminating in difficult-to-treat resistant P. aeruginosa (DTR-PA). Managing DTR-PA presents a daunting clinical challenge characterised by a narrow therapeutic armamentarium, treatment delays, and high attributable mortality. To bridge the gap between complex molecular microbiology and bedside decision-making, this narrative review employs a pragmatic, clinical vignette-based approach. Through six representative fictional scenarios of pneumonia and BSI, we systematically dissect the underlying mechanisms of resistance and their direct therapeutic implications. The vignettes explore combinations of intrinsic adaptations-such as Pseudomonas-derived cephalosporinase (PDC/AmpC) hyperexpression, OprD porin loss, and efflux pump upregulation-as well as the acquisition of serine- (e.g., GES) and metallo-β-lactamases (e.g., VIM, NDM, IMP). Grounded in the updated 2026 Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines, we evaluate the optimal deployment of newer β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations. We highlight the specific preference for ceftolozane-tazobactam in pneumonia, the roles of ceftazidime-avibactam and imipenem-relebactam, and the critical use of cefiderocol for metallo-β-lactamase producers and highly resistant phenotypes. Furthermore, the review addresses pressing clinical controversies: the superiority of targeted monotherapy over historical, toxic combination regimens; the risks of unconditionally applying "shorter-is-better" duration paradigms to DTR-PA; and the alarming frequency of treatment-emergent cross-resistance among novel agents. We also clarify common clinical misconceptions, such as the limited utility of meropenem-vaborbactam and aztreonam-avibactam against specific pseudomonal mechanisms. Ultimately, effective DTR-PA management precludes class-based empirical assumptions. By providing a phenotype-driven bedside aide-mémoire, this review reinforces that rapid recognition, direct agent-specific antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD)-optimised dosing, and prompt source control remain the absolute cornerstones of survival for patients afflicted by these formidable infections.

articles.title: Circulating NLRP3 Inflammasome Activation Is Associated With Sepsis-Associated Acute Kidney Injury and Disease Severity: A Prospective Pilot Study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI) is a severe and prevalent complication in critically ill patients, characterized by high mortality and a lack of reliable biomarkers that reflect inflammatory pathway activation and disease severity. Although the NLRP3 inflammasome is known to mediate inflammatory responses, pyroptosis, and renal injury, its clinical relevance in human SA-AKI remains poorly defined. This study aimed to characterize the expression profiles, dynamic trajectories, and clinical associations of circulating NLRP3 inflammasome components in patients with SA-AKI. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Thirty adult patients with sepsis (13 with SA-AKI and 17 without AKI) were prospectively and consecutively enrolled. Sepsis was defined according to the Sepsis-3 consensus criteria, whereas AKI was diagnosed and staged exclusively using the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. Serum protein levels of NLRP3, ASC, caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1, IL-1β, and IL-18, and transcript levels of NLRP3, ASC, and caspase-1, were determined on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 after enrollment using ELISA and quantitative real-time PCR. Statistical analyses included group comparisons, Spearman rank correlations, linear mixed-effects models, and exploratory receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses to assess concurrent group discrimination. Because samples were collected post-classification, these analyses describe post-diagnostic expression kinetics rather than prediction of future AKI onset. RESULTS: The expression of NLRP3 inflammasome-related molecules was significantly upregulated in the SA-AKI group and correlated with renal dysfunction and elevated illness-severity scores (SOFA and APACHE II). Exploratory ROC analyses suggested strong discrimination of concurrent AKI status for ASC, caspase-1, and NLRP3 transcript levels, with the strongest overall performance observed on day 3. These estimates are hypothesis-generating because of the small sample size and post-classification sampling. DISCUSSION: The NLRP3 inflammasome pathway is prominently activated in patients with SA-AKI and is closely associated with renal dysfunction and systemic illness severity. Circulating components of this pathway are candidate biomarkers of concurrent SA-AKI, but their ability to predict AKI onset or prognosis requires validation in larger prospective cohorts sampled before AKI develops.

articles.title: Incidence, Predictors, and Clinical Outcomes of Acute Kidney Injury in Critically Ill Patients: A Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract: Background Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent and serious complication among critically ill patients and is associated with prolonged hospitalization, increased need for organ support, and higher mortality. Objective The objective of the study is to determine the incidence of AKI among critically ill patients, identify its independent predictors, and evaluate its association with major clinical outcomes. Methods This retrospective observational study was conducted at Services Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan, from June 2023 to June 2026 and included 261 adult critically ill patients. Demographic characteristics, comorbidities, clinical severity scores, laboratory parameters, treatment-related factors, and clinical outcomes were extracted from medical records. Results AKI developed in 102 of 261 patients, corresponding to an incidence of 39.1%. Among patients with AKI, 42 (41.2%) had Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) stage 1, 34 (33.3%) had stage 2, and 26 (25.5%) had stage 3 disease. Compared with patients without AKI, those with AKI had higher intensive care unit (ICU) mortality (35 (34.3%) vs. 19 (11.9%)), in-hospital mortality (41 (40.2%) vs. 24 (15.1%)), and renal replacement therapy requirement (21 (20.6%) vs. 0 (0.0%)), as well as longer ICU and hospital stays and longer duration of mechanical ventilation (all p < 0.001). Factors independently associated with AKI included chronic kidney disease (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 3.12, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.34-7.28), vasopressor support at ICU admission (aOR 2.86, 95% CI 1.49-5.50), sepsis or septic shock (aOR 2.74, 95% CI 1.48-5.08), mechanical ventilation at ICU admission (aOR 2.09, 95% CI 1.08-4.04), increasing serum lactate (aOR 1.31, 95% CI 1.10-1.57), higher Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) score (aOR 1.09, 95% CI 1.04-1.14), and increasing age (aOR 1.03, 95% CI 1.01-1.05). Conclusion AKI affected more than one-third of critically ill patients and was associated with a greater observed clinical burden, including higher mortality, greater need for renal replacement therapy, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and longer ICU and hospital stays. Chronic kidney disease, sepsis or septic shock, vasopressor support at ICU admission, mechanical ventilation at ICU admission, higher serum lactate, higher APACHE II score, and increasing age were independently associated with AKI. Because clinical outcome comparisons were unadjusted, the observed differences in mortality, mechanical ventilation duration, and length of stay do not establish AKI as an independent determinant of these outcomes.

articles.title: Global heterogeneity and implementation gap in acute kidney injury prevention: Results from the AKI-PURIFY survey.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite substantial advances in critical care nephrology, the real-world implementation of diagnostic tools and evidence-based preventive strategies for acute kidney injury (AKI) in critically ill patients remains poorly defined. Understanding the gap between guideline recommendations and bedside practice is essential to inform targeted quality-improvement initiatives. The AKI-PURIFY survey was designed to provide a contemporary international overview of AKI diagnosis and management in the ICU, with emphasis on implementation of the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) preventive strategies and determinants with its adoption. We hypothesized that implementation of evidence-based preventive care varies across healthcare settings and is influenced by clinician training and organizational capacity. METHODS: AKI-PURIFY was a multicenter, international online survey endorsed by the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM), conducted between February and April 2024. Healthcare professionals involved in intensive care unit (ICU) management of AKI were invited to participate. The survey explored diagnostic strategies, implementation of the KDIGO kidney prevention strategy, renal replacement therapy practices, and perceived organizational and educational barriers. Multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted to identify factors independently associated with the use of diagnostic tools and the implementation of preventive strategies. RESULTS: A total of 703 respondents completed the survey. Routine implementation of the KDIGO kidney prevention strategy was reported by 36.3% of participants (47.0% among valid responses). Diagnostic practices varied across ICU and resource settings, and the use of AKI damage biomarkers remained low. In adjusted analyses, inadequate training (odds ratio [OR]=0.56, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.37 to 0.84, P=0.007) and higher organizational barrier scores (OR=0.78, 95% CI: 0.63 to 0.97, P=0.030) were independently associated with lower implementation. Clear income-level gradients were observed across diagnostic strategies, training adequacy, and organizational capacity. CONCLUSIONS: Adoption of guideline-recommended AKI prevention strategies remains inconsistent worldwide and is influenced by modifiable educational and system-level factors. Addressing this gap will require coordinated, context-sensitive strategies integrating structured training and scalable quality-improvement frameworks.

articles.title: The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines: The dissenting opinion.
articles.journal: The American journal of emergency medicine
articles.abstract: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) Guidelines once represented what was considered the pinnacle of care for patients with sepsis and septic shock. Unfortunately, over the past decade, successive iterations of the guidelines have drifted from what is now considered optimal care for critically ill patients with sepsis and septic shock. Moreover, the guidelines have shifted from recommendations intended to guide and support physicians based on the best available evidence, to mandated "bundles" which exert substantial influence over what is considered "standard of care" in sepsis management. This. Document is intended to serve as a refutation of sorts. A rebuttal to the most controversial and influential recommendations in the Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines, while also offering guidance on how clinicians might move beyond the protocolized, metric-based care that has become the current standard promoted by the SSC and similar organizations.

articles.title: Practices and barriers in PET/CT use for critically ill patients: an international survey.
articles.journal: European journal of nuclear medicine and molecular imaging
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: 2-deoxy-2-[18F] fluoro-D-glucose (FDG) Positron Emission Tomography/Computed Tomography ([18F]-FDG-PET/CT) offers high diagnostic sensitivity for occult infection, malignancy and inflammatory processes - conditions that frequently complicate critical‑care patients. Despite this potential, routine use of [18F]-FDG-PET/CT in the intensive care unit (ICU) remains sporadic and there are no formal guidelines to direct its application. The objective of the study is to describe current international practice, identify barriers to implementation, and provide a data‑driven foundation for future consensus recommendations on [18F]-FDG-PET/CT use in ICU patients. METHODS: An electronic questionnaire was disseminated worldwide through the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) and the European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM). The survey collected demographic information, hospital characteristics, availability and location of nuclear‑medicine services, clinical indications for [18F]-FDG-PET/CT in critically ill patients, frequency of use, workflow organization, and perceived obstacles. Forty‑one respondents from 16 countries completed the survey. RESULTS: Most participants worked in university hospitals (63%) and specialised either in ICU care (71%) or nuclear imaging (29%). A nuclear‑medicine department (NMD) was available in 78% of centres, but only 60% were co‑located with the ICU. [18F]-FDG-PET/CT was performed infrequently: 43% of users performed 1-5 scans per year and a fourth performed 1-2 scans per month. The use of PET/CT as primary diagnostic technique was infection (74%), followed by malignancy (57%) and fever of unknown origin (49%). Radiotracer administration occurred mainly in the NMD (77%) and specific dietary preparation protocols were present in only 50% of sites. Reported barriers included lack of standardised protocols, prolonged procedure duration, limited imaging slots, ambiguous indications, insufficient staff expertise, and logistical difficulties transporting unstable ICU patients. CONCLUSION: This international survey reveals marked heterogeneity in [18F]-FDG-PET/CT utilisation and significant practical obstacles in the ICU setting. The data highlight an unmet need for consensus guidelines and streamlined workflows to optimise the diagnostic value of [18F]-FDG-PET/CT in critical‑care patients. Findings will inform forthcoming joint recommendations by ESICM and EANM, ultimately aiming to enhance patient outcomes through evidence‑based imaging protocols.

articles.title: Acute kidney injury in hospitalized COVID-19 patients: predictors, risk factors, mortality, and renal recovery from a bi-center cohort in Palestine.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a prevalent and serious complication in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Data from low- and middle-income regions remain insufficient. OBJECTIVES: To examine the incidence, predictors, risk factors, renal recovery, and mortality of acute kidney injury (AKI) in hospitalized COVID-19 patients within a bi-center cohort in Palestine. METHODS: A retrospective cohort analysis involving 435 adult patients with confirmed COVID-19 infection admitted to Al-Makassed Hospital and Augusta Victoria Hospital in East Jerusalem from March 2020 to March 2022. Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) was categorized and staged in accordance with Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. We employed multivariable logistic regression to identify predictors of acute kidney injury and mortality. RESULTS: 32.2% (140 out of 435) of patients experienced AKI. The majority of AKI cases were male (60%) and over 60 years of age (74.3%). 70.7% of people with AKI experienced severe COVID-19. AKI was significantly associated with Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission (45%) and invasive ventilation. Stage 1AKI was observed in 60%, stage 2 in 21.4%, and stage 3 in 18.6% of cases. Renal recovery occurred in 63.6% of cases, whereas death reached 35.7%. AKI was a significant risk factor for mortality (OR 3.5, 95% Confidence Interval 2.16-5.66). Independent mortality predictors included severe COVID-19, ICU hospitalization, invasive ventilation, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, D-dimer, lactate), and increased peak creatinine and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels. A greater stage of AKI was significantly associated with worse renal outcomes and increased mortality (p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: AKI is a prevalent complication among hospitalized COVID-19 patients in Palestine, associated with elevated mortality and restricted renal recovery. The principal determinants of outcome are disease severity, intensive care unit management, and inflammatory load.

articles.title: Acute kidney injury in critically ill patients with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: a prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To identify clinical and biochemical factors associated with the development of acute kidney injury (AKI) in critically ill patients with severe hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) and to evaluate associated maternal and fetal outcomes. STUDY DESIGN: A prospective single-center cohort study was conducted in an Argentinian intensive care unit (ICU) between November 2017 and July 2022, including 179 women with severe HDP. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary outcome was the development of AKI, defined by either a pregnancy-adjusted admission serum creatinine threshold (>0.87 mg/dL) or fulfillment of Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. Secondary outcomes included maternal and fetal mortality. RESULTS: Out of 179 patients, AKI was diagnosed in 119 patients (66.3%) and was associated with higher illness severity scores and increased fetal mortality (18% vs. 5%; p = 0.022), In the final multivariable analysis, independent predictors of AKI included the corrected Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score (OR 1.37; 95% CI 1.04-1.81), serum uric acid (OR 1.03; 95% CI 1.01-1.05), lactate dehydrogenase (OR 1.01; 95% CI 1.00-1.01), and base excess (OR 0.87; 95% CI 0.78-0.96). HELLP syndrome represented the most severe phenotype, carrying the highest risk for advanced AKI and the need for renal replacement therapy. CONCLUSIONS: AKI is highly prevalent in critically ill patients with severe HDP and serves as a key determinant of adverse maternal and fetal prognosis, Simple biochemical markers and organ dysfunction scores enable early risk stratification, the limited specificity of standard criteria highlights the necessity for pregnancy-adapted diagnostic approaches.

articles.title: Early renal perfusion phenotypes and renal recovery in critically ill patients with or at risk for acute kidney injury: a prospective multicenter cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute kidney injury (AKI) in critical illness is heterogeneous, and conventional Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) classification may not capture early physiologic differences relevant to renal recovery. METHODS: Critically ill adults with or at risk for AKI were enrolled within 24 h of intensive care unit admission in a prospective multicenter cohort from six ICUs in China. Doppler ultrasound-derived semi-quantitative renal perfusion (SQP) and renal resistive index (RRI) were measured at admission, 24 h, and 48 h. Group-based trajectory modeling identified perfusion phenotypes, and associations with renal outcomes were evaluated using multivariable models. RESULTS: Among 456 patients, 216 (47.4%) had AKI at ICU admission and 253 (55.5%) met AKI criteria within 72 h. Two SQP phenotypes were identified: sustained-high perfusion (n = 224, 49.1%) and sustained-low perfusion (n = 232, 50.9%). Sustained-high SQP was associated with lower odds of persistent AKI in the primary model (adjusted odds ratio, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.35-0.89; P = 0.015), although this association was attenuated in expanded sensitivity models. Sustained-high SQP was also associated with less renal non-recovery within 7 days, faster recovery among patients with AKI at admission, and less RRT use on day 3 and day 7. RRI trajectories did not discriminate renal outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: Serial SQP phenotyping identified persistent low- and high-perfusion strata associated with kidney-specific recovery outcomes and may provide complementary bedside physiologic information, but external validation is required.Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05866250.

articles.title: Sustained Low-Efficiency Dialysis Versus Intermittent Hemodialysis in Critically Ill Patients with Severe Acute Kidney Injury.
articles.journal: Medical principles and practice : international journal of the Kuwait University, Health Science Centre
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The objectives of the study were to compare clinical efficacy, hemodynamic stability, and 90-day renal outcomes between Sustained low-efficiency dialysis (SLED) and Intermittent hemodialysis (IHD) in Medical intensive care unit (MICU) patients with severe Acute kidney injury (AKI). METHODS: This observational cohort study evaluated 300 patients with KDIGO Stage-2 or 3 AKI (SLED: n = 160; IHD: n = 140). Outcomes included MICU mortality, discharge renal recovery, stay duration, intradialytic complications, and 90-day renal preservation. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics were comparable. No significant differences emerged between SLED and IHD regarding MICU mortality (33% vs. 39%, p = 0.272) or renal recovery at discharge (61% vs. 54%, p = 0.223). However, SLED demonstrated superior safety, significantly lowering intradialytic hypotension (21% vs. 41%, p < 0.001) and the need for new vasopressors (11% vs. 22%, p = 0.011), while minimizing mean arterial pressure drops (12.12 ± 3.9 vs. 19 ± 6.36 mmHg, p < 0.001). SLED achieved shorter median MICU stays (14 vs. 16 days, p < 0.001). At 90-day, SLED survivors exhibited significantly lower Renal replacement therapy (RRT) dependence (11% vs. 24%, p = 0.014), reduced chronic kidney disease progression (26% vs. 34%, p = 0.044), and higher glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) (55.93 ± 7.69 vs. 45.86 ± 9.29 mL/min/1.73m2, p < 0.001).
