There were 1,736,509 births included in this analysis. Higher birthweights were associated with a significantly increased risk of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Births of infants in all birthweight groups ≥4,000 grams were associated with higher risk of delivery via operative vaginal or cesarean, maternal blood transfusion, Apgar score <7 at 5 minutes, NICU admission, neonatal assisted ventilation, neonatal seizures and infant death. Newborns ≥5,000 grams had the highest rates of adverse neonatal outcomes, including Apgar score <7 at 5 minutes (aRR 3.23, 95% CI 2.94-3.54), NICU admission (aRR 4.15, 95% CI 4.03-4.27), assisted ventilation (aRR 3.15, 95% CI 2.99-3.31), neonatal seizures (aRR 4.08, 95% CI 2.41-6.90) and infant death (aRR 2.91, 95% CI 1.98-4.29). When stratified by diabetes type, similar effect sizes were seen, although the adjusted risk of adverse outcomes was generally higher for those with gestational diabetes. Birthweights ≥4,000 grams were associated with increasingly higher risk of adverse outcomes among births complicated by diabetes. Future studies focused on targeted prenatal interventions to reduce risk for macrosomia as well as improve postnatal transitions are needed.

articles.title: Trust and Behavioural Intention to Use Artificial Intelligence Among ICU Nurses: An Empirical Structural Equation Modelling Study.
articles.abstract: AI-assisted systems in intensive care units face a major bottleneck because nurses lack trust and willingness to use them, limiting clinical impact. This study examined ICU nurses' trust and acceptance of AI using an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology model. A multicentre cross-sectional study was conducted via an online survey. Structural equation modelling was performed using SPSS AMOS for data analysis. The study adhered to the STROBE checklist for observational research reporting. From June to July 2025, ICU nurses participated in this study. Intention to use AI was moderately high. The model was rigorously tested and validated with data, confirming credibility and reliability. Cognitive trust significantly increased intention, and affective trust did so significantly but more weakly. Performance expectancy had no significant direct effect on intention or trust. Effort expectancy did not directly affect intention, but indirectly promoted adoption by strengthening cognitive and affective trust. Social influence directly boosted intention and acted indirectly through trust. Perceived risk did not directly lower intention, but indirectly hindered adoption by reducing both types of trust. Understanding the mechanisms by which critical care nurses utilise artificial intelligence in the ICU can help promote the adoption of AI in intensive care units. This study clearly shows trust is the key determinant of whether ICU nurses use AI. Belief in AI performance increases intention only when nurses trust the system. Colleague and leader support is the strongest route to build trust, whereas perceived risk erodes trust and discourages use. These results shift attention from utility to trust. We recommend a trust-first strategy for critical care: before deployment, ensure reliability, communicate risks transparently and have trusted experts demonstrate value, enabling safe, effective nurse-AI collaboration. Authors adhered to the STROBE checklist for cross-sectional studies. This study did not include patient or public involvement in its design, conduct, or reporting.

articles.title: External evaluation of serum osmolality equations in critical care: transportability and formula-dependent classification in MIMIC-IV and eICU.
articles.journal: Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry
articles.abstract: Serum osmolality equations are used in acute care, but their individual errors and dependence on the provenance of the reference result can limit interpretation in critical illness. We tested whether the Calderón B equation improves serum osmolality estimation in critically ill adults and how formula choice affects concentration classification. We analysed adult MIMIC-IV and eICU hospitalizations with complete chemistry at the first osmolality record within seven ICU days. The simple, Khajuria-Krahn, and Calderón B equations were compared without refitting using error, calibration, and classification. A previously fixed screening rule (Khajuria-Krahn ≥295 mOsm/kg for reference >300 mOsm/kg) was assessed descriptively in overlapping records. Confidence intervals used patient clusters in MIMIC-IV and hospital clusters in eICU. The analysis included 3905 MIMIC-IV and 3286 eICU hospitalizations. MIMIC-IV MAEs were 7.00, 6.73, and 8.66 mOsm/kg for the simple, Khajuria-Krahn, and Calderón B equations; Calderón B exceeded Khajuria-Krahn by 1.92 mOsm/kg (95% CI 1.80-2.05). Corresponding eICU MAEs were 9.20, 8.92, and 10.35 mOsm/kg; the difference was 1.43 (0.75-2.07). Excluding seven hospitals with formula-like patterns reversed the eICU comparison with the simple equation but not with Khajuria-Krahn. In the formula-pattern-excluded eICU high-glucose subset, Calderón B reduced low-side classification at 320 mOsm/kg while increasing high-side classification. Fixed-rule sensitivity was 90.6% in MIMIC-IV and 89.3% in eICU; specificity was 73.8% and 72.4%. Calderón B showed no transportable MAE advantage over Khajuria-Krahn. In the formula-pattern-excluded eICU high-glucose subset, formula choice changed classification direction, and hospital-level formula-like patterns materially affected eICU comparisons.

articles.title: Heterogeneous patterns and predictors of advance care planning engagement among intensive care nurses: A multicentre latent profile analysis.
articles.abstract: To identify distinct profiles of advance care planning (ACP) engagement among intensive care unit (ICU) nurses and examine factors associated with profile membership. A multicentre cross-sectional survey was conducted among ICU nurses in tertiary hospitals in China. ACP-related knowledge, attitudes, and practices were assessed using the Chinese version of the Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices regarding Advance Care Planning scale. Latent profile analysis was used to identify distinct engagement profiles, followed by multinomial logistic regression to examine factors associated with profile membership. Among 955 ICU nurses, three ACP engagement profiles were identified: Low Engagement (65.9%), Knowledge Dominant but Practice-Inactive (10.7%), and Positive Attitude with Knowledge Deficit (23.5%). Compared with the Low Engagement Profile, nurses with an undergraduate education were more likely to belong to the Positive Attitude and Practice with Knowledge Deficit Profile (aOR = 1.626, 95% CI:1.008 to 2.622, P = 0.046). More frequent care of end-stage patients was associated with higher odds of membership in the Knowledge Dominant but Practice-Inactive profile (aOR = 1.831, 95% CI:1.543 to 2.172, P < 0.001), whereas general clinical experience showed no significant association with profile membership. ACP engagement among ICU nurses was heterogeneous, with most nurses showing low engagement. Addressing specific knowledge deficits regarding advance directives, POLST, and surrogate decision-makers is essential. The identified profiles suggest that ACP education may need to be differentiated according to nurses specific knowledge, attitudinal, and practice needs, and that supervised clinical practice may be a potential component of future interventions. These profiles may potentially inform how critical care educators tailor training to specific knowledge and practice gaps. Future longitudinal or interventional studies are needed to determine whether such tailored approaches could strengthen nurses' capacity to engage patients in ACP.

articles.title: Analysis of patient safety culture in an intensive care unit.
articles.abstract: Studying the characteristics and level of development of a healthcare organization's safety culture is a necessary management strategy and constitutes the starting point for understanding and subsequently transforming it. Our main objective was to evaluate the patient safety culture in the intensive care unit of our hospital and identify existing strengths and weaknesses in order to detect potential areas for improvement and implement the necessary strategies. Descriptive, cross-sectional observational study. Sociodemographic and occupational variables were collected along with the validated and Spanish-translated Hospital Patient Safety Survey. The survey consists of 12 dimensions, with 3 groups of questions, rated on a 5-point Likert scale. Responses were classified as positive, neutral, or negative. Student's t-test, chi-square test, and ANOVA were used for bivariate analysis, with P < .05. Sixty-five questionnaires were obtained (98.48% response rate). The mean score for the safety culture perceived by nursing professionals was 7.62 ± 1.44. Fourteen professionals (21.4%) reported an adverse event in the last year, and 46 (70.8%) had recently received patient safety training. The dimensions with the highest scores were "Organizational Learning/Continuous Improvement'' and ``Teamwork in the Unit/Service", with 67.2 and 71.9 points, respectively. Nursing professionals perceive a positive safety culture in the intensive care unit, with particular strength in the areas of organisational learning/continuous improvement and teamwork. Furthermore, a higher perception of patient safety and a higher rate of adverse event reporting than previously documented have been observed.

articles.title: Reproducibility and variability of visual capillary refill time assessment by intensive care physicians: comparison with near-infrared spectroscopy and automated video analysis in a cross-sectional observational study.
articles.abstract: Capillary refill time (CRT) is a widely used bedside marker of peripheral perfusion in intensive care, and its clinical relevance has grown after recent randomized trials incorporated it into hemodynamic resuscitation algorithms. Reproducibility under routine conditions remains poorly characterized, and objective tools to reduce observer-dependent variability are lacking. We developed a custom Python-based software for automated colorimetric CRT analysis and compared visual assessment with this tool and near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) in a controlled experimental model. Eight healthy adult volunteers underwent three conditions: baseline, venous congestion at 50% of diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and congestion at 75% DBP. Tissue oxygen saturation (StO₂) was recorded continuously by NIRS every 3 s. Fingertip-pulp compression videos were obtained at 20, 40, 60, 80, and 240 s. Sixteen ICU clinicians assessed 2401 coded videos in random order. The Python colorimetric tool was applied to valid recordings. Reproducibility was evaluated with variance-component models, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), coefficients of repeatability (CR), and linear mixed-effects models. Mean visual CRT was 1.77 ± 0.65 s. No significant effects of congestion condition (F = 1.45, p = 0.23) or time (F = 1.48, p = 0.230) were detected; marginal R² was 0.04 and conditional R² was 0.44. Interobserver ICC was 0.52 (95% bootstrap CI 0.42-0.61), with a CR of 1.20 s; mean intraobserver ICC was 0.69 (range 0.42-0.84). Simulations showed ICC rising to 0.76 with three observers, 0.84 with five, and 0.92 with ten. NIRS (904 observations) detected significant condition- and time-related changes (p < 0.001); late-phase StO₂ differed by 8.46% between congestion levels, and nadir StO₂ was lower under greater congestion (p = 0.0018). Automated analysis of 53 recordings yielded a mean CRT of 3.89 ± 1.26 s, a significant congestion effect (F = 6.32, p = 0.016; marginal R² 0.12, conditional R² 0.48), and a mean between-condition difference of 0.68 s (p = 0.017). Visual CRT showed moderate reproducibility and did not detect graded perfusion changes. Both NIRS and the Python-based automated software identified condition-related differences that visual assessment missed. These results call for cautious interpretation of isolated CRT when small serial changes inform clinical decisions, and support further evaluation of automated approaches in critically ill patients.

articles.title: Clinical Features and Outcomes of Adenovirus Infections in Critically Ill Patients: A Retrospective Multicenter Case-Matched Analysis.
articles.abstract: Human adenovirus (HAdV) infection can lead to severe organ involvement in the ICU, particularly among immunocompromised patients. In this study of ICU patients with HAdV infection, we aimed to 1) determine the prevalence of HAdV disease, 2) identify risk factors for HAdV disease, and 3) evaluate its association with ICU mortality. Retrospective, multicenter, and propensity score case-matched study. Eight ICUs in France. Adult ICU patients admitted between January 2011 and January 2024 with at least one positive HAdV polymerase chain reaction result from any biological sample were included. HAdV infections were classified as either localized infections or systemic HAdV disease. None. A total of 169 patients were analyzed, including 115 patients (68%) classified as localized HAdV infection and 54 patients (32%) as HAdV disease. Hematologic malignancies were significantly more frequent in patients with HAdV disease (74% vs. 37%; p < 0.001). Twenty-three patients (43%) with HAdV disease received allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Pneumonia was the main end-organ manifestation (n = 36/54; 67%). By multivariate analysis, allogeneic HSCT (odds ratio [OR], 3.04) and corticosteroid therapy (OR, 2.89) were independently associated with HAdV disease. ICU mortality was 45% (n = 76). By multivariate analysis, HAdV disease (OR, 3.15), performance status greater than or equal to 2 (OR, 3.35), and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment scores at admission (OR, 1.17 per point) were independently associated with ICU mortality. Mortality remained significantly higher in the HAdV disease group (OR, 10.50) compared with matched ICU patients without HAdV infection. HAdV disease occurred in approximately one-third of ICU patients with HAdV infection, predominantly among those with hematologic malignancies or corticosteroid therapy, and was independently associated with mortality.

articles.title: Hyperoxaemia and outcomes following extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation in adult patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Patients are commonly exposed to hyperoxaemia during post-resuscitation care following extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR), yet its association with mortality and neurological outcomes remains uncertain. In this systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO registration: CRD42024586748), we searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Library from inception to 15 January 2026 for randomised trials and observational studies investigating the association between partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO2) levels and mortality at the longest available follow-up or neurological outcomes in patients receiving ECPR. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed, and results were reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). Subgroup analyses included predefined hyperoxaemia thresholds (>200 mmHg and > 300 mmHg). Risk of bias was assessed, and the certainty of the pooled estimates was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Ten studies comprising 5417 patients were included. Eight studies reported on mortality, and four reported neurological outcomes. Definitions of hyperoxaemia varied across the included studies, with the most common threshold being PaO2 > 300 mmHg. Hyperoxaemia was associated with higher mortality (OR = 1.83; 95% CI: 1.62-2.07; low certainty). This association persisted across subgroups with PaO2 > 300 mmHg (OR = 2.67; 95% CI: 1.07-6.64; low certainty) and PaO2 > 200 mmHg (OR = 2.36; 95% CI: 1.21-4.60; moderate certainty). Hyperoxaemia was also associated with lower odds of good neurological outcomes (OR = 0.68; 95% CI: 0.49-0.95; very low certainty). Hyperoxaemia after ECPR was associated with higher mortality and poor neurological outcomes. Appropriately designed RCTs are needed to confirm these associations and guide optimal oxygenation targets.

articles.title: Medical Students Want More Exposure to Biomedical Innovation.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Biomedical innovation is a core concept not traditionally included in medical school curricula, and exposure to and hands-on use of diagnostic and therapeutic technologies typically occur only during clinical rotations. By potentially delaying their exposure to innovation, entrepreneurship, and technology development, we may be missing an opportunity for early engagement. We surveyed medical students at a single US institution for an exploratory needs assessment to characterize their experiences and identify unmet educational opportunities in biomedical innovation, which we then used to guide our development of an interdisciplinary extracurricular program. Sixty-nine percent of medical students reported they had no exposure to biomedical innovation, yet 90% wanted to get involved, citing limited knowledge and resources as barriers. We developed an interdisciplinary extracurricular program to address this need, which emphasizes early exposure to technology development, experiential learning, multidisciplinary collaboration, and mentorship. Participants' evaluation forms (n = 229) indicated that each event (n = 38) was a worthwhile educational experience (98%). Despite having little exposure, medical students want to participate in biomedical innovation and valued our interdisciplinary educational program, which aligns well with ASAIO's mission of inspiring the next generation of early-stage biomedical innovators.

articles.title: Fecal microbiota transplantation modulates immunosuppressive cells and IgA secretion in a gut microbiota depletion model.
articles.abstract: The relationship between gut dysbiosis and host immune dynamics remains poorly understood. We used an antibiotic-induced gut microbiota depletion model following fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) via co-housing. Mice received an antibiotic cocktail for 4 weeks (Abx group), or for 2 weeks, followed by co-housing with healthy control mice for 2 weeks (CoA group), or kept under conventional housing for 2 weeks (Abx-CH group). The gut microbiota was assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing and Gram staining. Immune cell populations were analyzed via flow cytometry using antibodies for T cells, regulatory T cells (Tregs), IgA-secreting cells, PD-1+ cells, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) in the colon and blood. As a result, α- and β-diversity differed from Control in the Abx and Abx-CH groups, whereas the CoA group resembled Control. Three distinct enterotypes were identified with a recovery pattern (Lactobacillus), a pathobiome pattern (Klebsiella, Escherichia, Proteus), and an expanded pattern (Ruminococcus and Prevotella) through FMT. In the colon, the proportions of Tregs were significantly higher in Abx and CoA groups. IL-10⁺ Tregs tended to increase in the Abx and were significantly lower in the CoA group. IgA-secreting cells and fecal IgA levels in the CoA group were significantly higher than in the Abx group, respectively (6.1% vs. 0.5%, 427.0 vs. 83.7 μg/mL, CoA vs. Abx; p<0.05). In conclusion, FMT could influence the proportion of immune cells in response to gut microbiota modulation. IgA secretion could be upregulated by gut microbiota after FMT.

articles.title: Resting-State Functional MRI and Clinical Outcomes After Acute Disorders of Consciousness: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Accurate assessment and prognostication of patients with acute disorders of consciousness (DoC) after severe brain injury remain a substantial clinical challenge. Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) measures spontaneous, temporally correlated brain activity in the absence of external stimulation and provides objective insight into the integrity of large-scale neural networks that support brain function. Emerging evidence suggests that assessing neural integrity using rs-fMRI may improve outcome prediction in patients with acute DoC. This review summarizes the current evidence of rs-fMRI as an assessment tool during the acute phase of severe brain injury. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, we conducted a systematic literature search using MEDLINE and Embase databases from January 2006 to March 2026. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed empirical investigations of adult patients with acute DoC (<28 days postinjury) that examined associations between rs-fMRI measures and clinical outcomes. The systematic review protocol was registered in the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420251085923). Of 396 studies screened, 30 met eligibility criteria. Across these studies, a total of 800 patients (mean age = 48, 69% male) were scanned at a weighted average of 9.31 days after intensive care unit admission. Ten studies included patients exclusively with traumatic brain injury, 8 with cardiac arrest, 2 with encephalopathy, and 10 included mixed etiologies. The most frequently assessed resting-state networks were the default mode (n = 20) and executive control networks (n = 11), followed by visual (n = 6), salience (n = 6), sensorimotor (n = 6), and auditory (n = 5) networks. Across studies, significant associations between rs-fMRI measures and outcome were consistently reported, despite heterogeneity in methodology. The most commonly reported patient outcomes were functional or neurologic status, assessed at hospital discharge or between 3 and 12 months postinjury. Current evidence consistently demonstrates that rs-fMRI acquired during the acute phase of brain injury is associated with neurologic and functional outcomes in patients with DoC. In addition, rs-fMRI may help identify patients more likely to recover consciousness and achieve favorable functional outcomes by characterizing the integrity of large-scale brain networks. However, substantial heterogeneity and small sample sizes limit comparability across studies. Standardized acquisition and analysis frameworks, along with larger prospective studies, are needed to validate the clinical utility of rs-fMRI and support translation into an assessment tool after brain injury.

articles.title: Prehospital Fluid Resuscitation for Patients With Suspected Sepsis: The PITSTOP-Fluids Factorial Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: Early resuscitation with intravenous fluids is recommended for patients with sepsis. To determine the effect of liberal vs more conservative fluid resuscitation strategies in the ambulance on mortality among patients with suspected sepsis. Multicenter, 2 × 2 factorial randomized clinical trial conducted by 4 paramedic services and their destination hospitals in Ontario, Canada. Participants were adults with suspected sepsis, defined as suspected infection, fever (≥38.0 °C), and hypotension (systolic blood pressure [SBP] <100 mm Hg), and obtainable intravenous access. Patients were enrolled between March 23, 2020, and August 20, 2025, with last follow-up in December 2025. Patients were randomized to receive liberal fluids (up to 2 L of normal saline regardless of subsequent SBP) or usual care (fluids only when SBP <90 mm Hg and stopped when SBP ≥100 mm Hg) during prehospital care and until transfer of care in the emergency department. (Patients were additionally randomized to receive ceftriaxone vs placebo; analysis of which is reported separately.). The primary outcome was hospital mortality, defined as death prior to hospital discharge up to day 90. There were 17 secondary outcomes, including all-cause mortality at 90 days, hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor therapy, dialysis, and total fluids infused within 24 hours of hospital arrival. Among 1686 randomized patients, 1669 were eligible and 1646 were included in the primary outcome analysis (830 in the liberal fluids group and 816 in the usual fluids group). The median age of patients was 76 (IQR, 63-85) years and 938 (57.0%) were male. Most patients in both groups received a fluid bolus (826/848 [97.4%] in the liberal fluids group; 700/821 [85.3%] in the usual fluids group) during transport, but patients in the liberal fluids group received a larger volume (median, 1500 mL [IQR, 1000-2000 mL]) vs 500 mL [IQR, 175-800 mL] in the usual fluids group; difference, 910.1 mL [95% CI, 857.3-962.9 mL]). Hospital mortality was 149/830 (18.0%) in the liberal fluids group and 149/816 (18.3%) in the usual fluids group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.80-1.20]; unadjusted risk difference, -0.3 [95% CI, -4.0 to 3.4]; P = .82). Among the 17 secondary outcomes, all were similar between groups. Adverse events, including pulmonary edema during transport, were infrequent in both groups. A more liberal fluid resuscitation strategy for the prehospital management of patients with suspected sepsis did not reduce mortality compared with more restrictive usual care. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03068741.

articles.title: Vasopressin Versus Norepinephrine in Septic Shock: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials Focusing on Vasopressor Timing.
articles.abstract: Background and aimsThe optimal choice and timing of vasopressor therapy in septic shock remain uncertain. While norepinephrine is recommended as first-line treatment, vasopressin may offer potential benefits, particularly regarding renal outcomes. We aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of vasopressin versus norepinephrine, with a focus on timing of initiation.MethodsWe conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing vasopressin and norepinephrine in adult patients with septic shock. The primary outcome was short-term mortality. Secondary outcomes included renal replacement therapy (RRT), ICU length of stay, and serious adverse events. Random-effects models were used for the primary analyses, except for RRT, for which a fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel model was used because of concerns regarding small-study effects. Prespecified subgroup analyses evaluated initial randomized vasopressin strategy versus second-line vasopressin.ResultsSix randomized controlled trials including 1580 patients were analyzed. There was no significant difference in short-term mortality between vasopressin and norepinephrine (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.86-1.11; I2=0%). Vasopressin was associated with a significantly lower requirement for RRT (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.72-0.97; p = 0.016). No significant differences were observed in ICU length of stay (MD -0.18 days, 95% CI -2.30 to 1.94; I2=85.9%) or serious adverse events (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.76-1.50; I2=0%). Subgroup analysis showed a greater reduction in RRT with an initial randomized vasopressin strategy (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.50-0.84) than with second-line vasopressin (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.81-1.15), with a significant subgroup interaction (p = 0.014).ConclusionsVasopressin was associated with a reduced requirement for renal replacement therapy in patients with septic shock. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested a greater benefit with an initial vasopressin strategy compared with second-line vasopressin. No significant differences were observed in mortality, ICU length of stay, or serious adverse events.

articles.title: Real-Time Cumulative Fluid Balance Surveillance and Stewardship in Critical Care: From Prediction to Prevention of Fluid Overload.
articles.abstract: Fluid therapy is a crucial intervention in critical care, but the same treatment that restores perfusion during shock may become harmful when positive fluid balance persists after stabilization and contributes to organ dysfunction. A key conceptual distinction is that daily fluid balance (FB), cumulative fluid balance (CFB), and percent cumulative fluid balance (%CFB) are quantitative measurements, whereas fluid overload (FO) is a clinical state in which positive fluid balance is associated with or contributes to clinically meaningful organ dysfunction or morbidity. Building on the ADQI framework, an important bedside challenge is how to monitor the evolving CFB trajectory, identify the fluid sources driving accumulation, and recognize when a measurable positive balance has become clinically harmful FO. This review builds on the existing outcome-focused literature and offers a complementary implementation-oriented framework. We summarize the physiology of fluid equilibrium, contemporary terminology for FB, CFB, %CFB, and FO, and the bidirectional relationship between positive fluid balance, FO, and acute kidney injury (AKI). We then emphasize fluid profiling as a method to distinguish necessary resuscitation from potentially modifiable sources of fluid exposure, including maintenance fluids, medication carriers, flushes, diluents, and parenteral nutrition. Consistent with the ADQI emphasis on dynamic assessment across phases of fluid therapy, we suggest CFB monitoring as an evolving bedside signal by integrating %CFB, CFB trajectory and rate of change, daily weight, urine output, AKI stage, creatinine corrected for fluid balance, hemodynamics, respiratory status, and organ-specific tolerance. Finally, we outline a future research agenda centered on real-time electronic dashboards, prescribed CFB targets, predictive trajectory monitoring, renal angina-based risk stratification, urinary biomarkers, furosemide stress testing, pharmacy-nursing stewardship bundles, and pragmatic trials of structured de-resuscitation. The goal is to move beyond static numeric thresholds toward earlier recognition of adverse CFB trajectories and prevention of clinically harmful FO.

articles.title: Intracranial Pressure Waveform Response to Hypertonic Saline Bolus in Patients with Traumatic Brain Injury.
articles.abstract: We aimed to identify features of intracranial compliance (ICC) reflected in intracranial pressure (ICP) waveform morphology following bolus of 20% hypertonic saline (HTS) to manage intracranial hypertension. ICP was monitored during 89 HTS injections in ten patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and high intracranial hypertension. Pulse amplitude (AMP), P2/P1 ratio, pulse shape index (PSI), and normalized time to peak (TTP) were retrospectively analyzed over 3h including pre-, during, and postinjection interval. Trajectories of mean ICP and ICC surrogates were characterized using linear mixed models to assess individual contributions to the response following HTS injection. HTS injections induced transient decreases in all variables as follows: ICP [15.6 mmHg, 95% confidence interval (CI; 10.8, 20.3mmHg)], AMP [5.6 (3.5, 7.6mmHg)], P2/P1 [0.49 (0.32, 0.66)], PSI [0.65 (0.43, 0.87)], and TTP [0.054 (0.03, 0.07)]. Baseline P2/P1, TTP, and PSI showed predominantly between-patient variability [variance partition coefficient (VPC) = 0.56, 0.67, and 0.67, respectively], whereas baseline ICP and AMP showed greater within-patient variability (VPC = 0.18 and 0.24). Response-related features were also predominantly characterized by within-patient variability, with VPCs ranging from 0.20 to 0.27 for maximum decrease and from 0.13 to 0.23 for AAC. In random-intercept models, higher baseline ICP was associated with larger reductions in AMP (β = 0.13, p < 10-4), PSI (β = 0.02, p = 10-4), and TTP (β = 0.001, p = 0.034) following HTS administration, whereas baseline morphology metrics did not significantly improve the prediction of ICP reduction after adjustment for baseline ICP. When ICP nadir was modeled directly instead of the baseline-dependent change score, neither baseline ICP nor baseline morphology was significantly associated with ICP nadir. Adjustment for end-tidal CO2 (EtCO2) and prior osmotherapy did not materially alter these association patterns. ICP waveform morphology, as assessed by P2/P1, PSI, and TTP, is influenced by changes in intracranial pressure but also retains substantial patient-specific variability. In contrast, AMP is primarily driven by changes in intracranial pressure.

articles.title: Perioperative noise isolation for postoperative delirium in older adults undergoing hip surgery: a randomized clinical trial.
articles.abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is common in older adults undergoing hip surgery. Noise exposure is associated with increased delirium risk. We hypothesized that perioperative noise isolation would reduce POD in these patients. In this single-center, randomized, patient- and assessor-blind trial, 320 patients (aged ≥65 y) undergoing hip surgery under sevoflurane anesthesia were randomly assigned 1:1 using block randomization stratified by age, surgery type, and planned surgical ICU admission to noise isolation (earmuffs from anesthesia induction to tracheal extubation before awakening) or control (routine care). The primary outcome was the incidence of POD during the first 7 postoperative days or until hospital discharge. Among 316 patients (mean age 78 y; 71.8% female) who completed the study (158 per group), POD occurred in 19 (12.0%) patients in the noise isolation group vs. 36 (22.8%) in the control group (relative risk 0.53; 95% CI 0.32-0.88; P = 0.012). The absolute risk reduction was 10.8% (number needed to treat 9). The interventional effect remained significant after multivariable adjustment for stratification factors (adjusted odds ratio 0.42; 95% CI 0.23-0.80; P = 0.009) and after additional adjustment for Charlson Comorbidity Index (adjusted odds ratio 0.43; 95% CI 0.23-0.82; P = 0.010). Patients receiving noise isolation were less likely to experience moderate-to-severe pain and required less rescue analgesia. Perioperative noise isolation reduced the incidence of POD in older adults undergoing hip surgery. This simple, nonpharmacological intervention represents an immediately implementable strategy to enhance perioperative care. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2400082211).

articles.title: Predicting Energy Expenditure and Metabolic Tolerance for Medical Nutrition Therapy in Neurocritical Care: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Medical nutrition therapy (MNT) is a key determinant of outcome in critically ill patients, as both underfeeding and overfeeding are associated with unfavorable outcome. Optimal energy provision should consider both resting energy expenditure (REE) and the extent of catabolism to match the exogenous energy delivery to the patient's net demand and thereby maintain metabolic tolerance. Hence, we aimed to evaluate (1) the accuracy of predictive equations (PEs), (2) metabolic tolerance, and (3) REE in patients with acute brain injury. We conducted a prospective, single-center observational cohort study including mechanically ventilated neurocritical care patients with an expected intensive care unit stay of ≥ 10 days. REE was measured repeatedly using indirect calorimetry (IC) at predefined time points (days 0-10) and compared with commonly used PEs. Metabolic intolerance was defined as hypophosphatemia (< 0.65 mmol/L) and/or insulin requirement > 1 U/h. Multivariable mixed-effects models were used to identify predictors of metabolic intolerance and intraindividual REE variability. A total of 52 patients with 317 IC measurements were included. The Harris-Benedict formula showed the highest agreement among all tested equations, yet only 59% of estimates fell within 85-115% of measured REE. In patients with obesity (body mass index > 30 kg/m2), PEs showed clinically relevant bias (> 200 kcal). Metabolic intolerance occurred in 32% of observations and was independently associated with higher body temperature and higher proportions of administered relative to prescribed calories, while female sex was associated with lower risk. In mixed-effects models, resolving organ dysfunction disease severity was associated with greater REE variability (β = -44.1; 95% confidence interval, - 75.7 to - 12.6; p < 0.01). In neurocritical care patients, REE is highly dynamic and cannot be reliably estimated using PE, supporting the use of IC for energy assessment. Changes in disease severity may serve as a pragmatic trigger for reassessment. Overfeeding, male sex, and higher body temperature were associated with metabolic intolerance, underscoring the importance of precise energy assessment. Future studies should evaluate IC-guided, metabolic-tolerance-directed nutritional strategies to improve clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Graves' disease with thyroid storm: a truly grave disease.
articles.abstract: Graves' disease can be exacerbated by thyroid storm. This endocrine emergency is a very rare condition in children and adolescents, with a mortality rate of approximately 10%-30%. Here, we report on a 12-year-old girl with known Graves' disease who presented with pneumonia and thyroid storm (tachycardia, hyperpyrexia, hepatic failure, gastrointestinal manifestations [vomiting, diarrhea], and encephalopathy). She required immediate intensive care treatment including anti-thyroid medication, β‑blocker, and steroids as well as cooling and sedation. Twelve hours after admission, the patient developed cardiovascular collapse with asystole requiring immediate resuscitation. After intensive care treatment, the patient made a full neurological recovery within 1 week without any sequelae. Considering its substantial mortality rate, it is essential to include thyroid storm within the differential diagnosis in critically ill children and adolescents with Graves' disease.

articles.title: An Interpretable Machine Learning Model for Early Prediction of Septic Shock in Intensive Care Unit Patients: The Incremental Value of Cardiac Output.
articles.abstract: BackgroundEarly identification of septic shock is critical for timely resuscitation, yet conventional vital signs such as blood pressure exhibit physiological lag during the compensatory phase. Whether advanced hemodynamic parameters confer incremental predictive value within machine learning (ML) early warning frameworks remains unquantified.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study used the MIMIC-IV v3.0 database. From 7384 patients with hemodynamic monitoring records, 1716 adult ICU patients contributing 16,140 hourly prediction windows were analyzed. Patients were partitioned into a development set (n = 1372) and a held-out test set (n = 344). Two nested models predicted septic shock within 6 h: a baseline model using routine variables and an enhanced model adding cardiac output (CO), cardiac index (CI), stroke volume index (SVI), and systemic vascular resistance index (SVRI). XGBoost was the primary classifier. Patient-level cross-validation and clustered bootstrap evaluated discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility, while SHAP and ablation assessed feature contributions.ResultsThe enhanced model consistently outperformed the baseline across four algorithms. With XGBoost, cross-validated AUROC improved from 0.862 (95% CI 0.847-0.877) to 0.881 (0.867-0.894), a gain of 0.018 (0.010-0.027; DeLong p = 3.22 × 10-11). Sensitivity increased from 0.249 to 0.316 and F1 from 0.335 to 0.388. Held-out AUROC was 0.819 versus 0.844 (p = 2.06 × 10-6). Calibration was comparable, and the enhanced model provided greater net benefit at threshold probabilities of 0.01-0.49. SHAP ranked CO second only to lactate; removing CO reduced AUROC by 0.017 (0.008-0.024), whereas removing the derived indices had negligible effects.ConclusionsIncorporating cardiac output into routine monitoring models provides robust incremental value for early septic shock prediction. CO captures circulatory compromise masked by compensatory normotension and may support risk-stratified ICU surveillance.

articles.title: Ringer's lactate versus saline in the fluids in septic shock (FISSH) trial: a multicentre, blinded, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial.
articles.abstract: Despite fluid therapy being a hallmark of treatment for patients with septic shock, the optimal crystalloid to use in this setting remains unclear. We aimed to compare the effect of two different, commonly used crystalloids in patients with septic shock. In this multicentre, blinded, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial, adults (aged ≥16 years) at 30 academic and community hospitals across Canada and Saudi Arabia who were critically ill with septic shock were randomly assigned (1:1) via a web-based randomisation system to receive Ringer's lactate or 0·9% saline for all bolus and maintenance fluid throughout their intensive care unit (ICU) stay up to day 30, stratified by hospital. Randomisation used permuted blocks of undisclosed variable sizes. We included patients who had a systolic blood pressure lower than 90 mm Hg or a mean arterial pressure of less than 65 mm Hg after 1 L bolus or a serum lactate greater than 4 mmol/L, had a clinically suspected infection, and were within 6 h of emergency department presentation or ICU consultation. We excluded patients who had new raised intracranial pressure, had acute burn injury on more than 10% of the body surface area, were already receiving chronic or acute dialysis at the time of screening, or were admitted to ICU directly from the operating room, post-anaesthetic care unit, or another hospital or health-care facility. All bedside clinicians, patients, caregivers, research staff, and biostatisticians were masked to allocation. The primary endpoint was 30-day in-hospital mortality analysed on an intention-to-treat basis. The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03677102). Between Oct 6, 2018, and Feb 1, 2026, we screened 2457 patients and randomly assigned 1113, with a further ten excluded after randomisation (557 patients in the Ringer's lactate group and 546 in the saline group). 491 (44·5%) were female and 612 (55·5%) were male, the mean baseline APACHE II score was 24·7 (SD 8·8), and patients received a mean of 5844 mL (SD 4761) of study fluid. The mean baseline serum lactate was 4·8 mmol/L (SD 3·5) and the mean serum creatinine was 176·5 μmol/L (SD 126·4). 187 (33·6%) patients died in the Ringer's lactate group 180 (33·0%) died in the saline group (relative risk 1·02 [95% CI 0·86-1·21]; p=0·80). There were no serious adverse events. In this trial of patients who were critically ill with septic shock, Ringer's lactate compared with saline had no effect on 30-day in-hospital mortality. The Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Physician Services Incorporated Foundation.

articles.title: Exploring the Requirements of Clinicians for Transparent and Trustworthy Decision Support Systems in Intensive Care: Focus Group Study.
articles.abstract: Understanding how digital systems can support clinical decision-making is crucial, especially with the growing deployment of increasingly complex AI models. This complexity raises concerns about trustworthiness, affecting the safe and effective adoption of such technologies. In intensive care units (ICUs), where clinicians make high-stakes, time-sensitive decisions, decision support tools must be designed to align with clinical needs and cognitive workflows. A better understanding of decision-making processes and requirements for decision support tools is vital for providing effective solutions. This study investigates ICU clinicians' decision-making processes, their use of decision support systems (DSSs), and the design requirements for DSSs to ensure transparent and trustworthy recommendations. We conducted 2 virtual focus groups with 7 ICU clinicians from 1 hospital in September 2024. Participants included nurses, charge nurses, and medical doctors, each with at least three years of professional experience. The focus groups explored participants' perspectives on DSSs in relation to our study objectives. Reflexive thematic analysis was applied to the focus group transcripts, and analytic decisions were made inductively using open coding. Both semantic and latent coding were used. Following independent coding, a combined codebook was developed collaboratively, from which key themes and subsequent design recommendations were identified. Three core themes emerged from the analysis: ICU Decision-Making Relies on a Wide Range of Factors (theme 1); Complexity of Patient State Is Challenging for Shared Decision-Making (theme 2); and Acceptability and Usability of DSSs (theme 3). Five design recommendations derived from clinical input provide insights to inform future DSSs for intensive care: provide variable levels of detail (recommendation 1); support integration into existing clinical systems (recommendation 2); present explanations with additional contextual information (recommendation 3); prompt independent thought (recommendation 4); and facilitate communication of patient state (recommendation 5). DSSs have the potential to enhance ICU decision-making, but their adoption depends on alignment with clinicians' needs and workflows. To improve trust and usability, future systems must provide transparent recommendations, adapt to varying levels of patient complexity, and facilitate rather than replace human expertise. Our findings inform the development of transparent and trustworthy DSSs, which may improve their acceptance in ICU settings.

articles.title: Vector Flow Mapping Energy Loss and Pump Flow in Left Ventricular Assist Device Patients: A Transesophageal Echocardiography Pilot Study.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Left ventricular assist device (LVAD) support redirects intraventricular flow toward the inflow cannula. We examined whether vector flow mapping-derived energy loss (EL), a measure of viscous dissipation related to spatial velocity gradients, was associated with controller-displayed pump flow. This prospective single-center pilot enrolled 33 patients undergoing LVAD-related surgery with intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography; 31 HeartMate 3 recipients were analyzable. The maximum available peak EL across three views was the primary measure. Log-transformed maximum peak EL was associated with displayed flow after adjustment for pump speed and left ventricular end-diastolic diameter (B = 0.181, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.033-0.330), cannula angle (B = 0.204, 95% CI: 0.052-0.356), or aortic regurgitation grade (B = 0.204, 95% CI: 0.050-0.358). Among 28 complete cases, associations persisted using the mean of three view-specific peaks (B = 0.213-0.245; p = 0.007-0.019). In a 10-case interobserver reanalysis, maximum peak EL had an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.759 (95% CI: 0.294-0.934), with ratio limits of agreement of 0.56-2.41. Cannula angle and aortic regurgitation grade were not associated with EL. These preliminary findings support larger prospective studies but do not establish mechanism, measurement interchangeability, or clinical utility.

articles.title: Multidimensional Predictors of Post-Traumatic Stress in Relatives of Critically Ill Patients.
articles.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
articles.abstract: Relatives of critically ill patients frequently develop post-traumatic stress symptoms. Few studies have evaluated both psychological and ICU-related risk factors. We aimed to identify factors associated with post-traumatic stress symptom severity and probable post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in ICU relatives. In this prospective multicentre cohort study (FAME), we enrolled consecutive adults on mechanical ventilation for ≥48 h in 60 ICUs in France (15 December 2022-30 January 2024); for each patient, we enrolled one relative. The relatives completed validated instruments during the ICU stay and follow-up interviews at three and six months. The primary outcome was higher PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 [PCL-5] at 3 months. Associations were sought using multivariable logistic regression for PCL-5 scores ≥31 and multivariable linear regression for three-month PCL-5 scores. Of 1346 relatives, 936 (69·5%) completed PCL-5 at 3-month: 106 (11·3%) had probable PTSD and 358 (38·2%) clinically relevant post-traumatic stress symptoms. Factors associated with higher PCL-5 scores included pre-existing characteristics (social exclusion, living alone, perceived disability, and history of psychological trauma), early symptoms (anxiety, peritraumatic dissociation, and insomnia), and greater severity in the patients (vasopressor use and end-of-life decisions). Lower PCL-5 scores were associated with male sex and specific physician communication behaviours. Post-traumatic stress symptoms were common, and approximately one in nine relatives had probable PTSD at three months. Knowledge of early psychological markers may help identify relatives at risk, while improved communication practices may decrease the risk.

articles.title: Implementation of nurse-led frontal electroencephalography for early neurological assessment in patients after cardiac arrest: the FRONT study.
articles.abstract: Continuous electroencephalography (cEEG) is a valuable tool for neurological prognostication after cardiac arrest. However, registration is often delayed by time-consuming electrode placement and limited availability of EEG technicians. This study investigated the implementation of a frontal EEG (fEEG) configuration using 6 self-adhesive electrodes by nurses within 3 h of Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission in patients after cardiac arrest. The FRONT study followed a type 3 hybrid design. Nurses were trained to start an fEEG through a theoretical and practical session and were supported by a Step-by-Step interactive guide. Knowledge, attitude, and practice surveys were completed by nurses at baseline and after each fEEG application. Correct and timely application was measured prospectively in 60 patients. At baseline, the survey response rate was 46% (49/107); after application, it was 68% (41/60). Most nurses (84%) reported having sufficient knowledge of fEEG electrode placement and monitoring. The interactive guide was frequently used (98%) during fEEG initiation; the median application time was 20 min [IQR: 15-25]. All nurses found early fEEG monitoring meaningful; perception improved since implementation (3.98 ± 0.78 vs 4.54 ± 0.51, p < 0.001). During the implementation, an fEEG was applied in 88% of patients (53/60), including 73% (44/60) within 3 h. Electrode placement was confirmed as correct by EEG technicians in all evaluated patients. ICU nurses were able to apply fEEG monitoring with high levels of adoption, acceptability and fidelity following a short, multifaceted training program combined with an interactive guide. Further research is needed to clarify the interpretability, diagnostic performance, prognostic value, and clinical utility of nurse-led fEEG monitoring in post-resuscitation care. Early bedside EEG assessment by trained ICU nurses may facilitate timely neurological evaluation in routine clinical practice.

articles.title: Higher Quality Temperature Control Is Associated With Improved Outcomes Following Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Multicenter Validation Study.
articles.abstract: Hypothermic temperature control has not consistently demonstrated a neuroprotective effect, resulting in heterogeneity of use in clinical practice. We evaluated temperature control quality across 4 institutions and its association with clinical outcomes. Retrospective analysis of institutional registry data collected between 2021 and 2024 in survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with Glasgow Coma Scale Motor score less than 6 from 4 academic centers with established cardiac arrest programs. Eligible patients included those 18 years of age or older, treated with hypothermic temperature control (33-36°C) using a feedback-controlled device, and admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU). A temperature control quality score (0-6) was assigned for each patient. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. The secondary outcome was good neurologic outcome at hospital discharge, defined as a Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) score of 1-2. Univariable and multivariable logistic regressions quantified the relationship between quality of temperature control, as an ordinal variable, and outcomes. Among 356 included patients, most were male (N=224, 62.9%) with mean (standard deviation [SD]) age 58.1 (15.2) years. Most suffered a nonshockable arrest (N=262, 73.6%) and did not receive layperson CPR (N=225, 63.2%). Median [IQR] Pittsburgh Cardiac Arrest Category score was 4 [3,4], mean (SD) lactate 9.1 (4.1) mmol/L, and pH 7.09 (0.17). Median [IQR] preinduction time was 2.3 [1.5 to 3.5] hours and 150 (42.1%) were treated with early neuromuscular blockade. Adjusting for confounders in the multivariable model, an increase of one-point in the temperature control quality score was associated with improved survival at hospital discharge (odds ratio [OR] 1.32; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.07 to 1.64). A one-point increase in the quality score also resulted in a shift towards lower (improved) CPC score (OR 1.28; 95% CI, 0.05 to 1.55). The direction of effect was consistent across all centers. In unresponsive survivors of OHCA, an increase in temperature control quality was associated with improved survival and better neurologic outcome; however, confounding by site, injury severity, or perceived prognosis is possible. Lack of temperature control parameter standardization may influence efficacy and practice variability within pragmatic-design clinical trials possibly contributed to neutral trial results. Prospective trials evaluating the importance of temperature control quality and the population most likely to benefit from hypothermic temperature control are essential.

articles.title: Subphenotyping and precision medicine approaches to ARDS.
articles.abstract: Sixty years after its initial description, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remains defined by bilateral radiographic opacities and impaired oxygenation rather than by its underlying biology. This syndromic definition encompasses considerable clinical and biological heterogeneity, which may contribute to the ineffectiveness of pharmacotherapy trials to date. Subphenotyping aims to address this heterogeneity by identifying more homogeneous patient groups that differ in prognosis and/or treatment response. In this narrative review, framed by the research questions outlined in the 2023 European Society of Intensive Care Medicine guidelines, we synthesize current approaches to ARDS subphenotyping across complementary domains: clinical (etiology, rapidly improving ARDS), physiological (gas exchange, recruitability, elastance, and ventilatory ratio), morphological (focal versus non-focal radiological patterns), and biological (individual injury biomarkers and the hyperinflammatory and hypoinflammatory subphenotypes). We examine their pathobiological basis, temporal dynamics, and retrospective evidence for heterogeneity of treatment effect, and consider how parsimonious biomarker panels, machine-learning classifiers, and adaptive basket trial designs may support clinical implementation. Prospective validation across diverse populations, including resource-limited settings, remains a key priority.

articles.title: Discordance Between Guidelines and Practice in ICP Monitoring in Traumatic Brain Injury: Insights from the CENTER-TBI Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring is important in selected patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI). This study aims to quantify variability in ICP monitoring practices across European trauma centres, to analyse associations with patient and imaging characteristics and to explore concordance between the practice of ICP monitoring and guideline recommendations. In the Collaborative European Neurotrauma Effectiveness Research in Traumatic Brain Injury (CENTER-TBI) database, we assessed concordance between ICP monitoring and guideline recommendations, defined by a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score ≤ 8 and a positive computed tomography (CT) scan (Marshall score > 1) on presentation. To determine between-centre differences, the case-mix-adjusted percentage of ICP placements and duration of monitoring per centre were determined in the mixed-effects logistic regression model. To determine patient and imaging characteristics associated with the insertion of an ICP monitor, a mixed-effects logistic regression model was performed. Among 2138 patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), 921 patients (43%) received an ICP device. Among 900 patients meeting guideline recommendations for ICP monitoring, 571 (64%) received an ICP monitor. There were large between-centre variations in ICP-monitor placements and the duration of ICP monitoring [median odds ratio (MOR) 2.5, 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.1-2.8 and MOR 3.2, 95% CI 2.4-3.8, respectively]. Factors associated with ICP monitoring were a lower GCS score on admission [odds ratio (OR) 0.9, 95% CI 0.8-0.9], at least one pupil that was unreactive to light (OR 1.6, 95% CI 1.1-2.5) and the presence of CT abnormalities (i.e. contusion: OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.9-3.2). This study provides a detailed patient-level description of ICP monitoring decision-making. ICP monitoring decisions frequently extended beyond guideline criteria and were influenced by neurological, radiological and treatment-related considerations. The observed variation may reflect both differences in practice and limitations of existing guideline frameworks. These findings provide a foundation for future efforts aimed at developing ICP monitoring recommendations that are more closely aligned with real-world expert decision-making.

articles.title: Coma Epidemiology, Evaluation, and Therapy in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: Revisiting the Curing Coma(®) Campaign COME TOGETHER Survey.
articles.abstract: The Curing Coma Campaign (CCC) initiated a survey to assess global practices in coma management but lacked of sufficient data from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). A follow-up survey in India provided regional insights, which cannot be generalized to all LMICs. The aim of this study was to conduct a dedicated survey across various LMICs to understand local practices and challenges in the care of comatose patients. This was a cross-sectional online survey of 163 healthcare professionals from 32 LMICs, categorized into six geographical regions following the World Bank classification. The survey, an adaptation of the original COME TOGETHER questionnaire, covered coma definition, etiology, diagnostic tools, management, and prognostication. The majority of respondents were from South Asia (41.1%). Most worked in urban areas (96%), in government teaching hospitals (64%). There was substantial agreement on three cardinal features of coma: a Glascow Coma Scale (GCS) ≤ 8, absence of wakefulness, and failure to respond purposefully to stimuli. Traumatic brain injury (TBI) was the most common etiology (45%). GCS was the most frequently used assessment tool (96%). Most respondents reported no formal policy for the withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies (63%), and ethicists were rarely involved in such discussions (70%). The majority (76%) of respondents reported no patient follow-up after intensive care unit (ICU) discharge. This survey highlights significant variability and critical gaps in coma management across LMICs. The findings underscore the need for standardized protocols, targeted training for healthcare professionals, and international collaboration to improve patient outcomes in resource-limited settings.

articles.title: Protein and Energy Intake and Clinical Outcomes in Patients with Acute Kidney Injury during Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy: A Secondary Analysis of a Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Evidence on nutritional support's impact on outcomes in critically ill AKI patients receiving CRRT is limited. We evaluated associations between delivered energy/protein intake and mortality in this population. This was a secondary analysis of a prospective cohort study at King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital (March 2024-November 2025, NCT06254703), including critically ill adults with AKI on CRRT. Daily protein and calorie delivery were calculated from enteral, parenteral, and non-nutritional sources (glucose-containing solutions, propofol, citrate). Effluent urea nitrogen was measured daily to calculate normalized protein catabolic rate (nPCR). Outcomes included 28- and 90-day mortality, dialysis independence, renal recovery at days 28/90, and RRT-free days at day 28. Among 100 patients (median age 66 [IQR 51-77], 58% male, 54% 28-day mortality), non-survivors received less energy (15.8 vs 24.8 kcal/kg/day, p=0.001) and protein (0 vs 0.72 g/kg/day, p=0.002) than survivors. A J-shaped association linked protein intake to 28-day mortality: the lowest quartile (<0.09 g/kg/day) had markedly higher mortality (adjusted HR 8.63, 95% CI 3.75-19.8, p<0.001) after adjusting for sex and modified NUTRIC score. This quartile also showed the lowest dialysis independence and renal recovery rates at day 28 and fewest RRT-free days versus higher-intake quartiles. Total protein intake weakly correlated with nPCR (r=0.15, p=0.003) but not with BUN-to-creatinine ratio (r=0.09, p=0.07). In this hypothesis-generating analysis of critically ill AKI patients on CRRT, inadequate protein and energy delivery was associated with higher mortality, and lower protein intake with worse kidney outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of nutritional support during the first week after CRRT initiation. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06254703.

articles.title: Extreme Hypereosinophilia Revealing Disseminated Strongyloidiasis in a Critically Ill Patient.
articles.journal: The American journal of case reports
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND Extreme hypereosinophilia is an uncommon but clinically important laboratory finding that may indicate serious underlying disease. In tropical regions, parasitic infections, particularly Strongyloides stercoralis, should be considered. However, the diagnosis may be overlooked in critically ill patients with multiple concurrent infections. Because disseminated strongyloidiasis carries high mortality when diagnosis is delayed, early recognition and empirical anti-helminthic therapy are essential in endemic settings. CASE REPORT A 63-year-old Vietnamese farmer was transferred after 18 days of treatment for bacterial meningitis, intraventricular hemorrhage, Corynebacterium striatum pneumonia, and Candida auris infection. She remained critically ill and required respiratory support through a tracheostomy. Laboratory testing showed marked leukocytosis with extreme hypereosinophilia, severe anemia, profound hypoalbuminemia, acute kidney injury, electrolyte disturbances, and severe systemic inflammation. Arterial blood gas analysis confirmed hypoxemic respiratory failure. Given the extreme eosinophilia and endemic setting, disseminated strongyloidiasis was suspected, and empirical oral ivermectin was started before diagnosis. Strongyloides-specific IgG serology was positive, and Strongyloides stercoralis larvae were identified in sputum, confirming the diagnosis. The absolute eosinophil count declined from >10 000 cells/µL to 450 cells/µL by the next day, 180 cells/µL by treatment day 3, and 140 cells/µL by day 5. Her systemic condition remained stable for approximately 2 weeks; however, she subsequently developed recurrent intracranial hemorrhage and died in hospital. CONCLUSIONS This case highlights that strongyloidiasis should be considered in patients with unexplained marked eosinophilia, even when severe bacterial or fungal infections dominate the clinical presentation. In endemic regions, early clinical suspicion and timely empirical anti-helminthic therapy may be crucial to prevent potentially fatal disseminated strongyloidiasis, particularly in malnourished and medically complex patients.

articles.title: Early phosphate repletion and ventilator-free days in hypophosphatemic critical illness: a target trial emulation.
articles.abstract: Hypophosphatemia is common in critical illness, but whether prompt phosphate repletion improves patient-centered outcomes remains uncertain. To estimate the effect of phosphate repletion within 12 hours of incident hypophosphatemia on 28-day ventilator-free days. In this target trial emulation using MIMIC-IV 3.0, adults during their first ICU stay with an initial serum phosphate concentration <2.5 mg/dL within 48 hours of ICU admission were eligible. Treatment strategies were repletion within 12 hours versus no repletion within that grace period, with follow-up beginning at the 12-hour landmark. Stabilized inverse probability weighting was used to estimate average treatment effects on the primary outcome of 28-day ventilator-free days. Among 14,823 eligible patients, 6,995 received early repletion and 7,828 did not. Weighted covariate balance was adequate, with a maximum absolute standardized mean difference of 0.059. Early phosphate repletion did not improve 28-day ventilator-free days (MD -0.12 days, 95% CI -0.43 to 0.18, p = 0.424), ICU-free days, mortality, or renal replacement therapy. Among patients with repeat phosphate measurements, early repletion was associated with higher odds of phosphate normalization (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.24-1.50) and hyperphosphatemia (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.03-1.76). In this target trial emulation of critically ill adults, early phosphate repletion promoted biochemical normalization without improving patient-centered outcomes, suggesting selective rather than routine early repletion.

articles.title: Contribution of continuous renal replacement therapy to diquat elimination relative to native renal excretion in acute diquat poisoning.
articles.abstract: The quantitative contribution of continuous renal replacement therapy to diquat elimination remains poorly defined. We aim to quantify the contribution of continuous renal replacement therapy to diquat elimination and examine the influence of kidney function and treatment timing. In this prospective observational study, patients with acute diquat poisoning who received continuous renal replacement therapy and maintained urine output were enrolled between June 2020 and June 2025. Diquat removal was quantified using a mass-balance approach. The contribution fraction of continuous renal replacement therapy was defined as the amount removed extracorporeally divided by the sum of extracorporeal and concurrent urinary elimination. Linear mixed effects models were used to evaluate the factors associated with the contribution fraction. Twenty-eight patients underwent 76 continuous renal replacement therapy sessions. The median contribution fraction was 0.46 (interquartile range, 0.20-0.83). In mixed-effects analyses, the contribution fraction was inversely associated with estimated glomerular filtration rate (β = -0.004, 95% confidence interval -0.006 to -0.001; P = 0.010) and time from ingestion to continuous renal replacement therapy initiation (β = -0.005, 95% confidence interval -0.008 to -0.001; P = 0.012). At the patient level, continuous renal replacement therapy removal accounted for 22.1% (interquartile range, 9.1-52.3%) of urinary diquat excretion over 120 h. The relative contribution of continuous renal replacement therapy increased with declining kidney function and earlier treatment initiation, indicating that extracorporeal removal becomes more important when endogenous renal elimination is reduced and when circulating diquat concentrations remain high during the early phase after ingestion. In patients with acute diquat poisoning and preserved urine output, continuous renal replacement therapy contributed to diquat elimination, although native renal excretion remained the predominant elimination route. Its relative contribution was influenced by kidney function and treatment timing. Whether this removal translates into clinical benefit cannot be determined from this study and requires prospective evaluation.

A Machine Learning-Based Prognostic Risk Scoring Model for Patients with Coronary Artery Disease Admitted to the Intensive Care Unit Using Multi-Source Structured Clinical Data From the Information Mart for Intensive Care IV Database.
articles.abstract: Critical coronary artery disease (CAD) exhibits significant prognostic heterogeneity. Traditional scoring has limited efficacy in the early identification of high-risk patients. To develop a validated machine learning (ML)-based prognostic risk scoring model for critical CAD to predict adverse outcome risk based on multi-source structured clinical data from the medical information mart for intensive care IV (MIMIC-IV) database. A total of 5472 critically ill patients with CAD meeting the operational definitions of this study were retrospectively enrolled from the MIMIC-IV database and randomly divided into a training set and a test set at a 7 : 3 ratio. Fifty-two structured clinical indicators collected within the time window from 6 hours before intensive care unit (ICU) admission to 24 hours after admission were extracted. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression was applied in the training set to screen core variables based on 1-year all-cause mortality. Multiple ML algorithms were utilized to construct prognostic prediction models, with 1-year all-cause mortality as the primary outcome and 28-day in-hospital mortality as well as CAD-related ICU readmission rate as secondary outcomes. All model parameters and classification thresholds were predefined before performance evaluation in the test set. The test set was excluded from feature screening, parameter tuning, and threshold optimization procedures. Model performance was assessed via the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC of ROC), paired DeLong test, calibration curves, Brier score, calibration intercept, calibration slope, and decision curve analysis. The light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM) model with the highest AUC value was interpreted using SHapley additive exPlanations (SHAP). Additionally, sensitivity analysis with 5 sets of multiple imputations was performed. The 1-year all-cause mortality, 28-day in-hospital mortality, and CAD-related ICU readmission rate of the study population were 14.2%, 5.6%, and 9.1%, respectively. In the test set, the LightGBM model yielded AUC values of 0.896 and 0.898 for predicting 1-year all-cause mortality and 28-day in-hospital mortality, which were higher than those of other models. Nevertheless, paired DeLong tests revealed no statistically significant differences when compared with the logistic regression model (P = .062 and P = .642, respectively). The LightGBM model exhibited limited predictive performance for CAD-related ICU readmission rate (AUC = 0.690), with no significant difference in AUC relative to the logistic regression model (P = .238). SHapley additive exPlanations analysis identified the Charlson comorbidity index, history of coronary artery bypass grafting, and blood urea nitrogen as the top contributing variables of the LightGBM model. Thresholds derived from SHAP dependence plots were only interpreted as exploratory and model-dependent findings. The LightGBM model established in this study exhibited favorable performance for predicting mortality risk among critically ill patients with CAD in internal validation and was interpretable via the SHAP approach. It can provide quantitative references for early risk stratification and individualized clinical management of critically ill CAD patients in the ICU. However, only internal validation was conducted in the present study, and the model demonstrated suboptimal predictive efficacy and calibration for CAD-related ICU readmission. Therefore, external, multicenter, and prospective validations are required prior to its clinical implementation.

Integrating physiology and practice in critical care: hemodynamics and ventilatory mechanics for the beginner intensivist.
articles.abstract: This educational review provides a practical and evidence-informed overview of hemodynamic and ventilatory physiology for early-career intensivists. It integrates recent trials and expert consensus to explain how macro- and microcirculatory interactions, fluid responsiveness, vasopressor use, and mechanical-ventilation principles translate into bedside decision-making. Beyond summarizing physiology, this article emphasizes clinical reasoning, controversies, and limitations of monitoring approaches, aiming to strengthen conceptual understanding and promote individualized, physiology-guided critical care. Illustrative figures and summary tables support visual learning and reinforce the link between physiological concepts and clinical application. The review also highlights emerging frontiers, including Patient Self-Inflicted Lung Injury (P-SILI), the nuanced role of the pulmonary artery catheter in selected shock states, and ongoing challenges in bedside microcirculatory monitoring, which shape individualized critical care practice.
articles.ai_summary: This review summarizes hemodynamic and ventilatory physiology for early-career intensivists, integrating recent trials and expert consensus. It explains how macro- and microcirculatory interactions, fluid responsiveness, vasopressor use, and mechanical ventilation principles inform bedside decisions. The article also discusses emerging topics such as patient self-inflicted lung injury and the role of pulmonary artery catheters.
articles.ai_significance: Understanding these physiological principles helps clinicians tailor interventions to individual patients and avoid pitfalls of monitoring. It supports a physiology-guided approach that may improve patient outcomes.

articles.title: Neurosurgical intervention and ICU mortality in mechanically ventilated patients with acute brain injury: A post hoc analysis of a multicenter observational study.
articles.abstract: Mechanically ventilated patients with acute brain injury (ABI) frequently undergo neurosurgical procedures, but the differences between medically and surgically managed patients and ICU mortality remains uncertain because of disease heterogeneity and specific neurosurgical indication. We performed a post hoc analysis of the prospective ENIO multicenter observational study (NCT03400904), conducted from June 2018 to November 2020 in 73 ICUs across 18 countries. Adult neurocritical care patients with Glasgow Coma Scale score ≤12 before intubation, invasive mechanical ventilation for ≥24 h, and available data on neurosurgical intervention were included. The exposure was neurosurgical intervention versus conservative management. The primary outcome was ICU mortality. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used as the primary analytical approach; multivariable and mixed-effects logistic regression models and prespecified sensitivity analyses were used to assess robustness. Among 1510 included patients, 609 (40.3%) underwent neurosurgical intervention and 901 (59.7%) were managed without surgery. Crude ICU mortality was 7.1% in the neurosurgical group and 6.0% in the conservative-management group (p = 0.38). After IPTW in 1460 complete cases, baseline covariates were well balanced and neurosurgical intervention was not associated with ICU mortality (OR 1.12, 95% CI 0.73-1.70; p = 0.60). Findings were consistent in multivariable regression (OR 1.13, 95%CI 0.72-1.78; p = 0.56), mixed-effects models accounting for center-level clustering (OR 1.31, 95%CI: 0.77-2.22; p = 0.32), and sensitivity analyses restricted to patients with intracranial hemorrhage (OR 0.86, 95%CI 0.44-1.71; p = 0.66) or excluding patients who underwent decompressive craniectomy (OR 1.18, 95%CI 0.69-2.04; p = 0.54). After adjustment for confounding by indication, compared to medical management, neurosurgical intervention was not independently associated with ICU mortality among mechanically ventilated patients with ABI, despite substantially greater baseline severity in the surgical group. Future studies should evaluate procedure-specific effects, timing of intervention, withdrawal-of-care, and long-term functional outcomes.
