articles.title: Valvular Shock in the Cardiac Intensive Care Unit: Perioperative Care for Transcatheter Valve Interventions.
articles.abstract: Valvular heart disease is an uncommon but high-risk cause of cardiogenic shock requiring rapid, multidisciplinary management aimed at bridging patients to definitive surgical or transcatheter valve intervention. Early comprehensive Doppler echocardiography is essential, as clinical signs may be subtle. Distinguishing decompensated chronic valvular disease from acute unstable lesions guides urgency and treatment strategy. Medical stabilization and mechanical circulatory support vary markedly between stenotic and regurgitant lesions, and standard shock therapies may be harmful in specific contexts. Transcatheter approaches are preferred when feasible, though their expanding use introduces added complexity in cardiac intensive care.

articles.title: Endpoint-specific mortality associated with malignancy among adults with sepsis or septic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a major global health challenge and increasingly affects patients with complex conditions such as malignancy. Prior studies suggest higher mortality in this population, but interpretation is limited by aggregation of heterogeneous endpoints. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to clarify endpoint-specific prognostic associations between malignancy and mortality in adults with sepsis or septic shock. This study was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251141216). PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library and Epistemonikos were searched through 16 September 2025, for studies comparing all-cause mortality between sepsis patients with and without malignancy. Mortality endpoints were grouped as ICU, in-hospital, early, intermediate and extended follow-up mortality. Crude odds ratios (ORs) were estimated using random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup, meta-regression and sensitivity analyses were performed to explore heterogeneity and assess consistency. Among 105 eligible studies comprising 20,089,138 participants, 85 studies contributing 101 endpoint estimates were included in the primary synthesis. Pooled estimates were elevated across endpoints: ICU (OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.94-1.56), in-hospital (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.69-2.13), early (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.59-2.06), intermediate (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.72-3.03) and extended follow-up mortality (OR 2.41, 95% CI 1.70-3.42). Associations were sustained for haematologic malignancy, concentrated in in-hospital and early mortality for metastatic disease and more modest for solid tumours. Sensitivity analyses were directionally consistent, although risk ratio estimates were generally smaller than ORs. Exploratory meta-regression suggested that severity-related covariates may contribute to heterogeneity. Malignancy was associated with higher mortality among adults with sepsis or septic shock, with variation across mortality endpoints and clinical contexts. These findings support endpoint-specific prognostic assessment and highlight the need for future studies to incorporate more granular cancer characteristics. Because the primary estimates were unadjusted, results represent overall prognostic associations rather than independent causal effects.

Although most cases can be managed outside the intensive care unit, patients with RV failure, hemodynamic instability, or cardiac arrest require advanced monitoring and intervention. Management in this setting emphasizes rapid diagnosis and risk stratification, timely initiation of reperfusion therapies, and carefully tailored hemodynamic and respiratory support. Optimal outcomes rely on multidisciplinary collaboration, early escalation of care, and individualized, evidence-based decision-making.

articles.title: Prospective Observational Study Assessing Patient Characteristics, Management and Early Outcomes of Major Trauma Patients With Prehospital Shock. A preliminary report of the Sydney COAST study.
articles.abstract: Despite advances in trauma resuscitation, significant gaps remain in understanding how early physiological and biochemical derangements influence clinical outcomes. The Sydney 'Clinical Outcomes following Acute Shock in Trauma' (COAST) registry was developed by clinicians containing both prehospital and in-hospital data, allowing for the identification of risk factors that influence early mortality for major trauma patients with shock. This study reports the formation of the registry and the patient cohort enrolled over its first 12 months. A multi-centre, prospective registry of shocked adult trauma patients treated by prehospital medical teams and transported directly to a Sydney-based major trauma centre. Shock was defined as either (1) systolic blood pressure less than 100 mmHg, (2) shock index greater than one, (3) blood transfusion or (4) administration of inotropes. Descriptive statistics were used to report outcomes including injuries, pathology, transfusions, immediate intervention, mortality and length of stay. Two hundred fifty seven patients were enrolled. The predominant shock criteria for inclusion was hypotension (90% of cases), whilst 53% received prehospital blood transfusion. Interventional haemorrhage control was required in 31% of cases, whilst 74% received in-hospital transfusion. Injury severity was high (median injury severity score of 27). Four-hour mortality was 4.7% (9% at 24-h and 21% at 30-days). Consistent with recent observational studies, the Sydney COAST registry captured a cohort of critically ill trauma patients, not all of whom may have had haemorrhage. This will serve as an important dataset, allowing clinicians to better understand factors driving traumatic shock whilst exploring avenues for improving care in these cases.

articles.title: Earlier Application of Methylene Blue in Vasoplegic, Adrenergic Vasopressor-Resistant Patients is Associated with Better Clinical Outcomes. A Retrospective Analysis of 464 Patients.
articles.abstract: Severe shock hails a dismal prognosis for patients in intensive care units. Vasoplegic patients, refractory to adrenergic catecholamines face an increased risk for in-hospital mortality. However, the optimal timing for Methylene Blue (MB) in these vasopressor-resistant patients, remains unclear. This was a retrospective, single-center study conducted in the intensive care unit (ICU) of a tertiary medical center. 464 patients were included, 183 (39%) admitted to the general ICU and 281 (61%) to the cardiothoracic ICU. All patients developed vasoplegia and were treated with MB after a median time of 11.2 hours from admission. In the aggregated cohort, earlier MB administration was associated with lower ICU mortality (30% vs. 52%, p < 0.001), lower in-hospital mortality (41% vs. 59%, p < 0.001), lower 1-year mortality (46% vs. 62%, p < 0.001), and reduced need for continuous Veno venous hemofiltration (33% vs. 53%, p < 0.001). In survival analyses of the whole cohort, earlier MB administration was associated with reduced in-hospital mortality in univariate analysis (HR = 0.64; 95% CI 0.47-0.86, p = 0.003) and remained significant after multivariable adjustment (HR = 0.69; 95% CI 0.51-0.94, p = 0.018). ICU-specific analyses attenuated the association. In this retrospective, single-center cohort, earlier administration of MB was associated with improved clinical outcomes among ICU patients treated for vasoplegia, including lower mortality and reduced need for renal replacement therapy. Prospective studies are warranted to determine whether earlier MB administration should be incorporated into treatment protocols for adrenergic vasopressor-resistant vasoplegia.

Hemodynamic Effects of Three Different Mechanical Circulatory Support Strategies in Isolated Acute Right Heart Failure.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Although acute right ventricular failure (aRVF) is commonly treated with venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA ECMO), this approach may increase complications. We compared femoro-femoral VA ECMO, single-lumen cannula femoro-pulmonary artery (V-Pa), and double-lumen cannula right atrium-to-pulmonary artery (RA-Pa) support configurations in a swine model of ischemic aRVF-induced cardiogenic shock. Twenty-six adult German Landrasse swine were randomly assigned to the three study groups. Systemic oxygen delivery was the primary end-point; secondary end-points included hemodynamic parameters and complications. Systemic oxygen delivery remained stable during support without intergroup differences. Mean arterial pressure showed higher values in the V-Pa group compared with RA-Pa at 2 hours (65 ± 10 vs. 48 ± 8 mm Hg; p = 0.010) and 3 hours (62 ± 9 vs. 47 ± 10 mm Hg; p = 0.042). Mean pulmonary artery pressure was higher after V-A ECMO (20 ± 5 mm Hg) initiation compared with V-Pa (11 ± 5 mm Hg, p = 0.013) or RA-Pa (11 ± 3 mm Hg, p = 0.006) support. During support, the V-A ECMO group exhibited the lowest EtCO2 and highest carotid flow (p = 0.039 and p < 0.001, respectively). Challenges were noted with double-lumen cannulation due to anatomical constraints. Pulmonary artery cannulation-based support was noninferior to V-A ECMO in terms of oxygen delivery, with lower pulmonary pressures and preserved transpulmonary flow. Femoral vein-to-pulmonary artery configuration showed favorable short-term hemodynamics and easier cannulation compared with RA-Pa.

articles.title: Redefining blood pressure targets in refractory septic shock.
articles.abstract: Refractory septic shock was recently delineated by a set of clinical statements reflecting poor tissue perfusion despite adequate intravascular fluid volume and high doses of vasopressors. The concept of arterial pressure, which plays a pivotal role in the Sepsis-3 definition, was not incorporated by the panelists. The intensity of vasopressor treatment was found to be predominantly associated with mean arterial pressure. Indeed, the restoration of tissue perfusion is arguably the primary objective of resuscitation efforts. However, the loss of hemodynamic coherence-that is, the uncoupling between macrohemodynamics and microcirculation-suggests that, beyond a certain level of around 60-65 mmHg, tissue perfusion, as reflected by lactate and capillary refill time, is independent of arterial pressure in most patients. In this study, we propose a hypothesis derived from a physiological perspective, positing that the cost of increasing mean arterial pressure may increase disproportionately with rising norepinephrine requirements. In patients with refractory septic shock, the optimal level of arterial pressure should be investigated using time-limited challenge and adequate markers, such as capillary refill time and lactate. The approach to this evaluation should not be predicated on the analysis of isolated values; rather, it should be informed by a longitudinal and repeated examination of multiple markers that reflect global, regional, and local perfusion. Further research is necessary to ascertain the most effective strategy.
articles.ai_summary: The authors discuss refractory septic shock, noting that beyond a mean arterial pressure of about 60‑65 mmHg, tissue perfusion appears independent of arterial pressure. They propose that increasing MAP may incur higher norepinephrine costs and suggest evaluating MAP targets using repeated markers like capillary refill time and lactate rather than single values.
articles.ai_significance: This highlights that very high MAP targets may not improve tissue perfusion and could increase vasopressor burden, underscoring the need for individualized MAP goals in refractory septic shock.

articles.title: Total gastric and intragastric air volumes in immediate post-resuscitation whole-body computed tomography after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Association with airway management, aspiration, diaphragmatic position and initial blood gas analysis.
articles.abstract: Gastric distension (GD) may occur during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), but quantitative human data after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remain limited. We quantified gastric volumes after OHCA and explored associations with prehospital airway strategy, CT-defined aspiration, diaphragmatic position, and initial blood gases. This retrospective single-center study included OHCA patients undergoing post-resuscitation whole-body computed tomography (CT) within 180 minutes of emergency department (ED) admission between January 1, 2020, and March 31, 2025. Total gastric volume (TGV) and intragastric air volume (GAV) were quantified by CT volumetry. Of 255 identified patients, 120 underwent CT within 180 minutes. Median TGV was 594 mL and correlated strongly with GAV (p < 0.001). Among patients with an advanced airway at ED arrival, neither TGV (p = 0.20) nor GAV (p = 0.24) differed significantly between the tracheal airway (TA; n = 87) and supraglottic airway (SGA; n = 28) groups. CT-defined aspiration was numerically more frequent with SGA than TA (78.6% vs. 57.5%; OR 2.7; p = 0.071), whereas neither TGV nor GAV was associated with CT-defined aspiration. Weak positive correlations were observed between initial pCO2 and both TGV (ρ = 0.16; one-tailed p = 0.037) and GAV (ρ = 0.19; one-tailed p = 0.018). Gastric volumes were high in this selected post-OHCA immediate CT (< 180 minutes) cohort. No significant differences were detected according to recorded prehospital airway strategy, and gastric volume was not associated with CT-defined aspiration. Mechanisms and clinical consequences remain uncertain and require prospective studies before preventive/ therapeutic implications can be established.

articles.title: From clinical expertise to playable Code: AI-assisted development of a serious game for cardiac arrest awareness.
Managing Acute Asthma Exacerbations: A Survey Study of Real-world Practice Patterns and Specialty-related Differences.
articles.abstract: Although acute severe asthma (ASA) affects 55% of asthma exacerbations, variations in physicians' management of ASA have received less attention than practice trends for patients with stable asthma. Moreover, differences in care provided by specialists have not been addressed. This study aims to explore physicians' knowledge, attitudes, and practice trends regarding pharmacological and ventilatory management of ASA, and to verify practice variations between pulmonologists and non-pulmonologists. In this cross-sectional survey, a non-probability convenience sample of physicians entitled to manage ASA was surveyed using Google Forms to collect data on identification of exacerbations, triage decisions, pharmacological and ventilatory management practices, and beliefs about prognosis. Subgroup responses (pulmonologists versus non-pulmonologists) were compared. Ninety-three respondents were recruited mainly from the Middle East-North Africa region (59.1%), Europe (13.9%), and South/East Asia (12.9%). Sixty percent used predefined criteria to diagnose ASA, but these criteria were used less frequently for triage decisions. High-flow nasal cannula was readily available (93.5%), but "usually or mostly" used by only 29.03%. Pulmonologists demonstrated higher non-invasive ventilation (NIV) use "within and beyond" intensive care unit (P = 0.001), and more identified appropriate NIV settings (P = 0.048). 47% preferred individualizing the invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) mode. Multiple organ failure, cardiac arrest, asthma severity, and comorbid pneumonia were most frequently rated as strongly correlated with mortality or endotracheal intubation. Respondents believed that ASA patients who receive IMV after a failed NIV trial have worse prognosis. The use of pre-defined criteria for identifying ASA and triage decisions remains suboptimal. Several caveats related to optimal ventilatory settings exist, with significant differences between pulmonologists and non-pulmonologists.

articles.title: The SUBcutaneous Comprehensive UlTrasonographic (SUBCUT) protocol and Severity of Water and Edema Level Score (SWELS) for dynamic assessment of peripheral edema burden in critically ill patients: a prospective, longitudinal observational study.
articles.abstract: Excessive fluid resuscitation may lead to pathologic fluid accumulation and increased mortality. Cumulative fluid balance (CFB) correlates poorly with outcomes. Ultrasonographic central congestion metrics (VExUS/Lung ultrasound) inherently overlook critical fluid shifts within the peripheral reservoir. To bridge this diagnostic gap, we developed the SUBcutaneous Comprehensive UlTrasonographic (SUBCUT) protocol for standardized, semi-quantitative assessment of peripheral edema burden. Ultrasonographic assessment was performed bilaterally across six core anatomical regions using the SUBCUT protocol on days 1, 3, and 7. Individual sites were graded semi-quantitatively using the Ultrasonographic Subcutaneous Edema Grade (USEG, 0-4), yielding the Severity of Water and Edema Level Score (SWELS, 0-48) as the cumulative sum across 12 evaluation sites. The primary endpoint was ICU mortality, evaluating the prognostic performance of Day 3 SWELS. Among 111 patients analyzed (ICU mortality 23.4%; 26/111), baseline SWELS and CFB were similar between survivors and non-survivors. By Day 3, median SWELS surged in non-survivors (24 vs. 8; P < .001), yielding greater unadjusted, apparent discrimination than CFB (AUC 0.86 vs. 0.65). In competing-risk analysis, a 5-point increase in Day 3 SWELS was independently associated with ICU mortality (sHR, 1.51; 95% CI, 1.22-1.86; P < .001). Incorporating Day 3 SWELS into a contemporaneous clinical base model (Age, Admission Sepsis, Day 3 SOFA) enhanced model fit and discrimination (ΔAUC = 0.043; P = .008). The SUBCUT protocol provides a novel framework for assessing peripheral edema burden. At Day 3, its derivative, SWELS, demonstrates incremental prognostic association beyond contemporaneous organ dysfunction, offering an extravascular perspective for multi-compartment fluid mapping.

articles.title: Blood Pressure Estimation for Hemodynamic Monitoring Using Reduced Photoplethysmography Features in Intensive Care Units: Prospective Machine Learning Study.
articles.abstract: Continuous, noninvasive blood pressure (BP) monitoring is clinically important for managing hemodynamic instability in the intensive care unit (ICU). However, current ICU practice primarily relies on invasive arterial catheterization. While this is the clinical gold standard for continuous measurement, it carries risks such as infection and thrombosis and is typically limited to select critical care settings. To reduce reliance on invasive arterial lines, we developed an interpretable estimation framework for systolic blood pressure (SBP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) from single-sensor photoplethysmography (PPG). Synchronized PPG and arterial line 10-minute recordings from 100 patients in the ICU were analyzed. Using a hybrid feature selection strategy (RReliefF and intrinsic model-specific rankings), we reduced 201 initial features to an optimized subset of 30 core features. Model development and evaluation were designed to minimize information leakage and overfitting, incorporating nested cross-validation and patient-wise testing to assess generalizability across heterogeneous ICU populations. We developed and validated predictive models using machine learning techniques, specifically XGBoost (XGB), random forest, and support vector regression, with XGB serving as our primary model. Among the evaluated models, the Hybrid Top 30 XGB configuration provided the best balance between estimation performance, model compactness, and computational efficiency. The model achieved mean absolute errors of 8.61 mm Hg (SBP), 3.50 mm Hg (MAP), and 2.62 mm Hg (DBP). For MAP and DBP, mean difference (SD) values of -0.09 (4.54) mm Hg and -1.07 (3.51) mm Hg, respectively, satisfied the Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation numerical criteria, while performance corresponded to Grade A according to the British Hypertension Society grading criteria. Although SBP exhibited greater variability, estimation performance was largely preserved using a physiologically informed subset of 30 features (approximately 15% of the original feature set). Feature importance analysis revealed distinct physiological feature patterns across SBP, MAP, and DBP estimation. Interpretability analysis identified key predictors associated with wave reflection, systolic timing, low-frequency vasomotor activity, and autonomic regulation. By explicitly linking predictive features to underlying cardiovascular physiology, the proposed framework addresses a key limitation of existing black-box cuffless BP models. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that an optimized XGB framework using physiologically informed PPG features can provide accurate and computationally efficient BP estimation in ICU settings and may support the assessment of clinically relevant hemodynamic states using a single-sensor PPG platform. These findings provide a foundation for future development of more robust and generalizable interpretable BP estimation models and cuffless monitoring technologies.

articles.title: Cardiovascular physiology of respiratory support in acute cardiac critical illness: A hemodynamic guided approach.
articles.abstract: Respiratory support is traditionally regarded as a treatment for respiratory failure. However, interventions that modify pleural pressure, transpulmonary pressure, lung volume, or the work of breathing simultaneously influence venous return, ventricular loading conditions, pulmonary vascular resistance, ventricular interdependence, myocardial oxygen demand, cardiac output, and systemic perfusion. Consequently, similar respiratory interventions may produce different haemodynamic effects according to the predominant cardiovascular physiology. This narrative review examines heart-lung interactions during respiratory support in acute cardiac critical illness and proposes a physiology-based framework organized around three predominant haemodynamic phenotypes: left ventricular congestion/afterload excess, left ventricular low-output/cardiogenic shock, and right ventricular pressure overload/failure. Acute pulmonary embolism is considered an important aetiology of the latter phenotype rather than a separate haemodynamic category. We discuss how high-flow nasal oxygen, continuous positive airway pressure, bilevel non-invasive ventilation, and invasive mechanical ventilation modify cardiovascular physiology and how their effects may be anticipated and reassessed using clinical examination, systemic perfusion, haemodynamic monitoring, focused echocardiography, and lung ultrasound. These phenotypes are dynamic and may overlap or evolve during critical illness; therefore, the proposed framework should be regarded as a conceptual bedside approach rather than a validated therapeutic algorithm. Respiratory support may consequently be considered a cardiovascular as well as a respiratory intervention, requiring repeated assessment of both respiratory benefit and haemodynamic cost.
articles.ai_summary: This narrative review discusses how respiratory support interventions alter cardiovascular physiology in patients with acute cardiac critical illness. It proposes a framework based on three haemodynamic phenotypes—left‑ventricular congestion, low‑output cardiogenic shock, and right‑ventricular pressure overload—to guide assessment and management. The review emphasizes that respiratory support should be viewed as both a respiratory and cardiovascular intervention.
articles.ai_significance: Understanding the cardiovascular effects of respiratory support can help clinicians anticipate and mitigate potential haemodynamic complications in cardiac patients, improving overall management and outcomes.

articles.title: Survival after out of hospital cardiac arrest in relation to AED usage in a multi response system including AED equipped drones.
articles.abstract: Early defibrillation is a key determinant of survival in out‑of‑hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). In multi-response systems, it remains unclear which responders contribute most to early AED use and survival. This study compared first AED-attaching responders and their association with 30-day survival in a regional multi-response system. This registry‑based cohort study included OHCA cases in Västra Götaland Region, Sweden, between January 1, 2015, and December 31, 2024. Data were obtained from EMS, dispatch, and registry databases. The primary outcome was 30‑day survival. Among 9,413 OHCAs, EMS attached the first AED in 72% of cases, followed by on-duty first responders (ODFR) (18%), bystanders (6.0%), and community first responders (CFR) (4.5%). EMS attachment decreased from 77% to 67%, whereas CFR involvement increased from 1% to 13%. 30‑day survival was highest when AEDs were attached by bystanders (28%), compared with 9.0% for EMS, 8.7% for ODFR and 8.6% for CFR. Among witnessed OHCAs with an initial shockable rhythm, 30-day survival was highest in bystander-attached cases (62%), compared with 36% for CFR, 32% for ODFR, and 24% for EMS. In the multivariable analysis, bystander AED attachment was associated with higher odds of 30‑day survival compared with EMS (OR 2.25; 95% CI 1.77-2.85). In this multi-response system, survival was highest when AEDs were first attached by bystanders and remained higher after adjustment for known prognostic factors. This association likely reflects earlier access to defibrillation. These findings suggest that improving immediate access to defibrillation may have the greatest impact on OHCA outcomes.

articles.title: Early Prehospital Prediction of Neurological Outcome After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Derivation and External Validation of the MIRA-29 Score.
articles.abstract: Out-of-hospital cardiac (OHCA) arrest is a frequent emergency, and few patients will survive with good neurological outcome. Identification of patients with a low likelihood of meaningful recovery represents a major clinical challenge. Numerous scores have been developed to guide decision-making after OHCA, with variable goals and targets, but most of them have been validated on small cohorts, integrates variables not available in the prehospital field, or do have low prediction values. MIRA-29 score aimed to only rely on simple clinical variables, available in the prehospital setting. We hypothetized that such score will provide incremental neurological prognosis value at an early-stage following OHCA. MIRA-29 score was derived and internally validated over a five-year period on a prospective cohort of 1099 adult patients, including all OHCA treated by our territory dispatch center. Multivariate analysis identified independent variables within the database, that were used to optimize the prediction model using machine-learning and genetic algorithms. The score was subsequently validated externally on 82 696 patients extracted from the French national cardiac arrest registry (RéAC). Out from the 1099 patients, 85 patients (7.7%) had a favorable neurological outcome. Multivariate analysis identified five independent variables associated with neurological outcome: age, low-flow duration, number of external electric shock, epinephrine dose, and the OHCA site (street, public facility, home). After model optimization and machine-learning, age was not retained within the final model. External validation depicted a precision of 0.86 and a recall of 0.88 of the model. The F1-Score and accuracy are respectively 0.87 and 0.88, and specificity for a bad neurological prognosis is 0.99. MIRA‑29 strength lies on its ability to reliably identify patients with extremely high probability of poor neurological outcome, while being based on four simple clinical variables. The prospective validation of MIRA-29 in the clinical setting may evaluate its impact on clinical decision making.
articles.ai_summary: A prehospital score, MIRA‑29, was derived from 1,099 adult out‑of‑hospital cardiac arrest patients and externally validated in 82,696 cases. The model uses four simple clinical variables and achieved high accuracy (0.88) and specificity for poor neurological outcome (0.99).
articles.ai_significance: The score offers clinicians a rapid, data‑driven tool to identify patients with a very low likelihood of meaningful neurological recovery, potentially informing early triage and resource allocation decisions.

articles.title: RescQ(TM): One-year implementation and feasibility results of a digitally enabled support pathway for bystanders of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
articles.abstract: Bystanders to out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) are at significant risk of psychological distress, yet no standardised support pathway exists for them in the UK. RescQ™ is a digital-first bystander support pathway embedded within regional prehospital and cardiac arrest care services. To evaluate the feasibility of embedding RescQ™ into routine emergency medical services (EMS) practice leading to appropriate contact with bystanders involved in OHCA. Secondary aims were to describe digital access, demand for liaison officer (LO) support, identification of younger bystanders, and EMS clinician acceptability. Prospective one-year regional service evaluation of RescQ™ across Essex, UK. Bystanders involved in eligible OHCA events were registered by EMS clinicians and provided with immediate access to secure digital resources. Bystanders could self-refer for additional support through LO. During the one-year evaluation, 220 of 432 eligible OHCA incidents had at least one bystander identified and the incident entered into the RescQ™ pathway, representing an incident-level capture rate of 50.9%. Across these incidents, 298 bystanders were identified, of whom 260 eligible adults were registered with RescQ™. Of registered adult bystanders, 96.2% accessed the digital resources at least once. Among all identified bystanders, 30/298 (10.1%) were aged under 18 years. Approximately 10% of registered bystanders self-referred for additional personalised LO support. Among 25 EMS clinician survey respondents who had used RescQTM in clinical practice, ratings indicated acceptability. RescQ™ demonstrated the feasibility of identifying and supporting bystanders following OHCA through a digitally enabled pathway, achieving incident-level capture above the pre-specified feasibility threshold and high website access among registered adults. These findings support further multi-region evaluation of implementation, sustainability and scalability across different EMS systems.

articles.title: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrests due to foreign body airway obstruction: A CanROC registry, retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Foreign body airway obstruction (FBAO) is a treatable cause of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but North American data are limited. Exploratory retrospective cohort study of EMS-treated OHCAs using the Canadian Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium (CanROC) registry (2005-2023), classified as obviously FBAO-related or of no obvious cause (presumed cardiac). Logistic regression compared Utstein characteristics between etiologies and identified factors associated with prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to acute care discharge. Among 105,178 EMS-treated OHCAs, 1,106(1.1%) were obviously FBAO-related. Compared with cases of no obvious cause, obviously FBAO-related cases were older (median 73 vs 68 years, p<0.001), more often witnessed (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 6.98[5.36-9.25]), more often attended by trained bystanders (aOR 3.30[2.41-4.41]), and less often had a shockable rhythm (aOR 0.11[0.07-0.15]). Obviously FBAO-related cases more often achieved prehospital ROSC (62.7% vs 37.8%; OR 2.77[2.44-3.13]), but survival did not differ (10.6% vs 9.0%,p=0.094). Within the obviously FBAO-related cohort, ROSC was associated with witnessed arrest (aOR 1.66[1.13-2.43]) and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.95 per minute[0.92-0.99]). Survival was associated with younger age (aOR 0.76 per decade[0.61-0.93]), initial shockable rhythm (aOR 4.76[1.55-13.30]), and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.81 per minute[0.66-0.98]). Survival was 18.1% and 0.8% among obviously FBAO-related OHCAs with and without prehospital ROSC, respectively. Obviously FBAO-related OHCAs are uncommon but clinically distinct. ROSC is frequent, yet survival remains low and is associated with early prehospital factors, supporting choking prevention initiatives, bystander training, and rapid EMS response.

articles.title: Commercially available multimodal LLMs for EEG-based prognostication after cardiac arrest.
articles.abstract: Machine-learning and deep-learning approaches have been successfully applied to EEG-based prognostication in comatose patients after cardiac arrest (CA), but typically rely on task-specific signal processing, feature extraction, and model development. Here, we investigated whether two commercially available multimodal large language models (LLMs) could predict neurological outcome directly from EEG images. Thirty-three comatose patients on the first day after CA from a prospective cohort were included. For each patient, a single 10-second EEG segment displayed using a longitudinal bipolar montage was rendered as PNG image. ChatGPT 5.4. and Claude Opus 4.7 were instructed to estimate the probability for favorable outcome for each case based on the EEG and a generic information block describing conditions of recordings. Five different prompting strategies were used, including few-shot prompting where four exemplary EEGs (not from the 33 patients) were provided. Predictive performance was quantified using AUC and accuracy. Across prompting strategies, the AUC ranged from 0.86 to 0.99 for ChatGPT and from 0.74 to 1.00 for Claude. The highest accuracy achieved by both models was 93.9% using few-shot prompting. As reference, a previously published dedicated deep-learning model achieved 100% on the same cohort. In this exploratory study of a small cohort, multimodal LLMs showed variable but potentially promising discrimination for predicting favorable outcome from single EEG image in comatose patients after CA. Performance depended substantially on prompt design. These findings require confirmation in a larger cohort.

articles.title: Community First Responder Activation Reduces the Negative Impact of AED Distance on Bystander Defibrillation After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.abstract: Early defibrillation is critical for survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), yet bystander defibrillation remains uncommon despite the availability of automated external defibrillators (AEDs). We investigated whether HeartRunner community first responder activation increased the likelihood of bystander defibrillation and 30-day survival in relation to the distance to the nearest accessible AED. Linking data from the Danish Cardiac Arrest Registry, Danish AED Network, and HeartRunner application, we identified patients with OHCA eligible for HeartRunner activation during 2017-2021. Using street-network distances to the nearest accessible AED, we examined associations between HeartRunner activation, bystander defibrillation, and 30-day survival using multivariable logistic regression with interaction terms and targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE). Among 5,753 OHCAs (median age, 74 years; 64% male; 78% in private locations), HeartRunner activation (41%) was associated with higher bystander defibrillation across AED distances (p-interaction = 0.004), with no interaction for 30-day survival (p-interaction = 0.054). Predicted bystander defibrillation with versus without HeartRunner activation was 9.6% vs 5.5% at Q1 (389 m), 10.0% vs 4.3% at median (717 m), and 13.0% vs 4.8% at Q3 (1,183 m). TMLE estimated a 6.1-percentage-point higher probability of bystander defibrillation (95% CI, 4.5-7.8; p<0.001) and a modest 1.8-percentage-point increase in 30-day survival (95% CI, 0.1-3.6; p=0.038) with HeartRunner activation. HeartRunner activation attenuated the decline in bystander defibrillation with increasing AED distance following OHCA, without a corresponding distance interaction for 30-day survival. Overall, TMLE supported higher bystander defibrillation and suggested a modest increase in 30-day survival with HeartRunner activation.

articles.title: Anaesthetic management for first-trimester pregnancy termination in a patient with uncorrected persistent truncus arteriosus: a case report.
articles.abstract: Persistent truncus arteriosus (PTA) is a rare cyanotic congenital heart defect with substantial cardiovascular risk during pregnancy. We report a gravida 1, para 0, 20-year-old woman with unrepaired PTA undergoing suction curettage at 6 weeks and 2 days of gestation. She had chronic hypoxaemia and secondary erythrocytosis, with no chronic medications or previous surgery. Echocardiography showed a 16-mm ventricular septal defect with predominant right-to-left shunting, and approximately 50% truncal override. A left radial arterial catheter was placed before low-dose combined spinal epidural anaesthesia with isobaric bupivacaine 0.5% 6 mg (1.2 mL) administered intrathecally. Norepinephrine was infused at 0.02 μg/kg/min. Haemodynamics remained stable at baseline and oxygenation did not deteriorate below preprocedural levels; crystalloid administration was 100 mL and blood loss 10 mL. Intensive care unit monitoring continued through postoperative day 1, and she was discharged on day 2. The approach was feasible and well tolerated in this patient.

articles.title: The sepsis trial landscape: a domain-specific systematic review and meta-analysis of adult sepsis randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract: Despite decades of sepsis randomized clinical trials (RCTs), few therapeutic interventions have demonstrated reproducible mortality benefit. Whether this phenomenon reflects failure of individual therapies or broader limitations in sepsis RCT design remains unclear. We hypothesized that examining clinically distinct treatment domains would reveal differences in mortality effect estimates while identifying recurrent trial-design limitations shared across domains. Therefore, we performed a domain-specific meta-analysis of adult sepsis RCTs and evaluated the distribution of mortality effect estimates across treatment domains using a complementary landscape analysis framework and structured trial-design analysis. We conducted a meta-analysis of adult sepsis and septic shock RCTs published between 2000 and 2025 (PROSPERO CRD420261289221). Using PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL, two reviewers screened studies and extracted data. Trials were grouped into six treatment domains: initial resuscitation interventions, intravenous fluid quantity, intravenous fluid type, vasopressors, corticosteroids, and vitamin C-based therapies. Separate random-effects meta-analyses estimated pooled risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We also performed a complementary landscape analysis using Python to evaluate the distribution of mortality effect estimates relative to study sample size, as well as a structured thematic analysis to identify recurrent trial design constraints across treatment domains. Across 62 RCTs (n = 36,739), pooled mortality effects demonstrated no mortality benefit across each of the six treatment domains: resuscitation interventions (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77-1.01), intravenous fluid quantity (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.88-1.05), intravenous fluid type (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.89-1.01), vasopressors (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.88-1.07), corticosteroids (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.84-1.00), and vitamin C-based therapies (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.83-1.09). A landscape analysis showed wider dispersion of mortality effect estimates among smaller trials, whereas larger trial estimates generally clustered near the null. A structured thematic analysis using a prespecified trial-constraint framework identified recurrent design limitations across treatment domains, including delayed intervention timing, biologic and clinical heterogeneity, treatment contamination, and trial design and infrastructure constraints. Across the six prespecified treatment domains in sepsis, RCTs have not demonstrated consistent reductions in mortality. Recurrent trial-design limitations were common across treatment domains and may inform interpretation and future trial design.

articles.title: A Deep Learning-Based Prediction Model for Mortality in Severe COVID-19 Patients Requiring Intensive Care Unit Admission: A Multicenter Registry Analysis.
articles.abstract: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has been associated with substantial global mortality. Although artificial intelligence (AI)-based models have shown promise for mortality prediction, evidence focused specifically on critically ill patients remains limited. In addition, meaningful clinical implementation requires models that rely on a minimal set of readily available variables to enable rapid risk stratification. This study aimed to develop a deep learning-based model for predicting mortality in critically ill COVID-19 patients requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission, with an emphasis on efficiency and clinical applicability. This retrospective multicenter study included 900 critically ill patients with COVID-19 admitted to ICUs across 22 centers in Korea between January 1, 2020, and August 31, 2021. A deep learning-based tabular model was constructed, and systematic feature reduction strategies were applied to optimize predictive performance while enhancing practicality. Of the 900 patients, 365 (40.6%) survived and 535 (59.4%) died. Compared with survivors, non-survivors were older, demonstrated more severe clinical and chest X-ray (CXR) findings, had lower respiratory rate-oxygenation (ROX) indices, and required vasopressors and continuous renal replacement therapy more frequently (all P < 0.05). The initial model incorporating 66 variables achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.8500. Following stepwise feature selection, the model was reduced to seven key variables (age, C-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, pro-B-type natriuretic peptide, CXR infiltration, CXR consolidation, and ROX index), resulting in a simplified model with an AUC of 0.8247. A deep learning-based AI model was developed to support clinical decision-making in critically ill patients with COVID-19, offering an efficient and clinically practical approach to mortality risk assessment.

articles.title: Critically ill trauma in Portugal: a multicenter intensive care cohort study of frailty, organ dysfunction, and outcomes.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Multicenter data on critically ill trauma patients admitted to Portuguese intensive care units (ICUs) are lacking. We aimed to characterize their epidemiology, injury profile, organ dysfunction trajectories and outcomes, and to evaluate the prognostic performance of severity and frailty measures. Multicenter retrospective cohort study within the National Intensive Care Registry (RNMI) of adults (≥ 18 years) admitted to an ICU as a direct consequence of trauma (1 October-31 December 2024) in 32 of 50 voluntarily participating Portuguese ICUs; not nationally representative. SAPS II, ISS, TRISS, the Clinical Frailty Scale, daily SOFA scores, organ support, quality of life and mortality were collected. Prognostic performance was assessed by ROC analysis, multivariable logistic regression, calibration, and mixed-effects modelling of serial SOFA. 457 patients were included; median age 61 years (IQR 45-74), 72.0% male. Falls were the leading injury mechanism (46.9%). Traumatic brain injury (32.9%) and thoracic trauma (21.4%) predominated. Observed ICU and hospital mortality were 11.0% and 15.3%, respectively. SOFA scores were consistently higher in non-survivors from day one. SAPS II showed the highest discrimination for hospital mortality (AUC 0.874, 95% CI 0.825-0.924), followed by TRISS (0.758) and the Clinical Frailty Scale (0.702). SAPS II, day-1 SOFA, and frailty were independently associated with hospital mortality. SAPS II over-predicted mortality (observed/expected 0.64), whereas TRISS showed a non-significant tendency to under-predict it (1.32, 95% CI 0.99-1.72). In this multicenter cohort from 32 voluntarily participating ICUs, patients were older, with frequent falls, neurotrauma and thoracic injury, and moderate mortality. Organ dysfunction trajectories and frailty were associated with hospital mortality, but incremental predictive value was not assessed; both merit inclusion in future trauma registry frameworks.

articles.title: Does critical care training explain higher survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?, Letter to the Editor.
Reply to: Does critical care training explain higher survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?
Pre-eclampsia screening and prevention: Implementing FIGO guidelines in a Thai population.
articles.journal: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
articles.abstract: To evaluate the real-world implementation, screening performance, aspirin uptake, and safety of a FIGO (the International Federation of Gynecology & Obstetrics)-based first-trimester pre-eclampsia screening and prevention program. This retrospective cohort study included women initiating antenatal care before 14 weeks of gestation at a tertiary referral center in southern Thailand from 2021 to 2024. Screening incorporated maternal factors, mean arterial pressure, and uterine artery pulsatility index. Women with a calculated risk of 1:100 or greater were classified as being at high risk and offered aspirin 162 mg nightly. Outcomes included screening coverage, detection rates, aspirin uptake, pregnancy outcomes, and bleeding complications. Among 1713 pregnancies, 71 developed pre-eclampsia (4.1%), including 49 with severe features. Overall, 1106 women were screened (64.6%), but coverage reached 93.6% by the end of implementation. The screen-positive rate was 11.3%. Detection rates were 61.7% for overall pre-eclampsia, 69.6% for delivery before 37 weeks of gestation, 87.5% for delivery before 34 weeks of gestation, and 100% for delivery before 32 weeks of gestation, with false-positive rates of approximately 9%-11%. Aspirin uptake among screen-positive women was 99.2%. Pre-eclampsia was associated with higher rates of cesarean delivery, preterm birth, lower birth weight, and neonatal intensive care unit admission. No eclampsia, placental abruption, maternal intensive care unit admission, maternal death, stillbirth, or neonatal death occurred. After adjustment for potential confounders, aspirin was not associated with the risk of an estimated blood loss of 500 mL or more, and the risk of an estimated blood loss of 1000 mL or more did not differ significantly between groups. FIGO-based first-trimester screening was feasible in routine care, with increasing coverage as implementation matured, near-universal aspirin uptake, and clinically useful detection of preterm pre-eclampsia. Aspirin use was not significantly associated with severe bleeding.

articles.title: Capillary refill time at the admission of trauma patients: A prospective, observational study.
articles.abstract: The early identification of tissue perfusion is a significant challenge in the management of severe trauma cases. Capillary refill time (CRT) is a simple clinical marker of peripheral perfusion. The objective of this study was to ascertain the correlation between CRT and serum lactate levels in patients with severe trauma. A prospective, single-center observational study was conducted in a 20-bed intensive care unit (ICU) of a level 1 trauma center between April 2025 and January 2026. Adult patients who were directly admitted to the ICU from the scene of the accident for severe trauma, as defined by an injury severity score above 15, were included in the study. The CRT and serum lactate were measured on admission to the ICU. The primary endpoint was the association between admission serum lactate and admission CRT ≥ 3 s (abnormal CRT). Secondary analyses included the correlation between CRT and serum lactate at admission and the association between CRT and duration of vasopressor exposure during the first 3 days. Multivariate linear regression was performed on logarithmically transformed serum lactate, adjusted for age, core body temperature, prehospital weight-adjusted fluid administration, prehospital use of norepinephrine and prehospital timing. Of 627 patients screened, 196 were included in the analysis. The admission CRT was 2.4 [1.7-3.1] s with serum lactate level at 2.1 [1.3-3.4] mmol/L. Admission serum lactate did not differ significantly between the patients with abnormal CRT and those with normal CRT (2.6 [1.4-4.6] versus 1.9 [1.3-3.1] mmol/L; p = 0.07) while CRT and serum lactate levels were correlated (r = 0.33; p < 0.01). In multivariate analysis, continuous analysis of CRT was independently associated with serum lactate levels with a 15% increase in serum lactate per additional sec of CRT (95% CI 1.06-1.25; p < 0.01). Among patients with serum lactate >2 mmol/L, abnormal CRT was associated with longer vasopressor exposure at day 3 and increased ICU mortality. Admission lactate did not differ significantly between normal and abnormal CRT groups. Exploratory subgroup findings suggest that CRT may complement serum lactate in characterizing patients with severe trauma.

articles.title: How I Do It: An Intensivist's guide to RV Failure and Right Ventricular Assist Devices.
authors: Cardiology/CV Surgery Section, Pulmonary Vascular Disease and Cardiovascular Network.
articles.abstract: Right ventricular failure (RVF) is a high-mortality form of cardiogenic shock frequently encountered in critical illness and is often underrecognized due to its heterogeneous presentation. This article presents a physiology-driven, stepwise approach to the diagnosis and management of acute RVF using a longitudinal case in the intensive care unit. We highlight practical bedside tools for recognition, including point-of-care ultrasound and invasive hemodynamics, and review targeted strategies for preload optimization, afterload reduction, and contractility support. Special emphasis is placed on airway management, vasoactive medications, and timely escalation to mechanical circulatory support (MCS) in appropriately selected patients. This bedside "How I Do It" guide is written for intensivists and pulmonary/critical care clinicians and translates advanced hemodynamic and device concepts into practical decision points for acute care management.
articles.ai_summary: This guide outlines a physiology-driven, stepwise approach to diagnosing and managing acute right ventricular failure in the ICU. It emphasizes bedside tools such as point-of-care ultrasound and invasive hemodynamics, and reviews strategies for preload optimization, afterload reduction, contractility support, airway management, vasoactive medications, and timely escalation to mechanical circulatory support.
articles.ai_significance: Recognizing right ventricular failure early is critical because it carries high mortality in cardiogenic shock. Practical bedside tools and targeted interventions can improve identification and guide timely escalation to mechanical support, potentially improving outcomes.

articles.title: The occult hypoperfusion index: a bedside formula to identify undetected critical illness.
articles.abstract: The prehospital modified Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (mSOFA) score identifies patients with organ dysfunction but cannot detect normotensive occult hypoperfusion. To characterize the physiological correlation structure of mSOFA misclassification groups and to derive, internally validate and externally validate a bedside Occult Hypoperfusion Index (OHI) targeting undetected critical illness in patients classified as low acuity by the mSOFA. Prospective multicenter cohort study. Consecutive adults with acute illness attended by three physician-led emergency medical services. Prehospital mSOFA score computed from five point-of-care variables (mean arterial pressure, Glasgow Coma Scale [GCS], SpO₂/FiO₂ ratio, creatinine, and lactate). Primary outcome was all-cause mortality within 48 h of the index event. The index was then applied without refitting to an independent prospective cohort from Graz, Austria. Of 16,106 enrolled patients, 933 (5.8%) died within 48 h. Cross-tabulation of mSOFA threshold and mortality yielded 848 true positives (5.3%), 85 false negatives (FN, 0.5%), 2,136 false positives (13.3%), and 13,037 true negatives (80.9%). Correlation analysis revealed that the FN group was uniquely sparse, with a dominant lactate-GCS coupling of ρ=+0.616 (p<.001). This co-variation was formalized as OHI=lactate × (16 - GCS). Applied to the mSOFA < 5 subgroup (n = 13,122), the OHI achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.851 (95% CI, 0.816-0.885), outperforming lactate alone (0.755; DeLong p = .004) and GCS alone (0.630; DeLong p < .001). In the external cohort (n = 802; 67 deaths), the OHI at the pre-specified threshold achieved an area under the curve of 0.861 (95% CI, 0.699-0.990), with sensitivity 80.0% and specificity 74.8%, and showed no evidence of miscalibration. In a large prospective prehospital cohort, a multiplicative index derived from correlation analysis of mSOFA misclassification identified patients who died within 48 h despite being classified as low acuity. These findings are hypothesis-generating: the index was derived in one health system and externally validated in another, but the external estimates rest on few events and prospective evaluation before clinical use remains necessary. Consistent discrimination across three geographically distinct EMS systems in a leave-one-region-out analysis supports, but does not establish, its generalisability; this has now been extended to an independent cohort from a different country.

articles.title: Left Ventricular Unloading With Self-Expanding Pump During Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Acute Myocardial Infarction.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Increased left ventricular (LV) afterload and distension during venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) support may impede myocardial perfusion in acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Active LV unloading has been associated with improved outcomes. We report the first clinical use of a self-expanding percutaneous ventricular assist device (NyokAssist; magAssist, Suzhou, China) for LV unloading during VA-ECMO in a 56 year old man with AMI-related cardiogenic shock (CS). Successful coronary angiography and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) of the culprit left circumflex (LCx) lesion were performed with NyokAssist + VA-ECMO support. The patient was successfully weaned from VA-ECMO on post-procedure day 5 and remained on NyokAssist support alone for an additional 7 days before being transferred on VA-ECMO to a heart transplant center for consideration of advanced heart failure therapies due to limited myocardial recovery. No device-related complications were observed. This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of early implementation of a combined VA-ECMO and NyokAssist support strategy, enabling LV unloading, temporary hemodynamic stabilization, end-organ improvement, and VA-ECMO decannulation in a patient with AMI-related CS. As this report describes a single-patient experience, further clinical studies are warranted to define the safety, efficacy, and potential role of the use of NyokAssist in combination with VA-ECMO in the management of AMI-related CS.
articles.ai_summary: A 56‑year‑old man with acute myocardial infarction–related cardiogenic shock was treated with venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA‑ECMO) and a self‑expanding percutaneous ventricular assist device (NyokAssist). The patient was successfully weaned from VA‑ECMO after 5 days, continued on NyokAssist alone for 7 days, and was then transferred for advanced heart failure evaluation. No device‑related complications were reported.
articles.ai_significance: This case demonstrates that early LV unloading with a self‑expanding device can be technically achieved during VA‑ECMO support and may facilitate hemodynamic stabilization and decannulation in cardiogenic shock secondary to myocardial infarction. However, safety and efficacy remain unproven beyond this single experience.

articles.title: The global research landscape of emergency medical services in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
articles.abstract: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a major cause of death, and emergency medical services (EMS) are central to recognition, resuscitation, transport, and linkage to post-arrest care. Although previous bibliometric studies have mapped the broader cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation literature, the intersection of EMS and OHCA warrants focused characterization. We performed a retrospective bibliometric analysis of records indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection from 1972 through June 2026. The search combined OHCA terms with terms for EMS, paramedics, and emergency medical technicians. Annual output, research categories, journals, authors, and countries were described. VOSviewer version 1.6.20 was used for author co-authorship, keyword co-occurrence, and cited-reference co-citation analyses. The search identified 3,005 records. Annual output increased markedly after 2010, peaked at 244 publications in 2021, and remained above 200 publications per year from 2022 to 2025; 130 records were indexed for the partial 2026 year. Emergency Medicine (1,745; 58.1%) and Critical Care Medicine (1,014; 33.7%) were the most frequently assigned Web of Science categories. Resuscitation published 694 records (23.1%). The United States had the greatest country-level output (1,022; 34.0%), followed by Japan (375; 12.5%) and Canada (281; 9.4%). The most prolific author was Shin SD (98 publications). Co-authorship mapping showed registry-centered regional communities, while keyword analysis yielded ten interpreted domains spanning epidemiology, resuscitation interventions, dispatch, registries, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation, equity, and technology-related topics. Co-citation analysis identified four major intellectual communities. EMS-focused OHCA publications indexed in Web of Science show sustained output and international collaboration associated with established registries. Limited visibility of low- and middle-income settings within this database warrants further investigation. Equity, implementation, and digital and resuscitative technologies are potential areas for further research; the pooled network analysis does not establish their temporal growth.

articles.title: The Impact of Hospital Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Volume and Its Distribution Across ICUs on Adult Patients' Outcomes: An Analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry.
articles.abstract: Research from a prior era of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) found that higher hospital ECMO volume was associated with higher survival rates, but it did not examine whether distributing ECMO volume across multiple ICUs affected this relationship. Retrospective analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) registry. ECMO centers contributing to the registry. Adult patients required ECMO support from 2012 to 2023. None. We analyzed adult patients from the ELSO registry (2012-2023), adjusting for hospital factors and case mix using multivariable hierarchical logistic regression. The main outcome was in-hospital mortality. Hospital experience was measured by the annual number of adult ECMO cases and total ECMO hours. Volume-outcome associations were modeled for all centers and by total adult ICUs per center. We included 115,849 adults on ECMO across 495 hospitals. Model estimates showed small decreases in mortality odds with higher annual case counts (odds ratio [OR], 0.98; 95% CI, 0.97-0.99 per 10-case increase) and ECMO hours (OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99-1.00 per 1000 hr increase). Hospitals with one ICU had a median of 10 cases (interquartile interval [IQI], 3-25 cases), while those with four or more ICUs had a median of 50 (IQI, 28-91). Adjusted mortality was higher in centers delivering ECMO across four+ ICUs compared with one ICU (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.06-1.31), the annual case model (OR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06-1.26), and the annual ECMO hours model. Higher volume was associated with a reduction in the odds of mortality for hospitals with four+ ICUs compared with those with one ICU (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.96-1.00 per 10 cases and OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99-1.00 per 1000 hr). Higher hospital ECMO volume is associated with reduced mortality. Hospitals with more adult ICUs that perform ECMO may experience higher mortality, which may be explained by increased patient complexity and is offset by the higher center volume. More research is needed to better understand the optimum design of ECMO centers.

articles.title: Cycle-to-Cycle Prediction of Return of Spontaneous Circulation Using End-Tidal Carbon Dioxide Dynamics in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.abstract: Prognostication in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) commonly relies on static pre-resuscitation variables, although resuscitation is a rapidly evolving physiologic process. End-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2) is continuously available during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, but its sequential information has not been fully used for real-time prediction. We aim to develop and internally validate a cycle-to-cycle time-updated prediction model using sequential EtCO2 values to estimate the probability of return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) in the subsequent 2-minute resuscitation cycle. We conducted a multicenter retrospective study of adult OHCA patients from the NTUH-HYCARD database between 2016 and 2023. Event-level EtCO2 sequences were extracted from resuscitation records and standardized into 2-minute intervals for up to 30 minutes, consistent with Advanced Cardiac Life Support reassessment cycles. At each prediction time point, the model used EtCO2 values available from event onset to the current time point, without using future values. A two-layer long short-term memory model estimated the probability of ROSC in the subsequent cycle. Performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation at two levels: the event level (one prediction per event) and the cycle level (one prediction per 2-minute cycle). The final analysis included 1,651 event-level EtCO2 sequences from 1,480 patients; 583 events ended with ROSC. At the event level, the model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.876 (95% CI, 0.863-0.890) and a Brier score of 0.140 (95% CI, 0.131-0.149). When applied to every 2-minute cycle (17,029 prediction points; ROSC prevalence, 3.4%), the AUROC was 0.685 (95% CI, 0.664-0.706), and the model systematically overestimated ROSC probability (Brier score, 0.285; 95% CI, 0.268-0.303). Sequential EtCO2 dynamics showed good event-level discrimination for predicting ROSC in the subsequent cycle. When applied at each cycle, the model retained modest discrimination but overestimated ROSC probability, indicating that recalibration is required before cycle-to-cycle use.

articles.title: Neurological Outcomes of Rhythm Transitions in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest With Initial Nonshockable Rhythms: A Nationwide Population-Based Study.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the prognostic implications of rhythm transitions between asystole and pulseless electrical activity (PEA) in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with initial nonshockable rhythms. Nationwide population-based observational study. Nationwide OHCA Registry of South Korea, managed by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency. Consecutive adult (≥ 18 yr old) OHCA patients with nonshockable rhythms from January 1, 2016 to December 31, 2021. None. Patients were categorized into four groups based on rhythm changes during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR): asystole-to-asystole (A-A), asystole-to-PEA (A-P), PEA-to-asystole (P-A), and PEA-to-PEA (P-P). The primary outcome was good neurologic outcome at hospital discharge, defined as a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1-2. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to adjust for measured confounding. In the primary IPTW model, weighted risks of good neurologic outcome were 0.101% in A-A, 0.231% in A-P, 0.384% in P-A, and 0.874% in P-P. Compared with A-A, the odds of good neurologic outcome were higher in A-P (odds ratio [OR], 2.28; 95% CI, 1.78-2.93; risk difference [RD], 0.130 percentage points), P-A (OR, 3.80; 95% CI, 3.01-4.80; RD, 0.283 percentage points), and P-P (OR, 8.70; 95% CI, 6.98-10.83; RD, 0.773 percentage points). Compared with A-P, P-A had higher odds of good neurologic outcome (OR, 1.66; 95% CI, 1.39-1.99; RD, 0.153 percentage points). Asystole conversion to PEA during CPR was associated with a better neurologic outcome than persistent asystole. Although transitioning from PEA to asystole was associated with lower odds of a good outcome compared with persistent PEA, it was associated with a better outcome than A-P transitions. Recognizing these patterns may provide prognostic context beyond a single rhythm assessment.

articles.title: ECMO-Bridged Versus Elective LVAD Implantation: Comparable Long-Term Survival and Quality of Life in a 13-Year Single-Center Cohort.
articles.abstract: Background and Objectives: Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is an established rescue therapy for refractory cardiogenic shock. When weaning fails, urgent left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation under ongoing VA-ECMO support (a bridge-to-bridge strategy) is often the only path to survival. Whether this trajectory compromises long-term outcomes and quality of life (QoL) is unclear. Building on our group's previous report in a smaller institutional cohort, we now compare long-term survival and QoL between VA-ECMO-bridged and elective LVAD recipients in an expanded cohort with extended follow-up. Materials and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed all adult LVAD implantations at our institution between January 2012 and December 2024. Patients were grouped by urgency: VA-ECMO-bridged (urgent LVAD under ongoing VA-ECMO support) or elective (LVAD without prior mechanical circulatory support). LVAD or mechanical circulatory support device exchanges, post-cardiotomy cardiogenic shock, and pediatric cases were excluded. Survival was analyzed with the Kaplan-Meier method and the log-rank test. Quality of life was assessed prospectively with the EuroQol-5D-5L visual analogue scale and the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 at 3, 6 and 12 months and at the most recent follow-up. Results: Of 97 LVAD recipients, 38 (39%) were VA-ECMO-bridged, and 59 (61%) were electives. The bridged cohort was numerically younger (53.9 ± 14.3 vs. 57.9 ± 11.8 years, p = 0.16), with no difference in sex (78.9% vs. 88.1% male, p = 0.21) or etiology. Intensive care and hospital stays were significantly longer in the bridged group (33.6 vs. 12.6 days, p = 0.029; 58.1 vs. 32.8 days, p = 0.041). Crude mortality at last follow-up was 31.6% (12/38) versus 55.9% (33/59) over 37.5 ± 23.9 vs. 48.8 ± 38.0 months of follow-up; Kaplan-Meier survival did not differ between groups (log-rank p = 0.2310, 95% CI). Quality-of-life questionnaires were completed by 53 of 97 patients (54.6%). EQ-5D-5L visual analogue scale scores improved over the first year in both groups and were equivalent at last follow-up (66.9 ± 20 vs. 65.2 ± 20, p = 0.879); PHQ-9 indicated only mild depressive symptoms in both groups at long-term follow-up (6.0 ± 4.6 vs. 5.4 ± 5.2, p = 0.676). Conclusions: Among patients who survive LVAD implantation, VA-ECMO bridging was not associated with worse long-term survival or quality of life than elective LVAD, despite a markedly longer index hospitalization. This data should be read as showing acceptable outcomes in selected survivors rather than equivalence of an intention-to-bridge strategy, since patients who die on VA-ECMO before LVAD are not captured. Patient selection, rather than urgency itself, appears to drive outcomes.

articles.title: Cardiovascular disturbances and ward hypotension after major vascular surgery: a single-centre prospective cohort study.
articles.journal: Canadian journal of anaesthesia = Journal canadien d'anesthesie
articles.abstract: Postoperative hypotension can be caused by vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, severe hypovolemia, and obstruction. We sought to estimate the effects of these causes on the incidence of hypotension after major vascular surgery. We conducted a single-centre prospective cohort study of male and female adult patients undergoing major vascular surgery. We conducted point-of-care ultrasound and sidestream darkfield microscopy imaging to detect vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, severe hypovolemia, and obstruction. The primary outcome was hypotension (systolic blood pressure < 90 mm Hg or a vasopressor infusion) within 24 hr of surgery. We recruited 100 patients, of whom 89 had data available for analysis. Hypotension occurred in 20 participants (23%), vasodilation in 30 (34%), and myocardial dysfunction in 11 (12%). Severe hypovolemia and obstruction were not observed. The adjusted marginal risk difference of hypotension was 33% (95% confidence interval [CI], 14% to 53%; P < 0.001) for vasodilation and 41% (95% CI, 3% to 79%; P = 0.03) for myocardial dysfunction. Vasodilation increased the risk of intensive care unit admission by 27% (95% CI, 8% to 45%; P = 0.006) and of requiring a vasopressor infusion by 22% (95% CI, 4% to 39%; P = 0.02). Vasodilation and myocardial dysfunction increased the risk of postoperative hypotension, providing insight into the mechanistic development of postoperative hypotension. The absence of severe hypovolemia was surprising. Clinicians should assess for vasodilation and myocardial dysfunction as potential preludes to postoperative hypotension, potentially using point-of-care echocardiography and sidestream darkfield microscopy.

articles.title: Outcomes with Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis versus Mechanical Thrombectomy for Patients with Intermediate/High Risk Pulmonary Embolism: A Meta-Analysis of 24,090 Patients.
articles.abstract: Randomized trials comparing the outcomes with catheter-directed medical thrombolysis (CDT) versus mechanical thrombectomy (MT) for patients with intermediate/high risk pulmonary embolism (PE) are limited. This meta-analysis aimed to assess the clinical outcomes after CDT versus MT for patients with intermediate/high risk PE. Eligible studies compared CDT and MT for patients with intermediate/high risk PE underwent catheter-based therapies were retrieved from a comprehensive literature search for PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane CENTRAL through June 2026. Outcomes included all-cause mortality, major bleeding, and the length of intensive care unit (ICU) stay. Summary estimates were analyzed using a random effects model. A total of 18 studies (24,090 intermediate/high risk patients) were eligible for the analysis. CDT was associated with longer length of intensive care unit (ICU) stay (mean difference: 1.01 days, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.87-1.15) compared with MT. While there was no statistical difference between the two groups regarding the risk of all-cause mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.88, 95% CI 0.76-1.01, p = 0.068) and major bleeding (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.74-1.55, p = 0.705). Similarly, the incidence of other clinical outcomes; all-cause readmission, PE-related readmission, blood transfusion rates, length of hospital stay, cardiac arrest, and stroke, were similar between the two groups. Among patients with intermediate/high risk PE treated with catheter-based therapies, there was no difference regarding the clinical outcomes between CDT and MT, but CDT was associated with a longer ICU stay. Larger, well designed randomized trials are needed to confirm these findings.

articles.title: Local complications of peripheral intravenous vasopressor use with phentolamine as an antidote: a retrospective review.
articles.abstract: Prior studies have indicated that peripheral administration of vasopressors, particularly norepinephrine, can be considered safe, with local complications occurring in 0% to 1.8% of patients. Our study further explored the local skin complications from peripheral vasopressor administration treated with phentolamine in a large health care system. A retrospective chart review was performed on patients who received phentolamine for effects of local infiltration of pressors. Data were collected for demographics, vasopressor dose and duration of use, phentolamine dose and time after extravasation until administration, peripheral intravenous characteristics, as well as outcomes such as length of stay and mortality. Data on patients who did and did not require central venous catheter placement postextravasation were compared. Of 92 patients with infiltrated vasopressor intravenous access who required phentolamine, the mean age was 69, with 65% being female and a mean body mass index of 28 kg/m2. The most common sites of intravenous access were the antecubital fossa (33%) and forearm (27%). Mean number of hours prior to extravasation of peripheral vasopressors requiring phentolamine administration was 21 hours. Mean number of minutes prior to phentolamine administration after extravasation was 131 minutes. Seventy-six percent of patients did not any have significant ischemic tissue injury with extravasation, and 24% of patients had only minor bruising and erythema. Two significant reactions occurred, including deep vein thrombosis and local skin necrosis. Fifty-two percent of patients required a subsequent central venous line placement. The mean length of stay was 5.4 days in the intensive care unit and 11.8 days in the hospital, and in-patient mortality was 17%. In our large cohort of patients with extravasation from peripheral vasopressors managed with local phentolamine administration, severe tissue skin or soft tissue injury was rare.

articles.title: Transesophageal Echocardiography for Venous Gas Embolism During Ureteroscopic Instrument Exchange.
articles.abstract: Venous gas embolism is an uncommon but potentially catastrophic complication of endoscopic procedures. A 62-year-old man with bilateral urinary tract calculi, hydronephrosis, and renal insufficiency underwent right ureteroscopic treatment under general anesthesia. Approximately 40 min after surgery began, during exchange from a rigid to a flexible ureteroscope after placement of a ureteral access sheath, end-tidal carbon dioxide abruptly decreased to approximately 12 mmHg. The event was accompanied by an increase in peak airway pressure to 24 cmH2O, hypotension to 79/55 mmHg, progressive oxygen desaturation to 86%, and new atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 143 beats/min. Manual ventilation and lung auscultation did not identify an obvious airway cause. The procedure was stopped, 100% oxygen and positive end-expiratory pressure were applied, vasopressor support was initiated, and urgent transesophageal echocardiography was performed. The right ventricle was enlarged and full, with extensive gas-like echogenic material in the right heart and pulmonary artery. Serial echocardiography showed progressive reduction of the gas burden as hemodynamics stabilized. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit, extubated on postoperative day 2, and discharged on postoperative day 5. This case emphasizes the diagnostic value of an abrupt end-tidal carbon dioxide decrease combined with rescue transesophageal echocardiography when venous gas embolism is suspected during ureteroscopy.
articles.ai_summary: A 62‑year‑old man undergoing ureteroscopy developed sudden end‑tidal CO₂ drop, increased airway pressure, hypotension, desaturation, and atrial fibrillation. Urgent transesophageal echocardiography revealed extensive gas in the right heart and pulmonary artery, confirming venous gas embolism. The patient stabilized with supportive measures and was discharged after five days.
articles.ai_significance: This case demonstrates that venous gas embolism can present abruptly during ureteroscopic procedures and that transesophageal echocardiography can rapidly confirm the diagnosis and guide resuscitation.

articles.title: When the Filter Becomes the Source: POCUS Detection of Inferior Vena Cava Filter Thrombosis Extending Into the Right Atrium.
articles.abstract: Inferior vena cava (IVC) filters are used to prevent pulmonary embolism in patients with venous thromboembolism when anticoagulation is contraindicated. Although uncommon, filter thrombosis can result in thrombus propagation and potentially life-threatening embolic complications. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) provides a rapid bedside assessment of the heart, lungs, and may facilitate the prompt recognition of unexpected thromboembolic complications. A 43-year-old man with hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage was admitted to the intensive care unit requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support. Six days after admission, he developed sudden severe hypoxemia, tachycardia, and hypotension requiring reinitiation of norepinephrine. POCUS demonstrated bilateral anterior A-lines, left femoral and popliteal deep vein thrombosis, and preserved right ventricular (RV) function without echocardiographic evidence of RV strain. Catheter-based pulmonary angiography confirmed subocclusive thrombosis involving segmental branches of the right middle and lower lobes, which was treated with mechanical thromboaspiration, followed by IVC filter placement because anticoagulation was initially contraindicated. Four days later, he developed a new episode of acute hypoxemia despite remaining hemodynamically stable. Repeat POCUS demonstrated a large mobile thrombus in transit within the right atrium. Subcostal longitudinal imaging of the IVC demonstrated a large elongated thrombus attached to the IVC filter, with a freely mobile portion extending into the right atrium. Urgent mechanical thrombectomy and IVC filter replacement were performed. The new filter was positioned approximately 2 cm below the confluence of the hepatic veins with the inferior vena cava. Approximately 24 h later, follow-up POCUS showed no evidence of new thrombus formation. More than 2 weeks after admission, following a follow-up brain CT showing no significant progression of the intracerebral hemorrhage, anticoagulation with enoxaparin was initiated and progressively increased to a full therapeutic dose. This case highlights the value of POCUS for the prompt bedside recognition of an established and potentially life-threatening complication of IVC filter placement. Systematic bedside cardiac and venous ultrasound may identify thrombus propagation into the right atrium even in the absence of RV dilation or echocardiographic evidence of RV strain, facilitating timely endovascular intervention.
