First, we provide an overview of the interplay between patient and circuit related factors that determine brain perfusion and oxygen delivery in this critically ill patient population. Second, we highlight the importance of standardized multimodal neuromonitoring to detect evolving brain injury early and to guide individualized neurocritical care and ECLS management. Third, we identify modifiable ECLS factors and physiological targets which minimize secondary brain injury. We provide guidance on the titration of extracorporeal blood flow and blood pressure targets, the amount of sweep gas flow and oxygen fraction, temperature control and anticoagulation management. A comprehensive understanding of ECLS physiology and circuit-patient interactions, integrated with protocolized multimodal monitoring, enables individualized adjustment of modifiable ECLS settings to prevent or mitigate secondary brain injury.
articles.ai_summary: This review discusses how to prevent brain injury in patients on extracorporeal life support (ECLS) by optimizing brain perfusion and oxygen delivery. It highlights the importance of standardized multimodal neuromonitoring and individualized neurocritical care. The review provides guidance on adjusting ECLS settings to minimize secondary brain injury.
articles.ai_significance: Optimizing brain perfusion and preventing cerebral complications during ECLS is crucial for improving outcomes in critically ill patients, reducing mortality and long-term disability.

articles.title: SvO₂ response to red blood cell transfusion in cardiovascular surgical icu patients: a retrospective observational study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Red blood cell (RBC) transfusion decisions after cardiovascular surgery require integration of hemoglobin (Hb), hemodynamics, bleeding status, and oxygen supply-demand balance. Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO₂) reflects the global relationship between oxygen delivery and oxygen consumption, but an increase in SvO₂ does not necessarily indicate improved tissue oxygenation or clinical benefit. We evaluated acute SvO₂ changes after RBC transfusion in cardiovascular surgical ICU patients. METHODS: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of adult cardiovascular surgical ICU patients who received one RBC-equivalent transfusion with pre-transfusion Hb ≥ 7.5 g/dL and paired pre- and post-transfusion SvO₂ measurements. The primary outcome was an individual-level SvO₂ response, defined a priori as ΔSvO₂ ≥5% points from baseline to approximately 60 min after transfusion initiation. Multivariable regression was used to evaluate predictors selected a priori based on physiologic relevance to oxygen delivery and consumption. Receiver operating characteristic analysis was used to evaluate the discriminative ability of pre-transfusion SvO₂. RESULTS: 1,352 unique patients met the final inclusion criteria. Mean Hb increased from 9.82 ± 0.92 to 10.24 ± 0.98 g/dL, corresponding to a paired mean difference of 0.42 g/dL (95% CI, 0.38 to 0.46; P < 0.001). Mean SvO₂ changed minimally at the cohort level, from 73.79 ± 9.91% to 73.86 ± 9.37%, corresponding to a paired mean difference of 0.08% points (95% CI, -0.28 to 0.43; P = 0.671). Lower pre-transfusion SvO₂ was associated with a higher probability of an individual-level SvO₂ response. In multivariable logistic regression, pre-transfusion SvO₂ was associated with SvO₂ response (adjusted odds ratio, 0.89 per 1% increase; 95% confidence interval, 0.86-0.91; P < 0.001). Pre-transfusion SvO₂ showed moderate discrimination for SvO₂ response, with an area under the curve of 0.778 (95% confidence interval, 0.740-0.816). The Youden-derived cutoff was 69%, which should be interpreted as an exploratory predictor of acute SvO₂ rise rather than a transfusion trigger. CONCLUSIONS: Lower pre-transfusion SvO₂ was associated with acute individual-level SvO₂ increase after transfusion, but mean SvO₂ change was minimal. The association did not establish tissue oxygenation or clinical benefit and does not support using SvO₂, including the 69% cutoff, as a transfusion indication or trigger.
articles.ai_summary: Researchers studied how mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) changes after red blood cell transfusions in cardiovascular surgery patients. They found that lower pre-transfusion SvO2 levels were associated with an increase in SvO2, but overall SvO2 levels didn't improve much. SvO2 is not a reliable indicator of tissue oxygenation or clinical benefit.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings suggest that SvO2 should not be used as a transfusion trigger or indicator of tissue oxygenation in cardiovascular surgery patients.

articles.title: Neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest due to aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: a multicenter cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) due to aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) is rare but associated with extremely poor prognosis. Data on neurological outcomes and prognostic factors are limited. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective multicenter cohort study across 12 French neuro-ICUs including all adult patients admitted alive after OHCA-aSAH between 2014 and 2024. Demographics, cardiac arrest characteristics, aSAH severity, ICU management, and 6-month neurological outcomes (modified Rankin Scale, mRS) were collected. Firth penalized logistic regression was applied to explore predictors of favorable outcome. RESULTS: Among 15,907 SAH admissions, 164 patients had OHCA-aSAH. Median age was 54 [43-62] years; 47.5% were male. Only 8 patients (4.9%) achieved favorable outcome (mRS ≤ 3) while 156 (95.1%) had poor outcome (mRS ≥ 4), including 154 deaths (mRS 6). Low-flow duration tended to be shorter, epinephrine use lower, and pupillary abnormalities less frequent among survivors, although no independent statistical association could be confirmed. All patients receiving pre-hospital antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy (n = 14, 8.7%) had poor outcome. External ventricular drainage, ICP monitoring, and endovascular aneurysm treatment were more frequent, and ICU and hospital length of stay were longer, in survivors. One hundred and eight patients (65.8%) progressed to brain death within 1 [1-2] day. Penalized regression did not identify independent predictors of good outcome, though pupillary abnormalities and epinephrine use were associated with progression toward brain death. CONCLUSIONS: OHCA-aSAH carries a dismal prognosis, with < 5% achieving favorable neurological recovery. Selected patients may benefit from aggressive neurocritical care, and the high rate of brain death emphasizes the importance of organ donation pathways.

articles.title: Hyperlactatemia in sepsis and shock: a renal metabolic perspective.
articles.abstract: Hyperlactatemia is a frequent finding in critically ill patients and is traditionally interpreted as a marker of tissue hypoxia and anaerobic metabolism. However, in sepsis, septic shock, and other states of circulatory failure - including post-cardiac arrest syndrome - elevated lactate concentrations often occur despite preserved arterial oxygenation and adequate oxygen delivery. Increasing evidence indicates that lactate is a central metabolic intermediate whose circulating concentration reflects the balance between stress-induced production, cellular utilization, and organ clearance. While hepatic metabolism has long been considered the dominant pathway for lactate disposal, the kidneys - particularly proximal tubular cells - play a major and often underappreciated role in lactate utilization and clearance. Acute kidney injury (AKI), a common complication of sepsis, directly alters systemic lactate homeostasis. In this narrative review, we synthesize current knowledge on lactate biology in critical illness and examine the contribution of renal metabolism to hyperlactatemia in patients with sepsis-induced AKI. We propose that lactate should be interpreted as an integrated metabolic signal reflecting systemic stress and impaired clearance - rather than as a surrogate for hypoxia alone - with important implications for the management of septic AKI. The potential of urinary lactate as a marker of proximal tubular metabolic dysfunction and the emerging role of protein lactylation in modulating the inflammatory-to-reparative phenotypic transition are also discussed.
articles.ai_summary: Critically ill patients with sepsis and shock often have high lactate levels, but this doesn't always mean they're not getting enough oxygen. Lactate is a key metabolic intermediate that reflects the balance between production, utilization, and clearance. The kidneys play a significant role in lactate utilization and clearance, especially in patients with acute kidney injury.
articles.ai_significance: Understanding lactate biology in critical illness can help clinicians interpret lactate levels more accurately and develop more effective management strategies for septic acute kidney injury.

articles.title: Triple M overlap syndrome in the intensive care unit: differential diagnosis and management.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are increasingly used as first-line therapy for various malignancies and are associated with a growing spectrum of immune-related adverse events. While many toxicities are managed in the outpatient setting, a clinically significant subset progresses to life-threatening multisystem disease requiring intensive care. Among these, the Triple M overlap syndrome, characterized by concurrent myasthenia gravis-like disease, inflammatory myositis, and myocarditis, represents the most severe and lethal phenotype encountered in critical care. MAIN TEXT: Triple M overlap syndrome presents unique diagnostic and management challenges in critically ill patients. Clinical features frequently overlap with sepsis, pneumonia, thromboembolism, and cardiopulmonary disease, creating significant diagnostic uncertainty. In addition, traditional diagnostic tools such as myasthenia gravis antibody testing and early cardiac imaging may be normal or nondiagnostic early in the disease course. This review focuses on the recognition and management of Triple M overlap syndrome in the intensive care unit. We highlight key diagnostic pitfalls, including the frequent under-recognition of occult myocarditis and the limitations of electrophysiologic and serologic testing. A structured ICU-oriented approach is proposed, emphasizing early multisystem evaluation with creatine kinase, serial troponins, electrocardiography, and cardiac imaging, alongside concurrent assessment for infection. Management strategies include prompt discontinuation of ICIs, early initiation of corticosteroids, and escalation to intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange for severe neuromuscular involvement. Cardiac complications require close monitoring and early immunosuppression. Targeted therapies such as abatacept are discussed in the context of myocarditis, with current evidence limited primarily to cardiac involvement. This review emphasizes a practical ICU-oriented framework incorporating parallel evaluation for immune-mediated toxicity and infection in critically ill patients. CONCLUSION: Triple M overlap syndrome represents a high-risk and often underrecognized manifestation of ICI toxicity in critically ill patients. Early recognition, parallel evaluation for infection and immune-mediated disease, and coordinated multisystem management are essential to improving outcomes. Greater awareness and structured diagnostic approaches may reduce delays in treatment and associated mortality.

articles.title: Red Cell Transfusion in Critically Ill and Noncritically Ill Patients With Acute Myocardial Infarction and Anemia-A Subanalysis of the Myocardial Ischemia and Transfusion (MINT) Trial.
authors: Myocardial Ischemia and Transfusion (MINT) Trial Investigators
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Anemia is common in critically ill patients. In prior trials, a restrictive transfusion strategy was at least as effective as, and possibly superior to, a liberal strategy in critically ill adult patients. However, the Transfusion Requirements in Critical Care (TRICC) trial suggested that a restrictive strategy might be harmful in critically ill patients with ischemic heart disease. Our objective was to compare outcomes for restrictive and liberal transfusion strategies in critically ill and noncritically ill patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and anemia. DESIGN: Subgroup analysis of a parallel, two-arm randomized, controlled trial. SETTING: One hundred forty-four sites in the United States, Canada, France, Brazil, New Zealand, and Australia. PATIENTS: Adult patients with AMI and anemia enrolled in the Myocardial Ischemia and Transfusion (MINT) trial. Patients being treated in an ICU at randomization were considered critically ill. INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomly assigned to a restrictive (transfuse when hemoglobin < 7-8 g/dL) or liberal (transfuse when hemoglobin < 10 g/dL) transfusion strategy. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We determined the effect of transfusion strategy on death and the composite of death/myocardial infarction (MI) at 30 days among critically ill and noncritically ill patients. Of 3504 patients enrolled in MINT, 1679 (47.9%) were critically ill. At 30 days, death (11.9% vs. 6.5%) and death/MI (18.9% vs. 12.7%) occurred more frequently in critically ill patients compared with noncritically ill patients. A restrictive, compared with a liberal, transfusion strategy resulted in a nonsignificant increase in the risk of death by 9% (risk ratio [RR], 1.09; 95% CI, 0.77-1.54) and death/MI by 9% (RR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.85-1.38) in noncritically ill patients and a nonsignificant increase in the risk of death by 24% (RR, 1.24; 95% CI, 0.95-1.61; interaction p = 0.55) and death/MI by 21% (RR, 1.21; 95% CI, 0.99-1.47; interaction p = 0.52) in critically ill patients. CONCLUSIONS: There is no evidence that the overall MINT trial results, which generally favor a liberal transfusion strategy in AMI patients, apply differently to noncritically ill and critically ill patients.
articles.ai_summary: This study analyzed the effect of blood transfusion strategies in patients with acute myocardial infarction and anemia. It found that a restrictive transfusion strategy did not significantly reduce mortality in either critically ill or noncritically ill patients compared to a liberal strategy.
articles.ai_significance: Understanding the optimal blood transfusion strategy for critically ill patients with acute myocardial infarction and anemia is crucial for improving patient outcomes in the ICU.

articles.title: Compliance with the 2021 surviving sepsis campaign Hour-1 Bundle and impact on patient outcomes in a resource-limited setting: A quality improvement initiative in a referral hospital in Rwanda.
articles.abstract: Sepsis and septic shock are common life-threatening conditions associated with high mortality globally. Compliance with the Society of Critical Care Medicine's Hour-1 Bundle for sepsis management has the potential to improve outcome, but the bundle is infrequently applied in resource-constrained settings. We assessed level of compliance with the Hour-1 bundle among patients diagnosed with sepsis and septic shock at the Accident and Emergency Department (AED) or Intensive Care Unit (ICU) of University Teaching Hospital of Butare, Rwanda. We conducted training for nurses and doctors in the AED and ICU, with the goal of improving compliance. We re-assessed bundle compliance one month after the training. We used univariate and multivariate analyses to evaluate the association of compliance and fluid resuscitation with hospital mortality while adjusting for severity of illness and other covariates. Our finding showed that seventy-eight patients were enrolled during the pre-intervention period, and 82 in post-intervention. The overall compliance with at least 4 elements of the Hour-1 bundle before the intervention was 14%, and 76% after the intervention (p < 0.001). Mortality was lower in the post-intervention period than in the pre-intervention period (51.2% vs 74.4%; p = 0.003). Non-survivors had a significantly lower bundle compliance than survivors (35% vs 80%; adjusted OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.05-0.57; p = 0.004). Administered 2 liters of IV fluids and beyond during the first hour was independently associated with higher mortality (adjusted OR 19.38, 95% CI 5.63-66.75; p < 0.001). Findings from this Quality Improvement project suggest that compliance with the Hour-1 sepsis bundle in a resource-constrained setting can be improved with training, can improve outcome.. Administration of ≥2 liters during the first hour in those was independently associated with a higher in-hospital mortality, although bundle-compliant resuscitation was not. More research is needed, both on the implementation of sepsis bundles in resource-constrained settings, to assess if all bundle elements are as effective in these settings as recommended in the international guidelines.

articles.title: Anaphylactic shock caused by cefmetazole during induction of general anesthesia.
articles.journal: The journal of medical investigation : JMI
articles.abstract: A 52-year-old woman underwent bilateral mandibular wisdom tooth extraction under general anesthesia. Immediately after the intravenous administration of cefmetazole following anesthetic induction, she developed sudden hypotension, increased airway pressure, and decreased oxygen saturation. No cutaneous manifestations were initially observed, and hypotension was refractory to vasopressor therapy. Since anaphylactic shock was suspected, surgical drapes were removed, revealing generalized erythema. Intravenous adrenaline was promptly administered, which rapidly stabilized hemodynamics and the respiratory status. She was admitted to the intensive care unit for monitoring due to the risk of a biphasic reaction ; however, there was no recurrence and she was discharged on postoperative day two. Measurements of histamine and tryptase immediately after onset and 24 hours later confirmed anaphylactic shock. Subsequent prick and intradermal skin tests identified cefmetazole as the causative agent. Although anaphylactic shock due to cefmetazole is rare, this case highlights the potential of refractory hypotension as the initial manifestation even in the absence of skin symptoms. Under general anesthesia, skin findings may be concealed, potentially delaying a diagnosis. Therefore, anesthesiologists need to maintain a high index of suspicion for anaphylaxis in patients presenting with vasopressor-refractory shock following drug administration, regardless of cutaneous signs, and initiate prompt treatment with adrenaline. J. Med. Invest. 73 : 548-551, August, 2026.

articles.title: Early Identification of Sepsis-induced Acute Kidney Injury Utilizing NGAL, Cystatin C, Urine Output, and Serum Creatinine in a Porcine ( Sus scrofa) Model of Septic Shock: A comparative Study of Fluid and Vasopressor Strategies.
articles.abstract: Sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI) contributes significantly to ICU morbidity and mortality, yet early detection remains challenging due to the delayed response of conventional markers such as serum creatinine and urine output. This study aimed to evaluate the temporal patterns of early renal biomarkers-neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL) and cystatin C-compared with conventional functional markers in a porcine model of septic shock under three fluid and vasopressor resuscitation strategies. In a randomized experimental study, six Sus scrofa pigs underwent standardized septic shock induction and were allocated into three resuscitation groups: Ringer's lactate (30 mL/kg), fluid combined with early norepinephrine infusion, or early norepinephrine with maintenance fluids. Plasma NGAL, cystatin C, serum creatinine, and ultrasonographically assessed urine dynamics were measured sequentially alongside continuous hemodynamic monitoring. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures and nonparametric tests (p < 0.05). NGAL and cystatin C exhibited numerical temporal fluctuations across observation periods and differing trajectories among resuscitation strategies. Post-intervention decreases in NGAL and cystatin C coccurred in fluid-based groups, whereas early norepinephrine administration was followed by numerical increases. However, neither between-group nor within-group temporal changes reached statistical significance for NGAL, cystatin C, or serum creatinine. In this exploratory pilot study, NGAL and cystatin C displayed numerical temporal shifts during septic shock; however, these changes lacked statistical significance and cannot establish early SA-AKI detection. Given the unstandardized urine output criteria and non-significant creatinine kinetics, these findings represent exploratory evidence of renal biomarker dynamics rather than definitive diagnostic proof of SA-AKI.

articles.title: Escaping the ICU: A Gamified Escape Room for Septic Shock Education in Internal Medicine Residency.
articles.journal: MedEdPORTAL : the journal of teaching and learning resources
articles.abstract: Traditional didactic methods inadequately replicate the cognitive load and collaborative demands of critical care practice. This gap leaves residents entering high-acuity environments underprepared and with lower clinical confidence, precisely when patients need it most. We developed a gamified intensive care unit (ICU) escape room to address this gap in team-based critical care education for postgraduate year 1 (PGY-1) internal medicine residents with limited ICU exposure. We implemented the activity during a protected 4-hour academic half-day at the University of Hawai'i Internal Medicine Residency Program. Twenty-four PGY-1 residents participated in teams of 6 to 8 across 5 interconnected stations covering septic shock recognition, hemodynamic resuscitation, procedural decision-making, antimicrobial management, and complication mitigation. We assessed objective knowledge using a 10-item pre-post multiple-choice question assessment and self-reported confidence across 11 domains using 5-point Likert scales. Knowledge scores improved significantly (mean [SD]: pre, 6.00 [1.84] vs post, 7.71 [1.83]; P < .001; r = 0.67). Confidence improved across all 11 domains with moderate-to-large effect sizes (r = 0.58-0.71). Engagement was high: 100% reported enjoyment, 96% reported active concept recall, and 88% reported that time pressure did not impair concentration. Teamwork was rated favorably by 83% to 96% of participants. A gamified ICU escape room demonstrated significant gains in knowledge and confidence. Key lessons include the value of pilot testing, culturally resonant narrative framing, and a prescripted facilitator hint system. These findings support using gamified escape rooms as a feasible, low-resource approach to strengthen critical care readiness in residency training.

articles.title: Interpretable machine learning model for predicting major adverse kidney events within 30 days in critically ill patients with acute pancreatitis: development and validation in multicenter cohorts.
articles.abstract: Acute kidney injury is a frequent and serious complication of acute pancreatitis (AP), contributing to increased mortality and healthcare burden. Major adverse kidney events within 30 days (MAKE30) constitute a patient-centered composite endpoint for assessing kidney outcomes. However, effective tools for identifying patients at high risk of MAKE30 are lacking. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an interpretable machine learning model for predicting MAKE30 in critically ill patients with AP. Three clinical datasets were used. MIMIC-IV served as the development cohort, and external validation used eICU-CRD and a retrospective cohort from the Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University (AHSWMU). Feature selection combined least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression, the Boruta algorithm, and multivariable logistic regression. Seven machine learning algorithms were used to develop prediction models. Model performance was assessed in terms of discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) were used to interpret and visualize the final model. A total of 1,574 patients with AP from multiple centers were included. Six predictors were selected for model development: serum creatinine, red cell distribution width, albumin, aspartate aminotransferase, vasopressor use, and total bilirubin. The random forest model demonstrated favorable overall performance, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.863 in the internal validation cohort. Performance was consistent across the two independent external validation cohorts, with AUCs of 0.840 in eICU-CRD and 0.848 in AHSWMU. A web-based clinical risk calculator was developed to facilitate model use in clinical practice. The model developed in this study exhibited favorable performance and robust generalizability in predicting MAKE30 among critically ill patients with AP, providing reliable digital decision support for early risk stratification and individualized intervention strategies.

articles.title: Identification of hemodynamic sub-phenotypes in septic shock using joint trajectory modeling of vasopressor requirements and fluid accumulation: a MIMIC-IV database study.
articles.abstract: Patients with septic shock in critical care medicine often exhibit significant individual variability. Previous clinical assessments have largely relied on static severity scores at a single point in time to predict patient prognosis; however, this approach struggles to reflect the constantly changing clinical trajectory of patients during the resuscitation process. In recent years, research has gradually shifted from static assessments to dynamic observations. Dynamic trajectory observations may help characterize clinical heterogeneity and provide complementary prognostic information beyond static severity scores. This study is a retrospective cohort study based on the MIMIC-IV database, which included a total of 2,909 patients with septic shock meeting the Sepsis-3 criteria. We used a latent class mixture model to observe the dynamic trajectories of norepinephrine equivalents and cumulative fluid balance during the first 72 h following the onset of shock. Landmark analysis was used to assess changes in patient mortality risk before and after 72 h, and the Net Reclassification Improvement (NRI) and Integrated Discrimination Improvement (IDI) indices were employed to evaluate the improvement in model performance following the incorporation of dynamic trajectories. Because trajectory classification required data from the full 72-h observation window, the resulting classes could not be determined at shock onset and were therefore treated as retrospective descriptions of early resuscitation patterns rather than real-time predictors. Ultimately, four trajectory subtypes with distinct hemodynamic characteristics were identified. Class 1 presented with severe initial metabolic acidosis and required high-dose vasoactive agents, but demonstrated rapid subsequent improvement and a favorable overall prognosis. Class 2 was characterized by a less favorable clinical course and had the highest observed mortality rate (57.3%). Class 3, which constituted the largest proportion, recovered relatively quickly, with a rapid reversal of circulatory status and the best clinical outcomes. Class 4 was characterized by relatively low early vasopressor requirements, while its mortality hazard was higher among patients who survived beyond 72 h. The possibility of impaired cardiac reserve may help explain this pattern, although cardiac function was not directly assessed in this study. The combined model showed a modest improvement in discrimination over the baseline SOFA model, with a bootstrap-corrected AUROC increase of 0.010. The continuous NRI was 0.286 and the IDI was 0.016. Among patients initially classified as moderate risk by the SOFA score, 114 were reclassified into the high-risk category by the combined model, with an observed mortality rate of 61.4% in this subgroup. Joint trajectories of vasopressor requirements and fluid accumulation revealed heterogeneity in early resuscitation patterns among patients with septic shock. The combined model showed a modest improvement in discrimination beyond the baseline SOFA score, and trajectory information may provide complementary prognostic information. However, external validation and prospective evaluation are required to determine its clinical utility.

articles.title: Forty-eight-hour coagulation-perfusion recovery as a bedside reassessment framework in critical illness: a multidatabase landmark cohort study.
articles.abstract: The clinical course during initial intensive care unit (ICU) care provides information that admission severity scores do not directly describe. In this study, we evaluated a fixed 48 h reassessment framework that combines the coagulation and perfusion recovery status with the timing of observed recovery. We performed a retrospective 48 h landmark cohort study using MIMIC-IV (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV) and eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD). Adults who experienced their first ICU stays with an ICU length of stay of at least 48 h and survival to the landmark were included. In the primary MIMIC-IV sepsis analysis, coagulation recovery was defined by platelet count and international normalized ratio changes or normalization, and perfusion recovery was defined by lactate clearance or normalization. Trauma and high-coverage validation analyses used hemodynamic perfusion recovery based on the mean arterial pressure and/or shock index. Recovery speed was classified as rapid recovery, delayed recovery, persistent non-recovery, or progressive worsening. In MIMIC-IV sepsis, coagulation-only recovery (coagulation recovered but perfusion did not) and dual non-recovery were associated with a higher postlandmark 28-day mortality rate than dual recovery [adjusted odds ratios, 2.54 (95% CI, 2.16-3.00) and 2.62 (95% CI, 2.15-3.19)]. The mortality rate ranged from 18.8% with rapid recovery to 30.5% with progressive worsening. Associations persisted when repeated measurements were required. In a same-sample comparison, dynamic Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) plus lactate recovery and dynamic SOFA plus the joint phenotype had apparent area under the receiver operating characteristic curves of 0.7033 and 0.7038, respectively (DeLong's P = 0.7027; likelihood-ratio P = 0.3627). The MIMIC-IV trauma hemodynamic adaptation showed a risk gradient; eICU trauma candidates showed a non-monotonic pattern (ordinal trend P = 0.077). A fixed 48 h reassessment organizes observed coagulation and perfusion response into clinically interpretable recovery states. The sepsis findings support risk stratification among patients undergoing serial monitoring, with perfusion non-recovery carrying the clearest mortality association. This framework describes prognosis under ICU care rather than prescribing treatment; selective measurement and differences between validation cohorts define its present scope.

articles.title: Transportability, calibration, and alert burden of an hourly model for documented continuous vasopressor initiation: a retrospective three-database study.
articles.abstract: Clinical prediction models may retain discrimination across settings while losing probability calibration or a workable alert policy. We evaluated this distinction for hourly prediction of documented continuous vasopressor initiation. We used MIMIC-IV v3.1, eICU-CRD v2.0, and SICdb v1.0.8. Untreated adult stays contributed hourly landmarks from ICU hour 6 through 24 while still under observation. The outcome was first initiation within six hours and before ICU/unit exit; exit without initiation remained an operational non-event. Histogram-based gradient boosting (HGB) and logistic regression were fitted and selected in patient-disjoint MIMIC-IV reference-period groups. Evaluation used a separate MIMIC-IV group and two external databases. Source observations were range-checked before predictor summarization; SICdb hourly aggregates were withheld until the source hour had ended. These retrospective timing rules did not verify availability in live clinical information systems. Evaluation included 165,204 landmarks from 9,534 MIMIC-IV reference-period test stays; 2,745,224 landmarks from 168,636 eICU-CRD stays; 58,756 landmarks from 3,997 SICdb stays. HGB AUROCs were 0.770, 0.849, 0.695, respectively. Across 100 identifier-disjoint local-update splits, median Brier skill relative to a calibration-subset constant forecast was -0.168, -0.005, 0.023 before updating and 0.019, 0.025, 0.028 after full logistic recalibration. With thresholds targeting five raw alerts per 100 calibration rows, event detection after six-hour suppression was 0.406, 0.510, 0.275; false emitted alerts were 1.64, 1.52, 1.51 per 100 evaluation rows. Thresholds targeting 80% raw landmark sensitivity detected 0.885, 0.873, 0.883 of eligible events after suppression, while 63.8%, 50.7%, 86.9% of event-free stays received at least one false alert. Discrimination transferred unevenly, while calibration and alert performance remained setting-dependent. The evaluated model and alert policies are not ready for clinical deployment. Offline assessment against prespecified clinical criteria should precede any prospective silent evaluation.

articles.title: Interpretable machine learning for predicting 28-day mortality after cervical spinal cord injury: development and external validation.
articles.abstract: Cervical spinal cord injury (cSCI) is associated with substantial early mortality. We aimed to develop and externally validate an exploratory machine learning model for predicting 28-day mortality in critically ill patients with cSCI. This retrospective study used 232 patients from MIMIC-IV for development and 210 patients from the Second Hospital of Shanxi Medical University for external validation. The development cohort was divided into training and internal test sets at a stratified 70:30 ratio. Within ten-fold cross-validation repeated five times in the training partition, recursive feature elimination (RFE) and Boruta were applied independently, with their intersection used for feature selection; synthetic minority over-sampling was confined to each training fold. Eight algorithms were compared using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and exploratory decision curve analysis. An additional analysis of saved support vector machine (SVM) probability outputs assessed calibration. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) described model predictions. The SVM had the highest observed AUC among the evaluated models in the internal test cohort, 0.956 (95% CI, 0.895-1.000), and external cohort, 0.738 (95% CI, 0.664-0.812). The final training-set selection comprised APACHE II, APS III, temperature, age, glucose, bicarbonate, base excess, norepinephrine use, arterial pH, heart rate, and lactate. The SVM showed potential prognostic utility in the studied ICU populations. Prospective multicenter validation, confirmation of probability calibration, and assessment of clinical impact are needed before routine clinical implementation.

articles.title: Early systolic blood pressure trajectories and risks of 30-day mortality and new-onset atrial fibrillation in critically ill patients receiving dialysis: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: ObjectiveTo identify early systolic blood pressure (SBP) trajectory patterns and examine their associations with 30-day mortality and new-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) in critically ill patients receiving dialysis.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study included 2,716 dialysis patients from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database. Latent class trajectory modeling was applied to serial systolic blood pressure (SBP) measurements during the first 24 hours of intensive care unit admission. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was NOAF. Multivariable Cox and logistic regression models assessed trajectory-outcome associations, and interaction analyses evaluated the modifying effect of subgroups.ResultsFour model-derived SBP trajectory classes were identified: persistently-low (Class 1, 59.5%), moderate-declining (Class 2, 23.4%), high-dip-rebound (Class 3, 10.8%), and low-rise-fall (Class 4, 6.3%). Compared with Class 1, Classes 2 and 3 had lower adjusted hazards of 30-day mortality (Class 2: HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.41-0.61; p<0.001; Class 3: HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.48-0.81; p<0.001) and lower odds of NOAF (Class 2: OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.21-0.55; p<0.001; Class 3: OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.23-0.80; p=0.010). Class 4 showed no significant overall association with mortality (HR 1.12, 95% CI 0.86-1.47; p=0.390) or NOAF (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.43-1.69; p=0.724). In time-varying analyses, Class 2 was associated with lower mortality at all assessed timepoints and Class 3 at days 7, 14, and 28. Class 4 showed higher mortality at day 2 and lower mortality at day 28 relative to Class 1. Exploratory analyses showed a significant interaction between SBP trajectory class and vasoactive-agent use for 30-day mortality, but not for NOAF.ConclusionsEarly SBP trajectory patterns were associated with 30-day mortality and subsequent NOAF in critically ill patients receiving dialysis. These observational findings do not establish causality or validated incremental predictive value.

articles.title: Association between geriatric nutritional risk index and prognosis of patients with cardiac arrest: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: ObjectivesThe aim of this study was to examine the association between Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI) and prognosis of patients with cardiac arrest (CA).MethodsThis retrospective cohort study included 650 patients from the MIMIC-IV database, with the GNRI, a composite index of nutritional risk and physiological vulnerability, calculated within 24 hours of ICU admission. The primary endpoints were 30-, 90-, and 365-day mortality. We assessed the association between GNRI and mortality using Kaplan-Meier curves, multivariable Cox regression, and restricted cubic splines, followed by propensity score matching, subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses and exploratory decomposition analyses. A nomogram incorporating GNRI and LASSO-identified predictors was developed to predict 365-day mortality, with performance evaluated using ROC curves, calibration plots, decision curve analysis, and internal bootstrap validation. The model was additionally applied to the eICU database in an exploratory cross-outcome transportability analysis.ResultsKaplan-Meier analysis showed that lower GNRI was associated with higher all-cause mortality at 30, 90, and 365 days (log-rank P < 0.05 for all). After multivariable adjustment, the hazard ratios per one-unit increase in GNRI were similar in magnitude and direction at the three time points. Exploratory decomposition analyses indicated that BUN, INR and bicarbonate may account for part of this association. The combined nomogram showed moderate discrimination for 365-day mortality with acceptable calibration and clinical utility, although GNRI added little incremental discrimination beyond the five other predictors. Discrimination for in-hospital mortality was similar in a cross-outcome transportability analysis in eICU.ConclusionsA lower GNRI at ICU admission was associated with higher all-cause mortality after CA, with similar effect estimates across 30, 90 and 365 days. The combined nomogram offered moderate discrimination for long-term mortality, although GNRI contributed little incremental information beyond conventional predictors, and these findings require validation in cohorts with complete nutritional data.

articles.title: Consent for intensive care research involving adults who lack decision-making capacity: A jurisdictional analysis of Australia's fragmented framework.
articles.journal: Critical care and resuscitation : journal of the Australasian Academy of Critical Care Medicine
articles.abstract: Critically ill adults frequently cannot consent to research because of sedation, delirium, shock or mechanical ventilation, yet safe intensive care depends on evidence generated in this population; several treatments once regarded as standard care proved harmful when finally tested in randomised trials. The ethical framework for enrolling adults who lack decision-making capacity is national-the National Health and Medical Research Council National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research (2025), in effect since 23 June 2026-but legal authority for substitute consent is conferred by eight state and territory statutes that differ in terminology, in decision-maker hierarchies, in whether they address research at all, and whether they permit enrolment in an emergency. Mapping four representative study archetypes across all eight jurisdictions shows that the lawful basis for enrolling the same patient shifts with study design as much as with geography; differing statutory definitions, tribunal involvement and the transition to the 2025 National Statement produce material and avoidable inconsistency. Contemporary Australian intensive care trials show that practice has converged on the National Statement while the underlying legislation has not; the resulting inconsistency risks inequity, underrepresentation of critically ill patients, and bias in the evidence generated. We set out principles for reform (Box 1): nationally consistent framing of substitute consent for research-common terminology and legal principles, an explicit emergency-research pathway in every jurisdiction, and consistent interpretation within each jurisdiction-developed with consumers and with the clinicians and clinical research nurses who obtain consent, and taken forward with formal endorsement from the relevant professional bodies.

articles.title: Global Leadership Initiative on a Malnutrition-Based Muscle Assessment Using Multiple Methods in Critically Ill Patients: A Prospective Observational Study.
articles.abstract: BackgroundMuscle mass assessment is integral to the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) for critically ill patients. Despite its importance, an optimal muscle volume assessment has yet to be established. We herein performed various muscle volume and nutritional assessments and conducted an exploratory evaluation of muscle volume assessment methods that may be clinically meaningful for critically ill patients.MethodsThis single-center prospective cohort enrolled adults expected to require mechanical ventilation for >2 days who ambulated independently before hospitalization. Computed tomography (CT)-derived total skeletal muscle mass at third lumbar vertebra (CT-MM) from retrospectively reviewed scans served as the reference. Within 24 h of intensive care unit (ICU) admission, we measured mid-upper arm circumference (AC), calf circumference, bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA)-derived fat-free muscle volume and intracellular water-based muscle volume (BIA-Muscle-ICW), femoral cross-sectional area, ultrasound-derived femoral muscle thickness (ultrasound-FMT), ultrasound-derived upper-limb muscle thickness, and resting energy expenditure. Malnutrition followed GLIM. Reduced muscle mass used the CT-MM index.ResultsFifty-two patients were included, 13 with GLIM-defined malnutrition. BIA-Muscle-ICW correlated most strongly with CT-MM (r = 0.80, p < 0.001). The other measures also correlated consistently, and all intercorrelated. For CT-defined sarcopenia, ultrasound-FMT index (AUC = 0.88), BIA-Muscle-ICW index (AUC = 0.83), and AC (AUC = 0.85) demonstrated good discrimination. Additionally, BIA-Muscle-ICW correlated most strongly with resting energy expenditure (r = 0.61, p < 0.001).ConclusionThe muscle volume indices assessed herein mutually correlated in critically ill patients, suggesting the potential of incorporating these measures, particularly BIA-Muscle-ICW, into initial GLIM at ICU admission. BIA-Muscle-ICW index, ultrasound-FMT index, and AC demonstrated strong discriminative performance for diagnosing sarcopenia.

articles.title: The Role of Diagnostic Tools in the Management of Ventilator Associated Lower Respiratory Tract Infections.
articles.journal: Seminars in respiratory and critical care medicine
articles.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) remains a leading healthcare-associated infection in intensive care units and is closely associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation, excessive antimicrobial exposure, higher costs, and poor clinical outcomes. Despite decades of clinical trials and guideline development, bedside diagnosis remains limited by the absence of a biological reference standard. Conventional criteria combine nonspecific clinical, radiographic, and microbiological findings and cannot reliably distinguish parenchymal infection from airway colonization, endotracheal tube biofilm, or sterile pulmonary inflammation. Syndromic multiplex polymerase chain reaction panels, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, and host response profiling have greatly increased analytical sensitivity and shortened the time to microbiological information. They have also exposed the amount of microbial and inflammatory noise present in the ventilated airway. Detection of an organism, a resistance determinant, or systemic inflammation does not by itself establish causality. This review examines the strengths and limitations of clinical scores, imaging, respiratory sampling, conventional culture, rapid molecular assays, antimicrobial resistance testing, systemic and alveolar biomarkers, host transcriptomics, breath analysis, and artificial intelligence-based models. It proposes that VAP should be approached as a time-updated probability of tissue invasive infection rather than a binary diagnosis. A practical host-pathogen attribution framework should integrate the timing and trajectory of respiratory deterioration, specimen quality, relative pathogen burden and dominance, resistance and virulence signals, local and systemic host responses, prior antimicrobial exposure, and competing diagnoses. Diagnostic tests should be ordered only when a predefined management decision is linked to the result, followed by structured reassessment at 48 to 72 hours. This approach may improve antimicrobial targeting while reducing treatment of colonization and other noninfectious mimics.

articles.title: Bedside ECMO Cannulation by Intensivists and Emergency Physicians.
articles.abstract: The number of centers capable of initiating extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for critically ill patients with refractory cardiac or respiratory failure is expanding. Historically, patients were taken to the operating room or catheterization laboratory for ECMO cannulation by cardiothoracic surgeons and perfusionists. More recently, non-surgeons who have undergone specialized training are performing percutaneous ECMO cannulation and initiation of support at the bedside at some centers. This approach is attractive, in part, because of the timely initiation of ECMO and avoidance of the risk of patient deterioration during transport to a procedural area. The purpose of this article is to provide a roadmap for intensivists and emergency physicians to lead ECMO bedside procedures including veno-venous (VV), veno-arterial (VA), and hybrid veno-arteriovenous (V-AV) cannulation at ECMO-capable centers. These procedures demand cognitive and technical skills that are already foundational to critical care practice, including vascular access guided by point-of-care ultrasound and leadership during a dynamic resuscitation. A team-based approach to bedside ECMO cannulation is presented and illustrated with figures and video, including preparation, procedural execution, subsequent patient management, and programmatic considerations such as training and credentialing requirements.

articles.title: Liberation from Veno-venous Extracorporeal Life Support (VV-ECLS) for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): the Liberate VV-ECLS study: an international survey.
articles.abstract: The use of veno-venous extracorporeal life support (VV-ECLS) for severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) has increased substantially worldwide. However, approaches to liberation from extracorporeal support remain poorly defined, with no standardized protocols or validated readiness criteria. What are the global practices for VV-ECLS liberation among Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) centers? Where is there variability in readiness assessment, liberation strategies, and use of standardized protocols? We formulated a cross-sectional survey of 25 questions regarding liberation practices among ECLS providers. Questions focused on assessed parameters for readiness to liberate, determination of liberation success, and strategies to optimize it. Surveys were distributed electronically to 765 institutions globally registered with ELSO between July 1st and Aug 15th, 2022. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize responses. Of 765 centers contacted, 340 (44%) responded, with 209 (61%) reporting use of VV-ECLS. Most centers were adult-focused, intensivist-led programs with moderate annual volumes. Most respondents (58%) prioritized VV-ECLS liberation before liberation from mechanical ventilation. Readiness for liberation was most determined by improvement in oxygenation under lung-protective ventilation (92%) and respiratory system compliance (90%), while fewer centers used inspiratory effort indices (34%). Liberation strategies were heterogeneous, with progressive reduction of sweep gas flow being most common (40%). Liberation trial duration varied widely (median 120 minutes; mean 497 ± 635 minutes), and most centers performed one trial per day. Arterial blood gas abnormalities (90%) and clinical signs of respiratory distress were the primary indicators of liberation failure. Only 42% of centers reported using a formal liberation protocol. VV-ECLS liberation practices vary substantially across centers and are largely guided by institutional experience rather than standardized evidence. These findings highlight the need for validated physiologic predictors and protocolized strategies to optimize safe and timely liberation from VV-ECLS.

articles.title: The Current State of Ventilator Liberation Practices and Outcomes in the United States-A Report From the Ventilator Liberation For Kids (VentLib4Kids) Collaborative.
articles.journal: Pediatric critical care medicine : a journal of the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies
articles.abstract: Describe and explore interunit baseline ventilator liberation practices and outcomes related to the 2023 Pediatric Ventilator Liberation Guidelines within the original cohort of Ventilation Liberation For Kids (VentLib4Kids) Collaborative units. Observational cohort study. Nineteen VentLib4Kids ICUs in the United States (13 general medical/surgical, five cardiovascular, and one mixed). First planned extubation attempt where code status allowed reintubation in patients younger than 19 years old, endotracheally intubated for any indication between July 1, 2023, and June 30, 2024. None. A total of 2315 ventilator courses were included. Most were 28 days to younger than 6 years old (65.5%) and had a lower respiratory infection diagnosis (23.8%). Prematurity (13.2%) was the most common comorbidity. Spontaneous breathing trial exposure demonstrated the highest guideline concordance at 74.6% (median; interunit range [IUR], 49.6-100%), whereas maximal inspiratory pressure testing was lowest (3.7%; IUR, 0-62.4%). Most courses (55.5%; IUR, 19.8-99%) included an air leak test. Among those without an air leak noted or greater than 25 cmH2O, 70.1% were exposed to dexamethasone in concordance with the guidelines. Initiation of dexamethasone greater than or equal to 6 hours before extubation predominated (81.1%) at a median dose of 0.5 mg/kg/dose in exposed groups. Planned postextubation high-flow nasal cannula (44.3%) and bilevel positive airway pressure (18.6%) were most common. Unit-level use of any planned postextubation noninvasive respiratory support ranged from 20.6% to 100%. Among infants, planned continuous positive airway pressure was used in 6.7% of subjects. Among all courses, 10.4% (IUR, 4.5-19.2%) ended with extubation failure (reintubation within 48 hr). Baseline VentLib4Kids practices demonstrate varying degrees of concordance with guideline recommendations along with significant interunit variation. These results align with prior international survey data and support the need for structured, multicenter quality improvement and guideline implementation strategies.

articles.title: Integrating Glycemic Variability and Stress Hyperglycemia Ratio to Stratify Mortality Risk in Patients with Sepsis-Associated AKI.
articles.abstract: BackgroundSepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI) is a common and severe complication in intensive care units. Although glycemic variability (GV) and stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR) are associated with adverse outcomes in critical illness, their combined prognostic value in SA-AKI remains unclear.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study included patients with SA-AKI from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database. The primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess associations of GV and SHR with mortality. Predictive performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis.ResultsA total of 2638 patients were included. Both GV and SHR were independently associated with increased risks of in-hospital and 1-year mortality. Patients with concomitantly high GV and SHR had the highest mortality risk (OR 1.754, 95% CI 1.321-2.329, P < .001; HR 1.340, 95% CI 1.124-1.598, P = .001). The combined GV-SHR model yielded slightly higher AUCs than either marker alone, with values of 0.700 for in-hospital mortality and 0.708 for 1-year mortality.ConclusionCombined assessment of GV and SHR improves mortality risk stratification in critically ill patients with SA-AKI and may facilitate early identification of high-risk patients.

articles.title: Should ventilatory efficiency be considered when trading tidal volume against respiratory rate? Author's reply.
The path towards precision transfusion medicine in critical care: focus on patient physiology, not only on study populations.
ICU Mortality Associated With Clinically Important Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Multistate Analysis.
articles.abstract: Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding may increase mortality and time to discharge from the ICU. Conventional analyses ignore timing and treat bleeding as a binary event. We evaluated the association between time-dependent clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding and ICU mortality. A multicenter cohort study using data from an international stress ulcer prophylaxis trial. A total of 4821 invasively ventilated adult participants. None. A multistate model was specified with two transient ICU states (bleed-free and post-bleed) and four absorbing states (ICU discharge or death, each with or without bleeding). The Aalen-Johansen method was used to estimate transition and state occupancy probabilities and to describe risks of different clinical courses. Follow-up was censored at 90 days. We fit two Cox models for time to death in the ICU regressing on time-dependent bleeding history while adjusting for age, sex, baseline Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score, admission category (medical/surgical/trauma), vasopressor/inotrope use and renal replacement therapy on study day 1 and randomized allocation of pantoprazole or placebo; a second model also adjusted for time-dependent covariates of advanced life support (invasive mechanical ventilation, vasopressor/inotrope use, and renal replacement therapy). Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding developed in 104 patients (2.2%) in the ICU. Median ICU length of stay for those who experienced bleeding was 19 days (interquartile range [IQR], 11-30 d) vs. 9 days (IQR, 5-15 d) for those who did not. Accounting for immortal time bias, the time-dependent indicator of clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding was associated with increased ICU mortality (hazard ratio, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.13-2.15). At any time, patients who experienced bleeding had approximately 1.6 times the hazard of ICU mortality compared with those without a history of bleeding. Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding as a time-dependent event is associated with an increased risk of ICU mortality.

articles.title: High-Flow Nasal Cannula Versus Conventional Oxygen Therapy in Adults With De Novo Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis With Trial Sequential Analysis.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the efficacy of high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) compared with conventional oxygen therapy (COT) in adults with de novo acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) using a meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA). MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from database inception to April 7, 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing HFNC with COT in adults with de novo AHRF. Two investigators independently performed study selection, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and certainty assessment, with discrepancies resolved through discussion. A total of 13 RCTs involving 4294 patients were included in the analysis. Compared with COT, HFNC was associated with a lower risk of intubation (Risk ratio [RR], 0.88; 95% CI, 0.78-0.99; low certainty), but not mortality (RR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.83-1.10; moderate certainty). TSA indicated that the cumulative evidence was insufficient to establish a conclusive effect for either outcome. Although HFNC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in hospital length of stay (mean difference, -0.84 d; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.43; low certainty), the clinical importance of this reduction remains uncertain. No significant differences were observed in escalation of therapy (RR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.75-1.01; very low certainty), ICU admission (RR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.50-1.39; very low certainty), or ICU length of stay (mean difference, -0.10 d; 95% CI, -0.82 to 0.61; very low certainty). In adults with de novo AHRF, HFNC may reduce the need for endotracheal intubation but probably does not improve survival compared with COT.

articles.title: Multiplex PCR in suspected ventilator-associated pneumonia: for which settings, and at what price?
Opioid-Sparing Pain Control in Lung Transplantation: A Single-Center Experience with Intraoperative Intercostal Nerve Cryoablation.
articles.abstract: Postoperative pain following lung transplantation is substantial and contributes to opioid exposure, delirium risk, and prolonged recovery. We evaluated the impact of intraoperative intercostal nerve cryoablation on postoperative opioid use, delirium incidence, and early clinical outcomes. We conducted a single-center retrospective matched cohort study of adult lung transplant recipients. Patients who underwent intraoperative intercostal nerve cryoablation (intervention) were compared with a historical matched cohort of recipients who did not undergo cryoablation (control). The primary outcome was cumulative opioid use, measured in oral morphine milligram equivalents (MME), during the first 14 postoperative days. Secondary outcomes included delirium incidence, ventilator days, intensive care unit and hospital lengths of stay, and early postoperative complications. The study included 19 patients in the cryoablation group and 38 matched controls. Cryoablation was associated with a reduction in cumulative opioid use through postoperative day 14 (428 MME vs. 603 MME, p=0.681). Rates of postoperative delirium were slightly lower in the intervention group (58% vs. 66%, p=0.571). Cryoablation was not associated with increased complications. There were trends toward shorter median ventilator duration and total hospital length of stay in the intervention group, although results were not statistically significant. Intraoperative intercostal nerve cryoablation is a feasible and safe adjunct in lung transplantation and is associated with reduced early postoperative opioid use. These findings support further prospective evaluation of cryoablation as an opioid-sparing strategy in lung transplant recipients.

articles.title: High-Frequency Chest Wall Oscillation in Critical Care: A Systematic Review.
articles.journal: Respiration; international review of thoracic diseases
articles.abstract: Airway secretion retention represents a major clinical challenge in critically ill patients, promoting gas exchange impairment and atelectasis, precipitating failure of noninvasive respiratory support, and prolonging invasive mechanical ventilation, with an associated increase in respiratory-related complications and mortality. High-frequency chest wall oscillation (HFCWO) is a noninvasive airway clearance technique widely used in chronic respiratory diseases, but its role in the intensive care unit (ICU) remains unclear. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the available evidence on the efficacy and safety of HFCWO in adult ICU patients. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane Library from inception to December 2025 in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Studies evaluating HFCWO in adult ICU patients, including those receiving invasive or noninvasive respiratory support, were eligible. Primary outcomes included duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, and mortality. Secondary outcomes included impact on secretion airway clearance and its radiographic/functional surrogates as well as safety and treatment tolerance. A limited number of studies met the inclusion criteria, mainly small randomized controlled trials and observational studies, characterized by substantial heterogeneity in patient populations, intervention protocols, and assessed outcomes. HFCWO effects on clinically meaningful primary endpoints, including duration of mechanical ventilation, length of ICU stay, and mortality, remain variable and inconclusive. Overall, HFCWO was well tolerated and appeared to enhance secretion clearance, with some studies reporting modest improvements in oxygenation and respiratory mechanics. Current evidence suggests that HFCWO is a safe and feasible airway clearance strategy in selected ICU patients with secretion burden and without proved effects on the main clinical outcomes. Lack of physiopathologically driven criteria for selection of patients more likely to respond to HFCWO either alone or integrated with other cough-assisting techniques may partially explain these scanty findings from the overall published studies. This precludes its routine use in clinical practice. Well-designed, adequately powered randomized trials are needed to define patient selection criteria, optimal timing, and the true clinical impact of HFCWO in the ICU setting.

articles.title: Handling of the Non-Assessable Verbal Glasgow Coma Scale and Computed Illness Severity in Critically Ill Adults with Acute Brain Injury: A Retrospective Analysis.
articles.abstract: BackgroundThe Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) contributes to illness-severity scores. The verbal component cannot be observed in intubated patients; the MIMIC Code Repository sets "No Response-ETT" rows to a total of 15.ObjectiveTo quantify non-assessable verbal GCS examinations and describe how their handling changes computed severity, the analyzed population and mortality-model performance.Materials and MethodsRetrospective MIMIC-IV cohort (Boston, 2008 to 2022) of adults with acute brain injury (first intensive care unit stay per hospitalization); a "No Response-ETT" verbal entry was non-assessable. Five GCS derivation strategies were compared; four used the lowest eye-plus-motor examination of the first 24 h. The eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD; United States, 2014 to 2015) supported replication.ResultsOf 14,230 stays, 45.2% had a non-assessable verbal examination; 47.5% of ventilated stays had none assessable in the first 24 h. A non-assessable lowest examination was associated with mechanical ventilation (adjusted odds ratio, 32.8; 95% CI, 27.8 to 38.6). The official first-day GCS was 15 in 44.7% of 14 215 stays; 94.1% of default-rule totals of 15 were incompatible with the eye-plus-motor sum charted at that examination. With one mortality-model specification refitted per GCS derivation on the same stays, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.749 (95% CI, 0.739 to 0.760) with the official first-day GCS and 0.820 (0.812 to 0.828) with an eye-and-motor (Brennan) estimate. Complete-case analysis excluded 5509 of 14 192 stays and 72.8% of deaths. In eICU-CRD, stays with an unscored GCS component had higher mortality (16.6% vs 9.2%), but totals of 12 or more were no more frequent after the first documented ventilation entry (17.3%) than before (19.5%).ConclusionIn this cohort, how a non-assessable verbal GCS was handled changed computed severity and the analyzed population. Studies and benchmarks that use GCS-based severity should report the handling rule.

articles.title: Language Concordance in Critical Care: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Language barriers are associated with differences in care delivery processes and outcomes in critical care settings, with differences despite language assistance services. Less is known about outcomes associated with language concordant care. Language concordance is a linguistic match between a patient's preferred language and the language used by their care team. We undertook a systematic review to examine the measurement and impact of language concordant care delivery during critical illness, inclusive of the critical care recovery period after hospitalization. A systematic review was conducted in PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Embase, and Cochrane of English-language publications from database inception to March 3, 2026. Studies that investigated adults in critical care and post-ICU recovery clinic settings that included measurement of language concordance were included. Study quality was evaluated by the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist. Of 1,682 unique records identified, 11 were eligible for inclusion (128,181 total patients; mean [sd] age, 68.4 [17.9 yr]; 72,872 [56.9%] male and 55,082 [43.1%] female). Six studies assessed clinical decision-making. Reported outcomes included code status changes, family conferences, communication complexity, delirium, length of stay, mechanical ventilation, and mortality. Due to significant heterogeneity in study analyses and reported outcomes, data were not pooled for quantitative analysis. Current evidence suggests that language-concordant care may influence clinically meaningful processes of critical care, warranting interventional studies to guide care delivery recommendations.

articles.title: Association of Care Intensity With Survival and Long-Term Cost-Effectiveness in Sepsis Without Initial Organ Support After Emergency Admission: A Multicenter Cohort Study in Japan.
articles.abstract: To identify subgroups of patients hospitalized for community-acquired sepsis without initial organ support who may derive survival and cost-effectiveness benefits from ICU or high-dependency care unit (HDU) admission. Retrospective cohort study. A 140-hospital Japanese database (April 2016-March 2024). Adults admitted via emergency ambulance for community-acquired sepsis not requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, mechanical ventilation, catecholamines, or renal replacement therapy before or on the antimicrobial-initiation day. None. We compared ICU and HDU admissions, each vs. general ward (GW) admission, balancing patient characteristics using overlap propensity-score weighting. In-hospital mortality was estimated as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs using modified Poisson regression. Cost-effectiveness was measured by the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) in 3-year costs per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Among 28,211 patients (GW, 18,349; HDU, 8,706; ICU, 1,156), ICU and HDU admissions were not associated with lower mortality overall (HDU vs. GW; RR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.92-1.06 and ICU vs. GW; RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.92-1.22). However, HDU admission was associated with lower mortality among patients with Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score greater than or equal to 6 (RR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.75-0.99) or Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score less than or equal to 12 (RR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.71-0.92). Under the Japanese (50,000 USD/QALY) and U.S. (100,000 USD/QALY) thresholds, ICU and HDU admissions were not cost-effective overall (ICERs > 200,000 USD/QALY). However, the HDU subgroup with GCS score less than or equal to 12 (ICER, 47,738 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 45,918-49,558) was cost-effective under both thresholds, and that with SOFA score greater than or equal to 6 (ICER, 55,319 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 52,018-58,624) met the U.S. threshold. ICU or HDU admission was not associated with survival or economic benefits overall, whereas HDU subgroups (SOFA score ≥ 6 or GCS score ≤ 12) were associated with lower mortality and better cost-effectiveness. These findings may help optimize resource allocation.

articles.title: A Guytonian Atlas of Venous Return in Septic Shock: Reconstruction of Hemodynamic States.
articles.abstract: To reconstruct venous return physiology across published studies of septic shock and characterize the distribution of circulatory states represented in the literature. Exploratory physiologic reconstruction study. Secondary analysis of published hemodynamic observations. Adult patients with septic shock reported in studies containing sufficient information for reconstruction of mean circulatory filling pressure analogue (Pmca) and related parameters including venous return driving pressure (VRdP) and resistance to venous return (RVR). None. A total of 150 observations were available. Median Pmca, central venous pressure (CVP), VRdP, and RVR were 17.3 mm Hg, 9.0 mm Hg, 7.9 mm Hg, and 1.04 mm Hg/min/L, respectively. Empirical quartiles identified four recurrent circulatory phenotypes: reduced filling pressure/gradient, preserved venous return, elevated venous pressure, and high-resistance venous return. The preserved venous return pattern demonstrated the highest median cardiac output (CO), whereas the high-resistance pattern exhibited the lowest flow despite comparable filling pressures. In exploratory adjusted analyses incorporating available vasopressor exposure and fluid-therapy context, VRdP remained strongly associated with CO (β, 1.03 L/min/mm Hg; 95% CI, 0.80-1.25; p < 0.001). When Pmca and CVP were entered separately, Pmca was positively associated with CO (β, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.79-1.25; p < 0.001), whereas CVP was inversely associated with CO (β, -1.03; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.80; p < 0.001). Published hemodynamic observations in septic shock occupy distinct Guytonian phenotypes characterized by different combinations of circulatory filling pressure, venous pressure, and RVR. Reconstruction of venous return geometry may provide a physiologic framework for interpreting circulatory heterogeneity in septic shock.

articles.title: National Early Warning Score 2-Guided Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle Care for Adults With Suspected Sepsis in the Emergency Department: A Hybrid Type 1 Effectiveness-Implementation Stepped-Wedge Randomized Controlled Trial Pilot Study (NEWS-1 TRIPS).
articles.abstract: To increase the uptake of the Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle, we implemented a novel sepsis care model (National Early Warning Score [NEWS]-1 care), in which the Hour-1 Bundle is objectively triggered by a high NEWS-2 (≥ 5). We aimed to determine the feasibility of a full-scale type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation trial of this model. A pilot type 1 hybrid trial, comprising a stepped-wedge cluster randomized controlled trial and mixed-methods implementation evaluation with staff focus group interviews and an anonymous survey guided by the Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance framework. Four emergency departments in Hong Kong. Adult patients of 18 years or older with a clinical diagnosis of infection requiring hospitalization and a NEWS-2 greater than or equal to 5. Implementation of the Hour-1 Bundle when NEWS-2 was greater than or equal to 5. The primary outcome was the feasibility of a full-scale hybrid trial, evaluated based on 14 progression criteria. Preliminary clinical effectiveness and safety were assessed, alongside implementation barriers and facilitators. During the implementation phase, compliance with lactate, blood culture, and antibiotics increased significantly. All progression criteria were met, except for suboptimal overall bundle compliance (56.1%). Exploratory intention-to-treat analysis (standard care group, n = 102; NEWS-1 group, n = 98) showed no significant between-group difference in 30-day all-cause mortality (standard care group, 3.9%; NEWS-1 group, 9.2%; absolute risk difference, 5.3%; 95% CI -1.6% to 12.1%); in-hospital, 90-day all-cause, or sepsis-related mortality; need for mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, intensive care, or surgery; or ventilator-free days and adverse events. Implementation evaluation identified 15 barriers and 13 facilitators. The effectiveness of NEWS-1 care remained uncertain, though adverse events were rare. A full-scale hybrid stepped-wedge trial is feasible but requires a much larger sample size. Real-world implementation barriers and facilitators should be considered in sepsis management guidelines.

articles.title: The Impact of Hospital Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Volume and Its Distribution Across ICUs on Adult Patients' Outcomes: An Analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry.
articles.abstract: Research from a prior era of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) found that higher hospital ECMO volume was associated with higher survival rates, but it did not examine whether distributing ECMO volume across multiple ICUs affected this relationship. Retrospective analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) registry. ECMO centers contributing to the registry. Adult patients required ECMO support from 2012 to 2023. None. We analyzed adult patients from the ELSO registry (2012-2023), adjusting for hospital factors and case mix using multivariable hierarchical logistic regression. The main outcome was in-hospital mortality. Hospital experience was measured by the annual number of adult ECMO cases and total ECMO hours. Volume-outcome associations were modeled for all centers and by total adult ICUs per center. We included 115,849 adults on ECMO across 495 hospitals. Model estimates showed small decreases in mortality odds with higher annual case counts (odds ratio [OR], 0.98; 95% CI, 0.97-0.99 per 10-case increase) and ECMO hours (OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99-1.00 per 1000 hr increase). Hospitals with one ICU had a median of 10 cases (interquartile interval [IQI], 3-25 cases), while those with four or more ICUs had a median of 50 (IQI, 28-91). Adjusted mortality was higher in centers delivering ECMO across four+ ICUs compared with one ICU (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.06-1.31), the annual case model (OR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06-1.26), and the annual ECMO hours model. Higher volume was associated with a reduction in the odds of mortality for hospitals with four+ ICUs compared with those with one ICU (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.96-1.00 per 10 cases and OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99-1.00 per 1000 hr). Higher hospital ECMO volume is associated with reduced mortality. Hospitals with more adult ICUs that perform ECMO may experience higher mortality, which may be explained by increased patient complexity and is offset by the higher center volume. More research is needed to better understand the optimum design of ECMO centers.

articles.title: A Telemedicine Intervention for Spontaneous Awakening and Breathing Trials in Small and Large ICUs.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the effect of a tele-critical care (TCC) daily audit-and-feedback intervention on spontaneous awakening trial and spontaneous breathing trial protocol compliance. Pre-post quality improvement study. Single health system composed of 14 hospitals in the Midwestern United States. A total of 8909 patients of 18 years or older receiving mechanical ventilation via endotracheal tube for more than 1 calendar day between October 01, 2022 and September 20, 2024. Daily in the early afternoon, TCC nurses reviewed mechanically ventilated patients to determine whether a spontaneous awakening trial and spontaneous breathing trial had occurred. They contacted the bedside nurse if no trial had occurred and no weaning exclusion criteria were noted during a manual chart review. The coprimary outcomes were the proportion of ventilator days during each ventilator episode with documentation of spontaneous awakening trials and spontaneous breathing trials. Linear mixed effects models were used to examine the effect of the intervention on each outcome stratified by ICU size (large ≥ 15 beds or small < 15 beds). Spontaneous awakening trial documentation improved over time throughout the entire period, but the rate of improvement increased significantly after the telemedicine intervention (preintervention slope: 0.2% increase per 30 d; 95% CI, -0.2% to 0.6% and postintervention slope: 1.4% increase per 30 d; 95% CI, 1.0% to 1.9%; p < 0.001 for intervention-time interaction). The telemedicine intervention was associated with a step increase in spontaneous breathing trial documentation in small ICUs (absolute increase, 12.8%; 95% CI, 8.7-16.9%) but not in large ICUs (absolute increase, -0.1%; 95% CI, -1.8% to 1.6%; p = 0.02 for intervention-ICU size interaction). The telemedicine intervention was associated with increased spontaneous awakening trials and spontaneous breathing trials selectively in small ICUs. Telemedicine may have promoted practice standardization in small ICUs where exposure to ventilated patients was infrequent. Local ICU characteristics may impact the effectiveness of TCC interventions.

articles.title: Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System Therapy in Severe Amlodipine Overdose: Two Cases and Review of the Literature.
articles.abstract: BackgroundCalcium channel blocker (CCB) overdose is a significant cause of cardiovascular drug overdose-related mortality, with amlodipine emerging as the most frequently implicated agent in serious intoxication. Current management strategies for CCB poisoning include vasopressors, high-dose insulin therapy, and other adjunctive treatments. The unique pharmacodynamic profile of amlodipine can lead to severe and persistent vasoplegic shock that is refractory to conventional therapy.
