The Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System (MARS), an albumin dialysis technique capable of removing protein-bound toxins, has been proposed as a potential adjunctive therapy in cases of refractory vasodilatory shock associated with severe amlodipine poisoning.MethodsWe report two cases of severe amlodipine poisoning complicated by refractory vasodilatory shock treated with the Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System (MARS). A targeted PubMed search was also performed to identify published reports of calcium channel blocker intoxication with severe shock treated with MARS. Only reports describing amlodipine ingestion, either alone or with co-ingested agents, were included.ResultsBoth cases involved severe amlodipine poisoning complicated by refractory vasodilatory shock with multiorgan dysfunction requiring multiple vasopressors, high-dose insulin therapy, mechanical ventilation, and renal replacement therapy. Initiation of MARS was temporally associated with progressive hemodynamic stabilization, including reductions in vasopressor requirements and improvement in lactate levels. In the first case, MARS was successfully continued during prone ventilation for severe acute respiratory distress syndrome. In the second case, persistent cardiopulmonary failure required extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Reinitiation of MARS during ECMO support was associated with improved lactate clearance and reduced vasopressor requirements.ConclusionsSevere amlodipine poisoning can result in profound and persistent vasodilatory shock with multiorgan dysfunction despite multiple conventional and adjunctive therapies. MARS may represent a useful adjunctive therapy in selected cases and can be integrated into complex critical care strategies, including prone ventilation and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.

articles.title: From pneumonia to ARDS: a dynamic pulmonary-systemic framework.
Prognostic relevance of protein prescriptions based on adjusted body weight in critically ill overweight or obese patients - analysis of a large international database.
articles.abstract: ESPEN currently recommends using adjusted body weight (aBW) to guide protein prescriptions for critically ill overweight or obese patients. The prognostic relevance of this concept is unknown. We analyzed a subset of a large international point prevalence survey of nutritional practice in 785 intensive care units (ICUs) worldwide. Patients were included if they had been in the ICU for at least 96 h and had a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m². We modelled the association between early average protein intake (days 1-4 after ICU admission) and the cause-specific adjusted hazards of in-ICU death and ICU discharge alive within a competing risks framework. Intake was normalized to aBW, defined as ideal body weight plus 25% of the difference between actual and ideal body weight. 9,068 patients were analyzed. There was no evidence of an association between early protein intake and ICU discharge alive. In contrast, very low protein intake (below approximately 0.45 g/kg aBW/day) was associated with a higher hazard of in-ICU death. Above this threshold, there was no clear evidence of a further association between protein intake and the hazard of in-ICU death. The strongest association was observed at 0 g/kg aBW/day (adjusted hazard rate 1.41 i.e. an estimated 38% higher risk, 95% confidence interval 1.17-1.69). Early protein intake does not appear to be associated with time to ICU discharge among survivors. However, in critically ill patients with overweight or obesity, very low protein intake during the early acute phase may be associated with less favorable in-ICU outcomes.

articles.title: Impact of antibiotic prophylaxis on the occurrence of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia in trauma patients (antiVAP): a propensity score-weighted, retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Short-course antibiotic prophylaxis has been associated with a reduced risk of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) in selected populations, particularly patients with acute brain injury. However, its role in severely injured trauma patients remains controversial. This multicentre, retrospective cohort study, conducted in 15 French trauma centres, included severely injured adults who required mechanical ventilation initiated within 24 h of admission and continued for at least 48 h. Propensity score-based analyses assessed the association between early antibiotic prophylaxis (initiated within the first 24 h of management and continued for up to 72 h) and patient outcomes. The primary outcome was early-onset VAP; secondary outcomes included late-onset VAP, extrapulmonary infections, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU and hospital length of stay, and 30-day mortality. A total of 1,321 trauma patients were included. Antibiotic prophylaxis was administered to 746 patients (56%), with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid used in more than 90% of cases. Early-onset VAP occurred in 240 of 746 patients (32%) who received antibiotic prophylaxis and in 195 of 575 (34%) who did not. After inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with early-onset VAP (weighted odds ratio [wOR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.66-1.22; p = 0.48). A cause-specific Cox model accounting for the competing risk of death before day 7 yielded similar results (cause-specific hazard ratio [csHR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.71-1.07; p = 0.19). Antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with improve of secondary outcomes. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis in severely injured trauma patients was not associated with a reduced risk of early-onset VAP. Gov ID NCT07059039 - Registration date: July, 10th 2025.

articles.title: The Effect of Guanfacine on Delirium in Surgical and Trauma ICU Patients: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the feasibility of conducting a randomized controlled trial investigating guanfacine for ICU delirium, including assessment of recruitment, retention, protocol adherence, and data completeness, while estimating treatment effects to inform future trial design. Single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial conducted from November 2020 to February 2023. Surgical and Trauma ICUs at the University of Alabama at Birmingham Hospital. One hundred critically ill adults with Confusion Assessment Method-ICU-confirmed delirium randomized 1:1 to guanfacine or placebo. Patients received 2 mg guanfacine or matching placebo nightly for up to 14 days, or until ICU discharge or delirium resolution. Primary feasibility outcomes included protocol adherence (target ≥ 90%), retention (target ≥ 80%), recruitment rate (target ≥ 2 patients/mo), and data completeness (target ≥ 95%). Most feasibility targets were achieved: protocol adherence was 100%, retention was 100%, and data completeness was 100%. Recruitment was significantly impacted by COVID-19 pandemic disruptions, achieving 0.9 patients/wk during active recruitment periods.For clinical outcomes, in unadjusted analyses, median delirium and coma-free days were higher with guanfacine than placebo (2 [interquartile range [IQR], 0-6] vs. 1 [IQR, 0-4]; p = 0.02); however, this association was not statistically significant after adjustment for prespecified baseline covariates. ICU and hospital length of stay and duration of mechanical ventilation did not differ significantly between groups. No hemodynamic differences or safety concerns were observed. This pilot study successfully supports feasibility for a definitive trial, with excellent protocol adherence, adequate retention, and preliminary signals that warrant further evaluation. Although adjusted analyses were not statistically significant, the observed unadjusted difference in delirium and coma-free days and favorable safety profile support progression to a multicenter trial informed by these pilot estimates.

articles.title: Metabolic Health Modifies the Obesity Paradox in Critically ill Patients: A Phenotype-Based Risk Stratification Tool from the MIMIC-IV Database.
articles.abstract: BackgroundThe prognostic significance of obesity in critically ill patients remains controversial, partly due to the simplistic use of body mass index (BMI) without considering metabolic heterogeneity. We aim to evaluate whether combining BMI with metabolic health status provides superior risk stratification for all-cause mortality in ICU patients using the MIMIC-IV database.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study analyzed 31 171 adult ICU patients from the MIMIC-IV database. Patients were classified into six phenotypes based on BMI categories (normal, overweight, or obese) and metabolic health status (healthy vs unhealthy, defined by hypertension, diabetes or hyperlipidemia). The primary outcomes included 7-day, 30-day, and 90-day all-cause mortality. We applied survival curve analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression, with subgroup analyses stratified by sex, age, and illness severity.ResultsAmong metabolically healthy patients, BMI category did not significantly affect mortality. However, in metabolically unhealthy patients, a clear graded protective association emerged: the metabolically unhealthy obese (MUO) phenotype conferred the strongest survival benefit (adjusted HRs: 0.63, 0.65 and 0.64 for 7-day, 30-day and 90-day mortality, respectively), followed by metabolically unhealthy overweight (MUOW, adjusted HRs: 0.73, 0.70 and 0.69 for 7-day, 30-day and 90-day mortality), while the metabolically unhealthy normal weight (MUNW) patients showed the weakest protection. Such a survival benefit was significantly amplified in males and in patients with higher illness severity.ConclusionsAmong ICU patients, metabolic health status, rather than BMI alone, is the key determinant of prognosis. For metabolically unhealthy patients, higher BMI was associated with a graded survival advantage, particularly in those with greater illness severity. The proposed six-phenotype classification provides a simple, admission-available bedside tool for early risk stratification and may inform individualized nutritional and metabolic management in critical care.

articles.title: COVID-19 Is Not an Independent Risk Factor for Post-Intensive Care Syndrome: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: BackgroundPost-intensive care syndrome (PICS) affects many ICU survivors, leading to persistent physical, cognitive, and mental health issues. The COVID-19 pandemic raised concerns about whether SARS-CoV-2 infection increases PICS risk. This study aimed to evaluate whether COVID-19 is an independent risk factor for PICS and to identify other contributing factors.MethodsThis retrospective cohort included 92 patients treated for respiratory failure in three ICUs at Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin between July 2020 and September 2021. Patients were divided into COVID-19 (n = 49) and non-COVID-19 (n = 43) groups. At three months post-discharge, outpatient assessments consisted of demographic data, ICU-related variables, and evaluations of physical (handgrip dynamometry, Timed Up and Go test), cognitive (Mini-Cog, Animal Naming Test), and psychological health (PHQ-4). PICS was defined as at least one abnormal test; severity was graded by the number of affected domains. Logistic and ordinal regression analyses assessed whether COVID-19 was independently associated with PICS prevalence and severity.ResultsPICS was present in 71.4% of COVID-19 and 62.8% of non-COVID survivors (p = 0.378). Multivariable analysis showed no significant association between COVID-19 and PICS or its severity (OR = 1.46; 95% CI 0.50-4.23; p = 0.486; and OR = 1.09; 95% CI 0.45-2.68; p = 0.845, respectively).ConclusionsCOVID-19 was not independently associated with PICS in ICU survivors. Both groups experience high rates of long-term impairments, highlighting the importance of rehabilitation and follow-up care for all ICU survivors.

articles.title: Low Physical Activity and Reported Barriers Among Survivors of Critical Illness: A Mixed-Method Study.
authors: Trajectories of Recovery after ACutE and cRitical illness (TRACER) study group
articles.abstract: To examine physical activity levels in survivors of critical illness across 6 months, and to understand the barriers and facilitators of physical activity. Prospective, longitudinal, convergent mixed-methods study. Functional testing laboratory. Adults admitted to the ICU for at least 72 hours with acute respiratory failure or sepsis. None. Patients wore an accelerometer starting at hospital discharge, at 3- and 6-month follow-up to quantify daily step counts. At 6 months, physical function and patient-reported outcomes were collected in-person, with a subset of participants completing semi-structured interviews. Eighty-two patients were enrolled, with 67 (82%) having physical activity data with median age of 60 years (interquartile range [IQR], 52-66 yr), 54% male, and ICU stay 9.0 days [IQR, 5.8-17.0 d]. The median daily steps were 1358 (IQR, 742-2799) in 50 patients at baseline, 2305 (IQR, 1081-3898) in 54 patients at 3 months, and 2826 (IQR, 1609-4781) in 44 patients at 6 months. Higher comorbidity burden and earlier measurement associated with lower step counts. At 6 months, patients walked a mean of 344 ± 169 meters on the 6-minute walk test and reported being sedentary a median of 300 min/days (150-480 min/d). Eleven participants completed interviews, yielding three themes: 1) "a marathon, not a sprint": the extended ICU recovery trajectory; 2) engagement in physical activity is highly regulated by personal context; 3) value-driven and motivation-informed physical activity decisions. Mixed-methods integration demonstrated that qualitative themes expanded upon quantitative findings to explain nonlinear recovery patterns, contextualizing persistent sedentary behavior, and revealing that motivational and behavioral gaps are not captured by accelerometry. Survivors showed gradual improvement in daily steps over 6 months yet remained below recommended activity levels. Survivorship and attrition biases may lead to overestimation of step counts, further warranting larger studies. Integrating quantitative and qualitative data reveals modifiable contextual factors that may inform the design of pragmatic physical activity interventions.

articles.title: Normocapnia Versus Mild Hypercapnia During Lung Protective Ventilation in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Target Trial Emulation.
articles.abstract: This trial emulation aimed to answer the question: Among patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) who receive lung protective ventilation with low tidal volume, is normocapnia through an increase in respiratory rate associated with lower mortality than mild hypercapnia? Target trial emulation. Hospitals of the ARDS Network and Prevention and Early Treatment of Acute Lung Injury (PETAL) Network. Patients with ARDS enrolled in seven ARDS Network and PETAL Network randomized controlled trials. None. A target trial was emulated, assigning participants in a 1:1 ratio to normocapnia (target Paco2 35-45 mm Hg) or mild hypercapnia (target Paco2 50-55 mm Hg) for 4 days following the initiation of lung protective ventilation. The primary outcome was 90-day in-hospital mortality. Of 5367 potentially eligible subjects, 292 patients were assigned to normocapnia and 292 to mild hypercapnia. Separation in Paco2 values was preserved over the 4-day period of emulated intervention. Both groups had median pH greater than or equal to 7.33. Bicarbonate levels, driving pressure, tidal volume, and dead-space fraction did not differ clinically significantly between groups, while median respiratory rate was 33.0 breaths/min in the normocapnia vs. 28.0 breaths/min in the mild hypercapnia group (p < 0.001). Death within 90 days occurred in 84 of 292 patients (28.8%) in the normocapnia group and in 84 of 292 patients (28.8%) in the mild hypercapnia group (log-rank p = 0.842). This result persisted in subgroups such as older (≥ 65 yr) and obese (body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m2) patients. Among patients with ARDS who received lung protective ventilation, normocapnia through an increase in respiratory rate was not associated with lower mortality than mild hypercapnia. As this finding is derived from a trial emulation, it should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for significant residual bias.

articles.title: Predictive performance of bedside physiological parameters for the failure of prophylactic non-invasive ventilation after extubation.
articles.abstract: Extubation failure is associated with increased mortality. Whether bedside physiological variables can identify patients at risk of reintubation during prophylactic NIV after extubation is unknown. In this post hoc analysis of a multicenter physiological study, 60 hypoxemic adults at high risk of extubation failure underwent two 1-hour NIV sessions after planned extubation, with oronasal and full-face masks in randomized crossover order. We assessed the magnitude of airway occlusion pressure (Pocc), the esophageal pressure swing (ΔPes), SpO₂/FiO₂, respiratory rate, tidal volume, dynamic lung elastance (EL,dyn), ROX index [(SpO₂/FiO₂)/respiratory rate] and the pressure-oxygenation index (POX, SpO₂/FiO₂ divided by Pocc). Prophylactic NIV failure was reintubation for respiratory failure within 7 days. Discrimination was assessed by ROC analysis. Fourteen patients (23%) experienced NIV failure. Pocc yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.83 (95% CI, 0.71-0.95) with the oronasal mask and 0.83 (95% CI, 0.72-0.95) with the full-face mask, showing greater discriminative performance than tidal volume (AUCs, 0.55 and 0.53), respiratory rate (0.54 and 0.38), SpO₂/FiO₂ (0.51 and 0.50), and the ROX index (0.54 and 0.38; all p < 0.05). By contrast, the discriminative performance of Pocc did not differ from that of EL,dyn (AUCs, 0.72 and 0.73; p = 0.08 and 0.11), POX (AUCs, 0.82 and 0.81; p = 0.68 and 0.29), or |ΔPes| (AUCs, 0.83 and 0.82; p = 1.00 and 0.64). During prophylactic NIV, Pocc discriminated NIV failure better than conventional bedside variables, with no detectable difference from directly measured inspiratory effort. External validation is required.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of oliceridine versus remifentanil for analgesia in mechanically ventilated critically ill adults (CO-ROAM): a multicenter, assessor-blinded, non-inferiority randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: Remifentanil provides effective analgesia during invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), but its utility is limited by opioid-related adverse events. Oliceridine, a G protein-biased μ-opioid receptor agonist, may decouple analgesia from these effects, but lacks evidence in critically ill patients. This multicentre, assessor- and patient-blinded, non-inferiority randomised controlled trial was conducted across 19 intensive care units (ICUs) in China. Adults receiving IMV were randomised 1:1 to oliceridine or remifentanil, titrated to a Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool score below 3. The primary endpoint was time in target analgesic range (TTR; non-inferiority margin -10%). Of 307 randomised patients, 304 comprised the modified intention-to-treat population (151 oliceridine, 153 remifentanil). Median TTR was 96.0% versus 92.3% (absolute difference 3.7%, 95% CI -0.3-5.7%). Oliceridine was associated with fewer mild-to-moderate adverse drug reactions (ADRs), occurring at 15.9 versus 22.2 events per 100 patient-days (IRR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52-1.00, P = 0.049), and a lower rate of respiratory depression during the study period (0% vs. 4.6%, P = 0.015). Post-extubation respiratory depression (0% vs. 7.9%, P = 0.005) and analgesic-sedation costs were both lower with oliceridine. IMV duration, ICU stay, and 28-day mortality did not differ. Subgroup analyses identified a nominal ADR benefit in patients with Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II > 17 and a larger nominal TTR difference in those without acute respiratory distress syndrome. Oliceridine provides non-inferior analgesia to remifentanil with a more favourable respiratory safety profile and lower costs in critically ill adults. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06454292 (registered June 11, 2024).

articles.title: Metabolic response during neuromuscular electrical stimulation in critically ill patients with deep sedation: a prospective observational study.
articles.abstract: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) is a potential strategy to counteract skeletal muscle atrophy in critically ill patients unable to engage in early mobilization. However, it is difficult to confirm whether the exercise load applied by NMES is sufficient to elicit a physiological effect in patients under sedation or with impaired consciousness, as the appropriate stimulus intensity and exercise load of NMES are generally assessed using subjective responses. This study aimed to evaluate changes in energy expenditure during NMES in sedated, mechanically ventilated patients using indirect calorimetry. This single-center observational study included 22 mechanically ventilated patients under deep sedation in the intensive care unit (ICU). Energy expenditure was measured using indirect calorimetry during NMES sessions. The primary outcome was the difference in energy expenditure before and during NMES. Multivariable linear regression analysis was performed to calculate the adjusted mean difference in energy expenditure. A clinically meaningful increase in energy expenditure attributable to NMES was predefined as 150 kcal/day, which was assumed based on an increase in energy expenditure when sitting on the edge of the bed. In total, 26 NMES sessions involving 22 participants were included in the analysis. The mean energy expenditure was 1,137 ± 170 kcal/day pre-NMES and 1,350 ± 228 kcal/day during NMES. The adjusted increase in energy expenditure during NMES was 213.8 kcal/day (95% confidence interval, 137.1-290.3). This increase reached statistical significance when tested against the predefined threshold of 150 kcal/day (P = 0.02). The exercise load provided by NMES could be objectively assessed by measuring increases in energy expenditure. Although a statistically significant increase in energy expenditure was observed during NMES compared to pre-NMES levels, the magnitude of this increase was minimal. Further research is needed to determine whether NMES protocols that enhance energy expenditure are associated with muscle mass preservation, strength maintenance, and the prevention of ICU-acquired weakness.

articles.title: Consensus on a core outcome set for ventilation trials in critically ill patients with acute brain injury: results of an international Delphi consensus study.
articles.abstract: Clinical research evaluating mechanical ventilation liberation in patients with acute brain injury (ABI) shows substantial outcome heterogeneity, limiting evidence synthesis. We aimed to develop an internationally endorsed core outcome set (COS) and a hierarchical composite endpoint for ventilation trials in neurocritical care. Following COS-STAD/COS-STAP standards, we conducted a 4-round international Delphi study. Candidate outcomes were identified via a scoping review. A multidisciplinary panel from 31 countries scored outcomes using a 9-point GRADE scale. Inclusion required >70% rating as "critical" (score 7-9) and ≤15% as "not important" (1-3). Two consensus meetings were held to categorize outcomes, select representative measures, and ratify a hierarchical composite endpoint. 78 stakeholders participated in Round 1; 60 completed all rounds (23.1% attrition). Fifty-four outcomes achieved Delphi consensus. At Consensus Meeting 1, these were organized into 16 categories; the highest-scoring outcome per category was selected. Three outcomes were not ratified due to disease-specificity (NIH Stroke Scale) or lack of universal applicability (brain death, coma-free days). The final COS comprised 13 outcomes across 5 domains: respiratory function, survival, complications, functional status, and quality of life. A 3-level hierarchical composite endpoint was ratified at Consensus Meeting 2: (1) intensive care unit survival, (2) no reintubation within 72 hours, and (3) days alive without mechanical ventilation. This study establishes the first COS for ventilation weaning trials in ABI patients. Widespread adoption of these 13 outcomes and the hierarchical composite endpoint will standardize reporting, enable meaningful evidence synthesis, and facilitate clinical translation in neurocritical care. Core Outcome Measures in Effectiveness Trials (COMET) Initiative, registration number 2320.

articles.title: Long-Term Mortality in Sepsis Survivors: A Population-Based Study During 15 Years.
articles.abstract: To evaluate long-term mortality among sepsis survivors in Catalonia over a 15-year period and to identify factors associated with increased mortality within 2 years after hospital discharge. Retrospective population-based cohort study. Acute-care hospitals in Catalonia, Spain. Adult and pediatric patients hospitalized with sepsis between 2005 and 2019 identified using the International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision, Clinical Modification and International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification codes for infection and acute organ dysfunction. Patients who died during hospitalization, were transferred to another facility, or represented readmission episodes were excluded. None. Data were obtained from the Catalan Minimum Basic Dataset of Acute-Care Hospitals, with longitudinal follow-up through the Central Registry of Insured Persons. Comorbidities were assessed using the Charlson comorbidity index. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to identify predictors of long-term mortality. Among 296,554 hospital admissions for sepsis, 237,075 patients (79.9%) survived to hospital discharge. Of these, 42% died (99,571) within 2 years. Long-term mortality increased significantly with age, ranging from 5.8% in patients younger than 15 years to 62% in those older than 84 years (p < 0.0001), and with comorbidity burden (21%, 38%, 51%, and 67% for Charlson index 0, 1-2, 3-4, and ≥ 5, respectively; p < 0.0001). Neoplasia (hazard ratio [HR], 2.011), liver cirrhosis (HR, 1.562), and dementia (HR, 1.304) were the comorbidities most strongly associated with mortality. Longer hospital stays were also associated with increased mortality. A progressive decline in long-term mortality was observed during 2017-2019. Long-term mortality among sepsis survivors remains high, with more than 40% dying within 2 years after hospital discharge. These findings support the need for structured post-sepsis care strategies focused on high-risk patients, improved continuity of care, and prevention of long-term sepsis-related complications.

articles.title: Systemic corticosteroids in critical illness: an evidence-based framework for clinical decision-making.
articles.abstract: Systemic corticosteroids are pivotal in managing inflammation-driven critical illnesses, yet bedside translation remains inconsistent. This systematic review establishes an evidence-based framework for clinical decision-making by horizontally synthesizing contemporary evidence across severe community-acquired pneumonia (sCAP), acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and septic shock. A systematic electronic search was conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library up to early 2026. Peer-reviewed randomized controlled trials (RCTs), systematic reviews, and meta-analyses published in English were eligible. Data regarding population characteristics, dosing regimens, initiation timing, duration, and safety profiles were independently extracted and qualitatively synthesized. Landmark trials define context-dependent efficacy: early hydrocortisone continuous infusion significantly reduces 28-day mortality in sCAP (CAPE COD), while a 10-day dexamethasone regimen improves ventilator-free days and survival in moderate-to-severe ARDS (DEXA-ARDS). In septic shock, early hydrocortisone-fludrocortisone combination accelerates shock resolution and lowers 90-day mortality (APROCCHS). These outcomes align with distinct pharmacological profiles: hydrocortisone provides dual glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid activity to restore vascular tone, whereas dexamethasone exerts potent transrepression of proinflammatory transcription factors. To mitigate steroid-induced harm, protocolized safety targets are essential, including maintaining blood glucose at 140-180 mg/dL and actively monitoring for secondary infections. Corticosteroids do not exert a uniform class effect. Bedside success requires personalized, protocolized regimens optimized by scenario-specific timing, dosing, and proactive adverse-event monitoring.

articles.title: Individualized treatment effects of high flow nasal oxygen in immunocompromised patients.
articles.abstract: High flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) has become a common first-line practice for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (ARF). In immunocompromised patients, ARF is the leading cause of ICU admission, yet a randomized trial found no overall benefit of HFNO in this population. To assess whether baseline characteristics influence HFNO's effectiveness in preventing invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in immunocompromised patients with ARF. A causal forest machine-learning algorithm was derived in the HIGH trial (776 patients randomized to HFNO or conventional oxygen) to predict the HFNO effects on day-28 IMV incidence. Patients with a "do-not-intubate" order (n = 72) were excluded. Model performance was validated through 500 bootstrap iterations and patients were categorized into terciles based on predicted HFNO benefit. Transportability of the model was assessed in an independent observational cohort (818 patients). Among the 704 participants, HFNO's average effect on day-28 IMV was not significant. However, substantial heterogeneity in treatment responses was identified (predicted benefit: from 20.2% [IQR 15.5%-23.9%] absolute IMV risk reduction with HFNO to 7.4% risk reduction [2.9%-11.2%] with conventional oxygen). Patients with the highest predicted benefit were older, more frequently solid organ transplant recipients, less neutropenic, more severely hypoxemic/tachycardic, but with lower non-respiratory sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) scores. In this subgroup, HFNO was associated with a significant lower incidence of IMV. In the observational cohort, the benefit-ranking performance was preserved, although absolute effect estimates were less calibrated. These results suggest HFNO might benefit specific immunocompromised patients with ARF. Further prospective studies are needed to validate these findings.

articles.title: Defining ARDS: globalization and personalization to better serve the world-part 2.
Defining ARDS: Globalization and personalization to better serve the World - Part 1.
Sense of Coherence in Patients After Intensive Care Treatment: A 1-Year Follow-Up Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Patients endure physical, mental and cognitive symptoms after critical illness, and coping is vital to their healing process. Little research exists on associations between sense of coherence (SOC) and patients' health improvements after intensive care unit (ICU) discharge. To describe the trajectory of SOC and how demographic, clinical and psychosocial variables affect SOC in discharged ICU patients during 12 months of follow-up. A prospective cohort substudy of a neutral randomized controlled trial in Norway involving discharged ICU patients receiving nurse-led follow-up consultations or standard care. Data were collected in the ward (baseline) and after 3, 6 and 12 months. Univariate and multivariate linear mixed models for repeated measures were fitted with SOC-13 score as the dependent variable. We included 523 patients with a median of three ICU days, median age 57 years, 47% females, 54% receiving mechanical ventilation and stable SOC during follow-up. Higher SOC was associated with increased age (B = 0.12, 95% CI [0.05, 0.18]), no prior mental health problems (B = 6.69, 95% CI [4.19, 9.19]), no prior use of psychotropics (B = 2.37, 95% CI [0.16, 4.58]) and lower post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) at baseline (B = 5.56, 95% CI [3.50, 7.61]). Low educational level (B = -2.25, 95% CI [-4.10, -0.40]), higher pain interference at baseline (B = -0.46, 95% CI [-0.84, -0.08]) and less social support 3 months later (B = -5.93, 95% CI [-7.87, -3.99]) were associated with lower SOC. During 12 months after ICU discharge, SOC remained stable. Higher age, no previous mental health problems or use of psychotropics, and lower PTSS were associated with higher SOC. Low education, more pain and low social support were associated with lower SOC. More vulnerable patients deserve greater attention during general rehabilitation after ICU treatment due to low SOC.

articles.title: Intensive Care Unit Patients' Perspectives and Experiences in Using Virtual Reality Technology: A Qualitative Meta-Synthesis.
articles.abstract: As Intensive Care Unit (ICU) survival improves, attention has shifted towards patients' psychological well-being and recovery. Although Virtual Reality (VR) is increasingly used in critical care, patients' experiences of VR interventions have not been comprehensively synthesised. To synthesise qualitative and mixed-methods evidence regarding ICU patients' perceptions, experiences and implementation-related considerations associated with VR interventions. A qualitative systematic review and thematic synthesis following Thomas and Harden's three-stage approach was conducted. Eight databases were searched from inception to September 2025. Studies employing qualitative methods or components of mixed methods exploring ICU patients' firsthand VR experiences were included. Methodological quality was appraised using the JBI checklist. Eight studies involving 247 participants were included. Four analytical themes were synthesised: (A) VR as a restorative escape, (B) VR as a route from passive endurance to active participation, (C) Patient readiness and personal preference shape VR engagement, and (D) VR as a co-produced intervention requiring contextual and relational adaptation. ICU patients perceived VR as a valuable tool that provided restorative escape and enabled active recovery, yet multiple barriers shaped its feasibility. Implementation should consider comfortable devices, customisable content and staff training. These findings inform patient-centred VR design in the ICU. VR offers a non-pharmacological approach that may support patient well-being and recovery during an ICU stay. It can provide meaningful focus and relief from distress, while encouraging engagement with rehabilitation. Nurses play a key role in facilitating sessions and assessing patient readiness. Implementation may be enhanced by comfortable, bed-compatible devices, customisable content and staff training. While not all patients may be suitable candidates, VR appears generally acceptable and could be integrated into individualised care plans. The review protocol had been registered in PROSPERO (International prospective register of systematic reviews). The registration number is CRD420251074650.

articles.title: Seven versus 14 days of polymyxin-based therapy for ventilator-associated pneumonia due to carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii : A randomised feasibility trial.
articles.journal: Lung India : official organ of Indian Chest Society
articles.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) due to carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii ( CRAB ) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality in intensive care units (ICUs), yet the optimal antibiotic duration of therapy remains uncertain. We compared outcomes of 7-day versus 14-day polymyxin-based therapy for CRAB-VAP. We conducted a single-centre, open-label, randomised feasibility trial in a tertiary-care respiratory ICU from March 2017 to October 2024. Patients with microbiologically confirmed CRAB-VAP who met predefined clinical stability criteria on day 7 were randomised 1:1 to either discontinue antibiotics on day 7 or continue treatment for 14 days. Treatment comprised intravenous colistin or polymyxin B with adjunctive nebulised colistin. The primary outcome was relapse of CRAB-VAP. Secondary outcomes included antibiotic-free days through day 28, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU and hospital length of stay, and 28-day all-cause mortality. We randomised 41 patients (7-day n = 22; 14-day n = 19). Relapse occurred in 1 (4.5%) versus 2 (10.5%) patients (risk ratio [RR] 0.43; 95% CI: 0.04, 4.31) in the 7-day versus 14-day groups, respectively. The 7-day group had more antibiotic-free days (mean difference: 6.9 days; 95% CI: 5.1, 8.7 days). Acute kidney injury occurred in 0% versus 31.6% (RR 0.07; 95% CI: 0.004, 1.15). Other outcomes, including 28-day mortality (45.5 vs 63.2%; RR 0.72; 95% CI: 0.40, 1.30), were similar. In clinically improving CRAB-VAP, a 7-day discontinuation strategy was feasible. Clinical outcome estimates, including relapse and mortality, were imprecise and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. These findings support evaluation in larger, adequately powered multicentre trials.

articles.title: Methodological Considerations Regarding the Safety of Enteral Feeding in Patients on High-Flow Nasal Cannula.
From Single-Point Respiratory Load to Continuous Load Assessment: Rethinking the Physiological Benefits of High-Flow Nasal Oxygen After Extubation.
Preextubation Respiratory Effort As a Physiologic Guide to Postextubation High-Flow Nasal Oxygen.
Certainty of Evidence and Interpretation of Effects in Inhaled Antibiotics for Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia.

Probability Is Not Evidence of Benefit: A Critical Appraisal of the Bayesian Reanalysis of the Restricted Versus Liberal Positive End-Expiratory Pressure in Patients Without Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RELAx) Trial.
Complications of Midazolam-Containing Versus Midazolam-Free Analgosedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adult ICU Patients: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) patients requiring mechanical ventilation (MV) frequently need analgosedation strategies that combine analgesia and sedation. Analgosedation, often administered with midazolam, is widely employed in middle and low-income countries, but it carries a substantial risk of complications, particularly in older or comorbid patients. Acknowledging these complications is critical for patient safety and quality of care. To examine complications associated with midazolam-containing versus midazolam-free analgosedation in mechanically ventilated adult intensive care unit patients. This systematic review was conducted according to the PRISMA guidelines. A comprehensive search of Scopus, MEDLINE (PubMed), and Web of Science identified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published between 2015 and 2025. Studies meeting predefined eligibility criteria underwent risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane RoB2 tool. Nine RCTs were included. Midazolam-containing analgosedation regimens were generally associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation, increased respiratory depression and higher incidence of neurological complications, particularly delirium. In contrast, midazolam-free analgosedation regimens, especially those using short-acting opioids, were associated with shorter mechanical ventilation duration and fewer haemodynamic incidents. ICU length of stay and healthcare costs favoured opioid-only analgosedation protocols, although mortality findings were inconsistent across studies. Compared with midazolam-free analgosedation, midazolam-containing analgosedation regimens in mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients are associated with a higher incidence of respiratory and neurological complications. Opioid-only protocols appear to offer a more favourable complication profile and may facilitate earlier weaning and shorter ICU stays. These findings support cautious use of midazolam and emphasize the importance of individualized, goal-directed analgosedation strategies. Enhancing critical care nursing staff's awareness of complications associated with different analgosedation regimens is essential to promote vigilant clinical monitoring, thereby reducing adverse events and supporting safer patient management.

articles.title: Effects of neurally adjusted ventilatory assist on mortality in critically ill patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.journal: The Journal of international medical research
articles.abstract: ObjectivePatient-ventilator asynchrony is associated with poor outcomes. Previous data have shown that neurally adjusted ventilatory assist reduces patient-ventilator asynchrony. This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed whether neurally adjusted ventilatory assist reduces mortality compared with conventional ventilation modes and whether this effect differs between invasive and noninvasive modes of neurally adjusted ventilatory assist.MethodsWe searched the PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Controlled Clinical Trials databases up to 18 July 2026. Randomized controlled trials comparing neurally adjusted ventilatory assist with other modes were included. The primary outcomes were intensive care unit mortality, hospital mortality, mechanical ventilation success rate, and 28-day ventilator-free days. Two authors screened the studies for eligibility, extracted the data, and completed the data table. Study quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool 2.0. Summary estimates were reported as risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals for dichotomous data and as mean differences with 95% confidence intervals for continuous data.ResultsNine randomized controlled trials involving 842 patients (389 receiving neurally adjusted ventilatory assist and 453 receiving conventional ventilation) were included. In patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation, compared with conventional modes, neurally adjusted ventilatory assist reduced intensive care unit mortality (risk ratio = 0.72, 95% confidence interval: 0.53-0.99) and hospital mortality (risk ratio = 0.71, 95% confidence interval: 0.56-0.90) and increased the mechanical ventilation success rate (risk ratio = 1.13, 95% confidence interval: 1.04-1.22) and the number of 28-day ventilator-free days (mean difference = 3.48, 95% confidence interval: 0.97-6.00). In patients receiving noninvasive ventilation, neurally adjusted ventilatory assist did not significantly reduce hospital mortality (p = 0.23; I2 = 0%) or increase the mechanical ventilation success rate (p = 0.66; I2 = 0%), and 28-day ventilator-free days were reported only in the invasive mechanical ventilation trials.ConclusionNeurally adjusted ventilatory assist during invasive mechanical ventilation was associated with lower intensive care unit and hospital mortality, a higher mechanical ventilation success rate, and a greater number of 28-day ventilator-free days, whereas no such benefit was demonstrated during noninvasive ventilation. The evidence for noninvasive neurally adjusted ventilatory assist remains limited.

articles.title: Effect of Nurse-Delivered Chlorhexidine Versus Saline Oral Care on Ventilator-Associated Events in Medical Intensive Care Patients: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the effectiveness of nurse-delivered oral care using 0.12% chlorhexidine versus normal saline in reducing ventilator-associated events and improving clinical and oral health outcomes among adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation in a medical intensive care unit. Single-center, parallel-group, assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial. Adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation were randomly allocated to receive oral care with either 0.12% chlorhexidine or normal saline every eight hours until extubation or discharge from the ICU. The primary outcome was ventilator-associated events. Secondary outcomes included ventilator-associated pneumonia, duration of mechanical ventilation, length of stay in the intensive care unit, mortality in the intensive care unit, oral health status and intervention-related adverse events. A total of 141 participants were randomized. No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in ventilator-associated events, ventilator-associated pneumonia, duration of mechanical ventilation, length of stay in the intensive care unit, mortality in the intensive care unit, oral health status, or intervention-related adverse events. In this single-center superiority randomized controlled trial, nurse-delivered oral care with 0.12% chlorhexidine did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in ventilator-associated events compared with normal saline. Given the wide confidence intervals and lower-than-expected event rates, these findings do not confirm equivalence but suggest that routine chlorhexidine may provide limited incremental benefit over standardized mechanical oral hygiene in medical intensive care unit patients. Intensive care nurses might prioritize the consistent implementation of structured, evidence-based oral care protocols. Routine use of chlorhexidine may provide limited additional benefit over normal saline in this patient population. This study addresses the ongoing uncertainty regarding the effectiveness of chlorhexidine for routine oral care in mechanically ventilated adults. No significant differences were observed between chlorhexidine and normal saline in ventilator-associated events, clinical outcomes, oral health outcomes, or adverse events. These findings add to the growing body of evidence suggesting that the incremental benefit of chlorhexidine beyond standardized mechanical oral care may be limited and support further adequately powered multicenter trials to define its role in different intensive care populations. This study adhered to the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials guideline. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05913856. Available at: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05913856. The trial was registered after participant recruitment had commenced because of an administrative delay. No changes were made to the study design, eligibility criteria, outcomes, or analysis plan after registration. No Patient or Public Contribution.

articles.title: Airway Pressure Release Ventilation Versus Conventional Ventilation in Adults With or at Risk for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials.
articles.abstract: To assess whether airway pressure release ventilation (APRV) reduces mortality compared with conventional invasive ventilation in adults with established acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute lung injury, or conditions considered to confer a high risk of ARDS. We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception through August 15, 2026. We analyzed parallel-group randomized trials using random-effects models. Mortality at trial-defined follow-up was the primary outcome. We used Cochrane RoB 2 to assess risk of bias and GRADE to assess certainty of evidence. CRD420251170819. Nine trials involving 585 participants were included. No mortality benefit was demonstrated (risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.72-1.26). Ventilator-free days showed no clear difference (mean difference [MD] 3.83 days, 95% CI - 1.69 to 9.34; I²=83%). APRV was associated with a higher PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio (MD 56.21 mm Hg, 95% CI 24.63-87.79; I²=84%) and shorter ICU stay (MD - 2.53 days, 95% CI - 4.43 to - 0.64; I²=71%). Ventilation duration showed no clear difference (five trials, 413 participants; MD - 2.44 days, 95% CI - 4.96 to 0.09; I²=78%). Peak airway pressure was lower and mean airway pressure was higher with APRV. This synthesis does not establish that APRV improves survival, ventilator-free days, or ventilation duration. Oxygenation and ICU-stay findings require caution because populations, protocols, outcome timing, and risk of bias varied. Certainty of evidence was low to very low. These data do not establish mortality equivalence or superiority over contemporary lung-protective ventilation. CRD420251170819; registered 17 October 2025.

articles.title: An Approach to Navigating the Lorazepam Challenge Test for Catatonia in Critical Care Settings.
articles.abstract: Catatonia often occurs in the setting of psychiatric illness; however, it is also found in other medical conditions, especially within critical care settings. The lorazepam challenge test (LCT) is a key diagnostic and therapeutic intervention for catatonia; however, no specific guidance exists for patients within the intensive care unit (ICU). This review synthesizes psychiatric and critical care literature to propose a structured LCT framework adapted to the ICU. Specific indications and contraindications across gradients of catatonia likelihood and medical complexity are reviewed, along with practical dosing and monitoring recommendations. An interdisciplinary collaborative workflow is also outlined along with post-LCT documentation standards. Our structured approach offers a practical foundation for future standardized protocols, education, and catatonia research in critical care.

articles.title: Application of Electrical Impedance Tomography-Guided Pulmonary Rehabilitation Strategy in Patients with Respiratory Failure.
articles.abstract: This study investigated pulmonary rehabilitation strategies guided by electrical impedance tomography (EIT) in patients with respiratory failure. A total of 92 patients with respiratory failure admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) of a tertiary Grade A hospital in Chongqing from July 2024 to January 2025 were selected and randomly divided into a control group and an experimental group, with 46 cases in each group, using a random number table. The control group received conventional pulmonary physical therapy nursing strategies. The experimental group additionally received EIT-guided positioning, vibratory sputum clearance, and early mobilization. Relative regional tidal-ventilation distribution, PaO₂/FiO₂, respiratory rate, and pulse oxygen saturation were assessed at baseline and on the following three days; ICU stay, and delirium incidence were also compared. Finally, 44 cases in the control group and 44 cases in the experimental group completed the study. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed significant time effects across the four ventral-to-dorsal layers and significant group and interaction effects for the dorsal layer. Dorsal ventilation share was higher in the experimental group on days 2 and 3, but not significantly different on day 1. No significant group, time, or interaction effects were found for the four lung quadrants. The experimental group had higher PaO₂/FiO₂, shorter ICU stay (6.55 vs. 7.75 days), and lower delirium incidence (25.0% vs. 45.5%). Respiratory rate decreased, and pulse oxygen saturation increased over time in both groups, without significant group or interaction effects. The EIT-guided strategy may improve regional ventilation distribution and oxygenation, shorten ICU stay, and reduce delirium in patients with respiratory failure.

articles.title: Excessive Tidal Volume During Noninvasive Ventilation: Mechanisms of Harm Leading to Worse Clinical Outcomes.
Ventilation distribution assessed by electrical impedance tomography during robot-assisted laparoscopic prostatectomy: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: During robot-assisted laparoscopic prostatectomy (RALP), the combination of intra-abdominal pressure and a steep Trendelenburg position increases the risk of alveolar collapse and shifts the center of ventilation toward the abdomen, leading to intraoperative and postoperative hypoxia. This study evaluated whether fixed positive end-expiratory pressure(PEEP) 10 cmH2O, compared with zero PEEP (ZEEP), maintained a more central ventilation distribution during RALP as assessed by electrical impedance tomography (EIT). Sixty-five adult patients undergoing RALP were randomly assigned to either a PEEP 0 cmH2O group or a PEEP 10 cmH2O group. The primary endpoint was the mean center of ventilation (COV), as assessed using EIT. Secondary endpoints included other EIT parameters: the region of interest, global inhomogeneity index, and regional ventilation delay, as well as the P/F ratio, pulmonary compliance, peak airway pressure, and driving pressure (ΔP). Hemodynamic effects, lung injury biomarkers, and inflammatory cytokines were also evaluated. EIT and ventilator parameters were recorded at 6 time points: pre-intubation, post-intubation, during the Trendelenburg position, during pneumoperitoneum, pre-extubation, and post-extubation. Arterial blood gas and hemodynamic data were collected at the same points, plus 4 hours after ICU admission and again at ICU discharge. Lung injury biomarkers and inflammatory cytokines were measured pre- and postoperatively. The group-by-time interaction for COV was not statistically significant (P = .057). In exploratory Tukey-adjusted comparisons, COV was closer to 50% in the PEEP 10 group after intubation (PEEP 0 vs PEEP 10: 58.2% vs 53.4%; P = .038) and before extubation (58.6% vs 53.1%; P = .007). ΔP was lower, and lung compliance was higher, in the PEEP 10 group during the Trendelenburg position and pneumoperitoneum. No improvement in the P/F ratio or consistent between-group differences in major hemodynamic variables, KL-6, or IL-6 were observed. During RALP, with a fixed PEEP of 10 cmH2O, there was no group-by-time interaction effect observed for COV. However, in exploratory time-point comparisons, it was associated with a tendency for ventilation to be more centrically shifted after intubation and before extubation, and was also associated with an attenuated increase in ΔP and an attenuated decrease in lung compliance during the Trendelenburg position and pneumoperitoneum.

articles.title: Chlorhexidine within a standardized oral-care bundle for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia: a pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover trial in six medical intensive care units.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chlorhexidine (CHX) has been a long-standing component of oral-care bundles for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), but recent evidence has questioned its benefit in non-cardiac-surgery ICU. We evaluated whether adding 0.12% CHX to standardized oral-care bundle provides incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU. METHODS: We conducted a prospective, pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover (AB/BA) trial in six adult medical ICUs of a single tertiary-care academic hospital in Bhubaneswar, India. ICUs were randomized as three ICUs of two Period of 9 months with the multicomponent oral-care bundle without chlorhexidine and three with the same bundle plus 0.12% chlorhexidine with a 1-month wash-in and re-training interval. Consecutive adults ventilated for ≥ 48 h were included. The primary outcome was VAP incidence density (Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (CPIS) > 6) as per 1,000 ventilator-days. Secondary outcomes were 28-day all-cause mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, 28- day ventilator-free days, Beck Oral Assessment Scale (BOAS) and Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) scores. The primary model was a population-averaged Poisson generalized estimating equation (GEE) and adjustment for treatment, period, sequence, age, sex, APACHE II, and SOFA. RESULTS: A total of 1,035 patients (637 No CHX, 398 CHX) accrued 10,024 ventilator-days (5,918 vs. 4,106). Groups were well balanced at baseline (mean age ≈ 55 years; APACHE II ≈ 19.6; SOFA ≈ 13.4). VAP occurred in 100/5,918 ventilator-days (16.9 per 1,000) vs. 77/4,106 (18.8 per 1,000) (No CHX vs. CHX). The adjusted Poisson incidence rate ratio was 1.08 (95% CI 0.84-1.38; p = 0.56). 28-day mortality was 28.7% vs. 26.4% (no CHX vs. CHX) (adjusted OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.65-1.15; p = 0.33). ICU length of stay was longer in the CHX arm (adjusted mean difference + 0.89 days, 95% CI + 0.19 to + 1.58; p = 0.013). BOAS and CPOT scores did not differ. CONCLUSIONS: In this trial, adding 0.12% chlorhexidine to a standardized oral-care bundle did not reduce VAP incidence density or 28-day mortality and was associated with a modest increase in ICU length of stay. Routine CHX use provided no clear incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU population. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical Trials Regisrty- India (CTRI) identifier [CTRI/2024/02/062201], registered [01 February 2024].

articles.title: Impact of a Nurse-Led, Target-Directed Light Sedation Strategy on the Incidence of Delirium in Septic Patients in the Emergency Intensive Care Unit.
articles.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the impact of a nurse-led, target-directed light sedation strategy on delirium incidence and short-term outcomes in septic patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation in the emergency intensive care unit (EICU).MethodsWe analyzed 221 consecutive septic patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation for more than 24 h at a single center (January 2022-May 2024). Based on a sedation protocol change, patients were assigned to conventional sedation group (control, n = 123) or nurse-led, target-directed light sedation group (exposed, n = 98). The primary outcome was delirium incidence. Secondary outcomes included delirium-free days (DFD-28), ventilator-free days (VFD-28), mechanical ventilation duration, EICU length of stay, and 28-day mortality. Multivariable logistic regression examined the independent association between the nurse-led strategy and delirium risk.ResultsDelirium occurred less frequently in the nurse-led sedation group than in the control group (20.4% vs 37.4%, P = .007). The exposed group had shorter mechanical ventilation duration and EICU length of stay (both P < .05), whereas VFD-28 did not differ significantly between groups. The two groups did not differ significantly in 28-day mortality (28.6% vs 26.0%, P = .671) or in the rate of airway-related adverse events. On multivariable analysis, the nurse-led strategy was independently associated with a lower risk of delirium (OR = 0.428, 95% CI: 0.215-0.854, P = .016). Subgroup analyses showed that this protective benefit was consistent across age strata, disease severity levels, and comorbidity burden.ConclusionIn septic patients undergoing mechanical ventilation, a nurse-led, target-directed light sedation strategy was associated with reduced delirium incidence, shorter mechanical ventilation duration, and decreased EICU length of stay, without increasing adverse events. However, no improvement in 28-day mortality was observed. Further validation through multicenter prospective randomized controlled trials is warranted to assess long-term efficacy and safety.

articles.title: Ventilator-associated pneumonia after traumatic brain injury: a timing-sensitive ecological framework of neuroimmune-pulmonary vulnerability.
articles.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is frequent after traumatic brain injury (TBI), but its biological meaning and outcome impact remain incompletely defined. Traditional models emphasise mechanical ventilation, aspiration, colonisation, endotracheal tube biofilm, and hospital pathogens. These mechanisms remain essential, but they do not fully explain the early clustering, heterogeneous susceptibility, changing bacteriology, and variable mortality effect observed after TBI. Severe brain injury creates an early vulnerable host state through impaired consciousness and airway protection, neuroimmune dysregulation, autonomic and endocrine activation, altered pulmonary immune surveillance, and, in many patients, extracranial trauma, shock, transfusion, or thoracic injury. These processes interact with ventilation, antibiotic pressure, and rapid respiratory microbiome disruption. Early VAP may reflect abrupt loss of control after injury and intubation, whereas late VAP may reflect persistent or secondary failure driven by biofilm maturation, antibiotic selection, multidrug-resistant pathogens, and intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired immune dysfunction. Clinically, VAP consistently prolongs ventilation, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and resource use, while its independent effect on mortality is phenotype- and context-dependent. This model proposes a timing-sensitive ecological framework in which established mechanisms may converge early and with particular clinical intensity after severe TBI, creating a vulnerable host-microbe state that may lower the threshold for clinically apparent infection. Future studies should distinguish isolated TBI from polytrauma, compare TBI with other acute brain injuries and non-neurological ventilated populations, and incorporate dynamic immune, microbial, and trajectory-based outcomes. VAP after TBI should be viewed as a timing-sensitive interaction between ventilator exposure and early host vulnerability, not as a distinct disease entity or as a pneumonia pathway unique to traumatic brain injury. The TBI-focused contribution lies in the early convergence of otherwise non-unique mechanisms: impaired airway control, aspiration risk, neuroimmune-endocrine activation, treatment exposure, dysbiosis, and extracranial injury burden, rather than in any single TBI-specific mechanism. Isolated TBI and TBI with polytrauma are biologically different phenotypes and should be separated in future studies. Early and late VAP may represent different phases of loss of pulmonary host-microbe containment; this distinction is probabilistic rather than TBI-specific in itself and requires validation in TBI-stratified cohorts. Mortality remains clinically relevant but context-dependent; VAP more consistently modifies recovery trajectory, ventilator dependence, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and possibly neurological recovery.

articles.title: Bacterial epidemiology and attributable mortality of Ventilator-associated pneumonia before and after COVID-19 pandemic (2018-2021).
articles.abstract: BackgroundVentilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in mechanically ventilated patients. The COVID-19 pandemic has profoundly modified VAP epidemiology and microbial ecology.MethodsWe conducted a prospective multicenter cohort study within the REA-REZO network (≈20% of French ICU beds), 1 January 2018-31 December 2021. All adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation were included. VAP was defined according to ECDC criteria. Primary endpoints were VAP incidence density (per 1000 ventilation-days) and 30-day attributable mortality. Secondary endpoints included resistance patterns and pre-pandemic versus pandemic trends.ResultsAmong 98,047 patients, 12,251 patients developed VAP, with an incidence of 18.9/1000 ventilation-days. Peak incidence occurred at day 10 (29/1000 ventilation-days). Thirty-day attributable mortality was 4.9% [95% CI 3.7;6.2], rising to 7.2% [6.0;8.5] at 60 days. Gram-negative bacteria accounted for 78.0% of isolates, predominantly Enterobacterales (46%) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (20%). Third-generation cephalosporin resistance reached 27% in Enterobacterales and 25% in P. aeruginosa. The COVID-19 patients had a higher VAP rate (19.5% vs 9.7%, p<0.001) and mortality (36.9% vs 31.0%, p<0.001).ConclusionsVAP remains highly prevalent in French ICUs with substantial attributable mortality. The COVID-19 pandemic nearly doubled VAP incidence and worsened resistance profiles. Intensified prevention bundles during the first 10 days of ventilation and reinforced antimicrobial stewardship are critical.

articles.title: Intermittent or Continuous Renal-Replacement Therapy in Acute Kidney Injury.
articles.journal: The New England journal of medicine
articles.abstract: The preferred method of renal-replacement therapy for acute kidney injury in critically ill patients remains uncertain. In this multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned critically ill adults with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy to undergo intermittent hemodialysis or continuous renal-replacement therapy as the initial treatment. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event - defined as death, dependence on renal-replacement therapy, or a serum creatinine concentration more than 25% above the baseline value - by day 90. The trial was stopped early after sequential interim analyses showed a sustained signal of higher mortality with intermittent hemodialysis than with continuous renal-replacement therapy. A total of 554 patients underwent randomization, with 272 patients assigned to undergo intermittent hemodialysis and 282 to undergo continuous renal-replacement therapy; 535 patients (260 in the intermittent group and 275 in the continuous group) were included in the intention-to-treat population. A major adverse kidney event occurred by day 90 in 203 patients (78.1%) in the intermittent group and in 197 patients (71.6%) in the continuous group (adjusted absolute risk difference, 6.28 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.22 to 13.79). Death by day 90 occurred in 164 patients (63.1%) and in 147 patients (53.5%), respectively. Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates at day 90 were 63.3% and 53.6% (hazard ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.63). The most common complication potentially related to acute kidney injury or renal-replacement therapy was hypotension, which occurred in 179 patients (68.8%) in the intermittent group and in 183 patients (66.5%) in the continuous group. Among critically ill patients with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy, intermittent hemodialysis as the initial treatment approach was not shown to be noninferior to continuous renal-replacement therapy with respect to major adverse kidney events by day 90 and was associated with higher mortality. (Funded by the French Ministry of Health; ICRAKI ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06032884.).

articles.title: Beyond 28-Day Mortality: The Unfinished Story of Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Survivorship.
Adjunctive therapeutic plasma exchange as rescue therapy in septic shock due to streptococcal infection: a multicentric retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Septic shock due to streptococcal infection (SRSS) carries a high mortality and is in part driven by toxin-mediated inflammation. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) may modulate the septic host responses by removing injurious mediators while replenishing protective plasma factors, but data specific to SRSS is lacking. We performed a retrospective, multicenter, cohort study of adults with SRSS between 2012-2024. Patients from three tertiary care ECMO centers in Germany and Switzerland were included requiring (i) streptococcal spp. detected in blood or primary focus and (ii) septic shock according to sepsis-3 definition. Adjunctive TPE with fresh frozen plasma at the intensivists` discretion was compared with standard of care (SOC). The primary outcome was 90-day-hospital mortality. Key exploratory outcomes included 24-h kinetics of vasoactive-inotropic score(VIS) and lactate, as well as SRSS-related complications. Results were validated in a 1:1 propensity score-matched (PSM) cohort. Of 149 patients, 31 (20.8%) received TPE and 118 (79.2%) SOC. TPE patients were more severely ill at baseline: SOFA 14 (IQR 13.5-15) vs 11 (IQR 8-14) (p<0.001); lactate 6.4 vs 2.8 mmol/L (p<0.001); Vasoactive-Inotropic-Score (VIS) 70.7 vs 23.3 (p<0.001); more frequent invasive ventilation (87% vs 65%), VV-ECMO (36% vs 19%), and renal replacement therapy (96.8% vs 52.5%). Overall, 90-day hospital mortality was 27.5% (TPE 29.0%, SOC 27.1%). Following SOFA-score adjustment, TPE was associated with lower mortality risk (aHR 0.67 [95% CI 0.5-0.9]; p=0.009). This was validated in the PSM cohort, with an aHR for TPE of 0.44 (95% CI 0.3-0.8); p=0.002. Mixed-effects modeling demonstrated a significant VIS reduction only with TPE (fixed effect 24-h change, p=0.027) and improved lactate decrease versus SOC. In SRSS, adjunctive TPE was associated with rapid hemodynamic stabilization and improved lactate kinetics. Exploratory adjusted survival analyses support prospective evaluation of TPE in SRSS.

articles.title: Molecular Subtypes in Acute Respiratory Illness and Sepsis.
articles.journal: Seminars in respiratory and critical care medicine
articles.abstract: Sepsis and acute respiratory illness are clinical syndromes that encompass profound biological heterogeneity. The resulting heterogeneity of treatment effect is now widely understood as the explanation to why immunomodulatory trials in critical care have not me their study endpoints, thereby misclassifying effective therapies as futile while concealing harm in biologically ineligible subgroups. High-dimensional molecular profiling offers a route to resolve this heterogeneity into tractable subgroups or subtypes. Here we review molecular subtypes across adult and paediatric sepsis, pneumonia, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), spanning transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic platforms. Blood transcriptomic frameworks derived independently in multiple countries, and subsequently harmonized by international consensus efforts, converge on recurring immune archetypes: a myeloid inflammatory state dominated by neutrophil activation; a mixed myeloid and lymphoid dysregulated state carrying the highest mortality; and a relatively immunocompetent state with preserved lymphocyte function and the most favourable clinical trajectory. Plasma proteomic and metabolomic profiling recapitulate this architecture at orthogonal molecular layers, arguing that these archetypes are platform-independent rather than artefacts of any single technology. Cross-syndrome convergence is asymmetric, which plausibly reflects the methodological differences between top-down latent class analysis in ARDS and bottom-up unsupervised clustering in sepsis. Secondary analyses of randomized controlled trials consistently show subtype-dependent responses to treatment strategies, with a coherent directionality with potential benefit in hyperinflammatory states, and harm in immunosuppressed or adaptive immune-prevalent states. Subtype membership is not static; trajectory, not baseline assignment, most strongly encodes prognosis. Realising precision critical care now requires prospective, subtype-stratified trials of which none has yet been completed.

articles.title: Optimizing post-extubation respiratory support in high-risk patients.
ARDS at 60: beyond lung protection to lung repair.
Phenotyping ARDS: A pragmatic path forward with the POLARIS international cohort.
Clinical Outcomes and Complications of Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) in Adult Patients With COVID-19 in Central and Eastern Europe: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.journal: Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is a rescue therapy for severe COVID-19-related acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). International datasets do not consistently report Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) separately. We aimed to assess mortality, clinical characteristics, and complications of ECMO-treated COVID-19 patients across the CEE region. MATERIAL AND METHODS We conducted a systematic review with single-arm meta-analyses of observational studies. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from January 2020 to August 2025 for studies reporting ECMO outcomes in adult (≥18 years) COVID-19 patients from CEE countries, with at least 10 ECMO-treated patients. Conference abstracts and overlapping cohorts were excluded. The study protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251077593). RESULTS Twelve studies included 802 patients from 6 countries. Pooled in-hospital mortality was 65% (95% CI 0.57-0.72; I²=70.6%; 10 studies; n=691), and ICU mortality was 61% (95% CI 0.47-0.74; I²=85.8%; 7 studies, n=526). Country-level in-hospital mortality estimates were 54% for the Czech Republic and 76% for Poland but were descriptive because of the small number of studies and wide CIs. Mean pre-ECMO mechanical ventilation duration was 4.8 days (95% CI 3.7-5.8; I²=4.4%), ECMO duration was 17.8 days (95% CI 12.8-22.9; I²=79.8%), and ICU length of stay was 23.6 days (95% CI 7.5-39.7; I²=92.6%). Serious bleeding occurred in 40% (95% CI 22-61%; I²=85.7%). Certainty was very low for all pooled outcomes. CONCLUSIONS These CEE-specific estimates provide regional benchmarks, but substantial heterogeneity and very low certainty limit international comparisons and country-level interpretation. Standardized regional registries, prospective multicenter data, harmonized complication reporting, and long-term outcome assessment are needed.

articles.title: Antibiotic Stewardship in Nonoperative Facial Trauma: Necessary or Not?
articles.abstract: Closed facial fractures are common and often treated nonoperatively. Routine systemic antibiotic prophylaxis is controversial because infection rates are low and antibiotics can cause harm. We assessed whether prophylactic antibiotics reduce infectious complications in closed, nonoperative facial fractures. A systematic review was conducted of adults with closed, nonoperative facial fractures (emergency department, inpatient, intensive care unit). PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched from inception through September 19, 2025. Studies compared systemic prophylaxis versus none and/or ≤24 hours versus >24 hours. Seven US studies comprising 3274 patients met the inclusion criteria. Across studies, fracture-related infection rates were low and were not reduced by prophylactic antibiotics. In the largest prospective multicenter cohort, Mian et al reported a 30-day facial fracture-associated infection rate of 1.0%, with no significant benefit for ≤24 hours or >24 hours of prophylaxis compared with none (adjusted odds ratio 1.24-1.32). Orbital and zygomatic cohorts reported no infectious complications regardless of prophylaxis strategy. In sinus-involving and intensive care unit cohorts, fracture-site infection and sinusitis were rare; most infectious events were pneumonia or ventilator-associated pneumonia rather than facial fracture-specific infections. Longer antibiotic exposure was associated with isolated cases of Clostridioides difficile colitis. Available evidence does not support routine systemic prophylaxis for uncomplicated closed, nonoperative facial fractures. The strongest inference applies to patients without another indication for antibiotics. Current data do not identify fracture-specific subgroups in whom prophylaxis improves outcomes; accordingly, management should emphasize local care, return precautions, and structured follow-up.

articles.title: Impact of Erector Spinae Block on Postoperative Analgesia and Hospital Recovery in Coronary Artery Bypass Surgery: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis, Meta-Regression, and Sequential Trial Analysis.
articles.abstract: The erector spinae plane block (ESPB) is a promising regional technique for cardiac surgery. We evaluated the efficacy of ESPB regarding analgesia and in-hospital outcomes in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing ESPB versus control in adults undergoing CABG (CRD42025645045). Primary outcomes were opioid consumption (24 h/48 h) and pain intensity. Secondary outcomes included extubation time and intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay. Data were pooled using random-effects models. Meta-regression and trial sequential analysis (TSA) were used to assess sources of heterogeneity and robustness, respectively, while the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations framework provided the certainty of the evidence for each outcome. Twelve studies (704 patients) were analyzed. ESPB significantly reduced the morphine milligram equivalent consumption at 24 h (mean difference (MD) -19.05 mg; 95% confidence interval (CI) [-22.50 to -15.61]; P < 0.001; high certainty) and 48 h (MD -19.42 mg; 95% CI [-28.75 to -10.09]; P < 0.001; moderate certainty). Pain scores, by the Numerical Rating Scale, were lower within 12 h (MD -0.93; P < 0.001; moderate certainty) and at 24 h (MD -0.58; P = 0.016; low certainty). ESPB shortened extubation time (MD -2.50 h; high certainty) and ICU stay (MD -12.55 h; moderate certainty). TSA confirmed robust evidence for opioid reduction, early pain relief, and extubation benefits. ESPB provides effective early analgesia, reduces perioperative opioid requirements, and accelerates recovery in CABG, representing a fundamental complement to conventional isolated intravenous analgesia. Future research should investigate continuous techniques.

articles.title: Prevalence of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder in Iranian Intensive Care Unit Survivors and Related Factors: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit survivors are discharged with various psychological complications, among which post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is one of the most significant. The main aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of PTSD and its associated factors among Iranian intensive care unit (ICU) survivors. This systematic review and meta-analysis included studies published in English and Persian from 2000 to 2025. Electronic gateways and databases, including MEDLINE via PubMed, MEDLINE via OVID, ISI Web of Knowledge, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library, Magiran, Wiley, Scientific Information Database (SID), and Google Scholar, were searched. Study quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklist. Data were analyzed using STATA software (version 17.0, StataCorp/LC, USA). Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic, and a random-effects model was applied to estimate pooled prevalence. A significant level of P<0.001was considered. The pooled prevalence of PTSD in Iranian ICU survivors was 36.4% (95% CI: 23.5-48.3; I2=98.75%; P<0.001). The prevalence in Iranian women, 51.47% (95% CI: 45.01-57.92; I2=97.52%), was higher than in Iranian men, 48.53% (95% CI: 42.08-54.99; I2=97.52%). Common related factors included older age, prolonged ICU hospitalization, history of psychiatric disorders, mechanical ventilation, and drug abuse. The prevalence of PTSD among Iranian ICU survivors is relatively high. Identification of associated factors underscores the need for early screening, comprehensive follow-up programs, and targeted psychological interventions, particularly for high-risk populations.

articles.title: Analysis of the etiology of infection and antimicrobial resistance in chronic critically ill patients: a longitudinal study.
articles.journal: Journal of critical care medicine (Universitatea de Medicina si Farmacie din Targu-Mures)
articles.abstract: Hospital acquired infections and sepsis play an important role both as a triggering factor for chronic critically illness [CCI] and as a common complication of this syndrome. The aim of this study is to describe the clinical progression of sepsis episodes in CCI patients in the intensive care unit [ICU] of a Brazilian public hospital. A retrospective longitudinal study was conducted in a general ICU, from July 2022 to June 2023. The convenience sample consisted of 779 patients. Demographic, clinical, and microbiological data were analyzed. The incidence of CCI was 20.9% (n=166).
