Less is known about outcomes associated with language concordant care. Language concordance is a linguistic match between a patient's preferred language and the language used by their care team. We undertook a systematic review to examine the measurement and impact of language concordant care delivery during critical illness, inclusive of the critical care recovery period after hospitalization. A systematic review was conducted in PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Embase, and Cochrane of English-language publications from database inception to March 3, 2026. Studies that investigated adults in critical care and post-ICU recovery clinic settings that included measurement of language concordance were included. Study quality was evaluated by the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist. Of 1,682 unique records identified, 11 were eligible for inclusion (128,181 total patients; mean [sd] age, 68.4 [17.9 yr]; 72,872 [56.9%] male and 55,082 [43.1%] female). Six studies assessed clinical decision-making. Reported outcomes included code status changes, family conferences, communication complexity, delirium, length of stay, mechanical ventilation, and mortality. Due to significant heterogeneity in study analyses and reported outcomes, data were not pooled for quantitative analysis. Current evidence suggests that language-concordant care may influence clinically meaningful processes of critical care, warranting interventional studies to guide care delivery recommendations.

articles.title: Nitric oxide, prone positioning, and sedation and analgesia in mechanical ventilation.
articles.abstract: There are complementary treatments to mechanical ventilation in critically ill pediatric patients that are essential for optimizing oxygenation, gas exchange, and adaptation to respiratory support. Inhaled nitric oxide is a selective pulmonary vasodilator useful in specific situations such as pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular failure, and refractory hypoxemia, especially as rescue therapy, although its routine use in pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) has not been found to improve survival. The prone position improves ventilation/perfusion distribution, promotes alveolar recruitment, and reduces ventilator-associated lung injury, making it a valuable adjunctive strategy in patients with severe ARDS and persistent hypoxemia. Although its impact on pediatric survival is still being evaluated, it represents a physiologically sound tool for protective ventilation. Protocolized sedation and analgesia are essential to ensure comfort, synchrony with the ventilator, and prevention of complications such as delirium, withdrawal syndrome, or oversedation. The rational use of opioids, alpha-2 agonist sedatives, and neuromuscular blocking agents, along with monitoring using validated scales, allows for optimized clinical outcomes and reduced adverse effects. The individualized combination of these strategies is currently a cornerstone of advanced respiratory support for critically ill pediatric patients.

articles.title: The quality of delirium discussions during interprofessional ICU rounds: a mixed-methods study.
articles.abstract: Interprofessional rounds serve as the primary forum for care planning in the ICU, including implementation of evidence-based practices such as delirium screening. Whether validated screening results are communicated effectively during rounds-and whether they translate into action-remains poorly understood. How frequently and with what quality are delirium screening results discussed during interprofessional ICU rounds? We recorded, transcribed, and analyzed interprofessional rounding discussions from two ICUs in a large academic hospital. Both ICUs screen for delirium using the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist (ICDSC). We used quantitative analysis to determine how often the ICDSC was mentioned during rounds and how often abnormal scores prompted action planning, and qualitative content analysis with hybrid inductive and deductive coding to characterize the nature and content of delirium discussions during rounds. We analyzed 392 rounding discussions about 215 unique patients. The ICDSC score was mentioned during 213 (54%) discussions: 118 (55%) indicated subsyndromal delirium (ICDSC 1-3) and 44 (21%) indicated delirium (ICDSC ≥ 4). In ICDSC-anchored discussions, 67 (31%) included a plan to prevent or manage delirium. Content analysis identified five themes in these discussions: 1) "Tick the Box": rounding checklists treated as an end rather than a prompt for deeper discussion; 2) "Looking for a Solution": agitation prompting nuanced investigation; 3) "Don't Call It What It Is": reliance on imprecise descriptors of mentation; 4) "We Can't Assess For That": delirium assessment precluded by neurological injury or sedation level; and 5) "Direct Omissions": no mention of mental status. Implementation gaps in delirium care exist despite the use of validated tools for delirium assessment in the ICU. These results emphasize the need to test interventions that build the shared knowledge and vocabulary necessary for interprofessional ICU teams to prevent, diagnose, and treat delirium.

articles.title: Acute Neurotoxicity Syndromes from Immunotherapy: Emergency and ICU Management.
articles.abstract: Advances in cancer immunotherapy have transformed survival outcomes and driven widespread adoption of these treatments. However, as the population receiving immunotherapy has grown, neurologic complications have increasingly emerged, with rates of 1 to 3% among patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors and 26.9% among chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy recipients across all FDA-approved products. This review focuses on the early recognition and acute management of neurologic toxicities associated with immunotherapy, with particular emphasis on immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) related to CD19 and BCMA-directed CAR T cell therapies. Herein we synthesize current understanding of clinical phenotypes and risk factors for severe neurotoxicity, and review evidence-based approaches to diagnostic evaluation, including neuroimaging, electroencephalography, and laboratory markers. Practical management strategies for severe cases are discussed, including corticosteroid initiation, cytokine-directed immunomodulatory therapies, exploratory therapies, and neurocritical supportive care for fulminant cerebral edema and status epilepticus. We address less common but high-risk neurologic complications associated with CAR T cell therapy beyond ICANS. Lastly, we touch upon key clinical findings and treatments for acute neurologic complications related to immune checkpoint inhibitors, bispecific T cell engagers, tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, and engineered T cell receptor therapies.

articles.title: Structured Patient and Family-Centered Rounding in the ICU is Associated With Increased Family Confidence in Staff Compassion and Perceived Quality of Information Shared.
articles.abstract: Determine whether inviting families to participate in structured, multidisciplinary rounding in the ICU can lead to improved quality of information shared and greater overall confidence in the care delivered to patients. Pre- and postimplementation observational study based on surveys provided by the Society of Critical Care Medicine-Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute initiative. Academic teaching hospital with 21 medical (closed unit) and 25 surgical (open unit) ICU beds. Family members and care providers of critically ill adults of 18 years and older. Families and clinicians were surveyed before and after implementation of a quality initiative to promote greater patient and family-centeredness in daily ICU rounds, using a structured and scripted rounding template. Additional information was gathered regarding provider attitudes toward the incorporation of families in rounds. In pre-and postintervention periods, 36 and 28 families were surveyed in the MICU, and 44 and 42 families were surveyed in the SICU, respectively. In pre-and postintervention periods, respectively, 53 and 48 clinicians were surveyed in the MICU, and 46 and 28 clinicians were surveyed in the SICU. Clinician perceptions improved favorably in the MICU, with statistically significant improvements falling under the category of family welcoming, presence, and participation in decision-making; less so in the SICU. Family perceptions improved in almost all parameters in the MICU, with statistical significance achieved in perceived interest in patient needs, control of agitation and pain, and consistency and honesty of information shared. Similar patterns were observed in the SICU but did not reach statistical significance. Structured, multi-disciplinary rounding with regular inclusion of family members and bedside nurses was associated with significantly greater family confidence in the quality and honesty of information shared, and an increase in perceived compassion in the care provided by ICU staff. Clinician perceptions regarding family inclusion on rounds were generally positive.

articles.title: Quetiapine-induced neuroleptic malignant syndrome in a patient with traumatic brain injury: a case report.
articles.abstract: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a rare but life-threatening complication of antipsychotic therapy that can be mistaken for paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity (PSH) in traumatic brain injury (TBI), particularly when creatine kinase elevation is modest or when symptoms fluctuate. We report the case of a 54-year-old man with severe TBI who developed episodic PSH-like manifestations during recovery. Initial PSH-directed treatment was effective. However, after reintroduction of high-dose quetiapine, he began to exhibit recurrent manifestations resembling PSH that were refractory to treatment. Although the fluctuating clinical course and only modest creatine kinase (CK) elevation initially favored PSH, the clear temporal association with quetiapine reexposure supported a diagnosis of NMS. Discontinuation of quetiapine and initiation of NMS-targeted management resulted in rapid clinical improvement. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of distinguishing NMS from PSH in critically ill patients with TBI and underscores the importance of cautious reintroduction and gradual titration of antipsychotics, as well as early consideration of NMS even in the absence of marked CK elevation.

articles.title: The Effect of Guanfacine on Delirium in Surgical and Trauma ICU Patients: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the feasibility of conducting a randomized controlled trial investigating guanfacine for ICU delirium, including assessment of recruitment, retention, protocol adherence, and data completeness, while estimating treatment effects to inform future trial design. Single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial conducted from November 2020 to February 2023. Surgical and Trauma ICUs at the University of Alabama at Birmingham Hospital. One hundred critically ill adults with Confusion Assessment Method-ICU-confirmed delirium randomized 1:1 to guanfacine or placebo. Patients received 2 mg guanfacine or matching placebo nightly for up to 14 days, or until ICU discharge or delirium resolution. Primary feasibility outcomes included protocol adherence (target ≥ 90%), retention (target ≥ 80%), recruitment rate (target ≥ 2 patients/mo), and data completeness (target ≥ 95%). Most feasibility targets were achieved: protocol adherence was 100%, retention was 100%, and data completeness was 100%. Recruitment was significantly impacted by COVID-19 pandemic disruptions, achieving 0.9 patients/wk during active recruitment periods.For clinical outcomes, in unadjusted analyses, median delirium and coma-free days were higher with guanfacine than placebo (2 [interquartile range [IQR], 0-6] vs. 1 [IQR, 0-4]; p = 0.02); however, this association was not statistically significant after adjustment for prespecified baseline covariates. ICU and hospital length of stay and duration of mechanical ventilation did not differ significantly between groups. No hemodynamic differences or safety concerns were observed. This pilot study successfully supports feasibility for a definitive trial, with excellent protocol adherence, adequate retention, and preliminary signals that warrant further evaluation. Although adjusted analyses were not statistically significant, the observed unadjusted difference in delirium and coma-free days and favorable safety profile support progression to a multicenter trial informed by these pilot estimates.

articles.title: Composite Endpoints in Critical Care Delirium Trials.
articles.abstract: Delirium is an abnormal mental status, commonly occurring among critically ill patients, in which a person's attention and awareness change acutely. Delirium is associated with negative outcomes, including death. Furthermore, a longer duration of delirium is associated with long-term cognitive impairment in survivors of critical illness. Hence, there is a need for novel interventions that reduce the duration of delirium; however, measuring and analyzing "duration of delirium" as an endpoint in randomized trials is challenging due to the episodic nature of delirium and the competing events of coma and death, which can bias analyses of duration of delirium. Given these challenges, delirium trials have adopted one of two composite endpoints: delirium- and coma-free days, defined as the number of days alive without delirium or coma for both survivors and nonsurvivors, and an alternative composite that ranks death as the worst state and orders days alive without delirium or coma among survivors. To date, these composite endpoints have not been rigorously evaluated. Hence, herein we use data from the Maximizing Efficacy of Targeted Sedation and Reducing Neurologic Dysfunction (MENDS) trial to motivate the use of composite endpoints in critical care delirium trials, discuss how to define the effect of treatment on each composite endpoint and their clinical interpretability, and present a method for visualizing how the treatment effects accrue over the course of follow-up. Based on these analyses, we provide practical recommendations for the use of composite endpoints in critical care delirium trials, which could be extended to other randomized trials that rely on similar composite endpoints.

articles.title: Circulating Cell-Free Mitochondrial DNA, Delirium, and Long-Term Cognitive Impairment in Critically Ill Adults With Sepsis: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: During sepsis, circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA (ccf-mtDNA) is released and elevated due to cell injury, augments the immune response, and may contribute to organ dysfunction. Delirium is common and deleterious during sepsis, but little is known about the relationship between mitochondrial injury and delirium during sepsis. We sought therefore to examine associations between ccf-mtDNA and delirium and other clinical outcomes during sepsis. Multicenter, prospective cohort study. Medical and surgical ICUs in university and community hospitals in Nashville, TN. Four hundred eighty patients with sepsis plus shock and/or acute respiratory failure. None. We measured ccf-mtDNA in plasma collected on multiple days (study days 1, 3, and 5) during sepsis and assessed participants bid for delirium and coma using the validated Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU and Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale. We then assessed survivors' cognitive function 3 and 12 months after hospital discharge using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status. During sepsis, the adjusted odds of delirium were 7% lower for individuals at the 75th percentile of ccf-mtDNA compared with those at the 25th percentile (odds ratio [OR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.86-0.99; p = 0.048). ccf-mtDNA was marginally associated with in-hospital mortality (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.99-1.20; p = 0.08), but was not associated with coma (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.90-1.05; p = 0.31) or 3-month (beta, 0.23; 95% CI, -1.58 to 2.05; p = 0.80) and 12-month (beta, -0.36; 95% CI, -2.13 to 1.42; p = 0.69) cognitive outcomes. In this multicenter, prospective cohort study, higher levels of ccf-mtDNA were associated with lower odds of delirium, a result that contradicted our hypothesis. This provocative finding should be interpreted cautiously until replicated and explained by future studies.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of oliceridine versus remifentanil for analgesia in mechanically ventilated critically ill adults (CO-ROAM): a multicenter, assessor-blinded, non-inferiority randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: Remifentanil provides effective analgesia during invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), but its utility is limited by opioid-related adverse events. Oliceridine, a G protein-biased μ-opioid receptor agonist, may decouple analgesia from these effects, but lacks evidence in critically ill patients. This multicentre, assessor- and patient-blinded, non-inferiority randomised controlled trial was conducted across 19 intensive care units (ICUs) in China. Adults receiving IMV were randomised 1:1 to oliceridine or remifentanil, titrated to a Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool score below 3. The primary endpoint was time in target analgesic range (TTR; non-inferiority margin -10%). Of 307 randomised patients, 304 comprised the modified intention-to-treat population (151 oliceridine, 153 remifentanil). Median TTR was 96.0% versus 92.3% (absolute difference 3.7%, 95% CI -0.3-5.7%). Oliceridine was associated with fewer mild-to-moderate adverse drug reactions (ADRs), occurring at 15.9 versus 22.2 events per 100 patient-days (IRR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52-1.00, P = 0.049), and a lower rate of respiratory depression during the study period (0% vs. 4.6%, P = 0.015). Post-extubation respiratory depression (0% vs. 7.9%, P = 0.005) and analgesic-sedation costs were both lower with oliceridine. IMV duration, ICU stay, and 28-day mortality did not differ. Subgroup analyses identified a nominal ADR benefit in patients with Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II > 17 and a larger nominal TTR difference in those without acute respiratory distress syndrome. Oliceridine provides non-inferior analgesia to remifentanil with a more favourable respiratory safety profile and lower costs in critically ill adults. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06454292 (registered June 11, 2024).

articles.title: Metabolic response during neuromuscular electrical stimulation in critically ill patients with deep sedation: a prospective observational study.
articles.abstract: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) is a potential strategy to counteract skeletal muscle atrophy in critically ill patients unable to engage in early mobilization. However, it is difficult to confirm whether the exercise load applied by NMES is sufficient to elicit a physiological effect in patients under sedation or with impaired consciousness, as the appropriate stimulus intensity and exercise load of NMES are generally assessed using subjective responses. This study aimed to evaluate changes in energy expenditure during NMES in sedated, mechanically ventilated patients using indirect calorimetry. This single-center observational study included 22 mechanically ventilated patients under deep sedation in the intensive care unit (ICU). Energy expenditure was measured using indirect calorimetry during NMES sessions. The primary outcome was the difference in energy expenditure before and during NMES. Multivariable linear regression analysis was performed to calculate the adjusted mean difference in energy expenditure. A clinically meaningful increase in energy expenditure attributable to NMES was predefined as 150 kcal/day, which was assumed based on an increase in energy expenditure when sitting on the edge of the bed. In total, 26 NMES sessions involving 22 participants were included in the analysis. The mean energy expenditure was 1,137 ± 170 kcal/day pre-NMES and 1,350 ± 228 kcal/day during NMES. The adjusted increase in energy expenditure during NMES was 213.8 kcal/day (95% confidence interval, 137.1-290.3). This increase reached statistical significance when tested against the predefined threshold of 150 kcal/day (P = 0.02). The exercise load provided by NMES could be objectively assessed by measuring increases in energy expenditure. Although a statistically significant increase in energy expenditure was observed during NMES compared to pre-NMES levels, the magnitude of this increase was minimal. Further research is needed to determine whether NMES protocols that enhance energy expenditure are associated with muscle mass preservation, strength maintenance, and the prevention of ICU-acquired weakness.

articles.title: Consensus on a core outcome set for ventilation trials in critically ill patients with acute brain injury: results of an international Delphi consensus study.
articles.abstract: Clinical research evaluating mechanical ventilation liberation in patients with acute brain injury (ABI) shows substantial outcome heterogeneity, limiting evidence synthesis. We aimed to develop an internationally endorsed core outcome set (COS) and a hierarchical composite endpoint for ventilation trials in neurocritical care. Following COS-STAD/COS-STAP standards, we conducted a 4-round international Delphi study. Candidate outcomes were identified via a scoping review. A multidisciplinary panel from 31 countries scored outcomes using a 9-point GRADE scale. Inclusion required >70% rating as "critical" (score 7-9) and ≤15% as "not important" (1-3). Two consensus meetings were held to categorize outcomes, select representative measures, and ratify a hierarchical composite endpoint. 78 stakeholders participated in Round 1; 60 completed all rounds (23.1% attrition). Fifty-four outcomes achieved Delphi consensus. At Consensus Meeting 1, these were organized into 16 categories; the highest-scoring outcome per category was selected. Three outcomes were not ratified due to disease-specificity (NIH Stroke Scale) or lack of universal applicability (brain death, coma-free days). The final COS comprised 13 outcomes across 5 domains: respiratory function, survival, complications, functional status, and quality of life. A 3-level hierarchical composite endpoint was ratified at Consensus Meeting 2: (1) intensive care unit survival, (2) no reintubation within 72 hours, and (3) days alive without mechanical ventilation. This study establishes the first COS for ventilation weaning trials in ABI patients. Widespread adoption of these 13 outcomes and the hierarchical composite endpoint will standardize reporting, enable meaningful evidence synthesis, and facilitate clinical translation in neurocritical care. Core Outcome Measures in Effectiveness Trials (COMET) Initiative, registration number 2320.

articles.title: Vibroacoustic music therapy for postoperative delirium in the ICU: the VIMUD-ICU single-center exploratory randomized controlled trial.
Establishing curriculum priorities for intensive care recovery education: an international Delphi study.
articles.abstract: To effectively support recovery, intensive care unit (ICU) clinicians require training to identify patients at risk of post-intensive care syndrome and implement interventions during and after ICU admission. This study aimed to identify and prioritise curriculum topics for educating interprofessional ICU clinicians on evidence-based ICU recovery care across the continuum of critical illness. A two-round e-Delphi study followed by a structured consensus meeting endorsed by the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) was conducted. A steering committee generated an initial list of curriculum topics. In round 1, participants rated topic importance (9-point Likert scale) and suggested additional topics. In round 2, they rated newly identified topics and ranked priorities. Topics reaching consensus (≥70% rating as critical [7-9]; ≤15% rating as not important [1-3]) were discussed during the final consensus meeting. Participants' mean age was 43.5 (±10.5) years and they were predominantly female (n = 90, 66.7%). Priority topics included early mobilisation during ICU admission, post-intensive care syndrome, delirium prevention and management, implementation of the ABCDEF bundle, and cognitive support and rehabilitation. The final set of learning modules for a future curriculum was established. Priority topics and learning modules for an expert-developed curriculum framework for ICU recovery were established with interprofessional ICU clinicians through a structured international consensus process with moderate levels of participant retention between the two Delphi rounds and full consensus agreement among experts. This framework may support in delivering recovery-focused care across the continuum of critical illness.

articles.title: External Validation of a Machine Learning Model for Delirium Risk.
articles.abstract: Although external validation of machine learning (ML)-based delirium risk models is a key stage in the model development pipeline, few published reports exist. Moreover, ML-based delirium risk models commonly degrade in performance during external validation. To examine the performance of a fusion multimodal with natural language processing (NLP) delirium risk stratification model in live clinical practice with cross-hospital external validation. This quality improvement study evaluated live clinical deployment of the model among patients 60 years or older who were admitted to non-intensive care units at Mount Sinai Hospital (MSH), with external validation performed at Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital (MSM), from December 1, 2024, to December 31, 2025. Primary outcomes were performance of the risk stratification model, assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and monthly delirium detection rates. A 2 × 2 confusion matrix was created, and the 4 cells were used to calculate model performance metrics and compare associated diagnostic yield between premodel deployment and active model deployment periods. The overall sample included 33 095 admissions to non-intensive care units at MSM and MSH (mean [SD] age, 74.86 (9.22) years; 15 601 women [47.1%], 17 271 men [52.2%]). A total of 9020 MSM inpatient admissions were assigned a delirium risk score by the risk stratification model during live clinical operations and were compared to 21 186 MSH inpatient admissions that were assigned a risk score by the same model. Age at admission significantly differed between patients at MSM and MSH (MSM: median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years vs MSH: 72.62 [66.64-79.65] years; P < .001). Patients from MSM and MSH also significantly differed by sex, race and ethnicity, surgical vs medical primary diagnosis, length of stay, and dementia prevalence rate. Among 11 909 MSM patients, patients in the pre-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 78.00 [71.00-85.00] years) were significantly older than those in the post-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years) (P < .001). The AUROC of the model was 0.91 (95% CI, 0.90-0.92) for MSM and 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93-0.94) for MSH. The positive predictive value of the model was 25.9% for MSM and 19.4% for MSH. For MSM, the mean monthly delirium detection rate significantly increased from 9.23% (95% CI, 8.07%-10.38%) to 19.59% (95% CI, 17.32%-21.85%) after model deployment (P < .001). In this quality improvement study, an ML-based delirium risk stratification model maintained acceptable discriminative performance during external deployment without retraining and was similar to its performance at the development site without retraining. Model deployment was also associated with increased diagnostic yield but a high false positive rate. These findings provide further evidence of the potential generalizability of the model.

articles.title: Incidence of Intensive Care Unit Delirium After Heart Surgery: A Feasibility Study of a Forest Environment Intervention.
articles.abstract: Postoperative delirium is a serious complication in intensive care units (ICUs), particularly following cardiac surgery. It is associated with circadian rhythm disruption, sleep disturbances and adverse outcomes. ICU environments often lack natural time cues, which may exacerbate circadian misalignment and increase delirium risk. The primary aim of the study was the evaluation of the implementation of two chronotherapeutic ICU interventions regarding recruitment, implementability and safety. Its secondary aim was to descriptively assess postoperative delirium across intervention groups. This randomized feasibility study was conducted in a tertiary cardiac surgery ICU in Austria. Adult patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery were allocated to one of three groups: (1) forest environment, (2) light exposure or (3) standard ICU care. Interventions were applied for 12 h daily. Delirium was assessed at three postoperative time points using the confusion assessment method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) and intensive care delirium screening checklist (ICDSC). This study was conducted between March 2020 and 2025. Seventy-seven patients were enrolled, and 64 remained in the final analytical cohort. Interventions were delivered within routine care. Patients and ICU staff did not report intervention-related concerns. Implementation challenges included ICU restructuring, patient transfers due to COVID-19 and deviations from randomized allocation because of operational constraints. No intervention-related adverse events occurred. Delirium assessments were limited at several time points because of sedation, early ICU discharge or transfer. Across all groups, postoperative delirium was detected in 5 of 130 CAM-ICU completed assessments (3.8%) and 8 of 115 ICDSC completed assessments (6.9%), precluding inferential group comparisons. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions were feasible and safe in ICU care. Feasibility results highlighted challenges related to ICU logistics, sedation-related assessment limitations and pandemic-related disruptions. The unexpectedly low delirium incidence limited conclusions regarding intervention efficacy. Future trials should include larger high-risk populations and prospectively defined feasibility outcomes. Optimized ICU environments, including noise reduction and light management, may support delirium prevention. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions are feasible additions to routine ICU care.

articles.title: Effect of preoperative video-based digital educational program on incidence of delirium and length of hospital stay following coronary artery bypass grafting: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.journal: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care
articles.abstract: Postoperative delirium is common after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) and is associated with prolonged hospitalization and delayed recovery. Non-pharmacological educational interventions may improve outcomes, but evidence on structured video-based education for delirium prevention remains limited. To evaluate the effect of a preoperative video-based educational program on postoperative delirium incidence and hospital length of stay among patients undergoing CABG surgery. A parallel-group randomized controlled trial was conducted at Queen Alia Heart Institute, Jordan, between October 2025 and January 2026. Adult patients scheduled for elective first-time CABG surgery were randomized into intervention and control groups. Both groups received standardized multidisciplinary preoperative education through the institutional Preoperative Clinic, while the intervention group additionally received an 8-minute structured Arabic video-based educational program. Postoperative delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU). Among 226 randomized participants, 213 were analyzed (105 intervention; 108 control). Delirium incidence was lower with intervention (7.6%vs 25.0%, p < .001) and remained significantly associated with study group after adjustment (OR = 3.14, 95% CI: 1.08-9.14, p = .036). Hospital stay was shorter in the intervention group unadjusted (8.38 vs 10.58 days, p < .001), but not after adjustment (B = -0.656, p = .182). Preoperative video-based education was associated with lower postoperative delirium incidence, while its association with shorter hospital stay was not maintained after adjustment. Larger multicenter trials are warranted.

articles.title: Methodological Considerations Regarding Family Confusion Assessment Method Scoring in Delirium Screening for Spanish-Speaking ICU Patients.
Complications of Midazolam-Containing Versus Midazolam-Free Analgosedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adult ICU Patients: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) patients requiring mechanical ventilation (MV) frequently need analgosedation strategies that combine analgesia and sedation. Analgosedation, often administered with midazolam, is widely employed in middle and low-income countries, but it carries a substantial risk of complications, particularly in older or comorbid patients. Acknowledging these complications is critical for patient safety and quality of care. To examine complications associated with midazolam-containing versus midazolam-free analgosedation in mechanically ventilated adult intensive care unit patients. This systematic review was conducted according to the PRISMA guidelines. A comprehensive search of Scopus, MEDLINE (PubMed), and Web of Science identified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published between 2015 and 2025. Studies meeting predefined eligibility criteria underwent risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane RoB2 tool. Nine RCTs were included. Midazolam-containing analgosedation regimens were generally associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation, increased respiratory depression and higher incidence of neurological complications, particularly delirium. In contrast, midazolam-free analgosedation regimens, especially those using short-acting opioids, were associated with shorter mechanical ventilation duration and fewer haemodynamic incidents. ICU length of stay and healthcare costs favoured opioid-only analgosedation protocols, although mortality findings were inconsistent across studies. Compared with midazolam-free analgosedation, midazolam-containing analgosedation regimens in mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients are associated with a higher incidence of respiratory and neurological complications. Opioid-only protocols appear to offer a more favourable complication profile and may facilitate earlier weaning and shorter ICU stays. These findings support cautious use of midazolam and emphasize the importance of individualized, goal-directed analgosedation strategies. Enhancing critical care nursing staff's awareness of complications associated with different analgosedation regimens is essential to promote vigilant clinical monitoring, thereby reducing adverse events and supporting safer patient management.

articles.title: Application of Electrical Impedance Tomography-Guided Pulmonary Rehabilitation Strategy in Patients with Respiratory Failure.
articles.abstract: This study investigated pulmonary rehabilitation strategies guided by electrical impedance tomography (EIT) in patients with respiratory failure. A total of 92 patients with respiratory failure admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) of a tertiary Grade A hospital in Chongqing from July 2024 to January 2025 were selected and randomly divided into a control group and an experimental group, with 46 cases in each group, using a random number table. The control group received conventional pulmonary physical therapy nursing strategies. The experimental group additionally received EIT-guided positioning, vibratory sputum clearance, and early mobilization. Relative regional tidal-ventilation distribution, PaO₂/FiO₂, respiratory rate, and pulse oxygen saturation were assessed at baseline and on the following three days; ICU stay, and delirium incidence were also compared. Finally, 44 cases in the control group and 44 cases in the experimental group completed the study. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed significant time effects across the four ventral-to-dorsal layers and significant group and interaction effects for the dorsal layer. Dorsal ventilation share was higher in the experimental group on days 2 and 3, but not significantly different on day 1. No significant group, time, or interaction effects were found for the four lung quadrants. The experimental group had higher PaO₂/FiO₂, shorter ICU stay (6.55 vs. 7.75 days), and lower delirium incidence (25.0% vs. 45.5%). Respiratory rate decreased, and pulse oxygen saturation increased over time in both groups, without significant group or interaction effects. The EIT-guided strategy may improve regional ventilation distribution and oxygenation, shorten ICU stay, and reduce delirium in patients with respiratory failure.

articles.title: Impact of a Nurse-Led, Target-Directed Light Sedation Strategy on the Incidence of Delirium in Septic Patients in the Emergency Intensive Care Unit.
articles.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the impact of a nurse-led, target-directed light sedation strategy on delirium incidence and short-term outcomes in septic patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation in the emergency intensive care unit (EICU).MethodsWe analyzed 221 consecutive septic patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation for more than 24 h at a single center (January 2022-May 2024). Based on a sedation protocol change, patients were assigned to conventional sedation group (control, n = 123) or nurse-led, target-directed light sedation group (exposed, n = 98). The primary outcome was delirium incidence. Secondary outcomes included delirium-free days (DFD-28), ventilator-free days (VFD-28), mechanical ventilation duration, EICU length of stay, and 28-day mortality. Multivariable logistic regression examined the independent association between the nurse-led strategy and delirium risk.ResultsDelirium occurred less frequently in the nurse-led sedation group than in the control group (20.4% vs 37.4%, P = .007). The exposed group had shorter mechanical ventilation duration and EICU length of stay (both P < .05), whereas VFD-28 did not differ significantly between groups. The two groups did not differ significantly in 28-day mortality (28.6% vs 26.0%, P = .671) or in the rate of airway-related adverse events. On multivariable analysis, the nurse-led strategy was independently associated with a lower risk of delirium (OR = 0.428, 95% CI: 0.215-0.854, P = .016). Subgroup analyses showed that this protective benefit was consistent across age strata, disease severity levels, and comorbidity burden.ConclusionIn septic patients undergoing mechanical ventilation, a nurse-led, target-directed light sedation strategy was associated with reduced delirium incidence, shorter mechanical ventilation duration, and decreased EICU length of stay, without increasing adverse events. However, no improvement in 28-day mortality was observed. Further validation through multicenter prospective randomized controlled trials is warranted to assess long-term efficacy and safety.

articles.title: Ventilator-associated pneumonia after traumatic brain injury: a timing-sensitive ecological framework of neuroimmune-pulmonary vulnerability.
articles.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is frequent after traumatic brain injury (TBI), but its biological meaning and outcome impact remain incompletely defined. Traditional models emphasise mechanical ventilation, aspiration, colonisation, endotracheal tube biofilm, and hospital pathogens. These mechanisms remain essential, but they do not fully explain the early clustering, heterogeneous susceptibility, changing bacteriology, and variable mortality effect observed after TBI. Severe brain injury creates an early vulnerable host state through impaired consciousness and airway protection, neuroimmune dysregulation, autonomic and endocrine activation, altered pulmonary immune surveillance, and, in many patients, extracranial trauma, shock, transfusion, or thoracic injury. These processes interact with ventilation, antibiotic pressure, and rapid respiratory microbiome disruption. Early VAP may reflect abrupt loss of control after injury and intubation, whereas late VAP may reflect persistent or secondary failure driven by biofilm maturation, antibiotic selection, multidrug-resistant pathogens, and intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired immune dysfunction. Clinically, VAP consistently prolongs ventilation, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and resource use, while its independent effect on mortality is phenotype- and context-dependent. This model proposes a timing-sensitive ecological framework in which established mechanisms may converge early and with particular clinical intensity after severe TBI, creating a vulnerable host-microbe state that may lower the threshold for clinically apparent infection. Future studies should distinguish isolated TBI from polytrauma, compare TBI with other acute brain injuries and non-neurological ventilated populations, and incorporate dynamic immune, microbial, and trajectory-based outcomes. VAP after TBI should be viewed as a timing-sensitive interaction between ventilator exposure and early host vulnerability, not as a distinct disease entity or as a pneumonia pathway unique to traumatic brain injury. The TBI-focused contribution lies in the early convergence of otherwise non-unique mechanisms: impaired airway control, aspiration risk, neuroimmune-endocrine activation, treatment exposure, dysbiosis, and extracranial injury burden, rather than in any single TBI-specific mechanism. Isolated TBI and TBI with polytrauma are biologically different phenotypes and should be separated in future studies. Early and late VAP may represent different phases of loss of pulmonary host-microbe containment; this distinction is probabilistic rather than TBI-specific in itself and requires validation in TBI-stratified cohorts. Mortality remains clinically relevant but context-dependent; VAP more consistently modifies recovery trajectory, ventilator dependence, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and possibly neurological recovery.

articles.title: European Society of Intensive Care Medicine consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit.
articles.abstract: A human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit (ICU) aims to integrate person-centred care, communication, emotional support, equity, and collaboration into ICU environments. The European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) developed a consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the ICU following a systematic, multi-phase, evidence-informed methodology incorporating the views of ICU professionals, academics, and patient and family representatives. This international multidisciplinary panel of 46 members conducted rapid reviews addressing 20 Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes (PICO) questions across six domains: person-centred care; communication and transparency; emotional well-being; equity, diversity, and inclusion; ICU environment; technology and innovation. Based on the evidence synthesis, 53 draft statements were developed and evaluated through a two-round eDelphi study. The final set of statements was discussed and ratified at an expert consensus meeting with the initial panel of experts and with patients and family representatives. A total of 201 international stakeholders participated in round 1 and 149 in round 2. Members of the expert consensus meeting ultimately endorsed 43 consensus statements. Key recommendations supported flexible family visitation, structured interdisciplinary communication, empathy-based staff training, psychological support for patients and ICU professionals, culturally responsive care, environmental interventions to improve sleep and reduce delirium, and the integration of digital supported technologies. The consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the ICU provides a comprehensive framework for clinicians with evidence-informed directions to deliver high-quality practice across diverse ICU settings. By prioritising person-centred care, communication, inclusivity, and well-being alongside responsible technological innovation, the experiences and outcomes of patients, families, and ICU professionals may improve.

articles.title: The overall effects of virtual reality interventions on ICU patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients frequently experience psychological distress, pain, sleep disruption, and motor impairments. Virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a promising nonpharmacological adjunct to improve these outcomes, yet existing evidence remains fragmented and inconsistent. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized recent clinical trials to evaluate the effectiveness of VR on mental health, pain, sleep, functional outcomes, and delirium in adult ICU patients. This review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (2020) guidance and was registered in International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42023482529). Eight databases were searched for randomized controlled trials published between January 2000 and September 2025. Eligible studies included adult ICU patients receiving immersive or non-immersive VR interventions. Primary outcomes were anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD); secondary outcomes included pain, sleep quality, lower-limb function, and bedside balance. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB tool, and certainty of evidence was graded using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation. Twenty randomized controlled trials were identified, involving a total of 1551 patients. This meta-analysis showed that VR intervention helped improve anxiety (standardized mean difference [SMD] = -0.67, 95% confidence interval [CI: -1.00 to -0.35], P < .0001), depression (SMD = -0.46, 95% CI [-0.72 to -0.21], P = .0004), PTSD [mean difference = -5.48, 95% CI (-9.36 to -1.59), P = .006], lower-limb function score [mean difference = 2.83, 95% CI (1.99 to 3.67), P < .001] and sleep quality (SMD = 0.70, 95% CI [0.47 to 0.92], P < .0001), but had no significant effect on pain score (SMD = -0.57, 95% CI [-1.49 to 0.36], P = .23) and bedside balance score (SMD = 0.61, 95% CI [-0.44 to 1.66], P = .25). Most studies were assessed as having varying degrees of risk of bias. All evidence was rated from very low to moderate. VR interventions may confer meaningful benefits for anxiety, depression, PTSD, and sleep quality in adult ICU patients, and may improve lower-limb function in selected populations. However, evidence for analgesic effects and bedside balance remains inconclusive. Standardized VR protocols, objective outcome assessment, and adequately powered multicenter trials are needed to clarify the clinical value of VR in ICU care.

articles.title: Clinical safety, tolerability, and efficacy of fospropofol disodium for sedation: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: Fospropofol disodium (fospropofol) is a water-soluble prodrug of propofol with a distinct pharmacological and tolerability profile. However, evidence regarding the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of fospropofol across broader sedation contexts and different comparators remains insufficiently synthesized. This systematic review summarized current research findings on fospropofol to clarify its clinical role and guide future research. This systematic review was registered prior to initiation (PROSPERO CRD42023477740). Comprehensive searches were performed in PubMed, Web of Science, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via Ovid, Embase via Ovid, ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to 26 August 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating fospropofol for sedation and reporting extractable efficacy or safety outcomes were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated according to the GRADE approach. Meta-analysis was performed for clinically comparable evidence groups, with other findings synthesized according to SWiM principles. This systematic review included 10 original studies, comprising six procedural-sedation trials and four trials for ICU sedation. Quantitative synthesis was conducted for two comparable evidence groups, whereas the remaining outcomes were synthesized narratively. In three endoscopic procedural-sedation trials, fospropofol 6.5 mg/kg achieved a higher sedation success than 2 mg/kg (RR 3.27, 95% CI 2.62-4.08). In mechanically ventilated ICU patients, hypotension risk did not clearly differ between fospropofol and propofol (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.67-1.28). Procedural studies showed a dose-dependent pattern in sedation efficacy, whereas ICU studies generally reported comparable target-sedation attainment between fospropofol and comparator sedatives. Paresthesia/pruritus was commonly reported, while rates of cardiorespiratory adverse events varied across settings and doses and showed no consistent comparative advantage for fospropofol. Evidence for injection pain and satisfaction was limited. Certainty of evidence ranged from high to very low, mainly because of risk of bias and imprecision. Fospropofol can provide effective sedation across procedural and ICU settings, but its efficacy and safety profiles vary according to dose, comparator, and clinical setting. Higher doses may improve procedural-sedation efficacy but may also increase adverse effects in some settings. Current evidence does not establish a consistent cardiorespiratory safety advantage for fospropofol over other sedatives, and further adequately powered randomized trials are needed to clarify its comparative safety and optimal clinical role.

articles.title: Music Therapy During Weaning From Invasive Mechanical Ventilation in the ICU: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The study examined the effect of daily music therapy on weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in the ICU, with a primary focus on weaning duration. Secondary agitation, sedation, and analgesia doses, pain, delirium, and perceived stress after 90 days were assessed. Additionally, total IMV and ICU stay durations and tracheostomy rates were studied. Physiologic parameters were assessed in the music therapy group (MG). The study also aimed to promote the humanization of critical care through a biopsychosocial and creative music therapy approach. DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups: control group receiving standard care during weaning and MG receiving music therapy additionally. SETTING AND PATIENTS: Adult critically ill patients (n = 100) admitted to a general ICU who received IMV for at least 48 hours. INTERVENTIONS: MG received daily, individualized music therapy sessions averaging 25 minutes, based on patient needs and musical preferences, which included music relaxation, music listening, and clinical improvisation. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: No significant difference in weaning duration was observed between groups (p = 0.97). Patients in the MG group showed significant improvements in agitation and sedation levels (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) on days 1 and 3 (p = 0.048, 0.005, and 0.024) and a lower percentage required propofol (p = 0.028). No significant difference in perceived pain (Visual Analog Pain Scale). The MG obtained lower Perceived Stress Scale-14 scores (p = 0.24). Additionally, MG significantly reduced tracheostomy rates (14%; p = 0.025). Median total IMV and ICU stay duration were shorter in the MG group, but not significantly (p = 0.206 and 0.203). Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygenation showed no significant difference before and after music therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Music therapy may serve as a nonpharmacological complementary adjunct during weaning by reducing agitation, sedation, and tracheostomy rate. It may potentially decrease perceived stress and IMV and ICU stay durations. Further research is warranted.

articles.title: Open Visiting Policy and Delirium in Adult Patients in ICUs: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
authors: and the Padova Intensive Care Unit (PADUA-ICU) Group
articles.abstract: To critically evaluate the comparative effects of open or flexible family presence policies vs. restricted or traditional family presence policies on the occurrence of delirium and other major outcomes among adult patients admitted to ICUs. We conducted a comprehensive electronic search of MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to November 21, 2025. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing open or flexible vs. restricted ICU visiting policies in adult patients. The primary outcome extracted was delirium occurrence. Secondary outcomes included the duration of invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), ICU length of stay, hospital-acquired infections, and ICU mortality. Thirteen RCTs comprising 3861 patients were included. Random-effects models showed that compared with restricted policies, open/flexible family presence reduced delirium occurrence (risk ratio [RR], 0.48; 95% CI, 0.29-0.81; low certainty) and IMV duration (mean difference [MD], -0.36 d; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.26 d; low certainty). The intervention did not affect the ICU length of stay (MD, 4.21 d; 95% CI, -4.65 to 13.07 d; very low certainty), the rates of hospital-acquired infections (RR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.81-1.23; low certainty), or ICU mortality (RR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.72-1.08; very low certainty). Open/flexible ICU family presence may reduce delirium and shorten the duration of IMV slightly, without increasing infections or ICU mortality, although the certainty of evidence is low and heterogeneity remains substantial.

articles.title: Ventilatory Management in Neurocritical Versus Non-Neurocritical Care Patients: A Pooled Analysis From the PRIME Database.
authors: PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS (PRoVENT), PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries (PRoVENT-iMiC), and Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes (ENIO) investigators
articles.abstract: To describe ventilatory management in neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients and determine whether specific ventilator settings are associated with development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and mortality in neurocritical care patients. The primary endpoint was a diagnosis of ARDS after initiation of invasive ventilation; one secondary endpoint was ICU mortality. Post hoc pooled analysis of harmonized individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies combined into the PRIME database. PRIME is a harmonized pooled database comprising individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies on ventilatory management in critically ill patients: "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS" (PRoVENT), "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries" (PRoVENT-iMiC), and "Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes" (ENIO). We excluded patients with ARDS at the start of ventilation. Demographic and clinical characteristics, ventilator settings, respiratory variables, arterial blood gas values, and clinical outcomes were extracted from the harmonized PRIME database. Derived ventilation parameters included tidal volume normalized to predicted body weight, driving pressure, respiratory system compliance, mechanical power, ventilatory ratio, and Pao2/Fio2 ratio. This analysis included 3848 patients, including 1702 neurocritical care and 1920 non-neurocritical care patients. Based on recorded ventilatory variables, neurocritical care patients received lower median tidal volumes (Vts), positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. They had lower median driving pressure (ΔP), mechanical power (MP) of ventilation, and ventilatory ratio, as well as higher respiratory system compliance compared with non-neurocritical care patients. These differences were consistently observed at both assessed time points. ARDS was diagnosed more frequently in neurocritical care patients than in non-neurocritical care patients (8.7% vs. 3.9%; p < 0.001), while ICU mortality was lower (14.3% vs. 22.8%; p < 0.001). Among neurocritical care patients, those who developed ARDS were ventilated with lower median Vt and higher Fio2 and had higher median ΔP and MP. Vt normalized for predicted body weight in neurocritical care patients was independently associated with the development of ARDS. In this cohort, ventilatory management at the initial and 48-hour assessments differed between neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients, particularly with respect to key ventilator settings like Vt, positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. In neurocritical care patients, ARDS was more often diagnosed than in non-neurocritical care patients.

articles.title: Isoflurane-Based Inhaled Sedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adults With Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: The SAVE-ICU Randomized Clinical Trial.
authors: SAVE-ICU Investigators and the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group
articles.abstract: Rigorous evidence for inhaled sedation using isoflurane in mechanically ventilated patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) is limited. To evaluate whether an inhaled sedation strategy lowers hospital mortality compared with usual care intravenous sedation strategy in mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF. Pragmatic, effectiveness, open-label, superiority, randomized clinical trial in 14 intensive care units (ICUs) in Canada. Adults (≥18 years) receiving sedation for less than 72 hours and receiving mechanical ventilation for AHRF from non-COVID respiratory failure (ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen [Pao2] to fraction of inspired oxygen [Fio2] <300 mm Hg) or COVID-19 were enrolled between September 2020 and March 2025 with follow-up through June 2025. Patients were randomized to an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed or to a usual intravenous sedation care strategy. Sedatives were titrated to achieve the desired target sedation score guided by clinical teams and continued until extubation or death. Primary outcome was all-cause hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU- and ventilator-free days at day 30; hospital-free days at day 60; use of refractory hypoxemia adjunctive therapies; delirium- and coma-free days at day 14; and quality-of-life and disability scores at 3 months. Of 786 patients randomized, 780 were included in the primary analysis (mean age, 61.1 years; 34.0% female; 73.7% non-COVID AHRF, mean Pao2:Fio2 ratio, 152.6 mm Hg); 385 in the inhaled sedation and 395 in the intravenous sedation groups. In the inhaled sedation group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients received concomitant intravenous sedation on any day during the first 14 days after randomization. At hospital discharge, 161 of 379 patients (42.5%) in the inhaled sedation group had died, compared with 171 of 390 patients (43.8%) in the intravenous sedation group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.84 to 1.14]; P = .85). There was no effect modification in prespecified subgroup analyses for age, sex, and COVID-19 status. ICU-, ventilator-, and hospital-free days were similar between groups. The inhaled sedation group received more adjunctive therapies for hypoxemia (239 [63.9%] vs 214 [55.0%]; between-group difference, 8.89% [95% CI, 1.95% to 15.83%]) and had fewer delirium- and coma-free days (between-group difference, -0.95 [95% CI, -1.69 to -0.22]). There was no difference in quality-of-life and disability scores between groups. In mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF, an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed did not reduce hospital mortality compared with an intravenous sedation strategy. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04415060.

articles.title: State-of-the-art review: ß-blockade in critical illness.
articles.abstract: Critical illness is characterised by activation of the sympathetic nervous system which plays an important adaptive role in maintaining cardiovascular stability and organ perfusion. However, excessive sustained adrenergic stimulation may become maladaptive, contributing to tachyarrhythmias, myocardial injury, immune dysregulation, metabolic derangements, and organ dysfunction. This state-of-the-art review evaluates the role of ß-blocker therapy as a potential strategy to modulate or counteract the adrenergic response in critically ill patients. Current data suggest that their use remains highly context-dependent and controversial. There are established benefits in selected scenarios, including acute myocardial infarction, tachyarrhythmias, hypertensive emergencies, thyroid storm, and prevention of variceal bleeds. In contrast, evidence is limited or conflicting in septic shock, traumatic brain injury, acute heart failure, burns and other critical care syndromes. Concerns include impairment of compensatory cardiovascular responses, reduction of cardiac output, hypotension, and compromised organ perfusion. Furthermore, the safety and efficacy of ß-blockade appear to depend on the type and dose of ß-blocker, patient phenotype, timing of initiation, hemodynamic reserve, and whether therapy represents continuation of chronic treatment, withdrawal and re-initiation, or de novo initiation during acute illness. This review highlights major gaps in knowledge, including the absence of reliable indicators to identify patients most likely to benefit, uncertainty regarding optimal treatment targets and monitoring strategies, and limited randomised evidence in heterogeneous ICU populations. A phenotype-driven, physiology-guided approach that accounts for hemodynamic status, sympathetic spectrum and timing of ß-blocker therapy is likely required to optimise outcomes.

articles.title: Respiratory mechanics modifies the impact of ventilator settings on clinical outcome in patients with acute brain injury.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate whether respiratory system elastance (ERS) modifies the associations of tidal volume (VT) and respiratory rate with clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated patients with acute brain injury. METHODS: In this post hoc analysis of the VENTIBRAIN study, ERS was computed as the ratio of driving pressure (ΔP) to VT/PBW. Effect modification by ERS on outcome associations was assessed. RESULTS: In 1158 patients, VT was similar across ERS tertiles (median 7.9, 7.6 and 7.1 mL/kg), resulting in a marked ΔP gradient across tertiles (median 5, 9, and 12 cmH2O). Higher VT was associated with lower ICU mortality in patients with low ERS (OR 0.52, 95%CI 0.36-0.74) but not in those with high ERS (OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.89-1.51; Pint < 0.001). Higher respiratory rate was associated with worse outcomes, particularly at low ERS, with the association attenuating at higher ERS. The Bayesian optimal VT/PBW decreased continuously with ERS, from 11.4 mL/kg at ERS 0.5 cmH2O/(mL/kg) (≈ ΔP 6 cmH2O) to 4.4 mL/kg at ERS 2.5 cmH2O/(mL/kg) (≈ ΔP 11 cmH2O), while the optimal respiratory rate increased from 15 to 19 breaths/min. At constant alveolar ventilation, 1-cmH2O ΔP increase had comparable prognostic impact to ≈ 3 breaths/min respiratory rate increases. These results were consistent irrespective of ARDS diagnosis. CONCLUSIONS: The impact of ventilator settings is modulated by ERS. A physiological framework for VT adjustment could consider ΔP along with the respiratory rate required to maintain isocapnia, with outcome effects governed by a trade-off of ≈ 3 breaths/min per 1-cmH2O change in ΔP.

articles.title: Decades of intensive care medicine trials: what randomised evidence has changed, corrected, and still questions to resolve.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have reshaped intensive care medicine (ICM), a discipline defined by acute, interacting organ failures, time-sensitive decisions, biological uncertainty, and heterogeneous recovery trajectories. Many interventions supported by strong physiological rationale failed to improve patient-centred outcomes, whereas durable advances often emerged from optimisation of supportive care, avoidance of iatrogenic harm, and reassessment of established practices. METHODS: We conducted an interpretive historical review of landmark multicentre RCTs in adult ICM from the early 1990s onwards. PubMed searches, reference lists from major trials and reviews, and international guidelines were used to identify trials with conceptual influence on practice, guidelines, physiological reasoning, therapeutic strategy, research priorities, de-implementation, or outcome framing. Evidence was organised into overlapping paradigms rather than rigid chronological periods. FINDINGS: Across haemodynamic support, mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, antimicrobial treatment, nutrition, glucose control, transfusion, and sedation, landmark RCTs describe more than therapeutic expansion. Early biological and haemodynamic trials exposed the limits of reductionist strategies in syndromic critical illness. Protocol-driven approaches improved timeliness and consistency, but later pragmatic trials showed that rigid targets and invasive algorithms often added little once high-quality usual care was established. More recent trials challenge the assumption that greater intervention intensity improves outcomes, emphasising timing, disease phase, baseline risk, heterogeneity, patient selection, and treatment-related harm. Modern ICM RCTs have clarified not only what works, but what can be reduced, delayed, avoided, or applied selectively. Future progress requires biologically informed, context-sensitive trials focussed on meaningful survival, recovery, and long-term function.

articles.title: Intracranial pressure physiology, monitoring and individualized management in the acute brain injured patient.
articles.abstract: Acute brain injury (ABI), including traumatic brain injury, ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke, is associated with high morbidity and mortality, which is driven not only by the primary brain injury, but also by the development of secondary cerebral insults. Among these, raised intracranial pressure (ICP) plays a central pathophysiological role, acting both as a consequence and a driver of ongoing brain injury through mechanical deformation and cerebral ischemia. Although invasive intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring has a longstanding and ongoing role in neurocritical care management, the interpretation and clinical use of ICP remain controversial. Traditional management strategies rely on fixed ICP thresholds (e.g., > 22 mmHg) to trigger a standardized stepwise escalation of therapy; however, growing clinical evidence indicates that tolerance to ICP elevation varies widely across patients, disease entities, and physiological contexts. This review summarizes the physiological determinants of ICP, including intracranial compliance, cerebrospinal fluid dynamics, cerebral blood volume, and systemic factors, and describes the mechanisms underlying intracranial hypertension. We discuss limitations of using fixed ICP thresholds and highlight emerging concepts, such as ICP burden, waveform morphology, cerebral autoregulation, and functional brain monitoring, as tools to individualize ICP interpretation. The role of invasive and noninvasive ICP monitoring (nICP) modalities is reviewed, emphasizing the complementary value of nICP in guiding decision-making when invasive monitoring is unavailable or contraindicated. Particular attention is given to the integration of ICP within multimodal neuromonitoring frameworks assessing cerebral perfusion, oxygenation, and metabolism. Finally, we explore future perspectives, including the potential of artificial intelligence-based approaches to analyse complex neuromonitoring data, predict secondary insults, and move toward actionable, patientspecific therapeutic strategies. Collectively, these advances support a shift from a uniform, threshold-driven approach toward individualized, physiology-informed management of intracranial hypertension.

articles.title: Rethinking Muscle Wasting in Critical Illness: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Myofiber Size and Protein Turnover.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To identify biological findings underlying skeletal muscle dysfunction in adults with critical illness and meta-analyze myofiber cross-sectional area and protein turnover variables. DATA SOURCES: Six databases were electronically searched from inception to January 2025. STUDY SELECTION: We included original studies reporting biological findings obtained from skeletal muscle biopsies of adults with critical illness. DATA EXTRACTION: Bibliometrics, characteristics of the patients/controls, and biological findings were extracted in duplicate. Descriptive statistics of biological findings were performed. Random-effects meta-analyses investigated mean differences (MDs) in myofiber cross-sectional area and protein turnover compared with controls. DATA SYNTHESIS: From 22,035 titles screened, 75 studies ( n = 2,023 patients; n = 642 controls) published between 1988 and 2024 were included, with 48 unique patient datasets. Biopsies were mainly collected from vastus lateralis (64 [85%] studies) during the first ICU week (50% of studies) and post-ICU (9%). Biological findings included predominant type II myofiber atrophy with necrosis and structural degeneration, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory/fibrotic changes, and upregulated ubiquitin-proteasome/autophagy pathways. Data from six studies ( n = 100 patients; 193 controls) indicated that cross-sectional area was 22% lower in patients with critical illness before (MD, -689 µm 2 ; 95% CI, -1265 to -113 µm 2 ; p = 0.02) and after (MD, -775 µm 2 ; 95% CI, -1512 to -37 µm 2 ; p = 0.04) ICU discharge. Across seven studies ( n = 126 patients; 61 controls) protein synthesis was not significantly different in patients with critical illness compared with controls (MD, 0.007%/hr; 95% CI, -0.010 to 0.027; p = 0.36). Protein degradation pathway markers were significantly higher (standardized MD ranging, 0.5-1.7) in data from 11 studies ( n = 439 patients; 163 controls). CONCLUSIONS: Muscle wasting during critical illness reflects multifaceted biological disturbances. While myofiber size is significantly lower in patients with critical illness, pooled analyses show no significant differences in muscle protein synthesis compared with non-ICU controls, whereas protein degradation markers are consistently higher.

articles.title: Geographic Access to Care and Mortality in Cardiogenic Shock: A Nationwide Cohort Analysis.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Timely access to advanced care is critical for patients with cardiogenic shock (CS), yet the impact of regional disparities in hospital arrival time on mortality remains unclear. OBJECTIVES: To investigate whether regional disparities in hospital arrival time are associated with in-hospital and long-term mortality among patients with CS. DESIGN: Population-based, nationwide cohort study. SETTING: Tertiary hospitals in South Korea, using data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database and regional hospital accessibility indicators from the Korea Transport Institute. PARTICIPANTS: A total of 80,263 adults (≥ 18 yr) admitted to an ICU with a diagnosis of CS between 2017 and 2022. The study population was stratified by estimated hospital arrival time using region-level average daytime travel times (< 10, 10-30, 30-60, and > 60 min) for the present study. INTERVENTIONS: None. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was all-cause mortality, including in-hospital and post-discharge mortality. Multivariable logistic and Cox regression models were used to assess associations. RESULTS: Median estimated hospital arrival time was 9.15 minutes. In-hospital mortality increased progressively with longer arrival times: 29.6% (< 10 min), 33.5% (10-30 min), 34.9% (30-60 min), and 38.8% (> 60 min). Compared with less than 10 minutes, the adjusted odds ratios for in-hospital mortality were 1.27 (95% CI, 1.23-1.32), 1.24 (95% CI, 1.14-1.35), and 1.51 (95% CI, 1.29-1.75), respectively. At 1-year follow-up, the adjusted hazard ratios for all-cause mortality were 1.16 (95% CI, 1.14-1.19 for 10-30 min), 1.16 (95% CI, 1.09-1.21 for 30-60 min), and 1.31 (95% CI, 1.19-1.43 for > 60 min), relative to less than 10 minutes. These associations were consistent in both de novo and acute-on-chronic CS. CONCLUSIONS: Longer hospital arrival times are significantly associated with increased in-hospital and long-term mortality in patients with CS. These findings underscore the need for system-level interventions, such as regionally coordinated shock networks and early prehospital triage, to ensure timely access to definitive care.

articles.title: Impact of Erector Spinae Block on Postoperative Analgesia and Hospital Recovery in Coronary Artery Bypass Surgery: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis, Meta-Regression, and Sequential Trial Analysis.
articles.abstract: The erector spinae plane block (ESPB) is a promising regional technique for cardiac surgery. We evaluated the efficacy of ESPB regarding analgesia and in-hospital outcomes in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing ESPB versus control in adults undergoing CABG (CRD42025645045). Primary outcomes were opioid consumption (24 h/48 h) and pain intensity. Secondary outcomes included extubation time and intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay. Data were pooled using random-effects models. Meta-regression and trial sequential analysis (TSA) were used to assess sources of heterogeneity and robustness, respectively, while the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations framework provided the certainty of the evidence for each outcome. Twelve studies (704 patients) were analyzed. ESPB significantly reduced the morphine milligram equivalent consumption at 24 h (mean difference (MD) -19.05 mg; 95% confidence interval (CI) [-22.50 to -15.61]; P < 0.001; high certainty) and 48 h (MD -19.42 mg; 95% CI [-28.75 to -10.09]; P < 0.001; moderate certainty). Pain scores, by the Numerical Rating Scale, were lower within 12 h (MD -0.93; P < 0.001; moderate certainty) and at 24 h (MD -0.58; P = 0.016; low certainty). ESPB shortened extubation time (MD -2.50 h; high certainty) and ICU stay (MD -12.55 h; moderate certainty). TSA confirmed robust evidence for opioid reduction, early pain relief, and extubation benefits. ESPB provides effective early analgesia, reduces perioperative opioid requirements, and accelerates recovery in CABG, representing a fundamental complement to conventional isolated intravenous analgesia. Future research should investigate continuous techniques.

articles.title: Current strategies of cerebral oxygenation monitoring in general intensive care units: a narrative review.
articles.journal: Journal of critical care medicine (Universitatea de Medicina si Farmacie din Targu-Mures)
articles.abstract: Cerebral hypoxia represents the final metabolic consequence of sustained intracranial pressure and impaired autoregulation. Continuous cerebral oxygen monitoring is essential to prevent secondary ischemic injury in neurocritical care particularly in severe traumatic brain injury, malignant infarction, and aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage. It also guides management of systemic disturbances such as shock, sepsis, and respiratory failure and is increasingly used perioperatively in high-risk cardiac, carotid, and neurosurgical procedures. To synthesize physiological principles, monitoring modalities, and clinical applications of cerebral oxygenation across neurocritical care and perioperative settings, emphasizing bedside interpretation and integration within multimodal neuromonitoring. PubMed and Scopus were searched (January 2010-January 2025) using MeSH terms and keywords including "cerebral oxygenation," "brain tissue oxygen tension," "jugular bulb saturation," and "near-infrared spectroscopy." Fifty-eight English-language studies (randomized controlled trials, observational studies, reviews, and editorials) were included. Non-English publications, animal studies, conference abstracts, unavailable full texts, and non-peer-reviewed articles were excluded. Brain tissue oxygen tension, jugular bulb oximetry, and near-infrared spectroscopy provide complementary insights. Brain tissue oxygen tension is invasive and region-specific (<25 mmHg indicates high risk), jugular bulb oximetry reflects global cerebral oxygen extraction, and near-infrared spectroscopy enables noninvasive regional trend monitoring. Multimodal neuromonitoring integrating these with intracranial pressure, transcranial Doppler, and electroencephalography improves detection and management of secondary ischemia. In neurocritical care, invasive monitoring supports targeted interventions, whereas in ICU and perioperative settings, multimodal strategies balance diagnostic yield and feasibility. Cerebral oxygen monitoring should be routinely implemented in high-risk patients. Multimodal neuromonitoring should be prioritized to detect hypoxia early and guide individualized cerebral perfusion strategies. Near-infrared spectroscopy should be used for continuous monitoring, while invasive modalities should be reserved for high-risk neurocritical patients. Standardized thresholds and protocolized approaches should be established through prospective, outcome-driven research.

articles.title: Characteristics and outcomes of unplanned extubation in adult ICU: two-year retrospective observational cohort study.
articles.journal: Journal of critical care medicine (Universitatea de Medicina si Farmacie din Targu-Mures)
articles.abstract: Description of unplanned extubation rate, and characteristics of patients who experienced it. A two-year retrospective descriptive study conducted in a 120-bed closed ICU in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Adult mechanically ventilated patients who experienced UE were included. Data on demographics, airway management, staffing ratios, and clinical outcomes were analyzed. Results: Out of 4,054 mechanically ventilated patients, 226 experienced UE, to an incidence rate of 0.52 per 100 ventilator days. Majority of events were self-extubations (77.4%) and occurred during the day shift (61.5%). Median (IQR) distance from the endotracheal tube (ETT) tip to carina was 6.2 (4.6 - 7.8) cm, indicating relatively superficial positioning. Re-intubation was required in 57.5% of cases within 48 hours. Overall 28-day mortality rate was 22.6%. Accidental extubation patients were more frequently reintubated (90% vs. 48%) with a higher 28-day mortality rate (44% vs. 16.6%).
