In the early "golden hours" of sepsis, low cefepime levels (affecting up to 70% of cases) may lead to organ dysfunction progression, treatment failure, and antimicrobial resistance. Empiric dose escalation to overcome low levels can increase the risk of dose-dependent neurotoxicity. We developed and qualified a population pharmacokinetic model using patient weight and estimated glomerular filtration rate from creatinine and cystatin C that, in simulation, improved attainment of effective and safe drug levels. To describe the Beta-Lactam Optimization and Outcomes Management (BLOOM) 1 pragmatic feasibility trial. This single-center, cluster-randomized, pragmatic feasibility trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07287332) was approved with a waiver of informed consent. Participants are critically ill adults (age ≥ 18 yr), hospitalized at Mayo Clinic (Rochester, MN), who are receiving cefepime for suspected or documented sepsis. A screening tool embedded in the electronic health record (EHR) identifies eligible patients newly initiated on cefepime (≤ 1 previous dose in 48 hr) who are then randomized to care groups (clusters) that use an individualized dosing algorithm (intervention) or usual-care dosing (control). Exclusions are cephalosporin allergy, acute kidney injury, kidney replacement therapy, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and missing inputs required for the algorithm (weight, creatinine, cystatin C). Recruitment began on January 15, 2026, and is expected to conclude by January 2027 (target enrollment, ≥ 300 patients). For eligible patients, EHR-embedded clinical decision support prompts the cluster-assigned dosing approach, with final dose decisions made by the clinical team. Feasibility, fidelity, and exploratory pharmacokinetic and clinical outcomes will be assessed using mixed methods. This workflow-integrated pragmatic feasibility trial will determine whether personalized cefepime dosing can be implemented in routine practice to optimize timely sepsis therapy while maintaining safety.

articles.title: Carbapenem Renal Dose Discordance and Acute Kidney Injury in the Intensive Care Unit: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.journal: The Journal of pharmacy technology : jPT : official publication of the Association of Pharmacy Technicians
articles.abstract: Renal function changes rapidly in the intensive care unit (ICU), and carbapenem dosing above renal-adjusted recommendations is a potentially preventable medication safety issue. To evaluate the association between carbapenem renal dose discordance and acute kidney injury (AKI); treatment failure was exploratory. This ethics-approved retrospective cohort included adults receiving carbapenems for at least 48 hours in a Vietnamese hospital ICU (January 2024-April 2026). Discordance was at least 1 day above renal-adjusted recommendations based on estimated Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance and clinical indication. Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes criteria defined AKI. Robust Poisson regression estimated adjusted risk ratios (aRRs). Matched outcome models additionally adjusted for Glasgow Coma Scale category and septic shock. A post hoc Bonferroni threshold of α = .003125 was applied. Of 490 patients, 78 (15.9%) had discordant dosing. Acute kidney injury occurred in 28/78 (35.9%) with discordant dosing versus 18/412 (4.4%) with concordant dosing. Discordance was associated with AKI in the primary analysis (aRR, 8.061; 95% confidence interval [CI], 4.135-15.714; P < .001) and among 68 matched pairs (aRR, 5.937; 95% CI, 2.112-16.694; P = .001). Associations with treatment failure did not meet the corrected threshold in the primary analysis (aRR, 1.586; 95% CI, 1.023-2.458; P = .039) or among matched pairs (aRR, 1.164; 95% CI, 0.723-1.875; P = .532). Carbapenem renal dose discordance was associated with AKI, although causation cannot be established. Daily renal dose review by pharmacists is a practical medication safety target that warrants prospective evaluation.

articles.title: Impact of frailty on acute kidney injury in patients followed-up in the intensive care unit.
articles.journal: Ulusal travma ve acil cerrahi dergisi = Turkish journal of trauma & emergency surgery : TJTES
articles.abstract: Frailty in elderly patients is an important determinant of clinical outcomes in intensive care units, particularly in relation to acute kidney injury (AKI). This study investigated the association between frailty and AKI in the geriatric population. This prospective observational study included 120 patients. Frailty was assessed via the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) and the Edmonton Frail Scale (EFS). Patients were categorized according to the presence or absence of AKI. Demographic data, frailty scores, laboratory parameters, and clinical outcomes, including mortality, mechanical ventilation, and vasopressor use, were compared. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were used to identify factors associated with the development of AKI. The mean age of the participants was 79.7±7.5 years. Comorbidities such as diabetes and hypertension were common, and AKI was observed in 29.1% of patients. The incidence of AKI was significantly higher among patients classified as frail according to the CFS (p=0.002). Patients with AKI presented increased mortality rates and an increased need for mechanical ventilation and vasopressors. The AKI group presented significantly lower hemoglobin, platelet, and albumin levels and higher baseline creatinine levels. Multivariate analysis revealed that elevated baseline creatinine was an important predictor of AKI. Frailty assessed by the CFS was associated with AKI development in unadjusted analyses; however, this association was not maintained after multivariable adjustment. No significant association was observed between AKI and frailty assessed by the EFS. Baseline serum creatinine was the only independent predictor of AKI. These findings suggest that frailty assessment, particularly using the CFS, may serve as a complementary clinical tool for early risk recognition and patient stratification rather than an independent predictor of AKI. AKI development in critically ill older adults appears to be multifactorial.

articles.title: Reversal of severe diuretic resistance by dexmedetomidine-associated polyuria in type 1 cardiorenal syndrome: a case report.
articles.abstract: Dexmedetomidine is a selective α2-adrenergic agonist widely used for sedation in intensive care settings. Although hypotension and bradycardia are well-recognized adverse effects, dexmedetomidine-associated polyuria is a rare and unpredictable adverse effect. An 84-year-old man with ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy, permanent atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease was admitted to the Cardiac Intensive Care Unit with type 1 cardiorenal syndrome, severe systemic and pulmonary congestion, oliguria, and acute kidney injury. Despite continuous intravenous furosemide infusion, sequential nephron blockade, and dual vasoactive support with norepinephrine and dobutamine, the patient developed persistent oligo-anuria and worsening congestion. Dexmedetomidine infusion was initiated for psychomotor agitation and disorientation. Shortly thereafter, urine output abruptly increased to approximately 250 mL/h, accompanied by rapid decongestion and improvement in renal function. Following dexmedetomidine withdrawal, oliguria, congestion and renal dysfunction recurred. Rechallenge with dexmedetomidine again induced profound polyuria, with urine output peaking at 650 mL/h and a 10-kg weight loss over 48 h, allowing de-escalation of diuretic therapy and withdrawal of vasoactive support. The Naranjo score was 6, supporting a probable causal relationship. This case demonstrates a reproducible temporal association between dexmedetomidine administration and profound polyuria, confirmed by positive rechallenge. To our knowledge, this is the first report in which dexmedetomidine-associated polyuria was temporally associated with reversal of severe diuretic resistance and clinically meaningful decongestion in type 1 cardiorenal syndrome. Recognition of this rare adverse effect may be relevant in critically ill cardiac patients.

articles.title: Building Consensus Among Intensive Care Nurses on the Scope of Practice for Registered Nurses Deployed to Intensive Care During Surge Events: A Real-Time Delphi Study.
articles.abstract: Disaster events that overwhelm health system capacity often require the deployment of nurses from non-critical care clinical areas to supplement the specialist intensive care workforce. However, the role of deployed registered nurses in intensive care is poorly defined and without clear role boundaries, experienced intensive care nurses often bear disproportionate supervisory burdens, and deployed staff may assume clinical responsibilities for which they are inadequately prepared. Developing a scope of practice for deployed nurses is essential for safe, effective surge responses. To achieve expert consensus on the scope of practice of deployed registered nurses in a surged intensive care unit. A Real-Time Delphi study was conducted using a web-based platform. A 65-item survey was administered to a panel of experienced Australian intensive care nurses and educators with expertise in training and/or supervising nurses deployed to intensive care during surge events. Participants rated activities that could potentially be undertaken by deployed registered nurses in a surged intensive care setting using a 5-point Likert scale across two dimensions: appropriateness for delegation and importance within a tiered nursing model. Consensus was defined a priori as ≥ 70% agreement. Free-text comments were analysed thematically. Fifteen expert panellists completed the survey. Of the 69 items assessed, 33 reached consensus and were retained as constituting the scope of practice for registered nurses deployed to intensive care. Consensus items spanned neurological observation, basic cardiovascular monitoring, gastrointestinal care, fluid balance documentation, and essential nursing cares. No consensus was reached for mechanical ventilation, non-invasive ventilation or renal replacement therapy. This study resulted in a consensus-derived scope of practice for deployed registered nurses in a surged intensive care. The findings establish clear role boundaries to support safe, tiered nursing care during future surge events and provide a foundation for developing targeted upskilling programs. The findings offer intensive care clinicians, educators, and health services a practical foundation for planning surge nursing models before surge events occur. Clearer role delineation may also reduce uncertainty for deployed nurses and lessen the supervisory burden on experienced intensive care staff.

articles.title: Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy During Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation as a Marker of Persistent Organ Support Burden and Post-Decannulation Mortality in Adult Cardiovascular Critical Care: A 9-Year Cohort Study.
articles.journal: Journal of cardiothoracic and vascular anesthesia
articles.abstract: To evaluate whether continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) use during extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) serves as a clinical marker of persistent organ support burden and is associated with survival to hospital discharge and post-decannulation mortality among patients successfully separated from ECMO. Retrospective cohort study. Tertiary cardiovascular center, 2017-2025. Adults (n = 1,224) supported with ECMO, of whom 918 (75.0%) had cardiac failure, 245 (20.0%) underwent extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and 1,164 (95.1%) initially received veno‑arterial (V‑A) ECMO. CRRT use at any point during the ECMO course; patients without CRRT served as the comparator. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge; secondary analysis examined post‑decannulation death in patients successfully separated from ECMO. Primary severity‑adjusted models included age, sex, ECMO indication, intra‑aortic balloon pump use, pre‑ECMO lactate, and log‑transformed vasoactive‑inotropic score. CRRT was used in 519 (42.4%) patients. Survival to discharge was significantly lower with CRRT than without (149/513 [29.0%] v 380/700 [54.3%]; unadjusted odds ratio [OR], 0.34; 95% CI, 0.27-0.44), and the association remained after severity adjustment (adjusted OR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.28-0.48). Additional sensitivity models adjusting for pre-ECMO Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score (n = 1,056; adjusted OR, 0.38; 95% CI, 0.29-0.50) and pre-ECMO Survival After Veno-Arterial ECMO score in V-A ECMO (n = 1,052; adjusted OR, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.27-0.47) confirmed the consistency of this association. Among 676 patients successfully separated from ECMO, post-decannulation death occurred in 80 of 230 (34.8%) with CRRT and 66 of 446 (14.8%) without CRRT (adjusted OR, 2.69; 95% CI, 1.81-3.99). CRRT use during ECMO marked a high-risk cardiovascular critical care phenotype with greater persistent organ support burden, lower discharge survival, and higher post-decannulation mortality. These associations should be interpreted as prognostic rather than causal; CRRT status may provide pragmatic information for risk stratification after ECMO separation.

articles.title: HEMATOLOGICAL AND RENAL BIOMARKERS IN CRITICALLY ILL PATIENTS WITH COVID-19 IN A BRAZILIAN ICU: A RETROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY.
articles.abstract: and Objectives: Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is associated with high morbidity and mortality, especially in critically ill patients. This study aimed to evaluate the behavior of hematological and renal biomarkers and their association with mortality in brazilian ICU patients with COVID-19. This retrospective cohort study included 52 adult patients admitted to a Brazilian ICU between June 2020 and September 2021. Hematological parameters, urea, creatinine, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR) were assessed at admission and at the final outcome. Statistical analyses were performed in two stages: first, comparisons were made between sexes (male vs. female); subsequently, patients were stratified into survivors and non-survivors for group comparisons. Between-group analyses were conducted using the Mann-Whitney U test, with paired comparisons performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of mortality. Patients who died during hospitalization (non-survivors, n=29) showed higher levels of urea, creatinine, leukocytes, and neutrophils, and lower hemoglobin and platelet counts compared to survivors (n=23) (p<0.001). Renal and hematological alterations were independently associated with mortality. Dynamic changes in hematological and renal biomarkers are strongly associated with mortality. Serial monitoring may improve risk stratification in critically ill COVID-19 patients.

articles.title: Types of adult intensive care units and admissions in Türkiye between 2018 and 2023: a nationwide cohort study.
articles.journal: Canadian journal of anaesthesia = Journal canadien d'anesthesie
articles.abstract: Türkiye has one of the highest intensive care unit (ICU) bed capacities among middle-income countries but also globally. Nevertheless, little is known about the characteristics of ICUs in Türkiye, their temporal trends, and ICU admissions and readmissions. We sought to analyze the structural characteristics of all adult ICUs and the clinical profiles of ICU admissions across Türkiye. We conducted a retrospective nationwide cohort study using data from the Turkish Ministry of Health National Electronic Database. We analyzed adult ICU admissions across all levels and types over 6 years (2018-2023) and documented patient demographics, comorbidities, admission diagnoses, and ICU outcomes. We retrieved data on 3,362,539 ICU admissions. Among 22 ICU types, mixed ICUs accounted for the highest proportion of admissions (31.4%), followed by coronary (23.7%), anesthesiology (14.3%), medical (6.1%), and surgical (6.0%) ICUs. The proportion of mixed ICU beds decreased from 44.0% in 2018 to 25.1% in 2023. Most ICU beds were in state (public) hospitals (50.8%), followed by private hospitals (34.8%). The number of ICU beds increased from 2019, with a notable rise in state hospitals after 2020. The average number of ICU admissions was 659 per 100,000 population annually. The median patient age was 65 [interquartile range, 39-91] yr, and the ICU mortality was 15.5%. The leading admission diagnoses were respiratory failure (10.1%), cerebrovascular disease (7.1%), and acute kidney injury (5.2%). Hypertension (67.5%) and coronary artery disease (44.8%) were common comorbidities, particularly in nonsurvivors. The 7-day ICU readmission rate was 3.0%. The present comprehensive analysis of ICU admissions in Türkiye between 2018 and 2023 highlights a shift toward specialization with a decrease in mixed ICUs. The impact of ICU diversity on resource use and patient outcomes requires further evaluation.

articles.title: Tunneled Dialysis Catheter for KRT for Acute Kidney Injury in the Intensive Care Unit: CON.
Robotic-Assisted Partial Nephrectomy in a Solitary Kidney in a von Hippel-Lindau Renal Cell Carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is a rare autosomal dominant tumor syndrome caused by germline mutations in the VHL gene. Patients may develop multiple, bilateral, and recurrent renal cell carcinomas (RCCs), posing a major therapeutic challenge, particularly in those with a solitary kidney, where preservation of renal function is critical to prevent end-stage renal disease and dialysis dependence. This case demonstrates the surgical management of multiple renal tumors in a solitary kidney. A 37-year-old man with VHL disease (c.257C > G, p.P86R mutation) and a solitary right kidney following previous left radical nephrectomy presented with three progressive clear cell RCC (ccRCC) lesions, the largest measuring 4.8 cm, despite ongoing treatment with belzutifan, a HIF-2α inhibitor. A transperitoneal robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy (RAPN) was performed. A fourth tumor was identified intraoperatively. Complete excision of all tumors with negative surgical margins was achieved. Postoperatively, severe acute kidney injury (AKI) developed, requiring continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), which was complicated by forearm necrosis resulting from calcium substitution paravasation. An additional complication included a right pneumothorax. Following intensive care management, including pleural drainage, renal function gradually recovered, and CRRT was discontinued on postoperative day 8. This case demonstrates that RAPN can provide tumor control while preserving renal tissue in patients with VHL-associated multifocal RCC and a solitary kidney. However, the procedure carries a substantial risk of severe postoperative AKI requiring temporary renal replacement therapy.

articles.title: Efficacy and Safety of Nafamostat Mesilate Injection in Patients Receiving Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy: A Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: The objective of the study was to assess the efficacy and safety of nafamostat mesilate injection in patients receiving continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Dichotomous and continuous outcomes were analyzed using fixed-effect or random-effects models to estimate odds ratios (ORs) or mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Eight studies involving 1,189 patients were included in the meta-analysis. Compared with no anticoagulation, nafamostat mesilate injection was associated with lower mortality (OR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.44-0.76; p < 0.001) and longer filter lifespan (MD, 7.00; 95% CI, 1.50-12.50; p = 0.01). These estimates were derived predominantly from nonrandomized studies and should be interpreted with caution. However, no significant difference was found between nafamostat mesilate injection and no anticoagulation in bleeding complications (OR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.51-2.34; p = 0.82), total duration of CRRT (MD, 4.46; 95% CI, -0.13-9.04; p = 0.06), the proportion of patients requiring transfusion (OR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.54-1.03; p = 0.07), and intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay (MD, -0.24; 95% CI, -3.85-3.37; p = 0.90) in patients receiving CRRT. The available evidence suggests that nafamostat mesilate injection may be associated with lower mortality and longer filter lifespan compared with no anticoagulation in patients receiving CRRT. However, no clear difference was observed in bleeding complications, total duration of CRRT, the proportion of patients requiring transfusion, or ICU length of stay. These findings are limited by the predominance of nonrandomized designs, small numbers of studies, and substantial heterogeneity. Additional adequately powered randomized studies are needed before clinical benefit can be considered established.

articles.title: Intermittent or Continuous Renal-Replacement Therapy in Acute Kidney Injury.
articles.journal: The New England journal of medicine
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The preferred method of renal-replacement therapy for acute kidney injury in critically ill patients remains uncertain. METHODS: In this multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned critically ill adults with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy to undergo intermittent hemodialysis or continuous renal-replacement therapy as the initial treatment. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event - defined as death, dependence on renal-replacement therapy, or a serum creatinine concentration more than 25% above the baseline value - by day 90. RESULTS: The trial was stopped early after sequential interim analyses showed a sustained signal of higher mortality with intermittent hemodialysis than with continuous renal-replacement therapy. A total of 554 patients underwent randomization, with 272 patients assigned to undergo intermittent hemodialysis and 282 to undergo continuous renal-replacement therapy; 535 patients (260 in the intermittent group and 275 in the continuous group) were included in the intention-to-treat population. A major adverse kidney event occurred by day 90 in 203 patients (78.1%) in the intermittent group and in 197 patients (71.6%) in the continuous group (adjusted absolute risk difference, 6.28 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.22 to 13.79). Death by day 90 occurred in 164 patients (63.1%) and in 147 patients (53.5%), respectively. Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates at day 90 were 63.3% and 53.6% (hazard ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.63). The most common complication potentially related to acute kidney injury or renal-replacement therapy was hypotension, which occurred in 179 patients (68.8%) in the intermittent group and in 183 patients (66.5%) in the continuous group. CONCLUSIONS: Among critically ill patients with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy, intermittent hemodialysis as the initial treatment approach was not shown to be noninferior to continuous renal-replacement therapy with respect to major adverse kidney events by day 90 and was associated with higher mortality. (Funded by the French Ministry of Health; ICRAKI ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06032884.).

articles.title: Population pharmacokinetics of oseltamivir and oseltamivir carboxylate in critically ill adults receiving veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation without renal replacement therapy - an ASAP ECMO study.
articles.abstract: To characterise the population pharmacokinetics of oseltamivir and oseltamivir carboxylate in critically ill adults receiving veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) without renal replacement therapy (RRT), and to compare oseltamivir carboxylate exposure with an exploratory exposure-response threshold and published pharmacokinetic data. This multinational ASAP ECMO analysis included 8 critically ill adults receiving oseltamivir 75 mg every 12 hours during VV-ECMO. Serial blood samples were collected over a dosing interval, and oseltamivir and oseltamivir carboxylate concentrations were measured using a validated assay. Population pharmacokinetic modelling was performed in Monolix using an integrated parent drug-metabolite model. Fifty-eight plasma concentration-time points were available for analysis. The cohort was relatively young and 63% had augmented renal clearance (ARC). A one-compartment model best described both oseltamivir and oseltamivir carboxylate, with a transit compartment required to account for delayed metabolite formation. Median oseltamivir carboxylate exposure was generally comparable to values reported in healthy adults and critically ill patients receiving standard dosing. Median oseltamivir carboxylate area under the concentration-time curve from 0-12 hours (AUC0-12) was lower in patients with ARC than in those without (1877.78 vs. 8253.39 ng·h/mL; p=0.07). Only 2 of 8 patients achieved the primary exploratory exposure-response threshold (AUC0-12 ≥7000 ng∙h/mL) and none of the 5 patients with ARC achieved this threshold. Marked variability and lower exposure were observed in adults receiving VV-ECMO without RRT, particularly ARC patients. Higher doses may be required in ARC patients, but the optimal dosing regimen remains undefined. Routine dose escalation is not supported by current evidence.

articles.title: Dysnatremia in critically ill burn patients: incidence, timing and association with kidney outcomes.
articles.abstract: Dysnatremia is common in critically ill patients and has been linked to poor outcomes and renal prognosis. Burn patients are particularly vulnerable, but the prognostic significance of dysnatremia in this population remains unclear. We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 1,758 burn patients admitted to a French burn center between 2011 and 2023. Dysnatremia was defined as at least one episode of hyponatremia (<135 mmol/L) or hypernatremia (>145 mmol/L) during intensive care unit (ICU) stay. The primary endpoint was the incidence of dysnatremia; secondary endpoints included major adverse kidney events (MAKE) at ICU discharge and acute kidney injury (AKI) occurrence and severity. Dysnatremia occurred in 56.3% of patients (n = 990), with hyponatremia in 50.5% (n = 888) and hypernatremia in 23.8% (n = 418). MAKE at ICU discharge did not differ between hyponatremic and normonatremic patients (12.6% vs. 10.9%, p = 0.304) but was sixfold higher with hypernatremia (32.3% vs. 5.4%, p < 0.001). After adjustment for age and burned total body surface area, hypernatremia was independently associated with MAKE at ICU discharge (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 4.03; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.92-5.56; p < 0.001), whereas hyponatremia was not (aHR 1.15; 95% CI: 0.85-1.55; p = 0.377). Clustering analysis identified three phenotypes: Cluster B (severe burns, worst outcomes), Cluster A (older patients, mostly hyponatremic, intermediate outcomes), and Cluster C (younger patients, mild burns, best outcomes). Dysnatremia affects over half of burn patients. Sodium disturbances should be viewed as markers of systemic severity, warranting close monitoring and preventive strategies.

articles.title: Association between intracatheter Ca²(+) trajectory and extracorporeal circuit coagulation in unplanned early withdrawal among patients receiving CRRT: a retrospective cohort study.
Early Serum Creatinine Change and Multidimensional Clinical Determinants of Kidney Replacement Therapy in Acute Kidney Injury.
articles.abstract: Background: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a dynamic clinical syndrome, and a single serum creatinine measurement may not adequately reflect the severity or progression of renal dysfunction. The aim of this study was to assess whether early changes in serum creatinine provide better discrimination for renal replacement therapy (RRT) requirement than admission creatinine alone and to identify clinical factors associated with RRT and short-term renal outcomes. Methods: This retrospective observational cohort study included 115 adults with AKI admitted to the Nephrology Department or Intensive Care Unit of Sibiu County Clinical Emergency Hospital between January 2018 and December 2025. Clinical, biochemical, hemodynamic, fluid-balance and nephrotoxic exposure data were analyzed. Serum creatinine was assessed at admission or transfer to the Nephrology Department or Intensive Care Unit (time zero) and at 24 and 48 h thereafter. Multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic analyses were used to evaluate factors associated with RRT requirement and an eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 at 30 days. Creatinine change was defined as the absolute difference from the value measured at study entry. Results: Fifty-two patients required RRT. The 48 h change in serum creatinine showed better discrimination for RRT requirement than admission creatinine (AUC 0.758 vs. 0.634; DeLong p = 0.012). An exploratory, cohort-derived 48 h creatinine-change threshold of 0.79 mg/dL showed a sensitivity of 90.4% and a specificity of 52.4% for distinguishing RRT status. In multivariable analysis, vasopressor requirement, maximum serum potassium and positive 24 h fluid balance were independently associated with RRT, while the overall model showed high apparent discrimination (AUC 0.925). RRT requirement was also associated with an eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 at 30 days (adjusted OR 2.84, 95% CI 1.02-7.91). Conclusions: The 48 h creatinine change showed modest apparent discrimination of RRT status, but these findings are exploratory and do not establish prospective prediction. Patients requiring RRT also had greater hemodynamic instability, hyperkalemia and positive fluid balance and were more likely to have an eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 at 30 days. Serial assessment of renal function, together with the patient's clinical and metabolic status, may therefore be more informative than a single creatinine measurement.

articles.title: Prognostic Value of the Delta Neutrophil Index for Predicting 28-Day Mortality in Intensive Care Unit Patients with Candidemia.
articles.abstract: Candidemia is associated with substantial mortality in critically ill patients, and early identification of patients at increased risk of death remains challenging. The delta neutrophil index (DNI), an automated hematological parameter reflecting circulating immature granulocytes, has been proposed as a prognostic marker in sepsis, but its role in candidemia remains unclear. This retrospective study included adults who developed candidemia during intensive care unit hospitalization between January 1, 2020, and December 31, 2023; patients with neutropenia, haematological malignancy receiving ongoing chemotherapy, or granulocyte colony-stimulating factor therapy were excluded. Patients were classified as survivors or non-survivors according to 28-day all-cause mortality after blood culture collection. DNI, leukocyte count, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin were evaluated 24 hours before, at the time of, and 24 hours after blood culture collection. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with mortality, and receiver operating characteristic analysis assessed the prognostic performance of DNI. Among 246 patients, 132 survived and 114 died. Non-survivors had higher APACHE II scores and more frequent acute kidney injury. DNI and procalcitonin levels were significantly higher in non-survivors at all three time points. In the primary multivariable model, acute kidney injury, DNI at blood culture collection, and procalcitonin at blood culture collection were independently associated with mortality; the association of DNI was attenuated and no longer statistically significant after further adjustment for Candida species and antifungal therapy. DNI showed limited discrimination, with area under the curve values ranging from 0.608 to 0.625; the highest value was observed at blood culture collection (0.625), with a cutoff of 2.4, 43.0% sensitivity, and 82.6% specificity. DNI may aid mortality risk stratification in candidemia but should not be used as a standalone prognostic marker.

articles.title: Resting Energy Expenditure in Mechanically Ventilated Surgical-Trauma Patients With and Without Acute Kidney Injury: a single-center retrospective study.
articles.journal: Journal of renal nutrition : the official journal of the Council on Renal Nutrition of the National Kidney Foundation
articles.abstract: To compare resting energy expenditure (REE) measured by indirect calorimetry (IC) in mechanically ventilated surgical-trauma critically ill patients with and without acute kidney injury (AKI); to evaluate differences in REE by sex, age, and body mass index (BMI); and to assess associations between REE, psoas muscle index (PMI) measured using computed tomography scans, and lean body mass (LBM) estimated by predictive equations. This single-center retrospective cohort study conducted at a tertiary academic medical center included mechanically ventilated critically ill adults admitted between 01/01/2012 and 12/31/2023. Exclusion criteria were pediatric, pregnant, or incarcerated patients; quadriplegia, paraplegia, cystic fibrosis; abnormal respiratory quotients; Medical ICU admission; major burns (≥20% TBSA); parenteral nutrition initiated on or after IC; tracheostomy on admission; discharge or death while ventilated; or absence of a nutrition prescription. Of 794 patients screened, 180 met inclusion criteria (AKI n=84; no AKI n=96). At baseline, patients with and without AKI differed significantly in age (59.9 vs 55 years; P = 0.046), BMI (32.2 vs 28.8 kg/m2; P = 0.046), CKD (23.8% vs 3.13%; P < 0.001), and serum creatinine (1.49 vs 0.84 mg/dL; P < 0.001). Of patients with AKI, 71.4% had stage I AKI and 20.2% required renal replacement therapy (RRT). No significant difference in mean REE was observed between patients with and without AKI (1,642 vs 1,665 kcal/day; P = 0.380) . REE was significantly higher in males compared with females (1,806 vs 1,425 kcal/day; P < 0.001), in patients aged 18-65 versus >65 years (1,768 vs 1,428 kcal/day; P = 0.002), and in obese versus non-obese patients (1,841 vs 1,500 kcal/day; P < 0.001). In multivariable linear regression, higher BMI (P = 0.003) and male sex (P = 0.028) were independently associated with higher REE, while AKI was not. LBM estimated by predictive equations was more strongly correlated with REE than PMI (P < 0.001), and correlation strength did not differ by AKI status. Measured REE did not differ between ventilated surgical-trauma patients with and without AKI. REE differed by sex, age, and obesity status, and AKI was not associated with within-group differences. BMI and sex were identified as independent predictors of REE. Estimated LBM was strongly correlated with REE independent of AKI status. Given possible residual confounding, further investigation is needed.

articles.title: Machine Learning-Based Mortality Prediction for Mechanically Ventilated Liver Failure Patients: A Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract: To develop a mortality prediction model for patients with liver failure who require mechanical ventilation (MV) in ICU. This retrospective study utilized data from the MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV (v3.0) databases. Variables included demographics, liver function markers, ventilator parameters, severity scores, comorbidities, use of vasoactive drugs and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) as well as length of ICU and hospital stay. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Five machine learning algorithms were applied: logistic regression, decision tree, Bagging, neural network, and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost). The dataset was randomly split into a training set (70%) and a test set (30%). Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and calibration plots. Predictive factors were ranked for the best-performing model by importance. A total of 2336 patients were identified from the MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV databases. On the test set, the AUC values for each model were as follows: logistic regression (0.836), decision tree (0.768), neural network (0.774), Bagging (0.854), and XGBoost (0.875). Calibration curves showed good agreement for all models except the neural network. Among the 5 algorithms, XGBoost demonstrated the highest predictive performance. The top 5 predictors identified were length of hospital stay, SAPS II score, use of vasoactive drugs, total bilirubin and length of ICU stay. Machine learning-based models can effectively predict in-hospital mortality in liver failure patients receiving mechanical ventilation. Among the 5 algorithms tested, the XGBoost model achieved the best overall performance.

articles.title: A Multidomain Biomarker Score for Predicting Acute Kidney Injury and Renal Replacement Therapy Initiation in Critically Ill Adults.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: We evaluated the Renal-Inflammatory-Nutritional-Metabolic Index (RIN-IM), a previously published 0-10-point composite biomarker score, for acute kidney injury (AKI) and renal replacement therapy (RRT) initiation in an independent intensive care unit (ICU) cohort. Methods: This retrospective study included 480 adults admitted to two ICUs between October 2023 and August 2026. RIN-IM was calculated within 24 h of admission from creatinine, albumin, systemic immune-inflammation index (platelet count × neutrophil count/lymphocyte count), pan-immune-inflammation value (neutrophil count × platelet count × monocyte count/lymphocyte count), and triglyceride-glucose index (triglyceride and admission glucose concentrations). Patients were classified by RIN-IM Score as low-risk (0-3 points), intermediate-risk (4-6 points), or high-risk (7-10 points). Among patients without AKI or acute RRT initiation at or before the 24-h landmark, subsequent incident AKI was the primary outcome and RRT initiation was the secondary renal outcome. Twenty-eight-day all-cause mortality was evaluated descriptively. Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic analyses were performed. Results: AKI occurred in 189 patients (39.4%), RRT was initiated in 72 (15.0%), and 157 (32.7%) died within 28 days. In the low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups, AKI frequencies were 16.0%, 40.0%, and 62.0%; RRT initiation frequencies were 3.3%, 12.2%, and 30.0%; and 28-day mortality was 18.0%, 32.2%, and 48.0%, respectively (all p < 0.001). Adjusted odds ratios per score point was 1.31 (95% confidence interval, 1.16-1.48) for AKI and 1.47 (1.25-1.73) for RRT initiation. Areas under the curve were 0.862 and 0.903, respectively, exceeding those of Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment. Conclusions: Higher RIN-IM scores were associated with AKI, RRT initiation, and higher observed 28-day mortality. The score may support early renal risk stratification, pending prospective assessment of calibration and clinical utility.

articles.title: Rethinking Oliguria in the ICU: From Threshold to Trajectory.
Association Between Albumin-Bilirubin Index and Clinical Outcomes in Septic Acute Kidney Injury Patients.
articles.abstract: BackgroundThe albumin-bilirubin index (ALBI) has been reported as a prognostic marker in various clinical conditions; however, its value in patients with septic acute kidney injury (AKI) has not been clearly evaluated. This study aimed to investigate the association between ALBI and clinical outcomes in this population.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study used data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database. ALBI was analyzed as both a continuous variable in the primary analysis and a categorical variable according to tertiles in sensitivity analysis. The primary outcomes were 28-day, 60-day, 90-day, and 1-year all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included intensive care unit (ICU) transfer, septic shock, and disease severity. Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate the association between ALBI and mortality, and restricted cubic spline analyses were performed to assess potential nonlinearity. Subgroup analyses were further conducted to examine the consistency across different sub-group populations.ResultsOverall, 6700 patients with septic AKI were included. In adjusted Cox models, each 1-standard deviation increase in ALBI was associated with higher risks of 28-day mortality (HR 1.16, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.10-1.22), 60-day mortality (HR 1.14, 95% CI 1.10-1.19), 90-day mortality (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.08-1.18), and 1-year mortality (HR 1.10, 95% CI 1.06-1.14). The association between ALBI and mortality was generally consistent across most prespecified subgroups. Higher ALBI was also linked with septic shock (odds ratio [OR] 1.15, 95%CI 1.08-1.21, P < .001), ICU transfer (OR 1.09, 95%CI 1.02-1.16), and greater disease severity. RCS curves showed a nonlinear increase in mortality risk with ascending ALBI. Sensitivity analyses based on ALBI tertiles yielded broadly consistent findings.ConclusionHigher ALBI was independently associated with increased short- and long-term mortality and adverse clinical outcomes in septic AKI patients.

articles.title: Mechanical ventilation-associated AKI: toward a multimodal and kidney-protective ventilatory framework.
articles.abstract: Mechanical ventilation-associated acute kidney injury (AKI) represents a complex manifestation of lung-kidney cross-talk driven by hemodynamic alterations, neurohumoral activation, systemic inflammation and disturbances in gas exchange and acid-base homeostasis. Beyond static ventilatory settings, increasing evidence suggests that dynamic fluctuations in airway and perfusion parameters, including static driving pressure (ΔP), positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), mean airway pressure (Pmean), and effective renal perfusion pressure (eRPP) may substantially influence renal vulnerability during mechanical ventilation. This comprehensive narrative review synthesizes current mechanistic and clinical evidence on the relationship between mechanical ventilation and AKI and proposes an integrated framework for future research on the interplay between ventilatory stress, venous congestion, renal perfusion, and inflammatory injury. Emerging bedside tools such as renal Doppler indices, venous excess ultrasound score (VExUS), and kidney injury biomarkers are discussed as components of an integrated physiologic approach for early recognition and risk stratification of ventilator-associated AKI. We further propose a multimodal conceptual framework integrating respiratory mechanics, congestion assessment, perfusion monitoring, and biomarkers to support individualized kidney-protective ventilation strategies. Future research should prioritize standardized physiologic monitoring, time-varying exposure analyses, causal mediation approaches, and prospective multicenter studies to better define renal-protective ventilatory targets and advance precision critical care.

articles.title: Clinical prediction models in cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury (CSA-AKI) is a frequent postoperative complication associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Clinical prediction models (CPM) may identify high-risk patients enabling targeted preventive interventions and improved outcomes. The objective of the study was to identify available CPMs for the risk of developing CSA-AKI and summarize their performance. A systematic search of studies published in Pubmed, Scopus, the Chocrane Library and Web of Science was conducted, including studies that developed or validated CPMs for CSA-AKI in adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass. Data were extracted by two independent reviewers. Summary measures of diagnostic performance were calculated when feasible using random-effects models. Calibration and sensitivity analyses were also performed. The pooled incidence of CSA-AKI was 26.3% (95% CI, 26.0-26.4), whereas CSA-AKI requiring renal replacement therapy (CSA-AKI RRT) occurred in 2.2% of patients (95% CI, 2.1-2.2). Among validated CPMs, Thakar 2005 demonstrated the best predictive performance for CSA-AKI RRT: pooled AUC 0.80 (95% CI, 0.77-0.82), sensitivity of 0.87, and a specificity of 0.49 at a threshold of ≥ 3 points. Calibration analyses indicated underestimation of risk. The Mehta 2006 and Wijeysundera 2007 models also demonstrated good discrimination. Discrimination for the prediction of milder stages of CSA-AKI was poorer, but newer models such as the Demirjian 2022 model showed promising performance. Accurate and well-validated CPMs can facilitate risk stratification for CSA-AKI which can influence clinical practice and research. Thakar 2005 demonstrated very good discrimination for predicting CSA-AKI RRT, whereas more validation studies for the prediction of milder stages of CSA-AKI are warranted.

articles.title: Association of Oliguria With Acute Kidney Injury, Chronic Kidney Disease, and Mortality: Determining the Optimal Threshold in Critically Ill Patients.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Oliguria is a key prognostic indicator of acute kidney injury (AKI), yet the consensus definition (< 0.5 mL/kg/hr) is increasingly questioned. We aimed to determine thresholds of lowest mean diuresis (LMD) associated with AKI, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and mortality. DESIGN: Retrospective observational study. SETTING: Uppsala University Hospital ICU, Sweden. PATIENTS: A total of 4999 adults (≥ 18 yr) without preexisting CKD admitted to the ICU between 2017 and 2024. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: LMD was calculated over 3, 6, 12, and 24 hours (LMD3h-LMD24h). Generalized additive models were used, adjusting for Simplified Acute Physiology Score 3 estimated mortality ratio and gender. Outcomes were AKI within 7 days of LMD (Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes creatinine criteria), incident CKD after ICU discharge, and 90-day mortality. All LMD time frames were significantly associated with AKI, CKD, and death (p < 0.0001). Thresholds for AKI were 0.43, 0.41, 0.42, and 0.53 mL/kg/hr; for CKD, 0.21, 0.21, 0.31, and 0.43 mL/kg/hr; and for mortality 0.16, 0.18, 0.24, and 0.39 across LMD3h-LMD24h. CONCLUSIONS: The risk of mortality or persistent kidney injury, reflected by incident CKD, increases at a lower urine output threshold than the current AKI definition. These findings support the idea of filtration deficit, urine output, and tissue injury as different dimensions of AKI and should influence future AKI definitions.

articles.title: Fluid Therapy in Mechanically Ventilated Critically Ill Adult Patients.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Fluid therapy is ubiquitous in the intensive care unit (ICU) but carries risks, especially in mechanically ventilated patients. Contemporary global practice across dose, indication, and type is unknown. OBJECTIVE: To characterize ICU fluid practices in mechanically ventilated adults. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: International prospective observational cohort study between April 2024 and July 2025, across 206 ICUs in 41 countries on 6 continents. Consecutive adult patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation within 3 days of ICU admission and ventilated 24 hours or more. Exclusion criteria were age younger than 16 years and transfer under mechanical ventilation from another ICU. EXPOSURES: Fluid volume, indication, and type after intubation. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Key measures included (1) total infused volume and daily fluid balance over 7 days after intubation; (2) the indication for fluid therapy over the first 3 days after intubation; (3) the proportion of total administered fluid volume attributable to each fluid type over the first 3 days after intubation. RESULTS: Among 2454 patients analyzed (median age, 63 years [IQR, 49-73 years]; 63.6% [1560] male), median daily fluid input peaked on day 1 at 3.0 L (IQR, 2.2-4.0 L) and declined to 2.6 L (IQR, 1.8-3.5 L) through day 6. Daily fluid balance (median, 0.9 L; IQR, 0.1-1.9 L on day 1) decreased to less than 0.3 L (IQR, -0.5 to 1.2 L) by day 3 and remained near-neutral through day 6. Maintenance and replacement fluids (to meet daily requirements and to correct ongoing losses; 31.9%) and creep fluids (to deliver medications and maintain catheter patency; 30.9%) were the primary indications, whereas resuscitation (to restore circulating blood volume; 16.0%) accounted for a smaller proportion. Isotonic balanced crystalloids (48.9%) and isotonic saline (0.9% sodium chloride) (27.0%) were common; colloids were rare (1.3%). Substantial between-site variation persisted after adjustment for case-mix. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this prospective international cohort study, fluid therapy varied widely among mechanically ventilated critically ill patients, with maintenance and creep fluids-rather than resuscitation fluids-accounting for most total volume.

articles.title: The Easiest Decision in the Room: Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in Cirrhosis.
Heterogeneous Treatment Effects of Renal Replacement Therapy in Critically Ill Patients: A Multicenter Observational Study Using a Japanese ICU Registry.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Randomized trials evaluating the timing of renal replacement therapy (RRT) have informed current practice toward more conservative initiation strategies because of the lack of mortality benefit from early initiation. However, the optimal indications for RRT to offer lifesaving benefits remain uncertain. We aimed to estimate heterogeneous treatment effect of RRT and to identify patient groups associated with benefit or harm. DESIGN: Multicenter observational study. SETTING: A nationwide intensive care registry in Japan, Japanese Intensive Care Patient Database. PATIENTS: Adult patients who were admitted to the ICUs from 2018 through 2023 were included, excluding those with end-stage kidney disease, early death, readmission, or normal renal function. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Exposure was RRT during the ICU stay. Hospital mortality was the primary outcome. After 1:1 propensity score matching to adjust for confounding, 18,794 patients (9,397 per group) were analyzed. On average, RRT was associated with higher hospital mortality (risk difference, 6.1% points [95% CI, 3.4-8.7]). However, our machine learning-based causal forest algorithm showed substantial heterogeneity of treatment effects heterogeneity of treatment effects (HTEs) (rank-weighted average treatment effect, -8.2 percentage points [95% CI, -9.7 to -6.7]). Patients characterized by elevated serum creatinine, reduced urine output, and elevated blood urea nitrogen levels showed potential mortality benefit from RRT, whereas relatively preserved renal function was more likely to be associated with harm. CONCLUSIONS: Although RRT was associated with an increased risk of hospital mortality overall, HTEs were identified in selected subgroups that may benefit from RRT. These findings support a data-driven approach to defining clinically applicable optimal RRT indications to guide more judicious use of RRT.
articles.ai_key_stats: n=18,794, risk difference 6.1% points (95% CI 3.4-8.7), HTEs rank-weighted average treatment effect -8.2 percentage points (95% CI -9.7 to -6.7)
articles.ai_summary: This study used a large Japanese ICU registry to investigate the effects of renal replacement therapy (RRT) on hospital mortality. While RRT was associated with higher hospital mortality overall, the study found that certain subgroups of patients may benefit from RRT, such as those with elevated serum creatinine, reduced urine output, and elevated blood urea nitrogen levels.
articles.ai_significance: These findings suggest that RRT may not be beneficial for all critically ill patients, and that a more nuanced approach to its use is needed, taking into account individual patient characteristics.

articles.title: Net Ultrafiltration Rate and Mortality in Critically Ill Patients: A Multicenter Cohort Study With Analysis of Fluid Balance Changes.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To investigate the association between net ultrafiltration (NUF) rate and fluid balance changes with 28-day mortality in critically ill patients receiving continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). DESIGN: Multicenter retrospective observational study. SETTING: Data from two European mixed medical-surgical ICUs: University Hospital Bern, Switzerland, and Amsterdam University Medical Center, the Netherlands. PATIENTS: Adult critically ill patients receiving CRRT for at least 24 hours. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We studied 973 critically ill adults undergoing a total of 6914 days of CRRT. NUF rates and fluid balance changes were calculated from hourly data and categorized into four predefined groups. NUF rates were classified as no NUF, low (< 1.01 mL/kg/h), moderate (1.01-1.75 mL/kg/h), or high (> 1.75 mL/kg/h). Fluid balance change was stratified as negative (< -1.5 L/day), moderate negative (-1.5 to -0.5 L/day), neutral (-0.5 to 0.5 L/day), or positive (> 0.5 L/day). Using multivariable regression, random forest modeling, and mediation analysis, we observed no independent association between NUF rate and 28-day mortality after accounting for fluid balance. Mediation analysis suggested that the apparent survival advantage observed among patients with higher NUF rates was largely mediated through achievement of a more negative fluid balance, rather than a direct effect of NUF rate itself. In contrast, more positive fluid balance changes were linked to adverse clinical outcomes including 28-day mortality. CONCLUSIONS: In this two-center cohort of CRRT patients, NUF rate was not independently associated with mortality. Instead, the key determinant of outcome was fluid balance change. These findings suggest clinicians should not make NUF decisions in isolation, but rather should be using NUF as a means to achieve patient-specific fluid balance targets.
articles.ai_key_stats: n=973, no independent association between NUF rate and 28-day mortality, fluid balance change linked to adverse outcomes including 28-day mortality
articles.ai_summary: This study investigated the relationship between net ultrafiltration rate and fluid balance changes in critically ill patients receiving continuous renal replacement therapy. The results showed that fluid balance change, not net ultrafiltration rate, was the key determinant of outcome. The study found that more positive fluid balance changes were linked to adverse clinical outcomes.
articles.ai_significance: These findings suggest that clinicians should prioritize achieving patient-specific fluid balance targets over focusing solely on net ultrafiltration rate in critically ill patients receiving CRRT.

articles.title: Decades of intensive care medicine trials: what randomised evidence has changed, corrected, and still questions to resolve.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have reshaped intensive care medicine (ICM), a discipline defined by acute, interacting organ failures, time-sensitive decisions, biological uncertainty, and heterogeneous recovery trajectories. Many interventions supported by strong physiological rationale failed to improve patient-centred outcomes, whereas durable advances often emerged from optimisation of supportive care, avoidance of iatrogenic harm, and reassessment of established practices. METHODS: We conducted an interpretive historical review of landmark multicentre RCTs in adult ICM from the early 1990s onwards. PubMed searches, reference lists from major trials and reviews, and international guidelines were used to identify trials with conceptual influence on practice, guidelines, physiological reasoning, therapeutic strategy, research priorities, de-implementation, or outcome framing. Evidence was organised into overlapping paradigms rather than rigid chronological periods. FINDINGS: Across haemodynamic support, mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, antimicrobial treatment, nutrition, glucose control, transfusion, and sedation, landmark RCTs describe more than therapeutic expansion. Early biological and haemodynamic trials exposed the limits of reductionist strategies in syndromic critical illness. Protocol-driven approaches improved timeliness and consistency, but later pragmatic trials showed that rigid targets and invasive algorithms often added little once high-quality usual care was established. More recent trials challenge the assumption that greater intervention intensity improves outcomes, emphasising timing, disease phase, baseline risk, heterogeneity, patient selection, and treatment-related harm. Modern ICM RCTs have clarified not only what works, but what can be reduced, delayed, avoided, or applied selectively. Future progress requires biologically informed, context-sensitive trials focussed on meaningful survival, recovery, and long-term function.

articles.title: Circulating NLRP3 Inflammasome Activation Is Associated With Sepsis-Associated Acute Kidney Injury and Disease Severity: A Prospective Pilot Study.
articles.abstract: Sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI) is a severe and prevalent complication in critically ill patients, characterized by high mortality and a lack of reliable biomarkers that reflect inflammatory pathway activation and disease severity. Although the NLRP3 inflammasome is known to mediate inflammatory responses, pyroptosis, and renal injury, its clinical relevance in human SA-AKI remains poorly defined. This study aimed to characterize the expression profiles, dynamic trajectories, and clinical associations of circulating NLRP3 inflammasome components in patients with SA-AKI. Thirty adult patients with sepsis (13 with SA-AKI and 17 without AKI) were prospectively and consecutively enrolled. Sepsis was defined according to the Sepsis-3 consensus criteria, whereas AKI was diagnosed and staged exclusively using the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. Serum protein levels of NLRP3, ASC, caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1, IL-1β, and IL-18, and transcript levels of NLRP3, ASC, and caspase-1, were determined on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 after enrollment using ELISA and quantitative real-time PCR. Statistical analyses included group comparisons, Spearman rank correlations, linear mixed-effects models, and exploratory receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses to assess concurrent group discrimination. Because samples were collected post-classification, these analyses describe post-diagnostic expression kinetics rather than prediction of future AKI onset. The expression of NLRP3 inflammasome-related molecules was significantly upregulated in the SA-AKI group and correlated with renal dysfunction and elevated illness-severity scores (SOFA and APACHE II). Exploratory ROC analyses suggested strong discrimination of concurrent AKI status for ASC, caspase-1, and NLRP3 transcript levels, with the strongest overall performance observed on day 3. These estimates are hypothesis-generating because of the small sample size and post-classification sampling. The NLRP3 inflammasome pathway is prominently activated in patients with SA-AKI and is closely associated with renal dysfunction and systemic illness severity. Circulating components of this pathway are candidate biomarkers of concurrent SA-AKI, but their ability to predict AKI onset or prognosis requires validation in larger prospective cohorts sampled before AKI develops.

articles.title: Severe Propofol Infusion Syndrome Managed With Multimodal Critical Care: A Case Report.
articles.abstract: Rapid cardiovascular collapse with severe metabolic derangement during propofol sedation should raise concern for propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS). A 21-year-old man with previous traumatic brain injury presented with refractory status epilepticus requiring mechanical ventilation and prolonged propofol sedation. Following four days of infusion, he developed abrupt bradycardia, cardiogenic shock, severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, hypertriglyceridemia, and significant left ventricular dysfunction. The combination of prolonged propofol exposure and rapidly evolving multiorgan failure was considered consistent with PRIS. Propofol was discontinued immediately. Management included administration of multiple vasoactive infusions, sodium bicarbonate, calcium chloride, dual high-effluent continuous renal replacement therapy via two dialysis circuits, high-dose euglycemic insulin, and enteral L-carnitine. Hemodynamic improvement occurred within approximately six hours, followed by recovery of cardiac and renal function. He was discharged from the intensive care unit on day 30 and later returned home after rehabilitation without dialysis dependence. This case highlights the importance of early recognition of PRIS and rapid escalation of individualized organ support in severe presentations, while acknowledging that the contribution of individual adjunctive therapies cannot be determined from a single case.

articles.title: Leptospirosis presenting with cholestatic jaundice: Hepatic features and clinical outcomes.
articles.abstract: Leptospirosis is a zoonotic infection with a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations. Hepatic involvement is common, particularly in severe forms, such as Weil's disease, and poses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. We retrospectively evaluated the general characteristics and outcomes of patients diagnosed with leptospirosis at Harran University, Department of Gastroenterology between May 2019 and September 2025. We included 30 patients (86.7% male) with a median age of 45 years (range: 18-78 years); the median total bilirubin at presentation was 9.1 mg/dL (range: 2.5-49.0 mg/dL). All patients showed features of moderate-to-severe liver injury. A total of 18 (60%) patients developed acute kidney injury, 10 (33.3%) had pulmonary involvement, myocarditis was identified in 3 (10%) patients, and 5 (16.7%) patients exhibited neurological manifestations. All patients received antibiotics (doxycycline, cephalosporins, and carbapenems). Corticosteroids were given to nine patients. Therapeutic plasma exchange was performed in 12 (40%) patients. Seventeen (56.7%) patients required intensive care unit (ICU) admission, and 3 (10%) required invasive mechanical ventilation. Median creatinine (2.1 vs. 1.2 mg/dL, p=0.004) was higher, pulmonary involvement was more common (52.9% vs. 7.7%, p=0.017), plasma exchange (58.8% vs. 15.4%, p=0.026) and corticosteroid use (52.9% vs. 0%, p = 0.003) were more common among patients admitted to the ICU than among those not admitted to the ICU. Two (6.7%) patients did not respond to therapy and died during follow-up. Leptospirosis presenting with liver injury and pulmonary involvement is associated with a higher probability of ICU admission. Corticosteroids and/or plasma exchange can be used, but prospective studies are necessary to reveal their prognostic relevance in patients presenting with severe leptospirosis.

articles.title: Harmonizing the diagnosis of citrate accumulation - a call for standardized criteria.
articles.abstract: Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) has emerged as the gold-standard strategy for continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), yet its widespread adoption remains hindered by perceived complexity, heterogeneous protocols, unclear contraindications, and inconsistent terminology. A central challenge lies in the recognition and management of citrate accumulation, for which no single, reliable biomarker exists. The total-to-ionized calcium (tCa/iCa) ratio is widely utilized as a sensitive surrogate, but its specificity is limited by multiple confounding factors, including serum albumin concentration, acid-base status, and exogenous calcium administration. Current evidence supports a paradigm shift from reliance on static thresholds toward a dynamic, physiology-based assessment to define citrate accumulation. The kinetics of the tCa/iCa ratio, when interpreted alongside evolving metabolic parameters, particularly lactate trends, systemic ionized calcium, and acid-base status, provide a more robust framework for identifying citrate accumulation. Crucially, an elevated tCa/iCa ratio should not indiscriminately prompt the discontinuation of RCA. Targeted adjustments to the CRRT prescription can often safely mitigate citrate burden while preserving circuit patency. In the absence of a validated and widely available method for the direct measurement of plasma citrate levels, we propose a stepwise approach incorporating routinely measured screening tools and confirmatory parameters. Studies incorporating direct plasma citrate concentration measurements should be conducted to validate these criteria alongside readily available bedside surrogate markers. Refining this framework is essential to enhance the safe implementation of RCA and ultimately improve outcomes in critically ill patients.

articles.title: Vancomycin dosing in critically ill patients receiving renal replacement therapy: a critical appraisal of the toxicity threshold and external validation.
Epidemiology of Critically Ill Patients With Cirrhosis Undergoing Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy: A Contemporaneous Parallel Analysis of the HRS-HARMONY and CRRTnet Registries.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Describe the epidemiology of patients with cirrhosis/acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) receiving continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) pertaining to process factors including renal replacement dose, modality, and circuit anticoagulation. SETTING: Academic tertiary care hospitals in the United States and Canada. DESIGN AND PATIENTS: We performed a parallel study of contemporaneous data from the HARMONY and CRRT network (CRRTnet) databases to describe the epidemiology and process of CRRT care of cirrhosis/ACLF patients receiving CRRT in the ICU. We evaluated clinical and CRRT process factors (dialysis dose, anticoagulation) with the primary outcome of in-hospital mortality. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: The HARMONY cohort (n = 245; median age, 57 yr; 41% female) and CRRTnet cohort (n = 206; 58 yr; 39% female) demonstrated similar overall survival to hospital discharge (HARMONY, 34%; CRRTnet, 30%). In HARMONY, the two most common causes of acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring CRRT were acute tubular necrosis (73%) and hepatorenal syndrome-AKI (13%), with no significant difference between survivors and nonsurvivors (p = 0.24). In HARMONY, higher chronic liver failure-C ACLF scores (hazard ratio, 1.03 [95% CI, 1.01-1.05]; p < 0.001) were independently associated with increased in-hospital mortality. In CRRTnet, the most common CRRT modality was continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (83.8%), and the most common anticoagulation strategy was regional citrate anticoagulation (58.0%) or no anticoagulation (35.8%). CRRT prescribed dose greater than 30 mL/kg/hr was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (multivariable regression; odds ratio, 2.69; 95% CI, 1.3-5.64; p = 0.01). Of survivors in CRRTnet, 64% were transitioned to intermittent hemodialysis (IHD) before hospital discharge. CONCLUSIONS: Critically ill cirrhosis/ACLF patients initiated on CRRT in the absence of liver transplantation had high in-hospital mortality. These patients were prescribed higher initial CRRT doses (median total effluent > 30 mL/kg/hr), with higher CRRT dose independently associated with increased in-hospital mortality. Of ICU survivors, 64% were transitioned to IHD at ICU discharge. Despite concerns for citrate toxicity, citrate regional anticoagulation was commonly employed in these patients.

articles.title: Landscape of Biomarker Use in Critically Ill Patients: Systematic Evidence Map of Acute Kidney Injury and Implications for Practice.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Create systematic evidence maps of novel biomarkers of kidney injury from a mapping review to guide future implementation in patient care. DATA SOURCES: PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase. STUDY SELECTION: Systematic evidence maps included clinical trials and observational studies in critically ill patients, investigating novel kidney biomarkers for acute kidney injury (AKI). DATA EXTRACTION: Six thousand eight hundred five records were screened, and 1116 studies were included that related to one or more novel biomarkers and AKI. DATA SYNTHESIS: Adult populations accounted for 78.6% of the studies, and 93.3% used a cohort design to investigate AKI biomarkers. Mixed critically ill populations, cardiac surgery, and sepsis were identified as the most frequently studied clinical contexts in 69.5% of the studies. Systematic evidence maps were synthesized for biomarker studies to predict AKI (n = 944), prognosticate clinical outcomes (n = 647), diagnose AKI etiology (n = 109), enrich clinical trials (n = 6), and manage AKI (n = 12). Implementation strategies for patient care included surveilling patients at risk of AKI, including patients undergoing surgery and those exposed to multiple nephrotoxic drugs. CONCLUSIONS: Substantial clinical evidence assessing the accuracy of biomarkers compared with diagnosis of AKI exists, with fewer practical trials in clinical use. Still, guidance on implementation approaches can be gleaned from evaluations using biomarkers for the management of critically ill patients, particularly in surgical and nephrotoxin-exposed populations where evidence is available. This review identifies the landscape of current evidence and highlights priorities for future management and enrichment trials needed to bridge the gap between predictive accuracy and clinical decision-making.

articles.title: Tailored strategies for vitamin C, D, iron, and carnitine in critical illness.
articles.abstract: Micronutrients are essential cofactors for metabolic, immune, and cellular processes. Low plasma concentrations are frequent in ICU patients but poorly reflect tissue stores. Inflammation drives redistribution and utilisation, while disease, reduced intake, impaired absorption, dilution, and increased losses may contribute to true deficiency. Plasma values, therefore, cannot distinguish redistribution from deficiency, making individualised requirement estimation difficult. This narrative review focuses on four micronutrients of recent high interest, aiming to address some missing links in critical illness. Current guidelines recommend routine provision of basal micronutrient requirements for all ICU patients, with additional monitoring and increased doses reserved for high-risk groups with losses. Plasma measurements, often the only available tool, should be interpreted alongside inflammatory markers, clinical context, and risk factors. Large RCTs of vitamin C have mainly yielded neutral or negative results, which may reflect unguided supplementation across heterogeneous populations without accounting for timing, duration, dosing strategies, and biochemical formulation variability; alternatively, vitamin C may simply be ineffective as an early intervention in critical illness. Available evidence from ICU vitamin D trials indicates signals of outcome benefit, but the evidence is heterogeneous and trial sizes are limited, preventing firm ICU-specific recommendations. Ongoing large trials are expected to clarify effects of high-dose strategies. Iron status spans a narrow therapeutic window: iron deficiency and anaemia are highly prevalent during and after ICU, yet iron overload and ferroptosis-related toxicity also contribute to organ dysfunction. Targeted, hepcidin-guided intravenous (I.V.) iron therapy appears promising to safely correct deficiency. Both carnitine deficiency and high blood levels are associated with worse outcomes in ICU patients. Risk factors for alterations in carnitine concentrations include CRRT, renal and hepatic dysfunction, valproate use, inflammation, and wound losses. Supplementation should be evaluated in a stepwise approach to detect potentially excessive levels in a dose-finding RCT. New biomarkers and analytical approaches are needed to differentiate redistribution from deficiency, capturing dynamic changes over time. Future approaches should move beyond plasma measurements toward cellular and functional biomarkers that better reflect stores and biological activity. Given current limitations, testing should be selective to where results are expected to alter management, include CRP, and timing guided by underlying risk. Research should prioritise precision strategies with better biomarkers and longitudinal sampling to account for dynamic risk, needs, losses, and responses.

articles.title: Acute kidney injury and renal replacement therapy: a critical synthesis of metabolic derangements and nutritional implications.
articles.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) affects up to 50% of critically ill patients and is frequently complicated by severe metabolic derangements, requiring the initiation of replacement therapy (RRT) in 10-15% of cases. Despite substantial progress in the diagnosis of AKI and optimisation of RRT delivery, the nutritional management of these patients remains an underexplored area. AKI is increasingly recognised as a systemic metabolic disorder extending beyond impaired renal clearance. Key metabolic alterations include mitochondrial dysfunction, dysregulated gluconeogenesis, increased proteolysis and altered amino acid metabolism, with accelerated nitrogen wasting. These abnormalities are further amplified by acute systemic stress states, including sepsis, systemic inflammation, trauma, burns, liver dysfunction and multiorgan failure. RRT introduces additional metabolic consequences through extracorporeal losses of amino acids and micronutrients. Conversely, citrate anticoagulation, glucose-containing dialysate, and lactate-buffered solutions represent sources of clinically relevant calories. Current nutritional recommendations are largely extrapolated from heterogeneous intensive care populations. Available evidence suggests that AKI primarily influences energy balance rather than energy expenditure, which appears broadly comparable to that of other critically ill populations. While evidence specific to AKI is limited, protein provision of approximately 1.2-1.3 g/kg/day is generally recommended during critical illness. However, higher intakes of up to 1.7-2.5 g/kg/day may be considered in patients receiving RRT to offset extracorporeal amino acid losses and increased protein catabolism. In this setting, emerging concepts such as metabolic tolerance and biomarker-guided metabolic phenotyping may facilitate individualised nutritional strategies. AKI, particularly when requiring RRT, is associated with profound and dynamic metabolic disturbances that substantially influence energy and protein requirements, thereby making nutrition an integral component of organ support therapies. Future research should evaluate precision nutrition strategies that tailor nutritional support to the phase of critical illness, measured energy expenditure, metabolic tolerance, and RRT-related nutrient losses and gains. Such studies should prioritise patient-centred outcomes, including physical function and recovery, in addition to nutritional and metabolic endpoints.

articles.title: What place for pragmatic RCTs in intensive care?
articles.abstract: Pragmatic trials test the effectiveness of an intervention within real-life clinical practice, prioritising applicability and generalisability. By contrast, explanatory trials evaluate the efficacy of an intervention under optimal conditions and in well-defined populations, aiming to minimise bias and confounding and to maximise the treatment effect. The majority of large-scale, multicentre academic ICU studies are overall pragmatic in nature but have repeatedly failed to demonstrate outcome differences against control populations. This relates in part to the marked heterogeneity of ICU populations, often with enrolment based on syndromic categories such as sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, shock and acute kidney injury with significant inter-individual biological variability. Any beneficial treatment effects in specific, often unidentified, subsets are diluted or cancelled out by no effect or even harm in others. A second important factor underlying the lack of intervention effect is suboptimal performance of the trials, particularly poor protocol adherence, which undermines the likelihood of showing benefit, particularly when reliant on intention-to-treat analyses. In this article we discuss these issues and provide some suggestions for improvement.
articles.ai_summary: This article discusses the limitations of pragmatic randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in intensive care units (ICUs). Pragmatic RCTs often fail to demonstrate outcome differences due to heterogeneity of ICU populations and suboptimal trial performance. Suggestions for improvement are provided.
articles.ai_significance: Understanding the limitations of pragmatic RCTs in ICUs is crucial for developing effective treatment strategies and improving patient outcomes.

articles.title: Urinary kidney injury molecule-1 as a diagnostic biomarker for persistent severe acute kidney injury: a systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Despite the vast amount of literature dedicated to biomarkers and acute kidney injury (AKI), the persistent state of AKI has been relatively neglected. The objective of this study was to systematically review relevant studies and evaluate the diagnostic value of urinary kidney injury molecule 1 (uKIM-1) for persistent severe AKI in adults. We searched the PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials databases up to December 2025. Eligible studies included adult patients and assessed the diagnostic value of uKIM-1 for persistent severe AKI. The Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) was used for quality assessment. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, area under the curve (AUC) and diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) values were calculated via a Bayesian bivariate diagnostic meta-analysis model. Eight studies with 2349 patients were selected for meta-analysis. 378 patients were diagnosed with persistent severe AKI. The included studies were published between 2011 and 2025 and involved heterogeneous clinical settings, including intensive care, emergency department, postoperative, sepsis, COVID-19, and liver transplantation populations. The estimated sensitivity of uKIM-1 was 0.67 (95% CrI, 0.59-0.75), and the specificity was 0.73 (95% CrI, 0.61-0.84). The pooled DOR was 5.91 (95% CrI, 2.91-11.20), and the AUC was 0.75 (95% CrI, 0.62-0.84). Sensitivity analyses using alternative cutoff selections and prior specifications showed generally stable estimates. This Bayesian meta-analysis indicates that uKIM-1 has moderate diagnostic value for persistent severe AKI in adults. Current evidence does not support its use as a standalone biomarker, and future studies should evaluate its incremental value in combination with other biomarkers and clinical variables.

articles.title: Vancomycin optimised dosing regimens for critically ill patients receiving renal replacement therapy.
