authors: European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases (ESCMID) Study Groups for Infections in Critically Ill Patients (ESGCIP) and the ESCMID PK/PD of Anti-Infectives Study Group (EPASG)
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Optimal dosing of vancomycin in critically ill patients receiving renal replacement therapy (RRT) is uncertain due to high pharmacokinetic variability. We aimed to develop individualised vancomycin dosing recommendations that optimise efficacy while minimising toxicity. METHODS: Prospective, international, pharmacokinetic study enrolling critically ill patients treated with vancomycin and various RRT modalities. A population pharmacokinetic model was developed, externally validated and applied to perform Monte Carlo dosing simulations. We calculated the probability of each dosing regimen to achieve the efficacy target against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (ratio of the area under the concentration-time curve to the minimum inhibitory concentration (AUC0-24 h/MIC) ≥ 400) without exceeding the toxicity threshold (AUC0-24 h ≥ 700 mg.h/L). RESULTS: We enrolled 65 critically ill patients from 6 countries receiving continuous RRT (50.8%) or sustained low-efficiency dialysis (49.2%). The model was developed using 1318 pre- and post-filter plasma and effluent concentrations and validated with a new dataset (19 critically ill patients, 124 pre-filter plasma concentrations), with 47.4% patients concomitantly treated with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Predictive performance was high (median prediction error =-13.4%). Simulations showed that dosing requirements were dependent on actual body weight and RRT intensity and duration (p < 0.05). An optimised dosing nomogram was subsequently developed considering these clinical characteristics. CONCLUSIONS: Actual body weight and RRT intensity and duration are the main determinants of vancomycin dosing requirements in critically ill patients treated with RRT. Efficacious, non-toxic dosing may be guided by the optimised nomogram.

articles.title: Determinants of Delayed Recovery of Consciousness After Analgosedation Discontinuation in the ICU: Insights From Patients With COVID-19 Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Prolonged disorders of consciousness are common in critically ill patients receiving mechanical ventilation and are often attributed to prolonged sedative exposure in the setting of decreased drug clearance and/or reduced metabolism. Here, in a large sample of critically ill COVID patients obtained over a short period, we tested the assumption that prolonged unconsciousness following benzodiazepine and/or propofol sedation can be attributed to residual exposure. Further, we examine associations between clinical variables on time to recovery of consciousness (RoC) as a framework for the broader critically ill population. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study. SETTING: Massachusetts General Hospital, Weill Cornell Medicine, Columbia University Irving Medical Center. PATIENTS: Seven hundred eighty-four patients with COVID-19 critical illness in Spring-Summer 2020. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We estimated the latest expected RoC (LERoC) using models of sedation exposure that account for sedative-specific pharmacokinetics and critical illness. Our primary exposure variable was a time-weighted dose of analgosedative agents at benzodiazepine and/or propofol cessation; our primary outcome was time to RoC. We estimated relative risks for late RoC (i.e., after LERoC) via multinomial logistic regression. Among individuals with late RoC, we fit a multivariate subdistribution hazard model for time to RoC. Seventy-three percent of patients had RoC before hospital discharge, yet 34% of patients achieving RoC did not do so within pharmacologically plausible sedative elimination times. Patients with late RoC were older and exhibited hypoxemia and acute kidney injury. Patients with dexmedetomidine as an adjunct sedative had a disproportionately larger incidence of early recovery. Patients with early vs. late RoC did not have significantly different discharge dispositions. CONCLUSIONS: In our cohort, the time to RoC was commonly prolonged beyond that expected from sedation exposures alone. These data may aid clinicians and families with expectations of RoC and warrant investigation of alternative determinants of delayed RoC in this population.

articles.title: Sodium bicarbonate therapy in severe metabolic acidemia: an individual patient data meta-analysis of the BICAR-ICU and BICAR-ICU2 trials.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Two randomized trials (BICAR-ICU and BICAR-ICU2) evaluated intravenous sodium bicarbonate therapy in patients with severe metabolic acidemia but yielded inconclusive results. We performed an individual patient data meta-analysis to assess its effects on 90-day mortality and renal replacement therapy (RRT) use, and search for heterogeneity of treatment effects across prespecified subgroups. METHODS: We performed an individual patient data meta-analysis of the BICAR-ICU and BICAR-ICU2 trials, including adults with severe metabolic acidemia (pH ≤ 7.20). Patients were randomized to receive intravenous sodium bicarbonate titrated to a pH ≥ 7.30 or no sodium bicarbonate. The primary outcome was 90-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included RRT initiation and dialysis-free days. Prespecified subgroup analyses explored treatment-effect heterogeneity by acidemia depth (pH ≤ 7.10 vs. > 7.10), severe acute kidney injury (AKI) status, and serum lactate (< 2mmol/L vs. ≥2mmol/L). RESULTS: A total of 1,016 patients was included (509 sodium bicarbonate, 507 control). Sodium bicarbonate therapy did not significantly reduce 90-day mortality compared to control (58.3% vs. 60.6%; risk ratio [RR], 0.96; 95%CI, 0.86-1.07; p = 0.51). However, it significantly reduced RRT initiation (34.8% vs. 50.7%; RR, 0.69; 95%CI, 0.60-0.79; p < 0.001, number needed to treat: 6.3) and increased dialysis-free days (incidence rate ratio, 1.10; 95%CI, 1.06-1.14; p < 0.001). A significant interaction was observed with acidemia depth (p-for-interaction = 0.006): in patients with pH ≤ 7.10, sodium bicarbonate reduced 90-day mortality (RR, 0.80; 95%CI, 0.68-0.93; p = 0.004); no benefit was seen with pH > 7.10 (RR, 1.05; 95%CI, 0.92-1.21; p = 0.47). No significant interactions were observed for severe AKI status (p-for-interaction = 0.11) nor serum lactate (p-for-interaction = 0.22). CONCLUSIONS: Sodium bicarbonate therapy did not reduce overall 90-day mortality but decreased RRT use and suggested a mortality benefit in patients with the most profound acidemia (pH ≤ 7.10). These findings invite a reconsideration of current paradigms, suggesting timely correction of severe metabolic acidemia to avoid RRT in some patients.
articles.ai_summary: This study combined data from two previous trials to assess the effect of sodium bicarbonate therapy on patients with severe metabolic acidemia. It found that while sodium bicarbonate did not reduce overall mortality, it did decrease the need for renal replacement therapy and may benefit patients with the most severe acidemia.
articles.ai_significance: These findings suggest that timely correction of severe metabolic acidemia may help avoid the need for renal replacement therapy in some patients, and may change current clinical practice paradigms.

articles.title: Nutrition Therapy in Critically Ill Adults.
articles.journal: The New England journal of medicine
articles.abstract: In the acute phase of critical illness, adults have severe catabolism, inflammation, muscle loss, and gut dysfunction, all of which shape nutritional requirements. Early enteral nutrition supports gut integrity and microbiome health, but trials have shown that early short-term parenteral nutrition is a safe alternative when enteral feeding is not possible. Large trials have shown that early full-dose energy delivery offers no benefit over restrictive dosing and may increase gastrointestinal and metabolic complications, findings that support a restrictive nutrition strategy, especially in patients who have circulatory shock or are at risk for refeeding syndrome. Similarly, large trials have shown no advantage of high-dose over standard-dose protein and suggest harm in patients with acute kidney injury. Because adverse events are common with enteral nutrition, safe nutrition delivery requires gradual advancement, strategies for prevention of refeeding syndrome, glycemic control, and avoidance of routine gastric residual volume monitoring. Patient heterogeneity underscores the need for precise, biomarker-guided, phase-specific nutrition to preserve lean muscle mass and improve recovery.

articles.title: Genomic dynamics of antimicrobial resistance transmission between bacteria from intensive care unit surfaces and from critically ill patients.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Intensive Care Unit (ICU) is an environment where multiple factors that predispose to the transmission of Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) coexist. Genomic sequencing is a technology that enables a better understanding of how AMR genes are transmitted within the ICU environment. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the genomic dynamics of the transmission of antimicrobial resistance genes between bacteria from ICU surfaces and bacteria from critically ill patients. METHODS: A cross-sectional analytical study. Surface swab samples were collected from the ICU, including suction units, infusion pumps, stethoscopes, dialysis machines, monitors, ventilators and gas valves, as well as samples from critically ill patients with infections. Species were identified using microbiological microplate panels; antibiotic susceptibility testing was carried out to assess AMR; and whole-genome sequencing was performed on isolates that were multidrug-resistant (MDR). The sequencing was carried out using a nanopore long-read sequencer and the results were analysed using specialised bioinformatics tools. RESULTS: A total of 130 positive isolates were identified, of which 96 (73.85%) were from environmental samples and 34 (26.15%) from patient samples. Forty (30.76%) MDR species were identified. The most common MDR species were Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii. The most frequently detected AMR genes were blaNDM-5 and blaOXA-23. The most common plasmids were IncFIB(K)_1_Kpn3, Col440I and IncL/M(pMU407)_1_pMU407. A clonal outbreak of Acinetobacter baumannii ST 2 was detected on the dialysis machine, stethoscopes and patient samples. Evidence of horizontal transfer of resistance genes via plasmids conjugation was found in samples taken from suction units, oxygen valves and tracheal secretion in three cases. CONCLUSION: The findings of this research show that antimicrobial resistance genes are transferred between bacteria on surfaces and bacteria in critically ill patients, and that this transfer occurs in both directions.

articles.title: Interpreting protein dose trials in critical illness: a guide for the bedside clinician.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Critical illness induces a catabolic state, associated with profound muscle wasting and functional disability in survivors. Based on evidence at the time of development, international critical care nutrition guidelines recommend providing higher protein doses than in healthy populations. MAIN BODY: Three recent international multi-centre randomised trials (total n = 5633 patients) have compared higher protein doses to usual protein doses in critically ill patients. Based on the primary outcomes, these trials concluded that higher protein doses did not improve time-to-discharge alive or number of days free of the index hospital and alive at day 90, with worse functional recovery using the EQ-5D-5L health utility score over 180 days. Supported by evidence from recent trials, it appears preferable to commence protein delivery at low doses once patients are haemodynamically stable and increase progressively over the first 5 days to deliver a maximum of 1.2 g/kg/day. Based on current trial data, this upper limit may represent a safer alternative to doses >1.2 g/kg/day, acknowledging that the optimal dose may be lower. Subgroup analyses suggest that patients with an acute kidney injury may be particularly vulnerable to higher protein. There are no data to indicate the minimum protein dose that can be safely delivered to critically ill patients over their entire ICU stay. While existing trials included patients with a prolonged ICU stay, no trial identifying this cohort pre-randomisation has been conducted. It cannot be excluded that higher protein doses may provide benefit later in recovery, when the anabolic resistance to dietary protein observed early in the ICU admission has subsided. Evidence is also lacking on optimal protein targets for patients after ICU discharge. CONCLUSION: In critically ill adults, we suggest that protein doses be commenced at a low dose and increased progressively to a maximum of 1.2 g/kg/day based on recent randomised trials.
articles.ai_summary: Three large international trials compared high protein doses to usual doses in critically ill patients. The results showed no benefit to high protein doses, and instead suggest starting with low doses and increasing over time. This may be especially important for patients with acute kidney injury.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings have significant implications for ICU nutrition practice, suggesting a shift away from high protein doses and towards a more gradual and individualized approach to protein delivery.

articles.title: Implementation of the kidney protection strategy in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury - a multi-center prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The international Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines recommend the implementation of a kidney protection strategy (KPS) in patients at high risk of and with Acute Kidney Injury (AKI). However, real-world implementation of this strategy in critically ill patients with AKI is unclear. We quantified timely and sustained adherence to KPS in critically ill adults with moderate-to-severe (KDIGO stage 2 or 3) AKI and explored associations with clinical outcomes. METHODS: This was a multicenter, prospective cohort study enrolling adult patients with moderate or severe AKI requiring vasopressors and/or mechanical ventilation across five centers in Europe. The primary endpoint was adherence to the KPS, which included hemodynamic monitoring, sustained optimization of mean arterial pressure (MAP) > 65 mmHg, monitoring of serum creatinine and urine output, and avoidance of hyperglycemia, radiocontrast agents and nephrotoxins when possible, within 12 h after AKI diagnosis for 48 h or until ICU discharge. Exploratory analyses examined associations between adherence and renal outcomes. RESULTS: A total of 258 patients were enrolled (median age 69 years [IQR 62-75]; 65% male; median SOFA 10 [IQR 8-13]). The complete KPS was implemented in 80 patients (31%; 95% CI, 25.5-37.2%). Adherence to individual components of the KPS varied widely with optimization of MAP showing the lowest implementation rate (33%). In exploratory analyses accounting for death as a competing risk, KPS adherence was associated with a lower incidence of AKD beyond day 7 (subdistribution hazard ratio [SHR] 0.64; 95% CI, 0.41-0.99; p = 0.046), a higher incidence of renal recovery at hospital discharge (SHR 6.02; 95% CI, 4.00-9.05; p < 0.0001), and a lower incidence of RRT within 30 days (SHR 0.12; 95% CI, 0.02-0.91; p = 0.04). After multivariable adjustment, the association with renal recovery remained robust (adjusted SHR 6.29; 95% CI, 3.08-12.85; p < 0.0001). A clear dose-response relationship was observed between the number of implemented KPS components and renal outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: In critically ill patients with moderate-to-severe AKI, the complete KDIGO-recommended kidney protection strategy was implemented in approximately one-third of patients, and full KPS adherence was associated with a higher rate of renal recovery at hospital discharge.
articles.ai_summary: This study looked at how well a kidney protection strategy was implemented in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury. They found that about a third of patients received the full strategy, and those who did had a higher rate of kidney recovery. The study also found a link between the number of strategy components implemented and better kidney outcomes.
articles.ai_significance: This study is important for ICU clinicians because it highlights the need to implement a kidney protection strategy in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury to improve kidney recovery rates.

articles.title: The role of hemoadsorption in septic shock: toward a personalized approach.
articles.abstract: A dysregulated host response to infection is central to the pathophysiology of sepsis and may culminate in life-threatening organ dysfunction. Given that this process is largely characterized by concurrent pro- and anti-inflammatory activation, immunomodulatory strategies have long been explored in sepsis research. Among these, extracorporeal removal of circulating cytokines, inflammatory mediators and other soluble factors through non-specific hemoadsorption with macroporous styrene-divinylbenzene sorbents has been proposed as a potential therapeutic approach. Its adoption into clinical practice has largely been based on pathophysiological considerations rather than on evidence from large, well-designed randomized clinical trials. Over the past 15 years, most of the available evidence has been predominantly derived from small, single-center cohorts, reports from registries and heterogeneous prospective studies with substantial variability in patients' selection, timing, and treatment intensity. In addition, the precise mechanisms of action of hemoadsorption remain incompletely understood. Although several meta-analyses have attempted to synthesize the existing data, the overall quality and heterogeneity of the included studies limit the strength and reliability of their conclusions. As a result, current guideline recommendations are largely based on expert opinions rather than high-certainty evidence. This position statement aimed to provide a concise overview of the biological rationale, current evidence, and contemporary clinical practice related to hemoadsorption in critically ill patients.
articles.ai_summary: Researchers reviewed the evidence on hemoadsorption in septic shock, finding that current guidelines are based on expert opinions rather than high-certainty evidence. Hemoadsorption involves removing inflammatory mediators from the blood, but its effectiveness and mechanisms of action are not well understood. More research is needed to determine its role in treating septic shock.
articles.ai_significance: This study highlights the need for more robust clinical trials to establish the effectiveness of hemoadsorption in septic shock, which could lead to more personalized and effective treatment approaches in the ICU.

articles.title: Sodium Bicarbonate for Critically Ill Adults with Metabolic Acidosis and Shock.
articles.journal: The New England journal of medicine
authors: SODa-BIC Investigators and the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Clinical Trials Group
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Metabolic acidosis is common in critically ill patients and is associated with organ dysfunction and death. Sodium bicarbonate is used to correct acidemia, but its benefit in patients with metabolic acidosis who are receiving vasopressors remains uncertain. METHODS: In this pragmatic, adaptive, double-blind, randomized trial, we assigned adults with metabolic acidosis (pH, <7.30; base excess, no more than -4 mmol per liter; and partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide, ≤45 mm Hg without intubation or ≤50 mm Hg with intubation) who were receiving vasopressors in the intensive care unit (ICU) to receive either sodium bicarbonate or placebo (5% dextrose). Sodium bicarbonate or placebo was infused for up to 5 hours, with the infusion rate adjusted for a target pH of at least 7.30 and base excess of at least 0 mmol per liter. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event, defined as death, use of renal-replacement therapy, or persistent renal dysfunction, within 30 days. RESULTS: A total of 500 patients were enrolled in 55 ICUs across seven countries; 245 patients were assigned to receive sodium bicarbonate and 255 to receive placebo. A major adverse kidney event within 30 days occurred in 98 of 244 patients (40.2%) in the sodium bicarbonate group and in 100 of 254 patients (39.4%) in the placebo group (adjusted difference, 1.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -7.1 to 9.4; P = 0.78). Renal-replacement therapy was used within 30 days in 16.8% of the patients in the sodium bicarbonate group and in 20.9% of those in the placebo group (adjusted difference, -3.9 percentage points; 95% CI, -10.6 to 2.7). In-hospital mortality by day 30 was 25.4% in the sodium bicarbonate group and 24.0% in the placebo group (adjusted difference, 1.8 percentage points; 95% CI, -5.6 to 9.2). Four patients (1.6%) in the sodium bicarbonate group had an adverse effect, as compared with none in the placebo group (P = 0.06). CONCLUSIONS: The use of sodium bicarbonate in critically ill patients with metabolic acidosis receiving vasopressors did not lead to a lower risk of major adverse kidney events within 30 days than placebo. (Funded by the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia; SODa-BIC ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05697770.).
articles.ai_summary: Researchers conducted a randomized trial of 500 critically ill patients with metabolic acidosis and shock to see if sodium bicarbonate reduced kidney damage. The results showed no difference in kidney damage or mortality between patients who received sodium bicarbonate and those who received a placebo. The study found that sodium bicarbonate did not provide a benefit in reducing kidney damage or improving outcomes in critically ill patients.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings are significant for ICU clinical practice as they suggest that sodium bicarbonate may not be beneficial in reducing kidney damage or improving outcomes in critically ill patients with metabolic acidosis and shock. Clinicians may need to reconsider using sodium bicarbonate in these patients.

articles.title: Rethinking Fluid Balance: The Shift Toward Deresuscitation in Critical Care.
articles.journal: Advances in kidney disease and health
articles.abstract: Intravenous fluid therapy is central to resuscitating critically ill patients, yet accumulating evidence shows that excessive fluid administration and positive fluid balance contribute directly to respiratory failure, acute kidney injury, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and mortality. Modern fluid stewardship reframes intravenous fluids as pharmacologic agents with dose-dependent toxicity and emphasizes the ROSE (Resuscitation, Optimization, Stabilization, and Evacuation) model. Observational studies consistently link fluid overload (often defined as fluid balance >5% baseline weight) to worse outcomes, and early or protocolized deresuscitation (removal of accumulated fluid once perfusion goals have been achieved) through diuretics or ultrafiltration can reliably achieve negative fluid balance and improve pulmonary parameters without increasing acute kidney injury. Randomized trials of restrictive strategies demonstrate improved ventilator-free days and shortened length of stay but no mortality benefit, underscoring the need for individualized, physiology-guided approaches. Evidence for active deresuscitation remains mixed. Diuretic-based protocols can lower mortality and reduce renal replacement therapy use in select populations, while ultrafiltration studies highlight the importance of avoiding both insufficient (<1 mL/kg/h) and excessive (>1.75 mL/hg/h) fluid removal rates. Knowledge gaps persist around optimal timing, patient selection, hemodynamic monitoring, and fluid removal targets. Ongoing trials aim to refine protocolized resuscitation and better define strategies to safely restore euvolemia, mitigate organ dysfunction, and improve outcomes in critical illness.

articles.title: Acute Kidney Injury After Hematopoietic Stem CellTransplantation.
articles.journal: Advances in kidney disease and health
articles.abstract: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is a curative intervention for various hematologic malignancies. However, it is associated with an exceptionally high rate of acute kidney injury with a cumulative incidence of 55%. The risk is highest for unmatched allogeneic transplantation involving myeloablative conditioning regimens. The need for kidney replacement therapy can approach 21% especially in critically ill recipients with unacceptably high all-cause and nonrelapse mortality. Various factors predispose to kidney injury extending from the toxicity of conditioning regimen to a myriad of complications spanning up to 100 days post-transplantation. An understanding of this timeline as well as the pathophysiology of the various processes facilitates early recognition and prompt management. Advances in therapeutics bring optimism in improving outcomes and minimizing progressive tissue injury.

articles.title: Effects of higher versus lower protein intake in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: The optimal protein dose for critically ill patients remains uncertain, and emerging evidence suggests that the effects of higher protein intake may differ across clinically relevant subgroups. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating protein delivery in critical illness adults (up to July 2026). Higher and lower protein groups were defined according to each trial's original allocation. Primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included mechanical ventilation (MV) duration, Intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay (LOS), muscle outcomes, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), biochemical outcomes, and adverse events. Results were reported as risk ratios (RRs) or mean difference (MD) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA) was performed to control for random error, and the certainty of evidence was rated using the GRADE framework. Thirty three RCTs involving 11,622 participants were included. No significant differences were observed between higher and lower protein groups for all-cause mortality (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.08), MV duration (MD -0.48, 95% CI -1.08 to 0.13), or ICU LOS (MD -0.18, 95% CI -0.86 to 0.51), with TSA confirming these null findings. Some muscle metrics favored the higher protein group; however, there was a trend towards poorer HRQoL (SMD -0.12, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.00). The higher protein group showed improved nitrogen balance (MD 5.58, 95% CI 2.89 to 8.27) and higher serum albumin levels (SMD 0.18, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.29), but increased urea (MD 2.06, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.64) and blood urea nitrogen concentrations (MD 2.94, 95% CI 1.32 to 4.56). Sensitivity analyses restricted to 27 isocaloric-design trials yielded consistent results. Subgroup analyses revealed that higher protein intake was linked to increased mortality in patients with acute kidney injury (RR 1.46, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.87); however, higher protein intake combined with rehabilitation interventions was associated with reduced mortality (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.93), shorter MV duration (MD -1.45, 95% CI -2.61 to -0.29), and beneficial muscle effects. Higher protein intake was not associated with better clinical outcomes. While it may increase mortality in patients with AKI, combining it with physical rehabilitation yields survival and clinical benefits, warranting confirmation in future factorial RCTs. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251109618, identifier [CRD420251109618].

articles.title: SIRT5 deficiency exacerbates sepsis acute renal injury by activating ACSL4/FTH1 axis dependent ferroptosis.
articles.abstract: Sepsis‑associated acute kidney injury (S‑AKI) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients, yet effective targeted therapies remain lacking due to an incomplete understanding of its pathogenesis. Ferroptosis, an iron‑dependent form of regulated cell death driven by lipid peroxidation, has recently been implicated in AKI, but the upstream regulators of this process in sepsis remain undefined. Here, we identify SIRT5, a mitochondrial NAD ⁺ ‑dependent desuccinylase, as a critical endogenous suppressor of ferroptosis in S‑AKI. Using a cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) murine model and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)‑stimulated HK‑2 proximal tubular cells, we show that SIRT5 expression is significantly downregulated in septic kidney injury. Renal tubular‑specific ablation of Sirt5 exacerbated CLP‑induced renal dysfunction, structural damage, and tubular cell death, whereas AAV9‑mediated SIRT5 overexpression attenuated these pathological changes. Mechanistically, SIRT5 deficiency tipped the balance of the ACSL4/FTH1 axis toward ferroptosis: it increased ACSL4‑dependent membrane lipid remodeling and reduced FTH1‑mediated iron sequestration, accompanied by suppression of the antioxidant enzyme GPX4. Consequently, lipid peroxidation, iron overload, and mitochondrial damage were markedly amplified. Notably, knockdown of ACSL4 in SIRT5‑deficient HK‑2 cells effectively reversed lipid peroxidation, iron accumulation, and cell death, establishing ACSL4 as a key downstream effector of SIRT5‑mediated ferroptosis suppression. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized SIRT5-ACSL4/FTH1 regulatory axis that governs ferroptotic susceptibility in renal tubular cells during sepsis, and suggest that pharmacological restoration of SIRT5 activity or blockade of ACSL4‑driven ferroptosis may offer novel therapeutic avenues for S‑AKI.

articles.title: A secondary analysis of the SODa-BIC randomized clinical trial using multiple hierarchical composite outcomes.
articles.abstract: The Sodium Bicarbonate for Metabolic Acidosis in the ICU (SODa-BIC) trial assessed the effect of sodium bicarbonate on Major Adverse Kidney Events at 30 days (MAKE30) in critically ill patients with metabolic acidosis. Although the trial demonstrated no significant difference in the primary outcome, the individual components showed differing magnitudes and directions of effect; we undertook an exploratory analysis of the SODa-BIC trial using different hierarchical outcomes to better understand potential treatment effects of sodium bicarbonate. Post-hoc analysis of the SODa-BIC trial. All patients included in the SODa-BIC trial were eligible. The primary outcome was a win ratio analysis with a hierarchy consisting of death, requirement for renal replacement therapy, persistent renal dysfunction, and hospital length of stay. Several sensitivity and subgroup analyses were conducted. The primary analysis resulted in 59,250 pairs from 488 patients. Consistent with the SODa-BIC analysis, there was no overall evidence of a treatment effect of sodium bicarbonate, with a win ratio of 0.97 (95%CI 0.79 - 1.19) and a Desirability of Outcome Ranking probability of 0.49 (95%CI 0.45 - 0.54). A majority of pairwise comparisons were resolved by mortality and hospital length of stay. Evidence of significant treatment effect modification was observed across subgroups defined by acute kidney injury and severity of acidemia. In this post-hoc analysis of the SODa-BIC trial, the use of hierarchical composite outcomes did not alter the neutral overall interpretation of the original trial. However, this analysis provides additional insight into the relative contribution of individual components of the primary outcome.

articles.title: Machine learning for predicting mortality in patients with sepsis and its associated complications: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Sepsis remains a leading cause of death in intensive care units worldwide and may be accompanied by complex complications, including encephalopathy, coagulopathy, acute kidney injury, myocardial dysfunction, and delirium, each of which substantially increases the risk of poor outcomes. Machine learning, a promising approach for prognostic prediction, can capture complex nonlinear relationships among clinical risk factors. However, its predictive performance in sepsis and its specific complications remains unclear. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for relevant literature through April 2026. Studies that aimed to develop or validate machine learning models to predict mortality in adult patients with sepsis and its associated complications were included. The random-effects or bivariate model was used to calculate the AUC, sensitivity, and specificity. Overall, machine learning models show moderate predictive performance for short-term mortality in sepsis, with a combined AUC of 0.82 for the training set (46 studies, 15 models) and 0.79 for the validation set (50 studies, 25 models). Logistic regression is the most widely evaluated model, demonstrating stable performance (validation AUC = 0.81). Integrated methods, including random forest and XGBoost, performed equally well, with AUCs between 0.81 and 0.83 in both groups. Although LightGBM and DL-CMT achieved the highest AUCs in the training and validation sets, respectively, both estimates were based on a single study. Among the complications, the evidence for sepsis-associated encephalopathy (AUC = 0.81, 3 studies) and sepsis-induced coagulopathy (AUC = 0.80, 4 studies) is the most conclusive and best demonstrated. Sepsis-associated acute kidney injury showed moderate and stable performance (validation AUC = 0.79, 4 studies). Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy showed significant attenuation from training to validation (AUC 0.84 vs 0.78, all from a single study), and random forest performed well in training (AUC = 0.98) but was not widely reported. Septic shock reached the highest AUC (0.95), but this was based on a single study. The predictive utility of sepsis-associated delirium is limited (AUC = 0.67, 1 study), and sepsis-induced myocardial injury is moderate (AUC = 0.77, 1 study).For long-term mortality, evidence is extremely lacking. Only SAE (AUC 0.88 during training and 0.86 during validation) and SCRS (combined AUC 0.76) provided single study estimates, ruling out reliable conclusions. In this meta-analysis, machine learning models showed moderate predictive performance for short-term mortality in sepsis. Among complications, SAE and SIC had the strongest evidence and best performance, whereas SAD showed limited utility. Evidence for long-term mortality was extremely scarce. These findings support the potential role of machine learning in early prognostic risk stratification, yet they also highlight the urgent need for rigorous external validation and higher-quality studies, particularly for under-investigated complications.

articles.title: Meta-analysis of the effect of nafamostat mesilate versus no-anticoagulation regimens in adult patients undergoing continuous renal replacement therapy.
articles.abstract: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is a critical treatment for critically ill patients with acute kidney injury. However, effective anticoagulation of the extracorporeal circuit remains a clinical challenge. Nafamostat mesilate (NM), a serine protease inhibitor, possesses localized anticoagulation properties; however, its efficacy and safety in high-bleeding-risk populations have not been systematically evaluated. To compare the efficacy and safety of NM anticoagulation and no-anticoagulation regimens in patients undergoing CRRT. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cohort studies were retrieved from PubMed, Web of Science, MEDLINE, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature, the Cochrane Library, Wanfang Database, Chinese National Knowledge Infrastructure, and the Chinese Biomedical Literature Database. We included studies on adult patients receiving CRRT where the intervention and control groups were treated with NM anticoagulation and no-anticoagulation regimens, respectively. Primary outcomes included filter lifespan, number of filters used, coagulation indicators, bleeding events, and in-hospital mortality. The meta-analysis was conducted using RevMan 5.4 software. Eight studies involving 969 patients were included. The meta-analysis demonstrated that, compared with the control group, the NM group had a significantly prolonged filter lifespan (P = 0.01) and a reduced number of filters used (P < 0.0001). The activated partial thromboplastin time (P = 0.89), prothrombin time (P = 0.88), and international normalized ratio (P = 0.60) showed no significant differences. Both groups demonstrated clinically similar risks of bleeding events (P = 0.53). However, the NM group demonstrated a significantly reduced in-hospital mortality, compared with the control group (P = 0.02). The NM anticoagulation regimen effectively extended the CRRT filter lifespan, reduced resource consumption, and improved patient survival outcomes without increasing the bleeding risk, demonstrating particular value for high-bleeding-risk populations. Future multicenter RCTs are warranted to validate applicability of NM in non-East Asian populations. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261399024, identifier: PROSPERO CRD420251077578.

articles.title: Bloodstream Infections After Cardiac Surgery: Pathogen Distribution, Antimicrobial Resistance, and a Nomogram Prediction Model.
articles.abstract: Postoperative bloodstream infection (BSI) is a severe complication following cardiac surgery, associated with significant mortality. This study aims to characterize pathogen profiles, antimicrobial resistance and independent risk factors for BSI in a Chinese cardiac surgery cohort. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of postoperative BSI in patients who underwent cardiac surgery at the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University from January 2019 to December 2024. Patients who developed postoperative BSI were identified and a 1:1 propensity score matched analysis were performed to adjust for baseline characteristics of patients. Univariate and multivariate analysis were applied to identify independent risk factors for postoperative BSI. R software was used to construct a prediction nomogram, followed by internal validation. During the study, a total of 10,007 patients underwent heart surgery, and 164 pairs of patients were successfully matched using propensity score matching. Gram-negative bacteria were the most common pathogens (64.1%), followed by Fungi (18.2%) and Gram-positive bacteria (17.6%). Among Enterobacterales, 33.8% were carbapenem-resistant, with carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) accounting for 63.6% of K. pneumoniae isolates. Meanwhile, 85.0% (17/20) of A. baumannii isolates were multidrug-resistant A. baumannii (MDRAB). The 90-day mortality rate in the BSI group was 39.0%, significantly higher than that in the non-BSI group (4.9%, P < 0.001). Multivariate logistic regression identified impaired cardiac function (New York Heart Association II-IV, NYHA II-IV) (OR=5.583, 95% CI:2.681-11.627), pulmonary infection (OR =4.053, 95% CI:1.692-9.710), emergency surgery (OR=9.629, 95% CI:2.962-31.301), coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) (OR=2.796, 95% CI:1.096-7.134), continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT Postoperative ICU stay ≥ 14 d) (OR=4.758, 95% CI:1.854-12.211) and postoperative ICU stay ≥14 d (OR=14.616, 95% CI:6.765-31.577) as independent risk factors for postoperative BSI. The nomogram showed good discrimination and calibration after internal validation, with an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.913 and a mean absolute calibration error of 0.026. Postoperative BSI in cardiac surgery patients is associated with high mortality. A nomogram based on impaired cardiac function (NYHA II-IV), pulmonary infection, emergency surgery, CABG, CRRT and postoperative ICU stay ≥14 d displayed high accuracy and consistency in predicting the risk of postoperative BSI. These results facilitate early risk stratification and guide preventive strategies in high-risk cardiac surgical patients.

articles.title: Exploratory associations of composite inflammatory-immune markers with 28-day and 1-year all-cause mortality in patients with sepsis: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Inflammation and immune dysregulation are central to sepsis pathobiology, but the prognostic value of a broad panel of composite inflammatory-immune indices remains incompletely defined. We evaluated the associations of 18 composite inflammatory-immune markers with 28-day and 1-year all-cause mortality in sepsis patients. This single-center retrospective cohort study included 396 adult patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) with sepsis. Eighteen inflammatory-immune indices were calculated from blood tests obtained within the first 24 h after ICU admission. Per-1-standard deviation (SD) multivariable Cox models were used to evaluate each marker's association with 28-day and 1-year all-cause mortality. Subgroup analyses were performed by age (<75 vs. ≥75 years), sex, and sepsis-associated acute kidney injury status, with multiplicative interaction terms. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses were used to assess nonlinearity. Among 396 patients, 174 (43.9%) died within 28 days and 230 (58.1%) died within 1 year. In the primary per-1-SD multivariable Cox analyses, higher C-reactive protein-to-lymphocyte ratio (CLR) and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR) were associated with higher 28-day mortality (CLR: HR 1.313, 95% CI 1.145-1.505; P<0.001; PLR: HR 1.253, 95% CI 1.114-1.410; P<0.001) and 1-year mortality (CLR: HR 1.258, 95% CI 1.104-1.435; P<0.001; PLR: HR 1.193, 95% CI 1.071-1.329; P = 0.001). Higher lymphocyte-to-HDL-C ratio (LHR) was inversely associated with both endpoints (28-day: HR 0.759, 95% CI 0.626-0.920; P = 0.005; 1-year: HR 0.819, 95% CI 0.703-0.954; P = 0.010). Other markers showed endpoint-dependent or otherwise variable associations. Most formal interaction tests did not indicate heterogeneity by age, sex, or sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI) status; nominal interactions were observed for pan-immune-inflammation value with age for both endpoints and with SA-AKI status for 1-year mortality. RCS analyses showed nonlinear associations of log10-transformed PLR and CLR with both endpoints and an approximately linear inverse association of log10-transformed LHR with 28-day mortality. Higher CLR and PLR and lower LHR were independently associated with both short- and long-term mortality in patients with sepsis. However, the findings were derived from a single-center retrospective cohort without independent validation and do not establish clinical prediction utility. Further multicenter studies are required to validate these markers before they can be considered for clinical risk stratification.

articles.title: Longitudinal Multicenter Susceptibility Trends of Ceftazidime/Avibactam and Imipenem/Relebactam and Dose Optimization in Critically Ill Patients with Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales Bloodstream Infections.
articles.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) bloodstream infections cause high mortality in critically ill patients, where altered pharmacokinetics undermine treatment. Comparative data on ceftazidime/avibactam (CZA) and imipenem/relebactam (IMR) remain scarce, especially in patients with augmented renal clearance (ARC) or receiving continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). We analyzed 27,771 bloodstream infection (BSI) Enterobacterales isolates (1543 CRE) from 61 Chinese hospitals (2022-2024) for species distribution and susceptibility to CZA, IMR and other antibiotics. Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) assessed the joint probability of target attainment (PTA) and joint cumulative fraction of response (CFR) of IMR in ARC or CRRT patients. Among BSI CRE, carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) predominated (75.4%), followed by carbapenem-resistant Escherichia coli (CREC) (11.7%) and carbapenem-resistant Enterobacter cloacae (CRECL) (6.7%). Against CRKP, IMR exhibited superior activity to CZA (MIC9 0 2/4 vs >32/4 mg/L). Against CREC and CRECL, both agents showed limited activity, though IMR maintained lower MIC9 0 (8/4 vs >32/4 mg/L). CZA resistance among CRE rose from 17.1% in 2021 to 33.6% in 2023, then fell to 18.8% in 2024; IMR resistance remained lower, declining from 15.5% in 2022 to 13.1% in 2024. In ARC patients, IMR achieved joint PTA >90% but suboptimal CFR against CRKP (83.6%/81.4%) and failed against other CRE. In patients with continuous veno-venous hemofiltration (CVVH), 1.25 g, 1 g, and 0.75 g q6h achieved optimal CFR (>90%) against CRKP; only the two highest doses reached suboptimal levels (>80%) against other CRE. In patients with continuous veno-venous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF), 1.25 g and 1 g q6h achieved optimal CFR against CRKP; against non-CRKP, only 1.25 g q6h reached suboptimal coverage. IMR is a valuable option for CRKP infections, especially in patients on CRRT. But its coverage varies by species, and it falls short in ARC patients and against non-CRKP pathogens. Dosing should be guided by species identification, susceptibility results, renal function, CRRT modality, and local resistance surveillance.

articles.title: Early risk assessment model for sepsis-associated acute kidney injury combining quantitative contrast-enhanced ultrasound and biomarkers: a prospective pilot study.
articles.abstract: Sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI) is associated with high mortality in the intensive care unit (ICU), yet early diagnosis remains challenging due to the diagnostic lag of conventional functional biomarkers. We aimed to develop and validate a Ridge-penalized multimodal model integrating quantitative renal contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) with clinical biomarkers for early SA-AKI risk stratification. Adult septic patients were prospectively enrolled in a 35-bed general ICU. Quantitative renal CEUS parameters-including peak intensity (PI), time to peak (TTP), mean transit time (MTT), and area under the time-intensity curve (TIC-AUC)-and routine clinical variables were collected within 24 h of admission. SA-AKI was defined according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes criteria within 7 days. A multimodal Ridge logistic regression model (Model C) was developed using stratified 5-fold cross-validation (λ1SE rule) and compared with CEUS-only (Model A) and clinical-only (Model B) candidate models. Internal validation was performed using 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Multivariable Firth-penalized regression was used to evaluate independent predictors. Among 63 analyzed patients, 25 (39.7%) developed SA-AKI at a median lead time of ICU day 2 (IQR: day 1-day 3) post-admission; none met AKI criteria at baseline. Quantitative CEUS revealed significant cortical hypoperfusion (PI and TIC-AUC) and prolonged microvascular transit (MTT) in the SA-AKI group (all P < 0.05), while other temporal or slope parameters showed non-significant trends. Model C achieved superior discrimination with a bias-corrected area under the curve (AUC) of 0.852 (95% CI: 0.789-0.932), outperforming Model A (0.818) and Model B (0.740). At the optimal threshold, Model C yielded 80.0% sensitivity and 84.2% specificity. Decision curve analysis confirmed higher standardized net benefit for Model C across threshold probabilities of 0.15-0.60. Adjusted age and baseline serum cystatin C confirmed lower PI (aOR = 0.31), lower TIC-AUC (aOR = 0.31), and prolonged TTP (aOR = 2.1) as independent predictors (all P < 0.05). Quantitative renal CEUS parameters are independent early indicators of SA-AKI. Integrating renal CEUS with clinical biomarkers offers a promising, noninvasive strategy for early SA-AKI risk stratification up to 48 h before clinical diagnosis. https://www.chictr.org.cn/, identifier ChiCTR2300067267.

articles.title: The SMuRF-less paradox in ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction: a retrospective hospital-based two-cohort study.
articles.abstract: Patients with ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) without standard modifiable cardiovascular risk factors (SMuRFs) exhibit paradoxically increased mortality. We aimed to characterize associations with adverse outcomes and identify potential drivers. We included patients with STEMI from a hospital-based cohort in Lanzhou, China (n = 6,892; 2014-2023) and the US Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV; n = 4,480; 2008-2019). SMuRF-less status was defined as the absence of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and smoking, with obesity included in sensitivity analyses. Primary outcomes were 30- and 365-day all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes were major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCEs), 7-day delirium and acute kidney injury (AKI). Associations were estimated using adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and Fine-Gray competing-risk analyses performed for 7-day delirium and AKI. SMuRF-less patients comprised 17.2% (n = 1,182) of the Lanzhou cohort and 13.6% (n = 608) of the MIMIC-IV cohort. SMuRF-less status was associated with higher 30-day mortality in both cohorts (Lanzhou: aHR, 1.37; 95% CI, 1.09-1.71; MIMIC-IV: 1.67, 1.39-2.01). In landmark analyses, SMuRF-less status was not significantly associated with mortality during days 31-365 in Lanzhou (1.68; 0.84-3.37) but was associated with higher mortality in MIMIC-IV (1.34; 1.02-1.77). SMuRF-less status was not significantly associated with MACCEs in Lanzhou. In MIMIC-IV, SMuRF-less status was associated with a higher risk of 7-day delirium (1.40; 1.17-1.67) but was not associated with 7-day AKI (1.05; 0.94-1.17). For both 7-day delirium and AKI, competing-risk analyses yielded consistent findings. In subgroup analyses, excess 30-day mortality was greater among patients in Lanzhou not receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, those not receiving intra-aortic balloon pump, and those with Killip class I-III (P for interaction <0.05). Sensitivity analyses incorporating obesity showed similar associations for 30-day mortality in Lanzhou (1.40; 1.12-1.76) and MIMIC-IV (1.63; 1.33-1.99), as well as for 7-day delirium (1.33; 1.09-1.62). SMuRF-less status was independently associated with increased early mortality in both cohorts and a higher risk of delirium in the MIMIC-IV cohort. This excess risk was not fully explained by measured clinical and physiological markers, suggesting that residual risk may extend beyond conventional modifiable cardiovascular risk factors.

articles.title: Case Report: Raw grass carp gallbladder ingestion and acute liver injury.
articles.abstract: Raw grass carp gallbladder ingestion for folk medicinal purposes may cause severe acute liver injury driven by the hepatotoxin 5α-cyprinol sulfate, yet high-dose human poisoning cases remain infrequently documented. We report a 60-year-old male (60 kg body weight) who developed severe intoxication 22 h after consuming six raw gallbladders from grass carps of approximately 1.5 kg each. Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea occurred within 2 hours of ingestion. Laboratory testing on admission demonstrated extreme hepatocellular injury (ALT 6285 U/L, AST 9321 U/L). Conventional hepatoprotective agents plus pre-hospital haemoperfusion yielded limited biochemical improvement. While admitted to the intensive care unit, the patient received one session of double plasma molecular adsorption system, three sessions of plasma exchange and four sessions of continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT, CVVHDF modality) alongside comprehensive supportive care. Liver function normalized within 14 hospital days; no acute kidney injury was observed. Complete symptomatic recovery was documented at the 4-week follow-up visit, though longer-term outcomes remain unknown given the limited follow-up duration. Toxin-mediated hepatocyte damage is partially supported by pre-clinical cyprinol-sulfate experimental work; many downstream oxidative, mitochondrial, endoplasmic-reticulum and inflammatory molecular pathways remain hypothetical and are largely extrapolated from unrelated liver-injury models, without direct validation in human carp-gallbladder-poisoning tissue specimens. Biochemical improvement was temporally associated with multimodal extracorporeal purification, but causal therapeutic benefit can't be proven from this uncontrolled single case; spontaneous hepatic regeneration may also contribute to recovery. This case highlights substantial hazards associated with folk-health beliefs promoting raw fish-gallbladder consumption, emphasising the need for early clinical recognition of fish-gallbladder poisoning.

articles.title: Oliguria in critically ill patients: physiological or pathological?
articles.abstract: Urine output (UO) is a major clinical sign, available at the bedside for all patients, all over the world. Currently, oliguria is defined according to the KDIGO guidelines as a UO < 0.5 mL/kg/h over 6 h. The threshold was originally selected by expert consensus and has since been associated with adverse outcomes. However, the optimal cut-off remains uncertain and its bedside relevance is regularly challenged by clinicians. Observational studies have suggested that transient or mild oliguria may not consistently be associated with adverse outcomes. Indeed, mild oliguria may capture episodes of physiological water retention rather than pathological kidney injury with structural damage. However, oliguria remains one of the main triggers for fluid or diuretic administration in intensive care units. Improving the understanding of oliguria at the bedside and its influence on clinical decisions requires a thorough knowledge of the physiological mechanisms underlying urine formation and the pathophysiology of oliguria. In this review, we describe the process of urine formation and explain the different physiological and pathological mechanisms leading to oliguria. We further discuss how pathological and physiological oliguria can be differentiated at the bedside, highlighting the role of clinical tools, biomarkers and imaging techniques. Finally, we examine how this distinction may inform clinical decision making, and guide interventions.

articles.title: Trends and Frontiers in nutritional management for ICU patients with kidney dysfunction: a bibliometric and knowledge mapping study.
articles.abstract: Patients with kidney dysfunction in the intensive care unit (ICU) are at high risk of metabolic disturbances and malnutrition, yet the research landscape of nutritional management in this population remains incompletely characterized. This study aimed to map the knowledge structure, research hotspots, and temporal trends in this field. Publications from 2001 to 2025 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and analyzed using VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and bibliometrix. Scopus was used for cross-database comparison, while representative clinical studies retrieved from PubMed were descriptively summarized to provide clinical context for the bibliometric findings. A total of 551 publications were included, with publication output increasing overall from 2001 to 2025. Research activity was concentrated mainly in North America and Europe. Keyword analysis identified major themes related to acute kidney injury, renal replacement therapy, nutritional support, prognosis, and clinical outcomes. Temporal analyses showed that earlier research focused more on acute renal failure, RRT, and nitrogen balance, whereas nutritional risk, protein provision, and clinical outcomes became more prominent in later years. Burst analysis further identified "outcome," "impact," "hospitalized patients," and "malnutrition" as active recent keywords. This study indicates sustained research interest in nutritional management for ICU patients with kidney dysfunction. Research has broadened from RRT-related metabolic concerns to nutritional assessment, protein provision, and clinical outcomes. Protein dose and escalation timing, nutrient replacement during CRRT, and the use of nutritional risk assessment to guide treatment remain important questions for future clinical studies.

articles.title: Ceftazidime-avibactam monotherapy versus combination therapy for carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacterial infections: a secondary meta-analysis of predominantly critically ill cohorts.
articles.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacterial (CR-GNB) infections pose a critical threat to global public health, particularly in critically ill patients where treatment options are severely limited. Ceftazidime-avibactam (CAZ/AVI) is a novel β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combination that has become a cornerstone therapy, yet its optimal use-as monotherapy or in combination with other agents-remains debated. To systematically evaluate the comparative efficacy, renal safety, and risk of on-treatment resistance emergence between CAZ/AVI monotherapy and combination therapy in adult patients with confirmed CR-GNB infections. Because individual-patient data were unavailable, pooled estimates are derived from mixed cohorts in which approximately 82% of participants were ICU-admitted critically ill patients (critically ill is defined as intensive care unit admission or APACHE II score ≥15). This study is a secondary reanalysis of the aggregate dataset compiled by Hsu et al. (2024); no de novo systematic search was performed. Studies comparing CAZ/AVI monotherapy versus any combination regimen for the treatment of CR-GNB infections were eligible. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality. The secondary outcomes included in-hospital, 14-day, and 90-day mortality; clinical cure; microbiological eradication; acute kidney injury (AKI); and on-treatment resistance emergence. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. The heterogeneity was assessed via I2 statistics, and publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger's test. Subgroup analyses were prespecified by pathogen type, infection site, combination regimen, geographic region, and study design. Twenty-five studies (23 retrospective cohorts and two prospective cohorts) enrolling 2,676 patients were included. The pooled 30-day mortality was 31.2% in the combination group and 32.8% in the monotherapy group, with no significant difference (RR = 0.91, 95% CI 0.79-1.04, P = 0.17; I2 = 34%). In-hospital mortality (RR = 1.00, 95% CI 0.78-1.27), 14-day mortality (RR = 1.54, 95% CI 0.26-9.28), and 90-day mortality (RR = 1.18, 95% CI 0.64-2.18) showed no significant between-group differences. Clinical cure rates were comparable (RR = 0.95, 95% CI 0.84-1.08; I2 = 39%). Microbiological eradication did not differ significantly between groups (RR = 1.15, 95% CI 1.00-1.33; P = 0.05; I2 = 31%). AKI incidence did not differ overall (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.69-1.22; I2 = 42%), although a post hoc analysis showed a non-statistically significant trend toward higher nephrotoxicity for polymyxin-containing combination regimens (RR = 1.28, 95% CI 0.94-1.74). On-treatment resistance emergence did not differ significantly between groups (RR = 0.71, 95% CI 0.42-1.21; P = 0.21; I2 = 19%). Subgroup analyses consistently showed no mortality benefit across pathogen types, infection sites, or specific combination agents. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings, and no significant publication bias was detected. This secondary meta-analysis, based on the aggregate dataset compiled by Hsu et al. (2024), suggests that CAZ/AVI combination therapy does not confer a statistically significant survival or clinical cure advantage over monotherapy in patients with CR-GNB infections, although it was associated with a non-significant trend toward higher microbiological eradication and lower on-treatment resistance emergence. Given the predominantly observational nature of the included studies, high-quality randomized controlled trials are urgently warranted to guide clinical decision-making. Until higher-certainty evidence becomes available, these very-low-certainty findings support cautious, individualized decision-making: CAZ/AVI monotherapy may be a reasonable default therapeutic option for many patients, whereas combination therapy could be considered in selected high-risk scenarios, carefully balancing the unproven microbiological signals against increased toxicity and cost.

articles.title: Interpretable machine learning model for predicting major adverse kidney events within 30 days in critically ill patients with acute pancreatitis: development and validation in multicenter cohorts.
articles.abstract: Acute kidney injury is a frequent and serious complication of acute pancreatitis (AP), contributing to increased mortality and healthcare burden. Major adverse kidney events within 30 days (MAKE30) constitute a patient-centered composite endpoint for assessing kidney outcomes. However, effective tools for identifying patients at high risk of MAKE30 are lacking. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an interpretable machine learning model for predicting MAKE30 in critically ill patients with AP. Three clinical datasets were used. MIMIC-IV served as the development cohort, and external validation used eICU-CRD and a retrospective cohort from the Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University (AHSWMU). Feature selection combined least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression, the Boruta algorithm, and multivariable logistic regression. Seven machine learning algorithms were used to develop prediction models. Model performance was assessed in terms of discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) were used to interpret and visualize the final model. A total of 1,574 patients with AP from multiple centers were included. Six predictors were selected for model development: serum creatinine, red cell distribution width, albumin, aspartate aminotransferase, vasopressor use, and total bilirubin. The random forest model demonstrated favorable overall performance, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.863 in the internal validation cohort. Performance was consistent across the two independent external validation cohorts, with AUCs of 0.840 in eICU-CRD and 0.848 in AHSWMU. A web-based clinical risk calculator was developed to facilitate model use in clinical practice. The model developed in this study exhibited favorable performance and robust generalizability in predicting MAKE30 among critically ill patients with AP, providing reliable digital decision support for early risk stratification and individualized intervention strategies.

articles.title: Survival and clinical outcomes of critically ill COVID-19 patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation in Palestine: A multicenter retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Critically ill patients with COVID-19 often require invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), which is associated with increased fatality rates. There is a lack of data on survival and outcomes in resource-limited settings such as Palestine. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the survival rate and clinical outcomes of COVID-19 patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation in Palestinian intensive care units (ICUs) and to explore clinical factors associated with mortality in this critically ill cohort. We conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study of all adult COVID-19 patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation and hospitalized in the intensive care units (ICUs) of three prominent Palestinian hospitals from August 1, 2020, to April 30, 2021. We rigorously extracted comprehensive data on demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, and outcome characteristics from patients' medical records. Of the 150 patients necessitating invasive mechanical ventilation, only 13 (8.7%) survived to hospital discharge. Younger age was associated with survival in univariable analysis (OR = 0.948, p = 0.006). Coronary artery disease was more frequent among non-survivors (p = 0.041), and peak creatinine levels were significantly higher among non-survivors (p = 0.008). In univariable analysis, pressure-control ventilation mode (OR = 4.416, p = 0.022), lower minimum FiO2 (OR = 0.883, p = 0.001), and lower minimum inspiratory pressure (OR = 0.478, p = 0.010) were associated with survival. These results should be interpreted with caution, as they most likely reflect variations in disease severity and underlying lung mechanics rather than a direct effect of the ventilation mode. Remdesivir use was associated with higher odds of survival in univariable analysis (OR = 5.783, p = 0.004). The median duration of invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) was 15 days for survivors compared to 6 days for non-survivors (p < 0.001). Survivors had a longer IMV duration, reflecting a prolonged clinical course rather than a causal effect. The median length of stay in the intensive care unit (ICU) was 27 days for survivors versus 11 days for non-survivors. Acute kidney injury (60.7%) and cardiovascular complications (45.3%) were associated with worse outcomes. Tracheostomy was more frequently observed among survivors in univariable analysis. Morbid obesity was associated with survival in univariable analysis. The survival rate among critically ill COVID-19 patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation in Palestine was very low. Survival was associated with younger age and lower peak creatinine levels, while acute kidney injury and cardiovascular complications were associated with worse outcomes. Given the retrospective design and small number of survivors, these associations should be interpreted as exploratory rather than independent predictors of survival. These findings highlight the challenges of managing critically ill patients during a pandemic in a resource-constrained healthcare system and the importance of strengthening critical care capacity and preparedness for future health emergencies.

articles.title: Early serum chloride trajectory phenotypes and prognostic transportability across two critical care databases in acute brain injury.
articles.abstract: Studies of chloride after acute brain injury have largely relied on static measurements, and the cross-database transportability of dynamic phenotypes remains uncertain. We conducted a retrospective 72-h landmark study of adults with traumatic brain injury, intracerebral hemorrhage, or nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage in MIMIC-IV v3.1 and eICU-CRD v2.0. A four-class quadratic group-based trajectory model (GBTM) was derived without reference to outcomes in MIMIC-IV and transported to eICU-CRD with all parameters fixed. Fine-Gray models, with live discharge treated as a competing event, evaluated post-landmark in-hospital mortality; incident acute kidney injury (AKI) during 72-168 h was exploratory. Fifty database-specific multiply imputed datasets incorporated posterior-probability class draws. We included 1,817 MIMIC-IV patients (382 deaths) and 1,154 eICU-CRD patients (197 deaths). The trajectories were low-stable (C1), mid-stable (C2; reference), high-rising (C3), and very-high rise/plateau (C4). In MIMIC-IV, mortality associations differed across trajectories (global p < 0.001); adjusted subdistribution hazard ratios versus C2 were 1.87 (95% CI 1.18-2.95) for C1, 1.49 (1.11-2.01) for C3, and 2.96 (1.95-4.48) for C4. The corresponding eICU-CRD estimates were 0.77 (0.35-1.70), 0.77 (0.50-1.18), and 1.21 (0.71-2.07), with global p = 0.166. No clear association between trajectory class and incident AKI was observed in either database. Early chloride trajectory phenotypes were identifiable in both databases, whereas their prognostic associations varied between databases. These observational findings support structural phenotype transportability while underscoring the need for external evaluation before prognostic interpretation.

articles.title: A machine learning-based model for predicting 28-day mortality in ICU patients identified through radiotherapy-related records: validation using public databases and a single-center cohort.
articles.abstract: Critically ill patients with documented radiotherapy-related records represent a population in whom early short-term mortality assessment may be clinically relevant. We aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning model for predicting 28-day mortality in patients who remained observable through the first 24 h after ICU admission. We included patients from MIMIC-IV for model training (n=908), the MIMIC-III CareVue subset v1.4 for temporal testing (n=499), and the eICU/local cohorts for external validation (n=118). Eligibility was determined solely by radiotherapy-related diagnosis or procedure records, which were not used as model predictors. Model predictors were derived primarily from information recorded during the first 24 h after ICU admission. Missing data were handled using multiple imputation. LASSO regression was used for feature selection in the training cohort. Seven machine-learning models were compared based on their discrimination, and the selected model was further evaluated using calibration, decision-curve analysis, and SHAP interpretation. A sensitivity analysis excluding sepsis and acute kidney injury was performed. The 28-day mortality rates were 11.56% (105/908), 11.62% (58/499), and 12.71% (15/118) in the training, temporal testing, and external validation cohorts, respectively. LASSO selected chloride, SOFA score, RDW, respiratory rate, sepsis, and acute kidney injury. In the temporal testing cohort, random forest achieved the highest observed AUC (0.868; 95% CI, 0.815-0.917) and showed greater discrimination than SOFA-based benchmarks, six-variable logistic regression, and ANN in paired comparisons. In the external validation cohort, random forest showed an AUC of 0.785 (95% CI, 0.650-0.909). After exclusion of sepsis and acute kidney injury, the observed AUC decreased to 0.843 in temporal testing and 0.713 in external validation; the paired confidence intervals for both AUC differences included zero. A six-variable random forest model showed useful discrimination for 28-day mortality among ICU patients identified through radiotherapy-related records and maintained moderate discrimination in external validation. SHAP analysis enhanced model interpretability by illustrating the contribution of routinely available general ICU variables. Radiotherapy-related records served solely to define the study population; this study did not evaluate radiotherapy exposure or radiotherapy-specific mechanisms. These findings support further evaluation of the model for prognostic risk stratification in larger prospective cohorts.

articles.title: Prediction of acute kidney injury in ICU patients with cirrhosis and sepsis: a multicenter machine learning study.
articles.abstract: To develop and validate a machine learning model based on routinely available clinical variables for early risk stratification of acute kidney injury in intensive care unit (ICU) patients with cirrhosis and sepsis. In this retrospective multicenter cohort study, data were derived from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV v3.1) database and an independent ICU cohort from the Second Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University. Adult patients with cirrhosis who met Sepsis-3 criteria at ICU admission were included. Clinical variables obtained at the early stage of ICU admission were used as candidate predictors. Feature selection was performed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression combined with the Boruta algorithm. Seven machine learning algorithms, including random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), artificial neural network (ANN), light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM), support vector machine (SVM), decision tree, and logistic regression (LR), were developed and compared. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration, and decision curve analysis. Model interpretability was assessed using Shapley Additive Explanations. A total of 2,491 ICU patients with cirrhosis and sepsis were included, among whom 61% developed AKI. Fourteen variables were selected for model construction, including ascites, vasopressors, SOFA, SAPS II, weight, hemoglobin, platelet count, WBC, albumin, sodium, creatinine, prothrombin time, total bilirubin, respiratory rate. In the internal validation cohort, RF and XGBoost demonstrated comparable discrimination, both achieving an AUC of 0.839, while the RF model showed good calibration. In the external validation cohort, the RF model achieved the highest AUC (0.755; 95% CI, 0.686-0.820) among the evaluated models and provided a favorable clinical net benefit across a clinically relevant range of threshold probabilities. SHAP analysis indicated that creatinine, disease severity scores, coagulation parameters, and inflammatory markers were the most influential predictors, with effect directions consistent with known hepatorenal pathophysiology. A machine learning-based model using routinely available clinical variables can provide accurate and interpretable early prediction of AKI in ICU patients with cirrhosis and sepsis. This model may facilitate timely risk stratification and support clinical decision-making. Further prospective studies are warranted to validate its clinical utility and real-world implementation.

articles.title: SGLT2 inhibitors in sepsis and critical illness: a precision-medicine perspective on mechanisms, evidence, and future trial design.
articles.abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have transformed chronic cardiorenal care, but their role in sepsis and critical illness remains uncertain. This Review evaluates whether the anti-inflammatory, endothelial-stabilizing, metabolic, mitochondrial, and renal effects of SGLT2 inhibition can be translated into clinically meaningful benefit across the sepsis continuum. The mechanistic rationale is strong because several proposed drug effects map closely to recognized sepsis pathways, including endothelial barrier failure, immunometabolic dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, regulated cell death, septic cardiomyopathy, and sepsis-associated acute kidney injury. However, clinical evidence remains limited and heterogeneous. Observational prior-use studies suggest favorable associations but are vulnerable to confounding, while the first large randomized trial in acute critical illness, DEFENDER, found no overall clinical benefit of dapagliflozin in a broad ICU population. Exploratory analyses have nevertheless generated signals related to diuresis, fluid balance, and loop-diuretic usage, supporting a more targeted research strategy. Current evidence does not support routine initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors during acute sepsis or septic shock outside clinical trials, particularly during active shock, fasting, unstable renal perfusion, or metabolic stress. Future studies should avoid all-comer sepsis designs and instead focus on phenotype-enriched populations, safer timing windows such as stabilization or de-resuscitation, and post-ICU cardiorenal recovery. Mechanism-aligned endpoints, structured safety monitoring, biomarker-informed enrichment, and adaptive translational trial designs will be essential to determine whether SGLT2 inhibition can move from biologic plausibility to clinical utility in sepsis and critical illness.

articles.title: Kidney effects of inhaled nitric oxide in critically ill patients: from pathophysiological considerations to clinical implications.
articles.abstract: Inhaled nitric oxide is widely used as a selective pulmonary vasodilator in critical care, yet its renal effects remain controversial. While existing reviews mostly focus on indications for inhaled nitric oxide and its impact on outcomes, limited data exist on its renal effects, since it was thought to act only locally in the lungs. This review examine the clinical evidence regarding kidney outcomes associated with inhaled nitric oxide across major indications and provide an integrated mechanistic analysis of nitric oxide signaling in renal physiology and pathophysiology. Nitric oxide is produced by nitric oxide synthases using L-arginine as a substrate. It acts as a smooth muscle relaxation factor and ultimately causes vasodilation through its effect on cyclic guanosine monophosphate. Nitric oxide plays a pivotal role in renal hemodynamic regulation, glomerular filtration, tubular function, and microcirculatory homeostasis. The net renal effect of inhaled nitric oxide likely reflects the balance between improved nitric oxide signaling and oxidative stress generation. Available clinical data suggest that the renal impact of inhaled nitric oxide is context-dependent. In acute respiratory distress syndrome, higher-level evidence indicates a potential increase in acute kidney injury, possibly related to oxidative and nitrosative stress. Conversely, in cardiac bypass surgery, inhaled nitric oxide may confer nephroprotection by restoring nitric oxide bioavailability during hemolysis and free hemoglobin-mediated nitric oxide scavenging. In other conditions, including organ transplantation, pulmonary hypertension, sepsis, and hemolytic disorders, evidence remains limited or inconclusive. Overall, current evidence does not support a uniform renal effect of inhaled nitric oxide, indicating the need for prospective studies with predefined renal endpoints to clarify its clinical relevance.

articles.title: Incidence and mortality of invasive fungal infections among patients admitted in intensive care units in India: findings from a multicentric registry-based study (2023-25).
articles.journal: The Lancet regional health. Southeast Asia
articles.abstract: Invasive fungal infections (IFIs) are challenging to treat in critical care, particularly among patients treated in Intensive care units (ICUs). The existing evidence on IFIs from India remains fragmented. This study characterises IFI incidence, risk factors, resistance pattern, treatment and outcome among patients admitted to ICUs. This multicentre observational study leveraged registry data on IFIs among patients admitted to 63 ICUs in eight Advanced Mycology Diagnostic and Research centres in India between January 2023 and November 2025. Patients with proven and probable IFI according to European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer/Mycoses Study Group Education and Research Consortium (EORTC/MSGERC) 2020 and the modified Aspergillus intensive care unit (AspICU) 2020 criteria were included. IFI incidence to hospital admission, all-cause in-hospital mortality, pathogen distribution and antifungal susceptibility were recorded. Mortality-associated factors were estimated using multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards analysis. Among 178,417 ICU admissions, 2500 IFI patients were identified with an incidence of 14/1000 admissions (95% CI 13.5-14.6) and all-cause mortality of 53.6% (95% CI 51.7-55.6%).
