Invasive candidiasis was the most frequently reported (57.1%), followed by invasive aspergillosis (37%), mucormycosis (3.4%), trichosporonosis (1.8%), pneumocystis pneumonia (1.1%), and cryptococcosis (1.2%). Median age of the patients was 45 years (IQR: 26-60), with 61.9% males and 38.1% females. Among candidiasis, Candida tropicalis predominated (35.6%), while Candida auris exhibited high fluconazole resistance (61.7%) and elevated amphotericin B minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) (40.7%). Aspergillus fumigatus (50.8%) and Aspergillus flavus (38.7%) predominated among culture-positive aspergillosis, with generally low MICs. Exploratory multivariable analyses showed that sepsis, chronic liver disease, immunosuppression, corticosteroid exposure, and total parenteral nutrition were associated with higher mortality in invasive candidiasis, whereas mechanical ventilation, corticosteroid exposure, and immunosuppression were associated with higher mortality in invasive aspergillosis. The study findings highlight a high IFI burden and mortality among patients admitted in ICUs of India, with mortality exceeding 50%, underscoring the need for continuous surveillance, rapid diagnostics, infection control and antifungal stewardship. This study was funded by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Delhi (Grant ID: 157401).

articles.title: Deimplementation of Tradition-Based Enteral Feeding Practices to Improve Clinical Outcomes.
articles.journal: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
articles.abstract: Enteral feeding is common in acute and critical care but there are many elements to this practice that are steeped in confusion and lack evidence. This article will focus on verification of feeding tube (FT) placement methods and timing, medication administration by FTs, unnecessary holding or stopping of enteral formula, gastric residual volumes, and volume-based feeding. Supporting evidence for these practices will be reviewed and recommendations made for evidence-based alternatives and possible deimplementation.

articles.title: Effectiveness of three nasoenteral tube securement technologies in critically ill adults: A pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover trial.
articles.journal: International journal of nursing studies advances
articles.abstract: Nasoenteral tube stability is essential for the success of enteral nutritional therapy in critically ill patients. However, comparative evidence regarding the effectiveness and safety of available securement technologies remains limited, particularly concerning the balance between tube stability and preservation of skin and mucosal integrity. To compare the effectiveness and safety of three nasoenteral tube securement technologies in critically ill patients. A pragmatic, cluster-randomized, crossover, controlled, superiority, triple-blind clinical trial. The study was conducted in intensive care units at three large Brazilian hospitals. A total of 217 patients were included and received one of three securement strategies according to their intensive care unit-period allocation: manufactured securement using acrylate adhesive tape (control; n=75), a dedicated device with acrylate adhesive (n=72), or a dedicated hydrocolloid-based device (n=70). The participants were prospectively monitored during nasoenteral tube use. Outcomes included tube displacement and inadvertent removal, securement durability, device-related skin and mucosal injuries, and interruption of enteral nutritional therapy. Comparisons between groups were performed using generalized linear mixed models and survival analysis. No statistically significant differences were observed among the groups regarding nasoenteral tube displacement or inadvertent removal. The hydrocolloid group showed a higher risk of securement failure compared to the control group (hazard ratio=1.93; 95% confidence interval: 1.28-2.90; p=0.002) but a lower incidence of medical adhesive-related skin injury (7.1%) than the control group (34.7%) and the acrylate group (38.9%). The lower incidence of medical adhesive-related skin injury in the hydrocolloid group compared with the control group corresponded to an absolute risk reduction of 28% and a number needed to treat of 3.6. There were no significant differences among the groups regarding mucosal membrane injury or the duration of enteral nutrition therapy interruption. Dedicated securement technologies did not demonstrate superiority over improvised securement methods in preventing displacement or inadvertent removal of the enteral feeding tube. However, the hydrocolloid-based device reduced the medical adhesive-related skin injury incidence, despite showing lower securement durability. These findings highlight a trade-off between mechanical stability and the preservation of skin integrity, reinforcing that the choice of securement technology should be individualized, taking into account the patient's risk profile and the care setting. The trial was registered in the Brazilian Registry of Clinical Trials (ReBEC; RBR-10hr8nzd).

articles.title: Hemoglobin glycation index and mortality in critically ill atrial fibrillation patients: A retrospective cohort study from the MIMIC‑IV database.
articles.abstract: The hemoglobin glycation index (HGI), a marker of individual glycation propensity, has demonstrated prognostic value in cardiometabolic diseases. Its association with outcomes in critically ill patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) remains poorly characterized, particularly over the longer term. In this retrospective cohort study, we analyzed data from 2458 ICU patients with AF in the MIMIC-IV database. HGI was calculated as the difference between measured glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) and the value predicted from fasting plasma glucose. The primary endpoints were 30-day and 365-day all-cause mortality. We employed Kaplan-Meier analysis, Cox proportional hazards models, restricted mean survival time (RMST), and restricted cubic splines. Subgroup analyses were exploratory. Prespecified sensitivity analyses addressed bias via exclusion of continuous enteral/parenteral nutrition or dextrose fluids, restriction of HbA1c to within 7 days, exclusion of recent transfusion or extreme hemoglobin, and a lipid complete-case analysis. The analysis revealed a reverse J-shaped relationship between HGI and all-cause mortality. Patients in the lowest HGI quartile (Q1) faced the highest risk of death across all time points. RMST was significantly shorter in Q1 versus Q2. Adjusted spline curves confirmed this nonlinear association, with inflection points at HGI values of -0.54 (30-day) and -0.65 (365-day). In the fully adjusted model, the Q2 versus Q1 hazard ratio (HR) was 0.704 (95% CI: 0.530-0.933) for 30-day and 0.714 (0.552-0.924) for 365-day mortality. Directionally consistent estimates were observed across all sensitivity analyses, for example, excluding enteral/parenteral nutrition [0.641 (0.464-0.885)], restricting HbA1c to 7 days [0.611 (0.408-0.913)], excluding transfusion/extreme hemoglobin [0.713 (0.527-0.964)], and lipid complete-case [0.647 (0.455-0.920)]. Subgroup analyses did not identify significant effect modification after FDR correction; however, these analyses were underpowered. In this MIMIC-IV cohort of critically ill AF patients, HGI exhibits a reverse J-shaped association with mortality, indicating that low HGI, and to a lesser extent high HGI, may identify higher-risk phenotypes. These findings require external validation and should not be interpreted causally. Integrating HGI into initial metabolic profiling could enhance risk stratification and inform personalized monitoring strategies in the ICU, pending prospective confirmation.

articles.title: Association between early increased energy and protein delivery and 60-day in-hospital mortality relative to nutrition risk after cardiac surgery: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.journal: JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition
articles.abstract: It is unclear whether nutrition risk modifies the associations of early increased energy and protein delivery with mortality in cardiac surgery patients. This retrospective cohort study used data from the International Nutrition Survey. The analysis included critically ill adults who underwent major cardiac surgery and did not permanently progress to exclusive oral feeding during the first 4 full days in the intensive care unit. Nutrition delivery and adequacy were averaged over these 4 days. Logistic regression was used to evaluate the mNUTRIC score as a modifier of the associations between early nutrition and 60-day in-hospital mortality. A total of 292 patients were included; 57 (19.5%) died in hospital within 60 days. Decedents received significantly more nutrition compared to 60-day hospital survivors. After multivariable adjustment, early increases in energy and protein delivery were not significantly associated with 60-day in-hospital mortality. The mNUTRIC score did not significantly modify the association between nutrition exposure and mortality. Patients with mNUTRIC scores of 6-9 had higher 60-day in-hospital mortality than those with scores of 0-5 (24% versus 13%; odds ratio 2.2; 95% CI: 1.1-4.2; P = 0.017). For each 1-point increase in the mNUTRIC score, the odds of 60-day in-hospital mortality were multiplied by 1.3 (95% CI: 1.1-1.6, P = 0.008). In cardiac surgery patients who continued to need enteral and parenteral nutrition, the mNUTRIC score did not identify patients who benefited from early increases in energy and protein delivery.

articles.abstract: Few areas of clinical nutrition have been as humbled, or as energized, by recent evidence as the care of the critically ill [...].

articles.title: Comparison of formula-derived nasogastric tube insertion lengths in neurosurgical critically ill adults: A retrospective radiographic study.
articles.abstract: Estimating nasogastric tube insertion depth is a routine bedside step, but insufficient insertion may leave the tip or side holes short of the stomach, whereas excessive insertion may result in coiling or overly deep placement. Reported accuracy of body-surface measurement methods varies substantially, partly because previous studies have used different placement thresholds, anatomical reference points, tube designs and outcome definitions, making comparisons difficult. To compare five formula-derived nasogastric tube insertion lengths in neurosurgical critically ill adults using continuous radiographic quantification of intragastric tube length and a hierarchical outcome approach. Single-centre retrospective study. The study was conducted in the neurosurgical intensive care unit and affiliated wards of a tertiary teaching hospital in Shenyang, China. Adults who underwent nasogastric tube placement with post-insertion chest radiography between November 2016 and October 2024 were screened, and 108 patients were included. Software-assisted curved-path reconstruction was applied to post-insertion radiographs to quantify intragastric tube length distal to a radiographic cardia surrogate landmark. Five formula-derived insertion lengths were retrospectively calculated from recorded body-surface measurements: nose-earlobe-xiphoid, forehead-xiphoid, forehead-umbilicus, nose-earlobe-xiphoid plus 10 cm, and corrected nose-earlobe-xiphoid. Outcomes were gastric entry, minimum intragastric depth, and target-zone placement. A tube-specific sensitivity analysis assessed complete proximal side-hole clearance using a 3.8 cm threshold. The mean calculated nose-to-cardia length was 46.01 ± 4.48 cm. No formula-derived insertion length met all three placement criteria in every patient in this cohort. Target-zone placement occurred in 59/108 patients (54.6%, 95% confidence interval 45.2%-63.7%) with nose-earlobe-xiphoid and 56/108 patients (51.9%, 95% confidence interval 42.5%-61.0%) with forehead-xiphoid, whereas under-insertion occurred in 17.6% (95% confidence interval 11.6%-25.8%) and 38.0% (95% confidence interval 29.4%-47.4%) of cases respectively. Forehead-umbilicus and nose-earlobe-xiphoid plus 10 cm showed no under-insertion but over-insertion in 95.4% (95% confidence interval 89.6%-98.0%) and 90.7% (95% confidence interval 83.8%-94.9%) of cases, respectively. Corrected nose-earlobe-xiphoid showed an intermediate pattern. The tube-specific 3.8 cm side-hole clearance threshold produced lower clearance rates than the 3 cm minimum-depth criterion, particularly for forehead-xiphoid and nose-earlobe-xiphoid. The performance of formula-derived insertion lengths depended on the outcome criterion applied. The five formula-derived insertion lengths showed different trade-offs between under-insertion and over-insertion. Software-assisted continuous radiographic quantification of formula-derived intragastric tube length, together with reporting of tube side-hole configuration, may provide a more informative basis for evaluating nasogastric tube insertion depth. Not registered.

articles.title: High versus standard-protein provision and muscle loss in critically ill patients assessed by muscle ultrasound: A prospective ancillary study of a randomised controlled trial.
articles.abstract: Rapid skeletal muscle loss, a hallmark of critical illness, has been linked to delayed recovery, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and reduced quality of life. It has been suggested that increased enteral protein delivery may attenuate this muscle loss in critically ill patients. In this study, we examined the effect of high versus standard enteral protein provision on changes in M. rectus femoris cross-sectional area (RFCSA) in mechanically ventilated critically ill patients. We performed a prospective, pre-planned, single-centre ancillary study at Maastricht University Medical Centre, embedded within the quadruple-blinded randomised PRECISe trial, which evaluated the effect of standard (1.3 g/kg/day) versus high (2.0 g/kg/day) protein provision on functional recovery in critically ill patients. We included all patients who had baseline (<2 days after randomisation) and at least one follow-up ultrasound measurement of the M. rectus femoris. The primary outcome for this study was the change in RFCSA, measured during ICU stay and up to 30 days after randomisation. A total of 141 participants were included in this analysis (standard-protein group, n=75; high-protein group, n=66). RFCSA decreased over time in both groups, with a mean daily decrease of 0.077 ± 0.065 cm2 (95% CI, -0.10 to -0.05; p < 0.01) and -0.048 ± 0.047 cm2 (95% CI, -0.07 to -0.02; p < 0.01) in patients allocated to the standard- and high-protein groups, respectively. However, the overall change in RFCSA did not differ between groups (mean difference -0.098 cm2; 95% CI -0.24 to 0.044; p = 0.17). In mechanically ventilated critically ill patients, high enteral protein provision compared with standard enteral protein provision did not attenuate skeletal muscle loss, as assessed by ultrasound-derived RFCSA. The PRECISe trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04633421; https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04633421) on 23 October 2020.

articles.title: Efficacy Heterogeneity of Hemoperfusion Plus Continuous Venovenous Hemofiltration for Hypertriglyceridemia-Induced Acute Pancreatitis Stratified by Severity of Inflammatory Response.
articles.journal: Therapeutic apheresis and dialysis : official peer-reviewed journal of the International Society for Apheresis, the Japanese Society for Apheresis, the Japanese Society for Dialysis Therapy
articles.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the heterogeneity in the efficacy of hemoperfusion (HP) plus continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH) versus CVVH alone in reducing the incidence of severe acute pancreatitis (SAP) among patients with hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis (HTG-AP), stratified by the inflammatory marker C-reactive protein (CRP). In addition, we assessed secondary outcomes encompassing laboratory response, disease severity and organ function, healthcare resource utilization, and treatment-related indicators, so as to delineate the broader efficacy profile of the combination therapy and its relationship with the primary endpoint. Furthermore, we sought to identify a CRP-based therapeutic window for the combination therapy. This single-center retrospective study included 204 patients who were assigned to the HP + CVVH group (n = 103) or the CVVH group (n = 101). Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess the overall difference in efficacy between the two groups. Restricted cubic splines (RCS) were employed to analyze the nonlinear relationship between treatment efficacy and CRP levels and to identify a CRP-based therapeutic window. Secondary outcomes were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression for categorical variables and generalized linear models for quantitative variables. After multivariable adjustment, the incidence of SAP did not differ significantly between the HP + CVVH and CVVH groups (p > 0.05). RCS analysis revealed a significant interaction between treatment group and CRP levels. The conditional odds ratio for SAP (HP + CVVH vs. CVVH) was significantly below 1 only within a specific CRP range: 194.96-296.91 mg/L in the primary analysis and 200.77-285.81 mg/L after propensity score adjustment (p < 0.05). Regarding secondary outcomes, HP + CVVH was associated with significantly lower CRP, procalcitonin, and triglyceride levels on day 3, more SIRS-free days within 14 days, lower peak intra-abdominal pressure, shorter ICU length of stay, fewer CVVH sessions, earlier initiation of enteral nutrition, and higher blood purification-related costs (all p < 0.05). No significant differences were observed in organ failure-free days, incidence of pancreatic necrosis, hospital length of stay, total hospitalization cost, total morphine equivalent dose, carbapenem use, or duration of mechanical ventilation (all p > 0.05). HP + CVVH showed no overall superiority to CVVH alone in preventing SAP. Nevertheless, secondary outcome analyses demonstrated improved inflammatory control, faster resolution of systemic inflammatory response, reduced intra-abdominal pressure, and better recovery in several resource-related and treatment-related indicators, indicating measurable biological and clinical process benefits. These benefits, however, did not translate into a uniform reduction in SAP. The effect of HP + CVVH on the hard endpoint was conditional, nonlinear, and dependent on baseline inflammatory burden, with significant benefit confined to a specific CRP therapeutic window. Therefore, improvements in secondary endpoints should not be equated with hard-endpoint benefit, and the decision to initiate HP + CVVH should be individualized according to the intensity of the inflammatory response.

articles.title: The efficacy and safety of micronutrient complementation in adults during the acute phase of critical illness: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.journal: The American journal of the medical sciences
articles.abstract: Critically ill patients often experience metabolic imbalances and potentially low micronutrient blood levels that worsen oxidative stress and impair immune function. Despite guideline recommendations, micronutrient complementation is inconsistently applied due to accessibility issues and the lack of validated assessment tools during acute critical illness. This retrospective cohort study evaluated the impact of early intravenous micronutrient complementation on clinical outcomes in ICU patients using real-world electronic medical record data. Adult ICU patients at National Taiwan University Hsinchu Branch from July 2024 to November 2025 who received parenteral nutrition (PN) for at least 24 hours were included. Patients were divided into a treatment group receiving micronutrients within 72 hours of ICU admission and a control group without complementation. Primary outcomes included in-hospital mortality and infectious complications after day 6 of PN; secondary outcomes included ICU/hospital length of stay, inflammatory and metabolic biomarkers, organ support needs, and refeeding syndrome incidence. Among 462 patients analyzed, 213 received early micronutrient therapy. Baseline characteristics such as age (control 65.3±16.6 vs treatment 67.7±13.8 years), BMI (control 28.70±8.95 vs treatment 23.74±4.91 kg/m2), admission categories (control MICU 10.2%, SICU 43.7% vs treatment MICU 9.3%, SICU 36.8%), APACHE II score (control 16.8±8.5 vs treatment 17.3±8.1), and TISS score (control 20.5±7.5 vs treatment 19.6±6.2) were largely comparable. Thetreatment group significantly reduced infectious complications, with logistic regression confirming protective effects (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.20-0.49, p<0.001). Secondary outcomes showed no differences in LOS, vasopressor use, oxygen therapy, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) requirement, PN duration, or refeeding syndrome. The treatment group exhibited delayed enteral nutrition (EN) initiation (control 8.9 ± 8.9 days vs treatment 11.0 ± 10.7 days; p=0.02) but demonstrated significant improvements in inflammatory and metabolic parameters. The linear regression model were performed and demonstrated significantly reductions in C-reactive protein (CRP)(B = -10.91 mg/dL, 95% CI -13.16 to -8.65, p<0.001), serum lactate levels (B = -1.49 mmol/L, 95% CI -2.58 to -0.40, p=0.007), and time to lactate normalization (B = -0.90 days, 95% CI -1.64 to -0.16, p=0.017). In subgroup analysis, a total of 213 patients were included, of whom 138 received standard micronutrient complementation, and 75 received micronutrients with additional zinc complementation, which demonstrated further benefits. For instance, the group receiving additional Zn reduced infectious complications (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.21-0.85, p=0.02), shorter ICU LOD (B = -3.97 days, 95% CI-7.64 to -0.30, p=0.03), and faster lactate clearance (B = -1.17 days, 95% CI -1.87 to -0.47, p=0.09). These results support early comprehensive micronutrient complementation to enhance immune and metabolic recovery in critically ill patients and highlight the need for prospective biomarker-guided studies.

articles.title: Nutritional support in immunosuppressed critically ill patients.
articles.abstract: Immunosuppressed patients now make up a growing share of intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, largely as a result of advances in cancer treatment, organ transplantation, and immunomodulatory therapies. While their short-term ICU mortality may be similar to that of immunocompetent patients when illness severity is taken into account, these individuals often face longer ICU stays, more complications, and poorer long-term outcomes. In this context, artificial nutrition plays a central role in ICU management and represents a potentially modifiable intervention. Beyond meeting energy requirements, nutritional support may help sustain immune function, preserve gut integrity, and reduce the risk of infectious complications. Whenever possible, enteral nutrition should be favored, as it supports the intestinal barrier and gut-associated lymphoid tissue, even when delivered at low, trophic doses. Parenteral nutrition remains indispensable in the presence of intestinal failure but should be used cautiously, given its association with complications such as catheter-related bloodstream infections. Critical illness profoundly alters gut-immune interactions, promoting dysbiosis, increased intestinal permeability, and immune dysfunction - processes that may be further amplified by immunosuppressive therapies. This has fueled interest in immunonutrition strategies, including arginine, ω-3 fatty acids, glutamine, and nucleotides. However, evidence in immunosuppressed critically ill patients remains limited and inconsistent, preventing firm recommendations. Looking ahead, the integration of body composition assessment, immune-metabolic phenotyping, multi-omics technologies, and artificial intelligence may enable more personalized nutritional strategies. Future studies should focus on phenotype-specific randomized trials to better define the optimal route, composition, timing, and dosing of nutritional support in this complex population.

articles.title: Outcomes of SGLT2-inhibitor-induced euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis in a North Queensland intensive care unit: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Evidence on sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i)-associated euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis (EuDKA) in the intensive care unit (ICU) and its comparison with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is limited. This study aims to describe ICU characteristics, management and outcomes of SGLT2i-associated EuDKA, identify predictors of poorer outcomes and compare findings with T1DM-DKA. Single-centre retrospective cohort (2017-2023) of adults admitted to a Northern Queensland ICU. EuDKA was defined by plasma glucose <13.9 mmol/L plus ⩾1 of acidaemia, low bicarbonate, raised anion gap or ketonaemia, in patients with T2DM on SGLT2i. A comparator cohort comprised ICU admissions with T1DM-DKA. Demographics, precipitants, biochemistry, insulin therapy, and outcomes were extracted and analysed with non-parametric tests. Fourteen EuDKA and 31 T1DM-DKA admissions were included. EuDKA patients were older with more frequent comorbidities; First Nations Australians were over-represented. Presenting features were heterogeneous, with overlapping precipitants (commonly caloric restriction/fasting or intercurrent illness). Compared with T1DM-DKA, EuDKA had milder biochemical derangement and lower 24-h insulin dose but required longer insulin therapy and longer ICU length of stay; time to acidosis resolution was similar. In exploratory analyses, end-organ complications in type 2 diabetes were associated with longer ICU stay, while obesity and pre-admission insulin therapy were associated with prolonged acidosis duration. ICU-admitted SGLT2i-associated EuDKA differs clinically and in management from classical T1DM-DKA. Findings highlight diagnostic challenges, potential high-risk subgroups, and the need for prospective, multicentre studies to inform risk-based management in critical care.

articles.title: Clinical Phenotypes, Machine-Learning Risk Stratification and Treatment Outcomes of Constipation in Stroke Patients Receiving Enteral Nutrition: A Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract: Stroke-related complications and frequent feeding interruptions often compromise nutritional intake, making enteral nutrition (EN) a cornerstone therapy to improve nutritional status and support recovery. Nevertheless, constipation is highly prevalent and clinically consequential among stroke patients receiving EN, particularly in critically ill populations, where enteral nutrition-associated constipation can impede rehabilitation, increase complications and prolong intensive care unit (ICU) stay. This study aimed to explore potentially important determinants of enteral nutrition-associated constipation (ENAC) in patients with stroke using artificial intelligence approaches, characterise relevant clinical subgroups, compare internally validated machine-learning models and examine how the temporal availability of candidate predictors may influence model performance. Clinical data from patients admitted to a neurological intensive care unit between December 2019 and December 2023 were retrospectively analysed. K-means clustering was used to identify clinical subgroups. Six algorithms-logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting tree, XGBoost, LightGBM and Table PFN-3-were compared under temporally restricted and expanded retrospective feature frameworks using five repeats of nested five-fold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using ROC-AUC, average precision, Brier score, calibration and decision-curve analysis. Treatment outcomes were summarised descriptively. Among 362 patients, 233 (64.4%) had documented constipation. Table PFN-3 achieved the highest discrimination in both frameworks. The temporally restricted model yielded a ROC-AUC of 0.629 (95% CI 0.567-0.689), whereas the expanded retrospective model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.771 (95% CI 0.715-0.820), average precision of 0.857, Brier score of 0.177 and calibration slope of 0.965. The ROC-AUC increased by 0.142 (95% CI 0.090-0.201) after full-hospitalisation information was included. K-means clustering retained three subgroups (K = 3; silhouette coefficient = 0.108), with constipation frequencies of 67.35%, 56.98% and 88.89% in Clusters 0, 1 and 2, respectively. Among evaluable patients, observed relief was 80.3% with glycerin enema, 60.0% with lactulose, 72.7% with combination treatment and 65.7% with neither treatment; these treatment comparisons were descriptive. Table PFN-3 achieved the strongest internally validated performance, with the expanded retrospective framework combining good discrimination, strong precision-recall performance and close calibration. The 0.142 increase in ROC-AUC after completed hospital-course variables were incorporated quantifies the substantial discriminative information that emerges as hospitalisation evolves. Together with the distinct clinical phenotypes and descriptive treatment findings, these results establish a clinically relevant framework for trajectory-aware bowel monitoring and provide a clear rationale for developing dynamic, time-updated prediction models. By integrating machine-learning benchmarking, clinical phenotyping and observed treatment outcomes, this study identifies prolonged, treatment-intensive hospital trajectories as a particularly high-burden constipation phenotype and demonstrates that classification performance changes materially as hospital-course information accumulates. These findings support structured reassessment of bowel risk during neurological intensive care rather than reliance on a single static evaluation and provide a practical rationale for future dynamic monitoring tools.

articles.title: Application of Combined Gastric Tube Tip Manometry and Auscultation for Nasogastric Tube Positioning in Neurocritical Care Patients With Artificial Airways: A Prospective Diagnostic Pilot Study.
articles.abstract: Nasogastric tube placement is central to enteral nutrition support in neurocritical care patients. However, tube malposition, particularly accidental placement into the airway, can lead to fatal complications. To assess the accuracy of a combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation approach for confirming nasogastric tube placement in neurocritical care patients with artificial airways. This prospective study enrolled patients who underwent nasogastric tube insertion in the neurocritical care unit of a tertiary hospital in China between January 2025 and May 2025. Using chest X-ray as the reference standard, we compared the sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), positive likelihood ratio (PLR) and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) for gastric tube tip manometry alone, auscultation alone and their combination. In total, 120 patients participated. X-ray confirmed correct nasogastric tube positioning in 119 patients and malposition in 1 patient. For gastric tube tip manometry alone, the sensitivity was 97.48%, with a specificity of 0%, a positive predictive value (PPV) of 99.15% and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 0%. Auscultation alone yielded a sensitivity of 90.76%, a specificity of 100%, a PPV of 100% and an NPV of 8.33%. The combined manometry-plus-auscultation approach had a sensitivity of 88.24%, a specificity of 100%, a PPV of 100% and an NPV of 6.67%. The combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation method might serve as an adjunctive bedside strategy for confirming nasogastric tube placement in neurocritical care patients with artificial airways. However, only one malpositioned tube was observed in this study; the specificity and NPV should be interpreted with caution. When gastric aspirate cannot be obtained or immediate chest radiography is impractical, combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation provide a feasible, radiation-free bedside pathway for confirming nasogastric tube position; equivocal or negative bedside findings should still be verified radiographically before feeding. The study was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2300078001).

articles.title: Guided Tube Placement and Bridle Securement and Their Association With Complications, Delay and Retention: A Single-Centre Retrospective Cohort Analysis.
articles.abstract: Most intensive care unit (ICU), dysphagic or unconscious patients require feeding tube placement. Currently, standard placement is done 'blind' (unguided), secured by adhesive tape and tube position confirmed post-procedure by pH or X-ray checks. However, this carries an in-procedure risk of pneumothorax (0.43%) and contamination pneumonia (0.20%), made worse by tube loss requiring replacement. Immediate guidance-confirmed tube placement and bridle securement are associated with reduced risk and delay to treatment. To assess the association between guided tube placement and bridle securement with lung complications, delay to safe tube use and loss. UK tertiary care ICU and ward patient cohorts were obtained from quality improvement and audit studies. Retrospective, univariate and multivariable regression were used to determine the efficacy of guided versus blind tube placement and bridle versus tape securement. Compared to blind placement, guided tubes penetrated the respiratory tract less far beyond the carina (IRIS 0cm, Cortrak 11cm, blind: 17cm) and did not cause pneumothorax (0 vs. 5), whereas more were safely positioned (100% vs. 87.9%) and had a shorter delay to confirm tube position (0 h vs. 1.27 h). Compared with adhesive tape, bridle securement was associated with significantly lower odds of inadvertent tube removal (0.12:1) and approximately 5-7-fold higher odds of the tube remaining in situ until no longer required ('redundancy'), including in survivors and those transitioning directly to oral nutrition. Immediate guidance-confirmed tube placement and bridle securement were independently associated with reduced tube-related risk and delays to treatment and improved tube retention. Replacing current methods by staff trained in combined guided tube placement and bridle securement could eliminate most complications and deliver faster and more consistent treatment.

articles.title: Intermittent or Continuous Renal-Replacement Therapy in Acute Kidney Injury.
articles.journal: The New England journal of medicine
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The preferred method of renal-replacement therapy for acute kidney injury in critically ill patients remains uncertain. METHODS: In this multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned critically ill adults with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy to undergo intermittent hemodialysis or continuous renal-replacement therapy as the initial treatment. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event - defined as death, dependence on renal-replacement therapy, or a serum creatinine concentration more than 25% above the baseline value - by day 90. RESULTS: The trial was stopped early after sequential interim analyses showed a sustained signal of higher mortality with intermittent hemodialysis than with continuous renal-replacement therapy. A total of 554 patients underwent randomization, with 272 patients assigned to undergo intermittent hemodialysis and 282 to undergo continuous renal-replacement therapy; 535 patients (260 in the intermittent group and 275 in the continuous group) were included in the intention-to-treat population. A major adverse kidney event occurred by day 90 in 203 patients (78.1%) in the intermittent group and in 197 patients (71.6%) in the continuous group (adjusted absolute risk difference, 6.28 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.22 to 13.79). Death by day 90 occurred in 164 patients (63.1%) and in 147 patients (53.5%), respectively. Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates at day 90 were 63.3% and 53.6% (hazard ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.63). The most common complication potentially related to acute kidney injury or renal-replacement therapy was hypotension, which occurred in 179 patients (68.8%) in the intermittent group and in 183 patients (66.5%) in the continuous group. CONCLUSIONS: Among critically ill patients with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy, intermittent hemodialysis as the initial treatment approach was not shown to be noninferior to continuous renal-replacement therapy with respect to major adverse kidney events by day 90 and was associated with higher mortality. (Funded by the French Ministry of Health; ICRAKI ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06032884.).

articles.title: Resting Energy Expenditure in Mechanically Ventilated Surgical-Trauma Patients With and Without Acute Kidney Injury: a single-center retrospective study.
articles.journal: Journal of renal nutrition : the official journal of the Council on Renal Nutrition of the National Kidney Foundation
articles.abstract: To compare resting energy expenditure (REE) measured by indirect calorimetry (IC) in mechanically ventilated surgical-trauma critically ill patients with and without acute kidney injury (AKI); to evaluate differences in REE by sex, age, and body mass index (BMI); and to assess associations between REE, psoas muscle index (PMI) measured using computed tomography scans, and lean body mass (LBM) estimated by predictive equations. This single-center retrospective cohort study conducted at a tertiary academic medical center included mechanically ventilated critically ill adults admitted between 01/01/2012 and 12/31/2023. Exclusion criteria were pediatric, pregnant, or incarcerated patients; quadriplegia, paraplegia, cystic fibrosis; abnormal respiratory quotients; Medical ICU admission; major burns (≥20% TBSA); parenteral nutrition initiated on or after IC; tracheostomy on admission; discharge or death while ventilated; or absence of a nutrition prescription. Of 794 patients screened, 180 met inclusion criteria (AKI n=84; no AKI n=96). At baseline, patients with and without AKI differed significantly in age (59.9 vs 55 years; P = 0.046), BMI (32.2 vs 28.8 kg/m2; P = 0.046), CKD (23.8% vs 3.13%; P < 0.001), and serum creatinine (1.49 vs 0.84 mg/dL; P < 0.001). Of patients with AKI, 71.4% had stage I AKI and 20.2% required renal replacement therapy (RRT). No significant difference in mean REE was observed between patients with and without AKI (1,642 vs 1,665 kcal/day; P = 0.380) . REE was significantly higher in males compared with females (1,806 vs 1,425 kcal/day; P < 0.001), in patients aged 18-65 versus >65 years (1,768 vs 1,428 kcal/day; P = 0.002), and in obese versus non-obese patients (1,841 vs 1,500 kcal/day; P < 0.001). In multivariable linear regression, higher BMI (P = 0.003) and male sex (P = 0.028) were independently associated with higher REE, while AKI was not. LBM estimated by predictive equations was more strongly correlated with REE than PMI (P < 0.001), and correlation strength did not differ by AKI status. Measured REE did not differ between ventilated surgical-trauma patients with and without AKI. REE differed by sex, age, and obesity status, and AKI was not associated with within-group differences. BMI and sex were identified as independent predictors of REE. Estimated LBM was strongly correlated with REE independent of AKI status. Given possible residual confounding, further investigation is needed.

articles.title: Computed tomography-derived nasojejunal tube tip-to-gastric antrum path length and short-term outcomes in severe acute pancreatitis.
articles.abstract: Nasojejunal (NJ) feeding is commonly used in severe acute pancreatitis (SAP), but whether deeper tube advancement improves clinical outcomes is uncertain. Computed tomography (CT)-based three-dimensional reconstruction can quantify the in-situ tube trajectory. To determine whether CT-derived NJ tube path length is associated with short-term outcomes in patients with confirmed SAP. This prospective single-center observational cohort included 63 patients with confirmed SAP. CT-based three-dimensional reconstruction measured the curved path length from the gastric antrum-pylorus junction to the tube tip. The primary outcome was intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay. Associations were assessed using Spearman correlation and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II-adjusted median regression. Firth penalized logistic regression evaluated the exploratory composite outcome. Anatomical tube-tip position was independently classified on multiplanar CT. Median path length was 17.55 cm (interquartile range, 14.35-22.27 cm). Path length was not associated with ICU stay by Spearman analysis (rho = 0.055, P = 0.671) or adjusted median regression (difference per 5-cm increase = 0.192-day, 95% confidence interval: -0.922 to 1.305, P = 0.732). Post-CT ICU stay showed a similar null association. Anatomical position was duodenal in 28 patients, at the duodenojejunal flexure in 18, and jejunal in 17; path length correlated strongly with independently measured flexure-relative distance (rho = 0.997, P < 0.001). The exploratory composite outcome occurred in 17 patients, and path length remained non-significant in Firth regression. CT-derived NJ tube path length was not associated with ICU outcomes but closely reflected distal anatomical tube position. These findings do not establish an optimal advancement target.

articles.title: Current nutrition practices and additional reimbursement of intensive care units in Japan: A cross-sectional survey study.
articles.journal: JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition
articles.abstract: A unique reimbursement for early nutrition intervention was introduced in Japan to promote guideline-adherent nutrition practices in intensive care units. However, the current status of nutrition therapy implementation across Japanese intensive care units remains unclear. This cross-sectional survey study investigated intensive care units nationwide, led by the Japanese Society of Intensive Care Medicine. Facility characteristics, nutrition management structure, nutrition practices (nutritional assessment, nutrition planning, therapy implementation, and monitoring), and dietitian involvement were assessed. We examined relationships between reimbursement claim status and nutrition practices. Among 337 intensive care units, most performed nutritional assessment using at least one standardized tool and planned nutrition targeting 25-30 kcal/kg/day for energy and 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day for protein. Enteral nutrition-related practices were widely implemented. Of these, 255 intensive care units (75.7%) claimed the reimbursement; incentivized units more frequently implemented written enteral nutrition protocols, dietitian-conducted nutritional assessments, dietitian-led enteral nutrition design, and enteral nutrition initiation within 48 h. However, Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition assessment, indirect calorimetry, written protocols for parenteral nutrition/diarrhea/constipation, dietitian-led parenteral nutrition design, and post-intensive care unit nutritional follow-up remained limited even in incentivized units. In Japan, reimbursement incentives were positively associated with higher implementation of nutritional assessment, enteral nutrition-related practices, and dietitian involvement. To further advance specialized nutritional care, simultaneous system development may be warranted.

articles.title: Management of dysglycemia in critically ill adults: current evidence, clinical practice and future directions.
articles.abstract: Hyperglycemia is among the most common metabolic disturbances in critically ill patients, affecting up to 50% of adults admitted to intensive care units (ICUs), regardless of pre-existing diabetes. Both diabetes and stress-induced hyperglycemia are associated with increased risk of organ dysfunction, healthcare-associated infections, prolonged mechanical ventilation, longer ICU and hospital length of stay, and mortality. Clinical guidelines recommend initiating intravenous insulin therapy when blood glucose remains ≥180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) and targeting 140–180 mg/dL (7.8–10.0 mmol/L) for most critically ill adults. Recent advances in continuous glucose monitoring, computerized insulin dosing algorithms, automated insulin delivery systems and artificial intelligence-enabled clinical decision support are transforming glucose management in the ICU and have the potential to improve safety and efficiency. This review summarizes current understanding of the pathophysiology of stress hyperglycemia, the clinical consequences of dysglycemia, contemporary glucose targets, insulin therapy and glucose monitoring strategies. We also highlight emerging technologies, special patient populations and future directions expected to shape precision glycemic management for critically ill adults.

articles.title: Preserved anabolic skeletal muscle capacity in response to exercise and protein intake after critical illness.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Low muscle mass and persistent weakness are common after critical illness, but the mechanisms behind impaired recovery are incompletely understood. The aim of this study was to investigate the skeletal muscle anabolic response to combined resistance exercise and protein intake in intensive care unit (ICU) survivors, compared to matched controls without a history of critical illness. We hypothesised that residual anabolic resistance limits muscle regeneration after ICU stay. METHODS: Former patients were enrolled within 3 to 6 months of intensive care unit discharge. Muscle biopsies were obtained before and after resistance exercise using a flywheel leg extension ergometer, combined with ingestion of 24 g hydrolysed protein. Muscle protein fractional synthetic rate was determined from the incorporation of [ring-²H₅]phenylalanine into mixed-muscle protein during a primed continuous intravenous infusion. Anabolic and proteolytic pathways were measured using standard assays. Group-by-time differences were analysed using linear mixed models. The primary comparison was the between-group difference in pre-to-post change in muscle protein synthesis. RESULTS: Twenty ICU survivors (60 ± 12 years, 30% female, BMI 26.9 (IQR 22.9-28.7), SAPS 3 62.3 ± 15.8) and 20 age- and sex-matched controls were included. ICU survivors had significantly lower quadriceps muscle thickness (p = 0.02) and handgrip strength (p = 0.04) than controls. In ICU survivors, muscle protein synthesis from plasma precursor amino acids was higher at baseline than in controls (0.041%/hour vs. 0.030%/hour, p = 0.009), but increased less (Δ 0.031 vs. Δ 0.040%/hour, p = 0.04). Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis was similar between groups (0.071%/hour vs. 0.070%/hour, p = 0.70). At baseline, ICU survivors showed lower activation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway. In both groups, the intervention increased anabolic signalling, decreased initiation of autophagy and increased parts of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. CONCLUSIONS: In ICU survivors with persistent muscle loss and weakness, the increase in muscle protein synthesis after combined resistance exercise and protein intake was smaller than in controls, in the context of a higher baseline fractional synthetic rate. Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis rates were similar between groups. These findings provide the first mechanistic support for structured exercise-nutrition rehabilitation to promote muscle recovery after critical illness. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05261984), 2022-02-20.

articles.title: Refeeding Hypophosphatemia During ECMO Support: A Retrospective Cohort Study on Incidence, Predictors, and Association with Outcome.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Refeeding syndrome (RFS) is a potentially life-threatening complication of nutritional support in critically ill patients. Its incidence and clinical relevance in patients requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) are unknown. We retrospectively investigated the incidence, characteristics and clinical relevance of RFS in COVID-19 patients receiving venovenous (vv-)ECMO support. Methods: In a secondary analysis of 101 COVID-19 patients treated with vv-ECMO at a tertiary center, RFS was defined by a decrease of more than 0.16 mmol/L in serum phosphate to a value below 0.65 mmol/L within seven days of starting medical nutrition therapy (MNT), or a pre-existing phosphate below 0.65 mmol/L. Electrolyte trajectories, nutritional delivery, predictors of RFS, and the association with ICU mortality were analyzed. Robustness was assessed across alternative published definitions. Results: RFS developed in 46 of 101 patients (45.5%), with an incidence ranging from 23.8% to 84.2% depending on the definition applied. Patients with RFS had a lower body mass index and required significantly more phosphate substitution than those without (93.5% vs. 43.6%; p < 0.001). Early energy delivery did not differ between groups and was not associated with RFS. RFS was not associated with ICU mortality (41.3% vs. 41.8%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.80, p = 0.51), a finding consistent across all definitions examined. Conclusions: In this COVID-19 vv-ECMO cohort, refeeding-associated hypophosphatemia was frequent but not associated with caloric delivery or ICU mortality under close electrolyte monitoring. These hypothesis-generating findings do not support reducing caloric intake for isolated hypophosphatemia and require prospective confirmation.

articles.title: Clinical nutrition for critically ill patients: A practical appraisal of guideline gaps and perspectives for future research.
articles.abstract: Malnutrition and accelerated muscle wasting are frequent during critical illness and make nutritional support a central component of ICU care. Nutritional support is therefore central to ICU care, but its optimal timing, route, dose, and composition remain debated. Recent randomized trials have challenged the traditional objective of early full feeding and shifted practice toward progressive, phase-adapted, and tolerance-based nutrition. This narrative review compares current international guidelines for nutritional support in critically ill adults. Guidelines broadly agree that nutrition should be initiated early after clinical stabilization, acute-phase overfeeding should be avoided, energy and protein delivery should be increased progressively, and refeeding syndrome should be anticipated. However, important differences remain regarding acute-phase energy targets, protein dosing, enteral versus parenteral nutrition, supplemental parenteral nutrition, indirect calorimetry, and enriched enteral formulas. These discrepancies reflect differences in methodology, healthcare context, and interpretation of evidence largely derived from mechanically ventilated patients during the first ICU week. Several clinically important situations remain insufficiently addressed, including prolonged critical illness, obesity, sarcopenia, post-extubation nutrition, post-ICU rehabilitation, and nutrition after major surgery. Future research should move toward individualized strategies based on illness phase, metabolic trajectory, nutritional phenotype, tolerance, and recovery-oriented outcomes.

articles.title: Association between augmented enteral protein and muscle mass attenuation in critically ill patients: A sub-study of a cluster randomized crossover trial.
articles.journal: JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition
articles.abstract: Critically ill patients experience muscle wasting, impacting recovery. The associations between augmented enteral protein and muscle mass, strength, physical function, and quality of life are uncertain. We performed a sub-study in adult TARGET Protein participants from two sites between 23/11/2022-23/05/2023. Our exposure of interest was enteral formula with augmented protein (100 g protein/L) and comparator usual protein formula (63 g protein/L), which were isocaloric. Our primary outcome was the change in quadriceps muscle layer thickness from Days 1 to 7, determined by ultrasonography and compared between groups. Our secondary outcomes were group differences in handgrip strength, change in physical function, and quality of life. Data are numbers (%), mean (standard deviation), and differences with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Seventy-two patients were included (augmented protein n = 46, 61 (16)y, 65% male; usual protein n = 26, 56 (16)y, 46% male), 56 had primary outcome data (augmented protein n = 35; usual protein n = 21). Delivered protein was higher with augmented protein (1.2 (0.4) vs 0.8 (0.3) g/kg/day). Quadriceps muscle layer thickness decreased in both groups, with change from Days 1 to 7 similar (0.01 cm; 95% CI, -0.27, 0.28; P = 0.970). Left handgrip strength at ICU discharge and quality of life at Day 90 were similar. Augmented protein was associated with greater right handgrip strength at ICU discharge (6.23; 95% CI, 0.67, 11.79) and was associated with greater decline in physical function at ICU discharge (-15.00; 95% CI, -19.75, -10.25), but not at Day 90. No clear difference was detected in quadriceps muscle layer attenuation over 7 days between augmented enteral protein and usual protein. Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry identifier: ACTRN12622001465741.

articles.title: Clinical Course and Prognosis of the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition-Defined Malnutrition in Critically Ill Patients with Sepsis: A Multicenter Prospective Observational Study.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a critical condition with a high nutritional risk and mortality. Although the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) criteria have been proposed for diagnosing malnutrition, their clinical relevance in sepsis remains unclear. Therefore, we conducted a descriptive study on GLIM-defined malnutrition in intensive care unit (ICU) patients with sepsis to investigate its clinical course and prognosis. This was a multicenter prospective study conducted at 15 centers. Malnutrition was identified at ICU admission when both phenotypic and etiologic criteria were present. The primary outcome was a composite of in-hospital mortality or a decline in activities of daily living (Barthel Index <90) at discharge. Secondary outcomes included ICU length of stay, use of parenteral nutrition, and days to achievement of each ICU Mobility Scale level. Among 254 patients, 106 (41.7%) had malnutrition. The malnutrition group showed a significantly higher occurrence of the composite of in-hospital mortality and Barthel index <90 (76.4% vs. 64.2%, p = 0.04) and had significantly longer ICU stays (7 vs. 5, p = 0.001). Total nutrition delivery did not significantly differ between groups, while a higher percentage of patients in the malnutrition group received parenteral nutrition (57.6% vs. 43.2%, p = 0.02). Significant delays in achieving higher mobility levels were observed in the malnutrition group. GLIM-defined malnutrition in patients with sepsis was significantly associated with the composite outcome of in-hospital mortality or Barthel index <90 at discharge. These results suggest the clinical importance of an early GLIM assessment after ICU admission.

articles.title: The effects of intravenous glutamine supplementation in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Studies evaluating intravenous (IV) glutamine supplementation in critically ill patients have shown inconsistent results. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of IV glutamine on mortality, infectious complications, length of stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation. A systematic search of Ovid Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and KoreaMed was conducted from inception through October 2023 and updated in April 2025. Randomized controlled trials comparing IV glutamine supplementation with standard care in critically ill adults were included. Pooled estimates were calculated using random-effects models. A total of 10 randomized trials involving 1,593 critically ill patients were included in the analysis. IV glutamine supplementation was not associated with reduced overall mortality (risk ratio [RR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.77-1.13) or overall infection rates (RR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.63-1.18). No mortality benefit was observed in either non-surgical or surgical/trauma subgroups. Glutamine supplementation was associated with reduced pneumonia incidence (RR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.49-0.87) and shorter mechanical ventilation duration (mean difference, -0.97 days; 95% CI, -1.62 to -0.32); however, these findings were based on a limited number of small studies. Intensive care unit and hospital length of stay were longer in the glutamine group. IV glutamine supplementation was not associated with improved survival or overall infection rates in critically ill adults. Current evidence does not support routine IV glutamine supplementation in unselected critically ill patients.

articles.title: Evaluation of Chromium Picolinate Supplementation and Insulin Requirements in Critically Ill Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
articles.journal: The Journal of pharmacy technology : jPT : official publication of the Association of Pharmacy Technicians
articles.abstract: Chromium picolinate has been studied as an adjunct to improve glycemic indices in ambulatory type 2 diabetes mellitus, but its role in critically ill patients is unknown. To evaluate whether chromium picolinate supplementation was associated with reduced insulin requirements without worsening glycemic control in critically ill adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. We conducted a single-center retrospective pre-post cohort study of adult intensive care unit patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus or hemoglobin A1c ≥6.5% who received insulin and at least 4 consecutive chromium picolinate doses between July 2022 and January 2023. Patients served as their own controls during 24-hour pre- and post-chromium periods. The primary outcome was change in total daily insulin dose. Secondary outcomes included proportion of measured glucose values within 140 to 180 mg/dL, acute kidney injury, hypoglycemia, and exploratory Sequential Organ Failure Assessment-2 change. Among 91 screened patients, 45 met the inclusion criteria. Median total daily insulin dose decreased from 76.3 U/d (interquartile range [IQR], 40.1-96.9) before chromium to 40.0 U/d (IQR, 20.5-65.6) after chromium; the Hodges-Lehmann paired difference was -23.0 U/d (95% CI, -33.25 to -14.25; P < .0001). Proportion of measured glucose values within target did not differ significantly. No post-intervention hypoglycemia was observed, and 2 patients met the study-defined acute kidney injury criterion. Interpretation is limited by the retrospective design and absence of a concurrent control group. Chromium picolinate supplementation was associated with lower insulin requirements without worsening glycemic control. These hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation in prospective controlled studies.

articles.title: Plasma amino acid profiles reveal metabolic signatures of mortality and infection in critically ill surgical patients requiring parenteral nutrition: A longitudinal analysis.
articles.abstract: Surgical intensive care unit (SICU) patients experience high rates of adverse outcomes, underscoring the need for insights into pathophysiology. We aimed to evaluate associations between plasma amino acids (AAs), post-surgical mortality, and hospital-acquired infections in SICU patients requiring parenteral nutrition (PN). Secondary analysis of a multicenter trial including 148 adults receiving glutamine-supplemented or standard PN after major surgery. Levels of plasma AAs were quantified at baseline, Day 3, and Day 7. Mortality and infections were monitored through day 28. Associations between AAs and outcomes were assessed via generalized linear models adjusted for clinical covariates. Machine learning models evaluated the classification performance of AAs. At baseline, a four AA signature (plasma aspartate, histidine, leucine, and methionine concentrations) showed similar discrimination of 28-day mortality as the APACHE II score (AUC 0.88 vs. 0.78, DeLong test P = 0.28). Increased concentrations of these AA suggest impaired uptake and utilization. At baseline, BSI was best classified by a model that included decreased concentrations of alanine, cystine, glutamate, glutamine, and lysine (AUC 0.79), with glutamate elevated in cases. The best classification model for pneumonia at Day 7 included decreased cystine, lysine, ornithine, threonine, tyrosine, and valine concentrations (AUC 0.86). At baseline and Day 7, for any infections, the classification model included decreased glutamine, glycine, lysine, ornithine, proline, serine, threonine, and valine concentrations (AUC >0.79). Elevated essential AA concentrations were associated with SICU mortality, while lower levels of both essential and non-essential AAs were linked to hospital-acquired infections.

articles.title: Association of enteral nutrition reduction or discontinuation with diarrhea volume and caloric delivery in critically ill adults with diarrhea: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.journal: Nutrition in clinical practice : official publication of the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition
articles.abstract: When critically ill patients receiving enteral nutrition (EN) develop diarrhea, clinicians often reduce or discontinue EN, although evidence supporting this practice is limited. We examined the association between EN management after diarrhea and diarrhea volume in critical care patients. This single-center retrospective cohort study included adult intensive care unit patients who developed new-onset diarrhea (Bristol Stool Form Scale ≥6 on 2 consecutive days) during EN. Based on Day 1 EN management, patients were classified as continuation (infusion rate decrease <10 mL/h) or reduction/discontinuation (decrease ≥10 mL/h or complete discontinuation). The primary outcome was cumulative diarrhea volume (grams) on Days 1-2. Cumulative EN calories (kcal) on Days 1-2 was a key secondary outcome. Inverse probability of treatment weighting with regression adjustment accounted for 8 pre-specified confounders. Sensitivity analyses included alternative exposure thresholds and propensity score models. Of 135 patients analyzed (median age, 74 years; 32% female), 96 (71.1%) continued EN and 39 (28.9%) underwent EN reduction/discontinuation. After adjustment, the reduction/discontinuation group had lower cumulative diarrhea volume on Days 1-2 (adjusted mean difference, -183.4 g; 95% confidence interval [CI], -350.1 to -16.7; p = 0.033) but received substantially fewer calories (-1260.1 kcal; 95% CI, -1464.4 to -1055.9; p < 0.001). The direction of the reduction in diarrhea volume was consistent across sensitivity analyses. Reducing or discontinuing EN after diarrhea was associated with a modest reduction in diarrhea volume but a substantial caloric deficit. This trade-off should be considered when reducing EN for diarrhea.

articles.title: Evaluation of a device for insertion of a small intestinal feeding tube in the critically ill: A prospective multicentre international cohort study.
articles.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
articles.abstract: Critically ill patients sometimes require insertion of a feeding tube into the small intestine. This study evaluated the ease of placement of a proprietary small intestinal feeding tube incorporating a distal tip camera. investigator-initiated, industry-funded, prospective cohort study was conducted at four intensive care units across two countries. Patients were eligible if the treating clinician requested small intestinal feeding tube insertion. Operators were physicians or senior dietitians, and attempts were categorised as "inexperienced" (≤4 attempts) or "experienced" (≥5 attempts). The primary outcome was the overall probability of successful small intestinal placement. Secondary outcomes included procedural time and the posterior probabilities of success according to operator classification and experience, estimated using Bayesian hierarchical regression models incorporating minimally informative priors and random intercepts for clustering within operators. The device was used by 11 operators in 68 patients. Prior 24-h cumulative gastric residual volumes were 454 (standard deviation: 453) millilitres. The overall probability of success was 75% (95% credible interval: 61-86%). Experienced users and inexperienced users were successful in 30 of 38 (79%) and 21 of 30 (70%) attempts, respectively. Overall median (interquartile range) procedural times for successful versus unsuccessful placement were 23 (10-35) and 30 (20-42) minutes, respectively. In a multivariable analysis, the posterior probabilities of improved success (odds ratio >1) were 83% (gastrokinetic drug prescription), 82% (operative versus nonoperative admission), and 65% (device experience). The probability of successful small intestinal placement of feeding tubes by motivated clinicians in a critical care environment approximated the prespecified threshold of 80%, without the need for extensive specific device experience.

articles.title: Clinical applications of gastric point-of-care ultrasound in adult emergency and critical care: a scoping review.
articles.abstract: Point-of-care ultrasound (PoCUS) is a cornerstone of bedside assessment in emergency and critical care, providing rapid, radiation-free visualization of anatomy and pathology. Gastric PoCUS offers a non-invasive method to assess gastric content, volume, and motility, informing management of aspiration risk, airway interventions, and enteral feeding. Despite supporting evidence, its use remains limited and poorly standardized. The objective of this scoping review is to map the clinical applications of gastric PoCUS in adult emergency department (ED) and intensive care unit (ICU) patients. A scoping review was conducted according to PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Medline, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane, CINAHL, were searched from 1950 to May 2025 for studies evaluating gastric ultrasound in adult ED or ICU populations. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted, and charted data. Thirty-five studies met inclusion criteria. Clinical applications of gastric PoCUS among ED and ICU were clustered under three domains: aspiration risk assessment and airway management (n = 5); enteral nutrition and gastric residual volume monitoring (n = 12); and diagnostic evaluation or therapeutic monitoring (n = 18). Across studies, gastric PoCUS reliably differentiated gastric content types, estimated gastric volume, and informed airway and feeding decisions. In diagnostic contexts, gastric PoCUS enabled rapid bedside identification of gastric outlet obstruction, volvulus, intramural hematoma, and perforated viscus. No studies reported complications or harm caused by performing gastric PoCUS. Gastric PoCUS is a versatile bedside tool bridging diagnostic and therapeutic domains in emergency and critical care. It enhances patient safety, optimizes nutritional management, and reduces radiographic dependence. Standardization of scanning protocols, structured training, and multicenter outcome-based validation studies are needed to support routine integration in acute care.

articles.title: Effect of enteral nutrition nursing combined with gastrointestinal function monitoring on gastric retention and abdominal distension in neurosurgical patients.
articles.abstract: This study evaluated the clinical effects of enteral nutrition nursing combined with gastrointestinal function monitoring in neurosurgical patients receiving enteral nutrition. This single-center retrospective cohort study included 120 neurosurgical patients who received enteral nutritional support from June 2023 to June 2025. Sixty patients received routine enteral nutrition nursing (control group), and 60 received routine care plus dynamic gastrointestinal function monitoring (combined nursing group). Outcomes included gastric retention, abdominal distension, nausea and vomiting, overall gastrointestinal intolerance, enteral nutrition interruption, aspiration/reflux, nutritional delivery, gastrointestinal recovery, hospital and intensive care unit (ICU) stay, nutritional tolerance, and nursing satisfaction. Logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with gastric retention. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups (all P > .05). Gastric retention occurred less frequently in the combined nursing group than in the control group (15.0% vs 30.0%), although the difference did not reach statistical significance (P = .053). The combined nursing group had lower incidences of abdominal distension (16.7% vs 36.7%, P = .011), nausea and vomiting (11.7% vs 26.7%, P = .038), and overall gastrointestinal intolerance (20.0% vs 43.3%, P = .006). Time to achievement of enteral nutrition targets, gastric residual volume, time to recovery of bowel sounds, and time to first defecation were also more favorable (all P < .001). Enteral nutrition interruption was less frequent (8.3% vs 23.3%, P = .022), and hospital and ICU stays were shorter (both P < .01). Good nutritional tolerance and nursing satisfaction were more frequent in the combined nursing group (both P < .05). Multivariable analysis showed that the combined nursing model was associated with lower odds of gastric retention. Enteral nutrition nursing combined with gastrointestinal function monitoring was associated with improved gastrointestinal tolerance, more efficient nutritional delivery, earlier gastrointestinal recovery, and shorter hospital and ICU stays. A lower observed incidence of gastric retention was also noted, and adjusted analysis suggested an association with reduced odds of gastric retention.

articles.title: Prevalence of Chronic Complications After Inaugural Admission in Intensive Care Unit for Type 1 Diabetes in the SFDT1 Cohort: The INAUGURAL Study.
articles.abstract: Inaugural presentation at type 1 diabetes onset, as ketoacidosis, has been associated with poorer glycaemic control, but its relationship to diabetes-related complications remains unclear. We assessed the association between inaugural intensive care unit (ICU) admission and long-term diabetes-related outcomes in adults. This cross-sectional analysis used data from the Société Francophone du Diabète-Cohorte Diabète de Type 1 (SFDT1) cohort. We compared participants with and without an inaugural ICU admission regarding chronic complications, recent acute events, and cardiometabolic risk factors. Models were adjusted for age, sex, diabetes duration, smoking status, socioeconomic vulnerability, education, insulin therapy, HbA1c, and centre; interaction terms were tested. Among 3548 adults with type 1 diabetes (median duration 20 years [IQR 10-30]), 377 (10.6%) reported inaugural ICU admission. Retinopathy was more prevalent in the ICU group (36.6 vs. 31.4%; p < 0.05), including proliferative forms (11.1 vs. 7.7%; p < 0.05). These differences remained significant after adjustment (p < 0.05). An association with retinopathy was observed among individuals diagnosed before the age of 17 (OR = 1.5; 95% CI, 1.1-2.1; p = 0.015). Severe hypoglycaemia in the previous year was more frequent in the ICU group (15.4% vs. 10.5%; p < 0.01) and remained significant after adjustment (p < 0.05). No significant differences were observed for the other variables. In this multicentre cohort of adults with long-standing type 1 diabetes, inaugural ICU was associated with at least a 50% higher odds of severe hypoglycaemia and retinopathy, including proliferative forms. The association with retinopathy was mainly observed among individuals diagnosed at a young age. ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04657783).

articles.title: Decades of intensive care medicine trials: what randomised evidence has changed, corrected, and still questions to resolve.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have reshaped intensive care medicine (ICM), a discipline defined by acute, interacting organ failures, time-sensitive decisions, biological uncertainty, and heterogeneous recovery trajectories. Many interventions supported by strong physiological rationale failed to improve patient-centred outcomes, whereas durable advances often emerged from optimisation of supportive care, avoidance of iatrogenic harm, and reassessment of established practices. METHODS: We conducted an interpretive historical review of landmark multicentre RCTs in adult ICM from the early 1990s onwards. PubMed searches, reference lists from major trials and reviews, and international guidelines were used to identify trials with conceptual influence on practice, guidelines, physiological reasoning, therapeutic strategy, research priorities, de-implementation, or outcome framing. Evidence was organised into overlapping paradigms rather than rigid chronological periods. FINDINGS: Across haemodynamic support, mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, antimicrobial treatment, nutrition, glucose control, transfusion, and sedation, landmark RCTs describe more than therapeutic expansion. Early biological and haemodynamic trials exposed the limits of reductionist strategies in syndromic critical illness. Protocol-driven approaches improved timeliness and consistency, but later pragmatic trials showed that rigid targets and invasive algorithms often added little once high-quality usual care was established. More recent trials challenge the assumption that greater intervention intensity improves outcomes, emphasising timing, disease phase, baseline risk, heterogeneity, patient selection, and treatment-related harm. Modern ICM RCTs have clarified not only what works, but what can be reduced, delayed, avoided, or applied selectively. Future progress requires biologically informed, context-sensitive trials focussed on meaningful survival, recovery, and long-term function.

articles.title: Key principles for rehabilitation of critically ill patients with obesity.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Patients with obesity who are admitted to an ICU bring specific challenges for rehabilitation during and after critical illness. This narrative review explores impact of differences in body compositions and pathophysiology on outcomes to summarise interprofessional, patient-centred rehabilitation strategies across the trajectory of recovery. METHODS: The interprofessional expert panel reviewed major trials and guidelines, integrating their clinical expertise with the current evidence. RESULTS: Three distinct phenotypes potentially influence outcomes for survivors. Whilst patients with preserved muscle mass may have a survival advantage, the phenotypes characterised by ectopic visceral fat or sarcopenia are frequently complicated by multimorbidity and polypharmacy, likely increasing the risk of adverse effects such as suboptimal sedation, prolonged ventilation and immobilisation, malnutrition, and impaired recovery. Targeted respiratory interventions, including secretion-clearance techniques and appropriate patient positioning to prevent atelectasis, reduce the work of breathing. Optimisation of communication and swallowing function is an essential component for facilitating safe oral intake and promoting active patient participation in rehabilitation. Concurrently, targeted nutrition strategies combined with early, targeted, progressive mobilisation might mitigate ICU acquired weakness and support functional recovery. The availability of appropriate weight‑based equipment is fundamental to ensuring safe mobilisation for both patients and healthcare professionals. CONCLUSION: Interprofessional collaboration is central to optimising outcomes and should extend beyond the ICU to structured post-ICU follow-up to address persistent, worsening, or newly emerging health impairments. Early rehabilitation in critically ill patients with obesity should integrate physiological, logistical, and psychosocial considerations to support equitable and functional recovery.
articles.ai_summary: This study reviewed rehabilitation strategies for critically ill patients with obesity, identifying three distinct phenotypes that influence outcomes. Targeted interventions, including respiratory, nutrition, and mobilization strategies, can mitigate complications and support functional recovery.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings highlight the importance of interprofessional collaboration and early rehabilitation in critically ill patients with obesity, emphasizing the need to address physiological, logistical, and psychosocial considerations to support equitable and functional recovery.

articles.title: Net Ultrafiltration Rate and Mortality in Critically Ill Patients: A Multicenter Cohort Study With Analysis of Fluid Balance Changes.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To investigate the association between net ultrafiltration (NUF) rate and fluid balance changes with 28-day mortality in critically ill patients receiving continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). DESIGN: Multicenter retrospective observational study. SETTING: Data from two European mixed medical-surgical ICUs: University Hospital Bern, Switzerland, and Amsterdam University Medical Center, the Netherlands. PATIENTS: Adult critically ill patients receiving CRRT for at least 24 hours. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We studied 973 critically ill adults undergoing a total of 6914 days of CRRT. NUF rates and fluid balance changes were calculated from hourly data and categorized into four predefined groups. NUF rates were classified as no NUF, low (< 1.01 mL/kg/h), moderate (1.01-1.75 mL/kg/h), or high (> 1.75 mL/kg/h). Fluid balance change was stratified as negative (< -1.5 L/day), moderate negative (-1.5 to -0.5 L/day), neutral (-0.5 to 0.5 L/day), or positive (> 0.5 L/day). Using multivariable regression, random forest modeling, and mediation analysis, we observed no independent association between NUF rate and 28-day mortality after accounting for fluid balance. Mediation analysis suggested that the apparent survival advantage observed among patients with higher NUF rates was largely mediated through achievement of a more negative fluid balance, rather than a direct effect of NUF rate itself. In contrast, more positive fluid balance changes were linked to adverse clinical outcomes including 28-day mortality. CONCLUSIONS: In this two-center cohort of CRRT patients, NUF rate was not independently associated with mortality. Instead, the key determinant of outcome was fluid balance change. These findings suggest clinicians should not make NUF decisions in isolation, but rather should be using NUF as a means to achieve patient-specific fluid balance targets.
articles.ai_key_stats: n=973, no independent association between NUF rate and 28-day mortality, fluid balance change linked to adverse outcomes including 28-day mortality
articles.ai_summary: This study investigated the relationship between net ultrafiltration rate and fluid balance changes in critically ill patients receiving continuous renal replacement therapy.
