articles.abstract: We aimed to clarify the impact of early enteral nutrition support combined with comfort nursing on the prognosis of critically ill patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) who received ventilator-assisted ventilation. 100 critically ill patients admitted to our ICU were selected and randomly divided into the control group (CG) and the observation group (OG). The OG initiated early enteral nutrition support within 24 h after admission to ICU and received comfort nursing. The CG initiated enteral nutrition support after admission to the ICU based on monitoring biochemical indicators and received routine ICU nursing. The nutritional status, immune function, total malnutrition rate, incidence of pulmonary infection, ventilator weaning time and ICU hospitalization time of the two groups were measured and compared. The levels of albumin (ALB), total protein (TP), and globulin (GLB) in both groups were higher than those at admission to the ICU, while OG group were higher than CG group (P < 0.05). The PCT levels of both groups decreased compared to the levels during the period from admission to the ICU, while OG group was greater decrease than CG group (P < 0.05). The overall malnutrition rate in OG group was lower than that in CG group (P < 0.05). The incidence of pulmonary infection in OG group was lower than that in CG group (P < 0.05). The time to weaning from the ventilator and the ICU stay time in OG group were shorter than those in CG group (P < 0.05). For critically ill ICU patients undergoing ventilator assisted ventilation, early enteral nutrition support combined with comfort nursing can effectively reduce risk of malnutrition and pulmonary infection, enhance immune function, create convenient conditions for early weaning and early conversion to general wards, with broad clinical application prospects.

articles.title: Case Report: Acute complete esophageal obstruction associated with intraesophageal coagulation of RuiNeng enteral nutrition formula.
articles.abstract: Enteral nutrition is widely used in critically ill patients and in patients with dysphagia. However, mechanical obstruction associated with coagulation of an enteral formula within the esophagus is extremely rare and may be easily mistaken for ordinary reflux, aspiration, or tube blockage. We report the case of a 69-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) who received nasogastric tube feeding with RuiNeng enteral nutrition formula, a high-protein, fiber-containing formula, because of impaired consciousness and critical illness. During tube feeding, the patient developed regurgitation of medication, overflow of enteral formula from the oral cavity, marked resistance during aspiration and injection through the nasogastric tube, and withdrawal of a milky-white paste-like substance. Bedside gastroscopy revealed extensive retention of whitish solid coagulated material in the esophageal lumen, causing severe esophageal obstruction. Partial endoscopic removal and fragmentation of the coagulated material were performed, the remaining material was cautiously pushed into the stomach under direct endoscopic visualization, and a jejunal feeding tube was placed under direct endoscopic visualization. Based on the clinical course and published reports, this case was probably associated with suspected impaired opening of the esophagogastric junction, possible nasogastric tube malposition, migration, coiling, or ineffective passage into the stomach with subsequent retention of enteral formula in the esophagus, and coagulation of the high-protein formula in a locally acidic or low-motility environment. Because no objective pH measurement of esophageal contents or the coagulated material was available, these mechanisms should be interpreted as plausible hypotheses rather than directly proven findings. This case highlights that, in critically ill patients receiving high-protein or fiber-containing enteral formulas, abnormal reflux, sudden tube resistance, or milky-white paste-like aspirate should prompt immediate cessation of feeding, reassessment of tube position and esophageal patency, and early bedside endoscopic diagnosis and treatment when necessary.
articles.ai_summary: A 69-year-old man developed a rare esophageal obstruction from coagulated enteral nutrition formula, which was mistaken for reflux or tube blockage. Bedside gastroscopy revealed extensive retention of coagulated material in the esophagus. The patient underwent partial endoscopic removal and was switched to a jejunal feeding tube.
articles.ai_significance: This case highlights the importance of promptly recognizing and treating esophageal obstructions in critically ill patients receiving high-protein or fiber-containing enteral formulas to prevent serious complications.

articles.title: Enteral nutrition-related hyperglycemia in critical illness: cascade conceptual model and implications for precision nursing-a systematic review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hyperglycemia is a common complication in critically ill patients receiving enteral nutrition (EN). This review synthesizes evidence on its mechanisms, epidemiology, clinical implications, and nursing management to support precision glycemic care. METHODS: A systematic literature search identified 45 eligible studies, including randomized trials, retrospective studies, reviews, guidelines, and expert consensus statements. Given the lack of a universally accepted definition, enteral nutrition-related hyperglycemia was pragmatically defined as blood glucose ≥7.8 mmol/L occurring within 24-72 h after initiation of enteral nutrition. RESULTS: Reported incidence varies widely, from approximately 30-47% in general ICU populations to 60-80% following cardiac surgery, reflecting differences in definitions, patient characteristics, timing, and nutritional protocols. Based on thematic integration of existing evidence, we propose a six-level conceptual cascade framework, linking metabolic vulnerability, stress-hormone activation, exogenous substrate load, enteroinsular axis dysfunction, inflammation-mediated insulin resistance, and microbiota dysbiosis. Corresponding nursing strategies include diabetes-specific formulas, optimized feeding regimens, continuous glucose monitoring, and individualized insulin protocols within multidisciplinary care. These strategies may improve glycemic control; however, evidence for clinical outcome benefits remains limited and heterogeneous. CONCLUSION: Further prospective studies are needed to validate the model and refine precision nursing strategies.
articles.ai_summary: This systematic review of 45 studies examined the mechanisms and management of hyperglycemia in critically ill patients receiving enteral nutrition, proposing a six-level conceptual cascade framework to guide precision glycemic care.
articles.ai_significance: Understanding and managing enteral nutrition-related hyperglycemia is crucial for ICU clinical practice as it can lead to improved glycemic control, but further studies are needed to confirm its clinical benefits.

articles.title: Omega-3-rich fish oil lipid emulsions prevent sepsis-driven mesenteric hypoperfusion and multiorgan injury in a murine model.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND/AIM: Parenteral feeding is used in critically ill patients when enteral nutrition is inadequate or intolerable, or when the gastrointestinal tract is nonfunctional. Lipid emulsions play a major role in parenteral nutrition, supplying the necessary fatty acids and providing high-caloric density. We investigated the effects of various parenteral lipid emulsions on mesenteric perfusion, inflammation-induced oxidation, and organ damage in a lipopolysaccharide-induced mouse endotoxemia model. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Organ damage induced by lipopolysaccharide in septic mice was assessed histopathologically and biochemically, and an ultrasonic blood flowmeter was used to measure the impact of lipid emulsions on mesenteric blood flow. RESULTS: Lipopolysaccharide injection significantly reduced mesenteric blood flow when compared to saline controls (3.02 ± 0.10 mL/min vs 1.44 ± 0.10 mL/min, p < 0.05). Only fish oil emulsion treatment significantly abrogated this decrease (2.84 ± 0.39 mL/min, p < 0.05). None of the tested lipid emulsions prevented lipopolysaccharide-induced increases in liver and spleen weights. Fish oil reduced liver damage in septic mice, whereas specific dosages of olive and soybean oils caused significant histopathological liver and spleen damage even in the control animals. Furthermore, soybean and olive oil also significantly increased serum oxidative stress in the healthy control mice (2.55 ± 0.06 vs 4.93 ± 0.38 and 4.28 ± 0.12, p <0.05). CONCLUSION: Fish oil emulsions with high omega-3 fatty acid content abrogated the decrease in mesenteric blood flow and prevented liver damage in this experimental endotoxemia model.
articles.ai_summary: This study used a mouse model to investigate the effects of different lipid emulsions on mesenteric blood flow and organ damage in sepsis. Fish oil emulsions with high omega-3 fatty acid content were found to prevent a decrease in mesenteric blood flow and liver damage. Omega-3 fatty acids may help protect against sepsis-driven organ injury.
articles.ai_significance: This study suggests that fish oil emulsions could be beneficial in preventing organ damage in critically ill patients receiving parenteral nutrition, particularly those at risk of sepsis.

articles.title: Nutritional support for pressure injury: a bibliometric analysis of research trends.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pressure injury (PI) is a common complication closely associated with malnutrition. Nutritional support is critical for PI prevention and healing, but the overall research trends in this field remain unclear. PURPOSE: This bibliometric analysis aimed to explore trends in research on nutritional support for Pressure Injury (PI) patients, providing insights for healthcare professionals and researchers. METHODS: This study is a bibliometric analysis. Relevant English articles were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (WOSCC) and PubMed databases, with the search period spanning from the establishment of each database to February 2026. CiteSpace was employed to analyze the articles. RESULTS: A total of 1,380 publications were included in this study. The number of published articles showed a consistent growth trend, with a significant increase during 2019-2020. Regarding research output, the United States remains the core contributing country in this field, and Griffith University (Australia) ranks first in institutional output; Clinical Nutrition is the journal with the most published relevant studies, and Thomas DR is the most prolific author. Keyword clustering analysis identified 10 core research themes, including Pressure Injury, enteral nutrition, traumatic brain injuries, nursing home, retrospective study, risk factors, geriatric nutritional risk index, nutritional status, and intensive care unit. Emerging research hotspots are: palliative care, wound healing, and nutritional risk stratification factors in critically ill patients. The current research focus has been significantly concentrated on acute or critically ill patient populations. CONCLUSION: Nutritional support in Pressure Injury (PI) management has garnered growing research attention. Future studies should emphasize multidisciplinary collaboration to develop personalized, evidence-based protocols tailored to diverse patient conditions. Translational research is essential to optimize outcomes, especially for high-risk populations, and targeted nutritional strategies remain pivotal for effective PI management.
articles.ai_summary: This study analyzed 1,380 publications on nutritional support for pressure injury patients, finding a growing trend in research output and identifying key themes and emerging hotspots. The research focused on acute or critically ill patient populations, with a need for personalized, evidence-based protocols. Future studies should emphasize multidisciplinary collaboration and translational research to optimize outcomes.
articles.ai_significance: Understanding research trends in nutritional support for pressure injury patients is crucial for developing effective prevention and treatment strategies, particularly for high-risk populations in ICU settings.

articles.title: Mathematical analysis of the relationship between glucose and sodium in a large Swedish cohort of critically ill patients.
articles.abstract: Hyperglycemia causes compensatory decrease of plasma sodium concentration by an influx of water from the cellular compartment. When the glucose level is corrected, the sodium concentration will follow and increase to its original level. A complex MATLAB script incorporating the Katz and Hillier correction formulas was developed to evaluate the impact of hyperglycemia on sodium levels and to analyze sodium shifts in 9,863 patients across 297,714 paired sodium-glucose measurements. Intensive care unit (ICU) mortality and morbidity data were extracted for the full cohort to assess outcomes. 95.3% of the glucose values (283,686) implied a correction factor for the measured sodium levels in the cohort. Correction of all sodium values for hyperglycemia did not change the adjusted ICU mortalities. Increased maximum sodium shift/24 h starting from 4.00-5.99 mmol/L was related to increased independent ICU mortality. Correction of sodium levels by using Katz and Hillier formulas for hyperglycemia did not change the adjusted ICU mortalities. 602/9,863 (6.1%) patients showed a sodium shift more than 8 mmol/L/24 h. 31 patients (5.1%) were missed without correction for hyperglycemia by the Katz formula and 54 patients (9.0%) were missed without correction by the Hillier formula. Failure to correct sodium for hyperglycemia misses 5-9% of patients with large sodium shifts (>8 mmol/L per 24 hours). Additionally, a sodium shift as low as 4.00-5.99 mmol/L per 24 hours is an independent risk factor for increased ICU mortality.

articles.title: Construction and validation of a 28-day mortality prediction model for refeeding syndrome in critically ill patients.
articles.abstract: Refeeding syndrome (RFS) is a common and serious metabolic reaction during nutritional support in critically ill patients, associated with substantially increased mortality risk and poor prognosis. Existing studies mainly focus on predicting its occurrence, while predictive models for 28-day mortality risk remain lacking. This study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine learning model to support short-term prognostic assessment in clinical practice. Data for critically ill patients with RFS were extracted from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV, 2008-2019) as the internal cohort. A total of 8,705 patients were randomly assigned to training and test sets at a 7:3 ratio. Thirty-eight candidate variables were initially included, and feature selection was performed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) logistic regression. Three machine learning models were subsequently constructed, and the optimal model was validated using two independent datasets. Model interpretability was enhanced using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP). Kaplan-Meier curves were used to compare survival between the high- and low-risk, and nomograms were constructed to facilitate clinical application. Nine variables were ultimately selected to construct the logistic regression model. The model demonstrated excellent discriminative performance and generalizability, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.821, 0.809, and 0.731 in the internal test set, external validation set I (MIMIC-III), and external validation set II (the Affiliated Hospital of Yangzhou University), respectively. SHAP analysis identified partial pressure of oxygen, mean blood glucose level, and age as the key prognostic factors and further revealed nonlinear effects among the variables. Kaplan-Meier survival curves confirmed that the model significantly distinguished between the high- and low-risk groups across all cohorts (all p < 0.05). Decision curve analysis showed that the model provided favorable clinical net benefit in both external validation cohorts. The interpretable machine learning model developed in this study effectively predicts the 28-day mortality risk of RFS in critically ill patients, provides an objective reference for individualized clinical decision-making, and may help improve patient prognosis.

articles.title: Enteral nutrition interruption in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prevalence, causes, and clinical outcomes.
articles.abstract: Enteral nutrition interruption (ENI) is common in critically ill patients and may compromise nutritional delivery, but its prevalence, causes, and clinical consequences remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized evidence on ENI prevalence, contributing factors, clinical outcomes, and potential interventions. PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, and WanFang Data were searched from inception through December 2025. Studies of critically ill adults receiving enteral nutrition were eligible. The review followed PRISMA guidance and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251266654). Random-effects models, subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses, and GRADE assessments were performed. Forty-one studies involving 8,260 critically ill patients were included. Crude ENI prevalence ranged from 11.2% to 100%, with a median of 68.5% (IQR, 57.1%-96.6%). The estimated pooled prevalence was 79.2%, although heterogeneity was extreme (I 2 = 99%) and publication bias was evident (Egger's test, p < 0.001). Common causes included airway management, radiological or imaging procedures, gastrointestinal intolerance, and surgical procedures or preparation. ENI was associated with reduced energy adequacy (mean difference, -4.21 percentage points; 95% CI, -7.71 to -0.71; p = 0.02). No statistically significant association was observed with ICU length of stay (mean difference, -0.41 days; 95% CI, -2.05 to 1.23; p = 0.62). Short-term mortality was not statistically significantly associated with ENI (risk ratio, 1.86; 95% CI, 0.67-5.11), but the estimate was imprecise and heterogeneous (I 2 = 88%). ENI appears common and is predominantly procedure-related. It is associated with reduced energy adequacy, whereas its effects on ICU length of stay and short-term mortality remain uncertain because of inconsistent ENI definitions, substantial heterogeneity, publication bias, and limited outcome data. Standardized definitions, shorter peri-procedural fasting, improved gastrointestinal management, and multidisciplinary nutrition protocols may reduce avoidable interruptions. High-quality prospective studies and randomized trials are needed. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251266654.

articles.title: A nurse-led standardized bedside gastric ultrasound monitoring protocol for abdominal distension management in critically ill patients receiving enteral nutrition: a pragmatic, exploratory randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the feasibility and exploratory clinical effects of a standardized, nurse-led bedside gastric ultrasound-guided monitoring protocol for abdominal distension management in critically ill patients receiving enteral nutrition. In this single-center, pragmatic, exploratory randomized controlled trial, critically ill adults receiving enteral nutrition in the intensive care unit of Henan Provincial People's Hospital were assigned 1:1 to ultrasound-guided gastric residual volume (GRV) monitoring or syringe-aspiration monitoring. The primary outcome was abdominal circumference on day 7. Secondary outcomes included intra-abdominal pressure (IAP), exploratory biomarkers, gastric retention, feeding intolerance, and implementation measures. Of 112 patients assessed, 100 were randomized and 91 completed the 7-day protocol, giving an overall retention rate of 91%. In the intervention group, the median number of ultrasound assessments was 14 per patient (IQR, 10-19), and protocol adherence was 82/89 (92.1%). Day-7 abdominal circumference was lower in the intervention group after baseline adjustment (adjusted mean difference, -2.35 cm; 95% CI, -3.28 to -1.43; P < 0.001). Baseline-adjusted IAP was also lower (-1.68 mmHg; 95% CI, -2.51 to -0.86; P < 0.001). Feeding intolerance did not differ significantly between groups (31.9% vs. 47.7%; RR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.40-1.12; Fisher exact P = 0.139). Albumin was higher after baseline adjustment, whereas prealbumin did not differ significantly. The nurse-led protocol was feasible in this single-center population of non-intubated, relatively hemodynamically stable ICU patients and provided preliminary estimates for abdominal distension-related outcomes. The albumin result was exploratory and should not be taken as evidence of improved nutritional delivery. Secondary analyses were not adjusted for multiplicity and require cautious interpretation. The lack of prospective registration is a major limitation, and the findings do not apply to mechanically ventilated or hemodynamically unstable patients. The randomized design, outcomes, and analysis plan were specified in the ethics-approved protocol before enrollment. However, the separate requirement for registration in a public trial registry was overlooked, and the study was not prospectively registered [Ethics Committee of Henan Provincial People's Hospital, approval No. 2023(Ethics)127].

articles.title: Gastrointestinal point-of-care ultrasound for enteral nutrition management in critically ill adults: a scoping review.
articles.abstract: Gastrointestinal point-of-care ultrasound has been investigated as a non-invasive, bedside adjunct for gastrointestinal assessment and enteral-feeding decision-making in critical care; however, existing protocols and their outcome reporting remain fragmented. This scoping review mapped the existing evidence landscape on the use of gastrointestinal point-of-care ultrasound in the management of enteral nutrition in critically ill adults. Comprehensive searches in 10 databases (PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane, CINAHL, Scopus, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang, VIP, China Biological Medicine Literature Database) identified 5,123 records. Studies focusing on ultrasound-assessed gastrointestinal function to guide enteral nutrition, or to predict enteral nutrition intolerance and clinical prognosis, were screened, summarized, and descriptively analyzed. 49 unique studies were identified, including 36 interventional and 13 observational studies. Geographically, the synthesized evidence was heavily concentrated in China. Ultrasound indicators for gastrointestinal function included the gastric antrum (gastric residual volume, motility index, cross-sectional area), colon (colon diameter and peristaltic frequency), small intestine (small intestine diameter, wall thickness, peristalsis), and superior mesenteric artery hemodynamics. Observational studies showed Area Under the Curve point estimates frequently around or above 0.70, with substantial heterogeneity and no independent external validation reported for enteral nutrition intolerance and mortality. Among interventional studies, time to achieve feeding goals and intensive care unit length of stay were the most frequently evaluated outcomes (27/36), whereas in-hospital mortality was evaluated in only 8 of 36 studies; outcome reporting was heterogeneous and is presented descriptively. The synthesized literature suggests the potential utility of gastrointestinal point-of-care ultrasound as an objective, non-invasive bedside tool for gastrointestinal assessment and feeding protocol modulation. However, because no formal critical appraisal or pooled comparative or diagnostic analysis was performed, this review cannot establish clinical effectiveness, universal thresholds, or patient-important benefit. Future research priorities include consensus definitions and acquisition standards, effect estimates with confidence intervals and patient-important outcomes, inter-operator reliability and training evaluation, and external validation across diverse health systems.

articles.title: Knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding enteral nutrition interruption management in intensive care units: a multicenter cross-sectional study predominantly among nurses.
articles.abstract: Enteral nutrition (EN) is essential for critically ill patients, yet enteral nutrition interruption (ENI) is common in intensive care unit (ICU) and compromises nutrient delivery. ENI reflects clinical conditions, workflows, team collaboration, and bedside implementation, but how knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) interact remains unclear. To assess ENI-related knowledge, attitudes, and practices among ICU healthcare professionals, predominantly nurses, and examine their interrelationships and associations with training, demographic, and organizational factors. This multicenter cross-sectional survey included 478 ICU healthcare professionals from 14 hospitals in Shandong and Henan, China, between December 2025 and February 2026; 93.5% were nurses. Self-reported KAP were assessed using a validated questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, Spearman correlation, multiple linear regression, and observed-variable path analysis were conducted. Self-assessed knowledge scores were lower than attitude and practice scores, particularly for items related to the operational definitions of ENI. The three KAP domains were positively correlated, with the strongest correlation between knowledge and practice (ρ = 0.738, p < 0.001). Path analysis suggested that knowledge was associated with both attitudes and practices and that attitudes were also associated with practices. Bootstrap analysis further indicated a possible indirect association between knowledge and practice through attitudes (indirect effect = 0.339, 95% CI 0.246-0.438). EN-related training was associated with higher scores across all three domains, whereas EN team membership was associated with higher knowledge and practice scores. Several demographic and hospital characteristics showed domain-specific associations. The regression models explained a modest proportion of the observed variance (adjusted R 2 = 0.054-0.141). Among ICU healthcare professionals, predominantly nurses, self-reported ENI management practices were associated with knowledge and attitudes, with attitudes potentially playing an intermediary role. EN-related training was also associated with more favorable KAP scores, while organizational and workflow factors may contribute to the observed variation. These findings may help identify potential targets for future intervention development and evaluation but do not establish causal relationships or improvements in actual ENI management, nutrient delivery, or patient outcomes.

articles.title: Body mass index, diabetes, inflammation and survival in COVID-19: a retrospective study evaluating the obesity paradox in an urban hospital center.
articles.journal: Frontiers in clinical diabetes and healthcare
articles.abstract: Severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is associated with increased morbidity and mortality, particularly among patients with comorbidities such as diabetes and obesity. The combined influence of glycemic control, hyperglycemia, and body mass index (BMI) on disease severity remains incompletely understood, particularly in underserved urban populations. This retrospective study evaluated 478 adults hospitalized with confirmed COVID-19 between March and May 2020 at an urban academic medical center to examine the impact of diabetes, glycemic control, and body mass index (BMI) on clinical outcomes. Data collected included demographics, comorbidities, BMI, diabetes type, baseline hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), inflammatory markers, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, mechanical ventilation, hyperglycemia, and glucocorticoid use. Among patients with available HbA1c measurements, those with diabetes who developed cytokine storm had significantly higher mean HbA1c than those without cytokine storm. Obesity and overweight were highly prevalent, with 45% of patients classified as obese (BMI ≥30 kg/m²) and 29% classified as overweight (BMI 25-29 kg/m²). Diabetes was associated with increased ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, and steroid-induced hyperglycemia. Mortality was higher among older patients, Black patients, and those with diabetes, hypertension, hyperglycemia, greater glucocorticoid use, or ICU admission. Notably, patients with overweight or obesity demonstrated improved survival compared with those of normal weight, consistent with an obesity paradox in this urban cohort. Multivariable analysis identified steroid-induced hyperglycemia, obstructive sleep apnea, and higher methylprednisolone use as independent predictors of ICU admission, whereas higher BMI was associated with a lower risk of adverse outcomes. Diabetes and hyperglycemia were associated with greater COVID-19 severity, increased ICU utilization, and higher mortality, while higher BMI offered potential survival benefits. These findings highlight the complex interplay between metabolic dysfunction, obesity, and COVID-19 outcomes, suggesting the presence of an obesity paradox in hospitalized patients, and emphasize the importance of early recognition and management of diabetes and hyperglycemia to improve clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Interprofessional collaboration in emergency department nursing care for patients with diabetic ketoacidosis: a narrative review.
articles.abstract: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is an acute metabolic emergency requiring timely risk recognition, fluid resuscitation, insulin therapy, electrolyte correction, dynamic monitoring, and coordinated care transitions. These interdependent tasks pose substantial challenges to emergency nursing. This narrative review aimed to synthesise current evidence on interprofessional collaboration in emergency DKA nursing and propose a conceptual framework to support coordinated care. A structured narrative review was conducted using literature retrieved from PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and the Web of Science Core Collection from database inception to July 10, 2026. DKA-specific clinical and implementation evidence was integrated with broader literature on interprofessional collaboration, communication, and healthcare implementation. The evidence was synthesised using Donabedian's structure-process-outcome framework. Current collaborative approaches include nurse-led standardised pathways, risk-stratified subcutaneous insulin and non-intensive care unit management, collaborative medication management, laboratory and point-of-care monitoring, structured communication, digital decision support, and multidisciplinary discharge planning. Available evidence suggests that standardised collaborative pathways may improve the timeliness and consistency of care, shorten emergency department length of stay, and reduce intensive care resource use. However, evidence evaluating complete interprofessional nursing teams and nursing-sensitive outcomes remains limited. Based on the synthesis, a conceptual closed-loop collaboration framework comprising six interconnected stages was proposed: recognition and activation, shared risk stratification, coordinated monitoring and execution, escalation, care transition, and recurrence prevention. Effective interprofessional DKA nursing requires shared clinical information, explicit responsibility, timely feedback, and predefined escalation procedures, with emergency nurses serving as continuous information integrators and process coordinators. The proposed framework provides an evidence-informed approach to organising collaborative emergency care. However, it has not been prospectively validated, and further implementation research is required to evaluate its feasibility, safety, and effects on nursing-sensitive and patient outcomes.

articles.title: Medical nutrition therapy during the first 5 days of critical illness: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: The aim of this study was to describe the prescription of medical nutrition therapy for critically ill patients who were admitted to an intensive care unit during the first 5 days. In an observational, longitudinal, retrospective study conducted at the intensive care unit of a tertiary hospital in Mexico City, adult patients admitted from January to December 2018 and from November 2024 to February 2025 were included. Indications for fasting, the route of medical nutrition therapy (enteral nutrition-parenteral nutrition), caloric and protein intakes, sequential organ failure assessment score and lactate levels, and vasopressor requirements during the 5 days were evaluated. Delay in initiating medical nutrition therapy was defined as initiated after 48 h of intensive care unit admission. 100 critically ill patients were included; aged 53±18.8, and with a median sequential organ failure assessment score of 10 (7-12). The most frequent diagnoses at admission were pulmonary disease and septic shock. On the first day, 98% of patients were fasting, and 25% received high-dose vasopressor therapy (if the norepinephrine equivalent dose >0.3 μg/kg/min). Over 5 days, medical nutrition therapy transitioned progressively, predominantly from fasting through enteral nutrition (45%) and parenteral nutrition (11%). medical nutrition therapy delay in 54 patients and in a multivariate analysis was associated with age (OR 1.04; 95%CI 1.01-1.07), sequential organ failure assessment score (OR 1.20; 95%CI 1.02-1.40), and lactate levels (OR 1.8; 95%CI 1.10-3.00). Prescription of medical nutrition therapy in critically ill patients admitted to a intensive care unit during 5 days is dynamic, and in all patients, it is not possible to initiate at 48 h, associated with higher age and illness severity.

articles.title: Pathophysiology-guided nutritional strategies for persistent inflammation, immunosuppression, and catabolism syndrome: an immunometabolic perspective.
articles.abstract: Persistent inflammation, immunosuppression, and catabolism syndrome (PICS) is a phenotype of chronic critical illness characterized by unresolved inflammation, impaired immune competence, sustained catabolism, skeletal muscle loss, recurrent infections, and poor functional recovery. Although guideline-based nutritional support remains fundamental, persistent immunometabolic abnormalities may limit responsiveness to nutrient delivery and contribute to anabolic resistance, impaired substrate utilization, and defective tissue repair. This mini-review examines biological mechanisms limiting nutritional responsiveness in PICS and evaluates evidence for pathophysiology-guided nutritional strategies. A structured literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science was conducted from database inception through September 6, 2026, prioritizing English-language clinical guidelines, clinical studies, and mechanistic or translational evidence relevant to PICS, critical illness, nutritional responsiveness, and immunometabolic nutrition. We propose a framework addressing major barriers to recovery through strategies to restore anabolic responsiveness with protein, leucine, and rehabilitation; modulate inflammatory resolution and immune dysfunction with omega-3 fatty acids and arginine; optimize nutrient timing and circadian-metabolic regulation; and maintain a metabolic milieu conducive to nutrient utilization. Because direct interventional evidence in well-defined PICS populations remains limited, these strategies should complement rather than replace guideline-based nutritional support. The framework is conceptual and hypothesis-generating, and prospective PICS-specific studies incorporating biological stratification and clinically meaningful recovery outcomes are needed to determine its translational value.

articles.title: Beyond blood glucose targets: integrating glucose variability into acute glycemic care in French ICUs - a multicenter prospective study.
articles.abstract: Although hyperglycemia is a common adaptative response in hospitalized intensive care units (ICUs) patients, there are no recommendations regarding blood glucose management protocols. Consequently, practices differ between ICUs. We aimed to prospectively describe glucose management in French-speaking ICUs with the main objective to assess the impact of glucose management on glucose variability within the first 48 h of insulin infusion. A total of 650 patients from 38 ICUs across France and Belgium were included with 649 patients analyzed. Management with tighter glucose targets did not result in an increase in Glycemic Lability Index (OR 0.79, 95% CI [0.51-1.21]; p = 0.28) but episodes of severe hypoglycemia were more frequent in tight blood glucose control group. Nurse workload did not impact glucose variability significantly. Deviations from the protocol were frequent in 24.9% of cases, independently to the blood glucose target used. Percentage spent in the target range was significantly higher in the liberal group (p < 0.01). ICU mortality rate was higher in patients who had at least one episode of hypoglycemia <3.9 mmol/L (p = 0.04), and lower in patients with at least one episode of hyperglycemia >11.1 mmol/L (p = 0.04). Despite heterogenous practices through French speaking ICUs, management with tight blood glucose targets did not significantly impact glucose variability but was associated with higher incidence of severe hypoglycemia.

articles.title: Co-occurring leukocytosis and hyperglycemia identify patients at high risk of subsequent mortality after intracerebral hemorrhage: a 24-h landmark analysis in MIMIC-IV and eICU.
articles.abstract: White blood cell (WBC) count and glucose levels may jointly reflect physiological stress after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). We examined their associations with subsequent in-hospital mortality and whether they improved prediction beyond established clinical information. This retrospective study used the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) and the eICU Collaborative Research Database. Adults with ICH identified by diagnosis codes who were alive and hospitalized 24 h after intensive care unit admission were included. WBC > 10 × 109/L and glucose >140 mg/dL defined four groups: neither elevated, WBC elevation only, glucose elevation only, and both elevated. Logistic regression estimated adjusted associations, with bias reduction in the eICU cohort. Restricted cubic splines assessed nonlinear associations. Prediction models used the minimum first-day Glasgow Coma Scale score alone or a clinical baseline model that also included age, sex, blood pressure, and other laboratory measurements. Models were developed on MIMIC-IV and evaluated without updating in the eICU database. The MIMIC-IV and eICU landmark cohorts included 1,606 and 264 patients, with 332 and 42 subsequent deaths, respectively. Adjusted odds ratios for both markers elevated versus neither elevated were 2.98 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.04-4.36) in MIMIC-IV and 3.34 (95% CI, 0.97-11.54) in eICU. The glucose association in MIMIC-IV was nonlinear (p = 0.005), whereas the WBC curve varied with the spline specification. Among 229 eICU patients with both markers measured, adding the joint category to the clinical baseline model changed the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.796 to 0.811 (difference, 0.014; 95% CI, -0.012 to 0.039) and the Brier score, a measure of prediction error, by -0.0017 (95% CI, -0.0075 to 0.0041). Joint WBC-glucose elevation was associated with subsequent in-hospital mortality in MIMIC-IV, but estimates in the eICU cohort were imprecise. Additional predictive value remained uncertain, and continuous analyses did not establish a stable U-shaped association.

articles.title: Risk management of enteral nutrition-related complications in patients undergoing prone-position ventilation: a narrative review.
articles.abstract: Prone position ventilation (PPV) is a strategy for improving oxygenation in patients with severe hypoxemia, particularly those with acute respiratory distress syndrome. By redistributing transpulmonary pressure, improving ventilation-perfusion matching, and optimizing respiratory mechanics, prone positioning can improve oxygenation and clinical outcomes in selected critically ill patients. However, patients undergoing prone-position ventilation often present with severe disease, hypermetabolism, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and increased nutritional requirements. Early enteral nutrition is generally preferred when hemodynamic status is stable because it helps maintain intestinal mucosal integrity, supports immune function, and reduces the risk of nutrition-related deterioration. Despite these benefits, enteral nutrition during prone-position ventilation remains clinically challenging. Prone positioning, deep sedation, analgesia, neuromuscular blockade, delayed gastric emptying, impaired gastrointestinal motility, and increased intra-abdominal pressure may contribute to feeding intolerance and enteral nutrition-related complications, including high gastric residual volume, vomiting, gastroesophageal reflux, aspiration, diarrhea, feeding interruption, and ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). These complications may compromise nutritional delivery, prolong mechanical ventilation, and adversely affect prognosis. This review summarizes the pathophysiological mechanisms, major risk factors, clinical assessment indicators, and preventive management strategies for enteral nutrition-related complications in patients undergoing prone-position ventilation. Particular attention is given to glycemic control, intra-abdominal pressure monitoring, medication-related gastrointestinal dysfunction, nutritional biomarkers, endotracheal tube cuff pressure, feeding route selection, gastric residual volume assessment, post-pyloric feeding, prokinetic therapy, and positioning management. By integrating evidence and clinical practice considerations, this review aims to provide a practical framework for risk identification, early prevention, dynamic monitoring, and multidisciplinary management of enteral nutrition-related complications during prone-position ventilation.

articles.title: Comparative effects of continuous, cyclic, intermittent, and bolus enteral feeding on feeding intolerance and clinical outcomes in critically ill adults: a protocol for a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Enteral nutrition is recommended for critically ill adults unable to eat adequately. Continuous feeding predominates in intensive care, but cyclic, intermittent, and bolus regimens may confer advantages. Prior reviews combined intermittent and bolus feeding into a single category despite meaningful clinical differences. The comparative effects of all four modes remain uncertain. To compare the effects of continuous, cyclic, intermittent, and bolus enteral feeding on feeding intolerance and clinical outcomes in critically ill adults using a systematic review and network meta-analysis. We will conduct a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomised, cluster-randomised, cross-over, and quasi-randomised controlled trials in critically ill adults receiving gastric enteral nutrition. The intervention network will comprise continuous, cyclic, intermittent, and bolus feeding, classified from procedural details of the administered regimen rather than the terminology used by trial authors. MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, SinoMed, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform will be searched from inception without language restrictions. Two reviewers will independently select studies, extract data, and assess risk of bias using Cochrane RoB 2. The primary outcome will be feeding intolerance as defined by each trial, pooled only where definitions are clinically compatible. Key secondary outcomes, which will be presented in summary-of-findings tables, will be diarrhoea, vomiting, aspiration pneumonia, the proportion of prescribed energy delivered, intensive-care-unit mortality, and duration of mechanical ventilation. Additional secondary outcomes will include further gastrointestinal, respiratory, nutritional, glycaemic, clinical-course, and safety outcomes. Feeding intolerance is the sole confirmatory outcome; all secondary outcomes and all subgroup, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses are exploratory and will be interpreted according to prespecified rules. The false discovery rate will be controlled using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure within prespecified families of comparisons. When the evidence network is connected and transitivity is plausible, Bayesian random-effects network meta-analyses will estimate odds ratios, mean differences or standardised mean differences, and hazard ratios with 95% credible intervals, using arm-level likelihoods where arm-level data are available. Risk ratios from a binomial-log model will be examined in sensitivity analysis. Otherwise, random-effects pairwise meta-analyses (restricted maximum-likelihood estimation with the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment) or synthesis without meta-analysis will be undertaken. Transitivity, heterogeneity, global and local inconsistency, convergence, small-study effects, and robustness to alternative node classifications and prior distributions will be evaluated. Certainty of evidence for the primary and key secondary outcomes will be assessed using CINeMA for network estimates and GRADE for pairwise comparisons. This review will distinguish four clinically meaningful enteral feeding modes and integrate direct and indirect evidence while explicitly addressing uncertain classification and sparse network nodes. The findings may support nursing protocols, nutrition practice, and future critical-care nutrition research.

articles.title: Effects of enteral nutrition strategies on clinical outcomes in critically ill patients with shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Shock is a life-threatening clinical emergency that demands a sound treatment strategy. Nutritional support is among the key adjuvant therapies, but its application in shock remains controversial. This study explores how early enteral nutrition (EEN) affects the outcome of critically ill patients admitted with shock. This meta-analysis searched PubMed, the Cochrane Library, EMBASE, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) over a period from the inception of each database to October 31, 2025. Critically ill patients admitted with shock were included as the study cohort. The primary outcomes were 28-day mortality and 90-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU mortality, ICU length of stay (LOS-ICU), in-hospital mortality, hospital length of stay (LOS-H), ventilator-free days (VFD), nosocomial infection/reinfection, and adverse complications. Thirteen trials were included in this study. For the primary outcomes, EEN was not associated with 28-day mortality [relative risk (RR) = 1.03, 95% CI: 0.93-1.14] and 90-day mortality (RR = 1.04, 95% CI: 0.95-1.14). For secondary outcomes, EEN decreased LOS-ICU [standardized mean difference (SMD) = -0.28, 95% confidence interval (CI): -0.53 to -0.03] and LOS-H (SMD = -0.41, 95% CI: -0.61 to -0.21), without affecting VFD, nosocomial infection or reinfection, and Adverse reactions or complications. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested that the benefits of EEN varied by nutritional regimen. The high initial protein group was linked to lower LOS-ICU (SMD = -0.94, 95% CI: -1.59 to -0.30). The high initial calorie group was associated with shorter LOS-H (SMD = -0.12, 95% CI: -0.20 to -0.04), whereas the low initial calorie group reduced the adverse reactions or complications (RR = 0.44, 95% CI: 0.25 to 0.77). In critically ill patients with shock, EEN with high initial caloric or protein supply may reduce hospital stay, whereas low initial caloric early enteral nutrition is associated with fewer adverse reactions. Given post-hoc subgroup limitations and marked population heterogeneity, findings should be interpreted cautiously. Additional high-quality trials are needed to develop individualized nutritional strategies for these patients.Systematic Review Registration: identifier CRD420261282657.

articles.title: Trends and Frontiers in nutritional management for ICU patients with kidney dysfunction: a bibliometric and knowledge mapping study.
articles.abstract: Patients with kidney dysfunction in the intensive care unit (ICU) are at high risk of metabolic disturbances and malnutrition, yet the research landscape of nutritional management in this population remains incompletely characterized. This study aimed to map the knowledge structure, research hotspots, and temporal trends in this field. Publications from 2001 to 2025 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and analyzed using VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and bibliometrix. Scopus was used for cross-database comparison, while representative clinical studies retrieved from PubMed were descriptively summarized to provide clinical context for the bibliometric findings. A total of 551 publications were included, with publication output increasing overall from 2001 to 2025. Research activity was concentrated mainly in North America and Europe. Keyword analysis identified major themes related to acute kidney injury, renal replacement therapy, nutritional support, prognosis, and clinical outcomes. Temporal analyses showed that earlier research focused more on acute renal failure, RRT, and nitrogen balance, whereas nutritional risk, protein provision, and clinical outcomes became more prominent in later years. Burst analysis further identified "outcome," "impact," "hospitalized patients," and "malnutrition" as active recent keywords. This study indicates sustained research interest in nutritional management for ICU patients with kidney dysfunction. Research has broadened from RRT-related metabolic concerns to nutritional assessment, protein provision, and clinical outcomes. Protein dose and escalation timing, nutrient replacement during CRRT, and the use of nutritional risk assessment to guide treatment remain important questions for future clinical studies.

articles.title: Intensive vs. conventional glycemic control in critically ill cardiac patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract: Hyperglycemia is common during cardiac surgery and acute cardiac illness, but the balance between potential benefits and harms of lower glucose targets remains uncertain. PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched through 21 December 2024. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials comparing an intensive with a conventional glycemic-control protocol in adults undergoing cardiac surgery or experiencing an acute cardiac condition. Stroke and myocardial infarction were primary outcomes. Atrial fibrillation, 30-day mortality, infection, sepsis, acute renal dysfunction, intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay, and hospital length of stay were secondary outcomes. Risk ratios (RRs) or mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled. Prespecified disease-based subgroup analyses and interaction tests were performed. Sixteen unique randomized trials representing 6,525 participants were included. Intensive glycemic control was associated with fewer strokes (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.23-0.55; I 2 = 0%) but not fewer myocardial infarctions (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.82-1.13; I 2 = 9%). It was associated with lower risks of infection (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.37-0.67; I 2 = 0%) and acute renal dysfunction (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.57-0.94), but not with 30-day mortality (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.70-1.22), ICU stay (MD 3.03 h, 95% CI -0.84 to 6.89), or hospital stay (MD -0.02 days, 95% CI -0.50 to 0.46). Atrial fibrillation was lower after non-CABG cardiac surgery but not after CABG. Tests for interaction by cardiac condition were not significant. Lower-target protocols may reduce selected complications, particularly stroke and infection, but the evidence is heterogeneous and does not support routine glucose targets below current critical-care recommendations. Treatment should prioritize avoidance of both marked hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia, protocolized monitoring, and individualized targets. Larger contemporary trials that report hypoglycemia and glycemic variability are required.Systematic Review Registration: PROSPERO CRD42023418963.

articles.title: Early change in serum prealbumin adds predictive value for Day-7 enteral nutrition response in critically ill adults: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Single serum prealbumin (PAB) measurements are difficult to interpret during critical illness because they are strongly influenced by inflammation and disease severity. We investigated whether early changes in PAB after enteral nutrition (EN) initiation were associated with an operationally defined Day 7 EN response and added predictive value to that of routinely available clinical variables. This single-center retrospective cohort study screened 341 critically ill adults. The primary cohort comprised 263 patients with PAB measured at baseline, Day 3, and Day 7; an expanded sensitivity cohort comprised 271 patients with baseline and Day 3 PAB and ascertainable Day 7 EN outcomes, irrespective of Day 7 PAB availability. Day 7 EN response required energy target achievement ≥70%, protein delivery ≥1.0 g/kg/day, no gastrointestinal (GI)-related EN interruption >24 h, and no supplemental parenteral nutrition (PN) before assessment. We used multivariable logistic regression analyses, component-specific analyses, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, calibration, decision-curve analysis, restricted cubic splines, and 2,000-resample bootstrap validation. In the primary cohort, 154 of the 263 patients (58.6%) were responders. Each 10 mg/L increase in Day-3 ΔPAB was independently associated with higher odds of response (adjusted odds ratio 2.67, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.89-3.76; p < 0.001). Adding Day 3 ΔPAB to the clinical model increased the area under the curve (AUC) from 0.804 to 0.869 (ΔAUC 0.065, bootstrap 95% confidence interval 0.031-0.107; DeLong p < 0.001). In the expanded cohort, the corresponding adjusted odds ratio was 2.34 (1.72-3.19), and the AUC increased from 0.783 to 0.849 (ΔAUC 0.066; DeLong p = 0.001). Component analyses showed associations with energy and protein target attainment, whereas estimates for prolonged gastrointestinal interruption and supplemental parenteral nutrition were imprecise because these events were uncommon. An early increase in PAB was independently associated with Day 7 EN response and improved prediction beyond routine clinical, inflammatory, and nutritional variables. Day 3 ΔPAB should be interpreted as an adjunctive dynamic signal rather than a stand-alone marker of nutritional status, and external validation is required.

articles.title: Association between route of nutrition and serum I-FABP and MMP-9 levels in critically ill patients with acute ischemic stroke: a prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Gut barrier dysfunction and neuroinflammation are increasingly recognised as linked pathophysiological processes in acute ischaemic stroke (AIS). However, the influence of nutritional routes on these processes remains poorly characterised. To compare the longitudinal effects of enteral nutrition (EN) versus parenteral nutrition (PN) on serum intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP), a marker of intestinal epithelial integrity, and matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9), a marker of neuroinflammatory activity, in critically ill AIS patients. Prospective observational cohort study. A tertiary neurology intensive care unit (ICU) in Türkiye. Consecutive adults (≥18 years) admitted to the neurology ICU within 24 hours of a confirmed AIS diagnosis were enrolled between October 2024 and January 2026. Nutritional route was assigned by the treating clinician according to ESPEN guidelines. Serum I-FABP and MMP-9 concentrations were measured using commercial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits at baseline and on day 7. Longitudinal changes in serum I-FABP and MMP-9 concentrations between baseline and day 7, and their correlations with neurological severity (NIHSS). 73 patients (40 EN, 33 PN). Median age was 73 years (interquartile range, 64-80) and 37 (51%) were female. At baseline, I-FABP and MMP-9 levels were comparable between groups (all P>.05). Over the 7-day observation period, I-FABP trajectories diverged between groups (EN: 7.22 (2.68) to 6.69 (2.78) ng/mL; PN: 6.74 (3.09) to 7.82 (2.97) ng/mL), as did MMP-9 trajectories (EN: 11.5 (1.45) to 10.9 (2.31) ng/mL; PN: 11.3 (2.41) to 11.8 (1.87) ng/mL). At day 7, both biomarkers correlated significantly with NIHSS score (ρ=0.385 and ρ=0.440, respectively; both P<.001). Repeated measures analysis of covariance, adjusted for baseline NIHSS score, confirmed significant time × nutritional route interactions for both biomarkers (I-FABP: F[1,70]=4.22, P=0.044, P_FDR=.044, η2p=.057; MMP-9: F[1,70]= 4.76, P=.033, P_FDR=.044, η2p=0.064). In critically ill AIS patients, EN was associated with more favourable 7-day trajectories of gut barrier integrity and neuroinflammatory activity compared with PN, after adjustment for baseline stroke severity. Single-center design, biomarker sampling restricted to two time points, reliance on delivered rather than utilised nutritional measures, and non-randomised nutritional route assignment with residual potential for confounding by indication.

articles.title: Relationship Between Level of Consciousness, Pressure Ulcer Risk, and Pain Behaviors in Mechanically Ventilated Patients.
articles.abstract: Mechanically ventilated patients are vulnerable to pain, pressure injuries, and decreased levels of consciousness. This descriptive and correlational study examined the relationship between the level of consciousness, pressure injury risk, and pain behaviors in 150 patients treated in the intensive care units of a university hospital between November 2023 and February 2024. Data were collected using the Behavioral Pain Scale (BPS), Jackson/Cubbin Pressure Area Risk Assessment Tool, and Full Outline of UnResponsiveness (FOUR) Score. The mean FOUR Score was 6.78 ± 2.15, the mean Jackson/Cubbin score was 29.68 ± 2.79, and the mean BPS score was 4.73 ± 1.46. Pressure injury risk was significantly related to inotropic support and skin integrity (P < .001). Patients receiving enteral nutrition and those without sedation or inotropic support had higher BPS scores (P < .05). Weak positive correlations were found between the FOUR Score and both BPS (r = 0.190) and Jackson/Cubbin scores (r = 0.306). In conclusion, although patients had low consciousness and pain levels, regular assessment of pain, skin integrity, and consciousness remains essential for preventing complications and guiding individualized nursing care in intensive care settings.

articles.title: State-of-the-art review: ß-blockade in critical illness.
articles.abstract: Critical illness is characterised by activation of the sympathetic nervous system which plays an important adaptive role in maintaining cardiovascular stability and organ perfusion. However, excessive sustained adrenergic stimulation may become maladaptive, contributing to tachyarrhythmias, myocardial injury, immune dysregulation, metabolic derangements, and organ dysfunction. This state-of-the-art review evaluates the role of ß-blocker therapy as a potential strategy to modulate or counteract the adrenergic response in critically ill patients. Current data suggest that their use remains highly context-dependent and controversial. There are established benefits in selected scenarios, including acute myocardial infarction, tachyarrhythmias, hypertensive emergencies, thyroid storm, and prevention of variceal bleeds. In contrast, evidence is limited or conflicting in septic shock, traumatic brain injury, acute heart failure, burns and other critical care syndromes. Concerns include impairment of compensatory cardiovascular responses, reduction of cardiac output, hypotension, and compromised organ perfusion. Furthermore, the safety and efficacy of ß-blockade appear to depend on the type and dose of ß-blocker, patient phenotype, timing of initiation, hemodynamic reserve, and whether therapy represents continuation of chronic treatment, withdrawal and re-initiation, or de novo initiation during acute illness. This review highlights major gaps in knowledge, including the absence of reliable indicators to identify patients most likely to benefit, uncertainty regarding optimal treatment targets and monitoring strategies, and limited randomised evidence in heterogeneous ICU populations. A phenotype-driven, physiology-guided approach that accounts for hemodynamic status, sympathetic spectrum and timing of ß-blocker therapy is likely required to optimise outcomes.

articles.title: Sodium Bicarbonate for Critically Ill Adults with Metabolic Acidosis and Shock.
articles.journal: The New England journal of medicine
authors: SODa-BIC Investigators and the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Clinical Trials Group
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Metabolic acidosis is common in critically ill patients and is associated with organ dysfunction and death. Sodium bicarbonate is used to correct acidemia, but its benefit in patients with metabolic acidosis who are receiving vasopressors remains uncertain. METHODS: In this pragmatic, adaptive, double-blind, randomized trial, we assigned adults with metabolic acidosis (pH, <7.30; base excess, no more than -4 mmol per liter; and partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide, ≤45 mm Hg without intubation or ≤50 mm Hg with intubation) who were receiving vasopressors in the intensive care unit (ICU) to receive either sodium bicarbonate or placebo (5% dextrose). Sodium bicarbonate or placebo was infused for up to 5 hours, with the infusion rate adjusted for a target pH of at least 7.30 and base excess of at least 0 mmol per liter. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event, defined as death, use of renal-replacement therapy, or persistent renal dysfunction, within 30 days. RESULTS: A total of 500 patients were enrolled in 55 ICUs across seven countries; 245 patients were assigned to receive sodium bicarbonate and 255 to receive placebo. A major adverse kidney event within 30 days occurred in 98 of 244 patients (40.2%) in the sodium bicarbonate group and in 100 of 254 patients (39.4%) in the placebo group (adjusted difference, 1.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -7.1 to 9.4; P = 0.78). Renal-replacement therapy was used within 30 days in 16.8% of the patients in the sodium bicarbonate group and in 20.9% of those in the placebo group (adjusted difference, -3.9 percentage points; 95% CI, -10.6 to 2.7). In-hospital mortality by day 30 was 25.4% in the sodium bicarbonate group and 24.0% in the placebo group (adjusted difference, 1.8 percentage points; 95% CI, -5.6 to 9.2). Four patients (1.6%) in the sodium bicarbonate group had an adverse effect, as compared with none in the placebo group (P = 0.06). CONCLUSIONS: The use of sodium bicarbonate in critically ill patients with metabolic acidosis receiving vasopressors did not lead to a lower risk of major adverse kidney events within 30 days than placebo. (Funded by the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia; SODa-BIC ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05697770.).
articles.ai_summary: Researchers conducted a randomized trial of 500 critically ill patients with metabolic acidosis and shock to see if sodium bicarbonate reduced kidney damage. The results showed no difference in kidney damage or mortality between patients who received sodium bicarbonate and those who received a placebo. The study found that sodium bicarbonate did not provide a benefit in reducing kidney damage or improving outcomes in critically ill patients.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings are significant for ICU clinical practice as they suggest that sodium bicarbonate may not be beneficial in reducing kidney damage or improving outcomes in critically ill patients with metabolic acidosis and shock. Clinicians may need to reconsider using sodium bicarbonate in these patients.

articles.title: Individualising blood glucose control in ICU patients: evidence and practical implementations.
articles.abstract: Many intensive care unit patients develop hyperglycaemia, and this is associated with an increased risk of adverse outcomes. Landmark randomised controlled trials (RCTs) suggest the impact of lowering blood glucose to the healthy, age-adjusted fasting range, hereafter called tight glucose control, depends on the accuracy of the glucose control protocol and the nutritional strategy. In the context of early parenteral nutrition, a condition that induces severe, iatrogenic hyperglycaemia, tight glucose control significantly reduced morbidity and mortality compared to tolerating severe hyperglycaemia. In the absence of early parenteral nutrition, hyperglycaemia was less severe; tight glucose control, applied with a computerised protocol that avoided severe hypoglycaemia, did not impact mortality nor the duration of ICU dependency as primary endpoint in a large multicentre RCT, but was associated with a less pronounced benefit on selected morbidity outcomes. Conversely, tight glucose control, using a protocol that considerably increased the risk of severe hypoglycaemic events, concomitantly increased mortality; nevertheless, the cause of excess mortality in this trial remains unproven and other mechanisms may have contributed as well. Altogether, evidence suggests that severe and iatrogenic hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia should both be avoided. From a pathophysiologic point of view, tight glucose control may be superior in selected settings if it can be applied with a validated protocol that avoids severe hypoglycaemia. In the absence of such a protocol, the increased risk of severe hypoglycaemia may offset any benefit of preventing hyperglycaemia, and tolerating intermediate blood glucose targets is likely the default setting. In the paper, we suggest specific blood glucose targets that differ according to the clinical context. Future research should aim at strategies that further optimise the quality of blood glucose control and study whether these improve patient-centred outcomes, and investigate whether specific patient populations benefit from individualised targets.

articles.title: Induction Agents for Tracheal Intubation of Critically Ill Patients: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tracheal intubation is a common yet high-risk procedure in critically ill patients, with as many as one-half experiencing peri-intubation adverse outcomes. RESEARCH QUESTION: What is the comparative effectiveness and safety of various sedative agents used for endotracheal intubation of critically ill patients in the emergency department (ED), ICU, operating room, and prehospital setting? STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: We conducted a network meta-analysis and systematic review of randomized controlled trials. We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, PubMed, Cochrane, and trial registries from inception through December 10, 2025, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing ≥ 2 sedative agents in critically ill adults or children undergoing endotracheal intubation. Outcomes of interest were hemodynamic instability during intubation, hypoxemia, cardiac arrest, mortality, ICU and hospital length of stay, vasopressor use, adrenal insufficiency, and first-pass success. Reviewers screened, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool independently and in duplicate. We performed frequentist random-effects model network meta-analysis and used the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach to rate certainty in estimates. RESULTS: We included 21 RCTs enrolling 6,031 patients across ICU, ED, operating room, and prehospital settings. Compared with etomidate, more hemodynamic instability exists during intubation with ketamine (relative risk [RR], 1.31; 95% CI, 1.15-1.48; moderate certainty). Ketamine-propofol may decrease hemodynamic instability during intubation compared with etomidate (RR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.27-0.72; low certainty) and ketamine (RR, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.21-0.56; low certainty). Compared with etomidate, ketamine may decrease the need for the initiation of postintubation continuous infusion vasopressors (RR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.50-1.28; low certainty). Etomidate caused increased adrenal suppression compared with other agents. INTERPRETATION: Our results show that when considering sedation agents for endotracheal intubation of critically ill patients, etomidate probably causes less hemodynamic instability during intubation when compared with ketamine. However, etomidate may increase the need for the initiation of postintubation continuous infusion vasopressors when compared with ketamine and increases adrenal suppression. The clinical importance of these competing effects remains uncertain. Ketamine-propofol may decrease hemodynamic instability during intubation when compared with etomidate and ketamine, although the available evidence is too limited and uncertain to support firm conclusions, and further randomized trials are needed. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews; No.: CRD42024600739; URL: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/.

articles.title: Sodium Bicarbonate for Acute Metabolic Acidosis in Critically Ill Adults: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Acute metabolic acidosis is frequent in critical illness and may be managed with volume replacement therapy, sodium bicarbonate, and renal replacement therapy (RRT). BICARICU-1 and BICARICU-2 trials provided new evidence on bicarbonate therapy. We aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of sodium bicarbonate in critically ill patients. DATA SOURCES: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Medline, and the Cochrane Library for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating sodium bicarbonate vs. placebo in critically ill adults with acute metabolic acidosis. STUDY SELECTION: Only RCTs were selected. DATA EXTRACTION: Primary outcome was RRT; secondary outcomes were mortality, ICU length of stay, ventilator-free days, and vasopressor-free days. DATA SYNTHESIS: We performed Hartung-Knapp random-effects meta-analyses and trial sequential analysis (TSA) for primary outcomes. Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses with noninformative and weakly informative priors were used for sensitivity analysis. Four trials enrolling 1,111 patients were included. Sodium bicarbonate showed a nonsignificant trend toward lower mortality (risk ratio [RR], 0.84; 95% CI, 0.55-1.30); TSA indicated that the cumulative sample size remained far below the required information size, and the mortality effect is inconclusive. Sodium bicarbonate significantly reduced RRT use (RR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.61-0.78), and TSA supported firm evidence of benefit. Bayesian analyses estimated posterior probabilities of any mortality reduction (RR < 1) and reduced RRT use of 90.4% and 94.6%, respectively. Secondary outcomes remained imprecise, with a trend of toward more vasopressor-free days. CONCLUSIONS: In critically ill adults with acute metabolic acidosis, sodium bicarbonate significantly reduces RRT requirement, with Bayesian analyses suggesting a possibility of mortality benefit, although current evidence remains inconclusive. Larger RCTs or high-quality real-world studies are needed to confirm efficacy of sodium bicarbonate for mortality.
articles.ai_summary: This meta-analysis of 4 trials found that sodium bicarbonate reduced the need for renal replacement therapy in critically ill adults with acute metabolic acidosis, and may also lower mortality, although evidence is still inconclusive.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings suggest that sodium bicarbonate may be a useful treatment for critically ill patients with acute metabolic acidosis, but more research is needed to confirm its effects on mortality.

articles.title: Glycemic Ratio Is a Superior Predictor of Mortality Compared With Stress Hyperglycemia Ratio in Critically Ill Patients.
articles.journal: Journal of diabetes science and technology
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The glycemic ratio (GR), defined as the ratio of mean intensive care unit (ICU) blood glucose (BG) to estimated preadmission BG (EPBG), may provide superior prognostic insight compared with the single admission snapshot represented by the stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR, the ratio of ICU admission BG to EPAG). METHODS: This retrospective study included 4148 patients treated in a university-affiliated medical-surgical ICU from 2019 to 2023 who had >4 ICU BG measurements and a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) measured at admission. We compared SHR and GR prognostic ability for mortality, analyzed across prespecified GR and SHR bands, and calculated observed:expected mortality ratios (OEMRs). RESULTS: We observed a more sharply defined J-shaped relationship between GR and mortality compared with that generated by SHR. Mortality in the reference band of 0.8 to <1.0 for GR and SHR mortality was 7.5% vs 10.9%, respectively (P = .0087), and for the strata ≥1.4, mortality was 25.6% vs 20.5% (P = .0376). Compared with the reference band, GR < 0.8 and GR > 1.0 had higher OEMR (P < .0001 for each), but the OEMR for SHR <0.8 and >1.0 compared with the reference band was not significantly different. CONCLUSIONS: Glycemic ratio was superior to SHR as a predictor of mortality. This study demonstrates that a mean ICU BG level representing 80% to 100% of the patient's EPBG was associated with the lowest mortality rate in a heterogeneous cohort of critically ill patients. These results may inform current BG management strategies and should be considered when designing future interventional trials in the critically ill.
articles.ai_summary: This study compared two ways to predict mortality in critically ill patients: using a single blood glucose measurement at admission, and using a ratio of mean ICU blood glucose to estimated preadmission blood glucose. The study found that the ratio method was a better predictor of mortality. The best outcome was associated with a mean ICU blood glucose level that was 80-100% of the patient's preadmission level.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings may improve blood glucose management strategies in the ICU and inform the design of future clinical trials.

articles.title: A Cross-sectional Study to Examine the Prognostic Value of Glycated Hemoglobin Levels and Glycated Hemoglobin-adjusted Glycemic Variables in Patients with Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Dysglycemia, including both chronic hyperglycemia and stress-induced hyperglycemia, has been increasingly recognized as an important determinant of outcomes in critically ill patients. However, the prognostic value of glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)-adjusted glycemic indices in AECOPD remains poorly understood. OBJECTIVES: To assess the role of HbA1c and HbA1c-adjusted glycemic indices (glycemic gap, stress hyperglycemia ratio, and modified stress hyperglycemia ratio) in predicting outcomes in AECOPD. To determine the correlation between HbA1c-based adjusted glycemic variables in patients with AECOPD. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted on 102 patients admitted with AECOPD. HbA1c and admission glucose were measured, and HbA1c-adjusted glycemic indices were calculated. Outcomes, such as respiratory failure, intensive care unit admission, and mortality, were analyzed. RESULTS: Patients with adverse outcomes had significantly higher HbA1c, admission glucose, glycemic gap, and stress hyperglycemia ratio. Stress hyperglycemia ratio and glycemic gap showed superior predictive accuracy for adverse outcomes compared to HbA1c or admission glucose alone. CONCLUSION: HbA1c-adjusted glycemic indices are powerful predictors of clinical outcomes in AECOPD and can be used as simple, cost-effective prognostic tools in routine clinical practice.
articles.ai_summary: This study examined the relationship between glycated hemoglobin levels and glycemic variables in patients with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It found that HbA1c-adjusted glycemic indices, such as glycemic gap and stress hyperglycemia ratio, were strong predictors of clinical outcomes. These indices may be useful in predicting patient outcomes and guiding treatment decisions.
articles.ai_significance: Understanding the prognostic value of glycated hemoglobin levels and glycemic variables can help clinicians identify patients at high risk of adverse outcomes and tailor their treatment approach accordingly.

articles.title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring for Adult ICU Patients: A Meta-Analysis on Its Clinical Effectiveness.
articles.abstract: Critically ill patients often suffer from disrupted glucose metabolism, and well-managed blood glucose is a key determinant of clinical outcomes. While continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) is regarded as a viable alternative, its overall effectiveness in adult ICU patients remains controversial. This study aims to conduct a systematic evaluation on the effects of CGM versus conventional intermittent blood glucose monitoring on glycemic management among adult critically ill patients in ICUs. Literature searches were carried out across seven electronic databases including PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang Data and VIP, from database inception up to May 18, 2026. Included studies were RCTs that compared CGM with conventional intermittent glucose monitoring in adult ICU patients. A total of 22 eligible RCTs with 1,396 enrolled patients were incorporated into the meta-analysis. The pooled estimates showed that CGM was associated with a significant reduction in hypoglycemic events (RR = 0.41, 95% CI: 0.31-0.54, I2 = 24.9%) and average blood glucose levels (MD = -0.34 mmol/L, 95% CI: -0.55 to -0.13, I2 = 68.3%). The intervention also prolonged time in glycemic target range (MD = 10.12%, 95% CI: 6.03%-14.21%, I2 = 67.5%), cut down daily insulin use (MD = -22.17 U/day, 95% CI: -26.82 to -17.52, I2 = 37.7%), and reduced total mortality (RR = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.34-0.65, I2 = 0.0%). Our results suggest integrating CGM into routine ICU glycemic control strategies, particularly for patients with severe glycemic variability and high hypoglycemia risk.

articles.title: Nutrition Therapy in Critically Ill Adults.
articles.journal: The New England journal of medicine
articles.abstract: In the acute phase of critical illness, adults have severe catabolism, inflammation, muscle loss, and gut dysfunction, all of which shape nutritional requirements.
