Early enteral nutrition supports gut integrity and microbiome health, but trials have shown that early short-term parenteral nutrition is a safe alternative when enteral feeding is not possible. Large trials have shown that early full-dose energy delivery offers no benefit over restrictive dosing and may increase gastrointestinal and metabolic complications, findings that support a restrictive nutrition strategy, especially in patients who have circulatory shock or are at risk for refeeding syndrome. Similarly, large trials have shown no advantage of high-dose over standard-dose protein and suggest harm in patients with acute kidney injury. Because adverse events are common with enteral nutrition, safe nutrition delivery requires gradual advancement, strategies for prevention of refeeding syndrome, glycemic control, and avoidance of routine gastric residual volume monitoring. Patient heterogeneity underscores the need for precise, biomarker-guided, phase-specific nutrition to preserve lean muscle mass and improve recovery.

articles.title: Bedside identification of subphenotypes in acute respiratory failure (PHIND): a multicentre, observational cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a clinically defined, biologically heterogeneous condition with no proven disease-modifying therapies. Retrospective analyses have identified two biologically distinct subphenotypes (hyperinflammatory and hypoinflammatory) of ARDS, with differing outcomes and responses to therapy. Rapid identification of these subphenotypes in an actionable timeframe has previously not been possible. The PHIND study aimed to prospectively identify these subphenotypes and to demonstrate differing 60-day mortality. METHODS: The PHIND study was a prospective, multicentre, observational cohort study conducted in intensive care units (ICUs) within the National Health Service in the UK and the Health Service Executive in Ireland. Adult patients aged 18 years and older with ARDS or acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure (AHRF) were enrolled within 72 h of onset of the syndrome. Eligible patients were required to be receiving invasive mechanical ventilation, non-invasive ventilation, or high-flow nasal oxygen. Plasma interleukin (IL-6) and soluble TNF receptor-1 (TNFR1) were quantified at enrolment using a near-patient benchtop immunoanalyser (Randox multiSTAT) with a run time of approximately 1 h. Together with plasma bicarbonate measured from an arterial blood sample, these values were used to prospectively determine subphenotypes on an individual patient basis using a validated parsimonious logistic regression model. The primary outcome was 60-day mortality. The study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04009330. FINDINGS: Between Nov 22, 2019, and Sept 28, 2023, 1853 patients from 30 centres were screened for eligibility. Of these, 1328 were excluded and 525 were recruited into the study, with 512 individuals included. 308 (60%) patients were male, 204 (40%) were female, and mean age was 57·0 years (SD 15·1). 443 (87%) patients were white, 18 (4%) were Black, and 16 (3%) were Asian. 490 were subphenotyped using the near-patient assay: 89 (18%) were classified as hyperinflammatory and 401 (82%) as hypoinflammatory. The primary outcome of 60-day mortality was measured in 486 patients after four patients withdrew consent for confirmation of vital status. 60-day mortality was significantly higher in the hyperinflammatory group (45 [51%] of 88) than in the hypoinflammatory group (111 [28%] of 398; risk ratio 1·8 [95% CI 1·4-2·4], p<0·0001). After adjustment, hyperinflammatory patients had increased odds of 60-day mortality (adjusted odds ratio 2·7 [95% CI 1·6-4·4], p=0·0002). INTERPRETATION: Rapid identification of ARDS inflammatory subphenotypes using a near-patient assay was feasible and associated with many clinical characteristics and outcomes consistent with those described in earlier retrospective studies, including mortality, prevalence of sepsis, and incidence of metabolic acidosis. These findings support the implementation of precision medicine approaches in ARDS and the urgent need for prospective, subphenotype-stratified interventional trials. FUNDING: Innovate UK, Randox Laboratories, and Belfast Health & Social Care Trust.

articles.title: Implementation of the kidney protection strategy in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury - a multi-center prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The international Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines recommend the implementation of a kidney protection strategy (KPS) in patients at high risk of and with Acute Kidney Injury (AKI). However, real-world implementation of this strategy in critically ill patients with AKI is unclear. We quantified timely and sustained adherence to KPS in critically ill adults with moderate-to-severe (KDIGO stage 2 or 3) AKI and explored associations with clinical outcomes. METHODS: This was a multicenter, prospective cohort study enrolling adult patients with moderate or severe AKI requiring vasopressors and/or mechanical ventilation across five centers in Europe. The primary endpoint was adherence to the KPS, which included hemodynamic monitoring, sustained optimization of mean arterial pressure (MAP) > 65 mmHg, monitoring of serum creatinine and urine output, and avoidance of hyperglycemia, radiocontrast agents and nephrotoxins when possible, within 12 h after AKI diagnosis for 48 h or until ICU discharge. Exploratory analyses examined associations between adherence and renal outcomes. RESULTS: A total of 258 patients were enrolled (median age 69 years [IQR 62-75]; 65% male; median SOFA 10 [IQR 8-13]). The complete KPS was implemented in 80 patients (31%; 95% CI, 25.5-37.2%). Adherence to individual components of the KPS varied widely with optimization of MAP showing the lowest implementation rate (33%). In exploratory analyses accounting for death as a competing risk, KPS adherence was associated with a lower incidence of AKD beyond day 7 (subdistribution hazard ratio [SHR] 0.64; 95% CI, 0.41-0.99; p = 0.046), a higher incidence of renal recovery at hospital discharge (SHR 6.02; 95% CI, 4.00-9.05; p < 0.0001), and a lower incidence of RRT within 30 days (SHR 0.12; 95% CI, 0.02-0.91; p = 0.04). After multivariable adjustment, the association with renal recovery remained robust (adjusted SHR 6.29; 95% CI, 3.08-12.85; p < 0.0001). A clear dose-response relationship was observed between the number of implemented KPS components and renal outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: In critically ill patients with moderate-to-severe AKI, the complete KDIGO-recommended kidney protection strategy was implemented in approximately one-third of patients, and full KPS adherence was associated with a higher rate of renal recovery at hospital discharge.
articles.ai_summary: This study looked at how well a kidney protection strategy was implemented in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury. They found that about a third of patients received the full strategy, and those who did had a higher rate of kidney recovery. The study also found a link between the number of strategy components implemented and better kidney outcomes.
articles.ai_significance: This study is important for ICU clinicians because it highlights the need to implement a kidney protection strategy in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury to improve kidney recovery rates.

articles.title: Predictors and Mortality Determinants of Non-Thyroidal Illness Syndrome Among Patients in the Medical Intensive Care Unit in Northeastern Tanzania.
articles.journal: Clinical medicine insights. Endocrinology and diabetes
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS) frequently occurs in critically ill patients and reflects alterations in thyroid hormone metabolism without intrinsic thyroid disease. It has been increasingly recognized as a potential marker of disease severity and poor outcomes in intensive care settings, yet data from Sub-Saharan Africa remain limited. To determine the prevalence of NTIS and identify determinants of mortality among patients admitted to a medical intensive care unit (ICU) in northern Tanzania. METHODS: We conducted a prospective cohort study among 120 adult patients admitted to the medical ICU at a tertiary referral hospital between October 2024 and March 2025. Thyroid function tests (T3, T4, and TSH) were measured within 24 hours of admission. NTIS was defined based on characteristic biochemical patterns in the absence of known thyroid disease. Clinical, laboratory, and outcome data were collected prospectively. Associations were assessed using Chi-square tests and modified Poisson regression to estimate adjusted risk ratios (aRR) with 95% confidence intervals. RESULTS: The prevalence of NTIS was 23.3%. Overall mortality was 42.5%, with significantly higher mortality among patients with NTIS (67.9%) compared with those without NTIS (34.8%). NTIS remained independently associated with mortality after adjustment (aRR 8.05; 95% CI: 2.27-28.56; p=0.001). Patients with NTIS were also more likely to experience prolonged hospital stays. Although several clinical variables showed associations in bivariate analysis, most did not remain significant after adjustment. Illness severity, as reflected by clinical scoring systems, remained an important contributor to outcomes. CONCLUSION: NTIS is common among critically ill patients and is strongly associated with increased mortality. It may serve as a practical prognostic marker in ICU settings, particularly in resource-limited environments. Further multicenter studies are needed to validate its prognostic utility and integration into routine clinical practice.
articles.ai_summary: Researchers studied 120 critically ill patients in Tanzania and found that 23.3% had Non-Thyroidal Illness Syndrome (NTIS), which was strongly linked to higher mortality and longer hospital stays. NTIS is a common condition in ICU patients and may be a useful marker for predicting poor outcomes. Patients with NTIS had a much higher risk of death compared to those without NTIS.
articles.ai_significance: This study highlights the importance of NTIS as a potential prognostic marker in ICU settings, particularly in resource-limited environments. It suggests that NTIS could be used to identify patients at higher risk of mortality and inform clinical decision-making.

articles.title: Combined impact of glucose variability and mineral disorders on mortality and severe cardiorenal events in critically ill CKD patients: a multicenter cohort study.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Elderly critically ill ICU patients with CKD face high mortality. The independent and combined prognostic roles of glycemic variability (Glucose CV) and calcium-phosphate metabolic disorders in this population remain unconfirmed. METHODS: This retrospective study contained three cohorts: MIMIC-IV (n = 1,319, development), multicenter eICU (n = 996, validation), and Chinese hospital cohort (n = 1,069, clinical validation). Multivariable Cox regression and meta-analysis were applied. RESULTS: Elevated Glucose CV independently predicted 28- and 90-day mortality with predominant early risk. Concurrent hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia indicated the poorest prognosis, and high GV produced synergistic harmful effects in this subgroup. All results were verified by external cohorts. DISCUSSION: Targeted glycemic variability management and calcium-phosphate homeostasis correction may effectively improve survival of elderly critically ill CKD patients.
articles.ai_summary: This study looked at how glucose variability and mineral disorders affect critically ill patients with kidney disease. It found that both factors can increase the risk of death and severe complications, especially when combined. The study suggests that managing these factors could improve survival.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings are important for ICU clinicians because they highlight the need to closely monitor and manage glucose variability and mineral disorders in critically ill patients with kidney disease to improve their outcomes.

articles.title: Hemoglobin glycation index and short-term mortality in sepsis: a retrospective cohort study with external validation.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The hemoglobin glycation index (HGI) reflects interindividual variability in hemoglobin glycation beyond average glycemic exposure. Although stress-related dysglycemia is common in sepsis, the prognostic relevance of HGI in critically ill patients with sepsis remains unclear. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the MIMIC-IV database (n = 2,073) as the primary cohort. HGI was calculated as the difference between observed and predicted HbA1c based on admission glucose. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality. Findings were validated in an independent external cohort (n = 166). RESULTS: In the primary cohort, the 28-, 60-, and 90-day mortality rates were 23.25, 27.69, and 30.00%, respectively. Non-survivors exhibited significantly lower HGI levels than survivors (p < 0.001). Compared with the lowest HGI quartile (Q1), patients in the highest quartile (Q4) had a significantly lower risk of 28-day mortality (hazard ratio (HR) 0.70, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.52-0.94; p = 0.018) and 60-day mortality (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.58-1.00; p = 0.050). A similar but non-significant trend was observed for 90-day mortality (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.62-1.04; p = 0.101). In the external validation cohort, higher HGI was similarly associated with reduced 28-day mortality, supporting the robustness of the primary findings. CONCLUSION: Higher HGI was associated with lower short-term mortality in this retrospective cohort of critically ill patients with sepsis, with the strongest evidence observed for 28-day mortality. These findings suggest that HGI may provide prognostic information during the early phase of sepsis. Prospective studies are needed to validate these findings and determine their clinical utility.
articles.ai_summary: Researchers studied how a measure of hemoglobin glycation (HGI) affects short-term mortality in sepsis patients. They found that higher HGI levels were associated with lower mortality rates, especially within 28 days. This suggests HGI could be a useful prognostic tool in the early stages of sepsis.
articles.ai_significance: These findings could help clinicians predict patient outcomes and make more informed decisions in sepsis care. Further studies are needed to confirm the clinical utility of HGI in this context.

articles.title: Enteral nutrition-related hyperglycemia in critical illness: cascade conceptual model and implications for precision nursing-a systematic review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hyperglycemia is a common complication in critically ill patients receiving enteral nutrition (EN). This review synthesizes evidence on its mechanisms, epidemiology, clinical implications, and nursing management to support precision glycemic care. METHODS: A systematic literature search identified 45 eligible studies, including randomized trials, retrospective studies, reviews, guidelines, and expert consensus statements. Given the lack of a universally accepted definition, enteral nutrition-related hyperglycemia was pragmatically defined as blood glucose ≥7.8 mmol/L occurring within 24-72 h after initiation of enteral nutrition. RESULTS: Reported incidence varies widely, from approximately 30-47% in general ICU populations to 60-80% following cardiac surgery, reflecting differences in definitions, patient characteristics, timing, and nutritional protocols. Based on thematic integration of existing evidence, we propose a six-level conceptual cascade framework, linking metabolic vulnerability, stress-hormone activation, exogenous substrate load, enteroinsular axis dysfunction, inflammation-mediated insulin resistance, and microbiota dysbiosis. Corresponding nursing strategies include diabetes-specific formulas, optimized feeding regimens, continuous glucose monitoring, and individualized insulin protocols within multidisciplinary care. These strategies may improve glycemic control; however, evidence for clinical outcome benefits remains limited and heterogeneous. CONCLUSION: Further prospective studies are needed to validate the model and refine precision nursing strategies.
articles.ai_summary: This systematic review of 45 studies examined the mechanisms and management of hyperglycemia in critically ill patients receiving enteral nutrition, proposing a six-level conceptual cascade framework to guide precision glycemic care.
articles.ai_significance: Understanding and managing enteral nutrition-related hyperglycemia is crucial for ICU clinical practice as it can lead to improved glycemic control, but further studies are needed to confirm its clinical benefits.

articles.title: Numerical and Clinical Accuracy of the FreeStyle Libre 2 System: A Diagnostic Accuracy Study in Critically Ill Patients.
articles.journal: Clinical medicine insights. Endocrinology and diabetes
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The accuracy of the FreeStyle Libre 2 system in critically ill patients needing insulin therapy remains inadequately evaluated. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the clinical and numerical accuracy of continuous glucose monitoring (FreeStyle Libre 2) and capillary glucometry (StatStrip) compared with central laboratory glucose in critically ill patients requiring insulin therapy. METHODS: We conducted a diagnostic accuracy study, evaluating simultaneously two index tests, the FreeStyle Libre 2 and capillary glucose, compared to the central laboratory glucose (venous or arterial) as reference standard. The study included critically ill adult patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) with diabetes or stress hyperglycemia, requiring insulin therapy, and ventilatory or vasopressor support. Numerical accuracy was assessed using ISO 15197:2013 criteria and Mean Absolute Relative Difference (MARD). Clinical accuracy was evaluated using Clarke and Parkes error grid analysis. RESULTS: A total of 157 paired measurements were collected. FreeStyle Libre 2 showed a MARD comparable to capillary glucose (10.43% vs 7.58%; p=0.14). Neither method met ISO 15197:2013 numerical accuracy criteria. In the clinical accuracy analysis, FreeStyle Libre 2 classified 100% of measurements within zones A+B on both the Clarke and Parkes grids, whereas capillary glucose achieved 97.6% and 100%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: FreeStyle Libre 2 showed numerical accuracy comparable to capillary blood glucose and consistently reliable clinical performance in critically ill patients needing insulin therapy. These results support its potential as an alternative to capillary glucose monitoring in the ICU. More studies involving a greater number of hypoglycaemic events are required to confirm its effectiveness in this critical range.
articles.ai_summary: This study compared the accuracy of the FreeStyle Libre 2 system and capillary glucometry to central laboratory glucose in critically ill patients requiring insulin therapy. The FreeStyle Libre 2 showed comparable numerical accuracy and consistently reliable clinical performance. A total of 157 paired measurements were collected.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings support the potential use of the FreeStyle Libre 2 system as an alternative to capillary glucose monitoring in the ICU, but more studies are needed to confirm its effectiveness in preventing hypoglycemia.

articles.title: Effects of Iloprost on Nitric Oxide Biomarkers in Patients With Septic Shock and Severe Endotheliopathy.
articles.abstract: Septic shock is characterized by profound endothelial dysfunction, which may involve changes in the prostacyclin and nitric oxide (NO) pathways and contribute to immune dysregulation, coagulopathy, and vascular instability. Iloprost has shown potential to modulate NO biomarkers in non-septic conditions. We investigated whether treatment with the prostacyclin analog iloprost affected plasma concentrations of the NO biomarkers ADMA, SDMA, arginine, and homoarginine in patients with septic shock and severe endotheliopathy. This preplanned sub-study of the randomized, blinded COMBAT-SHINE trial enrolled 274 adult ICU patients with septic shock and severe endotheliopathy (defined as soluble thrombomodulin (sTM) > 10 ng/mL) who had consented to the use of data. Five participants from the full trial population withdrew consent. Participants were allocated to a 72-h infusion of iloprost (1 ng/kg/min) versus placebo. Plasma concentrations of ADMA, SDMA, arginine, and homoarginine were measured at 0, 24, 48, and 72 h. Changes in biomarker concentrations were assessed using linear mixed models, with predefined subgroup analyses. All results were considered exploratory. In explorative analyses, iloprost treatment, compared with placebo, did not statistically significantly change plasma concentrations of ADMA and SDMA (estimated difference in means -4% (95% CI: -13%, 6%; p = 0.4) and-2% (95% CI: -14%, 10%; p = 0.7), respectively), or plasma concentrations of arginine and homoarginine (estimated difference in means 9% (95% CI: -6%, 27%; p = 0.2) and 17% (95% CI: -3%, 42%; p = 0.10), respectively). None of the NO biomarkers changes over time (0-24 h, 24-48 h, or 48-72 h) differed between the iloprost and placebo groups (all p > 0.3). Findings were consistent across predefined subgroups. In this sub-study of a randomized clinical trial of adults in the ICU with septic shock and severe endotheliopathy, infusion of iloprost 1 ng/kg/min for 72 h did not affect plasma concentrations of the NO biomarkers ADMA, SDMA, arginine, and homoarginine. This substudy of a larger trial of iloprost versus placebo for sepsis outcomes (COMBAT-SHINE trial) examined specifically nitric oxide markers in a septic shock and epithelial injury cohort. Iloprost treatment at the tested dose did not appear to affect markers of nitric oxide measured as ADMA, SDMA, arginine or homoarginine levels.

articles.title: Gut microbiome-based interventions to prevent ICU-acquired infections: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Gut microbiome colonization with potential pathogens is common and often precedes clinical infection in the intensive care unit (ICU). Two key gut microbiome-based interventions seek to prevent infections yet use opposite approaches: selective digestive decontamination (SDD) utilizes antibiotics to eliminate potential pathogens, whereas biotic supplementation (prebiotics, probiotics, or synbiotics) aims to enrich beneficial microbes. In the absence of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) directly comparing these two interventions, this systematic review and meta-analysis sought to compare the effect sizes of SDD versus biotic interventions for mortality and infection-related outcomes. We searched PubMed for RCTs published between 2000 and 2025. Eligible studies recruited adult ICU patients, assessed SDD or biotics against a comparator (standard care or placebo), and reported on mortality and/or acquired infection-related outcomes. Pooled relative risks (RR) were calculated using random-effects models. Nine SDD trials involving 19,907 subjects and 29 biotic supplementation trials involving 5,483 subjects were included. When compared versus standard care or placebo, neither intervention significantly reduced overall mortality (SDD: RR = 0.96 [95%CI: 0.88-1.05]; biotics: RR = 0.93 [95%CI: 0.87-1.00]).SDD was associated with modestly lower observed risk for ICU acquired all-cause infections compared to biotics (SDD: RR = 0.76 [95%CI: 0.60-0.98]; biotics: RR = 0.82 [95%CI: 0.64-1.05], no statistically significant difference) and specifically lower risk for pneumonia (SDD: RR = 0.50 [95%CI: 0.26-0.96]; prebiotics and synbiotics: RR = 0.70 [95%CI: 0.54-0.90]). In conclusion, neither SDD nor biotics was significantly protective for mortality, but both types of interventions showed similarly promising protective associations with infections, especially pneumonia. The studies selected were heterogeneous, especially those testing biotic interventions.

articles.title: Endpoint-specific mortality associated with malignancy among adults with sepsis or septic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a major global health challenge and increasingly affects patients with complex conditions such as malignancy. Prior studies suggest higher mortality in this population, but interpretation is limited by aggregation of heterogeneous endpoints. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to clarify endpoint-specific prognostic associations between malignancy and mortality in adults with sepsis or septic shock. This study was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251141216). PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library and Epistemonikos were searched through 16 September 2025, for studies comparing all-cause mortality between sepsis patients with and without malignancy. Mortality endpoints were grouped as ICU, in-hospital, early, intermediate and extended follow-up mortality. Crude odds ratios (ORs) were estimated using random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup, meta-regression and sensitivity analyses were performed to explore heterogeneity and assess consistency. Among 105 eligible studies comprising 20,089,138 participants, 85 studies contributing 101 endpoint estimates were included in the primary synthesis. Pooled estimates were elevated across endpoints: ICU (OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.94-1.56), in-hospital (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.69-2.13), early (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.59-2.06), intermediate (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.72-3.03) and extended follow-up mortality (OR 2.41, 95% CI 1.70-3.42). Associations were sustained for haematologic malignancy, concentrated in in-hospital and early mortality for metastatic disease and more modest for solid tumours. Sensitivity analyses were directionally consistent, although risk ratio estimates were generally smaller than ORs. Exploratory meta-regression suggested that severity-related covariates may contribute to heterogeneity. Malignancy was associated with higher mortality among adults with sepsis or septic shock, with variation across mortality endpoints and clinical contexts. These findings support endpoint-specific prognostic assessment and highlight the need for future studies to incorporate more granular cancer characteristics. Because the primary estimates were unadjusted, results represent overall prognostic associations rather than independent causal effects.

articles.title: Persistent lymphopaenia in critically ill patients with and without sepsis: An Australian and New Zealand point prevalence study.
articles.journal: Critical care and resuscitation : journal of the Australasian Academy of Critical Care Medicine
authors: Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Point Prevalence Program and The George Institute for Global Health
articles.abstract: The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of persistent lymphopaenia, defined as an absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) < 1.0 × 109/L on both the first and second intensive care unit (ICU) days in patients with sepsis and the association of persistent lymphopaenia with advanced organ support. A prospective, multicentre, binational point prevalence study of adult patients treated in participating ICUs in June 2023 was conducted. Main outcome measures included prevalence of persistent lymphopaenia in patients with sepsis versus those without sepsis, hospital and ICU mortality, length of stay, and organ support patterns. Among 829 adult patients in 59 ICUs, 307 (37%) had persistent lymphopaenia, and 338 (40.8%) met sepsis criteria. Persistent lymphopaenia was associated with greater illness severity (mean Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score: 19.4 vs. 16.8, p < 0.001). Persistent lymphopaenia was more common in patients with sepsis than in those without sepsis (44.7% vs. 31.8%, p < 0.001); this difference remained after adjusting for predefined covariates (odds ratio: 1.51, 95% confidence interval: 1.12-2.03, p = 0.008). For patients with sepsis and persistent lymphopaenia, there was a 6% increase in mortality compared to those without lymphopaenia, although this did not reach statistical significance. For patients without sepsis, hospital length of stay was 16.5 days in those who had persistent lymphopaenia versus 14.4 days in those without persistent lymphopaenia (95% confidence interval: 0.5-3.7, p = 0.01). Persistent lymphopaenia is common in critically ill patients, particularly those with sepsis. Future prospective and interventional investigations are required to clarify the clinical significance of persistent lymphopaenia in critically ill adults and its potential as a therapeutic target.

articles.title: Association Between Daily Fluid Balance Trajectories and Dynamic Organ Failure Resolution (SOFA-2) in Sepsis: A Latent Class Growth Analysis of 16 262 Patients.
articles.abstract: BackgroundFluid management in sepsis has transitioned toward restrictive de-resuscitation during the intensive care unit (ICU) ebb phase (Days 3-7). The clinical heterogeneity of longitudinal fluid trajectories, their interaction with active therapeutic de-resuscitation, and their prognostic association with dynamic organ recovery evaluated under the 2025 SOFA-2 criteria require clarification in large multicenter databases.ObjectiveTo identify latent phenotypes of daily net fluid balance during the de-resuscitation phase and examine their independent associations with dynamic organ failure resolution and 28-day mortality after accounting for active de-resuscitation interventions.MethodsWe performed a retrospective observational cohort study of 16 262 adult septic patients from the MIMIC-IV v3.1 database who survived at least 72 h in the ICU. Daily net fluid balances (ml/kg/day) from Day 3 to Day 7 were modeled using group-based trajectory modeling without prior outcome stratification. Active de-resuscitation interventions, including cumulative intravenous loop diuretic dosing and renal replacement therapy (RRT), were extracted. Multivariable logistic regression and sensitivity analyses evaluated independent associations with 28-day mortality and longitudinal SOFA-2 trajectories.ResultsThree distinct trajectory phenotypes were identified: Class 1 (Rapid Recovery, 85.4%, n = 13 892), Class 2 (Late Response, 8.3%, n = 1354), and Class 3 (Persistent Failure, 6.3%, n = 1016). Class 1 maintained a steady, low net balance and experienced the lowest 28-day mortality (20.8%). Class 2 exhibited sustained high fluid retention until Day 5 before a delayed downward inflection, whereas Class 3 showed relentless fluid accumulation. Daily SOFA-2 scores resolved rapidly in Class 1 (decreasing from 4.24 on Day 3 to 1.18 by Day 7), whereas recovery was stalled in Class 2 (1.71 by Day 7) and persistently blunted in Class 3 (2.17 by Day 7). In multivariable logistic regression fully adjusted for baseline illness severity, loop diuretic exposure, and RRT, both Class 2 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.30, 95% CI 1.14-1.49; P < .001) and Class 3 (aOR 1.27, 95% CI 1.09-1.48; P = .002) were independently associated with increased 28-day mortality compared with Class 1. These associations remained consistent across sensitivity analyses restricted to non-RRT patients and loop diuretic users.ConclusionDiscrete longitudinal fluid balance phenotypes identify clinically distinct sub-populations during the de-resuscitation window of sepsis. Rather than proving direct causality, these trajectories serve as clinical markers of underlying endothelial integrity, intrinsic excretory capacity, and physiological responsiveness to de-resuscitation.

articles.title: The Role of Diagnostic Tools in the Management of Ventilator Associated Lower Respiratory Tract Infections.
articles.journal: Seminars in respiratory and critical care medicine
articles.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) remains a leading healthcare-associated infection in intensive care units and is closely associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation, excessive antimicrobial exposure, higher costs, and poor clinical outcomes. Despite decades of clinical trials and guideline development, bedside diagnosis remains limited by the absence of a biological reference standard. Conventional criteria combine nonspecific clinical, radiographic, and microbiological findings and cannot reliably distinguish parenchymal infection from airway colonization, endotracheal tube biofilm, or sterile pulmonary inflammation. Syndromic multiplex polymerase chain reaction panels, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, and host response profiling have greatly increased analytical sensitivity and shortened the time to microbiological information. They have also exposed the amount of microbial and inflammatory noise present in the ventilated airway. Detection of an organism, a resistance determinant, or systemic inflammation does not by itself establish causality. This review examines the strengths and limitations of clinical scores, imaging, respiratory sampling, conventional culture, rapid molecular assays, antimicrobial resistance testing, systemic and alveolar biomarkers, host transcriptomics, breath analysis, and artificial intelligence-based models. It proposes that VAP should be approached as a time-updated probability of tissue invasive infection rather than a binary diagnosis. A practical host-pathogen attribution framework should integrate the timing and trajectory of respiratory deterioration, specimen quality, relative pathogen burden and dominance, resistance and virulence signals, local and systemic host responses, prior antimicrobial exposure, and competing diagnoses. Diagnostic tests should be ordered only when a predefined management decision is linked to the result, followed by structured reassessment at 48 to 72 hours. This approach may improve antimicrobial targeting while reducing treatment of colonization and other noninfectious mimics.

articles.title: Integrating Glycemic Variability and Stress Hyperglycemia Ratio to Stratify Mortality Risk in Patients with Sepsis-Associated AKI.
articles.abstract: BackgroundSepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI) is a common and severe complication in intensive care units. Although glycemic variability (GV) and stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR) are associated with adverse outcomes in critical illness, their combined prognostic value in SA-AKI remains unclear.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study included patients with SA-AKI from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database. The primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess associations of GV and SHR with mortality. Predictive performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis.ResultsA total of 2638 patients were included. Both GV and SHR were independently associated with increased risks of in-hospital and 1-year mortality. Patients with concomitantly high GV and SHR had the highest mortality risk (OR 1.754, 95% CI 1.321-2.329, P < .001; HR 1.340, 95% CI 1.124-1.598, P = .001). The combined GV-SHR model yielded slightly higher AUCs than either marker alone, with values of 0.700 for in-hospital mortality and 0.708 for 1-year mortality.ConclusionCombined assessment of GV and SHR improves mortality risk stratification in critically ill patients with SA-AKI and may facilitate early identification of high-risk patients.

articles.title: Discordant evidence on corticosteroids in sepsis: a meta-research study.
articles.abstract: Despite an extensive evidence base of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and systematic reviews (SRs), current sepsis guidelines provide only weak recommendations for corticosteroid therapy, while available SRs report conflicting mortality conclusions. We aimed to characterize the evidence landscape of SRs evaluating corticosteroids for sepsis, including their clinical scope, underlying RCT evidence bases, mortality conclusions, and to explore potential sources of discordance. Meta-research study of SRs on corticosteroids in sepsis published between 2015 and 2025. Study-pool overlap was assessed using a SR×RCT inclusion matrix, Jaccard similarity (J), and hierarchical clustering. SRs and RCTs were classified according to standardized Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome (PICO) profiles. We explored discordance in short-term mortality conclusions among clinically comparable SRs and potential associations with study-pool composition, target populations, and methodological characteristics. Forty-two SRs including 121 unique RCTs were identified. More than half of pairwise SR comparisons shared no RCTs, and only three pairs showed high overlap (J > 0.8). SRs addressing similar intervention and target population profiles frequently relied on different study pools. Among 38 SRs with short-term mortality meta-analyses, 15 (39%) reported benefit and 23 (61%) no evidence of effect. Discordance occurred exclusively among SRs evaluating broad, non-specific corticosteroid strategies; conclusions were consistent for hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone (benefit) and hydrocortisone, ascorbic acid, and thiamine (no evidence of effect). SRs including adult sepsis ± shock populations more frequently reported benefit than those restricted to septic shock (62% vs 22%), although this comparison was based on only 22 SRs evaluating broad, non-specific corticosteroid strategies and estimates were imprecise. No single methodological or clinical factor consistently explained discordance. SRs addressing apparently similar clinical questions frequently synthesized different underlying evidence bases and reported discordant conclusions. When selecting SRs to inform clinical decisions and recommendations for sepsis management, clinicians and guideline developers should consider not only methodological quality and reported PICO, but also whether the included RCTs adequately represent the intended clinical question.

articles.title: Multiplex PCR in suspected ventilator-associated pneumonia: for which settings, and at what price?
The sepsis trial landscape: a domain-specific systematic review and meta-analysis of adult sepsis randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract: Despite decades of sepsis randomized clinical trials (RCTs), few therapeutic interventions have demonstrated reproducible mortality benefit. Whether this phenomenon reflects failure of individual therapies or broader limitations in sepsis RCT design remains unclear. We hypothesized that examining clinically distinct treatment domains would reveal differences in mortality effect estimates while identifying recurrent trial-design limitations shared across domains. Therefore, we performed a domain-specific meta-analysis of adult sepsis RCTs and evaluated the distribution of mortality effect estimates across treatment domains using a complementary landscape analysis framework and structured trial-design analysis. We conducted a meta-analysis of adult sepsis and septic shock RCTs published between 2000 and 2025 (PROSPERO CRD420261289221). Using PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL, two reviewers screened studies and extracted data. Trials were grouped into six treatment domains: initial resuscitation interventions, intravenous fluid quantity, intravenous fluid type, vasopressors, corticosteroids, and vitamin C-based therapies. Separate random-effects meta-analyses estimated pooled risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We also performed a complementary landscape analysis using Python to evaluate the distribution of mortality effect estimates relative to study sample size, as well as a structured thematic analysis to identify recurrent trial design constraints across treatment domains. Across 62 RCTs (n = 36,739), pooled mortality effects demonstrated no mortality benefit across each of the six treatment domains: resuscitation interventions (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77-1.01), intravenous fluid quantity (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.88-1.05), intravenous fluid type (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.89-1.01), vasopressors (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.88-1.07), corticosteroids (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.84-1.00), and vitamin C-based therapies (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.83-1.09). A landscape analysis showed wider dispersion of mortality effect estimates among smaller trials, whereas larger trial estimates generally clustered near the null. A structured thematic analysis using a prespecified trial-constraint framework identified recurrent design limitations across treatment domains, including delayed intervention timing, biologic and clinical heterogeneity, treatment contamination, and trial design and infrastructure constraints. Across the six prespecified treatment domains in sepsis, RCTs have not demonstrated consistent reductions in mortality. Recurrent trial-design limitations were common across treatment domains and may inform interpretation and future trial design.

articles.title: Association of Care Intensity With Survival and Long-Term Cost-Effectiveness in Sepsis Without Initial Organ Support After Emergency Admission: A Multicenter Cohort Study in Japan.
articles.abstract: To identify subgroups of patients hospitalized for community-acquired sepsis without initial organ support who may derive survival and cost-effectiveness benefits from ICU or high-dependency care unit (HDU) admission. Retrospective cohort study. A 140-hospital Japanese database (April 2016-March 2024). Adults admitted via emergency ambulance for community-acquired sepsis not requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, mechanical ventilation, catecholamines, or renal replacement therapy before or on the antimicrobial-initiation day. None. We compared ICU and HDU admissions, each vs. general ward (GW) admission, balancing patient characteristics using overlap propensity-score weighting. In-hospital mortality was estimated as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs using modified Poisson regression. Cost-effectiveness was measured by the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) in 3-year costs per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Among 28,211 patients (GW, 18,349; HDU, 8,706; ICU, 1,156), ICU and HDU admissions were not associated with lower mortality overall (HDU vs. GW; RR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.92-1.06 and ICU vs. GW; RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.92-1.22). However, HDU admission was associated with lower mortality among patients with Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score greater than or equal to 6 (RR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.75-0.99) or Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score less than or equal to 12 (RR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.71-0.92). Under the Japanese (50,000 USD/QALY) and U.S. (100,000 USD/QALY) thresholds, ICU and HDU admissions were not cost-effective overall (ICERs > 200,000 USD/QALY). However, the HDU subgroup with GCS score less than or equal to 12 (ICER, 47,738 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 45,918-49,558) was cost-effective under both thresholds, and that with SOFA score greater than or equal to 6 (ICER, 55,319 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 52,018-58,624) met the U.S. threshold. ICU or HDU admission was not associated with survival or economic benefits overall, whereas HDU subgroups (SOFA score ≥ 6 or GCS score ≤ 12) were associated with lower mortality and better cost-effectiveness. These findings may help optimize resource allocation.

articles.title: A Guytonian Atlas of Venous Return in Septic Shock: Reconstruction of Hemodynamic States.
articles.abstract: To reconstruct venous return physiology across published studies of septic shock and characterize the distribution of circulatory states represented in the literature. Exploratory physiologic reconstruction study. Secondary analysis of published hemodynamic observations. Adult patients with septic shock reported in studies containing sufficient information for reconstruction of mean circulatory filling pressure analogue (Pmca) and related parameters including venous return driving pressure (VRdP) and resistance to venous return (RVR). None. A total of 150 observations were available. Median Pmca, central venous pressure (CVP), VRdP, and RVR were 17.3 mm Hg, 9.0 mm Hg, 7.9 mm Hg, and 1.04 mm Hg/min/L, respectively. Empirical quartiles identified four recurrent circulatory phenotypes: reduced filling pressure/gradient, preserved venous return, elevated venous pressure, and high-resistance venous return. The preserved venous return pattern demonstrated the highest median cardiac output (CO), whereas the high-resistance pattern exhibited the lowest flow despite comparable filling pressures. In exploratory adjusted analyses incorporating available vasopressor exposure and fluid-therapy context, VRdP remained strongly associated with CO (β, 1.03 L/min/mm Hg; 95% CI, 0.80-1.25; p < 0.001). When Pmca and CVP were entered separately, Pmca was positively associated with CO (β, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.79-1.25; p < 0.001), whereas CVP was inversely associated with CO (β, -1.03; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.80; p < 0.001). Published hemodynamic observations in septic shock occupy distinct Guytonian phenotypes characterized by different combinations of circulatory filling pressure, venous pressure, and RVR. Reconstruction of venous return geometry may provide a physiologic framework for interpreting circulatory heterogeneity in septic shock.

articles.title: National Early Warning Score 2-Guided Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle Care for Adults With Suspected Sepsis in the Emergency Department: A Hybrid Type 1 Effectiveness-Implementation Stepped-Wedge Randomized Controlled Trial Pilot Study (NEWS-1 TRIPS).
articles.abstract: To increase the uptake of the Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle, we implemented a novel sepsis care model (National Early Warning Score [NEWS]-1 care), in which the Hour-1 Bundle is objectively triggered by a high NEWS-2 (≥ 5). We aimed to determine the feasibility of a full-scale type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation trial of this model. A pilot type 1 hybrid trial, comprising a stepped-wedge cluster randomized controlled trial and mixed-methods implementation evaluation with staff focus group interviews and an anonymous survey guided by the Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance framework. Four emergency departments in Hong Kong. Adult patients of 18 years or older with a clinical diagnosis of infection requiring hospitalization and a NEWS-2 greater than or equal to 5. Implementation of the Hour-1 Bundle when NEWS-2 was greater than or equal to 5. The primary outcome was the feasibility of a full-scale hybrid trial, evaluated based on 14 progression criteria. Preliminary clinical effectiveness and safety were assessed, alongside implementation barriers and facilitators. During the implementation phase, compliance with lactate, blood culture, and antibiotics increased significantly. All progression criteria were met, except for suboptimal overall bundle compliance (56.1%). Exploratory intention-to-treat analysis (standard care group, n = 102; NEWS-1 group, n = 98) showed no significant between-group difference in 30-day all-cause mortality (standard care group, 3.9%; NEWS-1 group, 9.2%; absolute risk difference, 5.3%; 95% CI -1.6% to 12.1%); in-hospital, 90-day all-cause, or sepsis-related mortality; need for mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, intensive care, or surgery; or ventilator-free days and adverse events. Implementation evaluation identified 15 barriers and 13 facilitators. The effectiveness of NEWS-1 care remained uncertain, though adverse events were rare. A full-scale hybrid stepped-wedge trial is feasible but requires a much larger sample size. Real-world implementation barriers and facilitators should be considered in sepsis management guidelines.

articles.title: Impact of antibiotic prophylaxis on the occurrence of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia in trauma patients (antiVAP): a propensity score-weighted, retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Short-course antibiotic prophylaxis has been associated with a reduced risk of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) in selected populations, particularly patients with acute brain injury. However, its role in severely injured trauma patients remains controversial. This multicentre, retrospective cohort study, conducted in 15 French trauma centres, included severely injured adults who required mechanical ventilation initiated within 24 h of admission and continued for at least 48 h. Propensity score-based analyses assessed the association between early antibiotic prophylaxis (initiated within the first 24 h of management and continued for up to 72 h) and patient outcomes. The primary outcome was early-onset VAP; secondary outcomes included late-onset VAP, extrapulmonary infections, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU and hospital length of stay, and 30-day mortality. A total of 1,321 trauma patients were included. Antibiotic prophylaxis was administered to 746 patients (56%), with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid used in more than 90% of cases. Early-onset VAP occurred in 240 of 746 patients (32%) who received antibiotic prophylaxis and in 195 of 575 (34%) who did not. After inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with early-onset VAP (weighted odds ratio [wOR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.66-1.22; p = 0.48). A cause-specific Cox model accounting for the competing risk of death before day 7 yielded similar results (cause-specific hazard ratio [csHR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.71-1.07; p = 0.19). Antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with improve of secondary outcomes. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis in severely injured trauma patients was not associated with a reduced risk of early-onset VAP. Gov ID NCT07059039 - Registration date: July, 10th 2025.

articles.title: Circulating Cell-Free Mitochondrial DNA, Delirium, and Long-Term Cognitive Impairment in Critically Ill Adults With Sepsis: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: During sepsis, circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA (ccf-mtDNA) is released and elevated due to cell injury, augments the immune response, and may contribute to organ dysfunction. Delirium is common and deleterious during sepsis, but little is known about the relationship between mitochondrial injury and delirium during sepsis. We sought therefore to examine associations between ccf-mtDNA and delirium and other clinical outcomes during sepsis. Multicenter, prospective cohort study. Medical and surgical ICUs in university and community hospitals in Nashville, TN. Four hundred eighty patients with sepsis plus shock and/or acute respiratory failure. None. We measured ccf-mtDNA in plasma collected on multiple days (study days 1, 3, and 5) during sepsis and assessed participants bid for delirium and coma using the validated Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU and Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale. We then assessed survivors' cognitive function 3 and 12 months after hospital discharge using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status. During sepsis, the adjusted odds of delirium were 7% lower for individuals at the 75th percentile of ccf-mtDNA compared with those at the 25th percentile (odds ratio [OR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.86-0.99; p = 0.048). ccf-mtDNA was marginally associated with in-hospital mortality (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.99-1.20; p = 0.08), but was not associated with coma (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.90-1.05; p = 0.31) or 3-month (beta, 0.23; 95% CI, -1.58 to 2.05; p = 0.80) and 12-month (beta, -0.36; 95% CI, -2.13 to 1.42; p = 0.69) cognitive outcomes. In this multicenter, prospective cohort study, higher levels of ccf-mtDNA were associated with lower odds of delirium, a result that contradicted our hypothesis. This provocative finding should be interpreted cautiously until replicated and explained by future studies.

articles.title: Low Physical Activity and Reported Barriers Among Survivors of Critical Illness: A Mixed-Method Study.
authors: Trajectories of Recovery after ACutE and cRitical illness (TRACER) study group
articles.abstract: To examine physical activity levels in survivors of critical illness across 6 months, and to understand the barriers and facilitators of physical activity. Prospective, longitudinal, convergent mixed-methods study. Functional testing laboratory. Adults admitted to the ICU for at least 72 hours with acute respiratory failure or sepsis. None. Patients wore an accelerometer starting at hospital discharge, at 3- and 6-month follow-up to quantify daily step counts. At 6 months, physical function and patient-reported outcomes were collected in-person, with a subset of participants completing semi-structured interviews. Eighty-two patients were enrolled, with 67 (82%) having physical activity data with median age of 60 years (interquartile range [IQR], 52-66 yr), 54% male, and ICU stay 9.0 days [IQR, 5.8-17.0 d]. The median daily steps were 1358 (IQR, 742-2799) in 50 patients at baseline, 2305 (IQR, 1081-3898) in 54 patients at 3 months, and 2826 (IQR, 1609-4781) in 44 patients at 6 months. Higher comorbidity burden and earlier measurement associated with lower step counts. At 6 months, patients walked a mean of 344 ± 169 meters on the 6-minute walk test and reported being sedentary a median of 300 min/days (150-480 min/d). Eleven participants completed interviews, yielding three themes: 1) "a marathon, not a sprint": the extended ICU recovery trajectory; 2) engagement in physical activity is highly regulated by personal context; 3) value-driven and motivation-informed physical activity decisions. Mixed-methods integration demonstrated that qualitative themes expanded upon quantitative findings to explain nonlinear recovery patterns, contextualizing persistent sedentary behavior, and revealing that motivational and behavioral gaps are not captured by accelerometry. Survivors showed gradual improvement in daily steps over 6 months yet remained below recommended activity levels. Survivorship and attrition biases may lead to overestimation of step counts, further warranting larger studies. Integrating quantitative and qualitative data reveals modifiable contextual factors that may inform the design of pragmatic physical activity interventions.

articles.title: Association Between the Neutrophil:Lymphocyte Ratio After Hospitalization for Sepsis and Long-Term Outcomes: A Population-Based Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Long-term outcomes after sepsis survival remain poor. No clinical laboratory tests are in use for stratifying long-term risk after sepsis, limiting the development of secondary prevention. The peripheral blood neutrophil:lymphocyte ratio (NLR) reflects innate and adaptive immune cell balance, and may reflect an immune milieu which is associated with long-term risk after sepsis. Accordingly, we evaluated the association between the NLR in the weeks after sepsis hospitalization discharge-a time when patients are routinely seen in post-ICU clinics-and long-term outcomes. Population-based cohort study. Ontario, Canada, 2010-2020. Adults discharged alive from a sepsis hospitalization. None. The exposure was the first outpatient NLR-derived from the complete blood count-measured 15-90 days after sepsis discharge. Among 37,250 survivors with available NLR, the median (interquartile range [IQR]) time-to-measurement was 34 days (22-54 d), and the median NLR was 2.7 (1.8-4.2). Within 1 year, 17,732 patients (47.6%) were rehospitalized or died (median [IQR] time-to-event, 82 d [27-185 d]). The frequency of rehospitalization or death increased across increasing NLR quartiles: 34.2%, 41.5%, 50.3%, and 64.4% (ptrend < 0.001). Compared with the lowest quartile, adjusted hazard ratios (95% CI) were 1.24 (1.18-1.29), 1.54 (1.48-1.62), and 2.25 (2.15-2.35) across higher quartiles. For most patients, NLR after sepsis returned to its patient-specific presepsis ambient level, which was itself prognostic. Among sepsis survivors, outpatient NLR measured 15-90 days after discharge is strongly associated with 1-year risk of rehospitalization or death. As a simple, widely available biomarker, the NLR may support early postsepsis risk stratification and inform development of secondary prevention strategies.

articles.title: The Post-Sepsis Neutrophil: Lymphocyte Ratio: A Population Signal in Search of Individual Meaning.
Beyond Febrile Neutropenia: Reframing Neutropenic Infection as a Clinical Spectrum in Oncology-A Narrative Review and Conceptual Framework.
articles.abstract: Febrile neutropenia is a critical emergency construct, but infection and sepsis can occur without fever. To examine the clinical evidence of nonfebrile neutropenic infection, potential mechanisms of an attenuated febrile response, physiological body-temperature variation, and limitations of clinical thermometry. A narrative review was supplemented by a targeted, transparently documented three-domain evidence map of published systematic syntheses, thermometry-accuracy studies, and oncology-neutropenia cohorts, updated on 1 November 2026. No new exhaustive systematic review or meta-analysis was performed. A synthesis of 36 studies (7636 healthy adults) reported site-specific oral and rectal temperature distributions of 35.73-37.41 °C and 36.32-37.76 °C (mean ± 2 SD), which do not establish a universal core-temperature interval. Peripheral and oral thermometers demonstrated pooled fever-detection sensitivities of 0.64 and 0.53, respectively, in non-neutropenia-specific populations. Nonfebrile infection proportions included 9/69 (13.0%) severe ICU infection episodes and 70/186 (37.6%) bloodstream infections without a recorded temperature ≥ 38.0 °C in a separate oncology-neutropenia cohort; an additional post-transplant corticosteroid cohort is discussed separately. These denominators do not permit a meaningful pooled incidence of afebrile neutropenic sepsis. Fever-based clinical pathways remain essential, but suspected infection, physiological deterioration, and organ dysfunction warrant evaluation irrespective of temperature.

articles.title: Long-Term Mortality in Sepsis Survivors: A Population-Based Study During 15 Years.
articles.abstract: To evaluate long-term mortality among sepsis survivors in Catalonia over a 15-year period and to identify factors associated with increased mortality within 2 years after hospital discharge. Retrospective population-based cohort study. Acute-care hospitals in Catalonia, Spain. Adult and pediatric patients hospitalized with sepsis between 2005 and 2019 identified using the International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision, Clinical Modification and International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification codes for infection and acute organ dysfunction. Patients who died during hospitalization, were transferred to another facility, or represented readmission episodes were excluded. None. Data were obtained from the Catalan Minimum Basic Dataset of Acute-Care Hospitals, with longitudinal follow-up through the Central Registry of Insured Persons. Comorbidities were assessed using the Charlson comorbidity index. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to identify predictors of long-term mortality. Among 296,554 hospital admissions for sepsis, 237,075 patients (79.9%) survived to hospital discharge. Of these, 42% died (99,571) within 2 years. Long-term mortality increased significantly with age, ranging from 5.8% in patients younger than 15 years to 62% in those older than 84 years (p < 0.0001), and with comorbidity burden (21%, 38%, 51%, and 67% for Charlson index 0, 1-2, 3-4, and ≥ 5, respectively; p < 0.0001). Neoplasia (hazard ratio [HR], 2.011), liver cirrhosis (HR, 1.562), and dementia (HR, 1.304) were the comorbidities most strongly associated with mortality. Longer hospital stays were also associated with increased mortality. A progressive decline in long-term mortality was observed during 2017-2019. Long-term mortality among sepsis survivors remains high, with more than 40% dying within 2 years after hospital discharge. These findings support the need for structured post-sepsis care strategies focused on high-risk patients, improved continuity of care, and prevention of long-term sepsis-related complications.

articles.title: Vasopressors as immunomodulators: a hidden axis in septic shock.
Systemic corticosteroids in critical illness: an evidence-based framework for clinical decision-making.
articles.abstract: Systemic corticosteroids are pivotal in managing inflammation-driven critical illnesses, yet bedside translation remains inconsistent. This systematic review establishes an evidence-based framework for clinical decision-making by horizontally synthesizing contemporary evidence across severe community-acquired pneumonia (sCAP), acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and septic shock. A systematic electronic search was conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library up to early 2026. Peer-reviewed randomized controlled trials (RCTs), systematic reviews, and meta-analyses published in English were eligible. Data regarding population characteristics, dosing regimens, initiation timing, duration, and safety profiles were independently extracted and qualitatively synthesized. Landmark trials define context-dependent efficacy: early hydrocortisone continuous infusion significantly reduces 28-day mortality in sCAP (CAPE COD), while a 10-day dexamethasone regimen improves ventilator-free days and survival in moderate-to-severe ARDS (DEXA-ARDS). In septic shock, early hydrocortisone-fludrocortisone combination accelerates shock resolution and lowers 90-day mortality (APROCCHS). These outcomes align with distinct pharmacological profiles: hydrocortisone provides dual glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid activity to restore vascular tone, whereas dexamethasone exerts potent transrepression of proinflammatory transcription factors. To mitigate steroid-induced harm, protocolized safety targets are essential, including maintaining blood glucose at 140-180 mg/dL and actively monitoring for secondary infections. Corticosteroids do not exert a uniform class effect. Bedside success requires personalized, protocolized regimens optimized by scenario-specific timing, dosing, and proactive adverse-event monitoring.

articles.title: Treating sepsis by targeting neutrophil extracellular traps: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Sepsis, a leading cause of death worldwide, is characterized by dysregulated host immune responses and multi-organ dysfunction. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are extracellular fibers from activated neutrophils that contribute to the immune response. However, excessive NETs formation during sepsis may exacerbate inflammation, thrombosis, and tissue injury, potentially affecting sepsis prognosis. We examined whether NETs-modulating interventions are beneficial in experimental sepsis models. Following PRISMA guidelines, this review analyzed studies from PubMed and Scopus that reported NETs-targeting therapies and included outcome measures. A meta-analysis of random-effects models using a restricted maximum likelihood estimation was performed with a priori moderators including NETs quantification tier, intervention timing relative to insult, and intervention class. In 33 included studies, the therapies significantly reduced NETs levels, while three studies increased NETs following treatment. The a priori moderators, NETs tier and treatment timing, were not significant, whereas intervention class significantly modified treatment effects. The treated groups had a lower risk of death and reduced IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-ɑ levels when compared to the control group. The treatments reduced tissue injury with considerable heterogeneity (I2=68.4%) and should be cautiously interpreted due to small study numbers. NETs modulation was significantly associated with a decrease in cytokine concentration and tissue injury. The heterogeneity of protocols, diverse outcome measures, publication bias, and overall poor reporting quality of the studies warranted conservative effect estimates and cautious interpretation of findings. Our meta-analysis suggests NETs modulation is associated with reduced mortality risk, attenuated organ injury, and decreased inflammation, based primarily on LPS endotoxemia rodent models. Notably, experimental protocols and model limitations impede the translatability of these therapies for clinical care at this stage of research. In accordance with the guidelines, our systematic review protocol is registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) registration number CRD420251124339 and was published with INPLASY on 20 August 2025.

articles.title: Reducing Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infections in ICUs: A Systematic Review of Barriers and Facilitators and Intervention Measures.
articles.abstract: Despite established guidelines, central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) remains a severe ICU complication due to cognitive and resource barriers hindering healthcare worker compliance. A systematic evaluation of these barriers and facilitators is currently lacking but is important for informing targeted implementation strategies for CLABSI prevention. To explore the barriers and facilitators to implementing CLABSI prevention in ICUs using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to provide evidence-based strategies for improvement. A PRISMA-guided systematic review was performed using PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, VIP, Wan fang, and CBM databases, up to August 2026. Eligible studies included qualitative, quantitative, or mixed-methods research on the barriers and facilitators to CLABSI prevention implementation among ICU healthcare workers. Two researchers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Data synthesis and intervention development were guided by the CFIR, with targeted strategies mapped using the CFIR-ERIC (Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change) matching tool. The literature search identified 1,780 records, of which 28 studies were ultimately included. The review identified 28 barriers and facilitators, which were synthesized into four major themes and mapped to 16 CFIR constructs across the catheter-care continuum. The most prominent barriers involved staff knowledge gaps, inconsistent adherence to recommended practices, limited resources, and insufficient leadership support. CFIR-ERIC mapping identified 11 Level 1 expert-endorsed implementation strategies, of which four were represented in the included literature and seven were identified as potential implementation gaps. CLABSI prevention in ICUs is influenced by multilevel implementation determinants spanning individual, organizational, and practice-related factors. A structured implementation-science approach may help healthcare organizations identify context-specific barriers and prioritize targeted strategies to support more consistent implementation of evidence-based CLABSI prevention practices. Improving CLABSI prevention may require multilevel strategies that combine targeted education and training, adequate resource allocation, leadership engagement, standardized clinical procedures, and ongoing audit and feedback. These strategies may help strengthen adherence to evidence-based practices, improve quality of care, and enhance patient safety in ICUs.

articles.title: Seven versus 14 days of polymyxin-based therapy for ventilator-associated pneumonia due to carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii : A randomised feasibility trial.
articles.journal: Lung India : official organ of Indian Chest Society
articles.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) due to carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii ( CRAB ) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality in intensive care units (ICUs), yet the optimal antibiotic duration of therapy remains uncertain. We compared outcomes of 7-day versus 14-day polymyxin-based therapy for CRAB-VAP. We conducted a single-centre, open-label, randomised feasibility trial in a tertiary-care respiratory ICU from March 2017 to October 2024. Patients with microbiologically confirmed CRAB-VAP who met predefined clinical stability criteria on day 7 were randomised 1:1 to either discontinue antibiotics on day 7 or continue treatment for 14 days. Treatment comprised intravenous colistin or polymyxin B with adjunctive nebulised colistin. The primary outcome was relapse of CRAB-VAP. Secondary outcomes included antibiotic-free days through day 28, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU and hospital length of stay, and 28-day all-cause mortality. We randomised 41 patients (7-day n = 22; 14-day n = 19). Relapse occurred in 1 (4.5%) versus 2 (10.5%) patients (risk ratio [RR] 0.43; 95% CI: 0.04, 4.31) in the 7-day versus 14-day groups, respectively. The 7-day group had more antibiotic-free days (mean difference: 6.9 days; 95% CI: 5.1, 8.7 days). Acute kidney injury occurred in 0% versus 31.6% (RR 0.07; 95% CI: 0.004, 1.15). Other outcomes, including 28-day mortality (45.5 vs 63.2%; RR 0.72; 95% CI: 0.40, 1.30), were similar. In clinically improving CRAB-VAP, a 7-day discontinuation strategy was feasible. Clinical outcome estimates, including relapse and mortality, were imprecise and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. These findings support evaluation in larger, adequately powered multicentre trials.

articles.title: Cefepime Dose Individualization in Early Sepsis: A Pragmatic Feasibility Trial Protocol.
authors: Beta-Lactam Optimization and Outcomes Management (BLOOM) Study Group
articles.abstract: Cefepime is a core antibiotic in sepsis treatment, yet standard dosing yields 10- to 30-fold exposure variability in critical illness. In the early "golden hours" of sepsis, low cefepime levels (affecting up to 70% of cases) may lead to organ dysfunction progression, treatment failure, and antimicrobial resistance. Empiric dose escalation to overcome low levels can increase the risk of dose-dependent neurotoxicity. We developed and qualified a population pharmacokinetic model using patient weight and estimated glomerular filtration rate from creatinine and cystatin C that, in simulation, improved attainment of effective and safe drug levels. To describe the Beta-Lactam Optimization and Outcomes Management (BLOOM) 1 pragmatic feasibility trial. This single-center, cluster-randomized, pragmatic feasibility trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07287332) was approved with a waiver of informed consent. Participants are critically ill adults (age ≥ 18 yr), hospitalized at Mayo Clinic (Rochester, MN), who are receiving cefepime for suspected or documented sepsis. A screening tool embedded in the electronic health record (EHR) identifies eligible patients newly initiated on cefepime (≤ 1 previous dose in 48 hr) who are then randomized to care groups (clusters) that use an individualized dosing algorithm (intervention) or usual-care dosing (control). Exclusions are cephalosporin allergy, acute kidney injury, kidney replacement therapy, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and missing inputs required for the algorithm (weight, creatinine, cystatin C). Recruitment began on January 15, 2026, and is expected to conclude by January 2027 (target enrollment, ≥ 300 patients). For eligible patients, EHR-embedded clinical decision support prompts the cluster-assigned dosing approach, with final dose decisions made by the clinical team. Feasibility, fidelity, and exploratory pharmacokinetic and clinical outcomes will be assessed using mixed methods. This workflow-integrated pragmatic feasibility trial will determine whether personalized cefepime dosing can be implemented in routine practice to optimize timely sepsis therapy while maintaining safety.

articles.title: Dual Protective Mechanisms of Neostigmine in Septic Shock: Cholinergic Anti-Inflammatory Pathway and Intestinal Barrier Preservation.
Certainty of Evidence and Interpretation of Effects in Inhaled Antibiotics for Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia.
Hypercapnia in Ventilated Sepsis: Signal, Target, or Lung-Protective Tradeoff?
Effect of Nurse-Delivered Chlorhexidine Versus Saline Oral Care on Ventilator-Associated Events in Medical Intensive Care Patients: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the effectiveness of nurse-delivered oral care using 0.12% chlorhexidine versus normal saline in reducing ventilator-associated events and improving clinical and oral health outcomes among adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation in a medical intensive care unit. Single-center, parallel-group, assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial. Adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation were randomly allocated to receive oral care with either 0.12% chlorhexidine or normal saline every eight hours until extubation or discharge from the ICU. The primary outcome was ventilator-associated events. Secondary outcomes included ventilator-associated pneumonia, duration of mechanical ventilation, length of stay in the intensive care unit, mortality in the intensive care unit, oral health status and intervention-related adverse events. A total of 141 participants were randomized. No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in ventilator-associated events, ventilator-associated pneumonia, duration of mechanical ventilation, length of stay in the intensive care unit, mortality in the intensive care unit, oral health status, or intervention-related adverse events. In this single-center superiority randomized controlled trial, nurse-delivered oral care with 0.12% chlorhexidine did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in ventilator-associated events compared with normal saline. Given the wide confidence intervals and lower-than-expected event rates, these findings do not confirm equivalence but suggest that routine chlorhexidine may provide limited incremental benefit over standardized mechanical oral hygiene in medical intensive care unit patients. Intensive care nurses might prioritize the consistent implementation of structured, evidence-based oral care protocols. Routine use of chlorhexidine may provide limited additional benefit over normal saline in this patient population. This study addresses the ongoing uncertainty regarding the effectiveness of chlorhexidine for routine oral care in mechanically ventilated adults. No significant differences were observed between chlorhexidine and normal saline in ventilator-associated events, clinical outcomes, oral health outcomes, or adverse events. These findings add to the growing body of evidence suggesting that the incremental benefit of chlorhexidine beyond standardized mechanical oral care may be limited and support further adequately powered multicenter trials to define its role in different intensive care populations. This study adhered to the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials guideline. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05913856. Available at: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05913856. The trial was registered after participant recruitment had commenced because of an administrative delay. No changes were made to the study design, eligibility criteria, outcomes, or analysis plan after registration. No Patient or Public Contribution.

articles.title: Intermittent or Continuous Renal-Replacement Therapy in Acute Kidney Injury.
articles.journal: The New England journal of medicine
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The preferred method of renal-replacement therapy for acute kidney injury in critically ill patients remains uncertain. METHODS: In this multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned critically ill adults with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy to undergo intermittent hemodialysis or continuous renal-replacement therapy as the initial treatment. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event - defined as death, dependence on renal-replacement therapy, or a serum creatinine concentration more than 25% above the baseline value - by day 90. RESULTS: The trial was stopped early after sequential interim analyses showed a sustained signal of higher mortality with intermittent hemodialysis than with continuous renal-replacement therapy. A total of 554 patients underwent randomization, with 272 patients assigned to undergo intermittent hemodialysis and 282 to undergo continuous renal-replacement therapy; 535 patients (260 in the intermittent group and 275 in the continuous group) were included in the intention-to-treat population. A major adverse kidney event occurred by day 90 in 203 patients (78.1%) in the intermittent group and in 197 patients (71.6%) in the continuous group (adjusted absolute risk difference, 6.28 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.22 to 13.79). Death by day 90 occurred in 164 patients (63.1%) and in 147 patients (53.5%), respectively. Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates at day 90 were 63.3% and 53.6% (hazard ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.63). The most common complication potentially related to acute kidney injury or renal-replacement therapy was hypotension, which occurred in 179 patients (68.8%) in the intermittent group and in 183 patients (66.5%) in the continuous group. CONCLUSIONS: Among critically ill patients with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy, intermittent hemodialysis as the initial treatment approach was not shown to be noninferior to continuous renal-replacement therapy with respect to major adverse kidney events by day 90 and was associated with higher mortality. (Funded by the French Ministry of Health; ICRAKI ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06032884.).

articles.title: Chlorhexidine within a standardized oral-care bundle for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia: a pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover trial in six medical intensive care units.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chlorhexidine (CHX) has been a long-standing component of oral-care bundles for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), but recent evidence has questioned its benefit in non-cardiac-surgery ICU. We evaluated whether adding 0.12% CHX to standardized oral-care bundle provides incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU. METHODS: We conducted a prospective, pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover (AB/BA) trial in six adult medical ICUs of a single tertiary-care academic hospital in Bhubaneswar, India. ICUs were randomized as three ICUs of two Period of 9 months with the multicomponent oral-care bundle without chlorhexidine and three with the same bundle plus 0.12% chlorhexidine with a 1-month wash-in and re-training interval. Consecutive adults ventilated for ≥ 48 h were included. The primary outcome was VAP incidence density (Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (CPIS) > 6) as per 1,000 ventilator-days. Secondary outcomes were 28-day all-cause mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, 28- day ventilator-free days, Beck Oral Assessment Scale (BOAS) and Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) scores. The primary model was a population-averaged Poisson generalized estimating equation (GEE) and adjustment for treatment, period, sequence, age, sex, APACHE II, and SOFA. RESULTS: A total of 1,035 patients (637 No CHX, 398 CHX) accrued 10,024 ventilator-days (5,918 vs. 4,106). Groups were well balanced at baseline (mean age ≈ 55 years; APACHE II ≈ 19.6; SOFA ≈ 13.4).
