articles.title: Amniotic fluid embolism following artificial rupture of membranes leading to hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and persistent vegetative state: A case report.
articles.abstract: Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) is a rare, catastrophic, and life-threatening condition that can occur during the peripartum period. It is thought to result from the entry of fetal cells and debris, present in amniotic fluid and rich in thromboplastin, into the maternal circulation, triggering disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), sudden cardiorespiratory collapse, and maternal and/or fetal deterioration. AFE remains a clinical diagnosis of exclusion, and management is primarily supportive. A 35-year-old woman at 40 weeks of gestation was admitted in active labor and underwent artificial rupture of membranes. Approximately two minutes later, she developed sudden and unexpected bradycardia, severe hypotension, cyanosis, and concurrent fetal bradycardia. On examination, the cervix was fully dilated; however, an attempted vacuum-assisted delivery during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was unsuccessful, and an emergency cesarean section was performed. The neonate was transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), while the mother was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) following cardiorespiratory arrest. DIC was diagnosed, and treatment for suspected AFE was initiated. Both the mother and neonate survived; however, the mother remained in a persistent vegetative state. This case highlights the critical importance of maintaining a high index of clinical suspicion for AFE in any parturient presenting with sudden bradycardia and hypotension. It further underscores the essential role of prompt multidisciplinary collaboration in optimizing maternal and neonatal outcomes.

articles.title: Causal mediation analysis of contact with COVID-19 patients and burnout syndrome in physiotherapists in Japan: secondary analysis of a multicentre observational study.
articles.abstract: Background: Physiotherapists played central roles in high-risk 'red-zone' care during COVID-19 and reported substantial distress, yet mechanisms linking exposure to burnout remain unclear.Objective: To examine whether the association between direct patient contact and burnout operates through a stress-related behavioural mediator (feeling like quitting/taking a break) and whether organisational resources moderate this pathway.Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of a nationwide, multicentre, web-based survey of Japanese physiotherapists engaged in COVID-19 care (March 2021). Burnout was defined using the Japanese MBI-GS case algorithm. Counterfactual mediation analysis with bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstraps (5,000 resamples) was used to estimate the average causal mediation effect (ACME), average direct effect (ADE), and total effect on the risk-difference scale. Models were adjusted for age, sex, years in practice, and cohabitation.Results: Burnout prevalence was 19.4%. A small indirect effect was observed (ACME = 0.00932; 95% CI 0.00188-0.0200), whereas the direct and total effects were not statistically significant. Appreciation/respect was associated with attenuation of the indirect effect (ACME = 0.00007), whereas endorsement of enhanced reimbursement for two-therapist care of critically ill patients was associated with a larger indirect effect (ACME = 0.00637; 95% CI 0.00122-0.0100). Because the primary mediation analysis used a binary mediator and binary outcome with logistic link functions, a formal ρ-based sensitivity analysis for unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding was not available under this specification.Conclusions: Among Japanese physiotherapists, the association between direct COVID-19 patient contact and burnout was consistent with an indirect pathway operating through a stress-related behavioural mediator. Recognition appeared to buffer this pathway, whereas reimbursement-linked resource strain appeared to amplify it. These findings suggest potentially relevant organisational targets for future intervention, but should be interpreted cautiously given the cross-sectional design and the causal assumptions required for mediation analysis.
articles.ai_summary: This study looked at Japanese physiotherapists who worked with COVID-19 patients and found that direct contact with patients contributed to burnout, but this effect was partly buffered by appreciation and respect from patients and colleagues. The study suggests that organisational resources, such as reimbursement for care, may also play a role in burnout. Burnout prevalence was 19.4% among the physiotherapists.
articles.ai_significance: These findings are relevant for ICU clinical practice as they highlight the importance of organisational resources and staff appreciation in mitigating burnout among healthcare workers, particularly during high-stress situations like the COVID-19 pandemic.

articles.title: Impact of direct transfer to critical care on mortality for patients who undergo emergency colorectal cancer resection: a national population-based cohort study in England.
articles.abstract: It is recommended that patients receiving emergency surgery and with 'high-risk' of morbidity and mortality should be transferred directly from theatre to critical care. Using a national, population-based cohort study, we estimated the effect of direct transfer to critical care on 90-day mortality after emergency colorectal cancer resection, and the variation amongst English NHS hospitals. Patients who underwent emergency colorectal cancer resection between December 2016 and November 2019 according to Hospital Episodes Statistics, National Bowel Cancer Audit or National Emergency Laparotomy Audit were included. Patients were identified as having a direct transfer to critical care through linkage with the Intensive Care National Audit and Research Centre Case Mix Programme. Multivariable logistic regression and propensity score methods were used to measure the effect of direct transfer to critical care on 90-day mortality. In total, 10,441 patients underwent an emergency colorectal cancer resection. Unadjusted 90-day mortality was higher in the direct transfer to critical care cohort (10.9%) than in patients without direct transfer to critical care (3.7%) (odds ratio [OR]: 3.16, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.65-3.77). There was no evidence of an association after risk adjustment (adjusted OR: 1.16, 95% CI: 0.94-1.43) or after propensity score analysis (weighted OR: 0.94, 95% CI: 0.69-1.27). For patients at high risk with a predicted mortality ≥5%, the proportion of patients with a direct transfer to critical care varied widely amongst hospitals (interquartile range 68%-92%; median 83%). Our findings suggest that apparent higher postoperative mortality in patients having direct transfer to critical care can be mostly explained by characteristics of patients, tumours, physiology and surgery. However, the extent to which direct transfer to critical care is used varies widely amongst hospitals. Further work to understand this variation has the potential to improve patient outcomes after emergency colorectal cancer resection.

articles.title: Piezo1 in acute and critical illnesses: From mechanosensing to organ dysfunction (Review).
articles.abstract: Acute and critical illnesses are typically accompanied by hemodynamic instability, tissue edema, mechanical ventilation and extracellular matrix remodeling. Abnormal shear stress, mechanical stretch, pressure loading and tissue deformation continuously reshape the local mechanical microenvironment. Piezo1 is a mechanosensitive cation channel that converts mechanical stimuli into intracellular signals dominated by Ca²+ influx and contributes to vascular homeostasis, immune regulation and tissue repair. In sepsis‑associated intestinal epithelial injury, pulmonary endothelial mechanical loading and infection‑related immune responses, Piezo1‑associated Ca²+ signaling has been implicated in intestinal barrier injury, mitochondrial stress and apoptosis, endothelial barrier disruption or protection, and enhanced host defense. The direction of its effects depends on the cell and experimental context and cannot be determined solely by the intensity or duration of activation. The present review summarizes the fundamental mechanisms of Piezo1‑mediated mechanosensing and mechanotransduction in sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, acute kidney injury and trauma/hemorrhagic shock. It also discusses the therapeutic potential and translational challenges of targeting Piezo1. Mechanical alterations in acute and critical illnesses may influence cellular processes, including inflammatory regulation, endothelial barrier function, mitochondrial stress and cell injury, through Piezo1‑associated signaling. However, direct evidence and the direction of effects vary between diseases, and shared mechanisms across organs remain to be validated. Defining the cell‑specific and stimulus‑ and disease stage‑dependent effects of Piezo1 may deepen understanding of organ dysfunction in acute and critical illness and provide a basis for research into interventions targeting mechanical signaling.

articles.title: Comparison of Emergency Surgery Score and Portsmouth Physiological and Operative Severity Score for Mortality and Morbidity in Emergency Laparotomies.
articles.abstract: Emergency laparotomy (EL) is associated with high morbidity and mortality worldwide. Reliable and rapid risk stratification tools are essential for predicting adverse outcomes and optimizing perioperative management. This study compared the predictive accuracy of the Emergency Surgery Score (ESS) and the Portsmouth Physiological and Operative Severity Score for the Enumeration of Mortality and Morbidity (P-POSSUM) in patients undergoing EL. In this retrospective cohort study, 230 adult patients who underwent EL were included between January 2017 and December 2021. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory variables were collected, and ESS and P-POSSUM were calculated for each patient. Outcomes included 30-d mortality, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, and postoperative complications. Discriminative performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, with area under the curve reported with 95% confidence intervals. Overall 30-d mortality rate was 13.9%, and 63.0% of patients required ICU admission. Both ESS and P-POSSUM demonstrated good discriminatory performance for 30-d mortality and ICU admission. ESS showed a numerically higher area under the curve for mortality than P-POSSUM; however, DeLong testing demonstrated no statistically significant difference between the models. For major postoperative complications, both models demonstrated acceptable discrimination, with comparable performance. Both ESS and P-POSSUM demonstrated comparable predictive accuracy for short-term outcomes following EL. ESS may offer practical advantages in emergency settings because it relies exclusively on preoperative variables, allowing early risk assessment and perioperative planning when operative information is not yet available.

articles.title: Analysis of outcome predictors in traumatic brain injury patients requiring intensive care management reveals an independent role of dynamic measures.
articles.abstract: Research in traumatic brain injury (TBI) mediation and outcome have developed many methods of assessing patient state and response. While several outcome calculators for TBI have been suggested, these calculators do not include all collected variables in the management of these patients; with a paucity of studies on how these hundreds of variables contribute statistically to long-term outcome. Thus, this work endeavors to assess the statistical relationships between commonly collected variables at admission, and during the first 24 h of critical care, with overall patient outcome. From a retrospective dataset of 1,266 TBI patients requiring intensive care, unique patient variables (including demographic, injury pattern, pathophysiological, treatment and biochemical/imaging biomarkers) were explored. Intra-variable and variable reduction analysis were completed with importance assessed through SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method. From all of this we developed predictive models to assess the 6-12-month Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) using general linear and XGBoost models. Of the 321 variables assessed, a final 36 variables were found to be the important and non-redundant, that included common variables (Glasgow coma scale (GCS), age, heart rate and blood pressure at scene of accident) and individualized measures (S100B level and long pressure reactivity). Survival based on these non-redundant variables resulted in an accuracy of 88.8% 0.723 AUC (0.65-0.795) vs the IMPACT LAB 80.9% 0.608 AUC (0.54-0.677). Notable combining the IMPACT LAB model with the non-redundant variables found an accuracy of 90.3% 0.765 AUC (0.693-0.838) and an improvement of the Nagelkerke R2 value from 0.317 to 0.499. These results found that overall general linear and XGBoost models behave similarly with an increase in non-IMPACT LAB variables performing better in XGBoost models. Broad categories of patient states like survival and favorable outcome can be determined by basic patient variables, however more dynamic measures of individualized response improve the predictive capacity for patient outcomes. Thus, to better understand patient state and more effectively monitor patient outcomes, dynamic and individualized patient physiology needs further evaluation.

articles.title: Massive Transfusion-Associated Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome After Liver Transplantation: A Case Report and Retrospective Estimate of the Sodium Load.
articles.abstract: A 67-year-old woman with acute-on-chronic liver failure and profound preoperative hyponatraemia (central-laboratory serum sodium 116 mmol/L preoperatively; 120.3 mmol/L on the first intraoperative blood gas) underwent emergency living-donor liver transplantation complicated by an estimated blood loss of 6200 mL. Resuscitation comprised 20 units of packed red blood cells (PRBC), 12 units of fresh frozen plasma (FFP), 34 units of cryoprecipitate, three units of apheresis platelets, approximately 7.7 L of crystalloid and albumin, 60 mL of 7% sodium bicarbonate and 70 mEq of potassium chloride, with no hypertonic saline. Serum sodium measured on the operating-room blood gas analyser rose from 120.3 to 132.5 mmol/L over 7 h (+12.2 mmol/L), and by 18 mmol/L between the preoperative central-laboratory value and arrival in the intensive care unit, exceeding the 8-10 mmol/L per 24 h limit recommended by the European Renal Best Practice guideline. She developed dysarthria and dysphagia after extubation on postoperative day (POD) 6 and severe tetraparesis with decreased consciousness on POD 7. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) on POD 7 (rapid protocol) reported no pontine lesion, whereas MRI on POD 19 showed T2 hyperintensity in the central pons and both thalami, consistent with osmotic demyelination syndrome with extrapontine involvement. A simple pooled Adrogué-Madias calculation, with its assumptions stated, estimated the sodium contributed by the infused products at roughly +10 to +17 mmol/L, the same order of magnitude as the observed rise. This case illustrates that blood products, isotonic crystalloids and sodium bicarbonate together can deliver a substantial sodium load during massive transfusion, that the load can be estimated approximately, and that an early MRI without a reported pontine lesion does not exclude osmotic demyelination.

articles.title: Perioperative factors associated with postoperative continuation of mechanical ventilation after initial burn surgery: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Early surgical intervention, including debridement and grafting, is crucial in acute burn injury management. Although early extubation in operating rooms (ORs) reduces intensive care unit length of stay and ventilator-associated complications, extubation feasibility following initial burn surgery remains uncertain. We investigated perioperative factors associated with postoperative continuation of mechanical ventilation (MV) after initial burn surgery. This retrospective study analyzed patients with burns who underwent acute-phase debridement between 2018 and 2024. Patients requiring postoperative MV were compared with those extubated in ORs. Factors independently associated with postoperative MV were identified using multivariate logistic regression analysis. Among 418 patients, 75 required postoperative MV. Age (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 1.03, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.00-1.06), percentage of total body surface area (%TBSA) burned (aOR = 1.08, 95% CI 1.03-1.12), preoperative intubation (aOR = 11.8, 95% CI 3.02-46.4), intraoperative fluid administration volume (ml/kg) (aOR = 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.06), and intraoperative maximum vasoactive-inotropic score (VIS) (aOR = 1.18, 95% CI 1.10-1.26) were independently associated with postoperative MV continuation. This association between the intraoperative maximum VIS and postoperative MV continuation was maintained in the sensitivity analysis excluding preoperatively intubated patients (aOR = 1.16, 95% CI 1.08-1.25). Age, %TBSA burned, preoperative intubation, intraoperative fluid administration volume, and maximum intraoperative VIS were independently associated with postoperative continuation of MV after initial burn surgery. Maximum intraoperative VIS may provide additional information regarding the hemodynamic component of perioperative severity by quantifying the intensity of vasoactive and inotropic support required during surgery.

articles.title: High-Frequency Chest Wall Oscillation in Critical Care: A Systematic Review.
articles.journal: Respiration; international review of thoracic diseases
articles.abstract: Airway secretion retention represents a major clinical challenge in critically ill patients, promoting gas exchange impairment and atelectasis, precipitating failure of noninvasive respiratory support, and prolonging invasive mechanical ventilation, with an associated increase in respiratory-related complications and mortality. High-frequency chest wall oscillation (HFCWO) is a noninvasive airway clearance technique widely used in chronic respiratory diseases, but its role in the intensive care unit (ICU) remains unclear. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the available evidence on the efficacy and safety of HFCWO in adult ICU patients. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane Library from inception to December 2025 in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Studies evaluating HFCWO in adult ICU patients, including those receiving invasive or noninvasive respiratory support, were eligible. Primary outcomes included duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, and mortality. Secondary outcomes included impact on secretion airway clearance and its radiographic/functional surrogates as well as safety and treatment tolerance. A limited number of studies met the inclusion criteria, mainly small randomized controlled trials and observational studies, characterized by substantial heterogeneity in patient populations, intervention protocols, and assessed outcomes. HFCWO effects on clinically meaningful primary endpoints, including duration of mechanical ventilation, length of ICU stay, and mortality, remain variable and inconclusive. Overall, HFCWO was well tolerated and appeared to enhance secretion clearance, with some studies reporting modest improvements in oxygenation and respiratory mechanics. Current evidence suggests that HFCWO is a safe and feasible airway clearance strategy in selected ICU patients with secretion burden and without proved effects on the main clinical outcomes. Lack of physiopathologically driven criteria for selection of patients more likely to respond to HFCWO either alone or integrated with other cough-assisting techniques may partially explain these scanty findings from the overall published studies. This precludes its routine use in clinical practice. Well-designed, adequately powered randomized trials are needed to define patient selection criteria, optimal timing, and the true clinical impact of HFCWO in the ICU setting.

articles.title: MPLA preconditioning protects against lethal radiation-combined burn injury with attenuation of KC/CXCL1-associated vascular leakage in mice.
articles.abstract: Radiation-combined burn injury (RCB), defined as concurrent irradiation and burn injury, is expected to be common in radiological or nuclear mass-casualty events and can be highly lethal. The mechanisms underlying the irradiation-burn interaction remain poorly understood, particularly whether it amplifies capillary leak and inflammatory mediator responses to drive early lethality. We examined whether repeated low-dose monophosphoryl lipid A (MPLA) preconditioning modulates this response and whether KC/CXCL1 contributes to vascular leakage. Male C57BL/6J mice underwent 6 Gy whole-body irradiation followed 1 h later by a 20% total body surface area full-thickness burn. MPLA (10 µg/mouse) or vehicle was administered intraperitoneally on days -4 and -3. We assessed 30-day survival, hemoconcentration, intravascular FITC-albumin retention, intestinal barrier endpoints, and cytokine/chemokine responses. A separate exploratory experiment evaluated pre-irradiation anti-KC/CXCL1 antibody treatment. Neither injury alone was lethal, whereas vehicle-treated RCB mice had 90% mortality (9 of 10 mice). Seven of these deaths occurred at 24-48 h after RCB. MPLA preconditioning increased 30-day survival from 10% to 80% (p = 0.0003) and eliminated deaths within 48 h. RCB induced hemoconcentration and tended to reduce FITC-albumin retention. Compared with vehicle-treated RCB mice, MPLA-preconditioned RCB mice had less hemoconcentration, significantly higher FITC-albumin retention, and lower mesenteric lymph node bacterial burden. MPLA preconditioning suppressed KC/CXCL1, which showed the largest absolute increase among measured cytokines/chemokines at 6 h. Anti-KC/CXCL1 antibody treatment significantly increased FITC-albumin retention at 6 h (p = 0.038). MPLA preconditioning improved survival after RCB. It may attenuate early inflammatory and vascular abnormalities. Exploratory antibody-treatment findings suggest a possible contribution of KC/CXCL1 to early vascular albumin leakage, warranting further validation.

articles.title: Effect of Different Single-Session Durations of Intermittent Pneumatic Compression on the Prevention of Deep Vein Thrombosis in Postoperative ICU Patients: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.journal: Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a common and potentially life-threatening complication in postoperative ICU patients. Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) is widely used for mechanical thromboprophylaxis; however, the optimal single-session duration of IPC remains unclear. This randomized controlled trial aimed to evaluate the efficacy of different single-session durations of IPC for preventing DVT in postoperative ICU patients. MATERIAL AND METHODS This prospective randomized controlled trial enrolled 138 patients who were randomized into 3 groups (n = 46 each) receiving IPC 3 times daily, with single-session durations of 40 minutes, 2 hours, or 6 hours. DVT incidence, coagulation parameters (D-dimer [mg/L] and fibrinogen [FIB; g/L]), and adverse events were compared on postoperative days 3 and 5. RESULTS Baseline characteristics were comparable among groups (P>0.05). The 6-hour group had a DVT incidence of 0% on both days, significantly lower than those in the 40-minute (15.21% and 32.61%) and 2-hour (8.70% and 34.78%) groups (P<0.05). No significant intergroup differences in D-dimer levels were observed (P>0.05); FIB levels significantly differed only on day 3 (P<0.05). Adverse events occurred in 6 patients (13.04%) in the 6-hour group, whereas none occurred in the other 2 groups. CONCLUSIONS Although 6-hour single-session IPC provides the most effective DVT prevention, it is associated with a higher risk of skin-related adverse events. Shorter, more frequent IPC (40 minutes or 2 hours per session, 3 times daily) may represent a preferable strategy for postoperative ICU patients due to its balance of efficacy, safety, and clinical feasibility.

articles.title: Evaluation of preoperative and perioperative characteristics in patients admitted to a postoperative intensive care unit: A prospective observational study.
articles.abstract: Postoperative intensive care unit (ICU) admission is commonly considered for patients perceived to be at increased risk of postoperative complications. This study aimed to describe the preoperative and perioperative characteristics of patients admitted to a postoperative ICU and to explore associations between routinely available clinical parameters, inflammatory biomarkers, and short-term outcomes. This prospective observational study included 126 adult patients admitted postoperatively to a tertiary reanimation ICU. Demographic characteristics, comorbidities, ASA physical status, anesthesia type, laboratory parameters, postoperative organ support requirements, ICU length of stay, and mortality were recorded. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio (CAR) were evaluated. Continuous and categorical variables were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test and chi-square or Fisher exact test, as appropriate. The mean age was 67.3 ± 16.1 years, and 114 (90.5%) patients were classified as ASA III. Abdominal surgery was the most common surgical category (56, 44.4%). Mean NLR and CAR values were 6.17 ± 8.36 and 1.17 ± 2.52, respectively. Two patients died (1.6%; exact 95% CI, 0.2-5.6%). Mortality was not significantly associated with NLR (P = .310), CAR (P = .845), admission SpO2 (P = .084), or hemoglobin level (P = .907). ICU length of stay showed an exploratory association with mortality (P = .004); given that only 2 deaths occurred, this observation cannot establish a prognostic relationship. In this selected postoperative ICU cohort, preoperative and perioperative characteristics did not clearly distinguish patients according to short-term outcomes. Because there was no non-ICU comparator cohort and mortality events were very limited, the findings should be interpreted cautiously. Larger multicenter studies are needed to evaluate whether these parameters can support postoperative ICU admission decisions.

articles.title: How Specialty Shapes Burnout in the Medical ICU: A Qualitative Study of Resident Experiences.
articles.abstract: The negative impacts of burnout in resident physicians have been widely documented, and burnout rates in the Medical Intensive Care Unit (MICU) are high. While burnout has been studied in physicians and other personnel in Intensive Care Units (ICUs), little attention has been given to resident physicians in the MICU. Our prior study demonstrated very high rates of burnout in residents in the MICU and was suggestive that non-internal medicine (non-IM) residents may be at an even higher risk of burnout than their internal medicine (IM) colleagues. This study aimed to determine and compare drivers and mitigators of burnout experienced by IM and non-IM (Family Medicine (FM) and Emergency Medicine (EM)) resident physicians rotating in the MICU. It also sought to identify drivers and mitigators of burnout that may be amenable to intervention strategies. Three different resident disciplines (IM, EM, and FM) hosted trained investigators who mediated focus groups of 4-12 trainees during protected teaching time between April 2022 and May 2023. The focus groups aimed at identifying contributors to and mitigators of burnout in the MICU. Trained scribes recorded notes from the conversation, which were later parsed into themes and compared across groups to determine if similar themes existed in other resident specialties. In this study, we identified common themes in the focus groups from residents of all specialties and themes unique to each specialty. Universal drivers of burnout included moral distress and ethical concerns and insufficient orientation. Multiple unique drivers for FM and EM residents were identified including decreased gratification (FM), guilt (FM),  communicating uncertainty to families (EM), managing chronic medical diseases (EM), and hierarchical relationships (FM & IM). Universal mitigators across all three specialties include meaningful patient experiences, time and access to food, and positive team dynamics. Drivers and mitigators of burnout vary across residency training specialties in the MICU, though common themes exist amongst different specialties. Identifying these themes creates opportunities for intervention strategies with the potential to improve resident satisfaction, training quality, and patient outcomes.

articles.title: Successful management of arrow‑rebound‑induced transcervical penetrating trauma with major vascular and pharyngolaryngeal injuries: A case report.
articles.abstract: Penetrating neck injury involving major vessels is highly lethal. Long-trajectory transcervical penetration caused by rebounding arrows is exceptionally rare in civilians, posing significant diagnostic and management challenges. A man in his early 50s presented to the emergency department approximately 2 hours after an arrow, rebounding from a nearby training target, penetrated his neck (entering above the left mandible, exiting on the right). He was conscious with minimal external bleeding but copious oropharyngeal secretions. Computed tomography angiography (CTA) revealed the arrow traversing the hyoid bone and oropharynx, abutting the right common carotid artery (CCA) and compressing the right internal jugular vein (IJV). Open neck injury; combined right CCA and IJV injury; hemorrhagic shock; pharyngolaryngeal trauma without aerodigestive perforation; and pulmonary infection with consolidation. Initial stabilization included arrow shaft shortening by firefighters. Emergency exploration under general anesthesia involved tracheotomy, cervical exploration, primary repair of the right IJV and CCA, and foreign body removal. Postoperative management in the intensive care unit included damage-control resuscitation (transfusion of 7.0 U packed red blood cells, 1100 mL plasma, and 10.5 U cryoprecipitate), antimicrobial therapy (cefuroxime, guided by cultures showing Staphylococcus epidermidis), early individualized anticoagulation (enoxaparin transitioned to rivaroxaban), and systematic correction of coagulopathy and electrolyte disturbances. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 12 with healed wounds. Follow-up at 1, 3, 6.5 months, 1, 2, and nearly 3 years showed intact neurological function. Imaging confirmed stable right IJV occlusion. Anticoagulation was discontinued at 1 month without subsequent bleeding or thromboembolism. Although long-term imaging was limited to a 6.5-month non-contrast computed tomography, the patient remained asymptomatic without signs of venous hypertension or neurological deficits throughout the follow-up period. High-quality preoperative computed tomography angiography with 3D reconstruction is critical for defining the relationship between the foreign body and vital structures. In selected patients, early individualized anticoagulation after excluding active bleeding may mitigate venous thrombosis. Systematic intensive care unit management of coagulopathy, electrolytes, and pulmonary complications is pivotal for survival.

articles.title: Association Between Lactate Levels upon ICU Admission After Liver Transplantation and the Burden of In-Hospital Complications: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Background: ICU-admission lactate after liver transplantation (LT) may reflect perioperative stress, but its association with cumulative morbidity remains unclear. Methods: This retrospective cohort included 457 adults undergoing first LT between October 2015 and July 2026. ICU-admission lactate was evaluated in four prespecified strata (<2, 2-<5, 5-<10, ≥10 mmol/L). Outcomes included the Comprehensive Complication Index (CCI), adapted early allograft dysfunction (EAD), Toronto graft dysfunction, MEAF, and death or retransplantation at 7 and 30 days. Analyses included multivariable regression, ROC analysis, and bootstrap validation. Results: Strata comprised 178, 210, 51, and 18 recipients. Median CCI increased from 29.6 to 89.3 (p < 0.001). After adjustment, the ≥10 mmol/L group had a 40.1-point higher median CCI than the <2 mmol/L group (95% CI 27.1-53.0). Adapted EAD increased from 24.2% to 83.3%, and severe Toronto dysfunction from 0.6% to 61.1%. Seven-day death or retransplantation increased from 0% to 61.1% (adjusted HR per lactate doubling 2.83, 95% CI 2.15-3.72; AUC 0.869). Adding lactate increased the 30-day AUC from 0.691 to 0.800 (optimism-corrected: 0.652 to 0.767). Conclusions: ICU-admission lactate was associated with postoperative morbidity and early adverse outcomes, supporting risk stratification pending external validation.

articles.title: Perioperative Impact of Incidental Durotomy in Elderly Patients Undergoing Elective Spine Surgery: A Multicenter European Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Incidental durotomy is among the most frequent intraoperative complications in spine surgery, yet elderly patients may be especially vulnerable to its downstream consequences because of frailty, multimorbidity, delayed mobilization, and postoperative neurocognitive complications. The literature suggests that durotomy is associated with increased perioperative resource utilization, whereas long-term functional outcomes are not well reported. We performed a retrospective multicenter cohort study across five European academic neurosurgical centers. Consecutive patients aged 65 years or older who underwent elective spine surgery between 2019 and 2024 were reviewed. Patients with incidental durotomy during the index procedure were compared with those without durotomy. Outcomes of interest included length of stay, thromboembolic events, postoperative infection, delirium, readmission, revision surgery, postoperative intensive care use, and discharge disposition. Among 723 included patients, 107 (14.8%) sustained an incidental durotomy. Operative time was longer in the durotomy cohort (median 178 vs 138 minutes; p < 0.001), as were length of stay (8 vs 5 days; p < 0.001), thromboembolic events (6.5% vs 1.8%; p = 0.010), and postoperative delirium (14.0% vs 5.2%; p = 0.001). In descriptive analyses of patients older than 75 years, median length of stay was 10 vs 6 days, delirium occurred in 17.7% vs 7.4%, and thromboembolic events occurred in 8.1% vs 2.2%. Postoperative infection, 30-day readmission, revision surgery, intensive care use, and discharge disposition were not significantly different between groups. In elderly patients undergoing elective spine surgery, incidental durotomy was associated mainly with increased perioperative morbidity rather than clearly worse short-term post-discharge outcomes. The signals for prolonged stay, delirium, and thromboembolic complications-especially in patients older than 75 years-support age-sensitive perioperative pathways emphasizing meticulous repair, early mobilization when clinically appropriate, delirium prevention, and close medical surveillance.

articles.title: Hemodynamic Management in Burn Patients with Vasopressor-Dependent Sepsis: A Preliminary Exploratory Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Background: Sepsis remains a leading cause of late mortality in critically ill burn patients. The optimal hemodynamic strategy, including vasopressor combinations, corticosteroids, and landiolol therapy, remains incompletely defined in this population. Objective: To examine factors associated with landiolol therapy, vasopressor strategies, and corticosteroid use in burn patients with vasopressor-dependent sepsis, and to evaluate their relationship with organ dysfunction and clinical outcomes. Methods: We conducted a preliminary exploratory retrospective cohort study in a specialized burn intensive care unit (ICU) over a three-year period (2022-2024). All mechanically ventilated adult burn patients who developed sepsis requiring vasopressor support during ICU stay were included. The primary exposure of interest was landiolol therapy; five outcomes were assessed for this exposure (ventilator-free days at day 28 after sepsis onset, duration of mechanical ventilation after sepsis onset, ICU length of stay after sepsis onset, acute kidney injury [AKI] after sepsis, and ICU mortality). Hydrocortisone administration and dual vasopressor therapy with norepinephrine plus vasopressin were evaluated as secondary descriptive exposures. Results: Thirty-one patients were included (mean age 55.8 ± 15.3 years; mean TBSA 40.2 ± 13.3%). ICU mortality was 35.5% (11/31). Landiolol was administered in 41.9% of patients; all treated patients were in sinus tachycardia (heart rate 111-140 beats/min), whereas all untreated patients had heart rates <95 beats/min at sepsis onset. No differences were detected for any outcome: ventilator-free days at day 28 (18 [0-23.5] vs. 0 [0-17] days; multiplicity-adjusted p = 0.97), mechanical ventilation duration after sepsis onset (10 [4.5-23] vs. 15 [4.75-53.25] days; multiplicity-adjusted p > 0.99), ICU length of stay after sepsis onset (41 [21-62] vs. 56 [15-106.25] days; multiplicity-adjusted p > 0.99), AKI (2/13 vs. 5/18; OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.08-2.93; multiplicity-adjusted p > 0.99), and ICU mortality (6/13 vs. 5/18; OR 2.23, 95% CI 0.50-10.00; multiplicity-adjusted p > 0.99). The shorter total mechanical ventilation duration in landiolol-treated patients (24 [7-38] vs. 53 [18.75-79.75] days) reflected shorter ventilation before sepsis onset (6 [3-16] vs. 16.5 [10-36.75] days) and the competing risk of early death (six of eleven deaths occurred within 28 days of sepsis onset). Dual vasopressor therapy (25.8%) and hydrocortisone (19.4%) identified phenotypes of greater shock severity. Conclusions: In this small preliminary retrospective cohort, protocolized landiolol therapy in sinus-tachycardic patients was feasible and achieved heart-rate targets, but was not associated with detectable differences in clinical outcomes. These exploratory findings warrant adequately powered prospective studies in this population.

articles.title: Network Trauma Research series: Modeling Trauma Complexity: Rodent Platforms for Studying Bone Healing and Hemorrhagic Shock.
articles.abstract: Polytrauma, defined as severe injury to multiple body regions often accompanied by physiological instability, remains a major global health burden with high morbidity and mortality. Among the most clinically relevant two-injury combinations, long-bone fractures and hemorrhagic shock are particularly important, as both critically influence systemic inflammation, remote organ dysfunction such as lung or kidney damage, and tissue regeneration itself. To improve translational understanding of these complex interactions, robust small-animal models, particularly murine systems, have been developed to experimentally dissect the biological mechanisms underlying fracture healing, hypovolemic shock, and their combined effects. This review provides a comprehensive overview of current rodent models for isolated fracture, hemorrhagic shock, and combination trauma. Key methodological variables, such as fracture induction methods, fixation strategies, hemorrhage protocols, anesthesia and analgesia, and the influence of age, sex, and comorbidities are outlined to support informed model selection. Additionally, this manuscript highlights the challenges and opportunities in designing clinically relevant "double-hit" models that mimic real-world trauma patterns while maintaining high reproducibility and animal welfare standards. Collectively, the summarized evidence underscores the importance of standardized, physiologically meaningful preclinical trauma models to advance mechanistic insights and foster the development of effective therapeutic interventions.

articles.title: Reimbursement of Severe Trauma Care Under the SwissDRG Prospective Payment System: 11-Year Evolution of Cost-Reimbursement Adequacy.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: The Swiss Diagnosis-Related Groups (SwissDRG) system, introduced in 2012, aimed to enhance cost transparency and reimbursement efficiency. However, trauma centers treating severely injured patients face financial challenges due to complex care needs and difficulties in estimating appropriate cost weights. This study assessed the adaptability of the SwissDRG prospective payment system since its implementation and identified key drivers of financial deficits in polytrauma care. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study at Lausanne University Hospital, including 382 adult polytrauma patients with an Injury Severity Score ≥ 16, treated from 2012-2019. Reimbursement was evaluated using three methods: MOOS, which grouped the entire population using tariffs from the first three years of SwissDRG implementation; ACTUAL, which compared costs and reimbursements per patient and per year; and RECODED, which simulated updated DRG classifications over an extended 11-year period, up to 2023. Statistical modeling identified the main drivers of financial deficits. Results: The MOOS method showed near-full cost coverage by 2015. The ACTUAL method revealed an average loss of CHF -2751 per patient and a cumulative deficit of CHF -1.05 million over 8 years, with intensive care unit (ICU)-related and polytrauma-specific DRGs as main contributors. In highly complex cases (ISS ≥ 20; 273/382 [71.5%]) mean losses reached CHF -3588. The RECODED method found full cost coverage only in 2021, despite substantial cumulative deficits needing decades of surplus to offset. Conclusions: Current SwissDRG reimbursement remains inadequate for complex trauma care. A more tailored model reflecting ICU costs, outlier penalties, and care complexity is urgently needed to sustain high-quality trauma services in Switzerland.

articles.title: Network Trauma Research Series: Modeling Trauma Complexity - In Vitro Models to Study Traumatic Lung Damage.
articles.abstract: Polytrauma, defined as severe injury to multiple body regions, frequently affects the head and thorax and induces a systemic immune response that can favor secondary infections such as pneumonia. In particular, thoracic trauma substantially increases the risk of post-traumatic pneumonia, as direct lung injury, impaired respiratory function, and the frequent need for mechanical ventilation predispose patients to pulmonary infections, thereby contributing to adverse clinical outcomes. To improve translational understanding of these interactions, complex in vitro models have been developed to experimentally dissect the biological mechanisms underlying injuries of the lung. This review provides a comprehensive overview of current in vitro lung models and their suitability to analyze trauma induced lung damage and following infection. Key methodological variables are the selection of appropriate cell lines, the modeling of air - liquid interface or barrier function and the simulation of the trauma. Importantly, experimental approaches should clearly distinguish between inflammatory stimulation and mechanical injury, as these represent distinct pathophysiological processes. Collectively, the models discussed herein highlight the importance of standardized and physiologically relevant in vitro trauma models for advancing mechanistic insights and facilitating the development of targeted therapeutic strategies.

articles.title: Physiologic, Metabolic, and Protein Redox Effects of Methylene Blue in a Porcine Hemorrhage Model.
articles.abstract: Methylene blue (MB) has established benefit in vasodilatory shock, and a potential role in hemorrhagic shock. Some evidence suggests that MB could lower anesthetic requirements. The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of MB on volatile anesthetic requirements (primary), metabolic markers (secondary), and protein redox modifications (tertiary) in a porcine hemorrhage model. This was a randomized 2 x 2 factorial animal study conducted at a tertiary medical center in 2019-2020. Forty swine were randomized to the following experimental interventions: hemorrhage (0 v. 30 mL/kg, at t = 0 min) and MB (0 v. 2 mg/kg, at t = 20 min). End-tidal isoflurane, blood pressure, and arterial blood gas parameters were recorded at prespecified intervals. Skeletal muscle was used for redox analyses. Group differences were investigated with mixed effects and one-way analyses of variance. There was no effect of MB on volatile requirements or metabolic markers (all P > 0.05). Hemorrhage was associated with 2.4 mg/dL higher lactate (95% CI, 1.4 to 3.4) and 23 mmHg lower mean arterial pressure (95% CI, 11 to 34). Hemorrhage was also associated with increased protein carbonyl levels (P < 0.001) that were non-significantly attenuated by MB (P = 0.130), and increased protein S-nitrosylation (P < 0.001) that was significantly attenuated by MB (P < 0.001). MB does not have a significant effect on volatile anesthetic requirements or systemic physiologic and metabolic responses during hemorrhagic shock. However, MB significantly attenuates protein S-nitrosylation and partially attenuates protein carbonyl accumulation.

articles.title: Tracheostomy after burn and inhalation injury: A tale of two patient populations.
articles.abstract: Severe burn injury is often accompanied by inhalation injury (II), facial burns, large-volume resuscitation, and prolonged critical illness, frequently requiring tracheostomy. Tracheostomy timing is well studied after trauma but comparative data in burn patients remain limited and conflicting and have not accounted for inhalation injury status. We retrospectively reviewed adults (age≥18) admitted 9/2022-3/2025 with burns and/or II requiring tracheostomy, examining demographics, comorbidities, tracheostomy timing, and clinical outcomes. Patients were compared by survival status, stratified by II, and by decannulation status. Of 51 patients identified, 43 met inclusion criteria-predominantly Black (48.8%) males (74.4%), mean age 52.1 ± 17.5 years, mostly flame burns (90.7%). Median total body surface area was 30.0% (IQR 26.5); nearly half (46.5%) had II. Most survivors (72.7%) were decannulated before discharge. Overall, tracheostomy timing did not affect survival. However, surviving II patients (n = 16) underwent tracheostomy earlier than non-survivors (n = 4) (9.4 ± 6.4 vs 19.8 ± 11.5 days, p = 0.024), whereas among patients without II the pattern reversed and was non-significant (survivors n = 17, 13.1 ± 4.3 vs non-survivors n = 6, 9.8 ± 5.0 days, p = 0.143). Burn patients requiring tracheostomy comprise two distinct populations with divergent timing-survival relationships. These single-center, quality-improvement findings are specific to our population and not generalizable; they motivated an internal, inhalation-stratified decision aid to individualize timing that we plan to evaluate prospectively. Presented in part at the Southeastern Surgical Congress (SESC), 2026.

articles.title: Sex Differences in ICU Assignment and Mechanical Ventilation for Patients with Myocardial Infarction.
articles.abstract: We aimed to examine sex-related differences in the allocation of intensive care and mechanical ventilation among patients with myocardial infarction. Understanding these differences may help identify potential disparities in critical care delivery and inform efforts to promote equitable treatment allocation. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the publicly available MIMIC-IV database, which contains de-identified electronic health records of ICU patients. We identified all adult patients (≥20 years) admitted to any ICU with a diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction using ICD codes. This study uses the denormalized MIMIC-IV ICU database to examine the hourly progression of patient treatments and outcomes. Women with MI were less likely than men to be admitted to cardiac specialty ICUs and had significantly higher mortality and lower odds of receiving mechanical ventilation. Patterns of ICU assignment revealed notable sex disparities as well. Women admitted with MI were less likely than men to be assigned to the CVICU but more likely to be placed in the Neuro-Intermediate ICU. The differences observed in this study may reflect the higher prevalence of atypical symptom presentation in women, which can lead to misdiagnosis and subsequent admission to non-specialty ICUs, including those oriented toward neurological conditions. The observed differences in ICU distribution do not establish their underlying causes, because the clinical indications and decision-making processes underlying ICU assignment were not evaluated. These real-world findings highlight the need to examine how sex influences ICU placement, and to consider policy and practice changes that reduce these biases.

articles.title: Evaluation of early hydrocortisone use for hemodynamic shock in adult burn patients with suspected critical illness related corticosteroid insufficiency.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency (CIRCI) presents as refractory hemodynamic shock in critically ill patients. Research on CIRCI and its treatment in burn patients is limited. We sought to review the use of corticosteroids in a burn population during their first week of hospitalization. The burn registry and the electronic medical records were queried for burn patients admitted between January 2015 and December 2025. The following variables were abstracted: demographics, burn history, hospital course, and treatments. Outcome variables included length of stay (LOS), infections, graft loss, pharmacological treatment, and mortality. The two groups were compared with Student's T-test and Chi Square where appropriate. A multivariant analysis was performed to determine independent predictors of CIRCI, infection and mortality. Significance was determined at p<0.05 level. The study group consisted of 87 patients in hemodynamic shock receiving vasopressors, with 47 also receiving corticosteroids. The corticosteroid group had larger burns (37.6 v 25.1%), more resuscitation (15.9 v 8.1 L), more vasopressor days (6.23 v 3.7 d), more ventilator days (19.72 v 7.83 d), more infections (66% v 34%) and longer LOS (51.53 v 26.05 d), all p<0.05. On multivariant analysis, variables independently related to the diagnosis of CIRCI were age and resuscitation fluids; to infection were corticosteroid use; and to mortality were age. Overall, over 50% of patients in hypotensive shock during their first week of treatment were diagnosed and treated with corticosteroids for suspected CIRCI. More study is needed to determine the appropriate role of corticosteroid use in early burn treatment.

articles.title: Surgeons' Immediate Postoperative Prediction After Major Emergency Abdominal Surgery.
articles.abstract: Major emergency abdominal surgery carries high morbidity and mortality, making accurate risk stratification important. Whether surgeons' immediate postoperative clinical judgment predicts outcomes and how it compares with established surgical risk models remains poorly characterized. Prospective single-center cohort of 411 patients undergoing major emergency abdominal surgery (February 2024-June 2025). Immediately after surgery, the operating surgeon estimated 30-d mortality (ordinal 10% intervals) and the risk of complications (0-10 scale). Discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]) and calibration (observed-to-expected ratio, calibration slope and intercept, Brier score) were assessed. Mortality discrimination was compared with National Emergency Laparotomy Audit and Portsmouth Physiological and Operative Severity Score for the enUmeration of Mortality and Morbidity using the DeLong test. Thirty-day mortality was 11% (47/411). Surgeon-estimated risk showed good discrimination for mortality (AUC: 0.89; 95% confidence interval: 0.85-0.94), comparable to National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (0.90) and Portsmouth Physiological and Operative Severity Score for the enUmeration of Mortality and Morbidity (0.86; P = 0.83 and P = 0.30). Surgeons systematically overestimated absolute mortality (mean predicted: 23% versus observed: 11%; observed-to-expected: 0.48; intercept: -1.17; slope: 1.20). For complications, discrimination was good for sepsis/multi-organ failure (AUC 0.81) and acceptable for intensive care unit admission (0.78) and cardiac complications (0.78), but poor for reoperation (0.62) and mechanical bowel obstruction (0.62), and absent for prolonged paralytic bowel dysfunction (0.51). Higher estimated risk was associated with increased odds of complications. Predicted discharge destination agreed moderately with observed (accuracy 74%; weighted κ 0.61). Surgeons' immediate postoperative assessment showed discriminatory performance of a similar magnitude to established models but systematically overestimated absolute risk and performed better for systemic than procedure-specific complications. This bedside estimate may aid early risk stratification but requires external validation before clinical use.

articles.title: The First 48 Hours: Incidence, Timing and Predictors of Adverse Events After ICU-To-Ward Transfer: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: The transition from the intensive care unit (ICU) to a general ward is a period of heightened vulnerability, yet the precise timing and modifiable predictors of adverse events remain poorly defined. To determine the incidence, timing and types of adverse events following ICU-to-ward transfer, evaluate the predictive accuracy of four early-warning scores and identify independent risk factors. A prospective cohort study of 207 adult patients transferred from ICUs to general wards at a tertiary university hospital over 20 months (March 2024-October 2025) was enrolled. Four early warning scores (PACS, MEWS, SWIFT, LACE) were calculated daily for 5 days post-transfer. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors. The total number Adverse events occurred in 52 patients (25.1%), most commonly ICU readmission (n = 46, 22.2%) and healthcare-associated infections (n = 29, 14.0%). Critically, 88% of events occurred within the first 48 h (day 1: 56.0%; day 2: 32.0%). SWIFT demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy at transfer (AUC 0.856). Mechanical ventilation was the strongest independent risk factor (OR 10.11), followed by prolonged ICU stay (OR 6.40), respiratory diagnosis (OR 4.99), > 3 invasive devices (OR 4.41) and comorbidities (OR 3.64). These five factors collectively explained 88.5% of adverse events. Adverse events affect one in four patients after ICU-to-ward transfer, with the vast majority occurring within the first 48 h. A simple set of readily identifiable risk factors can guide nursing surveillance and targeted interventions during this critical window. Bedside nurses should prioritize enhanced monitoring for patients with a history of mechanical ventilation, prolonged ICU stay, multiple invasive devices and significant comorbidities during the first 48 h post-transfer. Daily use of early-warning scores can inform monitoring frequency and rapid response activation.

articles.title: Effect of Progressive Muscle Relaxation and Nature Sounds on Alarm Fatigue in Intensive Care Unit Nurses: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) nurses are exposed to numerous alarms, many of which are unnecessary and lead to alarm fatigue. This phenomenon, caused by desensitization to alarm sounds, reduces nurses' responsiveness to critical alerts and threatens both their well-being and patient safety. Alarm fatigue has been linked to elevated stress, burnout and errors in patient care, underscoring the need for effective interventions. Progressive muscle relaxation involves the gradual and systematic contraction and relaxation of different muscle groups throughout the body and nature sounds use for decrease stress and alarm fatigue. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) and exposure to nature sounds in reducing alarm fatigue among ICU nurses. A three-arm, parallel, single-blinded randomized controlled trial was conducted. Ninety-six ICU nurses from three hospitals in southern Iran, were randomly assigned to one of three groups: PMR (n = 32), nature sounds (n = 32) or control (n = 32). Alarm fatigue was assessed using a validated alarm fatigue scale at baseline, immediately after the intervention and 2 months post-intervention. Both PMR and nature sound interventions significantly reduced alarm fatigue among ICU nurses (p < 0.001). Between-group comparisons showed significant differences between the PMR and control groups (p < 0.001) and between the nature sound and control groups (p < 0.001). No significant difference was observed between the PMR and nature sound groups (p = 0.650). PMR and exposure to nature sounds significantly reduced alarm fatigue among ICU nurses, as reflected in lower fatigue scores. These interventions improved nurses' capacity to manage stress and fatigue, thereby supporting better job performance and enhanced patient safety. Given their simplicity and accessibility, both approaches represent promising strategies for addressing alarm fatigue in critical care settings. Progressive muscle relaxation and nature sounds may offer practical, non-pharmacological approaches to managing alarm fatigue among intensive care unit nurses. These interventions could be incorporated into nurses' work routines, although further research is needed to confirm their effectiveness and long-term benefits.

articles.title: Incidence of Intensive Care Unit Delirium After Heart Surgery: A Feasibility Study of a Forest Environment Intervention.
articles.abstract: Postoperative delirium is a serious complication in intensive care units (ICUs), particularly following cardiac surgery. It is associated with circadian rhythm disruption, sleep disturbances and adverse outcomes. ICU environments often lack natural time cues, which may exacerbate circadian misalignment and increase delirium risk. The primary aim of the study was the evaluation of the implementation of two chronotherapeutic ICU interventions regarding recruitment, implementability and safety. Its secondary aim was to descriptively assess postoperative delirium across intervention groups. This randomized feasibility study was conducted in a tertiary cardiac surgery ICU in Austria. Adult patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery were allocated to one of three groups: (1) forest environment, (2) light exposure or (3) standard ICU care. Interventions were applied for 12 h daily. Delirium was assessed at three postoperative time points using the confusion assessment method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) and intensive care delirium screening checklist (ICDSC). This study was conducted between March 2020 and 2025. Seventy-seven patients were enrolled, and 64 remained in the final analytical cohort. Interventions were delivered within routine care. Patients and ICU staff did not report intervention-related concerns. Implementation challenges included ICU restructuring, patient transfers due to COVID-19 and deviations from randomized allocation because of operational constraints. No intervention-related adverse events occurred. Delirium assessments were limited at several time points because of sedation, early ICU discharge or transfer. Across all groups, postoperative delirium was detected in 5 of 130 CAM-ICU completed assessments (3.8%) and 8 of 115 ICDSC completed assessments (6.9%), precluding inferential group comparisons. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions were feasible and safe in ICU care. Feasibility results highlighted challenges related to ICU logistics, sedation-related assessment limitations and pandemic-related disruptions. The unexpectedly low delirium incidence limited conclusions regarding intervention efficacy. Future trials should include larger high-risk populations and prospectively defined feasibility outcomes. Optimized ICU environments, including noise reduction and light management, may support delirium prevention. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions are feasible additions to routine ICU care.

articles.title: Psychological Detachment Among Intensive Care Unit Nurses: A Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit nurses face sustained workload, vigilance and emotionally demanding care. Psychological detachment during non-work time is an important recovery experience, but evidence in this population remains limited. To describe psychological detachment among intensive care unit nurses and identify demographic, departmental psychological support resources availability, social support and burnout dimensions associated with it. A single-centre cross-sectional survey. Registered intensive care unit nurses from a tertiary grade A general hospital in eastern China were recruited by convenience sampling between June and July 2025. Participants completed demographic, psychological detachment, burnout and social support questionnaires. Descriptive analyses, univariate comparisons, correlation analyses and multivariable linear regression were performed. The study was reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology checklist. Of 220 questionnaires submitted, 199 valid responses were analysed (90.45%). The mean psychological detachment score was 11.68 ± 3.85. Mean emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation and personal accomplishment scores were 37.75 ± 8.15, 16.93 ± 4.87 and 25.91 ± 6.25, respectively. Psychological detachment correlated negatively with emotional exhaustion (r = -0.230, p = 0.001) and positively with subjective support (r = 0.175, p = 0.013). Departmental psychological support resources availability (B = 1.674, β = 0.216, p = 0.001), head-nurse position (B = -4.776, β = -0.195, p = 0.004) and emotional exhaustion (B = -0.115, β = -0.243, p < 0.001) were independently associated with psychological detachment. In this single-centre sample of intensive care unit nurses, the reported availability of departmental psychological support resources was associated with higher psychological detachment, whereas head-nurse position and emotional exhaustion were associated with lower psychological detachment. These findings suggest that critical care nursing managers may consider departmental psychological support resources availability, nursing position and emotional exhaustion when assessing recovery needs among intensive care unit nurses.

articles.title: Efficacy and Safety of Low-Dose Versus Standard-Dose Alteplase to Treat High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism.
articles.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses
articles.abstract: The optimal dosing of alteplase in patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism is widely debated. To evaluate outcomes in patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism who received alteplase at a low dose or a standard dose. This was a retrospective cohort analysis of 65 patients who received alteplase for high-risk pulmonary embolism at a large academic medical center between June 1, 2011, and August 31, 2022. Patients were placed in 2 cohorts according to initial dose: low-dose alteplase (50 mg) and standard-dose alteplase (100 mg). The primary outcome was sustained hemodynamic stability within 24 hours of the start of alteplase infusion. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, hospital and intensive care unit length of stay, and major bleeding. The primary outcome of sustained hemodynamic stability within 24 hours did not differ significantly between the 2 cohorts (achieved in 32% of patients in the low-dose group and 38% in the standard-dose group; P = .65). In-hospital mortality did not differ significantly between groups (48% in the low-dose group vs 45% in the standard-dose group; P = .81). Patients in the low-dose group had fewer days of mechanical ventilation than patients in the standard-dose group (1.5 vs 6 days; P = .03) and a smaller percentage had major bleeding (12% vs 25%; P = .34). In patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism, sustained hemodynamic stability within 24 hours did not differ significantly between low-dose and standard-dose alteplase treatment strategies. Low-dose alteplase may be an appropriate alternative dosing strategy for patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism.

articles.title: Effect of preoperative video-based digital educational program on incidence of delirium and length of hospital stay following coronary artery bypass grafting: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.journal: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care
articles.abstract: Postoperative delirium is common after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) and is associated with prolonged hospitalization and delayed recovery. Non-pharmacological educational interventions may improve outcomes, but evidence on structured video-based education for delirium prevention remains limited. To evaluate the effect of a preoperative video-based educational program on postoperative delirium incidence and hospital length of stay among patients undergoing CABG surgery. A parallel-group randomized controlled trial was conducted at Queen Alia Heart Institute, Jordan, between October 2025 and January 2026. Adult patients scheduled for elective first-time CABG surgery were randomized into intervention and control groups. Both groups received standardized multidisciplinary preoperative education through the institutional Preoperative Clinic, while the intervention group additionally received an 8-minute structured Arabic video-based educational program. Postoperative delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU). Among 226 randomized participants, 213 were analyzed (105 intervention; 108 control). Delirium incidence was lower with intervention (7.6%vs 25.0%, p < .001) and remained significantly associated with study group after adjustment (OR = 3.14, 95% CI: 1.08-9.14, p = .036). Hospital stay was shorter in the intervention group unadjusted (8.38 vs 10.58 days, p < .001), but not after adjustment (B = -0.656, p = .182). Preoperative video-based education was associated with lower postoperative delirium incidence, while its association with shorter hospital stay was not maintained after adjustment. Larger multicenter trials are warranted.

articles.title: Anesthetic management of right radical nephrectomy and inferior vena cava thrombectomy for giant renal cell carcinoma: a case report.
articles.journal: International journal of surgery case reports
articles.abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) with tumor thrombus extension into the inferior vena cava (IVC) represents a major surgical and anesthetic challenge because of the high risk of massive hemorrhage, hemodynamic instability, and intraoperative tumor embolism. We report the case of a 55-year-old man presenting with a large right renal mass measuring 14 × 14 × 13 cm, with a tumor thrombus extending from the right renal vein into the infrahepatic IVC. The patient underwent right radical nephrectomy with caval thrombectomy under general anesthesia and invasive hemodynamic monitoring. Anesthetic management focused on anticipating major blood loss, preventing thromboembolic complications related to thrombus manipulation, ensuring adequate blood product availability, and maintaining perioperative hemodynamic optimization. Intraoperative blood loss was estimated at 3500 mL, which necessitated transfusion of four units of packed red blood cells and four units of fresh frozen plasma. The intraoperative course was favorable, with satisfactory hemodynamic stability throughout the procedure, and the patient was subsequently transferred to the intensive care unit for postoperative monitoring. This case highlights the importance of meticulous multidisciplinary planning and perioperative anesthetic management in patients with locally advanced RCC and an IVC tumor thrombus to minimize potentially fatal hemorrhagic and thromboembolic complications. In summary, this report demonstrates the anesthesiologist's critical role in mitigating the severe hemodynamic and hemorrhagic risks of radical nephrectomy with IVC thrombectomy through meticulous, multidisciplinary perioperative planning. Specifically, this case emphasizes three key clinical messages: (1) early multidisciplinary planning is mandatory for complex urologic oncology; (2) continuous invasive hemodynamic monitoring combined with early vasopressor support is crucial to manage abrupt preload reductions during IVC clamping; and (3) proactive transfusion preparedness via a standardized massive transfusion protocol prevents coagulopathy during massive hemorrhage.

articles.title: Ventilator Modes Used to Facilitate Liberation From Mechanical Ventilation: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract: Liberation from invasive ventilation involves gradual decrements in respiratory support, spontaneous breathing trials, or both. Although various ventilator modes have been studied to facilitate weaning, the approaches used across trials for the highest risk patients are not well summarized. We sought to summarize the different ventilator modes and liberation strategies that have been investigated in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of critically ill adults at risk for difficult or prolonged weaning from invasive ventilation. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, and Cochrane Library databases from inception to January 2026. We conducted a scoping review of RCTs that enrolled critically ill adults (≥ 18 yr) who received invasive ventilation for greater than or equal to 24 hours and were considered to have either difficult or prolonged weaning (Weaning according to a New Definition [WIND] group "no wean," "difficult weaning," or "prolonged weaning") and compared two or more assisted ventilatory modes. We excluded trials that compared ventilatory modes for spontaneous breathing test (SBT) conduct, invasive vs. noninvasive ventilation, or tracheostomized patients at the time of randomization. We extracted data related to eligibility criteria, outcomes, and weaning protocols and assessed risk of bias using a modified Cochrane risk of bias tool in duplicate. Among 38 eligible trials, the most studied ventilatory modes were pressure support ventilation (71.1%, 27 trials) and synchronized intermittent or intermittent mandatory ventilation (31.6%, 12 trials). The most frequently studied automated modes were SmartCare/pressure support (15.8%, six trials) and proportional assist ventilation (15.8%, six trials). Weaning typically used a gradual reduction in support without a mode change (52.6%, 20 trials), or with intermittent SBTs (31.6%, 12 trials). Overall risk of bias was commonly high due to a probably high risk of selective reporting. Diverse modes and strategies have been evaluated to achieve liberation. Future research should focus on adequately powered, high-quality trials of the effect of commonly used and widely available modes and strategies on clinically important outcomes for liberation from mechanical ventilation of high-risk patients.

articles.title: Effects of neurally adjusted ventilatory assist on mortality in critically ill patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.journal: The Journal of international medical research
articles.abstract: ObjectivePatient-ventilator asynchrony is associated with poor outcomes. Previous data have shown that neurally adjusted ventilatory assist reduces patient-ventilator asynchrony. This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed whether neurally adjusted ventilatory assist reduces mortality compared with conventional ventilation modes and whether this effect differs between invasive and noninvasive modes of neurally adjusted ventilatory assist.MethodsWe searched the PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Controlled Clinical Trials databases up to 18 July 2026. Randomized controlled trials comparing neurally adjusted ventilatory assist with other modes were included. The primary outcomes were intensive care unit mortality, hospital mortality, mechanical ventilation success rate, and 28-day ventilator-free days. Two authors screened the studies for eligibility, extracted the data, and completed the data table. Study quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool 2.0. Summary estimates were reported as risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals for dichotomous data and as mean differences with 95% confidence intervals for continuous data.ResultsNine randomized controlled trials involving 842 patients (389 receiving neurally adjusted ventilatory assist and 453 receiving conventional ventilation) were included. In patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation, compared with conventional modes, neurally adjusted ventilatory assist reduced intensive care unit mortality (risk ratio = 0.72, 95% confidence interval: 0.53-0.99) and hospital mortality (risk ratio = 0.71, 95% confidence interval: 0.56-0.90) and increased the mechanical ventilation success rate (risk ratio = 1.13, 95% confidence interval: 1.04-1.22) and the number of 28-day ventilator-free days (mean difference = 3.48, 95% confidence interval: 0.97-6.00). In patients receiving noninvasive ventilation, neurally adjusted ventilatory assist did not significantly reduce hospital mortality (p = 0.23; I2 = 0%) or increase the mechanical ventilation success rate (p = 0.66; I2 = 0%), and 28-day ventilator-free days were reported only in the invasive mechanical ventilation trials.ConclusionNeurally adjusted ventilatory assist during invasive mechanical ventilation was associated with lower intensive care unit and hospital mortality, a higher mechanical ventilation success rate, and a greater number of 28-day ventilator-free days, whereas no such benefit was demonstrated during noninvasive ventilation. The evidence for noninvasive neurally adjusted ventilatory assist remains limited.

articles.title: Beyond COVID-19: Prolonged Versus Standard Prone Positioning in ARDS of Diverse Aetiologies.
articles.abstract: Prolonged prone positioning (PPP, > 24 h per session) was widely adopted during the COVID-19 pandemic, but its safety and efficacy in patients with moderate-to-severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remain uncertain in non-COVID-19 ARDS. This study compared clinical outcomes and safety of PPP versus standard prone positioning (SPP, 16-24 h) in a post-pandemic cohort. 239 patients with ARDS were categorized according to the duration of the first PP session. The primary outcome was 28-day all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included ventilator liberation, ICU discharge, pressure injuries and other complications. To mitigate potential treatment selection bias, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied. In total, n = 239 patients (PPP n = 130, SPP n = 109), 28-day mortality was similar between the PPP and SPP groups (39.0% vs. 35.0%, p = 0.53). No significant differences were observed in time to ventilator liberation (55.8% vs. 61.0%, p = 0.42) or ICU discharge by Day 28 (49.0% vs. 56.0%, p = 0.28). Although the cumulative duration and overall pressure injury rate by Day 7 did not differ, the PPP group had a significantly higher incidence of Stage II injuries (32.8% vs. 18.4%, p = 0.016), whereas Stage I injuries were more common in the SPP group (31.1% vs. 13.4%, p = 0.002). Independent risk factors for pressure injury included lower serum albumin (OR 1.11 per 1 g/L decrease, p = 0.002), cumulative prone duration (OR 1.05 per 1-h increase, p = 0.004) and longer mechanical ventilation (OR 1.07 per 1-day increase, p = 0.002). Facial edema occurred more frequently with PPP (57.7% vs. 32.1%, p < 0.001). Compared with SPP, PPP was not associated with a statistically significant difference in 28-day mortality, ICU discharge or ventilator liberation after IPTW adjustment. Given the observational design and the limited sample size of this study, this null finding should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and cannot be taken as evidence of therapeutic equivalence or causal ineffectiveness. PPP was associated with more severe (Stage II) pressure injuries; although cumulative prone duration did not differ significantly between groups, this may indicate that the temporal pattern of loading, rather than cumulative duration alone, contributes to injury severity.

articles.title: Airway Pressure Release Ventilation Versus Conventional Ventilation in Adults With or at Risk for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials.
articles.abstract: To assess whether airway pressure release ventilation (APRV) reduces mortality compared with conventional invasive ventilation in adults with established acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute lung injury, or conditions considered to confer a high risk of ARDS. We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception through August 15, 2026. We analyzed parallel-group randomized trials using random-effects models. Mortality at trial-defined follow-up was the primary outcome. We used Cochrane RoB 2 to assess risk of bias and GRADE to assess certainty of evidence. CRD420251170819. Nine trials involving 585 participants were included. No mortality benefit was demonstrated (risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.72-1.26). Ventilator-free days showed no clear difference (mean difference [MD] 3.83 days, 95% CI - 1.69 to 9.34; I²=83%). APRV was associated with a higher PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio (MD 56.21 mm Hg, 95% CI 24.63-87.79; I²=84%) and shorter ICU stay (MD - 2.53 days, 95% CI - 4.43 to - 0.64; I²=71%). Ventilation duration showed no clear difference (five trials, 413 participants; MD - 2.44 days, 95% CI - 4.96 to 0.09; I²=78%). Peak airway pressure was lower and mean airway pressure was higher with APRV. This synthesis does not establish that APRV improves survival, ventilator-free days, or ventilation duration. Oxygenation and ICU-stay findings require caution because populations, protocols, outcome timing, and risk of bias varied. Certainty of evidence was low to very low. These data do not establish mortality equivalence or superiority over contemporary lung-protective ventilation. CRD420251170819; registered 17 October 2025.

articles.title: Dysnatremia in critically ill burn patients: incidence, timing and association with kidney outcomes.
articles.abstract: Dysnatremia is common in critically ill patients and has been linked to poor outcomes and renal prognosis. Burn patients are particularly vulnerable, but the prognostic significance of dysnatremia in this population remains unclear. We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 1,758 burn patients admitted to a French burn center between 2011 and 2023.
