articles.title: Point-of-care ultrasound in hemodynamically unstable pulmonary embolism.
articles.abstract: The recent guideline from the American Heart Association on acute pulmonary embolism provides an updated framework for diagnosis, risk stratification, and management. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography remains the reference standard for confirming pulmonary embolism. However, in critically ill patients with hemodynamic or respiratory instability, transport for definitive imaging may be unsafe or impractical. In this context, bedside evaluation becomes central to early decision-making. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), particularly when performed as a multi-organ assessment integrating cardiac, pulmonary, and venous ultrasound, can rapidly identify signs of right ventricular dysfunction, detect thrombus in transit, and exclude alternative life-threatening causes of shock. Emerging evidence suggests that multi-organ POCUS has high diagnostic performance in critically ill patients with suspected pulmonary embolism. In unstable patients, bedside ultrasound may therefore provide clinically actionable information to support timely therapeutic decisions when definitive imaging is not immediately feasible.

articles.title: Induction agents for emergency tracheal intubation in critically ill adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Etomidate, ketamine, and propofol are all used as induction agents for emergency tracheal intubation in critically ill adults but it remains uncertain which agent should be preferable. METHODS: We searched MEDLINE and Embase (inception to December 2025) for randomized controlled trials comparing etomidate, ketamine, propofol, or ketamine-propofol combination (ketofol) for emergency or rapid sequence intubation in critically ill adults. We performed random-effects network meta-analysis using the frequentist framework. The primary outcome was short-term mortality (28-30 day, or ICU/in-hospital mortality when unavailable). Secondary outcomes included cardiovascular collapse, post-induction hypotension, vasopressor use, first-pass intubation success, and peri-intubation cardiac arrest. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the CINeMA framework. RESULTS: Nine trials (4,672 patients, four treatments) were included. Ketamine and etomidate probably result in similar mortality (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.80-1.16; [Formula: see text] = 30%; moderate certainty). Evidence for other mortality comparisons was very uncertain: ketamine vs propofol (OR 1.53, 0.80-2.93; 1 trial; low certainty) and etomidate vs propofol (OR 0.63, 0.32-1.24; indirect only; very low certainty). Compared with etomidate, ketamine probably increases cardiovascular collapse (OR 1.44, 1.20-1.71; moderate certainty) and may increase post-induction hypotension (OR 1.34, 1.07-1.68; low certainty) and peri-intubation vasopressor use (OR 1.45, 1.21-1.74; low certainty). There was probably little or no difference in first-pass intubation success or cardiac arrest. CONCLUSIONS: Etomidate and ketamine probably result in similar mortality, but confidence intervals are compatible with clinically important differences in either direction-ketamine probably causes more peri-intubation hemodynamic instability. Beyond one trial, no randomized evidence exists for propofol in emergency intubation of critically ill adults.
articles.ai_summary: This study compared three induction agents (etomidate, ketamine, and propofol) for emergency tracheal intubation in critically ill adults. The results showed that etomidate and ketamine probably result in similar mortality, but ketamine may cause more peri-intubation hemodynamic instability. The study also found that propofol has no randomized evidence for emergency intubation in critically ill adults.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings are important for ICU clinical practice as they provide guidance on the choice of induction agent for emergency tracheal intubation, which can impact patient outcomes and hemodynamic stability.

articles.title: Mechanical ventilation for ICU patient with obesity: current best practices and future directions.
articles.abstract: Obesity is increasingly prevalent among critically ill patients and profoundly alters respiratory mechanics, gas exchange, and cardiopulmonary interactions, complicating ventilatory management. Excess adipose tissue increases pleural pressure, reduces functional residual capacity, and promotes airway closure and atelectasis, increasing susceptibility to hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and ventilator-induced lung injury. These physiological alterations necessitate tailored ventilatory strategies distinct from those used in patients without obesity. Lung-protective ventilation using tidal volume indexed to predicted body weight remains the cornerstone of management, as lung size does not increase proportionally with body mass. Patients with obesity often require higher positive end-expiratory pressure to counteract elevated pleural pressure and prevent airway closure although optimal titration strategies remain uncertain. Interpretation of airway pressures requires caution, as increased chest wall elastance may result in elevated plateau and driving pressures without excessive lung stress. Adjunctive monitoring tools, including esophageal pressure measurement and electrical impedance tomography, may help individualize ventilatory management by improving assessment of transpulmonary pressure and regional ventilation. Airway management is particularly challenging in patients with obesity due to rapid oxygen desaturation and increased risk of difficult intubation; positive-pressure preoxygenation and video laryngoscopy improve procedural safety. Adjunctive therapies, such as prone positioning, non-invasive ventilation, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, are feasible and may provide benefit when clinically indicated. Liberation from mechanical ventilation requires careful assessment, and prophylactic non-invasive ventilation may reduce extubation failure in selected patients. Despite increasing recognition of obesity-specific physiology, most current recommendations are extrapolated from general ICU populations. Dedicated clinical trials are needed to define optimal ventilatory strategies and improve outcomes in this growing population of critically ill patients with obesity.

articles.title: Effect of Spatial Distance From the Crash Scene to a Critical Care Center on Traffic Fatality Rates in Japan.
articles.journal: The Tokai journal of experimental and clinical medicine
articles.abstract: To evaluate the association between spatial distance from the traffic-crash scene to the nearest critical care center and traffic-crash fatality in Japan. Using National Police Agency Traffic Accident Statistics Open Data for 2022-2024, we calculated the great-circle distance from each crash site to the nearest of 312 critical care centers, stratified crashes into 1-km bands, and grouped crashes into < 5 km, 5-15 km, and ≥ 15 km categories to compare fatality rate, crash type, roadway configuration, and time of day. Fatality rate rose approximately linearly with distance: 0.50% (< 5 km), 0.92% (5-15 km), and 2.29% (≥ 15 km), a 7.1-fold increase beyond 30 km versus the 0-1 km band. Crashes < 5 km were predominantly intersection- and pedestrian-related, whereas crashes ≥ 15 km were disproportionately single-lane, straight-road and single-vehicle events. Spatial distance to the nearest critical care center was strongly and consistently associated with traffic-crash fatality in Japan, reflecting systematic distance-related differences in crash patterns. Because this was an ecological, unadjusted analysis using great-circle distance as a proxy for transport time, an independent causal effect cannot be inferred. As 90% of crashes occur within 15 km of existing centers, time-based distance reduction via HEMS and physician-staffed ambulances appears more realistic than new facility construction.

articles.title: Healthcare Professionals' Perspectives on Nutritional Risk Screening Practices in Intensive Care Units: The Guide-in Nut National Survey.
articles.journal: Journal of human nutrition and dietetics : the official journal of the British Dietetic Association
articles.abstract: Nutritional risk screening is recommended for critically ill patients; however, little is known about how healthcare professionals implement it in practice. This study evaluated healthcare professionals' perspectives on nutritional risk screening, including implementation, use of validated tools, adherence to guideline recommendations, and perceived barriers. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among Brazilian physicians, nurses, and dietitians with at least 1 year of ICU experience. The questionnaire assessed participants' reported implementation of nutritional risk screening, use of validated tools, professional responsibilities, and perceived barriers. Logistic regression analyses identified factors associated with reported screening implementation. Adherence to recommended practices was evaluated using a Nutritional Risk Screening Implementation Score. A total of 145 professionals participated (98 dietitians, 35 nurses, and 12 physicians). 83.8% reported performing nutritional risk screening. Professionals working in private hospitals were more likely to report screening implementation than those working in public hospitals (adjusted OR 3.77; 95% CI 1.16-12.21). Dietitians were primarily responsible for screening and reported the highest frequency of validated tool use (98.7%). NRS-2002 was the most frequently reported tool (79.4%). Screening practice scores differed across professionals (p = 0.003), with nurses showing lower scores and greater uncertainty regarding screening tools. Nutritional risk screening was widely reported among ICU healthcare professionals in Brazil; however, variability remained regarding the use of validated tools and adherence to recommended practices. Hospital type was associated with reported screening practice, whereas differences across professional categories were observed in screening practice scores.

articles.title: Enhancing the Completeness of Incontinence-Associated Dermatitis Care in Intensive Care Unit: A Multifaceted Quality Improvement Intervention.
articles.abstract: To improve the completeness of incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD) care among intensive care unit (ICU) nurses and to reduce observed IAD incidence in critically ill patients through a structured quality-improvement intervention. IAD is a common and preventable skin complication in ICU patients, contributing to increased morbidity and healthcare burden. Despite the availability of evidence-based guidelines, inconsistencies in nursing practice often lead to suboptimal care and increased incidence of IAD. A quasi-experimental pre-post quality-improvement project guided by the SQUIRE 2.0 framework was conducted in a 12-bed medical ICU in southern Taiwan. Phase 1 comprised a local needs assessment, tool development, baseline observation, semi-structured interviews, and root-cause prioritization. Phase 2 comprised intervention development, implementation, and evaluation. The locally developed instrument included 10 cognitive items and 15 behavioural items. Content validity was reviewed by five experts; pilot testing involved 28 nurses. The multifaceted intervention comprised standardized protocols, education, multimedia tools, high-risk alerts, multidisciplinary discussion, and audit-feedback. Pre-post outcomes were compared using chi-squared or Fisher's exact tests, as appropriate. Care completeness increased from 50.4% (212/420) to 96.4% (405/420), an absolute increase of 46.0 percentage points. Observed IAD incidence decreased from 43.3% (84/194) to 21.9% (7/32). Extended monitoring from June 2024 to July 2026 identified 186 cases among 865 ICU admissions (non-duplicated ICU patients) (aggregate incidence, 21.5%). The intervention was associated with improved adherence to IAD-care practices and a lower observed incidence of IAD in the participating ICU. Because the study was uncontrolled and single-centre, causal inference and transferability are limited. The project provides a practical, reproducible model for supporting evidence-based IAD care in ICU settings.

articles.title: Rapid response vehicles vs mobile intensive care units in prehospital stroke-code care: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.journal: Emergencias : revista de la Sociedad Espanola de Medicina de Emergencias
articles.abstract: Rapid response vehicles (RRVs) are advanced life support resources similar to mobile intensive care units (MICUs), but without patient transport capacity; therefore, they require support from a basic life support ambulance for transport to hospital. In this study, we evaluated whether the RRV care model delays stroke-code care times compared with MICUs and compared their diagnostic accuracy. We conducted a retrospective study of stroke codes with a known onset time attended by SUMMA-112 during 2022. We compared baseline characteristics, care times (call, assessment, door), reperfusion treatments administered, and the accuracy of the M-DIRECT scale in identifying candidates for thrombectomy between patients attended by MICUs and RRVs. A total of 1,263 patients were included: 953 (75%) attended by MICUs and 310 (25%) by RRVs. We found no differences in call-to-assessment times (median, 27 minutes in both groups) or assessment-to-door times (median, 44 vs 46 minutes). There were no differences in the proportion of stroke diagnoses at discharge (79% vs 80%) or in the proportion of reperfusion treatments administered (thrombolysis and thrombectomy). The sensitivity rate of the M-DIRECT scale for thrombectomy treatment was 76% for MICUs and 67% for RRVs (P = .161). Care provided by RRVs showed care times similar to those observed with MICUs, with no significant differences in diagnostic accuracy, supporting their feasibility as a resource for the care of patients with acute stroke.

articles.title: Subtyping Physician Practice Patterns in the Intensive Care Unit.
articles.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine

articles.title: Earning a place in care by learning in it.
Dynamics of Mitochondrial Structure, Biogenesis and Function in Skeletal Muscle of Critically Ill Patients.
articles.abstract: To define the timing and phenotype of mitochondrial ultrastructural remodeling and electron transport chain (ETC) function in skeletal muscle during early critical illness. Secondary analysis of a prospective observational study with serial muscle biopsies. Adult ICU. Thirty-three mechanically ventilated ICU patients (median age, 49 yr; 27% women) with Sequential Organ Failure Assessment greater than or equal to 9 on three consecutive days; skeletal muscle biopsies of the vastus lateralis muscle at ICU day 5 (n = 29) and day 15 (n = 22). Healthy subjects served as controls. None. Vastus lateralis biopsies were analyzed by electron microscopy with stereology, quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), Western blotting, and spectrophotometric ETC enzyme assays (reported per tissue weight and normalized to citrate synthase [CS]). Intact mitochondrial profiles were reduced vs. controls (fold change vs. controls: day 5, 0.24 [0.18-0.34]; p = 0.039 and day 15, 0.20 [0.16-0.33]; p = 0.011) and disturbed profiles increased (day 5, 5.62 [3.20-7.17]; p < 0.001 and day 15, 5.20 [3.67-6.36]; p = 0.001), with reduced volume density of intact mitochondria (day 5, 0.33 [0.20-0.49]; p = 0.009 and day 15, 0.32 [0.21-0.50]; p = 0.005). Inner mitochondrial membrane surface-to-volume ratio was reduced at day 5 (0.69 [0.49-0.89]; p = 0.022) and remained unchanged at day 15. Complex III tissue activity was reduced at day 5 (85.6 [22.1-133.3] vs. 151.4 [100.5-205.0]; p = 0.015) and day 15 (50.5 [36.0-69.8]; p = 0.001), remaining reduced after CS normalization (day 5, 0.83 [0.34-1.49]; p = 0.040 and day 15, 0.87 [0.65-0.93]; p = 0.007). Complex IV activity remained reduced before and after CS normalization at both time points (all p < 0.001). CS activity declined by day 15 (56.3 [52.7-65.1] vs. 95.6 [80.1-133.0]; p = 0.001 and day 15 vs. day 5; p = 0.041). qRT-PCR and Western blot supported reduced ETC components and altered biogenesis signaling. Skeletal muscle mitochondrial ultrastructure is altered by ICU day 5 and remains abnormal at day 15, with persistent complex III/IV dysfunction after CS normalization. These findings define an early sustained mitochondrial remodeling phenotype in skeletal muscle during critical illness.

articles.title: What is your diagnosis? A life-threatening complication in severe acute pancreatitis.
Alarm Fatigue Across Critical Care Domains: Comparative Insights and Independent Predictors From a Cross-Sectional Multicenter Survey Study.
articles.abstract: Alarm fatigue, the desensitization to excessive false alarms, threatens patient safety and staff performance across critical care domains. It is unclear whether alarm fatigue differs between hospital departments. This study compared alarm fatigue among staff in the ICU, cardiac telemetry ward (CTW), and operating room (OR), and, secondarily, identified its independent determinants. Cross-sectional, multicenter survey study. ICUs, a CTW, and ORs. A total of 514 healthcare professionals working in the ICU, CTW, and OR. None. Alarm fatigue was assessed using the Dutch-translated Charité Alarm Fatigue Questionnaire, which includes alarm stress and alarm coping subscales. Participants also rated their self-perceived alarm fatigue on a 1-10 scale and the percentage of perceived false alarms. Telemetry staff reported the highest self-perceived alarm fatigue (B = 0.65; 95% CI, 0.06-1.24; p = 0.032) and perceived false alarms (B = 0.77; 95% CI, 0.23-1.30; p = 0.005), while OR staff reported the lowest (B = -1.01; 95% CI, -1.59 to -0.43; p < 0.001). Second, physicians (B = -0.13; 95% CI, -0.25 to -0.01; p < 0.031) and less experienced staff (< 3 mo; B = -0.34; 95% CI, -0.68 to -0.01; p = 0.046) reported lower alarm fatigue. Alarm fatigue varied significantly across departments and professions, being highest in telemetry staff and lowest among physicians and less experienced personnel. Targeted department-specific interventions and longitudinal research are necessary to mitigate alarm fatigue and enhance patient safety.

articles.title: Rapid molecular diagnostics for VAP: unresolved questions and directions for future research.
Learning at the bedside is not the same as reaching it.
Evaluation of Sequential Organ Failure Assessment-2 Performance Across Demographic Subgroups: An External Validation Using MIMIC-IV.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the discrimination and calibration of the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)-2 score for ICU mortality across demographic subgroups defined by age, sex, race and ethnicity, primary language, and insurance status. Retrospective cohort study. Single academic medical center in the northeastern United States (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA), using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV database (version 3.1), 2008-2022, a dataset external to the SOFA-2 development cohort. Adult patients (≥ 18 yr) with at least one ICU admission. The first ICU admission of the first qualifying hospitalization per patient was analyzed. None. First-day SOFA-2 scores were calculated from the worst values recorded during the first 24 hours of ICU admission across six organ systems, with ICU mortality as the primary outcome. Discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and calibration using intercept and slope, with subgroup differences in AUROC estimated by bootstrap resampling. Among 64,015 ICU patients (mean [sd] age, 64.6 [17.1] yr; 56.1% male; 66.1% White), overall AUROC was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.76-0.77). Discrimination declined significantly with age: AUROC, 0.85 (0.83-0.87) for ages 18-44 years vs. 0.72 (0.70-0.73) for ages 75 or older (ΔAUROC, -0.14 [95% CI, -0.16 to -0.11]), with systematic underprediction in older patients. Discrimination was significantly decreased among non-English speakers (ΔAUROC, -0.04) but did not differ across documented racial/ethnic groups. Patients with missing demographic information had markedly higher mortality than the overall cohort rate of 7.2% (14.1% for missing race/ethnicity; 23.1% for missing language). SOFA-2 demonstrated good overall performance but with clinically meaningful variation across subgroups, particularly with age and language. Patients with missing demographic data experienced markedly higher mortality. These findings argue for routine equity evaluation as a complement to traditional validation of clinical prediction tools.

articles.title: AI - Train with the best.
Shortening the Family Satisfaction in the ICU (FS-ICU): Development and Validation of a 12-Item Family Satisfaction Survey for Adult ICUs.
articles.abstract: To develop and validate a shorter Family Satisfaction in the ICU (FS-ICU) questionnaire that reduces survey length while preserving content and psychometric performance for quality improvement and benchmarking. The FS-ICU survey assesses family perceptions of care, communication, and decision-making and has been translated into multiple languages with implementation across diverse health care systems internationally. In a province-wide electronic implementation in Ontario, more than 40% of initiated surveys were incomplete, suggesting that survey length may limit practicality for large-scale quality improvement and benchmarking. Multistage study using provincial FS-ICU survey data and an independent multicenter validation dataset for item reduction, psychometric evaluation, agreement testing, and external validation of a shortened questionnaire. A 12-member expert working group, convened for a Critical Care Services Ontario initiative, used provincial web-based data from adult ICUs across Ontario to develop a shorter version, FS-ICUshort. External validation was applied to FS-ICUshort using a separate multicenter Canadian revised FS-ICU dataset. A 12-member expert working group led by Dr. Daren K. Heyland, including administrative staff, ICU clinical staff, patient experience specialists, and quality improvement specialists from Ontario, used provincial FS-ICU rollout data. None. Using empirical criteria and expert ratings, the FS-ICU was reduced from 29 to 12 items: seven in the satisfaction-with-care domain (FS-Care) and five in the communication and decision-making domain (FS-DM). FS-ICUshort showed high internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.93 for FS-Care, 0.86 for FS-DM, and 0.94 for total). Confirmatory factor analysis supported a two-factor structure with better fit than a single-factor model. Scores from FS-ICUshort closely matched full FS-ICU, with mean differences less than or equal to 1.1 points on a 0-100 scale and intraclass correlations of 0.97-0.99. External validation replicated these results. The 12-item FS-ICUshort maintains the core content and psychometric quality of the original FS-ICU while significantly reducing length, supporting routine use in ICU family experience measurement and benchmarking.

articles.title: ICU resilience, stress and support: perceptions of ICU professionals in an international ESICM survey.
"Bold and necessary experiments:" The redelegation of authority and responsibility to nurses at the origins of cardiac intensive care.
articles.abstract: Coronary Care Units (CCUs) were at the forefront of the development of intensive care in the 1960s and 1970s. The development of CCUs, and intensive care more broadly, was enabled by the interplay of expanding medical technology and the evolving role of nurses vis-à-vis physicians. This paper examines the history the CCU at New York Hospital, the teaching hospital of Cornell University School of Medicine and School of Nursing, with a particular focus on role of nurses in the unit's success. Drawing from historical archives of New York Hospital and the Cornell University School of Nursing, this paper argues that that nurses were co-creators, alongside physicians, of the NYH CCU, and demonstrates how nurses drew from the NYH CCU experience to expand critical care services at the local and national level, including by advocating for the creation of the NYH medical intensive care unit (MICU), leading a CCU nurse training program to expand regional CCU capability, and contributing expertise to a federally-sponsored national conference on CCUs. A close reading of this history offers lessons and insights as intensive care medicine moves into an uncertain future, chief among them that work of caring for critically ill patients requires the thoughtful integration of new technologies with hands on care.

Nurse-Led Interventions to Mitigate High-Alert Medication Errors in Critical Care: A Systematic Review of Effectiveness and Implementation Strategies.
articles.abstract: Intensive care units (ICUs) are high-risk environments where nurses administer the majority of high-alert medications, making them the final checkpoint in the medication-use process. However, evidence on nurse-led interventions specifically targeting high-alert medication errors has not been systematically synthesized across all ICU populations. This systematic review evaluated the effectiveness of nurse-led interventions in reducing high-alert medication errors in neonatal, paediatric and adult intensive care units and examined implementation strategies that enhance patient safety. We followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus for studies published between January 2000 and June 2026. Inclusion criteria required nurse-led interventions, measurement of high-alert medication error rates and critical care settings. The risk of bias was assessed. A narrative synthesis was performed due to heterogeneity in study designs and outcome measures. Six studies met the inclusion criteria. Interventions included simulation-based training, staff education, smart pump integration, clinical decision support systems and standardization of medication orders and protocols. All studies reported improvements in medication safety outcomes, including reductions in medication error rates, improved compliance, enhanced accuracy and increased efficiency. Secondary outcomes included improved compliance with PRN orders (from 62.0% ± 9.2% to 77.7% ± 10.1%), reduced medication dispensing time (to < 1 min) and cost savings ($90 000-$130 000 per year). Risk of bias was moderate to low in five studies and high in one study. Nurse-led multicomponent interventions are associated with reductions in high-alert medication errors and improvements in safety outcomes in critical care settings. However, technology alone is insufficient without workflow integration and nursing education. Education and standardization require concurrent process redesign for sustained improvement. Nurses should advocate for multicomponent strategies combining training, technology and standardized protocols. Healthcare organizations must ensure workflow integration to maximize the benefits of smart pumps and clinical decision support systems. Future research should employ rigorous designs, include diverse ICU settings and low- to middle-income countries and evaluate long-term sustainability.

articles.title: Nursing Mechanisms of Intravenous Medication Loss in Adult Intensive Care: A Mixed-Methods Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Adult ICU medication loss is reported using non-equivalent forms and denominators, limiting interpretation and intervention design. To examine loss measurement, nursing mechanisms, intervention evidence and balancing outcomes. Convergent segregated mixed-methods systematic review. Three databases were searched to 1 July 2026, with citation searching, metadata checks and an uncapped rerun of two capped PubMed arms. Quantitative results remained in native units; qualitative findings were synthesised separately and integrated. MMAT 2018 was applied by design category; two reviewers checked screening, extraction and appraisal. Of 768 screened records (576 primary; 192 rerun), 79 reports were assessed with retained sources. Four reports could not be retrieved. Twenty-five reports from 21 independent studies were included; the rerun added none. Categories were prepared-unused medication (11), post-order or post-event loss (7), partial-container residual (8), delivery-system residual (3) and material-flow loss (4); categories were nonexclusive. Denominators were explicit in 10 studies, partial in 5 and absent in 6. No studies met pooling criteria. Two qualitative studies generated six low-confidence CERQual findings. Intervention evidence was uncontrolled, modelled or proposal-based; balancing outcomes were uncommon. Adult ICU loss comprised non-equivalent quantities, not one waste prevalence, and no study related it to a patient outcome. Studies would need to specify loss form, numerator, denominator, observation window, workflow node, result origin and balancing outcomes alongside resource use. Order review before non-urgent preparation, reconstitution and checking, storage and return pathways, and syringe, pump and line handling are candidate targets; no controlled adult ICU study has shown reduced loss without affecting access, dose delivery, sterility, compatibility or workload.

Effects of Assertiveness Training on ICU Nurses' Resilience and Clinical Decision-Making: A Randomised Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: Nursing in the intensive care unit (ICU) is highly stressful, necessitating strong resilience and effective clinical decision-making. Grounded in the Stress and Coping Theoretical Framework and the Assertive Healthy Behaviour Model, assertiveness training is proposed as a strategy to empower nurses and improve these critical competencies. This study aimed to answer two questions: (1) Does an assertiveness training programme significantly improve the resilience scores of ICU nurses immediately post-intervention (T1) and at a 3-month follow-up (T2) compared to a control group? (2) Does it significantly improve their clinical decision-making scores at T1 and T2? A single-blind randomised controlled trial was conducted. ICU nurses were randomly allocated using a computer-based random number generator to either an intervention or a control group. The intervention group received an expert-designed assertiveness training programme (six 1.5-h sessions). The control group received only routine hospital programmes, consisting of standard annual in-service training focusing exclusively on basic clinical updates and safety protocols. Outcomes were measured at T0 (baseline), T1 (immediately post-intervention) and T2 (3-month follow-up) using the CD-RISC (Cronbach's α = 0.85) and PDAQ (Cronbach's α = 0.79). Data were analysed using repeated measures ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests. Among the 70 participating ICU nurses, there were no significant baseline differences between the groups at T0 (p > 0.05). The intervention group showed significantly higher resilience and clinical decision-making scores at both T1 and T2 compared to the control group (p < 0.01). Post hoc analyses revealed that these significant improvements occurred specifically between T0 and T1 (p < 0.01) and were strictly maintained at T2 (p < 0.01). An expert-designed assertiveness training programme significantly enhances and sustains the resilience and clinical decision-making abilities of ICU nurses. Nursing leaders should incorporate assertiveness communication training into standard professional development programmes to improve the quality of care and empower nursing staff. The findings provide practical guidance for nurse managers to integrate assertiveness training into ongoing hospital education programmes, thereby bolstering the psychological resilience of ICU nurses against stress and ultimately ensuring high-quality patient care and clinical safety in these high-pressure environments.

articles.title: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Prophylactic Dressings for Pressure Injury Prevention in Critically Ill Adults: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.abstract: Pressure injuries (PIs) remain an important preventable complication of critical illness. Preventive dressings are used as an adjunct to repositioning, support surfaces and skin care, but comparative evidence across dressing types and anatomical settings is sparse. To compare the efficacy and safety of prophylactic dressings and topical preventive strategies for PI prevention in critically ill adults and to examine whether conclusions were robust after separating device-related from body-site PIs. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, CINAHL and Web of Science from inception to July 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The primary outcome was any newly acquired PI. Secondary outcomes were Stage II or higher PI, sacrum-specific PI, heel-specific PI where separately reported and patient-level dressing-related skin injury. Random-effects frequentist network meta-analyses were performed. Multi-arm trials were reconstructed at arm level and brand arms mapping to the same treatment class were combined before analysis. A prespecified sensitivity analysis excluded the nasogastric-tube-related trial. Eleven RCTs involving 2259 participants were included. In the complete network, silicone foam reduced any new PI versus standard care (OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.16-0.68; p = 0.0027). This estimate was unchanged after exclusion of the device-related trial. The exclusion separated hydrocolloid and transparent film into a disconnected component, precluding valid indirect comparison of these treatments with standard care in the non-device network. For Stage II or higher PI, silicone foam showed a protective but imprecise effect (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.18-1.02; p = 0.0568). For sacrum-specific PI, silicone foam reduced risk (OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-0.60; p = 0.0007). Zinc oxide and Vaseline dressing estimates were large but arose from a single small multi-arm trial and had wide confidence intervals. Patient-level dressing-related skin injury did not show a clear difference between silicone foam and control (OR 1.46, 95% CI 0.28-7.64). Certainty was judged moderate for the silicone-foam findings for any PI and sacral PI, low for Stage II or higher PI and low or very low for most single-trial comparisons. The most reproducible evidence supports multilayer silicone foam as an adjunct for reducing overall and sacral PIs in critically ill adults. Evidence for preventing Stage II or higher PI is less precise, and estimates for other materials are limited by single trials, zero-event data or disconnected networks. Device-related PIs should be analysed separately from sacral and heel PIs because their mechanisms and preventive context differ. Preventive dressings should complement individualized repositioning, pressure-redistributing support surfaces, nutrition, moisture management and repeated skin assessment. For critically ill adults at high risk of sacral PI, multilayer silicone foam is supported by the most consistent randomized evidence in the current network. Evidence is insufficient to rank alternative materials reliably and device-related pressure injury requires site- and device-specific prevention rather than extrapolation from sacral dressing studies.

articles.title: Cost-Effectiveness of a Nurse-Led Pressure Injury Prevention Care Bundle Among Adult Intensive Care Patients: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the cost impact and cost-effectiveness of a newly developed pressure injury prevention care bundle (PIP-CB) compared with standard care in an adult intensive care unit from a hospital perspective. A randomized controlled trial with a prospectively planned economic evaluation. This study was conducted in an adult intensive care unit. The intervention consisted of an evidence-based and expert-informed PIP-CB. Cost analysis included direct medical costs such as nursing labour time and prophylactic product use, calculated using unit prices and utilization rates. Incremental cost-effectiveness analysis estimated the additional cost required to prevent one pressure injury and to delay injury onset by 1 day. Economic outcomes were assessed in Turkish lira (₺) and interpreted against a theoretical willingness-to-pay threshold based on Turkey's gross domestic product per capita. Ethical approval was obtained, and informed consent was secured from all participants. The mean total cost per patient was significantly higher in the intervention group (₺62,721.22 ± 36,431.75) than in the control group (₺39,752.24 ± 19,319.33). In both groups, patients who developed pressure injuries incurred substantially higher costs. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was ₺74,467.44 per pressure injury prevented and ₺3074.44 per day of delayed injury onset, both of which were below the theoretical willingness-to-pay threshold. While the PIP-CB raised short-term prevention costs, it proved cost-effective by lowering pressure injury-related expenses. Widespread use of this care bundle could substantially reduce preventable hospital-acquired pressure injury (HAPI) costs and ease the overall financial burden on healthcare systems. The cost-effectiveness of this nurse-led PIP-CB supports its adoption in routine intensive care nursing practice. By reducing the incidence and delaying the onset of HAPIs, it promotes efficient use of nursing and hospital resources while improving patient outcomes. These findings can inform clinical decision-making and resource allocation in intensive care settings. What problem did the study address? HAPIs are associated with prolonged intensive care stays and substantially increased healthcare costs. Hospital-acquired PIP-CBs are effective in reducing injury incidence, yet their economic value is rarely evaluated using randomized controlled designs. What were the main findings? This study provides a hospital-perspective economic evaluation of a newly developed hospital-acquired PIP-CB in an intensive care setting. The findings demonstrate that, although the care bundle significantly increased total healthcare costs, it was cost-effective relative to willingness-to-pay thresholds by reducing the incidence of pressure injuries and delaying their onset relative to its incremental cost. Where and on whom will the research have an impact? The findings support adoption of standardized prevention bundles in intensive care settings and can inform hospital administrators, clinicians and health policy decision-makers. CONSORT 2025 guidelines were followed. Patients and the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting or dissemination plans of this research because the study evaluated a clinical care process implemented within routine hospital practice. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06770686.

articles.title: Association between early serum sodium variability and in-hospital mortality among adult intensive care unit admissions recorded in the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database.
articles.journal: The Journal of international medical research
articles.abstract: ObjectiveSerum sodium abnormalities are common among critically ill patients; however, static measurements may not capture early fluctuations. This study evaluated the association between serum sodium variability measured within the first 48 h after intensive care unit admission and in-hospital mortality among adult intensive care unit admissions.MethodsThis retrospective observational cohort study used data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database (version 3.1); we included the data of 41,165 adult first intensive care unit admissions for whom at least three serum sodium measurements taken within the first 48 h after intensive care unit admission were available. Sodium variability defined as the SD of sodium measurements within the specified observation window. Multivariable logistic regression was adjusted for age, sex, selected comorbidities, mean sodium concentration, and electrolyte measurement count. Robustness analyses used a first 24 h window, excluded SD values ≥10 mmol/L, removed exact duplicate laboratory rows, tested nonlinearity with a natural cubic spline, and performed bootstrap internal validation.ResultsThe overall in-hospital mortality rate was 12.0% (4952/41,165). The mortality rates were 10.1%, 11.5%, 11.3%, and 15.2% across increasing quartiles 1-4, respectively, of sodium variability. Each 1 mmol/L increase in the SD of sodium concentrations was associated with higher adjusted odds of in-hospital death (odds ratio: 1.14; 95% confidence interval, 1.12-1.17; p < 0.001). The association persisted during a 24 h window (odds ratio: 1.12; 95% confidence interval, 1.10-1.15) and among admissions with mean sodium concentrations of 135-145 mmol/L (odds ratio: 1.14; 95% confidence interval, 1.11-1.18). Spline modeling supported a nonlinear association (p < 0.001). The optimism-corrected area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.765.ConclusionsGreater early serum sodium variability was associated with higher adjusted odds of in-hospital mortality. The retrospective design, selection of patients with repeated testing, and incomplete adjustment for acute illness severity and treatment preclude causal or clinical-use claims.

articles.title: Nocturnal intravenous gamma-hydroxybutyrate and sleep architecture in non-sedated intensive care unit patients: a polysomnographic experience.
Diagnosis: the forgotten ICU procedure.
Maternity versus non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy.
articles.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
articles.abstract: Substantial uncertainty exists regarding how healthcare system factors, especially care setting types, affect the uptake and implementation of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy screening in practice. Evidence suggests that the care environment may influence diagnostic processes. To assess the effectiveness of maternity and non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus or diabetes in pregnancy. We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) up to April 2026, and for controlled non-randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs) up to December 2025. We also searched CENTRAL to identify ongoing trials. We included RCTs and planned to include cluster-RCTs and NRSIs, but we did not find any. Eligible participants were pregnant women being screened for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) or diabetes in pregnancy. We defined maternity healthcare settings as those specialising in care for pregnant, birthing, and postpartum individuals, with appropriate screening protocols, and non-maternity healthcare settings as general medical environments lacking a focus on pregnancy and women's care. We considered any screening format (e.g. risk-factor-based screening) and any diagnostic test (e.g. one- and two-step oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT)). Critical health service outcomes were compliance with screening and follow-up guidelines, diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy, maternal emergency department visits during pregnancy, maternal antenatal hospitalisation, length of maternal hospitalisation, length of neonatal hospitalisation, and care accessibility. Critical maternal outcomes included hypertensive disorders, maternal death, intensive care admissions, hyperglycaemia requiring pharmacological treatment, infections, and postpartum glucose intolerance, including progression to diabetes, within 15 years after birth. Critical child-related outcomes encompassed perinatal death, neonatal intensive care admissions, preterm birth, neonatal hypoglycaemia, large-for-gestational-age, shoulder dystocia, and birth trauma. Further critical and important outcomes not included in the summary of findings tables can be found in the full text. We used the Cochrane RoB 2 tool to assess bias in the RCTs. We had planned to use ROBINS-I version 2 to assess bias in the NRSIs if we had identified any. We used standard Cochrane methodology. We planned to synthesise results for each outcome using meta-analysis where possible (inverse-variance or Mantel-Haenszel approaches; fixed-effect model). We used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome. We included one RCT with 781 participants: 390 were randomised to screening in a maternity healthcare setting and 391 were randomised to screening in a non-maternity healthcare setting. Except for screening compliance, trialists evaluated all outcomes using a per-protocol analysis instead of by original randomised groups. This approach created substantial disparities in sample sizes between settings and largely nullified the methodological protections typically provided by a randomised design. The trial evaluated screening for GDM only. We did not identify any ongoing studies or studies awaiting classification. Health service outcomes Screening in a maternity healthcare setting may increase compliance with screening and follow-up guidelines (risk ratio (RR) 1.69, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.53 to 1.87; 781 participants) and may improve care accessibility, assessed as time to access antenatal diabetes care, measured in days (mean difference (MD) -4.70, 95% CI -6.03 to -3.37; 690 participants), both with low-certainty evidence. We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.60 to 2.01; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and length of neonatal hospitalisation (MD 0.04, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.65; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No direct evidence was available on screening for diabetes in pregnancy as distinct from GDM. No data were reported on maternal emergency department visits, maternal antenatal hospitalisation, length of maternal hospitalisations, and costs. Maternal outcomes We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on pre-eclampsia (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.56 to 2.75; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The following outcomes were not reported: eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, maternal death, admission to intensive care, hyperglycaemia requiring pharmacological treatment, infections, and postpartum glucose intolerance. Child-related outcomes We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on: stillbirth or foetal death (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.93), admission to neonatal intensive care (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.71), preterm birth (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.41 to 2.71), neonatal hypoglycaemia (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.23 to 3.59), large-for-gestational-age (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.04), shoulder dystocia (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.70), and birth trauma (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.93), all with 690 participants each and very low-certainty evidence. An effect estimate for neonatal death was not estimable (maternity setting: 0/475; non-maternity setting: 0/215). There is insufficient evidence to determine whether screening for gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy in maternity healthcare settings compared with non-maternity healthcare settings improves health service, maternal, or child-related outcomes. Low-certainty evidence from a single study indicates that screening in maternity healthcare settings may result in a reduction in time to access antenatal diabetes care and may increase compliance. The effects on other outcomes remain unknown. Conducting studies using intention-to-treat analyses could bridge existing research gaps, enhancing effect estimates and certainty. This Cochrane review was funded by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the UNDP-UNFPA-UNICEF-WHO-World Bank Special Programme of Research, Development and Research Training in Human Reproduction (HRP). Protocol available via PROSPERO: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251108692.

Preserved anabolic skeletal muscle capacity in response to exercise and protein intake after critical illness.
articles.abstract: Low muscle mass and persistent weakness are common after critical illness, but the mechanisms behind impaired recovery are incompletely understood. The aim of this study was to investigate the skeletal muscle anabolic response to combined resistance exercise and protein intake in intensive care unit (ICU) survivors, compared to matched controls without a history of critical illness. We hypothesised that residual anabolic resistance limits muscle regeneration after ICU stay. Former patients were enrolled within 3 to 6 months of intensive care unit discharge. Muscle biopsies were obtained before and after resistance exercise using a flywheel leg extension ergometer, combined with ingestion of 24 g hydrolysed protein. Muscle protein fractional synthetic rate was determined from the incorporation of [ring-²H₅]phenylalanine into mixed-muscle protein during a primed continuous intravenous infusion. Anabolic and proteolytic pathways were measured using standard assays. Group-by-time differences were analysed using linear mixed models. The primary comparison was the between-group difference in pre-to-post change in muscle protein synthesis. Twenty ICU survivors (60 ± 12 years, 30% female, BMI 26.9 (IQR 22.9-28.7), SAPS 3 62.3 ± 15.8) and 20 age- and sex-matched controls were included. ICU survivors had significantly lower quadriceps muscle thickness (p = 0.02) and handgrip strength (p = 0.04) than controls. In ICU survivors, muscle protein synthesis from plasma precursor amino acids was higher at baseline than in controls (0.041%/hour vs. 0.030%/hour, p = 0.009), but increased less (Δ 0.031 vs. Δ 0.040%/hour, p = 0.04). Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis was similar between groups (0.071%/hour vs. 0.070%/hour, p = 0.70). At baseline, ICU survivors showed lower activation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway. In both groups, the intervention increased anabolic signalling, decreased initiation of autophagy and increased parts of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. In ICU survivors with persistent muscle loss and weakness, the increase in muscle protein synthesis after combined resistance exercise and protein intake was smaller than in controls, in the context of a higher baseline fractional synthetic rate. Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis rates were similar between groups. These findings provide the first mechanistic support for structured exercise-nutrition rehabilitation to promote muscle recovery after critical illness. This study was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05261984), 2022-02-20.

articles.title: Principles of drug dosing for obese patients in the intensive care unit.
articles.abstract: The increasing prevalence of severe obesity in intensive care unit (ICU) patients has led to several challenges with medication dosing. Doses listed in product labels or tertiary references typically do not account for the pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic variability encountered with obesity, leading to the potential for treatment failure or an adverse effect. The purpose of this review is to provide guidance for ICU clinicians when crafting pharmacotherapy regimens in critically ill patients with extreme obesity. A literature search was performed to identify relevant articles pertaining to the pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics of medications in obese patients. Articles describing both general treatment principles and medication specific assessments were retrieved. Bibliographies were searched for additional publications. Evidence guiding medication use in critically ill obese patients is limited by the small number of patients with more extreme forms of obesity, the lack of clinical outcome measurements, and the few studies that are specific to the ICU. Obesity-related alterations in pharmacokinetic parameters, such as apparent volume of distribution and drug clearance, may hinder attainment of pharmacodynamic targets. Individualized dosing strategies are essential to optimize therapeutic outcomes. This review provides dosing recommendations for selected ICU medications and proposes a practical framework to guide medication dosing decisions in this patient population. Drug dosing in critically ill obese patients should be individualized by assessing pharmacokinetic variability and whether pharmacodynamic goals can be achieved. Selecting the correct weight for weight-based calculations or dose for fixed regimens is paramount for achieving these goals. Consultation with a clinical pharmacist may be beneficial.

articles.title: Cluster Versus Individual Randomization in Prehospital, Emergency and Critical Care Trials: A Meta-Epidemiological Study.
articles.abstract: Cluster-randomized clinical trials (cRCTs) are pooled with individually randomized clinical trials (iRCTs) in meta-analyses. However, cRCTs are associated with methodological characteristics potentially inducing systematic differences compared with iRCTs. In acute settings, trial inclusion is time-sensitive, exacerbating inclusion-based biases. We conducted a meta-epidemiological study to assess deviations in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs in these settings. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed and Embase. We screened and identified all meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, or critical care within the last decade that included at least one cRCT and one iRCT. Data were extracted in duplicate from the meta-analyses. If overlapping trials were identified, results were pooled. The primary outcome was mortality; the secondary outcome comprised length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes. Using absolute ln(odds ratio [OR]) for mortality and absolute Hedges' g for the secondary outcome, mean differences (MDs) in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs were analyzed using mixed regression models, presented with 95% CIs. We identified 94 eligible meta-analyses; 44.7% reported on randomization type (cRCT or iRCT). We included 65 meta-analyses in quantitative analyses, encompassing 212 randomized clinical trials (39 cRCTs and 173 iRCTs) and 315,276 patients. No statistically significant difference in absolute ln(OR) for mortality between cRCTs and iRCTs was found (MD, -0.110; 95% CI, -0.093 to 0.313). For length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, a significant difference in absolute Hedges' g was found (MD, -0.202; 95% CI, -0.392 to -0.012). A systematic difference between cRCTs and iRCTs in length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, but not mortality, was identified, with cRCTs reporting smaller effect size magnitudes than iRCTs. With under half of identified meta-analyses reporting on randomization modality, these results highlight the need for improved transparency and statistical consideration of randomization type in future meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, and critical care.

articles.title: Geo-economic variations in structure and organization of intensive care units: the ISOREA survey.
articles.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
articles.abstract: Little is known on critical care services globally. This study aimed to describe ICU resources and organization across countries and assess variability by income group, between countries, and within countries. Participating centers provided structured data on hospital and ICU characteristics via electronic case report form (January 2018 to July 2020). Questionnaire included 237 items covering general characteristics (2 topics) and ICU resources and organization (18 topics). We computed standardized functional domain scores (ISOREA score), classified ICUs using Marshall criteria, and readiness for essential emergency and critical care using a modified Schell score. A total of 1,426 ICUs from five continents were recruited, and 1,225 were analyzed, from high-income countries (HICs, 58%), upper-middle-income (20%), and low/lower-middle-income countries (LLMICs, 22%). Most ICUs were in referral centers (90%) and large urban areas (80%). Most variables (93%) were significantly associated with income group, Most variables (93%) were significantly associated with income group, with 88% showing higher levels in HICs and lower levels in LLMICs. Six domains showed major disparities: extracorporeal support, respiratory support, emergency access to interventional radiology and surgery, neurology and trauma care, patient file and general monitoring, and cardiovascular and hemodynamic monitoring. According to the Marshall classification, 79% of ICUs in HICs were classified as level III, whereas 55% of ICUs in LLMICs were classified as level I. Domains with higher ISOREA scores varied primarily between countries, whereas lower-performing domains exhibited greater variability across ICUs within the same country. Adjustment for income group reduced, but did not eliminate, country-level clustering. Substantial disparities exist in ICU resources and organization across income groups, countries, and ICUs. ICU capacities appeared multidimensional, extending beyond resource limitations.

articles.title: Promoting equity, diversity and inclusion in intensive Care: a position paper of the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine.
Infections Acquired in the ICU Among Cancer and Other Immunosuppressed Patients: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: To compare the cumulative incidence of ICU-acquired infections (ICU-AIs) across distinct immunosuppression diagnostic categories (solid cancer, hematological cancer, other immunosuppression) and nonimmunosuppressed patients, accounting for competing risks of death and discharge. Retrospective cohort study using prospectively collected data. A total of 50 participating ICUs in Brazil. A total of 38,126 adult patients admitted between October 2019 and December 2021 with an ICU stay exceeding 48 hours and no infections diagnosed within the first 48 hours. None. The primary outcome was the incidence of the first ICU-AI during the ICU stay, evaluated using Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard ratios (sHR). In the multivariable competing-risk analysis, patients with hematological malignancies (sHR, 1.64; 95% CI, 1.01-2.65) and other immunosuppressive conditions (sHR, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.02-2.54) were associated with an increased cumulative incidence of ICU-AI, while solid malignancy was not significantly different from non-immunosuppressed patients (sHR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.68-1.14). Patients with hematological malignancies and other immunosuppressive conditions face a significantly higher risk of ICU-AIs.

articles.title: What's new in point-of-care lung ultrasound: reading the new recommendations.
A Quality Improvement Initiative to Achieve Provincial Implementation of a Web-Based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) Survey to Inform Patient-Centered Care.
articles.abstract: To review the web-based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) survey across all adult level 3 Ontario ICUs to capture patient and family experiences with critical care, and to evaluate feasibility, participation, and satisfaction scores. A province-wide, multisite quality improvement study using an electronic, key-based FS-ICU survey with prospectively collected anonymous data linked to encounters through a centralized database. All 83 adult level 3 ICUs (52 community, 31 academic) in ON, Canada, from July 1, 2019, to May 31, 2024. The population comprised adult ICU patients, family members, or substitute decision-makers, with one survey per ICU encounter regardless of length of stay or number of family members. ICUs implemented a web-based FS-ICU using a unique seven-digit key in three formats (Staff-Provided, Quick Response-Driven, Website-Code), supported by training, resources, and tablets, with no clinical care interventions beyond routine practice. Feasibility metrics included onboarding (keys generated per ICU admission), opening, participation, and completion rates, calculated for different centers using provincial data. Over the study period, 24,679 unique keys were generated for 353,400 ICU admissions (onboarding rate, 7.0%), 13,596 keys were opened (opening rate, 55.1%), and 7,542 surveys met the greater than or equal to 70% completion threshold (completion rate, 57.6% among opened surveys; reflection rate, 2.1% of ICU encounters). Survey initiation was highest with the Staff-Provided format (88.4% of keys initiated), and overall satisfaction was high, with mean FS with Care, 87.8; FS with Decision-Making, 84.4; and FS-TOTAL 86.5 on a 0-100 scale, with nursing care rated highest and adequacy of time for questions rated lowest. A provincial, web-based FS-ICU was implemented across all adult level 3 Ontario ICUs, producing a large dataset with high satisfaction scores. A small proportion completed the survey, highlighting feasibility and workflow barriers. Future efforts should improve activation and completion rates and integrate FS-ICU data into routine quality improvement to enhance patient- and family-centered care.

articles.title: ICU Physical Environments Used for Family Conferences: A Multimodal Qualitative Evaluation with ICU Team Members.
articles.abstract: Family-clinician communication is central to high-quality care for critically ill patients. Although previous work has focused on improving how and what is communicated, little is known about where this high-stakes communication takes place and how it is shaped by the physical environment. Our objectives were to characterize ICU spaces typically used for family conferences and identify modifiable environmental features that influence communication. We conducted a multimodal qualitative study of 17 spaces typically used for family conferences across four adult ICUs in a U.S. academic medical center. Healthcare design and architecture experts independently assessed architectural plans and photographs to characterize spatial features. Then, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 23 ICU team members (nurses, social workers, case managers) to elicit perspectives on and experiences within these spaces. We conducted qualitative content analysis using a combined inductive and deductive approach. A total of 17 family conference spaces across four adult ICUs in a U.S. academic medical center. A total of 23 ICU team members. None. The 17 analyzed spaces included designated family-communication rooms (n = 2), multipurpose rooms (n = 6), visitor lounges (n = 4), and public areas (n = 5; lobbies/hallways). Study participants preferred designated spaces, as they provide privacy, prevent interruption, and facilitate emotional support. Conversely, multipurpose and public areas are prone to distractions and interruptions from conflicting uses. We identified key environmental features that support communication: proximity to patients, flexible furniture layout, and nonclinical ambiance. Family conferences occur in a variety of physical environments in and around adult ICUs, ranging from intentionally designed rooms to elevator lobbies. ICU team members perceive that physical environments have an important influence on communication quality, and we identified pragmatic opportunities to improve existing spaces.

articles.title: Association of Tele-Critical Care Capability With Interhospital Transfers and Potentially Low-Value Transfers Among Critically Ill Medicare Beneficiaries.
articles.abstract: Interhospital transfer is essential for accessing specialized critical care services, yet it poses clinical risk and substantial burden for patients and the healthcare system. Tele-critical care (TCC) programs extend expertise to resource-limited hospitals and may influence transfer decisions by identifying patients requiring escalation or supporting local management. We examined the association between TCC capability at index ICU hospitalizations, interhospital transfer, and post-transfer outcomes. Nationwide retrospective cohort study using 2021-2023 Medicare claims linked to the American Hospital Association Annual Survey Database (AHAASD). U.S. acute care hospitals. Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries with ICU hospitalizations between 2022 and 2023. None. TCC capability was identified by AHAASD reporting and/or the presence of five or more TCC claims annually. The primary outcome was interhospital ICU transfer. Exploratory post-transfer outcomes included receipt of specialty procedures, death or hospice discharge within 1 day of transfer, in-hospital and 30-day mortality, and discharge disposition. Hierarchical logistic regression adjusted for patient demographics, comorbidities, acute organ failures, and transferring/accepting hospital characteristics, with transferring hospitals as random intercepts. Among 2,140,919 ICU hospitalizations, 33.4% occurred at 1,066 TCC-capable hospitals. Absolute transfer rates were similar (2.5% vs. 3.0%), but TCC capability was associated with higher adjusted odds of transfer (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.08; 95% CI, 1.01-1.14). In exploratory post-transfer analyses, transferred patients from TCC hospitals had greater illness severity yet were less likely to die or be discharged to hospice within 1 day of transfer (4.6% vs. 6.6%; aOR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.76-0.97) and more likely to be discharged home within 2 days (4.7% vs. 3.7%; aOR, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.03-1.33). TCC capability was associated with modestly increased transfer rates, fewer potentially low-value transfers, and improved post-transfer outcomes, suggesting improved transfer selection.

articles.title: Tools Measuring Health Literacy in Critically Ill Patients and Their Caregivers: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract: Health literacy, the ability to understand and use health information, is important for critically ill patients and their caregivers in the neonatal ICU (NICU), PICU, and adult ICU to make informed decisions and navigate complex care. This review aimed to identify and summarize tools used to assess health literacy in critically ill patients or their caregivers. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO through July 24, 2025. Included articles reported on tools to assess health literacy in critically ill patients or their caregivers. Two reviewers independently performed screening and data extraction. Two independent reviewers extracted data in Covidence. Data items included study characteristics (country in which the study was conducted, study funding, study setting) and health literacy tool characteristics (tool user, types of questions in the tool, method of tool administration, if the tool was created by the study team, and if a full version was available in the publication). We included 92 articles describing 84 health literacy tools. Tools measured: 1) topic-specific clinical knowledge (e.g., organ donation, cardiopulmonary resuscitation; n = 24/84, 29%; NICU: n = 9; PICU: n = 1; ICU: n = 14); 2) ICU prognosis, diagnosis, and treatment (n = 23/84, 27%; NICU: 6; PICU: 3; ICU: n = 15); 3) neonatal and parenting (n = 13/84, 15%; all NICU); 4) general health literacy abilities (n = 11/84, 13%; NICU: n = 6; PICU: n = 2; ICU: n = 7); 5) information needs (n = 4/84, 5%; NICU: n = 1; PICU: n = 0; ICU: n = 3); 6) readiness for discharge (n = 3/84, 4%; all NICU); 7) decision-making (n = 3/84, 4%; all NICU); 8) health-related behaviors (n = 2/84, 2%; NICU: n = 1; ICU: n = 1); and 9) research participation (n = 1/84, 1%; NICU). Although several health literacy tools exist, they often focus on individual knowledge of specific aspects of ICU care, with less attention to how understanding is produced within the clinical context through interactions among patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers. This may limit their ability to reflect how health literacy functions in critical illness. Assessment of health literacy requires pairing the appropriate tools with interaction-focused approaches to guide communication and support informed decision-making in ICU settings.

articles.title: Interpreting the HISTAP trial: the role of AKI criteria and cumulative exposure to hypotension. Author's reply.
Rapid molecular diagnostics in VAP: when faster results do not mean faster decisions.
Frontal cortical neuroinflammation and circulating biomarkers following cardiopulmonary bypass in sheep.
articles.abstract: Cerebral hypoxia and neuroinflammation have been implicated in neurocognitive disorders following cardiac surgery, but their postoperative trajectory and relationship with circulating biomarkers are poorly defined. We investigated cerebral tissue oxygenation, neuroinflammation, and plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration over 4 weeks after cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) in sheep. Sixteen adult Merino ewes underwent CPB with a 2-h aortic cross-clamp and recovered for either 48 h (n = 8) or 4 weeks (n = 8). Cerebral tissue oxygenation was monitored. Neuroinflammation was quantified by morphometric analyses of microglia and astrocytes in the frontal cortex in both CPB groups and a naïve control group (n = 8). Plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) were measured serially. Compared with pre-CPB baseline, cerebral tissue oxygenation did not change significantly in the 48-h or 4-week period. In the 48-h post-CPB group, microglial soma sphericity was reduced (0.79 ± 0.04 vs. 0.83 ± 0.02, P = 0.018) compared with naïve controls, indicating microglial activation. Astrocytic GFAP-positive area was also elevated (17 ± 2% vs. 10 ± 2%, P = 0.026). In the 4-week post-CPB group, these measures did not differ significantly from naïve controls. Plasma NfL rose from 138 [96-185] pg/mL at baseline to 198 [149-265] pg/mL at 48 h (P = 0.0007), while GFAP peaked at the end of CPB (14.4 [4.7-32.4] vs. 3.0 [1.3-4.5] pg/mL, P < 0.0001) and normalised by 48 h. CPB induced neuroinflammation characterised by frontal cortical microglial activation and astrogliosis, accompanied by temporal elevations in plasma GFAP and NfL. These findings identify microglial activation as a response to CPB in the setting of preserved tissue oxygenation and provide preliminary evidence of an association between perioperative neuroinflammatory changes and circulating biomarkers GFAP and NfL, supporting further investigation.

Delivery fidelity was high with variable uptake of optional components in a remote multicomponent rehabilitation intervention in intensive care unit survivors (iRehab): a mixed-methods fidelity assessment.
articles.abstract: What was the fidelity of a remote multicomponent rehabilitation intervention in intensive care unit survivors (iRehab) across the National Institutes of Health Behavior Change Consortium Treatment Fidelity framework domains (design, training, delivery, receipt and enactment)? iRehab participants (n = 429; 231 intervention, 198 standard care); interviews involved 20 intervention participants, 15 standard care participants and six intervention staff. A mixed-methods fidelity assessment was embedded within the process evaluation of a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Quantitative fidelity was assessed using structured checklists, participant-level tracking data and longitudinal monitoring of potential drift. Qualitative interviews explored fidelity processes across domains. Study design fidelity was maintained, with clear differentiation between the experimental intervention and standard care. Provider training included structured training, competency assessment and ongoing multidisciplinary support. Delivery fidelity was high for one-to-one sessions, with no systematic drift in sampled sessions. Of 231 participants allocated to iRehab, 169 (73%) attended at least five one-to-one appointments. The uptake of optional group-based components was more variable. Qualitative findings indicated participant understanding and engagement, whereas tracking data and participant accounts provided evidence of strategies being applied in daily life. The iRehab intervention was delivered with high delivery fidelity while allowing individualisation to patient needs. For physiotherapists, monitoring of fidelity should extend beyond attendance and exercise prescription to whether patients can independently apply rehabilitation strategies when symptoms, fatigue and everyday demands fluctuate. Defined core components, staff training, staff competency assessment, ongoing support and fidelity monitoring may help support consistent remote delivery.

articles.title: Between Beliefs and Reality: How to Help Family Members Deal With Prognostic Expectations for Critically Ill Patients.

Evaluating plasma ferritin and suPAR as treatable traits for critically ill patients with COVID-19 treated with anakinra: an exploratory analysis of the immune modulation domain of the REMAP-CAP randomised clinical trial.
articles.abstract: Identifying treatable traits in critically ill patients offers potential to enable a precision medicine approach to treatment. The aim of this exploratory analysis of the REMAP-CAP immune modulation domain was to evaluate whether plasma ferritin or soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (suPAR) represent treatable traits for anakinra in critically ill patients with coronavirus disease (COVID-19). An exploratory analysis of patients randomised within the COVID-19 immune modulation domain of the REMAP-CAP trial was conducted. Adults within 24 h of receiving respiratory or cardiovascular organ support in an ICU with suspected or microbiologically confirmed COVID-19 were included. Plasma ferritin was measured at study sites, and plasma suPAR measured in stored plasma samples. The primary outcome was organ support-free days (OSFD) until day 21. Analyses were performed using a Bayesian cumulative logistic regression model, and results are presented as the posterior median odds ratio (OR), along with 95% credible intervals (CrI), for anakinra being superior to control. In ferritin analyses, 1243 patients were included. Patients with increasing ferritin levels had numerically fewer OSFDs. The posterior probabilities of anakinra having benefit (OR > 1) were 64%, 71%, and 21% across increasing ferritin terciles, compared to 53% in analyses that did not adjust for ferritin levels. 145 patients were included in the suPAR analyses. Patients with high baseline plasma suPAR (≥ 6 ng/ml; n = 85) had numerically fewer OSFDs than patients with low plasma suPAR (-1.0 (-1.0, 9.0) vs. 13.0 (-1.0, 17.0)). The posterior probabilities of anakinra having benefit (OR > 1) were 94.8% (OR 2.28 [0.85-6.06]) in patients with low baseline suPAR, and 38.6% (OR 0.88 [0.39-2.00]) in patients with high baseline suPAR. Plasma ferritin does not identify patients with COVID-19 who benefit from treatment with anakinra, whilst anakinra may be beneficial in patients with low, rather than high, baseline plasma suPAR. These hypothesis-generating findings contrast with the results of clinical trials in non-critically ill patients with COVID-19. NCT02735707. Date of trial registration: 06/04/2016.

articles.title: Advancing a New Method of Care: The Scientific and Business Development of the eICU.
Arterial blood gas parameters as mortality predictors in critically ill patients admitted from the emergency department: a prospective observational cohort study.
articles.journal: Journal of critical care medicine (Universitatea de Medicina si Farmacie din Targu-Mures)
articles.abstract: Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis is rapidly available in emergency and intensive care settings and constitutes a core component of many critical illness scoring systems. Although ABG parameters are incorporated into many multidimensional critical illness scoring systems, their independent contribution to mortality prediction remains uncertain because these variables may change rapidly during the early course of critical illness and resuscitation. This study evaluated the prognostic performance of ABG parameters and validated severity scoring systems for predicting 28-day mortality in critically ill patients admitted from the emergency department (ED) to the intensive care unit (ICU). In this prospective observational cohort study, 242 adult patients admitted from the ED to the internal medicine ICU between January 2012 and March 2013 were enrolled. Admission ABG parameters (pH, PaCO2, PaO2, and HCO3 -) and severity scores (APACHE II, APACHE IV, and SAPS II) were recorded. The primary outcome was 28-day all-cause mortality. Prognostic discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Overall 28-day mortality was 47.1%. Non-survivors had significantly higher APACHE II, APACHE IV, and SAPS II scores than survivors (all p < 0.001). SAPS II demonstrated the best prognostic performance (AUC 0.720; 95% CI 0.659-0.776), significantly outperforming APACHE II and APACHE IV. In contrast, none of the individual ABG parameters independently predicted 28-day mortality (all p > 0.05). Multidimensional severity scoring systems, particularly SAPS II, provide superior prognostic discrimination compared with isolated ABG parameters in critically ill ED patients. Although ABG analysis remains essential for acute physiologic assessment, isolated blood gas variables appear insufficient as standalone mortality predictors in heterogeneous ICU populations.

articles.title: Thiamine-deficiency in the ICU-patient - When the plug is out.
articles.abstract: There is a notorious difficulty in judging micronutrient stores and requirements in critically ill patients and deficiency states will be rarely associated with clinical symptoms. A fundamental exception is vitamin B1, thiamine, a micronutrient of crucial importance in mitochondrial energy production. With thiamine deficiency "the energy plug is out", resulting in multiple organ dysfunctions, such as of brain, heart, kidney or respiratory system, lactate formation is increased, lactate clearance reduced, all fundamentally affecting the course of disease and prognosis of a patient. Several patient groups, such as malnourished subjects or patients with liver or kidney disease are already deficient prior to hospital or ICU admission, but there is also a high risk of developing deficiency during ICU stay. There are several well defined patient groups at risk, however, there is no need to measure plasma concentrations, as assays are mostly not available, costly and actually do not reflect the cellular status. There is quite solid evidence that thiamine may preserve / improve organ function (brain, heart, kidney), reduce blood lactate concentration and reduce mortality in various groups of critically ill patient. An extra thiamine supplementation should be given in high-risk patient groups, which bears no risk of inducing toxicity and is cheap, so we advocate to administer thiamine whenever a deficiency state is suspected.

articles.title: Targeted vs Standard Contact Precautions and Transmission of Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococci in Critically Ill Adults: A Pilot Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: Contact precautions are used commonly to prevent nosocomial transmission of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and vancomycin-resistant Enterococci (VRE).
